A value near 0.98 shows that the aluminium fin is almost isothermal, so little is gained from higher conductivity and the design is limited by the convection coefficient and surface area instead.

Answer: 0.979

(d)

The unfinned base area equals the plan area minus the fin footprints: A_un = (W − N·t)·L = (0.100 − 15 × 0.002) × 0.12 = 0.00840 m². The heat from the base is h·A_un·θ_b = 19.6 × 0.00840 × 50 = 8.2 W. The fins add N·q_f = 15 × 6.08 = 91.2 W. The total is Q = N·q_f + h·A_un·θ_b = 99.4 W. A 25 W driver would run with a base well under 75 °C, so this heat sink is generously sized for the load and could be shortened.

Answer: 99.4 W

(e)

A bare base of the same 100 mm × 120 mm plan area would dissipate Q_bare = h·W·L·θ_b = 19.6 × 0.100 × 0.12 × 50 = 11.8 W. The enhancement ratio is Q/Q_bare = 99.4/11.8 = 8.46. The fins increase the dissipation more than eightfold, using only a modest quantity of metal, so they are clearly justified. The ratio is limited because the 5 mm gaps between fins would in practice restrict the airflow and lower h; the more fins one adds, the more the coefficient falls, and an optimum spacing exists.

Answer: 8.46

Problem 5 [A1-085] Transient conduction lumped capacitance

A forging shop quenches 50 mm diameter steel balls (k = 40 W/(m·K), ρ = 7800 kg/m³, c = 470 J/(kg·K)) for use in a grinding mill. Each ball leaves the furnace at a uniform 850 °C and is dropped in an agitated oil bath at 60 °C, where the heat-transfer coefficient is 800 W/(m²·K). Once the ball reaches 400 °C it is lifted out and allowed to cool in still air at 35 °C, with a combined convection and radiation coefficient of 30 W/(m²·K), until it reaches 100 °C. Assume the properties are constant. Judge whether a lumped-capacitance (uniform temperature) analysis is acceptable before using it for the oil-bath stage, using the usual criterion.

  1. (a) Calculate the Biot number for the oil quench and decide whether the lumped model is acceptable. [3]
  2. (b) Find the time for a ball to cool from 850 °C to 400 °C in the oil, using the lumped model. [5]
  3. (c) Find the energy removed from one ball during the oil stage, in kJ. [4]
  4. (d) Find the time for the ball to cool from 400 °C to 100 °C in still air. [5]
  5. (e) Find the initial rate of temperature fall of the ball when first dropped in the oil, in K/s. [3]
(a)

The characteristic length for a sphere is the volume divided by the surface area, L_c = V/A = D/6 = 0.050/6 = 0.00833 m. The Biot number is Bi = h·L_c/k = 800 × 0.00833/40 = 0.167. The usual criterion for a lumped analysis is Bi < 0.1, so the quench in oil with Bi = 0.167 slightly exceeds it, giving a centre-to-surface temperature difference of roughly Bi/5, a few percent of the surface-to-fluid drop. The lumped result is therefore an approximation, acceptable for a first estimate but not for a quench-crack study; the air-cooling stage, with h = 30, has Bi = 0.0063 and is well within the criterion.

Answer: 0.167

(b)

With the lumped model, the energy balance ρVc·dT/dt = −hA(T − T∞) gives (T − T∞)/(T_i − T∞) = exp(−t/τ), where the time constant is τ = ρ·c·L_c/h. Substituting: τ = 7800 × 470 × 0.00833/800 = 38.19 s. Solving for the time, t = τ·ln[(T_i − T∞)/(T − T∞)] = 38.19 × ln[(850 − 60)/(400 − 60)] = 38.19 × ln(2.324) = 32.2 s. This is the immersion time before the ball is lifted out. Given the slight Bi excess in part (a), the real centre will lag by a few seconds, so a safe process sheet would add a margin.

Answer: 32.2 s

(c)

Energy removed equals the change in internal energy of the ball, Q = ρVc(T_i − T_f). The volume is V = πD³/6 = π × 0.050³/6 = 6.545 × 10⁻⁵ m³, giving a mass m = ρV = 0.511 kg. Then Q = 0.511 × 470 × (850 − 400) = 107973 J, which is 108.0 kJ per ball. This is also the heat the oil bath must reject per ball, and with a production rate in balls per hour the bath cooler can be sized directly. The calculation is exact for energy even if the temperature profile is not uniform, as long as T_f is taken as the volume-average temperature.

Answer: 108.0 kJ

(d)

In air, the lumped model is valid because Bi is very small. The time constant is τ_air = ρ·c·L_c/h = 7800 × 470 × 0.00833/30 = 1018 s. Then t = τ_air·ln[(T_f − T∞)/(T − T∞)] = 1018 × ln[(400 − 35)/(100 − 35)] = 1018 × ln(5.615) = 1757 s, about 29 minutes. The air stage is far slower than the oil stage, which shows the effect of the factor of about 27 between the coefficients. It also explains why the balls are stacked for slow cooling after the quench, if a tempering effect is wanted.

Answer: 1757 s

(e)

At the start, the rate of change follows directly from the lumped energy balance, dT/dt = −h(T − T∞)/(ρ·c·L_c). Substituting T = 850 °C and T∞ = 60 °C: dT/dt = −800 × (850 − 60)/(7800 × 470 × 0.00833) = −20.7 K/s. The negative sign denotes cooling. This rate decays exponentially with the time constant of part (b), so the cooling is fastest at the instant of immersion, which is when the thermal stress in the skin is greatest and cracking risk is highest. Lowering the agitation (and h) would reduce the initial rate.

Answer: 20.7 K/s

A1 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A1-086] Transient conduction Heisler charts or semi-infinite solid

A water main in northern Ontario is buried with its top at 1.2 m depth in soil that is initially at a uniform 12 °C. A cold snap holds the ground surface at a constant −15 °C for 30 days. Treat the soil as a semi-infinite solid with constant properties: thermal diffusivity 0.6×10⁻⁶ m²/s and thermal conductivity 1.5 W/(m·K). Ignore latent heat of freezing of the soil water and any snow cover, which makes the estimate conservative. The municipality wants to know whether 1.2 m cover is adequate, how deep the frost line (0 °C) reaches, how large the heat flux out of the ground is, and how long the cold must last to reach 1.5 m.

  1. (a) Calculate the soil temperature at 1.2 m depth after 30 days. [5]
  2. (b) Find the depth to which the 0 °C isotherm has penetrated after 30 days. [4]
  3. (c) Find the heat flux at the ground surface at t = 30 days, in W/m². [4]
  4. (d) Find the time, in days, for the 0 °C isotherm to reach a depth of 1.5 m. [4]
  5. (e) State whether the water main at 1.2 m depth is at risk of freezing after 30 days under the model, and give the reasoning. [3]
(a)

For a semi-infinite solid with a step change in surface temperature, (T − T_s)/(T_i − T_s) = erf[x/(2√(αt))]. The time is t = 30 × 86400 = 2592000 s, so 2√(αt) = 2 × √(0.6×10⁻⁶ × 2592000) = 2.494 m. The argument is x/(2√(αt)) = 1.2/2.494 = 0.481, and erf(0.481) = 0.5038. Then T = −15 + (12 − (−15)) × 0.5038 = -1.4 °C. The soil at pipe depth has therefore fallen from 12 °C to below freezing, since the cold penetrates to a depth of about twice √(αt), here more than a metre. The negative sign is meaningful only in the model, because the latent heat of freezing was ignored and would hold real soil near 0 °C.

Answer: -1.4 °C

(b)

The 0 °C condition requires erf(η) = (0 − T_s)/(T_i − T_s) = 15/27 = 0.5556, with η = x/(2√(αt)). Inverting the error function gives η = 0.5407. Then x_f = 2η√(αt) = 2 × 0.5407 × √(0.6×10⁻⁶ × 2592000) = 1.35 m. This depth is the position of the frost line in the model. Because latent heat of freezing was neglected, the real frost front would advance more slowly; the number is therefore a conservative upper bound on frost depth. As a check, the ratio 15/27 is only about 0.56, so the frost line sits at less than the characteristic penetration depth 2√(αt), which is about 2.5 m here.

Answer: 1.35 m

(c)

The surface flux for the step-change case is q″_s = k(T_i − T_s)/√(παt). Substituting: q″_s = 1.5 × 27/√(π × 0.6×10⁻⁶ × 2592000) = 40.5/2.2104 = 18.32 W/m². The flux is directed upward out of the ground. It falls as 1/√t, so the largest losses occur at the start of the cold snap, when the gradient at the surface is steepest. Multiplying by the exposed area and the time, integrating 2k(T_i − T_s)√(t/(πα)) gives the total energy removed per unit area. The flux is directed from the warm deep soil toward the cold surface, which is the direction in which the ground loses energy to the atmosphere during the cold snap.

Answer: 18.32 W/m²

(d)

The isotherm position follows x_f = 2η√(αt) with η = 0.5407 fixed by the temperatures. Solving for the time gives t = x_f²/(4η²α). With x_f = 1.5 m: t = 1.5²/(4 × 0.5407² × 0.6×10⁻⁶) = 3.206 × 10⁶ s, which is 37 days. The time scales with the square of depth, so doubling the cover depth multiplies the time to freezing by four. This is why increasing the cover is an effective measure: a modest extra depth buys a large increase in time before the ground freezes. The time exceeds the 30 days used above because the isotherm slows as it advances: depth grows only as the square root of time, so each extra 10 cm costs more days than the previous one.

Answer: 37 days

(e)

Compare the frost-line depth from part (b) with the pipe top at 1.2 m. The 0 °C isotherm reaches 1.35 m after 30 days, which is deeper than 1.2 m, and the soil temperature at 1.2 m from part (a) is -1.4 °C, below freezing. Under the model the pipe is therefore at risk: the frost line has passed it by 0.15 m. Because latent heat was neglected the real frost front is somewhat shallower, so the true margin is smaller than the model suggests, but the conclusion is the same for a stagnant pipe. Moving water adds heat and reduces the risk, whereas a dead-end branch is most exposed. The remedy is more cover or insulation, which part (d) helps quantify through the square-root-of-time scaling.

Answer: At risk (frost line passes below the pipe top)

Problem 2 [A1-087] Forced convection external flow

A resistance heating wire of 2.0 mm diameter is stretched across a duct to warm a laboratory airstream. The wire is nichrome (k = 15 W/(m·K)) and generates heat uniformly at 60 W per metre of length. Air at 20 °C flows across the wire at 15 m/s. Use air properties at the film temperature: ν = 1.60×10⁻⁵ m²/s, k = 0.0263 W/(m·K), Pr = 0.707, and treat them as constant. Use the Churchill and Bernstein correlation for the average Nusselt number of a cylinder in crossflow, Nu = 0.3 + [0.62 Re0.5 Pr1/3/(1 + (0.4/Pr)2/3)0.25]·[1 + (Re/282000)5/8]4/5. Neglect radiation and end effects. The designer also wants to know the effect of slowing the airstream to 5 m/s.

  1. (a) Calculate the Reynolds number based on the wire diameter. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the average Nusselt number and the convection coefficient. [4]
  3. (c) Find the wire surface temperature. [4]
  4. (d) Find the centreline temperature of the wire, given uniform internal heat generation. [4]
  5. (e) The airstream is slowed to 5 m/s with the same heat generation. Find the new wire surface temperature. [5]
(a)

The Reynolds number for crossflow over a cylinder uses the diameter as the length scale: Re_D = U·D/ν. Substituting: Re_D = 15 × 0.002/1.60×10⁻⁵ = 1875. This is in the range where the Churchill and Bernstein correlation, valid for Re·Pr above 0.2, applies without restriction. The flow is laminar at the front of the wire with separation behind it, so boundary-layer assumptions for flat plates should not be used. A Reynolds number of this size also indicates that the wake behind the wire will shed vortices, which can produce a faint audible tone in some arrangements.

Answer: 1875

(b)

Substituting Re = 1875 and Pr = 0.707 into the correlation: the first group is 0.62 × 18750.5 × 0.7071/3/[1 + (0.4/0.707)2/3]0.25 = 20.99, and the second group is [1 + (1875/282000)5/8]4/5 = 1.0347. Then Nu = 0.3 + 20.99 × 1.0347 = 22.02. The coefficient is h = Nu·k/D = 22.02 × 0.0263/0.002 = 289.6 W/(m²·K). This is the average over the circumference, which is higher at the front stagnation point and lowest near the separation point, so local wire temperature varies slightly around the circumference. The correlation was fitted to data over a wide range of Reynolds numbers and has an uncertainty of the order of 10 to 20 percent, so quoting h to more than three significant figures is not meaningful for design.

Answer: 289.6 W/(m²·K)

(c)

In steady state, all of the electrical heat generated per unit length leaves by convection from the surface: q′ = h·π·D·(T_s − T∞). Rearranging, T_s = T∞ + q′/(h·π·D). Substituting: T_s = 20 + 60/(289.6 × π × 0.002) = 20 + 60/1.8197 = 53.0 °C. The surface is only moderately warm because the 15 m/s airstream is efficient. The film temperature is then about 37 °C, close to the value at which the properties were stated; a second iteration with updated properties would shift h by under 2 percent, which is acceptable.

Answer: 53.0 °C

(d)

For a long solid cylinder with uniform generation q̇ and a surface temperature T_s, T(0) − T_s = q̇r₀²/(4k). The volumetric generation is q̇ = q′/(πr₀²), so q̇r₀²/(4k) = q′/(4πk). Substituting: ΔT = 60/(4π × 15) = 0.318 K. The centreline temperature is T_0 = T_s + ΔT = 53.0 + 0.318 = 53.3 °C. The temperature difference inside the wire is only a third of a kelvin, since the wire is small and conductive. The surface resistance controls the temperature, and the wire can be treated as isothermal for any practical purpose.

Answer: 53.3 °C

(e)

At 5 m/s: Re = 5 × 0.002/1.60×10⁻⁵ = 625, and the correlation gives Nu = 12.63, so h = 12.63 × 0.0263/0.002 = 166.1 W/(m²·K). The surface temperature is T_s = 20 + 60/(166.1 × π × 0.002) = 77.5 °C. The velocity is a third of the original, but the coefficient falls by about 43 percent, because h varies roughly as U0.5 to U0.6 for this range, so the wire temperature rises by 24.5 K. A wire at this temperature would still be well within a nichrome limit, but the trend shows how a loss-of-flow fault raises temperature and why such heaters have flow interlocks.

Answer: 77.5 °C

Problem 3 [A1-088] Forced convection internal flow

A process-water heater consists of a single straight stainless tube of 25 mm inside diameter wrapped in an electric heating jacket that supplies a uniform wall heat flux of 40 kW/m². Water enters at 25 °C and must leave at 65 °C at a flow rate of 0.30 kg/s. Evaluate properties at the mean bulk temperature of 45 °C: ρ = 990 kg/m³, cp = 4180 J/(kg·K), μ = 6.0×10⁻⁴ Pa·s, k = 0.637 W/(m·K). The tube is smooth drawn tubing with roughness 0.0015 mm. Use the Dittus and Boelter equation (n = 0.4 for heating) for convection, and the Haaland equation for the friction factor. Assume fully developed flow along the whole length, and a pump and motor efficiency of 65 percent.

  1. (a) Calculate the Reynolds number and the Prandtl number, and confirm the flow regime. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the heat transfer coefficient. [4]
  3. (c) Determine the heated tube length required. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the wall temperature at the tube outlet. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the electrical power required by the pump and motor to overcome friction in the tube. [4]
(a)

For internal flow, Re = 4ṁ/(πDμ) = 4 × 0.30/(π × 0.025 × 6.0×10⁻⁴) = 25465. The Prandtl number is Pr = cp·μ/k = 4180 × 6.0×10⁻⁴/0.637 = 3.94. Since Re is above 10 000, the flow is fully turbulent, and the Dittus and Boelter equation, valid for Re above 10⁴ and 0.6 < Pr < 160, applies. The correlation also requires L/D above about 10 for fully developed flow, which is checked after the length is known in part (c). The answer for part (a) is the Reynolds number.

Answer: 25465

(b)

With heating, the Dittus and Boelter equation is Nu = 0.023·Re0.8·Pr0.4. Substituting Re = 25465 and Pr = 3.94: Nu = 0.023 × 254650.8 × 3.940.4 = 133.2. Then h = Nu·k/D = 133.2 × 0.637/0.025 = 3394 W/(m²·K). This is a high coefficient typical of turbulent liquid flow in a small tube. It is essentially uniform along the tube under the fully developed assumption, so with constant wall flux the difference between wall and bulk temperature is also constant, equal to q″/h. The Dittus and Boelter correlation carries an uncertainty of about 25 percent, so a design margin on tube length is normally added when the heater power is fixed.

Answer: 3394 W/(m²·K)

(c)

The heat required by the water follows from the energy balance: Q = ṁ·cp·(T_out − T_in) = 0.30 × 4180 × 40 = 50160 W. The jacket supplies a uniform flux over the inner surface, Q = q″·π·D·L. Rearranging, L = Q/(q″·π·D) = 50160/(40000 × π × 0.025) = 15.97 m. The ratio L/D is 639, comfortably above 10, so the fully developed assumption is reasonable over nearly all the length. In practice such a length would be coiled, and the bends would increase both the heat transfer and the pressure drop slightly.

Answer: 15.97 m

(d)

With constant wall flux and a fully developed profile, the difference between wall and bulk temperature is constant: T_s − T_m = q″/h. At the outlet the bulk temperature is 65 °C, so T_s,out = T_m,out + q″/h = 65 + 40000/3394 = 65 + 11.8 = 76.8 °C. This is the hottest point in the tube and the one that controls tube material limits and any risk of local boiling or scale deposition. At 1 atm, the wall remains below the 100 °C boiling point, so there is no subcooled boiling and the single-phase correlation is valid.

Answer: 76.8 °C

(e)

First the friction factor from the Haaland equation: 1/√f = −1.8·log₁₀[(ε/D/3.7)1.11 + 6.9/Re] with ε/D = 6.00 × 10⁻⁵ gives f = 0.0244. The velocity is V = ṁ/(ρA) = 0.30/(990 × 4.909 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.617 m/s. The pressure drop is Δp = f(L/D)(ρV²/2) = 0.0244 × 638.7 × 990 × 0.617²/2 = 2935 Pa. The hydraulic power is Δp·ṁ/ρ = 2935 × 0.30/990 = 0.89 W. Dividing by the efficiency 0.65 gives the electrical power 1.37 W, negligible beside the 50 kW heating duty. The pump power is tiny compared with the heater duty, so friction heating of the water is negligible and the constant-flux heat balance is not affected.

Answer: 1.37 W

Problem 4 [A1-089] Natural convection

The vertical steel door of an industrial curing oven is 1.2 m high and 0.8 m wide. Its outer surface is at a uniform 60 °C and has an emissivity of 0.85. The surrounding room air and walls are both at 20 °C. Use air properties at the film temperature of 40 °C: ν = 1.70×10⁻⁵ m²/s, α = 2.4×10⁻⁵ m²/s, k = 0.0271 W/(m·K), Pr = 0.71, with β = 1/T_film for an ideal gas, and g = 9.81 m/s². Use the Churchill and Chu correlation for a vertical plate over the whole Rayleigh-number range, Nu = {0.825 + 0.387 Ra1/6/[1 + (0.492/Pr)9/16]8/27}². The door is a single flat plate; treat the room as a large enclosure and neglect the edges.

  1. (a) Calculate the Rayleigh number based on the door height. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the average natural convection coefficient. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the rate of heat loss by convection from the door. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the rate of heat loss by radiation from the door to the surroundings. [5]
  5. (e) Find the share of the total heat loss carried by radiation, and say how a low-emissivity foil on the door would change the heat loss. [4]
(a)

The Rayleigh number is Ra_L = gβ(T_s − T∞)L³/(να), with β = 1/T_film = 1/313.15 K = 0.00319 K⁻¹. Substituting: Ra_L = 9.81 × 0.00319 × (60 − 20) × 1.2³/(1.70×10⁻⁵ × 2.4×10⁻⁵) = 5.307 × 10⁹. Because Ra exceeds the usual transition value of about 10⁹, the boundary layer on the door is turbulent over much of its height, and the Churchill and Chu equation, which covers both regimes, is the appropriate choice. The Rayleigh number is the product of the Grashof and Prandtl numbers, and it measures the strength of buoyancy forces relative to viscous and thermal diffusion effects in the boundary layer.

Answer: 5.307 × 10⁹

(b)

The Nusselt number from the correlation: the bracketed denominator is [1 + (0.492/0.71)9/16]8/27 = 1.1929. The numerator term is 0.387 × Ra1/6 = 0.387 × 41.76 = 16.163. So Nu = (0.825 + 16.163/1.1929)² = 206.6. The coefficient is h = Nu·k/L = 206.6 × 0.0271/1.2 = 4.67 W/(m²·K). This is typical of natural convection in air, which is one or two orders of magnitude below forced convection. The low coefficient is the reason radiation matters so much, as shown in part (d). The Churchill and Chu relation is smooth across transition, which is why it is preferred here over separate laminar and turbulent forms.

Answer: 4.67 W/(m²·K)

(c)

The convective heat loss is q_conv = h·A·(T_s − T∞). The door area is A = H × W = 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 m². Substituting: q_conv = 4.67 × 0.96 × (60 − 20) = 179.2 W. This is the loss through the air alone. The value would rise with the temperature difference to the power of about 1.25 (laminar) or 1.33 (turbulent), because the coefficient itself increases with the driving temperature difference. A door at 80 °C would lose far more than the simple proportional increase. The air properties were evaluated at the film temperature, the mean of the surface and ambient values, which is standard practice for natural convection correlations.

Answer: 179.2 W

(d)

The door is a small body in a large enclosure, so q_rad = εσA(T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴). With T_s = 333.15 K and T_sur = 293.15 K: T_s⁴ = 1.232 × 10¹⁰ K⁴ and T_sur⁴ = 7.385 × 10⁹ K⁴, giving a difference of 4.933 × 10⁹ K⁴. Then q_rad = 0.85 × 5.67×10⁻⁸ × 0.96 × 4.933 × 10⁹ = 228.3 W. This is at least as large as the convective loss despite the modest 40 K temperature difference, because radiation depends on the difference of fourth powers. The equivalent radiation coefficient is 5.94 W/(m²·K). The temperatures must be in kelvin; using Celsius values in the fourth-power terms is a common mistake that gives a wrong answer.

Answer: 228.3 W

(e)

The total loss is q = q_conv + q_rad = 179.2 + 228.3 = 407.4 W. The radiation share is q_rad/q = 228.3/407.4 = 56 percent. A bright aluminium foil with emissivity around 0.1 would cut the radiation to about 26.9 W (it scales directly with ε), so the total falls to 206.0 W, a reduction of roughly 49 percent, while the convective loss is unchanged. The result shows that surface finish is as important as the air movement in controlling the loss of a warm vertical surface.

Answer: 56 %

Problem 5 [A1-090] Radiation exchange and view factors

In a vacuum drying chamber, a large flat heated platen at 650 K (emissivity 0.75) faces a parallel cooled panel at 300 K (emissivity 0.55). The gap is small compared with the plate dimensions, so edge effects are negligible and the view factor between the plates is one. The space between is evacuated, so only radiation transfers heat. Both surfaces are diffuse and grey. The designer proposes to insert thin, parallel radiation shields of emissivity 0.12 on both faces to cut the heat load on the cooled panel. Use σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴), and treat the shields as thin enough to have negligible conduction resistance.

  1. (a) Calculate the net radiative heat flux from the platen to the panel with no shield. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the flux with one shield inserted midway between the plates. [5]
  3. (c) Find the equilibrium temperature of the shield. [4]
  4. (d) Find the percentage reduction in heat flux produced by the single shield. [3]
  5. (e) Find the flux if three identical shields (each ε = 0.12 on both faces) are used in series. [4]
(a)

For two large parallel grey plates, q″ = σ(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴)/(1/ε₁ + 1/ε₂ − 1). The fourth-power difference is T₁⁴ − T₂⁴ = 1.785 × 10¹¹ − 8.100 × 10⁹ = 1.704 × 10¹¹ K⁴, and σ times it is 9662 W/m². The emissivity term is 1/0.75 + 1/0.55 − 1 = 2.1515. So q″ = 9662/2.1515 = 4491 W/m². This is a large load, about 4.5 kW per square metre, and it falls entirely on the cooled panel, which is why shielding is considered. The result is a heat flux, so a plate area is needed to get the load in watts.

Answer: 4491 W/m²

(b)

With a shield of emissivity ε₃ on both faces, the net radiation circuit has two gaps in series: platen to shield, and shield to panel. The sum of the gap resistances is 1/ε₁ + 1/ε₃ − 1 + 1/ε₃ + 1/ε₂ − 1 = 1/ε₁ + 1/ε₂ + 2/ε₃ − 2. Substituting: 1/0.75 + 1/0.55 + 2/0.12 − 2 = 17.818. The flux is q″ = 9662/17.818 = 542 W/m². A single low-emissivity shield cuts the flux by an order of magnitude, since its large reflectivity dominates the resistance. The shield position does not affect the flux, only its own temperature.

Answer: 542 W/m²

(c)

In steady state, the flux through each gap equals the flux q″ found in part (b). Apply the one-gap formula between the platen and the shield: q″ = σ(T₁⁴ − T₃⁴)/(1/ε₁ + 1/ε₃ − 1). The gap resistance is 1/0.75 + 1/0.12 − 1 = 8.667. Rearranging, T₃⁴ = T₁⁴ − q″·8.667/σ = 1.785 × 10¹¹ − 8.288 × 10¹⁰ = 9.562 × 10¹⁰ K⁴. Then T₃ = 556 K. The shield sits much closer to the platen temperature than to the panel, because the gap on the panel side has a larger resistance and the fourth-power law makes most of the temperature drop appear there.

Answer: 556 K

(d)

The percentage reduction is (q″₀ − q″₁)/q″₀ × 100, where q″₀ = 4491 W/m² is the unshielded flux and q″₁ = 542 W/m² is the shielded flux. So reduction = (4491 − 542)/4491 × 100 = 87.9 percent. Equivalently, the ratio of the resistances gives q₁/q₀ = 2.1515/17.818 = 0.121. This is the main benefit of the shield, but the effect is not a simple division by two as it would be for black surfaces; low emissivity makes the reduction far greater. Percentage reduction is a convenient way to report the benefit, because it does not depend on the plate area or on the absolute temperatures chosen.

Answer: 87.9 %

(e)

Each additional shield adds one more pair of surfaces. With N shields, the total resistance is 1/ε₁ + 1/ε₂ − 1 + N(2/ε₃ − 1), noting that each interior gap adds (2/ε₃ − 1) and the two outer gaps already counted give the combined constant. Check with N = 1: the formula gives 2.1515 + (2/0.12 − 1) = 17.818, matching the sum in part (b) once rounded, which verifies it. For N = 3: R = 2.1515 + 3 × (2/0.12 − 1) = 49.152. The flux is q″ = 9662/49.152 = 196.6 W/m². Further shields give diminishing returns in absolute terms, but each one removes about the same proportional amount.

Answer: 196.6 W/m²

A1 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A1-091] Heat exchanger LMTD method with tube-wall conduction and fouling

A double-pipe counterflow oil cooler is built from steel tube of inside diameter 20 mm and outside diameter 24 mm (k = 45 W/m·K). Engine oil flows in the annulus at 1.2 kg/s with cp = 2100 J/kg·K and is cooled from 95 °C to 60 °C. Cooling water enters the tube at 22 °C at 1.8 kg/s, cp = 4180 J/kg·K. The water-side film coefficient is 3200 W/m²·K and the oil-side film coefficient is 480 W/m²·K. Fouling resistances are 0.0002 m²·K/W on the outer (oil) surface and 0.0001 m²·K/W on the inner (water) surface, each referred to its own surface. Heat loss to the surroundings is negligible. Treat the tube as a single straight length of the stated section, with all passes in series.

  1. (a) Find the heat duty of the exchanger. [3]
  2. (b) Find the water outlet temperature. [3]
  3. (c) Find the log-mean temperature difference for counterflow. [4]
  4. (d) Find the overall heat transfer coefficient based on the outer tube surface, including wall conduction and both fouling resistances. [5]
  5. (e) Find the required tube length. [5]
(a)

Steady flow, no losses, constant specific heat. The duty is found from the oil side, where all temperatures are known: Q = ṁ_oil cp_oil (T_h,in − T_h,out) = 1.2 × 2100 × (95 − 60) = 1.2 × 2100 × 35 = 88200 W. This equals 88.2 kW. The water side must absorb the same amount by the first law applied to each stream separately, with no work and negligible kinetic and potential energy change, so Q = ṁ_w cp_w (T_c,out − T_c,in). A marker rewards stating the control-volume assumptions, writing the equation with substituted numbers, and keeping the unit consistent (W to kW). This value fixes the water outlet temperature in part (b) and the surface area in part (e).

Answer: 88.2 kW

(b)

Apply the energy balance to the water stream: Q = ṁ_w cp_w (T_c,out − T_c,in), so T_c,out = T_c,in + Q/(ṁ_w cp_w). Substituting: T_c,out = 22 + 88200/(1.8 × 4180) = 22 + 88200/7524 = 22 + 11.72 = 33.7 °C. The capacity rate of the water (7524 W/K) is larger than that of the oil (2520 W/K), so the water temperature rise (about 11.7 K) is much smaller than the oil temperature drop of 35 K. This outlet temperature is needed to build both terminal temperature differences for the counterflow LMTD in part (c). Check: the water outlet must stay below the oil outlet of 60 °C for the counterflow arrangement to be feasible, and it does.

Answer: 33.7 °C

(c)

For counterflow the terminal differences pair the hot inlet with the cold outlet and the hot outlet with the cold inlet. ΔT₁ = T_h,in − T_c,out = 95 − 33.72 = 61.28 K. ΔT₂ = T_h,out − T_c,in = 60 − 22 = 38.00 K. The log-mean difference is LMTD = (ΔT₁ − ΔT₂)/ln(ΔT₁/ΔT₂) = (61.28 − 38.00)/ln(61.28/38.00) = 48.7 K. The arithmetic mean would be about 49.6 K, so the log mean is slightly lower, which is expected because the two differences are unequal. The formula applies because U is taken as constant along the length and specific heats are constant.

Answer: 48.7 K

(d)

Write the series resistance per unit outer area: 1/U_o = 1/h_o + R_f,o + r_o ln(r_o/r_i)/k + R_f,i (r_o/r_i) + r_o/(r_i h_i). With r_o = 0.012 m and r_i = 0.010 m: 1/h_o = 1/480 = 0.002083; R_f,o = 0.000200; wall term = 0.012 × ln(1.2)/45 = 0.012 × 0.18232/45 = 0.0000486; R_f,i (r_o/r_i) = 0.0001 × 1.2 = 0.000120; inner film = 0.012/(0.010 × 3200) = 0.000375. Sum = 0.002827 m²·K/W. So U_o = 1/0.002827 = 353.7 W/m²·K. The oil film dominates the resistance (about 74 percent), so improving the water side would gain little. Referring every term to the outer area is the step markers look for.

Answer: 353.7 W/m²·K

(e)

The rate equation for a heat exchanger with constant U is Q = U_o A_o LMTD, with A_o = π D_o L for a single tube. Rearranging, A_o = Q/(U_o LMTD) = 88200/(353.7 × 48.72) = 5.12 m². Then L = A_o/(π D_o) = 5.12/(π × 0.024) = 67.9 m. In practice this length would be folded into a hairpin or multi-tube bundle. The fouling allowance is significant: without the two fouling resistances U_o would rise to about 399 W/m²·K and the length would fall by roughly 11 percent. State the assumption that U is uniform along the tube and that end effects are ignored.

Answer: 67.9 m

Problem 2 [A1-092] Heat exchanger effectiveness-NTU method with fouling what-if (economizer)

A boiler economizer is a shell-and-tube exchanger with one shell pass and two tube passes. Flue gas (cp = 1100 J/kg·K) flows at 4.5 kg/s and enters at 380 °C. Feedwater (cp = 4200 J/kg·K) flows at 3.2 kg/s and enters at 60 °C. Clean-condition tests give UA = 6200 W/K. After a season of soot and scale build-up on both sides, the plant engineer estimates UA has dropped by 25 percent. Treat both fluids as single-phase with constant properties and use the standard effectiveness expression for a one-shell, two-tube-pass exchanger. The plant manager wants the heat recovery that remains in the fouled condition.

  1. (a) Identify the minimum heat capacity rate and find NTU for the clean exchanger. [3]
  2. (b) Find the effectiveness of the clean exchanger. [4]
  3. (c) Find the heat recovered in the clean condition. [4]
  4. (d) Find the flue gas outlet temperature in the clean condition. [4]
  5. (e) After fouling, UA falls by 25 percent. Find the new heat recovery, assuming flow rates and inlet temperatures are unchanged. [5]
(a)

Capacity rates: C_gas = ṁ cp = 4.5 × 1100 = 4950 W/K; C_water = 3.2 × 4200 = 13440 W/K. The gas stream has the smaller rate, so C_min = 4950 W/K and C_max = 13440 W/K, giving a capacity ratio C_r = C_min/C_max = 0.3683. The number of transfer units is NTU = UA/C_min = 6200/4950 = 1.253. NTU is a non-dimensional size of the exchanger: values near 1 mean the exchanger is moderately large relative to the stream with the smaller capacity. Identifying C_min correctly is the step markers check first, because every later result uses it.

Answer: 1.253

(b)

For one shell pass and 2, 4, 6 ... tube passes the effectiveness is ε = 2 / [1 + C_r + (1 + C_r²)½ × (1 + exp(−NTU (1 + C_r²)½)) / (1 − exp(−NTU (1 + C_r²)½))]. First s = (1 + 0.3683²)½ = 1.0657. Then exp(−NTU s) = exp(−1.253 × 1.0657) = 0.2632. The bracket ratio is (1 + 0.2632)/(1 − 0.2632) = 1.7145. Substituting, ε = 2/(1 + 0.3683 + 1.0657 × 1.7145) = 0.6259. This is below the counterflow value for the same NTU and C_r, which is the penalty for mixed-direction flow in a two-pass shell-and-tube design.

Answer: 0.6259

(c)

The maximum possible heat transfer is set by the inlet temperature difference acting on C_min: Q_max = C_min (T_gas,in − T_water,in) = 4950 × (380 − 60) = 1584000 W. The actual duty is Q = ε Q_max = 0.6259 × 1584000 = 991427 W, which is 991 kW. This approach avoids iteration because the outlet temperatures are not known at the start; the effectiveness-NTU method is preferred over LMTD for exactly this reason. The result is checked in part (d) by applying the gas-side energy balance, and the water side follows from the same Q.

Answer: 991 kW

(d)

Apply the first law to the gas stream with no work and negligible kinetic energy change: Q = C_gas (T_gas,in − T_gas,out). Solving, T_gas,out = T_gas,in − Q/C_gas = 380 − 991427/4950 = 380 − 200.3 = 179.7 °C. The water outlet follows from T_w,out = 60 + Q/13440 = 133.8 °C. A practical point worth stating: flue gas leaving this cold risks acid-dew-point condensation on the tube surface if the fuel contains sulphur, so a designer would check the outlet against the dew point. The gas outlet must remain above the water inlet temperature of 60 °C, which it does.

Answer: 179.7 °C

(e)

The new conductance is UA' = 0.75 × 6200 = 4650 W/K, so NTU' = 4650/4950 = 0.939. C_r is unchanged because the flow rates are unchanged. Recompute s = 1.0657, exp(−NTU' s) = 0.3675, ratio = (1 + 0.3675)/(1 − 0.3675) = 2.1620. Then ε' = 2/(1 + 0.3683 + 1.0657 × 2.1620) = 0.5446. The new duty is Q' = ε' Q_max = 0.5446 × 1584000 = 862689 W = 863 kW. The loss of recovery is 128738 W, about 13.0 percent of the clean duty, so a 25 percent drop in UA causes a much smaller percentage drop in Q because the effectiveness curve flattens at higher NTU. That flattening is why modest fouling is tolerated before cleaning pays.

Answer: 863 kW

Problem 3 [A1-093] Steady-flow energy balance: expander versus throttle on a compressed-air main

A food plant reduces the pressure of a 2.5 kg/s compressed-air main from 900 kPa to 150 kPa through a throttling valve. The air arrives at 30 °C (303.15 K) after the dryer. Management is considering replacing the valve with an adiabatic turbo-expander of isentropic efficiency 0.78 that discharges at 150 kPa. Treat air as an ideal gas with cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and k = 1.4, with negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy. A downstream process cannot accept air colder than 10 °C (283.15 K), so an electric or gas-fired heater would restore the temperature after the expander. Shaft power is valued at 0.09 $/kWh, heat at 0.04 $/kWh, and the line runs 8000 h per year. The throttle itself produces no work and no cooling.

  1. (a) Find the expander exit temperature. [4]
  2. (b) Find the shaft power the expander delivers. [4]
  3. (c) Find the heater duty needed after the expander to bring the air back to 10 °C. [4]
  4. (d) Find the net annual value of replacing the valve, counting the power generated and the heat purchased. [4]
  5. (e) Recommend, with reasons, whether to install the expander and state what the figure in part (d) leaves out. [4]
(a)

Steady flow, adiabatic, ideal gas with constant cp. The isentropic exit temperature uses T₂s = T₁ (p₂/p₁)(k−1)/k = 303.15 × (150/900)0.2857 = 303.15 × 0.5993 = 181.7 K. The isentropic efficiency of a turbine is η = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s) = (T₁ − T₂)/(T₁ − T₂s) for constant cp, so T₂ = T₁ − η (T₁ − T₂s) = 303.15 − 0.78 × (303.15 − 181.7) = 208.4 K, which is -64.7 °C. The real exit is warmer than the isentropic one because irreversibility returns part of the work to the stream as internal energy. Note that the throttle keeps the air at 303.15 K for an ideal gas, since enthalpy is conserved.

Answer: 208.4 K

(b)

Apply the steady-flow energy equation to the expander as a control volume with one inlet and one outlet, adiabatic, with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes: W = ṁ (h₁ − h₂) = ṁ cp (T₁ − T₂). Substituting, W = 2.5 × 1.005 × (303.15 − 208.4) = 2.5 × 1.005 × 94.7 = 238 kW. The valve wastes this entire amount as an irreversible pressure drop, so it is the recoverable energy in the current arrangement. A marker rewards a correct sign convention (work out of the system positive), the correct choice of ΔT, and a unit check: kg/s × kJ/kg·K × K = kW. The value is before any mechanical or generator losses, which the problem tells us to ignore.

Answer: 238 kW

(c)

The heater is a constant-pressure steady-flow device with no work, so Q = ṁ (h₃ − h₂) = ṁ cp (T₃ − T₂). The target T₃ is the lowest acceptable temperature of 283.15 K. Then Q = 2.5 × 1.005 × (283.15 − 208.4) = 2.5 × 1.005 × 74.7 = 187.8 kW. This heat is a large fraction (79 percent) of the shaft power recovered, which is the core trade-off in the decision. Pressure drop in the heater is neglected. The result is the same whether the heater is electric or fired, but the energy price differs, as used in part (d). Stating that the heater is needed only because the expander cools the air well below the process limit earns the reasoning mark.

Answer: 187.8 kW

(d)

Hourly value of power = 238.0 kW × 0.09 $/kWh = 21.42 $/h. Hourly cost of heat = 187.8 kW × 0.04 $/kWh = 7.51 $/h. Net = 13.91 $/h, and over 8000 h the annual figure is 111293 $. The sign convention matters: power is a benefit and heat a cost. Equipment cost, maintenance, generator and gearbox losses and the pressure drop across the heater are excluded, so this is a gross value to compare against capital cost, not a profit. A careful answer also states the assumption that the line runs at full flow for all 8000 hours, because part-load operation would lower the expander efficiency and the saving.

Answer: 111300 $

(e)

On the numbers the expander recovers about 238 kW of shaft power from energy the valve destroys, and even after paying 188 kW of heating the net gross value is roughly 111293 dollars per year. That justifies a feasibility study. The recommendation depends on capital cost and payback: a payback under three years would normally be attractive. Items to check: generator efficiency and gearbox losses, which cut W by perhaps 10 to 15 percent; whether waste heat from the compressor aftercooler could replace purchased heat; part-load flow variation, since the main rarely runs at a constant 2.5 kg/s; the cost of a bypass valve for reliability; and whether the cold exhaust could be used for process cooling, which would offset the heater. A marker rewards a clear decision, one number from the analysis cited, and at least two sensible omitted factors.

Answer: Judgement, see worked solution

Problem 4 [A1-094] Entropy generation and isentropic efficiency: choosing between two steam turbines

A 15 kg/s steam flow at 4 MPa and 400 °C is to be expanded adiabatically in a turbine to a condenser pressure of 20 kPa. Two vendors bid. Machine A has an isentropic efficiency of 0.82 and machine B has 0.86. Machine B costs 1.8 million dollars more. The plant operates 7500 h per year and the electricity it displaces is worth 0.07 $/kWh. Use property data for water and steam from a reliable library (CoolProp or IAPWS). Take the dead-state temperature as 293.15 K, neglect kinetic and potential energy changes and heat loss, and neglect generator losses. The owner wants to know how irreversible machine A is and whether machine B pays back in a reasonable time.

  1. (a) Find the specific work output of machine A. [4]
  2. (b) Find the entropy generation per kilogram of steam in machine A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the work lost to irreversibility per kilogram in machine A. [3]
  4. (d) Find the additional power output obtained with machine B compared with machine A. [4]
  5. (e) Find the simple payback period of the additional investment for machine B, based on displaced electricity only. [5]
(a)

State 1 from the library: h₁ = 3214.5 kJ/kg and s₁ = 6.7714 kJ/kg·K. For the ideal expansion s₂s = s₁ at 20 kPa, which gives h₂s = 2230.5 kJ/kg (a wet mixture). Isentropic work is h₁ − h₂s = 984.0 kJ/kg. The first law for the adiabatic turbine gives w = h₁ − h₂, and the definition of isentropic efficiency gives w_actual = η (h₁ − h₂s) = 0.82 × 984.0 = 807 kJ/kg. The actual exit enthalpy is h₂ = h₁ − w = 2407.6 kJ/kg, and the exit quality is 0.915. A marker looks for the property source stated, the isentropic state fixed from s₁, and η applied to the work, not to the temperature.

Answer: 807 kJ/kg

(b)

For a steady adiabatic single-stream device the entropy balance reduces to s_gen = s₂ − s₁, since there is no heat transfer to carry entropy across the boundary. Fix the actual exit state from p₂ = 20 kPa and h₂ = 2407.6 kJ/kg, which gives s₂ = 7.3029 kJ/kg·K. Then s_gen = 7.3029 − 6.7714 = 0.5316 kJ/kg·K. The result is positive, as the second law requires; a negative value would signal an arithmetic or property error. A convenient cross-check is that s_gen must be zero at η = 1 and rise as the efficiency falls, which is consistent with this value for η = 0.82.

Answer: 0.5316 kJ/kg·K

(c)

The lost work (exergy destroyed) follows the Gouy-Stodola relation x_dest = T₀ s_gen. With T₀ = 293.15 K, x_dest = 293.15 × 0.5316 = 155.8 kJ/kg. This is 15.8 percent of the reversible work 984.0 kJ/kg. It is not the same as the plain enthalpy shortfall between the ideal and actual work (177.1 kJ/kg) because the exergy accounting weights the entropy generated by the dead-state temperature, and the steam leaves hotter than that. The two measures agree only for heat rejected at T₀. Units: kJ/kg·K times K gives kJ/kg, and the answer is a per-kilogram quantity, so multiplying by 15 kg/s would give the destruction rate in kW.

Answer: 155.8 kJ/kg

(d)

Machine B turns the same isentropic work into more output: w_B = 0.86 × 984.0 = 846.3 kJ/kg. The difference per kilogram is 846.3 − 806.9 = 39.4 kJ/kg, and the extra power at 15 kg/s is ΔP = 15 × 39.4 = 590.4 kW = 0.590 MW. Both machines share the same inlet state and the same ideal reference expansion, so the comparison is fair. Note that machine B extracts more work, so its exhaust enthalpy is lower (2368 against 2408 kJ/kg) and its exit quality lower (0.898 against 0.915); the condenser duty falls slightly but the exhaust is wetter. This is not needed here but is a useful remark.

Answer: 0.590 MW

(e)

Extra energy per year = 590.4 kW × 7500 h = 4428072 kWh. Annual value = 4428072 × 0.07 = 309965 $/year. Simple payback = additional capital / annual saving = 1 800 000 / 309965 = 5.81 years. Judgement: a payback of this length is compared with the plant life and the cost of capital. Under about 3 years most owners accept it; between 3 and 6 years it is acceptable for a long-life asset with stable load; beyond that, a lifetime discounted cash-flow analysis is needed. The calculation assumes constant load for 7500 h, no escalation in energy price, no extra maintenance for machine B and no generator losses. Any of these could move the answer, so the owner should test the sensitivity to the load factor.

Answer: 5.81 years

Problem 5 [A1-095] Ideal Rankine cycle: boiler pressure selection for a biomass plant

A 5 MW (net) biomass plant will use a simple ideal Rankine cycle with turbine inlet temperature 450 °C and a condenser held at 10 kPa (saturated liquid leaves the condenser). The designer is choosing between a boiler pressure of 3 MPa and 8 MPa. The turbine and pump are isentropic, pipe losses are neglected, and the net output of 5 MW is the turbine work minus the pump work. Blade erosion limits are a concern: the turbine manufacturer recommends an exit steam quality of at least 0.84 for the last stage. Use steam properties computed from a reliable library such as CoolProp or IAPWS. The owner asks for a recommendation that weighs thermal efficiency against exit moisture.

  1. (a) Find the thermal efficiency of the cycle with a boiler pressure of 3 MPa. [4]
  2. (b) Find the thermal efficiency with a boiler pressure of 8 MPa. [4]
  3. (c) Find the turbine exit quality at 8 MPa and say whether it meets the manufacturer limit. [3]
  4. (d) Find the steam mass flow rate needed to give 5 MW net at 8 MPa. [5]
  5. (e) Recommend a boiler pressure and justify the decision using the results above. [4]
(a)

Number the states 1 turbine inlet, 2 turbine exit, 3 condenser exit, 4 pump exit. From the library at 3 MPa and 450 °C: h₁ = 3344.8 kJ/kg. The isentropic expansion to 10 kPa gives h₂ = 2244.7 kJ/kg. Saturated liquid at 10 kPa has h₃ = 191.8 kJ/kg, and the isentropic pump to 3 MPa gives h₄ = 194.8 kJ/kg. Turbine work = h₁ − h₂ = 1100.1 kJ/kg, pump work = h₄ − h₃ = 3.0 kJ/kg, heat input = h₁ − h₄ = 3150.0 kJ/kg. Efficiency = (w_t − w_p)/q_in = (1100.1 − 3.0)/3150.0 = 0.3483. Show the T-s sketch or the state table; both earn credit for method.

Answer: 0.3483

(b)

Repeat with the same temperature and condenser. At 8 MPa and 450 °C: h₁ = 3273.3 kJ/kg. Isentropic expansion to 10 kPa gives h₂ = 2076.4 kJ/kg. The pump takes the saturated liquid at h₃ = 191.8 kJ/kg to h₄ = 199.9 kJ/kg. Then w_t = 1196.9 kJ/kg, w_p = 8.1 kJ/kg, q_in = 3073.5 kJ/kg, and η = (1196.9 − 8.1)/3073.5 = 0.3868. The pump work rises by a factor of about 2.7 compared with the 3 MPa case but remains small relative to the turbine work. Raising boiler pressure at fixed inlet temperature raises the mean temperature of heat addition and so improves efficiency.

Answer: 0.3868

(c)

The ideal expansion is at constant entropy. Take s₁ at 8 MPa and 450 °C from the library, then find the quality at 10 kPa where s₂ = s₁: x₂ = (s₂ − s_f)/(s_fg), which the library returns as x₂ = 0.788. The 3 MPa case gives x₂ = 0.858 for comparison. The manufacturer limit is 0.84, so the 8 MPa design fails by 0.052 and the 3 MPa design meets it. The exit stream carries about 21 percent liquid by mass, which erodes the last-stage blades. Reheat, a higher inlet temperature, or a moisture separator would be needed at 8 MPa. A state point on the T-s diagram inside the dome is the visual check.

Answer: 0.788

(d)

Net power equals mass flow times net specific work: Ẇ_net = ṁ (w_t − w_p). Net specific work at 8 MPa = 1196.9 − 8.1 = 1188.9 kJ/kg. Then ṁ = 5000 kW/1188.9 kJ/kg = 4.21 kg/s. For the 3 MPa design the mass flow would be 4.56 kg/s, about 8 percent larger, so the higher pressure also reduces steam flow and the size of the condenser and feed pump. Steady flow, a single stream, and negligible kinetic and potential energy changes are the stated assumptions. The thermal input is then ṁ q_in = 12926 kW.

Answer: 4.21 kg/s

(e)

The 8 MPa design is more efficient (0.3868 against 0.3483) and needs about 8 percent less steam for the same output, but its turbine exit quality of 0.788 is below the 0.84 limit, which risks blade erosion and loss of life. The 3 MPa design has an exit quality of 0.858, which is acceptable, at the price of a lower efficiency. A good recommendation is not to pick 8 MPa unchanged: either choose 3 MPa, or keep 8 MPa and add a mitigating measure such as reheat, a higher turbine inlet temperature if the superheater metallurgy allows, or a moisture-removal stage. Cost matters too, since an 8 MPa boiler and piping are heavier. Cite two numbers, state the trade-off, and propose a mitigation for full marks.

Answer: Judgement, see worked solution

A1 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A1-096] Rankine cycle with reheat: choosing the reheat pressure

A 150 MW (net) steam station uses an ideal reheat Rankine cycle. Steam leaves the boiler at 12 MPa and 520 °C, expands in the high-pressure turbine to the reheat pressure, is returned to the boiler and reheated to 520 °C, then expands in the low-pressure turbine to a condenser pressure of 7 kPa. Saturated liquid leaves the condenser. All turbines and the pump are isentropic. The designer is comparing reheat pressures of 3 MPa and 1 MPa, and wants the turbine exit quality to stay above 0.85. Use steam properties from a reliable library such as CoolProp or IAPWS, and neglect pressure drops in the boiler and reheater. The net output is turbine work minus pump work.

  1. (a) Find the thermal efficiency with a reheat pressure of 3 MPa. [4]
  2. (b) Find the thermal efficiency with a reheat pressure of 1 MPa. [4]
  3. (c) Find the exit quality of the low-pressure turbine for the 3 MPa reheat pressure. [3]
  4. (d) Find the steam mass flow needed for 150 MW net, using whichever reheat pressure gives the higher efficiency. [5]
  5. (e) Recommend a reheat pressure and say what other factors beyond these two numbers would influence the final choice. [4]
(a)

State table from the library: 1 boiler exit, 2 HP turbine exit at 3 MPa (s₂ = s₁), 3 reheater exit (3 MPa, 520 °C), 4 LP turbine exit (7 kPa, s₄ = s₃), 5 condenser exit (saturated liquid), 6 pump exit at 12 MPa. Values: h₁ = 3403.4, h₂ = 3004.3, h₃ = 3502.2, h₄ = 2265.4, h₆ = 175.4 kJ/kg. Turbine work w_t = (h₁ − h₂) + (h₃ − h₄) = 1635.8 kJ/kg. Pump work w_p = 12.1 kJ/kg. Heat in q_in = (h₁ − h₆) + (h₃ − h₂) = 3725.9 kJ/kg. Efficiency = (w_t − w_p)/q_in = 0.4358. Both heat additions, in the boiler and in the reheater, must appear in the denominator.

Answer: 0.4358

(b)

Only the reheat pressure changes, so states 1, 5 and 6 are unchanged. Now h₂ = 2765.1 kJ/kg at 1 MPa, h₃ = 3522.6 kJ/kg at 1 MPa and 520 °C, and h₄ = 2429.7 kJ/kg at 7 kPa. Then w_t = (h₁ − h₂) + (h₃ − h₄) = 1731.1 kJ/kg, and q_in = (h₁ − h₆) + (h₃ − h₂) = 3985.5 kJ/kg. Efficiency = (1731.1 − 12.1)/3985.5 = 0.4313. The lower reheat pressure puts more of the expansion in the low-pressure turbine, so more heat is added at a lower mean temperature, which lowers efficiency compared with the 3 MPa case. A T-s sketch showing the reheat line at each pressure supports the reasoning.

Answer: 0.4313

(c)

The LP expansion is isentropic from the reheater exit: s₄ = s₃ at 7 kPa. The library returns the quality directly: x₄ = 0.873. For the 1 MPa design the quality is 0.941. Both are above the 0.85 target, because reheating to 520 °C raises the entropy of the steam entering the LP turbine. Reheat is the standard way of avoiding the heavy moisture that a non-reheat cycle at 12 MPa would produce; the same cycle without reheat would give a quality of about 0.778. Calculation order: fix s₃, then find x from s = s_f + x s_fg at 7 kPa.

Answer: 0.873

(d)

The higher efficiency is found in part (a), the 3 MPa case (0.4358 against 0.4313). Net specific work for that option = 1623.8 kJ/kg. Net power equals ṁ times net specific work, so ṁ = 150 000 kW/1623.8 kJ/kg = 92.4 kg/s. The assumptions are steady flow with one steam stream, no extraction, and no losses. Heat input at this flow is ṁ q_in = 92.4 × 3725.9 = 344184 kW = 344 MW thermal, and the heat rejected is the difference between that and 150 MW. Check the units: kW divided by kJ/kg gives kg/s.

Answer: 92.4 kg/s

(e)

The 3 MPa reheat pressure gives the higher efficiency (0.4358 against 0.4313) with an exit quality of 0.873, above the 0.85 limit, so it is the better thermodynamic choice. The 1 MPa case also meets the quality limit but wastes efficiency. Common practice places the reheat pressure at about 15 to 25 percent of the boiler pressure, which here would mean roughly 2 to 3 MPa, consistent with the 3 MPa result. Non-thermodynamic factors: a higher reheat pressure shrinks the cold reheat and hot reheat piping and valves, since steam density is higher; it raises the required design pressure of the reheater tubes; the HP turbine exit temperature affects feedwater heater arrangements; and the plant would also compare the benefit against the added cost and control complexity. Give a decision and at least two such factors.

Answer: Judgement, see worked solution

Problem 2 [A1-097] Regenerative Rankine cycle with one open feedwater heater: choosing the extraction pressure

An ideal regenerative Rankine cycle receives steam at 10 MPa and 500 °C. A single open feedwater heater is fed by steam extracted from the turbine, and the remaining steam expands to a condenser at 10 kPa. Saturated liquid leaves the condenser and also leaves the open heater at the heater pressure. Two pumps are used, one before the heater and one after it. All turbine and pump processes are isentropic. The designer must choose between extraction at 0.5 MPa and 2 MPa. Use steam properties from a library such as CoolProp or IAPWS, and a mass basis of 1 kg of steam entering the turbine. The plant must deliver 100 MW net, and the net output is turbine work minus both pump works.

  1. (a) Find the fraction of steam extracted to the open feedwater heater at 0.5 MPa. [4]
  2. (b) Find the thermal efficiency with extraction at 0.5 MPa. [4]
  3. (c) Find the thermal efficiency with extraction at 2 MPa. [4]
  4. (d) Find the steam mass flow rate needed for 100 MW net with whichever extraction pressure gives the higher efficiency. [4]
  5. (e) Recommend an extraction pressure and say how the choice would change if the cycle had two open heaters. [4]
(a)

Number the states: 1 turbine inlet, 2 extraction point at 0.5 MPa, 3 turbine exit at 10 kPa, 4 condenser exit, 5 first pump exit at 0.5 MPa, 6 heater exit (saturated liquid at 0.5 MPa), 7 second pump exit at 10 MPa. From the library: h₂ = 2654.1, h₄ = 191.8, h₅ = 192.3, h₆ = 640.1 kJ/kg. An energy balance on the open heater, adiabatic and with no work, is y h₂ + (1 − y) h₅ = h₆. Solving, y = (h₆ − h₅)/(h₂ − h₅) = (640.1 − 192.3)/(2654.1 − 192.3) = 0.1819. This is the mass of extraction steam per kilogram entering the turbine; the remaining 1 − y continues to the condenser.

Answer: 0.1819

(b)

Turbine work per kg entering: w_t = (h₁ − h₂) + (1 − y)(h₂ − h₃) = (3375.1 − 2654.1) + 0.8181 × (2654.1 − 2089.7) = 1182.8 kJ/kg. Pump work: w_p = (1 − y)(h₅ − h₄) + (h₇ − h₆) = 0.8181 × (192.3 − 191.8) + (650.4 − 640.1) = 10.76 kJ/kg. Heat added in the boiler: q_in = h₁ − h₇ = 3375.1 − 650.4 = 2724.7 kJ/kg. Efficiency η = (w_t − w_p)/q_in = 0.4301. The fraction (1 − y) must multiply the LP turbine and first pump terms; forgetting it is the most common error.

Answer: 0.4301

(c)

Repeat at 2 MPa. Here h₂ = 2930.7, h₅ = 193.8, h₆ = 908.5 kJ/kg, so y = (908.5 − 193.8)/(2930.7 − 193.8) = 0.2611. Turbine work = (3375.1 − 2930.7) + (1 − 0.2611) × (2930.7 − 2089.7) = 1065.8 kJ/kg. Pump work = 10.87 kJ/kg. Heat in = h₁ − h₇ = 3375.1 − 917.9 = 2457.2 kJ/kg. Efficiency = 0.4293. Extracting at higher pressure raises the feedwater temperature entering the boiler, but takes steam that could still produce work in the lower stages of the turbine. The comparison with part (b) is therefore a genuine trade-off.

Answer: 0.4293

(d)

The higher efficiency is the case with 0.5 MPa extraction (0.4301). The net specific work for that case is 1172.0 kJ/kg. With Ẇ_net = ṁ w_net, the mass flow at the turbine inlet is ṁ = 100 000 kW/1172.0 kJ/kg = 85.3 kg/s. The extraction flow to the heater is then y ṁ = 15.5 kg/s, and the flow to the condenser is (1 − y) ṁ = 69.8 kg/s. These flows help size the heater and condenser. Steady flow and negligible kinetic and potential energy changes are assumed. Check that the heater flow and the condenser flow add back to the total, and use the net specific work, not the turbine work alone, as the basis.

Answer: 85.3 kg/s

(e)

The efficiencies are 0.4301 at 0.5 MPa and 0.4293 at 2 MPa, so 0.5 MPa extraction is better in this single-heater cycle. The gain from regeneration over the same cycle with no heater is shown by comparing with the plain Rankine efficiency; the heater lifts the average temperature of heat addition because the feedwater enters the boiler hotter. A single heater's best pressure lies roughly where the saturation temperature is midway between the condenser temperature and the boiler saturation temperature, about 140 to 180 °C here, which suggests 0.5 to 1 MPa. With two open heaters the temperature rise is split into three nearly equal steps, so the pressures would be spaced in roughly equal saturation-temperature increments, and the gain over one heater would be smaller than the first heater gave. Cite the numbers and state the principle for full marks.

Answer: Judgement, see worked solution

Problem 3 [A1-098] Otto cycle: compression ratio and knock limit for a motorcycle engine

A single-cylinder motorcycle engine of displacement 0.600 L is analysed with a cold-air-standard Otto cycle. Air at the start of compression is at 95 kPa and 305 K. Use cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, so that k = 1 + R/cv. Heat addition by combustion is 1500 kJ per kilogram of air. The designer is comparing compression ratios of 9.5 and 11.5. Fuel testing shows that knock begins if the end-of-compression temperature exceeds 800 K. The swept volume is the displacement, so the cylinder volume at bottom dead centre is the swept volume times r/(r − 1). Neglect residual gas and take each cycle to induct a fresh air mass at the stated conditions.

  1. (a) Find the thermal efficiency at a compression ratio of 9.5. [4]
  2. (b) Find the thermal efficiency at a compression ratio of 11.5. [4]
  3. (c) Find the temperature at the end of compression at a ratio of 11.5. [4]
  4. (d) Find the highest compression ratio that keeps the end-of-compression temperature at or below 800 K. [4]
  5. (e) Find the net work per cycle at r = 11.5, in joules. [4]
(a)

For the air-standard Otto cycle with constant specific heats, η = 1 − 1/rk−1. First k = 1 + R/cv = 1 + 0.287/0.718 = 1.3997, so k − 1 = 0.3997. Then rk−1 = 9.50.3997 = 2.4593, and η = 1 − 1/2.4593 = 0.5934. The efficiency depends only on compression ratio and k, not on the heat added, because the two constant-volume processes have equal ratios of absolute temperatures. A cold-air value of k = 1.4 is typical; real engines reach lower efficiency because of variable specific heats, heat loss and combustion that is not instantaneous.

Answer: 0.5934

(b)

Use the same formula with r = 11.5: rk−1 = 11.50.3997 = 2.6545, and η = 1 − 1/2.6545 = 0.6233. The gain over r = 9.5 is 0.0299 in absolute efficiency, or 5.0 percent of the lower value. The returns diminish: each extra unit of compression ratio buys less than the one before, because the 1/rk−1 term flattens. This is the thermodynamic argument for raising r; the mechanical and fuel arguments against it follow in the next two parts. Check: both values lie below the Carnot limit for the given temperatures, and both exceed what real spark-ignition engines achieve, which is typically 30 to 35 percent.

Answer: 0.6233

(c)

The compression stroke is isentropic for an ideal gas with constant specific heats: T₂ = T₁ rk−1 = 305 × 11.50.3997 = 305 × 2.6545 = 809.6 K. This is 536.5 °C. The result is compared with the knock threshold of 800 K: it is above the limit by 9.6 K. For information, the peak cycle temperature at constant-volume heat addition is T₃ = T₂ + q_in/cv = 809.6 + 1500/0.718 = 2899 K, which is far above any realistic engine value and shows how idealised the cold-air standard is.

Answer: 809.6 K

(d)

Set T₂ = T₁ rk−1 = 800 K and solve for r: r_max = (T₂/T₁)1/(k−1) = (800/305)1/0.3997 = 2.62302.502 = 11.16. Any ratio above this would be expected to knock with this fuel. The proposed ratio 11.5 is above this limit, so on this fuel it would be expected to knock, as part (c) showed. Even the compression ratio r_max leaves no margin for a hot day or a hot-running engine. A designer would therefore either keep 11.5 only with knock-sensing control that retards ignition, or choose a lower value such as 10.5, which gives T₂ of about 781 K, a safer margin, at a small cost in efficiency (0.6093 against 0.6233).

Answer: 11.16

(e)

First the air mass per cycle. Swept volume V_d = 0.600 L = 0.000600 m³, and V₁ = V_d r/(r − 1) = 0.000600 × 11.5/10.5 = 0.000657 m³. Then m = P₁V₁/(R T₁) = 95 × 0.000657/(0.287 × 305) = 0.000713 kg, using kPa·m³ = kJ. Net work per cycle w_net = η q_in = 0.6233 × 1500 = 934.9 kJ/kg, so W_net = m w_net = 0.000713 × 934.9 = 0.6668 kJ = 667 J. At 6000 rpm this single-cylinder four-stroke engine fires 50 times per second, so the indicated power would be 33.3 kW.

Answer: 667 J

Problem 4 [A1-099] Diesel cycle: effect of cutoff ratio on efficiency and mean effective pressure

A marine auxiliary diesel engine is modelled with the cold-air-standard Diesel cycle. The compression ratio is 17. Air at the start of compression is at 100 kPa and 300 K. Use cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, with k = cp/cv. The engine is to run at either a light-load cutoff ratio of 1.8 or a full-load cutoff ratio of 2.8, where the cutoff ratio is the ratio of the volume after heat addition to the volume at the end of compression. Heat is added at constant pressure and rejected at constant volume. Mean effective pressure is the net work per cycle divided by the swept (displacement) volume per unit mass, v₁ − v₂. Assume constant specific heats and an ideal cycle.

  1. (a) Find the thermal efficiency at a cutoff ratio of 1.8. [4]
  2. (b) Find the thermal efficiency at a cutoff ratio of 2.8. [4]
  3. (c) Find the heat added per kilogram of air at a cutoff ratio of 2.8. [3]
  4. (d) Find the mean effective pressure at a cutoff ratio of 2.8. [5]
  5. (e) A shipowner asks whether to prefer running at 1.8 or 2.8 cutoff ratio for fuel economy. Give a reasoned recommendation using the results. [4]
(a)

For the Diesel cycle η = 1 − (1/rk−1) × (r_ck − 1)/(k (r_c − 1)). First k = cp/cv = 1.005/0.718 = 1.3997. Then rk−1 = 170.3997 = 3.1034, so the compression temperature is T₂ = 300 × 3.1034 = 931.0 K. With r_c = 1.8, r_ck = 2.2767. The bracket is (2.2767 − 1)/(1.3997 × 0.8) = 1.1402. Therefore η = 1 − 1.1402/3.1034 = 0.6326. The same result is obtained from the heat terms, q_in = cp (T₃ − T₂) and q_out = cv (T₄ − T₁), as a cross-check. Efficiency is higher at light load.

Answer: 0.6326

(b)

Repeat with r_c = 2.8: r_ck = 2.81.3997 = 4.2257. The bracket is (4.2257 − 1)/(1.3997 × 1.8) = 1.2803. Then η = 1 − 1.2803/3.1034 = 0.5875. The efficiency has fallen by 0.0452, about 7.1 percent of the light-load value, because a larger cutoff ratio means more of the heat is added late in the power stroke, effectively at lower compression ratio. This is the thermodynamic reason that, for a fixed compression ratio, diesel efficiency decreases as load, and so cutoff ratio, increases. The Otto cycle of the same compression ratio would be more efficient still.

Answer: 0.5875

(c)

Heat is added at constant pressure between states 2 and 3, so q_in = cp (T₃ − T₂). The end-of-compression temperature is T₂ = 931.0 K, and since the cutoff ratio is T₃/T₂ at constant pressure, T₃ = 2.8 × 931.0 = 2606.9 K. Then q_in = 1.005 × (2606.9 − 931.0) = 1.005 × 1675.8 = 1684 kJ/kg. The peak temperature of 2607 K is an idealisation; real engines reach lower peak values because of dissociation, heat loss and variable specific heats. This heat input is later converted to net work using the efficiency from part (b), so q_in is also a check on part (d).

Answer: 1684 kJ/kg

(d)

The specific volume at the start of compression is v₁ = R T₁/P₁ = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.8610 m³/kg, and at the end of compression v₂ = v₁/r = 0.8610/17 = 0.05065 m³/kg. Net work per kilogram is w = η q_in = 0.5875 × 1684 = 989.4 kJ/kg (equally, q_in − q_out with q_out = cv (T₄ − T₁) = 694.8 kJ/kg). The mean effective pressure is MEP = w/(v₁ − v₂) = 989.4/(0.8610 − 0.05065) = 1221 kPa. This is a large figure for a naturally aspirated engine because the cold-air model ignores real losses. Units are consistent because kJ/kg divided by m³/kg gives kPa.

Answer: 1221 kPa

(e)

Per kilogram of air, the light-load setting (r_c = 1.8) has the higher efficiency (0.6326 against 0.5875), so it burns less fuel per unit of work. The full-load setting (r_c = 2.8) develops a much higher MEP (1221 kPa against 584 kPa at light load), so it gives more power from the same engine. The right answer therefore depends on the power the ship needs: running at light load is the economical choice only when that power is sufficient, and the engine should not be oversized and throttled back for long periods because real engines also lose efficiency at light load through friction. Mention the practical limits: peak pressure, smoke at high load, turbocharger matching, and the real effect of friction. State a decision tied to the load profile.

Answer: Judgement, see worked solution

Problem 5 [A1-100] Brayton cycle with regeneration: pressure ratio selection for a recuperated microturbine

A 20 MW recuperated gas-turbine generating set is being sized. Air enters the compressor at 300 K. The turbine inlet temperature is limited to 1250 K. Compressor and turbine isentropic efficiencies are 0.85 and 0.88, and the regenerator (recuperator) effectiveness is 0.80, defined from the compressor-exit and turbine-exit temperatures. Treat the working fluid as air with constant cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and k = 1.4 throughout, neglect pressure drops and the fuel mass flow, and treat the combustor as a pure heat addition. The designer is choosing between an overall pressure ratio of 5 and 10. Regeneration is most useful when the turbine exhaust is much hotter than the compressor exit.

  1. (a) Find the thermal efficiency at a pressure ratio of 5. [5]
  2. (b) Find the thermal efficiency at a pressure ratio of 10. [4]
  3. (c) Find the net specific work at a pressure ratio of 5. [3]
  4. (d) Find the air mass flow required for 20 MW using the option with the higher efficiency. [4]
  5. (e) Recommend a pressure ratio and explain how it would change for a simple (non-regenerative) cycle. [4]
(a)

States: 1 compressor inlet, 2 compressor exit, 3 turbine inlet, 4 turbine exit, 5 regenerator cold-side exit (combustor inlet). Isentropic factor x = 50.4/1.4 = 1.5838. Compressor exit T₂ = T₁ [1 + (x − 1)/η_c] = 300 × [1 + 0.5838/0.85] = 506.1 K. Turbine exit T₄ = T₃ [1 − η_t (1 − 1/x)] = 1250 × [1 − 0.88 × (1 − 1/1.5838)] = 844.5 K. The regenerator warms the compressed air: T₅ = T₂ + ε (T₄ − T₂) = 506.1 + 0.80 × (844.5 − 506.1) = 776.8 K. Heat added q_in = cp (T₃ − T₅) = 475.5 kJ/kg. Net work = cp [(T₃ − T₄) − (T₂ − T₁)] = 200.4 kJ/kg. Efficiency = w_net/q_in = 0.4215.

Answer: 0.4215

(b)

Repeat the sequence. x = 100.2857 = 1.9307. T₂ = 300 × [1 + 0.9307/0.85] = 628.5 K. T₄ = 1250 × [1 − 0.88 × (1 − 1/1.9307)] = 719.7 K. Regenerator exit T₅ = 628.5 + 0.80 × (719.7 − 628.5) = 701.5 K. The exhaust is now only slightly hotter than the compressor discharge, so regeneration recovers little: the regenerator saves only 73.4 kJ/kg of heat, against 272.1 kJ/kg at a pressure ratio of 5. Then q_in = 551.3 kJ/kg, w_net = 202.8 kJ/kg, and η = 0.3679. Efficiency with regeneration falls as pressure ratio rises, the reverse of the simple cycle.

Answer: 0.3679

(c)

Compressor work w_c = cp (T₂ − T₁) = 1.005 × (506.1 − 300) = 207.1 kJ/kg. Turbine work w_t = cp (T₃ − T₄) = 1.005 × (1250 − 844.5) = 407.5 kJ/kg. Net work w_net = w_t − w_c = 407.5 − 207.1 = 200.4 kJ/kg. For comparison, the net work at a pressure ratio of 10 is 202.8 kJ/kg, so the two options produce nearly the same work per kilogram of air; the net work is relatively flat near the optimum for this cycle, while the heat added is quite different. A regenerator changes the heat input but not the work, because it only moves heat inside the cycle.

Answer: 200.4 kJ/kg

(d)

The better option is the pressure ratio of 5, with η = 0.4215. The required flow follows from ṁ = Ẇ_net/w_net = 20 000 kW/200.4 kJ/kg = 99.8 kg/s. Heat input at that flow is ṁ q_in = 99.8 × 475.5 = 47454 kW, which is also 20 000/0.4215. Fuel flow is neglected as instructed. Practical remark: compressor and turbine diameters scale with the volumetric flow, so a lower pressure ratio at the same power gives larger machines in the compressor, and the recuperator core also grows with exhaust flow.

Answer: 99.8 kg/s

(e)

Between the two options the pressure ratio of 5 gives the higher efficiency, 0.4215, against 0.3679 for the other, with about the same net work per kg, so the recuperated set should run at a low pressure ratio. This is the opposite of a simple Brayton cycle, whose efficiency rises with pressure ratio until compressor and turbine losses dominate, so a simple-cycle machine would use a ratio of 10 or higher. The reason is the mean temperature of heat addition: at low pressure ratio the turbine exhaust is hot, and the regenerator replaces a large amount of fuel heat. At high pressure ratio the exhaust cools and the regenerator becomes ineffective. Constraints to mention include recuperator size and pressure loss, cost, and the turbine-exit temperature limit of the recuperator material.

Answer: Judgement, see worked solution

Exam A2: Kinematics and Dynamics of Machines

A2 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A2-001] Planar mechanism velocity analysis by instant centres

A four-bar linkage in a packaging machine has the ground pivots O2 and O4 spaced 0.40 m apart on a horizontal line, with O4 to the right of O2. The driving crank O2A is 0.12 m long and turns counter-clockwise at a constant 20 rad/s. The coupler AB is 0.38 m long and the follower O4B is 0.30 m long. Take the open configuration with B above the line O2O4. At the instant studied the crank makes 70° with the positive x-axis, measured counter-clockwise from O2. Point C is the midpoint of the coupler. Use instant-centre methods; a scale drawing is not required if you calculate the positions of the centres. Take counter-clockwise rotation as positive.

  1. (a) State the number of instant centres for this four-bar linkage and name the two that must be found by the Aronhold-Kennedy theorem. [2]
  2. (b) Locate I13 by calculating its distance from O2 along the line O2A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the angular velocity of the coupler AB. [5]
  4. (d) Find the angular velocity of the follower O4B. [5]
  5. (e) Find the speed of the midpoint C of the coupler. [4]
(a)

A mechanism with n links has n(n-1)/2 instant centres. With four links (ground 1, crank 2, coupler 3, follower 4) this gives 4 × 3 / 2 = 6. Four of them are permanent pin centres that are found by inspection: I12 at O2, I23 at A, I34 at B and I14 at O4. The remaining two, I13 (coupler relative to ground) and I24 (crank relative to follower), are not pins. The Aronhold-Kennedy theorem states that three bodies in relative planar motion have three instant centres lying on one straight line. Applying it to links 1, 2, 3 puts I13 on the line through I12 and I23, which is the line O2A extended. Applying it to links 1, 3, 4 puts I13 on the line through I34 and I14, the line BO4 extended. So I13 is the intersection of the extended lines O2A and O4B. I24 follows in the same way from the lines I12 I14 and I23 I34.

Answer: 6 (I13 and I24 by Kennedy)

(b)

First fix B. With O2 at the origin, A is at (0.12 cos 70°, 0.12 sin 70°) = (0.0410, 0.1128) m and O4 is at (0.40, 0). The distance AO4 is 0.3763 m. Intersecting a circle of radius 0.38 m about A with a circle of radius 0.30 m about O4 and taking the upper intersection gives B = (0.3724, 0.2987) m. I13 lies on the line O2A and on the line O4B, so solve O2 + s(cos 70°, sin 70°) = O4 + t × (unit vector O4 to B). Solving the two scalar equations gives s = 0.933 m, so I13 = (0.319, 0.877) m. The centre lies well beyond A on the extended crank line, because the coupler and follower are nearly parallel. Check: the distance from O4 to I13 along line O4B is consistent with the same point, which confirms the intersection.

Answer: 0.933 m

(c)

The coupler rotates about the instant centre I13, which is a point of zero velocity of link 3 relative to the ground. The velocity of A is perpendicular to O2A with magnitude vA = ω2 × O2A = 20 × 0.12 = 2.40 m/s. A is a distance AI13 = 0.813 m from the centre. Then ω3 = vA / AI13 = 2.40 / 0.813 = 2.952 rad/s. For the sense of rotation, note that A lies between O2 and I13 on the same line. The velocity of A is the same for both bodies, so rotation about O2 and rotation about I13 on opposite sides of A must be opposite in sense. Crank 2 turns counter-clockwise, so the coupler turns clockwise. Using the vector form ω3 = (rA × vA) / |rA|², with rA = A - I13, the result is ω3 = -2.952 rad/s (negative means clockwise).

Answer: -2.95 rad/s

(d)

Point B belongs to both the coupler and the follower. Its velocity is found from the coupler's rotation about I13: vB = ω3 × BI13. The distance BI13 is 0.580 m, so vB = 2.952 × 0.580 = 1.713 m/s, directed perpendicular to I13B. The same point also moves on a circle of radius O4B = 0.30 m about O4, so vB = ω4 × 0.30. Hence ω4 = vB / 0.30 = 1.713 / 0.30 = 5.712 rad/s in magnitude. The direction follows from the vector cross product of (B - O4) with vB, which gives ω4 = 5.712 rad/s. The positive sign means the follower turns counter-clockwise, opposite to the coupler, which is consistent with B moving to the left and slightly down, vB = (-1.71, -0.16) m/s. A cross-check using I24 would give the same ratio, but the direct route avoids locating it.

Answer: 5.71 rad/s

(e)

All points on the coupler move as if the coupler were rotating about I13 with angular velocity ω3, so the speed of any point is ω3 times its distance from I13. The midpoint is C = (A + B) / 2 = (0.2067, 0.2057) m. Its distance from I13 is CI13 = 0.680 m. Therefore vC = |ω3| × CI13 = 2.952 × 0.680 = 2.008 m/s. The velocity is perpendicular to the line from I13 to C. As a reasonableness check, vA = 2.40 m/s and vB = 1.713 m/s, and the speed of C is 2.01 m/s. It need not lie between them, because C is nearer to the centre of rotation than A is from the far side of the coupler. The velocity vectors of A, C and B are in proportion to their distances from I13, which provides a quick graphical check.

Answer: 2.01 m/s

Problem 2 [A2-002] Relative velocity and acceleration of a four-bar linkage

A four-bar linkage drives the sweep arm of a car-wash brush. The fixed pivots O2 and O4 lie 0.350 m apart on a horizontal line with O4 to the right of O2. The crank O2A is 0.100 m long, the coupler AB is 0.300 m long and the rocker O4B is 0.250 m long. The crank is driven counter-clockwise at a constant 30 rad/s and, at the instant of interest, makes 120° with the positive x-axis measured from O2. Take the configuration with joint B above the line O2O4. Use the loop-closure vector equation r2 + r3 = r1 + r4 and its time derivatives. Treat counter-clockwise rotation as positive, and give accelerations as magnitudes where a vector is asked for.

  1. (a) Determine the angular velocity of the coupler AB. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the angular velocity of the rocker O4B. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of point A. [3]
  4. (d) Determine the angular acceleration of the rocker O4B. [5]
  5. (e) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of point B. [4]
(a)

Write the loop closure as r2 ejθ2 + r3 ejθ3 = r1 + r4 ejθ4. Geometry first: A = (-0.0500, 0.0866) m, and the circle intersection with B above the ground line gives θ3 = 25.21° and θ4 = 120.95°. Differentiating once with respect to time: j ω2 r2 ejθ2 + j ω3 r3 ejθ3 = j ω4 r4 ejθ4. Separating real and imaginary parts gives two linear equations in the unknown ω3 and ω4. Substituting ω2 = 30 rad/s and the lengths and angles above and solving the 2 × 2 system gives ω3 = -0.167 rad/s. The negative sign shows that the coupler rotates clockwise at this instant while the crank turns counter-clockwise. The magnitude is tiny compared with ω2 because the crank (120°) and the rocker (121.0°) are almost parallel, so the coupler is very nearly in instantaneous translation.

Answer: -0.167 rad/s

(b)

The same two velocity equations contain ω4. With the matrix form [j r3 ejθ3, -j r4 ejθ4] × [ω3, ω4] = -j ω2 r2 ejθ2, the real and imaginary rows are solved together. The numbers are j r3 ejθ3 = (-0.1278 + j 0.2714), and -j r4 ejθ4 = (0.2144 + j 0.1286), with right-hand side (2.598 + j 1.500) m/s. The solution is ω4 = 12.018 rad/s. As a check, the velocity of B from the rocker is |ω4| × 0.250 = 3.005 m/s, and from the crank-coupler path it is the vector sum of vA (3.000 m/s) and the relative velocity ω3 × AB, which agrees. The positive value shows that the rocker turns counter-clockwise, the same sense as the crank. Because the coupler is almost translating, the rocker pin B moves at nearly the same speed as A.

Answer: 12.02 rad/s

(c)

Point A moves on a circle of radius 0.100 m about O2 with constant angular velocity, so the angular acceleration of the crank is zero and the tangential acceleration is zero. The acceleration of A is purely centripetal and is directed from A towards O2: aA = ω2² × r2 = 30² × 0.100 = 90.0 m/s². In complex notation the full expression is aA = (j α2 - ω2²) r2 ejθ2 with α2 = 0, giving the same magnitude. This acceleration is the starting point of the acceleration polygon, because the coupler then adds a normal term ω3² r3 towards A and a tangential term α3 r3 perpendicular to AB, while the rocker adds ω4² r4 towards O4 and α4 r4 perpendicular to O4B. Knowing aA fixes the first vector in the loop and makes the second-derivative equation solvable.

Answer: 90.0 m/s²

(d)

Differentiate the loop closure a second time, with α2 = 0: -ω2² r2 ejθ2 + (j α3 - ω3²) r3 ejθ3 = (j α4 - ω4²) r4 ejθ4. Collect the unknown angular accelerations on the left: j α3 r3 ejθ3 - j α4 r4 ejθ4 = ω2² r2 ejθ2 + ω3² r3 ejθ3 - ω4² r4 ejθ4. The right-hand side evaluates to (-26.4 + j 47.0) m/s², using ω3 = -0.167 and ω4 = 12.018 rad/s. The coefficient matrix is the same one used in the velocity solution, so solving the 2 × 2 system gives α3 = 180.5 rad/s² and α4 = -15.6 rad/s². The rocker still turns counter-clockwise but its angular acceleration is negative, so it is decelerating at 15.6 rad/s². The coupler angular acceleration is large and positive because the coupler is passing through its nearly translating state.

Answer: -15.6 rad/s²

(e)

Point B moves on a circle of radius 0.250 m about O4, so its acceleration has a normal component towards O4 and a tangential component perpendicular to O4B. Normal: aBn = ω4² × r4 = 12.018² × 0.250 = 36.1 m/s². Tangential: aBt = |α4| × r4 = 15.6 × 0.250 = 3.9 m/s². These components are mutually perpendicular, so aB = √(aBn² + aBt²) = √(36.1² + 3.9²) = 36.3 m/s². The complex form (j α4 - ω4²) r4 ejθ4 gives the identical magnitude. The result is smaller than aA = 90 m/s² because the rocker is turning more slowly than the crank, and the normal term dominates the tangential term. This value is what a designer would use in sizing pin bearings and the brush inertia load.

Answer: 36 m/s²

Problem 3 [A2-003] Slider-crank kinematics

An offset slider-crank forms the drive of a small reciprocating air compressor. The crank radius is r = 50 mm, the connecting rod is l = 210 mm between centres, and the line of stroke of the piston pin passes 20 mm above the crank-shaft centre, on the side towards which the crank pin rises as the crank turns from θ = 0. The crank turns at a constant 1800 rpm. Measure the crank angle θ from the line parallel to the line of stroke through the crank centre, so that the crank pin is at height r sin θ above the shaft centre. The position of the piston pin from the shaft centre along the stroke direction is x = r cos θ + √(l² - (r sin θ - e)²), with e = 20 mm. Analyse the compressor when θ = 40°.

  1. (a) Find the position x of the piston pin from the crank-shaft centre. [4]
  2. (b) Find the velocity of the piston pin at θ = 40°. [5]
  3. (c) Find the acceleration of the piston pin at θ = 40°. [5]
  4. (d) Find the angular velocity of the connecting rod at θ = 40°. [6]
(a)
