Use x = r cos θ + √(l² - (r sin θ - e)²) with r = 0.050 m, l = 0.210 m, e = 0.020 m and θ = 40°. The crank-pin height above the shaft centre is r sin θ = 0.050 × sin 40° = 0.03214 m. Subtract the offset: r sin θ - e = 0.01214 m. Then the rod's projection is √(l² - (r sin θ - e)²) = √(0.210² - 0.01214²) = 0.20965 m. The crank's own projection is r cos θ = 0.050 × cos 40° = 0.03830 m. Summing, x = 0.03830 + 0.20965 = 0.24795 m, which is 248.0 mm. Because the line of stroke is offset, x at this angle differs slightly from the in-line result, and the maximum x is reached a little after top dead centre. The answer is a reasonable check against the rod length plus crank radius, 260 mm.

Answer: 248.0 mm

(b)

The crank speed is ω = 1800 × 2π / 60 = 188.50 rad/s. Differentiate x with respect to time using θ = ωt: dx/dt = -ω r sin θ - ω (r sin θ - e) r cos θ / √(l² - (r sin θ - e)²). Substitute the values from part (a): the first term is -188.50 × 0.050 × sin 40° = -6.058 m/s. The second term is -188.50 × 0.01214 × 0.03830 / 0.20965 = -0.418 m/s. Summing the two terms gives vp = -6.476 m/s. The negative value means the piston is travelling towards the crank shaft. The speed of 6.48 m/s is typical of the mean piston speed range for a compressor of this size. The velocity is evaluated with a symbolic derivative, which gives the same answer as differentiating by hand.

Answer: -6.48 m/s

(c)

Differentiate the velocity again with respect to time, with ω constant. For brevity let q = r sin θ - e and s = √(l² - q²), so that dx/dt = -ω r sin θ - ω q r cos θ / s. With q' = ω r cos θ and q'' = -ω² r sin θ, the quotient rule gives d²x/dt² = -ω² r cos θ - (q'² + q q'')/s + q² q'² / s³. Evaluating at θ = 40° with q = 0.01214 m, s = 0.20965 m, q' = 7.220 m/s and q'' = -1141.9 m/s² gives a = -1544 m/s². The sign is negative, so the piston is accelerating towards the crank shaft. The magnitude is about 157 times gravity, which is why the inertia force of the reciprocating parts is a dominant design load in the connecting rod and bearings. The result was obtained by symbolic differentiation and agrees with the hand expansion.

Answer: -1544 m/s²

(d)

Let φ be the rod angle from the line of stroke. The geometry gives l sin φ = r sin θ - e, so sin φ = 0.01214 / 0.210 = 0.0578 and φ = 3.31°. Differentiate: l cos φ × dφ/dt = r cos θ × ω. Therefore ωrod = r ω cos θ / (l cos φ). Substituting, ωrod = 0.050 × 188.50 × cos 40° / (0.210 × cos 3.31°) = 7.220 / 0.20965 = 34.44 rad/s. The positive value means the rod swings in the sense of increasing φ. The rod angular velocity is needed for the rod's rotational kinetic energy and for the dynamic force analysis of the mechanism.

Answer: 34.4 rad/s

Problem 4 [A2-004] Grashof and transmission angle

A four-bar linkage operates the gate of a bottle-sorting machine. The fixed distance between the ground pivots is 280 mm. The driving crank is 140 mm long, the coupler is 320 mm long and the driven rocker is 260 mm long. The crank is driven at constant speed by the motor and the rocker pivot O4 lies on the same side of the coupler as the crank pivot O2. The designer needs the rocker to oscillate rather than rotate, and wants the transmission angle at the rocker end of the coupler to stay acceptable at every crank position. Define the transmission angle μ as the acute angle between the coupler and the rocker. The designer will also check the quick-return behaviour of the rocker. Take all angles in degrees.

  1. (a) Apply Grashof's criterion: calculate (p + q) - (s + l), where s and l are the shortest and longest link lengths and p and q the other two. [4]
  2. (b) State the type of mechanism that results from this chain with the ground link as given, and justify the answer. [3]
  3. (c) Find the minimum transmission angle over the whole crank cycle. [5]
  4. (d) Find the total angular swing of the rocker between its two extreme positions. [4]
  5. (e) Find the time ratio (longer stroke time to shorter stroke time) for a constant crank speed. [4]
(a)

Grashof's criterion says that at least one link can make a full revolution relative to the others only if the sum of the shortest and longest link lengths does not exceed the sum of the other two: s + l ≤ p + q. The four link lengths are 280 (ground), 140 (crank), 320 (coupler) and 260 (rocker). The shortest is s = 140 mm and the longest is l = 320 mm, so s + l = 460 mm. The other two links give p + q = 280 + 260 = 540 mm. The margin is (p + q) - (s + l) = 540 - 460 = 80 mm. A positive margin means the linkage is a Grashof chain, so continuous rotation of the shortest link is possible. A margin of zero would give a change-point (special-case) mechanism and a negative margin a non-Grashof triple rocker. The margin of 80 mm is large enough that small dimensional errors will not alter the classification.

Answer: 80 mm

(b)

The chain is Grashof, so the type depends on which link is fixed. The rule is that the link adjacent to the shortest link, when fixed, gives a crank-rocker. Here the shortest link is the 140 mm crank, and it is adjacent to the ground link (the ground is one of its two neighbours, the other being the coupler). With the ground fixed, the crank can make full revolutions while the 260 mm rocker, which is the link opposite the shortest link (the crank), swings through a limited angle. Therefore the mechanism is a crank-rocker. If the shortest link were fixed it would be a double-crank (drag link) and if the link opposite the shortest were fixed it would be a double-rocker. The required behaviour, a continuously driven crank and an oscillating rocker, matches the crank-rocker type, so the choice of ground link is correct.

Answer: Crank-rocker mechanism: the shortest link (the crank) is adjacent to the ground link, so it rotates fully while the rocker oscillates.

(c)

For a four-bar linkage the cosine rule applied to the diagonal between the crank pin and the rocker pivot gives cos μ = (b² + c² - d² - a² + 2ad cos θ2) / (2bc), with a = 140 (crank), b = 320 (coupler), c = 260 (rocker) and d = 280 (ground) in mm. The only variable is cos θ2, so cos μ is a maximum when θ2 = 0 (crank folded along the ground link towards the rocker pivot), which is where μ is a minimum. Substituting: (320² + 260² - 280² - 140² + 2 × 140 × 280) / (2 × 320 × 260) = (170000 - 98000 + 78400) / 166400 = 0.9038. Hence μmin = cos⁻¹(0.9038) = 25.3°. At θ2 = 180° the angle is 92.2°, whose acute value is 87.8°. The minimum of 25.3° is below the usual 40° guide value, so the drive would be poor at that end of the stroke.

Answer: 25.3 °

(d)

The rocker reaches its extreme positions when the crank and coupler are collinear (the toggle positions), at which the crank-pin to rocker-pivot distance is either a + b or b - a. First extreme: D1 = 140 + 320 = 460 mm. Second extreme: D2 = 320 - 140 = 180 mm. In the triangle formed by O2, O4 and B (sides d = 280, c = 260 and D), the angle ψ at O4 measured from the line O4O2 to the rocker follows the cosine rule: cos ψ = (c² + d² - D²) / (2cd). For D1 = 460: cos ψ1 = (67600 + 78400 - 211600) / 145600 = -0.4505, so ψ1 = 116.8°. For D2 = 180: cos ψ2 = (146000 - 32400) / 145600 = 0.7802, so ψ2 = 38.7°. The swing is |ψ1 - ψ2| = 78.1°. This is the useful angular range for the sorting gate.

Answer: 78.1 °

(e)

Because the crank turns at constant speed, the time ratio equals the ratio of the crank angles swept in the two rocker strokes. The crank angles at the toggle positions come from the triangle O2, O4, B: the crank angle θ2 is the angle at O2 between the line O2O4 and the line O2B, with cos θ = (d² + D² - c²) / (2dD). For D1 = 460 mm: cos θ = (78400 + 211600 - 67600) / (2 × 280 × 460) = 0.8634, so θ = 30.3°. For D2 = 180 mm, the crank is folded back on the opposite side of the pivot, so the crank angle is cos⁻¹((78400 + 32400 - 67600) / (2 × 280 × 180)) + 180° = 244.6°. The two angles between the toggle positions are 214.3° and 145.7°. Time ratio Q = 214.3 / 145.7 = 1.47. The rocker takes about 1.47 times longer on the slower stroke than on the faster return stroke.

Answer: 1.47

Problem 5 [A2-005] Cam profile and follower motion

A radial disc cam with an in-line knife-edge follower operates the inlet valve of a stationary engine rig. Starting from a dwell at the lowest position, the follower must rise 18 mm with cycloidal motion while the cam turns through 120°. The cam rotates at a constant 450 rpm and the base-circle radius is 35 mm. The follower then dwells at the top; only the rise is analysed here. Measure the cam angle θ from the start of the rise. The cycloidal rise follows s = h [θ/β - sin(2πθ/β) / (2π)], where h is the total rise, β the rise angle, and the pressure angle for an in-line follower satisfies tan φ = (ds/dθ) / (R0 + s). Analyse the follower when the cam has turned 45° from the start of the rise.

  1. (a) Calculate the follower displacement at θ = 45°. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the follower velocity at θ = 45°. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the peak follower acceleration during the rise. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the pressure angle at θ = 45°. [6]
(a)

The rise follows the cycloidal law s = h [θ/β - sin(2πθ/β) / (2π)]. Here h = 18 mm, β = 120° and θ = 45°, so θ/β = 45/120 = 0.3750. The argument of the sine is 2π × 0.3750 = 2.3562 rad, which is 135.0°. Then sin(135.0°) = 0.7071, and sin(2πθ/β) / (2π) = 0.7071 / 6.2832 = 0.11254. The bracket is 0.3750 - 0.11254 = 0.26246. Therefore s = 18 × 0.26246 = 4.724 mm. The follower has risen about 26 percent of the total lift after 37.5 percent of the rise angle, which is well behind a uniform rise, which would be 37.5 percent, because the cycloidal law starts and ends with zero velocity and acceleration.

Answer: 4.72 mm

(b)

First convert the cam speed: ω = 450 × 2π / 60 = 47.124 rad/s. Differentiating the cycloidal law with respect to time, using dθ/dt = ω, gives v = (h ω / β) [1 - cos(2πθ/β)], with β in radians (β = 120° = 2.0944 rad). Substituting: h ω / β = 0.018 × 47.124 / 2.0944 = 0.4050 m/s. Next, cos(135.0°) = -0.7071, so the bracket is 1 - (-0.7071) = 1.7071. The velocity is therefore v = 0.4050 × 1.7071 = 0.691 m/s. The peak velocity of this law is 2 h ω / β = 0.810 m/s at mid-rise, so the follower is at 85 percent of its peak speed at this angle. Velocity is positive, so the follower is moving away from the cam centre.

Answer: 0.691 m/s

(c)

Differentiating the velocity again gives a = (2π h ω² / β²) sin(2πθ/β). The sine term has a maximum value of 1, which occurs at θ = β/4 = 30° (and a minimum of -1 at θ = 90°). So the peak magnitude is amax = 2π h ω² / β². Substituting h = 0.018 m, ω = 47.124 rad/s (so ω² = 2220.7 rad²/s²) and β = 2.0944 rad (so β² = 4.3865 rad²): amax = 2π × 0.018 × 2220.7 / 4.3865 = 57 m/s². This is about 6 times gravity, which sets the spring force needed to keep the follower in contact with the cam. The acceleration is zero at the start and end of the rise, which is why the cycloidal law gives low shock loading. At 45° the acceleration is 40 m/s², about 71 percent of the peak.

Answer: 57 m/s²

(d)

For an in-line follower the pressure angle is tan φ = (ds/dθ) / (R0 + s), where ds/dθ is the slope of the displacement curve in metres per radian of cam rotation. From the cycloidal law, ds/dθ = (h / β) [1 - cos(2πθ/β)]. Using the earlier values, h / β = 0.018 / 2.0944 = 0.00859 m/rad, and the bracket is 1.7071, so ds/dθ = 0.01467 m/rad. The pitch radius at this angle is R0 + s = 0.035 + 0.00472 = 0.03972 m. Then tan φ = 0.01467 / 0.03972 = 0.3693, so φ = 20.3°. This is below the generally accepted limit of about 30° for a translating follower, but the base radius is not generous. A smaller base circle would raise this pressure angle quickly, so the designer should check it at the angle of maximum slope, which for this law is at mid-rise.

Answer: 20.3 °

A2 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A2-006] Spur gear geometry and gear trains

A two-stage compound spur gear reducer drives a conveyor head shaft. Stage one is a pinion of 18 teeth on the motor shaft meshing with a gear of 54 teeth. The 54-tooth gear shares a shaft with a pinion of 20 teeth, which meshes with an output gear of 60 teeth. Stage one has a module of 4 mm; both stages use standard full-depth 20° involute teeth (addendum equal to one module). The motor runs at 1200 rpm and delivers 7.5 kW, and the overall mechanical efficiency of the train is 95 percent. Analyse the first mesh for geometry and then the train as a whole. Assume the second stage is strong enough for the loads and do not consider tooth bending or contact stress.

  1. (a) Calculate the centre distance of the first mesh. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the contact ratio of the first mesh. [6]
  3. (c) Calculate the output shaft speed. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the torque available on the output shaft. [6]
(a)

For a standard spur gear pair the pitch circles are tangent, so the centre distance is the sum of the pitch radii: C = m (z1 + z2) / 2. The module m is 4 mm, the pinion has z1 = 18 teeth and the gear has z2 = 54 teeth. The pinion pitch radius is r1 = m z1 / 2 = 4 × 18 / 2 = 36 mm and the gear pitch radius is r2 = m z2 / 2 = 4 × 54 / 2 = 108 mm. Therefore C = 36 + 108 = 144 mm. The pitch circle of a gear is defined by the module and the tooth count, independent of the pressure angle, and the centre distance for a standard (zero profile shift) pair does not depend on the pressure angle either. Any machine-tool or bearing-housing layout would place the two shaft axes 144 mm apart.

Answer: 144 mm

(b)

The contact ratio is the length of the path of contact Z divided by the base pitch pb. Pitch radii are r1 = 36 mm and r2 = 108 mm; addendum radii are ra1 = 36 + 4 = 40 mm and ra2 = 108 + 4 = 112 mm. Base radii are rb = r cos 20°: rb1 = 33.829 mm and rb2 = 101.487 mm. The path of contact is Z = √(ra1² - rb1²) + √(ra2² - rb2²) - C sin φ = 21.345 + 47.375 - 49.251 = 19.469 mm. The base pitch is pb = π m cos φ = π × 4 × cos 20° = 11.809 mm. Therefore the contact ratio is 19.469 / 11.809 = 1.65. A value above 1 means that at least one tooth pair is always in contact, and a value of 1.65 means two pairs share the load for about 65 percent of the mesh.

Answer: 1.65

(c)

In a compound train, the gear 2 and pinion 3 are on one shaft and turn at the same speed. The speed ratio of a compound train is the product of the individual tooth-count ratios: (N1/N4) = (z2/z1) × (z4/z3) = (54/18) × (60/20) = 3 × 3 = 9. The output speed is therefore N4 = N1 / ratio = 1200 / 9 = 133.3 rpm. The intermediate shaft speed is 1200 / 3 = 400 rpm, and the second stage reduces it by another factor of 3. Each external mesh reverses the rotation, so there are two reversals and the output shaft turns in the same direction as the motor. Because both stages are external pairs, no idler is required. The overall reduction of 9:1 is split into two 3:1 stages, a comfortable ratio per stage for spur gearing.

Answer: 133.3 rpm

(d)

Power at the output shaft is the motor power multiplied by the efficiency: Pout = 7500 × 0.95 = 7125 W. The output angular velocity is ω4 = 2π N4 / 60 = 2π × 133.3 / 60 = 13.963 rad/s. The output torque is T4 = Pout / ω4 = 7125 / 13.963 = 510 N·m. As a check, the motor torque is 7500 / (2π × 1200 / 60) = 59.7 N·m, and multiplying by the speed ratio of 9 gives 537 N·m, which becomes 510 N·m after the 0.95 efficiency is applied. The torque has risen by almost the same factor as the speed has fallen, so power is conserved apart from the losses. The head shaft and its key must be sized for at least this torque, plus a service factor.

Answer: 510 N·m

Problem 2 [A2-007] Planetary gear trains

A winch drive uses a single simple planetary gear set with a sun gear of 24 teeth, three identical planet gears of 18 teeth each and an internal ring gear of 60 teeth, all of the same module. In normal hoisting the ring gear is held stationary by a brake, the sun gear is the input from the electric motor and the planet carrier is the output to the drum. The motor turns the sun at 1800 rpm counter-clockwise (positive) and applies 15 N·m. The set is 97 percent efficient. For a second duty, the drum brake is applied to hold the carrier stationary, the ring gear is released, and the sun again turns at 1800 rpm. Use the tabular or relative-velocity method, and take counter-clockwise rotation as positive. Planet speeds are absolute speeds of a planet about its own axis.

  1. (a) Find the speed of the carrier (drum shaft) for the normal duty with the ring held. [5]
  2. (b) Find the absolute speed of a planet gear about its own axis in the normal duty. [5]
  3. (c) Find the output torque on the carrier in the normal duty, allowing for the stated efficiency. [5]
  4. (d) For the second duty, with the carrier held and the ring free, find the ring gear speed (positive counter-clockwise). [5]
(a)

Write the basic relation for the gears, using the carrier as reference: (ωr - ωc) / (ωs - ωc) = -Ns / Nr, with Ns = 24 and Nr = 60. The negative sign appears because the sun is an external gear and the ring is internal, giving the planets a reversal between them. With the ring fixed (ωr = 0): -ωc / (ωs - ωc) = -24/60 = -0.4. Rearranging, ωc = 0.4 (ωs - ωc), so ωc (1.4) = 0.4 ωs, giving ωc = ωs × 0.4 / 1.4 = ωs / 3.5. This agrees with the standard result ωc = ωs / (1 + Nr/Ns) = 1800 / 3.5 = 514.3 rpm. The carrier rotates in the same sense as the sun, counter-clockwise. The reduction ratio of 3.5:1 is high for a single stage because the ring, not the carrier, is the fixed member.

Answer: 514.3 rpm

(b)

The planet meshes with the sun, an external pair, so relative to the carrier the planet turns in the opposite direction to the sun: (ωp - ωc) / (ωs - ωc) = -Ns / Np = -24/18 = -1.3333. First the sun speed relative to the carrier: ωs - ωc = 1800 - 514.3 = 1285.7 rpm. Then the planet speed relative to the carrier is -1.3333 × 1285.7 = -1714.3 rpm. The absolute spin of the planet is ωp = ωc + (-1714.3) = 514.3 - 1714.3 = -1200 rpm. The negative sign means the planet spins clockwise, opposite to the sun, as it must when meshing externally with it. The planet also orbits with the carrier at 514.3 rpm. A quick check from the ring mesh: relative to the carrier the ring turns at -514.3 rpm, and the internal mesh keeps the planet turning in the same sense as the ring.

Answer: -1200 rpm

(c)

With three members attached to the outside world (sun input, carrier output, ring held by the brake), the ring brake supplies the reaction torque. The energy balance is Pout = η Pin, with Pin = Tin ωs and Pout = Tout ωc. Then Tout = η Tin ωs / ωc = η Tin × ratio. Substituting: ωs / ωc = 3.5, Tin = 15 N·m and η = 0.97 gives Tout = 0.97 × 15 × 3.5 = 50.9 N·m. The ideal torque (η = 1) would be 52.5 N·m, so 1.6 N·m is lost to gear and bearing friction. The ring brake carries a reaction of Tout - Tin = 35.9 N·m in the sense that balances the torques on the whole assembly (sum of external torques on the set is zero). The brake and its connection to the housing must be designed for this reaction.

Answer: 50.9 N·m

(d)

With the carrier stationary (ωc = 0) the set behaves as a fixed-axis train, and the planets act as idlers between the sun and the ring. The tooth-count relation (ωr - ωc) / (ωs - ωc) = -Ns / Nr becomes ωr / ωs = -Ns / Nr = -24/60 = -0.4. Hence ωr = -0.4 × 1800 = -720 rpm. The minus sign means the ring turns clockwise, opposite to the sun. The sign is physically correct: the sun drives the planets in the opposite direction, and an internal ring meshing with the same planets turns in the same sense as the planets, which is opposite to the sun. The planet axle speeds relative to the housing are zero. The magnitude, 720 rpm, is much higher than the carrier speed in normal duty, because the speed ratio is now Ns/Nr instead of 1/(1 + Nr/Ns).

Answer: -720 rpm

Problem 3 [A2-008] Static force analysis of a mechanism

A four-bar linkage actuates a hinged access hatch. The ground pivots O2 and O4 are 0.300 m apart on a horizontal line, with O4 on the right. The input crank O2A is 0.100 m long and the output rocker O4B is 0.220 m long, joined by a coupler AB of 0.280 m. The crank is at 80° from the positive x-axis, with B above the ground line. A resisting torque of 120 N·m acts on the rocker about O4, from the hatch weight and seals. Treat the linkage as quasi-static: neglect the weights and inertias of the links, and neglect friction in the pins. The coupler carries load only at its two end pins. Use the two-force-member idea to find the driving torque on the crank, and a power balance to check the result against the velocity ratio.

  1. (a) Find the force carried by the coupler AB. [5]
  2. (b) Find the driving torque required on the crank O2A. [4]
  3. (c) Use a power balance to find the angular velocity ratio ω4/ω2 for this position. [4]
  4. (d) Find the input power needed if the crank turns at 15 rad/s. [3]
  5. (e) Find the transmission angle at B (the acute angle between the coupler and the rocker). [4]
(a)

Because the coupler has pin loads only at A and B and no friction, it is a two-force member: the force it transmits acts along the line AB. The geometry is fixed first. A = (0.0174, 0.0985) m, and the intersection of the 0.280 m circle about A with the 0.220 m circle about O4 (upper solution) gives B = (0.2706, 0.2180) m. The unit vector along AB is (0.9043, 0.4269). The moment of the coupler force about O4 balances the 120 N·m load on the rocker, so F × d4 = 120, where d4 is the perpendicular distance from O4 to the line AB. Evaluating d4 = |(B - O4) × u| = 0.2097 m, the force is F = 120 / 0.2097 = 572 N. The force is compressive or tensile depending on the sense of the load; its magnitude governs the buckling check for the coupler.

Answer: 572 N

(b)

The crank has the coupler force at A and a reaction at O2, plus the input torque. The coupler pushes on A along the line AB with magnitude F = 572 N. Taking moments about O2, the torque needed is T2 = F × d2, where d2 is the perpendicular distance from O2 to the line of action AB. Evaluating d2 = |A × u| = 0.0816 m. Therefore T2 = 572 × 0.0816 = 46.7 N·m. Since the load torque is 120 N·m and the driving torque is only 46.7 N·m, the linkage gives a torque amplification of 2.57, which is possible because the output rocker is turning more slowly than the crank, as the next part shows. The pin reaction at O2 has the same magnitude as F because the crank is a two-force member apart from the input torque, with no other external force.

Answer: 46.7 N·m

(c)

With no friction and no storage of energy in the massless links, the power delivered to the load equals the power supplied: T2 ω2 = T4 ω4 in magnitude. Rearranging, ω4 / ω2 = T2 / T4 = 46.7 / 120 = 0.389. This is also what the kinematics give: the ratio of the perpendicular distances d2 / d4 = 0.0816 / 0.2097 = 0.389, since both ends of the coupler move with the same velocity component along AB. The velocity component of A along AB is ω2 d2 and that of B along AB is ω4 d4, and those are equal for a rigid link. The two routes give the same ratio, so the force analysis and the velocity analysis are consistent. The rocker moves at less than half the crank speed in this position, which is why it can lift a heavy hatch.

Answer: 0.389

(d)

Input power is the torque times the angular velocity: P = T2 ω2. Substituting T2 = 46.7 N·m and ω2 = 15 rad/s gives P = 46.7 × 15 = 701 W. The output power is the load torque times the rocker speed, T4 ω4 = 120 × (0.389 × 15) = 701 W, which is the same, confirming the balance. In a real linkage friction in the four pins would raise the input power, so a motor chosen for this duty needs a margin. Because the geometry changes with crank angle, the torque ratio is only valid at 80° and the designer would repeat the calculation through the hatch travel to find the peak torque. The result here, about 0.70 kW, is modest for a hatch actuator.

Answer: 701 W

(e)

The transmission angle measures how efficiently the coupler force is turned into rocker torque. It is the acute angle between the line AB and the line BO4. Unit vectors from B are towards A: (-0.9043, -0.4269) and towards O4: (0.1338, -0.9910). The dot product is 0.3021, so the angle between them is cos⁻¹(0.3021) = 72.4°. The acute transmission angle is 72.4°. A value near 90° is ideal, because the whole coupler force acts tangentially on the rocker. Since the tangential component is F sin μ, the moment on the rocker is F × 0.220 × sin μ = 120.0 N·m, which equals the 120 N·m load within rounding. This confirms the geometry and the force found in part (a). Values below about 40° are normally avoided.

Answer: 72.4 °

Problem 4 [A2-009] Dynamic force analysis of a slider-crank

A single-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine has a bore of 90 mm, a crank radius of 50 mm and a connecting rod of 170 mm between centres. The reciprocating parts (piston, rings and gudgeon pin, plus the share of the rod mass assigned to the piston end) have a combined mass of 0.55 kg. The engine runs at a constant 3000 rpm. During the power stroke, when the crank is 30° past top dead centre, the cylinder gauge pressure is 2.4 MPa. Atmospheric pressure acts on the underside of the piston and can be ignored here. Take the connecting rod as massless apart from the lumped reciprocating mass, and neglect friction. The piston acceleration is a = -r ω² (cos θ + cos 2θ / n) towards the crank, with n = l / r. Analyse the engine at θ = 30°.

  1. (a) Calculate the gas force on the piston. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the inertia force of the reciprocating mass at this crank angle. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the crank-shaft torque produced by the net piston force at this angle. [7]
  4. (d) Calculate the side thrust of the piston on the cylinder wall. [5]
(a)

The gas force is the product of the gauge pressure and the piston crown area. The piston area is A = π d² / 4 with d = 0.090 m, so A = π × 0.090² / 4 = 0.006362 m². The pressure is 2.4 MPa = 2.4 × 10⁶ N/m². Hence Fg = p A = 2.4 × 10⁶ × 0.006362 = 15268 N. The force acts along the cylinder axis, pushing the piston towards the crankshaft in the power stroke. This is the force that the combustion process puts into the mechanism. Before it reaches the crank, part of it is used up to accelerate the piston and the rest of the reciprocating mass, which is considered in the next part. The value is about 1.6 tonnes-force, a typical order for a 0.64 litre single-cylinder engine at high cylinder pressure.

Answer: 15268 N

(b)

The crank angular velocity is ω = 3000 × 2π / 60 = 314.16 rad/s, so ω² = 98696 rad²/s². The rod-to-crank ratio is n = l / r = 0.170 / 0.050 = 3.4. The piston acceleration magnitude towards the crank is a = r ω² (cos θ + cos 2θ / n). Compute r ω² = 0.050 × 98696 = 4934.8 m/s². The bracket is cos 30° + cos 60° / 3.4 = 0.8660 + 0.1471 = 1.0131. So a = 4934.8 × 1.0131 = 4999.4 m/s², directed towards the crank. The inertia force needed to accelerate the mass is Fi = m a = 0.55 × 4999.4 = 2750 N. The piston is accelerating towards the crank at this angle, so this force is supplied by part of the gas force, and the force transmitted to the connecting rod is reduced by Fi. The acceleration of 510 g shows why high-speed engines use light pistons.

Answer: 2750 N

(c)

The net force transmitted along the cylinder axis to the connecting-rod pin is Ft = Fg - Fi = 15268 - 2750 = 12518 N. The rod angle comes from the geometry, sin φ = r sin θ / l = 0.050 × sin 30° / 0.170 = 0.1471, so φ = 8.46°. The force along the rod is Ft / cos φ = 12518 / 0.9891 = 12656 N. The perpendicular distance from the crank-shaft centre to the line of the rod is r sin (θ + φ) = 0.050 × sin (30.0° + 8.46°) = 0.050 × 0.6219 = 0.03110 m. The torque on the crank-shaft is T = Frod × arm = 12656 × 0.03110 = 394 N·m. This is the shaft torque at this instant; it is not the mean engine torque, which is much smaller because the torque is large only during the power stroke. The same value follows from T = Ft r sin(θ + φ) / cos φ.

Answer: 394 N·m

(d)

The connecting rod inclines at φ to the cylinder axis, so the force it exerts on the piston has a component perpendicular to the cylinder wall. This is reacted by the cylinder, because the piston can only move along the axis. The wall reaction is Fn = Ft tan φ. Using Ft = 12518 N and tan φ = 0.1487 (from sin φ = 0.1471), Fn = 12518 × 0.1487 = 1861 N. This side thrust presses the piston skirt against the thrust face of the cylinder, in the direction determined by the sense of crank rotation, and it grows with the rod angle and the net force. It is the reason for piston skirt lubrication and wear. Fn is 14.9 percent of the net piston force, so friction at the piston, with a typical coefficient of 0.05, would remove only about 93 N, justifying the frictionless assumption.

Answer: 1861 N

Problem 5 [A2-010] Flywheel sizing

A punch press in a metal-stamping shop is driven by a constant-torque electric motor through a flywheel on the crankshaft. Each punching stroke needs 5.0 kJ of work and the full press cycle takes 2.5 s, of which the work is taken during the 0.5 s of the stroke. Between strokes the motor, which gives constant power equal to the average demand, is the only energy source and the load is zero. The mean crankshaft speed is 180 rpm and the coefficient of speed fluctuation must not exceed 0.05. Assume the motor delivers the same power throughout the cycle, ignore friction, and treat all of the required inertia as concentrated in the flywheel. The flywheel is to be a solid steel disc of density 7850 kg/m³ and thickness 120 mm. Use Cs = (ωmax - ωmin) / ωmean.

  1. (a) Calculate the average power the motor must supply. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the maximum energy fluctuation per cycle that the flywheel must absorb and return. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the mass moment of inertia required for the flywheel. [5]
  4. (d) Find the diameter of a solid steel disc of 120 mm thickness that gives this inertia. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate the minimum shaft speed during the cycle. [3]
(a)

Over one complete cycle the energy supplied by the motor must equal the energy used by the punching stroke, otherwise the mean speed would drift. The work per cycle is 5.0 kJ and the cycle time is 2.5 s. Average power is energy divided by time: Pavg = E / T = 5000 / 2.5 = 2000 W, which is 2.00 kW. The motor can therefore be selected for about 2 kW plus a margin, instead of the much larger power that would be needed to meet the peak demand during the stroke: the stroke alone would demand 5000 / 0.5 = 10000 W, which is five times the average. This reduction of the motor size, by storing energy in the flywheel between strokes, is the main reason a flywheel is fitted to a punch press. The motor torque is assumed constant at the mean speed.

Answer: 2.00 kW

(b)

During the 0.5 s stroke the press takes 5000 J while the motor supplies only its constant average power for that time, Pavg × tp = 2000 × 0.5 = 1000 J. The remainder must come from the kinetic energy of the flywheel: ΔE = E - Pavg tp = 5000 - 1000 = 4000 J. During the 2.0 s between strokes the motor supplies 2000 × 2.0 = 4000 J, which exactly restores the 4000 J given up by the flywheel, so the energy balance over the cycle closes. The speed therefore falls steadily during the stroke and rises again after it, with the largest speed variation equal to the ΔE of 4000 J. The fluctuation of energy is the quantity that fixes the required flywheel inertia in the next part, because it is the largest change in kinetic energy between ωmax and ωmin.

Answer: 4000 J

(c)

The kinetic energy of the flywheel is ½ I ω². Between the maximum and the minimum speed the change is ΔE = ½ I (ωmax² - ωmin²) = I ωmean² Cs, using the usual approximation ωmean = (ωmax + ωmin)/2 and (ωmax - ωmin) = Cs ωmean. The mean angular velocity is ωmean = 180 × 2π / 60 = 18.850 rad/s, so ωmean² = 355.31 rad²/s². Rearranging, I = ΔE / (Cs ωmean²) = 4000 / (0.05 × 355.31) = 4000 / 17.765 = 225.2 kg·m². This is the total inertia required, which in this design is taken as that of the flywheel alone. Increasing Cs to 0.10 would halve the inertia, which is why a high allowable fluctuation, common on presses, gives a lighter flywheel. The result is large because the press runs slowly, and inertia varies inversely with the square of the speed.

Answer: 225.2 kg·m²

(d)

For a solid disc of radius r, thickness t and density ρ, the mass is m = ρ π r² t and the inertia about its axis is I = ½ m r² = ½ ρ π t r⁴. Solving for the radius: r⁴ = 2 I / (π ρ t). Substituting I = 225.2 kg·m², ρ = 7850 kg/m³ and t = 0.120 m: π ρ t = π × 7850 × 0.120 = 2959.4 kg/m². Then r⁴ = 2 × 225.2 / 2959.4 = 0.15217 m⁴. Taking the fourth root, r = 0.6246 m, so the diameter is D = 2r = 1.249 m. The mass of the disc is m = ρ π r² t = 1154 kg. The rim speed at mean speed is ω r = 18.850 × 0.625 = 11.8 m/s, which is far below the 30 to 40 m/s rim speed limit of cast iron, so the stress in the disc is not a concern.

Answer: 1.25 m

(e)

The coefficient of fluctuation is defined as Cs = (ωmax - ωmin) / ωmean, with ωmean taken as the arithmetic mean of the two extremes. Therefore ωmax = ωmean (1 + Cs/2) and ωmin = ωmean (1 - Cs/2). With ωmean = 180 rpm and Cs = 0.05: ωmax = 180 × (1 + 0.025) = 184.5 rpm and ωmin = 180 × (1 - 0.025) = 175.5 rpm. The speed range is 9.0 rpm, which is 5 percent of the mean speed, as specified. The minimum occurs at the end of the stroke, when the flywheel has given up its energy, and the maximum occurs just before the stroke begins. The operator would notice the press slowing by about 9 rpm during each punch. If the punch needs more consistent speed, the designer should reduce Cs, which increases the flywheel inertia in proportion.

Answer: 175.5 rpm

A2 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A2-011] Balancing of rotating masses

A cutting-tool spindle carries three eccentric attachments that lie in the same transverse plane. Attachment 1 has mass 4.0 kg at radius 150 mm and angle 0°. Attachment 2 has mass 3.0 kg at radius 200 mm and angle 90°. Attachment 3 has mass 5.0 kg at radius 120 mm and angle 210°. All angles are measured counter-clockwise from the same reference line on the shaft. The spindle turns at 3000 rev/min. A single balancing mass is to be fixed in the same plane at a radius of 100 mm. Treat the spindle as rigid and neglect the mass of the shaft itself.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the resultant unbalanced mass-radius product m·r of the three attachments. [5]
  2. (b) Find the balancing mass required at a radius of 100 mm. [5]
  3. (c) Find the angular position of the balancing mass, measured counter-clockwise from the reference line, on a 0 to 360° scale. [5]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the rotating force transmitted to the bearings at 3000 rev/min if the spindle were run unbalanced. [5]
(a)

For a rotating system in one plane the centrifugal forces are proportional to m·r, so balance requires the vector sum of m·r to be zero. Resolve along the reference line (x) and perpendicular (y). Σmr cosθ = 4.0(0.15)cos0° + 3.0(0.20)cos90° + 5.0(0.12)cos210° = 0.0804 kg·m. Σmr sinθ = 4.0(0.15)sin0° + 3.0(0.20)sin90° + 5.0(0.12)sin210° = 0.3000 kg·m. The resultant is R = √(Σx² + Σy²) = √(0.0804² + 0.3000²) = 0.3106 kg·m. This is the unbalanced m·r the balancing mass must cancel. Check the signs carefully: the third mass lies in the third quadrant, so it contributes negative x and negative y.

Answer: 0.3106 kg·m

(b)

The balancing mass must produce an m·r equal in magnitude to the resultant and opposite in direction. With the balancing radius r_b = 0.100 m, m_b r_b = R, so m_b = R / r_b = 0.3106 / 0.100 = 3.106 kg. A larger radius would reduce the mass needed, so the choice of 100 mm is a packaging constraint rather than a free design variable. The mass is reasonable compared with the 12 kg total of the attachments. State that the result assumes all four masses are in one plane, so only static (force) balance is needed and no couple arises.

Answer: 3.106 kg

(c)

The balancing mass sits opposite to the resultant vector. The resultant of the unbalanced masses has components (0.0804, 0.3000) kg·m. The balancing vector is therefore (−Σx, −Σy) = (-0.0804, -0.3000) kg·m. Its angle is θ_b = atan2(−Σy, −Σx) = atan2(-0.3000, -0.0804) = 255.00° after adding 360° where needed to put the angle on a 0 to 360° scale. Use atan2 or check the quadrant by hand, because a plain arctangent of the ratio would give an answer 180° out. A quick check: the balancing vector has a negative x component and a positive y component only if the resultant has the opposite signs.

Answer: 255 °

(d)

Run unbalanced, the net centrifugal force is F = (Σmr) ω², with ω = 3000 × 2π / 60 = 314.16 rad/s. Then F = 0.3106 × 314.16² = 30653 N. This force rotates with the shaft, so each bearing sees a once-per-revolution load whose magnitude is a share of F depending on the position of the plane. Because F varies with ω², halving the speed would cut it to one quarter, which is why balancing matters most for high-speed spindles. With the balancing mass fitted the net force is zero and only the weight and cutting loads remain.

Answer: 30650 N

Problem 2 [A2-012] Gyroscopic effects

A marine steam turbine rotor of mass 4500 kg and radius of gyration 0.45 m turns at 3000 rev/min in a ship. The bearings are 2.4 m apart. The ship pitches in simple harmonic motion about a transverse axis with an amplitude of 6° and a period of 20 s. The rotor axis lies along the ship's length, so pitching tilts the spin axis and produces a gyroscopic effect. Take the maximum pitching angular velocity as the amplitude of the angular displacement multiplied by 2π/T. Neglect the weight of the rotor and any change in speed of the rotor.

  1. (a) Find the polar moment of inertia of the rotor and its spin speed in rad/s. Give the spin speed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum angular velocity of pitching. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum gyroscopic couple acting on the rotor. [6]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the equal and opposite reaction forces at the two bearings caused by this couple. [6]
(a)

The moment of inertia of the rotor about its spin axis is I = m k² = 4500 × 0.45² = 911.3 kg·m². The spin speed is ω = 2πN / 60 = 2π × 3000 / 60 = 314.16 rad/s. Both quantities enter the gyroscopic couple C = I ω ω_p, where ω_p is the precession rate. Because the rotor is treated as a rigid body of constant speed, no angular acceleration of the spin needs to be considered. Note that the spin is a large number, so the couple will be large even for a modest pitching rate. Keep consistent SI units (kg, m, rad/s) throughout.

Answer: 314.2 rad/s

(b)

Pitching is simple harmonic, θ = θ_max sin(2πt / T), so the angular velocity is ω_p = θ_max (2π / T) cos(2πt / T) with maximum ω_p,max = θ_max × 2π / T. The amplitude is 6° = 0.1047 rad and T = 20 s, so ω_p,max = 0.1047 × 2π / 20 = 0.03290 rad/s. This is the largest rate at which the spin axis is turned, occurring as the ship passes through its mean pitch attitude. It is far smaller than the spin speed, which is why the gyroscopic equation C = Iωω_p is valid for the steady-precession approximation used here.

Answer: 0.0329 rad/s

(c)

The gyroscopic couple is the rate of change of angular momentum, C = I ω ω_p. Substituting the maximum precession rate gives C_max = 911.3 × 314.16 × 0.03290 = 9418 N·m = 9.418 kN·m. The couple acts about an axis perpendicular to both the spin axis and the axis of pitching, which here is the vertical axis. Its sense reverses when the bow rises and when it falls, so the couple is alternating at the pitching period. The result is the peak value; the bearings carry an alternating load between plus and minus this value.

Answer: 9.42 kN·m

(d)

The bearings resist the gyroscopic couple by a pair of equal and opposite forces separated by the bearing span L = 2.4 m. Taking moments, F L = C, so F = C / L = 9418 / 2.4 = 3924 N = 3.924 kN. One bearing is pushed up and the other down, and the directions swap each half period of pitching. These forces are in addition to the static load of the rotor weight, which is neglected in this question. A designer would add this alternating load to the static bearing reaction when sizing the bearings and housing.

Answer: 3.92 kN

Problem 3 [A2-013] Single degree of freedom free vibration

A rotary dryer drive of mass 150 kg is mounted at the midspan of a simply supported steel beam. The beam is 2.4 m long, with Young's modulus 200 GPa and second moment of area 8.5×10⁻⁶ m⁴. The mass of the beam is small compared with that of the drive and is neglected, so the system is a single degree of freedom mass on a spring with the beam acting as the spring. The drive is pulled down 6 mm at midspan and released from rest. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and assume no damping.

  1. (a) Find the stiffness of the beam at midspan. [5]
  2. (b) Find the natural frequency in rad/s. [5]
  3. (c) Find the natural frequency in hertz. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum speed of the drive during the free vibration that follows release. [6]
(a)

For a simply supported beam with a central point load, the midspan deflection is δ = W L³ / (48 E I), so the equivalent spring stiffness is k = W / δ = 48 E I / L³. Substituting, k = 48 × 200×10⁹ × 8.5×10⁻⁶ / 2.4³ = 5902778 N/m = 5902.8 kN/m. The static deflection under the weight of the drive follows from k as δ_st = m g / k = 0.249 mm, which is small compared with the 6 mm release displacement and confirms that the beam stays within the linear range. The beam mass is neglected as instructed; including a third of its mass would lower the frequency slightly.

Answer: 5903 kN/m

(b)

The equation of motion for an undamped single degree of freedom system is m ẍ + k x = 0, giving oscillation at ω_n = √(k / m). With k = 5902778 N/m and m = 150 kg, ω_n = √(5902778 / 150) = 198.37 rad/s. Use the stiffness from part (a) in N/m, not kN/m, otherwise the result is out by √1000. An equivalent route is ω_n = √(g / δ_st) with the static deflection in metres, which gives the same answer and offers a useful check on the arithmetic.

Answer: 198.4 rad/s

(c)

The cyclic frequency is f_n = ω_n / (2π) = 198.37 / (2π) = 31.57 Hz. The period of oscillation is T = 1 / f_n = 0.0317 s. Compare this with the rotor speed of the drive in service: if the dryer is driven at a shaft speed near 1894 rev/min, the beam would be excited near resonance, so this number is the one that a designer checks against operating speed. Note the distinction between rad/s and hertz, since the equation of motion uses angular frequency while specifications are often quoted in hertz.

Answer: 31.57 Hz

(d)

The free response from an initial displacement x₀ and zero initial velocity is x(t) = x₀ cos(ω_n t). The velocity is ẋ = −x₀ ω_n sin(ω_n t), whose maximum magnitude is x₀ ω_n. With x₀ = 0.006 m, v_max = 0.006 × 198.37 = 1.190 m/s. This occurs each time the mass passes through the static equilibrium position. Since there is no damping the amplitude stays constant, so this peak speed repeats every half cycle. Energy check: the elastic energy ½ k x₀² equals the kinetic energy ½ m v_max², which can be used to confirm the answer.

Answer: 1.19 m/s

Problem 4 [A2-014] Damped free vibration and logarithmic decrement

A vibration test is run on a hydraulic press frame idealised as a single degree of freedom system of effective mass 250 kg and effective stiffness 180 kN/m. The frame is struck and its free decay is recorded with an accelerometer and integrated to give displacement. The first peak amplitude is 12.0 mm and the peak after five complete cycles is 2.1 mm. The damping is viscous and linear. Treat the damping ratio as less than 0.2, but do not use the small-damping approximation: use the exact relationship between logarithmic decrement and damping ratio.

  1. (a) Find the logarithmic decrement of the system. [5]
  2. (b) Find the damping ratio using the exact relationship. [5]
  3. (c) Find the viscous damping coefficient of the frame. [5]
  4. (d) Find the damped natural frequency. [5]
(a)

The logarithmic decrement is the natural logarithm of the ratio of two successive peaks, and for peaks n cycles apart it is δ = (1/n) ln(x₁ / x_(n+1)). The ratio of successive peaks is the same for a linear viscous system, so using five cycles reduces measurement error. Here δ = (1/5) ln(12.0 / 2.1) = (1/5) ln(5.714) = 0.3486. The result is dimensionless. Using the ratio over several cycles rather than one is the standard approach because each individual peak reading carries a reading uncertainty that is shared out over n cycles.

Answer: 0.3486

(b)

The exact relation is δ = 2πζ / √(1 − ζ²). Solving for ζ gives ζ = δ / √(4π² + δ²). Substituting δ = 0.3486, ζ = 0.3486 / √(39.478 + 0.1215) = 0.0554. This is under 0.2, as the question expects. The small-damping approximation ζ ≈ δ / 2π would give 0.0555, which is close here, but the exact form removes the need for a judgement about when the approximation is acceptable. A damping ratio near 0.055 means the system is lightly damped and will oscillate many times before it settles.

Answer: 0.0554

(c)

The critical damping coefficient is c_c = 2√(k m) = 2√(180000 × 250) = 13416 N·s/m. The actual coefficient is c = ζ c_c = 0.0554 × 13416 = 743 N·s/m. Check units: k m has units (N/m)(kg) = N·s²/m² × ... which resolves to (N·s/m)² after the square root, as it should. This damping coefficient would be the value specified for a replacement damper, or compared with the value obtained from the manufacturer for the press mounts. It represents the energy dissipated per cycle through viscous action.

Answer: 743.2 N·s/m

(d)

The undamped natural frequency is ω_n = √(k / m) = √(180000 / 250) = 26.83 rad/s. The damped natural frequency is ω_d = ω_n √(1 − ζ²) = 26.83 × √(1 − 0.0554²) = 26.79 rad/s. The frequency is reduced only slightly by damping because ζ is small; the reduction is 0.15 percent. This is the frequency that the accelerometer trace actually shows between successive peaks, so it is also the frequency from which the period of the recorded decay can be checked, T_d = 2π / ω_d = 0.2345 s.

Answer: 26.79 rad/s

Problem 5 [A2-015] Forced vibration and resonance

A packaging machine of mass 120 kg is mounted on springs of total stiffness 2.0 MN/m, with viscous damping equivalent to a damping ratio of 0.10. A reciprocating feeder applies a vertical harmonic force of amplitude 800 N at a machine speed of 900 rev/min. The machine is constrained to move vertically only. After the transient decays, the motion is a steady harmonic response at the forcing frequency. Use the standard single degree of freedom steady-state results with a force applied directly to the mass.

  1. (a) Find the undamped natural frequency of the machine on its springs. [4]
  2. (b) Find the steady-state displacement amplitude. [6]
  3. (c) Find the phase angle by which the displacement lags the applied force. [4]
  4. (d) Find the amplitude of the force transmitted to the floor through the springs and dampers. [6]
(a)

The natural frequency of the sprung machine is ω_n = √(k / m) = √(2.0×10⁶ / 120) = 129.10 rad/s, which corresponds to 1233 rev/min. The forcing frequency is ω = 2π × 900 / 60 = 94.25 rad/s, so the frequency ratio r = ω / ω_n = 0.7300. The ratio is below 1, so the machine runs below resonance, but not by a large margin. Always compute both ω_n and r because the response in later parts depends on r rather than on ω_n alone.

Answer: 129.1 rad/s

(b)

The steady-state amplitude of a damped system under a force F₀ sin ωt is X = (F₀ / k) / √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²). The static deflection is F₀ / k = 800 / 2.0×10⁶ = 0.4 mm. With r = 0.7300 and ζ = 0.10, (1 − r²) = 0.4670 and 2ζr = 0.1460. The denominator is √(0.2181 + 0.0213) = 0.4893. So X = 0.4 / 0.4893 = 0.8174 mm. The magnification factor over static is 2.044.

Answer: 0.8174 mm

(c)

The phase lag of the displacement behind the force is φ = atan[2ζr / (1 − r²)], taking the angle in the correct quadrant (0 to 180°); for r < 1 it lies between 0 and 90°. Then φ = atan[0.1460 / 0.4670] = 17.36°. At low frequency the displacement is almost in phase with the force, at resonance the lag is 90°, and above resonance it tends to 180°. A value of 17.4° therefore tells us the machine is on the lower, stiffness-controlled side of the resonance curve but approaching it. The lag in time is φ / ω = 3.21 ms.

Answer: 17.36 °

(d)

The force reaching the floor is the sum of the spring force kX and the damper force c ω X, which are 90° apart. Its amplitude is F_T = X √(k² + (c ω)²) = k X √(1 + (2ζr)²), because c ω = 2ζ r k. Substituting, F_T = 2.0×10⁶ × 0.000817 × √(1 + 0.0213) = 1652.2 N. The transmissibility is F_T / F₀ = 2.065, so the springs amplify the force by that factor at this speed, which shows that these mounts are not acting as isolation. Isolation only occurs when r exceeds √2.

Answer: 1652 N

A2 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A2-016] Base excitation and vibration isolation

An avionics instrument package of mass 35 kg is carried on four identical rubber isolators acting in parallel with a total vertical stiffness of 60 kN/m and a damping ratio of 0.12. The rack to which the isolators are bolted vibrates vertically in simple harmonic motion with amplitude 2.0 mm at 40 Hz. The package is constrained to move vertically. Use the standard single degree of freedom model with harmonic base motion, and assume steady-state conditions.

  1. (a) Find the natural frequency of the isolated package in hertz. [4]
  2. (b) Find the frequency ratio at the excitation frequency of 40 Hz. [4]
  3. (c) Find the displacement transmissibility. [6]
  4. (d) Find the absolute displacement amplitude of the instrument package. [6]
(a)

The natural frequency of the package on its isolators is ω_n = √(k / m) = √(60000 / 35) = 41.40 rad/s. Converting to hertz, f_n = ω_n / 2π = 41.40 / 2π = 6.59 Hz. The four isolators act in parallel, so the stiffnesses have already been added to give the 60 kN/m quoted. The static deflection is mg/k = 5.72 mm; the relation f_n ≈ 15.8 / √(δ_st in mm) gives the same frequency and is a quick check commonly used for isolator selection.

Answer: 6.59 Hz

(b)

The excitation angular frequency is ω = 2π f = 2π × 40 = 251.33 rad/s. The frequency ratio is r = ω / ω_n = 251.33 / 41.40 = 6.0701. Because r is greater than √2 = 1.414, the package is in the isolation region, where the response is smaller than the base motion. If r were below √2 the isolators would amplify the motion. The ratio should be worked from the angular frequencies, not from a mix of Hz and rad/s, which is a common slip in this type of question.

Answer: 6.07

(c)

For harmonic base motion the displacement transmissibility is T = X / Y = √[(1 + (2ζr)²) / ((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)]. With ζ = 0.12 and r = 6.0701: 2ζr = 1.4568, so the numerator is 1 + 2.1224 = 3.1224. The denominator is (1 − r²)² + (2ζr)² = 1284.973 + 2.1224 = 1287.096. Hence T = √(3.1224 / 1287.096) = 0.0493. Isolation is effective because T is well below 1.

Answer: 0.04925

(d)

The absolute amplitude of the package is the transmissibility multiplied by the base amplitude: X = T × Y = 0.0493 × 2.0 mm = 0.0985 mm. This is the displacement of the mass relative to a fixed reference, not relative to the rack. The relative displacement across the isolators is larger and is what determines the working stroke of the mounts, so the clearance around the package must allow for it. The result confirms that the isolators cut the 2.0 mm rack motion down to about 99 micrometres at 40 Hz.

Answer: 0.09851 mm

Problem 2 [A2-017] Rotating unbalance

An electric motor with a total mass of 150 kg, including a rotor with a residual unbalance equivalent to 0.40 kg at an eccentric radius of 80 mm, is mounted on a base that behaves as a single degree of freedom system with vertical stiffness 900 kN/m and damping ratio 0.05. The motor runs at 1500 rev/min. The motor is free to move vertically only. Use the standard rotating-unbalance response, in which the exciting force amplitude is m₀ e ω² and the total mass M, including the unbalanced mass, vibrates.

  1. (a) Find the frequency ratio at the running speed of 1500 rev/min. [4]
  2. (b) Find the steady-state vertical amplitude of the motor at the running speed. [6]
  3. (c) Find the amplitude of the force transmitted to the foundation. [5]
  4. (d) Find the amplitude that would occur if the motor ran at resonance with the same damping ratio. [5]
(a)

The undamped natural frequency is ω_n = √(k / M) = √(900000 / 150) = 77.46 rad/s. The running speed gives ω = 2π × 1500 / 60 = 157.08 rad/s. Therefore r = ω / ω_n = 157.08 / 77.46 = 2.0279. The motor runs well above its natural frequency, with r about 2, which is the normal arrangement for machines mounted on soft supports. It must pass through resonance during start-up and run-down, so the amplitude at the critical speed (part d) is also of interest.

Answer: 2.028

(b)

For rotating unbalance the amplitude is X = (m₀ e / M) r² / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]. The unbalance ratio is m₀ e / M = 0.40 × 0.080 / 150 = 0.2133 mm. With r = 2.0279, r² = 4.1123, so (1 − r²)² = 9.6866 and (2ζr)² = 0.0411; the denominator is 3.1189. Then X = 0.2133 × 4.1123 / 3.1189 = 0.2813 mm. Above resonance the amplitude tends to m₀e/M, the mass centre being nearly stationary.

Answer: 0.2813 mm

(c)

The force reaching the foundation is the vector sum of the spring and damper forces: F_T = X √(k² + (c ω)²) = k X √(1 + (2ζr)²). Substituting, F_T = 900000 × 0.0002813 × √(1 + 0.0411) = 258.3 N. For comparison, the exciting force itself is m₀ e ω² = 0.40 × 0.080 × 157.08² = 790 N, so the mounts reduce the transmitted force below the exciting force, as expected for r > √2. A rotating machine that exceeded this force would risk fatigue of the foundation bolts.

Answer: 258.3 N

(d)

At resonance r = 1, and the amplitude expression reduces to X = (m₀ e / M) / (2ζ). Thus X_res = 0.2133 mm / (2 × 0.05) = 2.133 mm. This is about 8 times larger than the amplitude at the running speed, which shows why the speed must pass through the critical speed quickly during start-up, or why extra damping is provided if the machine has to dwell near it. The resonance condition is at ω = ω_n = 77.5 rad/s, or 740 rev/min.

Answer: 2.133 mm

Problem 3 [A2-018] Two degree of freedom systems and mode shapes

A press-and-bed assembly is modelled as two lumped masses in a vertical line. Mass m₁ = 800 kg (the bed) is connected to the floor by a spring of stiffness k₁ = 3.0 MN/m. Mass m₂ = 500 kg (the press head) is connected to m₁ by a spring of stiffness k₂ = 2.0 MN/m. Only vertical motion is considered, damping is neglected, and x₁ and x₂ are displacements of the masses measured from equilibrium. The characteristic equation for the squared natural frequencies is m₁m₂ω⁴ − [(k₁+k₂)m₂ + k₂m₁]ω² + k₁k₂ = 0.

  1. (a) Find the lower natural frequency. [5]
  2. (b) Find the higher natural frequency. [5]
  3. (c) Find the amplitude ratio X₂/X₁ in the first mode. [5]
  4. (d) Find the amplitude ratio X₂/X₁ in the second mode. [5]
(a)

Substitute the data into the given quartic. With λ = ω², a = m₁m₂ = 4 × 10⁵, b = −[(k₁+k₂)m₂ + k₂m₁] = -4.1 × 10⁹, c = k₁k₂ = 6 × 10¹². The discriminant is b² − 4ac = 7.21 × 10¹⁸, whose square root is 2.685 × 10⁹. The smaller root is λ₁ = (−b − √disc) / 2a = 1768.57 rad²/s². Then ω₁ = √λ₁ = 42.05 rad/s, or 6.69 Hz. The two roots must both be positive for a stable system with positive stiffnesses, which provides a check on the arithmetic.

Answer: 42.05 rad/s

(b)

The larger root of the same quadratic in λ = ω² is λ₂ = (−b + √disc) / 2a = (4.1 × 10⁹ + 2.685 × 10⁹) / 8 × 10⁵ = 8481.43 rad²/s². Hence ω₂ = √λ₂ = 92.09 rad/s, or 14.66 Hz. The sum of the two roots λ₁ + λ₂ should equal −b/a = 10250.00, and their product should equal c/a = 15000000.00; both identities hold, so the roots are consistent. Note that the frequencies bracket the uncoupled values √(k₁/m₁) = 61.24 rad/s and √(k₂/m₂) = 63.25 rad/s in the usual way.

Answer: 92.09 rad/s

(c)

The second equation of motion is m₂ẍ₂ + k₂(x₂ − x₁) = 0. For harmonic motion at ω this gives (k₂ − m₂ω²) X₂ = k₂ X₁, so X₂ / X₁ = k₂ / (k₂ − m₂ω²). For the first mode, ω² = 1768.57: k₂ − m₂ω² = 2 × 10⁶ − 500 × 1768.57 = 1.116 × 10⁶ N/m. Then X₂ / X₁ = 2 × 10⁶ / 1.116 × 10⁶ = 1.7926. The ratio is positive and greater than 1, so the masses move in phase, with the press head moving more than the bed.

Answer: 1.793

(d)

Use the same expression with the higher root ω² = 8481.43. Then k₂ − m₂ω² = 2 × 10⁶ − 500 × 8481.43 = -2.241 × 10⁶ N/m, and X₂ / X₁ = 2 × 10⁶ / -2.241 × 10⁶ = -0.8926. The ratio is negative, so in the second mode the masses move in opposite directions (out of phase), and there is a node between them. As a check, the first equation of motion gives the same ratio: X₂ / X₁ = (k₁ + k₂ − m₁ω²) / k₂ = (5 × 10⁶ − 800 × 8481.43) / 2 × 10⁶ = -0.8926.

Answer: -0.8926

Problem 4 [A2-019] Vibration absorbers

A centrifugal blower of mass 500 kg sits on springs of total stiffness 4.2 MN/m and runs at a constant 900 rev/min. A harmonic force of amplitude 1500 N at the running speed excites the blower vertically, and the response is severe. A tuned vibration absorber of mass 40 kg is to be fitted to the blower housing. The absorber spring is to be chosen so that the absorber natural frequency equals the running speed, which eliminates the steady motion of the blower. Neglect damping throughout.

  1. (a) Find the stiffness of the absorber spring required. [4]
  2. (b) With the absorber fitted, find the lower natural frequency of the combined system. [6]
  3. (c) With the absorber fitted, find the higher natural frequency of the combined system. [6]
  4. (d) Find the amplitude of motion of the absorber mass at the running speed. [4]
(a)

The absorber is tuned when its natural frequency equals the excitation frequency, √(k_a / m_a) = ω. The running speed gives ω = 2π × 900 / 60 = 94.25 rad/s. Therefore k_a = m_a ω² = 40 × 94.25² = 355306 N/m = 0.355 MN/m. The original natural frequency of the blower is √(4.2×10⁶ / 500) = 91.65 rad/s, which is close to the running speed, explaining the severe response. Tuning the absorber to the excitation, not to the blower's own natural frequency, is the key design point for a fixed-speed machine.

Answer: 0.3553 MN/m

(b)

With the absorber fitted, the two-degree-of-freedom system has the characteristic equation m m_a ω⁴ − [(k + k_a) m_a + k_a m] ω² + k k_a = 0. Coefficients: A = m m_a = 2 × 10⁴, B = −[(k + k_a) m_a + k_a m] = -3.599 × 10⁸, C = k k_a = 1.492 × 10¹². The discriminant root is 1.006 × 10⁸. The smaller root is ω² = (−B − √disc) / 2A = 6481.65, giving ω₁ = 80.51 rad/s, which is below the running speed (94.25 rad/s). The mass ratio μ = m_a / m = 0.080 controls how far the new frequencies are separated from the old one.

Answer: 80.51 rad/s

(c)

The larger root of the same equation is ω² = (−B + √disc) / 2A = 11511.60, so ω₂ = 107.29 rad/s. The running speed of 94.25 rad/s lies between ω₁ = 80.51 and ω₂ = 107.29 rad/s, so the machine is no longer close to a resonance. The two new frequencies straddle the running speed. The drawback of an undamped absorber is that the machine must pass through one of these resonances if started from rest, and that the absorber is only effective in a narrow band around the tuned frequency, since a change of speed brings the system close to one of these frequencies.

Answer: 107.3 rad/s

(d)

At the tuned frequency the blower mass has zero steady motion and the absorber spring force balances the exciting force: k_a x_a = −F₀. The absorber amplitude is therefore |x_a| = F₀ / k_a = 1500 / 355306 = 4.222 mm, and the motion is 180° out of phase with the force. The absorber spring force amplitude is exactly F₀ = 1500 N, which should be checked against the strength of the spring and the fatigue life of its attachment. The stroke is small, so mounting space is not a constraint, but the spring must carry 1500 N cyclically without yielding.

Answer: 4.222 mm

Problem 5 [A2-020] Torsional vibration of shafts

A steel solid shaft of diameter 40 mm and length 0.90 m connects two rotors. Rotor 1 is a motor armature with polar mass moment of inertia 2.4 kg·m², and rotor 2 is a pump impeller with polar mass moment of inertia 1.2 kg·m². The shear modulus of the steel is 79 GPa. The shaft mass is negligible compared with the rotors, the ends of the shaft are rigidly attached to the rotors, and the assembly is free to rotate in space, such as on low-friction bearings, so that it can twist in free torsional vibration.

  1. (a) Find the torsional stiffness of the shaft. [5]
  2. (b) Find the natural frequency of torsional vibration of the two-rotor system. [5]
  3. (c) Find the distance of the vibration node from rotor 1. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum torque in the shaft if the amplitude of rotor 1 is 0.020 rad. [6]
(a)

The polar second moment of area of the solid shaft is J = πd⁴ / 32 = π × 0.040⁴ / 32 = 2.5133 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴. The torsional stiffness of a shaft is k_t = G J / L = 79×10⁹ × 2.5133 × 10⁻⁷ / 0.90 = 22061 N·m/rad = 22.06 kN·m/rad. This is the torque needed per radian of relative twist between the two ends. Use metres for the diameter, otherwise J is wrong by a factor of 10¹². The shaft mass is neglected, so the whole shaft acts as a single massless torsional spring joining the two inertias.

Answer: 22.06 kN·m/rad

(b)

For two rotors on one shaft free to rotate, the equations are J₁θ̈₁ + k_t(θ₁ − θ₂) = 0 and J₂θ̈₂ − k_t(θ₁ − θ₂) = 0. One root is zero (rigid-body rotation) and the other gives ω_n² = k_t (J₁ + J₂) / (J₁ J₂). Substituting, ω_n² = 22061 × (2.4 + 1.2) / (2.4 × 1.2) = 27576.2, so ω_n = 166.1 rad/s, or 26.4 Hz. This is the frequency at which the twist oscillates. Compare it with the running speed and the torque pulsation frequencies of the motor to check for resonance risk.

Answer: 166.1 rad/s

(c)

In the single-node mode the rotors move in opposite directions and the node (a section of zero angular amplitude) lies between them. The shaft torque is the same on both sides of the node, and the angular momentum is conserved, so J₁θ₁ = −J₂θ₂. The node divides the shaft in the inverse ratio of the inertias, l₁ / l₂ = J₂ / J₁. With l₁ + l₂ = L, l₁ = L J₂ / (J₁ + J₂) = 0.90 × 1.2 / 3.6 = 0.300 m from rotor 1. The node is closer to the larger inertia, which is expected because the heavier rotor moves through the smaller angle.

Answer: 0.3 m

(d)

From J₁θ₁ = −J₂θ₂, the amplitude of rotor 2 is θ₂ = −(J₁ / J₂) θ₁ = −(2.4 / 1.2) × 0.020 = −0.040 rad. The relative twist is θ₁ − θ₂ = 0.020 − (−0.040) = 0.060 rad. The maximum torque is T = k_t × twist = 22061 × 0.060 = 1324 N·m = 1.32 kN·m. Equivalent route: the torque equals J₁ ω_n² θ₁ = 2.4 × 27576.2 × 0.020 = 1324 N·m. The shear stress is τ = T (d/2) / J = 105.3 MPa, which a designer compares with the fatigue limit of the shaft.

Answer: 1.324 kN·m

A2 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A2-021] Critical speed of shafts

A solid steel shaft of diameter 40 mm is carried in two self-aligning bearings 1.20 m apart, so it may be treated as simply supported. A single rigid disc of mass 25 kg is mounted at mid-span. For the steel take E = 207 GPa and ρ = 7850 kg/m³, and use g = 9.81 m/s². The shaft is part of a centrifugal blower drive that normally runs at 1200 rpm. The disc centre of mass is offset from the shaft axis by an eccentricity e = 0.10 mm. Treat the system as undamped and use the lateral (whirling) model of a single disc on a flexible shaft.

  1. (a) Find the static deflection at mid-span due to the disc weight alone, neglecting shaft mass. [4]
  2. (b) Find the first critical speed of the disc-on-massless-shaft model, in rpm. [4]
  3. (c) Find the shaft's own first critical speed with no disc, then use Dunkerley's equation to estimate the first critical speed of the combined system, in rpm. [6]
  4. (d) Using the Dunkerley critical speed as the natural frequency, find the whirl amplitude of the disc centre at 1200 rpm caused by the eccentricity. [6]
(a)

Second moment of area I = πd⁴/64 = π(0.040)⁴/64 = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴. For a simply supported beam with a central point load the deflection is δ = mgL³/(48EI). Substituting, δ = (25 × 9.81 × 1.20³)/(48 × 207×10⁹ × 1.2566 × 10⁻⁷) = 423.8 / 1.2486 × 10⁶ = 0.3394 mm. The shaft mass is neglected here, so this is the deflection of a massless beam under the disc weight alone. A marker looks for the correct beam formula, consistent SI units and an answer in millimetres. The deflection is small compared with the 1.2 m span, which supports the linear beam model used throughout this problem.

Answer: 0.3394 mm

(b)

For the single-disc model the lateral natural frequency equals √(k/m), and the shaft stiffness is k = mg/δ, so ωn = √(g/δ). Substituting, ωn = √(9.81/3.3942 × 10⁻⁴) = 170.01 rad/s. Converting, N = ωn × 60/(2π) = 1623 rpm. This is the speed at which the rotating shaft whirls with large amplitude, because the force from the disc eccentricity then coincides with the lateral natural frequency. Since the shaft mass was neglected, this value is an upper bound on the true critical speed. Rayleigh and Dunkerley methods both give lower, more realistic values once the distributed shaft mass is included, which is the purpose of the next part.

Answer: 1623 rpm

(c)

Shaft alone: the first lateral frequency of a uniform simply supported beam is ωs = (π/L)²√(EI/ρA). With A = πd²/4 = 1.2566 × 10⁻³ m², ωs = (π/1.2)² × √(26012.4/9.8646) = 6.854 × 51.35 = 352.0 rad/s. Dunkerley's equation adds the reciprocals of the squared frequencies: 1/ω² = 1/ωdisc² + 1/ωs² = 1/170.0² + 1/352.0², which gives ω = 153.1 rad/s, or 1462 rpm. Dunkerley always underestimates the true fundamental slightly, so it is a safe, conservative estimate. The combined critical speed is lower than either component alone, which is why the Dunkerley estimate is always the more conservative guide for setting the operating-speed margin of the blower.

Answer: 1462 rpm

(d)

Operating speed 1200 rpm corresponds to ω = 1200 × 2π/60 = 125.66 rad/s. The frequency ratio is r = ω/ωn = 125.66/153.1 = 0.8209. For an undamped disc with eccentricity e, the steady whirl amplitude is x = e r²/|1 − r²|. Substituting, x = 0.10 × 0.6738/|1 − 0.6738| = 0.207 mm. The amplitude is about double the eccentricity, because the blower runs only about 18 percent below the critical speed. A marker would also expect a comment that this margin is thin, that real damping, bearing flexibility and gyroscopic effects would shift the result, and that a wider separation of at least 20 to 25 percent would normally be sought.

Answer: 0.207 mm

Problem 2 [A2-022] Rigid body planar kinetics with energy methods

A uniform slender rod of mass 12 kg and length 1.80 m is hinged to a fixed frictionless pin at one end O. A small compact sphere of mass 5 kg is fixed to the free end of the rod; treat it as a point mass at the tip. The assembly is released from rest in the horizontal position and swings down in a vertical plane under gravity (g = 9.81 m/s²). Rod and sphere together form a single rigid body rotating about O. Neglect air resistance and the size of the sphere. The designer needs the dynamic loads on the pin to size the bracket that carries it.

  1. (a) Find the mass moment of inertia of the assembly about the pin O. [4]
  2. (b) Find the angular acceleration immediately after release, with the rod horizontal. [4]
  3. (c) Using conservation of energy, find the angular velocity when the rod reaches the vertical position. [6]
  4. (d) Find the vertical component of the pin reaction at O when the rod is vertical, and state the horizontal component. [6]
(a)

The rod about its end has I = mL²/3 = 12 × 1.80²/3 = 12.960 kg·m². The tip mass, treated as a point, adds ML² = 5 × 1.80² = 16.200 kg·m². Moments of inertia about the same axis simply add, so IO = 12.960 + 16.200 = 29.160 kg·m². The pin is a fixed axis, so this single moment of inertia governs both the dynamics and the kinetic energy of the rigid body. A marker rewards stating that the rod centre of mass is at L/2 and the sphere at L from the pin, which are the lever arms used in the next parts, and also using the end-pivot formula rather than the centroidal one.

Answer: 29.160 kg·m²

(b)

For rotation about a fixed axis, ΣMO = IOα. At the horizontal position the weights act at right angles to the rod, so the moment about O is mg(L/2) + Mg(L) = 12 × 9.81 × 0.90 + 5 × 9.81 × 1.80 = 105.95 + 88.29 = 194.24 N·m. The pin reaction passes through O and has no moment. Then α = 194.24/29.160 = 6.661 rad/s². The angular velocity is zero at release, so there is no centripetal term yet. The tip has tangential acceleration αL = 11.99 m/s², larger than g, which is possible because the heavy tip is dragged along by the rod.

Answer: 6.661 rad/s²

(c)

Energy is conserved because the pin is frictionless and only gravity does work. From horizontal to vertical, the rod centre falls L/2 = 0.90 m and the tip falls L = 1.80 m. Loss of potential energy: ΔV = mg(L/2) + Mg(L) = 194.24 J. Starting from rest, the kinetic energy at the bottom is ½IOω², so ½ × 29.160 × ω² = 194.24. Solving, ω² = 13.322 and ω = 3.650 rad/s. The tip speed is then ωL = 6.57 m/s. The angular velocity cannot be found from ΣM = Iα alone without integrating over the swing, which is why the energy method is preferred for this question.

Answer: 3.650 rad/s

(d)

At the vertical position the moment of gravity about O is zero, so α = 0 and there is no tangential acceleration. The horizontal pin reaction is therefore Ox = 0 N. Vertically, the combined body accelerates toward O with a centripetal term. Summing forces on the rigid body, Oy − (m + M)g = (m(L/2) + ML)ω², where the bracket is the first moment of mass about O. Substituting, Oy = 17 × 9.81 + (12 × 0.90 + 5 × 1.80) × 13.322 = 166.8 + 263.8 = 430.5 N upward. This is more than 2.5 times the combined weight, which a marker expects to see commented on for pin and bracket design.

Answer: 430.5 N

Problem 3 [A2-023] Planar mechanism velocity analysis by instant centres

A four-bar linkage in a packaging machine has a fixed pivot O2 at the origin and a second fixed pivot O4 located 0.400 m along the positive x-axis. The driving crank O2A is 0.120 m long, the coupler AB is 0.380 m long and the follower O4B is 0.250 m long. The crank is at θ2 = 70° measured counter-clockwise from the x-axis, and B lies above the line O2O4 (positive y). A designer must size the crank speed so that the follower reaches a specified angular velocity while the linkage is in this position, and uses the instant centre method to relate the two angular velocities.

  1. (a) Find the angle θ4 of the follower O4B, measured counter-clockwise from the positive x-axis. [5]
  2. (b) Locate the instant centre I24 of the crank and follower, giving its x-coordinate on line O2O4 measured from O2. [5]
  3. (c) Find the ratio ω4/ω2 from the instant centre positions (positive means the same sense). [5]
  4. (d) Find the crank speed in rpm that gives the follower an angular speed of 3.00 rad/s counter-clockwise in this position. [5]
(a)

Crank pin A = (0.120 cos 70°, 0.120 sin 70°) = (0.0410, 0.1128) m. The distance from A to O4 is D = 0.3763 m. B lies on a circle of radius 0.380 m about A and a circle of radius 0.250 m about O4. The foot of the common chord is at x = (b² − c² + D²)/(2D) = 0.2970 m from A along AO4, and the half-chord is h = √(b² − x²) = 0.2371 m. Taking the intersection with positive y gives B = (0.3954, 0.2500) m. Then θ4 = atan2(By, Bx − 0.400) = 91.05°, near vertical, with B slightly to the left of O4. Check: |O4B| = 0.250 m.

Answer: 91.05 °

(b)

By the Kennedy-Aronhold theorem, I24 lies on the line through I12 = O2 and I14 = O4, which is the x-axis, and also on the line through I23 = A and I34 = B. So I24 is the intersection of line AB with the x-axis. Direction AB = (0.3544, 0.1372). The parameter that brings y to zero is s = −Ay/ΔyAB = -0.8219, giving x = 0.0410 + -0.8219 × 0.3544 = -0.2502 m. This is 0.6502 m from O4, on the same side of both pivots, so the two pivots turn in the same sense. A marker looks for the stated theorem and a correct line intersection.

Answer: -0.2502 m

(c)

At the instant centre I24 the crank and follower have the same velocity, so ω2 × O2I24 = ω4 × O4I24, giving ω4/ω2 = O2I24/O4I24. Here I24 lies at x = -0.2502 m, so O2I24 = 0.2502 m and O4I24 = 0.6502 m. The instant centre lies outside the segment O2O4, on the same side of both pivots, so the two links turn in the same sense and the ratio is positive: ω4/ω2 = 0.2502/0.6502 = 0.3848. Cross-check with the vector loop: solving the 2×2 velocity equations from the loop closure gives the same ratio, ω4 = 0.3848 ω2. If I24 had fallen between the pivots the ratio would be negative, so the location test is what a marker checks.

Answer: 0.3848

(d)

The required follower speed is ω4 = 3.00 rad/s counter-clockwise. From part (c), ω4 = 0.3848 ω2, so ω2 = 3.00/0.3848 = 7.796 rad/s, counter-clockwise because the ratio is positive. Converting, N2 = ω2 × 60/(2π) = 74.4 rpm. The value applies only at this crank angle, because the velocity ratio of a four-bar linkage changes continuously through the cycle. A designer would therefore repeat the calculation at several crank angles, or choose the mean crank speed from the required cycle time, and check that the follower speed stays within its limit at the worst position.

Answer: 74.4 rpm

Problem 4 [A2-024] Relative velocity and acceleration of a four-bar linkage

A four-bar linkage drives a pick-and-place arm. Fixed pivots O2 and O4 are 0.240 m apart on a horizontal line, with O2 at the origin and O4 on the positive x-axis. The crank O2A is 0.080 m, the coupler AB is 0.220 m and the rocker O4B is 0.180 m. At the instant considered the crank angle is θ2 = 120° counter-clockwise from the x-axis and B lies above the ground line. The crank turns at constant ω2 = 20 rad/s counter-clockwise. The rocker bearing is rated for a maximum angular acceleration, and the designer must find the highest crank speed that respects that rating at this critical position.

  1. (a) Find the angular velocity ω4 of the rocker at this instant (counter-clockwise positive). [5]
  2. (b) Find the angular acceleration α4 of the rocker at this instant (counter-clockwise positive). [6]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of point B. [4]
  4. (d) The bearing limit is |α4| ≤ 600 rad/s². Find the highest constant crank speed in rpm that satisfies this at this position. [5]
(a)

Pin A = (-0.0400, 0.0693) m and the distance A to O4 is 0.2884 m. Intersecting the circles of radius 0.220 m about A and 0.180 m about O4 (B above the axis) gives B = (0.1599, 0.1612) m, so θ3 = 24.69° and θ4 = 116.43°. The velocity loop equation vA + vB/A = vB gives two scalar equations: -b sinθ3 ω3 + c sinθ4 ω4 = a ω2 sinθ2 and b cosθ3 ω3 - c cosθ4 ω4 = -a ω2 cosθ2. Solving the 2×2 system gives ω3 = 0.453 rad/s and ω4 = 8.855 rad/s. A positive value means counter-clockwise. A marker rewards a clear loop equation, the two components and a sensible check, such as the polygon closing.

Answer: 8.855 rad/s

(b)

Differentiating the velocity loop once more with α2 = 0 gives the acceleration equation. Its two components are -b sinθ3 α3 + c sinθ4 α4 = aω2² cosθ2 + bω3² cosθ3 - cω4² cosθ4 and b cosθ3 α3 - c cosθ4 α4 = aω2² sinθ2 + bω3² sinθ3 - cω4² sinθ4. The right-hand sides evaluate to -9.68 and 15.09 m/s². The coefficient matrix is the same as in the velocity problem, so solving it gives α3 = 81.1 rad/s² and α4 = -13.8 rad/s². The values are modest at 20 rad/s because the crank centripetal term aω2² = 32.0 m/s² is small, but it grows quickly with speed. Note that α4 grows with the square of the crank speed when ω2 is constant.

Answer: -13.8 rad/s²

(c)

Point B moves on a circle about O4 with radius c = 0.180 m, so its acceleration has a tangential part cα4 and a normal part cω4². Tangential: 2.5 m/s². Normal: 0.180 × (8.855)² = 14.11 m/s². In components, aB = (-α4 c sinθ4 - ω4² c cosθ4, α4 c cosθ4 - ω4² c sinθ4) = (8.5, -11.5) m/s². The magnitude is |aB| = 14.3 m/s², about 1.5 g. A marker accepts the vector route or the tangential and normal route, provided the two components are combined by Pythagoras. The acceleration of point B is the quantity that sets the inertia load on the coupler pin, so it is worth stating clearly with its units.

Answer: 14.3 m/s²

(d)

For constant crank speed with fixed geometry, every acceleration term scales with ω2², because both the aω2² source term and the velocity-squared terms scale that way. So α4 is proportional to ω2². At 20 rad/s the rocker angular acceleration is |α4| = 13.8 rad/s². Requiring |α4| ≤ 600 rad/s² gives ω2,max = 20 × √(600/13.8) = 131.76 rad/s. Converting, N = 1258.3 rpm. The limit applies only at this crank angle. The designer must scan the full cycle and take the lowest speed allowed over all positions, so this answer is an upper bound on the true allowable speed.

Answer: 1258.3 rpm

Problem 5 [A2-025] Slider-crank kinematics

A single-cylinder compressor uses an in-line slider-crank mechanism (no offset) with a connecting rod of length 0.340 m. The specification requires a piston stroke of 0.180 m. To limit ring wear the mean piston speed must not exceed 7.50 m/s. The designer must choose the crank radius, find the highest allowable shaft speed, and check the inertia loading on the wrist pin at top dead centre and the piston speed part-way through the stroke. Use the exact kinematic relations, not the first-harmonic approximation, and treat the shaft speed as constant. The compressor drives a small workshop air receiver and is belt driven from an electric motor.

  1. (a) Find the crank radius needed for the specified stroke. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum shaft speed in rpm that keeps the mean piston speed at 7.50 m/s. [4]
  3. (c) At that shaft speed, find the magnitude of the piston acceleration at top dead centre (crank angle 0°). [6]
  4. (d) At that speed, find the piston speed when the crank has turned 60° from top dead centre. [6]
(a)

For an in-line slider-crank the piston travels between top and bottom dead centre, a distance of (l + r) − (l − r) = 2r. The stroke is therefore S = 2r, so r = S/2 = 0.180/2 = 0.0900 m. The connecting rod length does not affect the stroke in the in-line case; it affects only the shape of the motion, such as the asymmetry between the two halves of the stroke. The rod-to-crank ratio is l/r = 0.340/0.0900 = 3.78, which is a typical value for compressors and keeps the maximum rod angle to 15.3°.

Answer: 0.0900 m

(b)

The piston makes one stroke each half revolution, so in one revolution it travels 2S. Mean piston speed is therefore vm = 2SN with N in revolutions per second. Rearranging, N = vm/(2S) = 7.50/(2 × 0.180) = 20.833 rev/s. Converting, the shaft speed is 1250.0 rpm, which is ω = 130.90 rad/s. The mean speed is only an average. The peak piston speed is higher, slightly above rω = 11.8 m/s, and that peak sets the lubrication regime at the rings, so a marker would credit a comment on this difference.

Answer: 1250.0 rpm

(c)

At top dead centre θ = 0, the exact piston acceleration is a = rω²(cosθ + (r/l)cos 2θ), which reduces to rω²(1 + r/l). Substituting, a = 0.0900 × 130.90² × (1 + 0.0900/0.340) = 1542 × 1.2647 = 1950 m/s², directed toward the crank centre. This is about 199 g. The inertia force on the wrist pin is the reciprocating mass times this value, so halving the piston mass halves the load. The (r/l) term raises the TDC acceleration compared with pure harmonic motion, showing why a shorter rod is worse for inertia loading.

Answer: 1950 m/s²

(d)
