The exact piston velocity is v = rω[sinθ + (r sinθ cosθ)/√(l² − r² sin²θ)]. At θ = 60°: sinθ = 0.8660, cosθ = 0.5, r sinθ = 0.0779 m. The square root is √(0.340² − 0.00607) = 0.3309 m. The bracket becomes 0.8660 + 0.1178 = 0.9838. With rω = 11.781 m/s, v = 11.590 m/s. This is well above the mean speed of 7.50 m/s, as expected near mid-stroke, and the piston is moving away from TDC. The velocity is not symmetric about mid-stroke because of the finite rod length, so the exact expression must be used instead of the harmonic approximation.

Answer: 11.590 m/s

A2 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A2-026] Grashof and transmission angle

A designer is sizing a crank-rocker linkage for a window-opener. The ground link is fixed at d = 0.450 m, the coupler is b = 0.380 m and the rocker is c = 0.300 m. The crank length a is still to be chosen and the crank must be able to rotate fully. The transmission angle, the acute angle between the coupler and the rocker, must not fall below 40° at any point in the cycle, otherwise the mechanism jams under load. The designer first tests a trial crank of 0.200 m and then adjusts it. Take the transmission angle at each extreme as the acute angle formed by the coupler and rocker lines.

  1. (a) Find the longest crank length for which the crank can still rotate fully (Grashof condition with the crank as the shortest link). [4]
  2. (b) For the trial crank a = 0.200 m, find the minimum transmission angle over the cycle. [6]
  3. (c) Find the longest crank length that keeps the minimum transmission angle at or above 40°. [6]
  4. (d) State what kind of linkage results if a is increased to 0.260 m, and what it means for a motor driving the crank. [4]
(a)

Grashof's rule states that for a four-bar linkage s + l ≤ p + q, where s and l are the shortest and longest links and p, q the other two. The longest link is the ground at 0.450 m. If the crank is the shortest, the condition is a + 0.450 ≤ 0.380 + 0.300, so a ≤ 0.680 − 0.450 = 0.230 m. With the crank adjacent to the ground and shortest, the linkage is a crank-rocker and the crank rotates fully. Beyond this length the inequality fails, no link can rotate fully, and the linkage becomes a triple-rocker. The marker looks for identifying the longest link correctly before applying the inequality, and for noting that the crank must also be the shortest link.

Answer: 0.230 m

(b)

The transmission angle μ between coupler and rocker follows from the cosine rule on the triangle formed by the coupler, the rocker and the diagonal from the crank pin to the ground pivot. Extreme values occur when the crank lies along the ground line. With the crank folded toward the rocker the diagonal is d − a = 0.250 m: cos μ1 = (b² + c² − 0.250²)/(2bc) = 0.7539, so μ1 = 41.1°. Extended, the diagonal is d + a = 0.650 m: cos μ2 = -0.8250, giving an obtuse angle of 145.6°, whose acute equivalent is 180° minus that, 34.4°. The minimum is the smaller value, 34.4°, which fails the 40° requirement.

Answer: 34.4 °

(c)

Both extremes must give at least 40°. Folded position: μ1 ≥ 40° requires (d − a)² ≥ b² + c² − 2bc cos40°, so a ≤ d − √(b² + c² − 2bc cos40°) = 0.2056 m. Extended position: the acute angle is 180° minus the obtuse angle, so we need the obtuse angle to be at most 140°, which gives (d + a)² ≤ b² + c² + 2bc cos40°, so a ≤ √(b² + c² + 2bc cos40°) − d = 0.1896 m. Both are upper bounds on a, so the smaller one governs: a = 0.1896 m. The extended position controls here, which is why the trial crank of 0.200 m failed even though the folded angle was acceptable. Checking, 0.1896 m is also inside the Grashof limit of 0.230 m, so the crank still rotates fully.

Answer: 0.1896 m

(d)

With a = 0.260 m the Grashof inequality is violated, since 0.260 + 0.450 = 0.710 m exceeds 0.380 + 0.300 = 0.680 m. No link can make a full turn, and the linkage becomes a triple-rocker (non-Grashof). A motor connected to the crank would stall when the crank reaches a limit position, or force the mechanism to lock up and overload the bearings, so a continuously rotating drive cannot be used. The designer would either shorten the crank to 0.230 m or less (and in practice to about 0.19 m to meet the transmission angle limit), or use an oscillating actuator such as a linear actuator or a reversing gearmotor with limit switches.

Answer: See working

Problem 2 [A2-027] Cam profile and follower motion

A radial roller-follower cam in a bottling machine must raise its follower by 30 mm using cycloidal motion while the cam turns through 90°, at a constant cam speed of 600 rpm. The follower line of action passes through the cam centre (no offset). The designer must limit the pressure angle during the rise to 30°, which fixes the minimum prime circle radius (the radius to the roller centre at the start of the rise), and then checks a chosen design with a 60 mm prime circle. For cycloidal rise the follower displacement is s = h(θ/β − sin(2πθ/β)/(2π)), where h is the rise and β the rise angle.

  1. (a) Find the maximum follower velocity during the rise. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum follower acceleration during the rise. [4]
  3. (c) Find the smallest prime circle radius that keeps the pressure angle at or below 30° throughout the rise. [7]
  4. (d) For a prime circle radius of 0.060 m, find the pressure angle at mid-rise. [5]
(a)

The cam speed is ω = 600 × 2π/60 = 62.83 rad/s, and the rise takes place over β = 90° = 1.5708 rad. For cycloidal motion the velocity is v = ω ds/dθ = (hω/β)(1 − cos(2πθ/β)). This is greatest when the cosine equals −1, at mid-rise, giving vmax = 2hω/β = 2 × 0.030 × 62.83/1.5708 = 2.400 m/s. The velocity is zero at both ends of the rise, which is what makes cycloidal motion free of velocity jumps. A marker expects the derivative to be taken with respect to the cam angle and then multiplied by the cam angular speed, not left as a per-radian slope.

Answer: 2.400 m/s

(b)

The acceleration is a = ω² d²s/dθ² = (2πhω²/β²) sin(2πθ/β). Its peak occurs at a quarter and three quarters of the rise, where the sine equals ±1, so amax = 2πhω²/β². Substituting, amax = 2π × 0.030 × 3947.8/2.4674 = 301.6 m/s², about 31 g. The acceleration is zero at start and end, so there is no jerk spike at the transitions, which is the main advantage over simple harmonic motion. The inertia force on the follower train is its mass times this value, and the roller-to-cam contact force must exceed it to avoid follower jump, so a spring preload would be sized from this figure.

Answer: 301.6 m/s²

(c)

For an in-line follower the pressure angle φ satisfies tanφ = (ds/dθ)/(Rp + s), where Rp is the prime circle radius. Requiring φ ≤ 30° at every angle gives Rp ≥ (ds/dθ)/tan30° − s. Using ds/dθ = (h/β)(1 − cos(2πθ/β)) and the cycloidal s, evaluate the right-hand side over the rise on a fine grid of angles. The largest value is 0.0525 m, which sets the minimum prime radius. At mid-rise alone the bracket is (2h/β)/tan30° − h/2 = 0.0512 m, and the true maximum lies close to it. So Rp,min = 0.0525 m, giving a minimum prime diameter of about 105 mm. A small cam therefore needs a lower rise or a longer rise angle.

Answer: 0.0525 m

(d)

At mid-rise θ = β/2, s = h/2 = 0.015 m and ds/dθ = 2h/β = 0.0382 m/rad. With Rp = 0.060 m, tanφ = 0.0382/(0.060 + 0.015) = 0.5093, so φ = 26.99°. This is inside the 30° limit, so a 60 mm prime radius is acceptable at mid-rise. Since the minimum permitted radius from part (c) is slightly lower than 60 mm, the design has a small margin everywhere in the rise. A marker also looks for the remark that the pressure angle should be checked at the angle of maximum slope, not only at the mid-point, and that a pressure angle above 30° risks jamming and high side loads on the follower guide.

Answer: 26.99 °

Problem 3 [A2-028] Spur gear geometry and gear trains

A pair of 20° full-depth involute spur gears must connect two parallel shafts whose centre distance is 150 mm. The speed ratio should be 3.00 reduction with a tolerance of ±3 percent, the module is 4 mm, and the pinion must not suffer undercutting. The pinion is driven at 1750 rpm by an electric motor. Standard full-depth teeth have addendum equal to one module. The designer first finds the smallest permitted pinion, chooses the tooth numbers that fit the centre distance, and then checks whether the contact is smooth enough (a contact ratio of at least 1.4 is wanted) and what output speed results.

  1. (a) Find the theoretical minimum number of pinion teeth that avoids interference with a rack, then state the whole number used. [4]
  2. (b) Choose whole-number tooth counts (pinion and gear) that fit the 150 mm centre distance with module 4 mm and give a ratio within 3 percent of 3.00. Report the actual speed ratio. [5]
  3. (c) Find the contact ratio of the chosen gear pair. [6]
  4. (d) Find the output speed of the gear in rpm. [5]
(a)

To avoid undercutting by a rack cutter, the minimum number of pinion teeth for full-depth teeth is Nmin = 2/sin²φ = 2/sin²20° = 2/0.11698 = 17.10. Since the tooth number must be a whole number and it cannot be lower than the theoretical value, the practical minimum is 18 teeth. The whole number used in the design is therefore not less than 18. A marker looks for the 2/sin²φ result and for rounding up rather than to the nearest integer. A smaller pinion could be used with profile shift or a larger pressure angle, but with standard teeth and no shift this limit stands.

Answer: 17.10 teeth

(b)

For a gear pair of module m the centre distance is C = m(Np + Ng)/2, so Np + Ng = 2C/m = 2 × 150/4 = 75 teeth. The ratio should be 3.00 within ±3 percent, so Ng/Np lies between 2.91 and 3.09, and Np must be at least 18. Trying Np = 18 gives Ng = 57 and a ratio of 3.167, outside the band. Np = 19 gives Ng = 56 and a ratio of 2.9474, which is 1.8 percent from 3.00 and acceptable. So the design is 19 teeth on the pinion and 56 teeth on the gear. A marker credits any pair satisfying all three conditions, with the arithmetic shown.

Answer: 2.9474

(c)

Pitch radii: Rp = mN/2 = 38.0 mm and Rg = 112.0 mm. Base radii are Rb = R cos20°, giving 35.708 mm and 105.246 mm. Addendum circle radii are R + m, so 42.0 mm and 116.0 mm. The length of the path of contact is Z = √(Ra,p² − Rb,p²) + √(Ra,g² − Rb,g²) − C sinφ = 22.111 + 48.779 − 51.303 = 19.587 mm. The base pitch is pb = πm cosφ = 11.809 mm. The contact ratio is mc = Z/pb = 1.659, which exceeds the 1.4 requirement, so on average more than one tooth pair carries the load.

Answer: 1.659

(d)

The output speed follows from the tooth ratio, since the pitch line velocity is common to both gears: n2 = n1 × Np/Ng = 1750 × 19/56 = 593.8 rpm. The gear turns in the opposite sense to the pinion, because the mesh is external. The actual ratio 2.9474 differs from the nominal 3.00 by 1.8 percent, which is why the output speed is 10.4 rpm different from the 583.3 rpm that an exact 3.00 ratio would give. If the driven machine has a strict speed tolerance this difference should be compared with it before the design is accepted. The pitch line velocity is v = ωpRp = 6.96 m/s, which sets the choice of gear quality.

Answer: 593.8 rpm

Problem 4 [A2-029] Planetary gear trains

A winch gearbox uses a simple epicyclic train with a sun gear, a set of identical planet gears carried on an arm, and an internal ring gear. A designer must obtain a 4.50:1 speed reduction by driving the sun gear and taking the output from the carrier while the ring gear is held fixed to the casing. The sun gear has 20 teeth and all gears share one module. Three equally spaced planets are used. The input shaft runs at 1800 rpm and delivers 50 N·m. Treat the train as lossless. The three planets share the load equally, the gearbox is mounted horizontally on a rigid frame, and the casing is bolted to the winch bed so that it can resist the ring gear reaction.

  1. (a) Find the number of teeth on the ring gear. [4]
  2. (b) Find the number of teeth on each planet gear, and state the assembly check for three planets. [3]
  3. (c) Find the carrier speed in rpm for the 1800 rpm input. [4]
  4. (d) Find the absolute angular speed of a planet gear about its own axis, in rpm (positive in the sense of the sun). [4]
  5. (e) Find the torque reaction that the casing must provide on the ring gear. [5]
(a)

With the ring fixed and the sun driving the carrier, the ratio from the tabular method is nsun/ncarrier = 1 + Nr/Ns. Setting this to 4.50 gives Nr/Ns = 3.50, so Nr = 3.50 × 20 = 70 teeth. The derivation: with the carrier held, the ring turns at −(Ns/Nr) times the sun speed; adding the carrier rotation to every gear and imposing zero ring speed gives the result. A marker expects either the tabular method or the formula speed ratio equation, with the fixed member correctly identified, and the sign of the ring gear motion stated. A higher ring-to-sun tooth ratio produces a larger reduction, but the ring then grows, so 4.5:1 is a typical single-stage limit.

Answer: 70 teeth

(b)

The planet meshes with the sun and the ring, so the geometry gives Nr = Ns + 2Np, because the diameter of the ring equals the sun diameter plus two planet diameters. Therefore Np = (Nr − Ns)/2 = (70 − 20)/2 = 25 teeth. For equal spacing of three planets, (Ns + Nr)/3 must be a whole number: (20 + 70)/3 = 30, which is an integer, so the three planets can be assembled at 120° intervals. If that quotient were fractional, the planets could not be fitted at equal spacing without shifting the teeth.

Answer: 25 teeth

(c)

The carrier speed equals the sun speed divided by the reduction ratio when the ring is fixed: nc = nsun/(1 + Nr/Ns) = 1800/4.50 = 400 rpm, in the same direction as the sun. As a check by the tabular method: with the carrier held, sun = +1 and ring = −Ns/Nr = −0.2857. Adding x = +0.2857 to every member makes the ring zero, the carrier +0.2857 and the sun 1.2857, so the sun-to-carrier ratio is 1.2857/0.2857 = 4.50. The carrier speed is 400 rpm for a sun input of 1800 rpm.

Answer: 400 rpm

(d)

Relative to the carrier, the planet turns opposite to the sun by the tooth ratio: nplanet/carrier = −(Ns/Np)(nsun − ncarrier) = −(20/25)(1800 − 400) = -1120 rpm. The absolute planet spin is the carrier speed plus this relative speed: 400 + (-1120) = -720 rpm. The negative sign means the planet spins in the opposite sense to the sun. The planet bearing sits between the planet and the carrier, so it runs at the relative speed of 1120 rpm, not the absolute 720 rpm, and the bearing life calculation should use 1120 rpm.

Answer: -720 rpm

(e)

For a lossless train, power in equals power out: Tin ωin = Tout ωout, so Tout = 50 × 4.50 = 225 N·m on the carrier. The sun, carrier and ring torques must sum to zero for a train in steady operation, since the casing is the only external support. Taking the sun input as +50 N·m and the carrier output as −225 N·m, the ring torque is the remainder: Tring = Tout − Tin = 225 − 50 = 175 N·m. This is the reaction the casing mounts must carry, and it acts opposite in sense to the carrier output torque. Marks go for equilibrium of torques and for stating that the ring reaction is not zero even though it does not rotate.

Answer: 175 N·m

Problem 5 [A2-030] Static force analysis of a mechanism

A reciprocating air compressor uses an in-line slider-crank mechanism with a crank radius of 60 mm and a connecting rod of length 220 mm. The cylinder bore is 100 mm and the gas pressure acting on the piston crown is 2.50 MPa gauge when the crank is 40° past top dead centre. At this instant inertia and friction may be ignored (a quasi-static analysis), because the compressor is running slowly during commissioning. The crank pin bearing is a plain journal with a length equal to 0.9 times its diameter, and the designer must size the pin for a limit on projected-area bearing pressure of 12 MPa.

  1. (a) Find the gas force on the piston. [4]
  2. (b) Find the connecting rod force at this crank angle. [4]
  3. (c) Find the torque the crank shaft must supply to balance the gas load at this instant. [6]
  4. (d) Find the minimum crankpin diameter in millimetres, based on the projected bearing area. [6]
(a)

The gas force is the pressure times the piston area: F = pπD²/4 = 2.50×10⁶ × π × 0.100²/4 = 2.50×10⁶ × 0.00785 = 19635 N = 19.635 kN. It acts along the cylinder axis. Gauge pressure is used because atmospheric pressure acts on both sides of the piston in an air compressor, depending on the construction, and the problem states gauge pressure acts on the crown. With friction and inertia ignored, the piston is in equilibrium under the gas force, the guide reaction and the connecting rod force, a three-force body with the rod force along the rod axis.

Answer: 19.635 kN

(b)

The rod angle φ follows from the geometry: sinφ = (r sinθ)/l = (0.060 × sin 40°)/0.220 = 0.1753, so φ = 10.10°. Resolving forces on the piston along the cylinder axis, the rod force is F/cosφ, because the guide reaction supplies the transverse component. So Frod = 19635/cos(10.10°) = 19944 N = 19.944 kN. The side thrust on the cylinder wall is F tanφ = 3496 N, which is a useful by-product for the guide and liner design. The rod is in compression, and the same force acts on the crank pin.

Answer: 19.944 kN

(c)

The rod force acts along the rod through the crank pin. Its moment about the crank centre is the force times the perpendicular distance, which equals r sin(θ + φ) for this geometry. So T = Frod r sin(θ + φ) = 19944 × 0.060 × sin(50.10°) = 1196.6 × 0.7671 = 918.0 N·m. As a cross-check, virtual work gives T = F × v/ω, and the piston velocity ratio v/ω = r sin(θ + φ)/cosφ gives the same value. The shaft torque is positive in the direction of rotation, meaning the gas is driving the crank, as in an engine. For a compressor the shaft must supply an equal and opposite torque.

Answer: 918.0 N·m

(d)

The crankpin carries the full rod force. The projected bearing area is d × L = d × 0.9d = 0.9d². The bearing pressure is p = Frod/(0.9d²) ≤ 12 MPa, so d ≥ √(Frod/(0.9 × 12×10⁶)) = √(19944/1.080 × 10⁷) = 43.0 mm. The design would round up to the next standard bearing size. Because the load is checked only at this crank angle, the designer must repeat the work at the point of peak force, and also include inertia at speed. The result is an indicative size only, and a marker looks for the use of projected area and the stated length-to-diameter ratio.

Answer: 43.0 mm

A2 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A2-031] Dynamic force analysis of a slider-crank

A single-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine for a portable generator has a crank radius of 45 mm and a connecting rod 150 mm long between centres. The aluminium piston assembly (piston, rings and pin) has a mass of 0.90 kg and the bore is 90 mm. The engine runs at a constant 4800 rpm. Neglect the mass of the connecting rod and all friction, and use the standard two-term approximation for piston acceleration, a = rω²(cos θ + (r/l) cos 2θ), directed toward the crankshaft, where θ is the crank angle from top dead centre (TDC). During the power stroke the gas pressure acting on the piston crown is 4.5 MPa (gauge) when θ = 30°. The designer also needs a speed limit that keeps the reversing inertia load on the piston pin acceptable.

  1. (a) Calculate the inertia force of the reciprocating piston assembly at TDC. [4]
  2. (b) Find the net force transmitted along the cylinder axis through the piston pin at θ = 30°. [4]
  3. (c) Find the force in the connecting rod at θ = 30°. [4]
  4. (d) Find the torque delivered to the crankshaft at θ = 30°. [4]
  5. (e) The piston pin is designed for a maximum inertia force at TDC of 15 kN. Find the highest permissible engine speed. [4]
(a)

Assume constant crank speed and a rigid mechanism. Crank speed ω = 4800 × 2π/60 = 502.7 rad/s. At TDC θ = 0, so cos θ = 1 and cos 2θ = 1. Piston acceleration a = rω²(1 + r/l) = 0.045 × 502.7² × (1 + 0.045/0.150) = 14781 m/s². Inertia force F = m a = 0.90 × 14781 = 13303 N. This is the reaction to the piston being decelerated, so at TDC it acts away from the crankshaft and tends to pull the piston from the pin. It is the largest value of the combined primary plus secondary inertia term in the cycle, and the figure the pin and rod bolts must be sized against.

Answer: 13303 N

(b)

Gas force: A = π(0.090)²/4 = 0.00636 m², so F_g = 4.5×10⁶ × 0.00636 = 28628 N. Piston acceleration at θ = 30°: a = rω²(cos 30° + 0.3 cos 60°) = 0.045 × 502.7² × (0.8660 + 0.15) = 11552 m/s², toward the crankshaft. The piston must be accelerated toward the crank, so the pin carries the gas force less the force needed to accelerate the piston assembly: F = F_g - m a = 28628 - 0.90 × 11552 = 18231 N. The inertia force reduces the load on the rod during the early power stroke, which is why peak rod loading occurs shortly after TDC rather than at it.

Answer: 18.23 kN

(c)

The rod angle follows from the geometry r sin θ = l sin φ, so sin φ = 0.045 × 0.5/0.150 = 0.150 and φ = 8.63°. The cylinder-axis force F = 18231 N is the axial component of the rod force, so F_rod cos φ = F. Hence F_rod = 18231/cos 8.63° = 18440 N. The side thrust on the cylinder wall is F tan φ = 2766 N, which the designer would use for piston skirt and liner checks. The rod force is only slightly larger than the cylinder-axis force because the rod angle is small at this crank position, and the rod is in compression.

Answer: 18.44 kN

(d)

The torque on the crank follows from power balance, F v = T ω, which gives the standard result T = F r sin(θ + φ)/cos φ. Substituting: T = 18231 × 0.045 × sin(38.63°)/cos 8.63° = 518.0 N·m. Check by components: the rod force F_rod acts along the rod, whose line is 38.63° from the crank direction, so the tangential component is F_rod sin(θ + φ) and the torque is that component times r, which gives the same value. The sign shows the engine is delivering positive torque at this position, and the result is the instantaneous value, not the cycle average.

Answer: 518 N·m

(e)

The limiting condition is the TDC inertia force, F = m r ω² (1 + r/l) ≤ 15 000 N. Solving for ω: ω² = 15 000/(0.90 × 0.045 × 1.3) = 284900, so ω_max = 533.8 rad/s. Converting, N = ω × 60/2π = 5097 rpm. The inertia force scales with the square of speed, so the existing 4800 rpm design produces 13303 N, which is 89 percent of the limit and leaves a modest margin. A 10 percent speed increase would raise the load by 21 percent. A lighter piston is the other design lever, since the load is directly proportional to mass.

Answer: 5097 rpm

Problem 2 [A2-032] Flywheel sizing

A sheet-metal punching press runs at 30 strokes per minute. Each stroke is a 2.0 s cycle in which the punch does 14.0 kJ of work, delivered at a uniform rate over the 1.2 s working part of the cycle; for the remaining 0.8 s the press is idling and absorbs no energy. A constant-torque electric motor drives the press through a reduction so that the flywheel shaft turns at a mean speed of 240 rpm. Friction losses are negligible. The speed of the flywheel must not vary by more than 8 percent of the mean speed between its maximum and minimum values (coefficient of speed fluctuation Cs = 0.08). The flywheel will be a solid steel disc 150 mm thick, density 7850 kg/m³, and the inertia of the other rotating parts can be ignored.

  1. (a) Find the power the motor must supply, taking the average over one cycle. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum fluctuation of energy that the flywheel must absorb and release in one cycle. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the mass moment of inertia required of the flywheel. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the outside radius of the solid disc flywheel. [5]
  5. (e) State the maximum shaft speed reached in the cycle. [2]
(a)

Because the motor torque is constant and losses are negligible, the motor must deliver the full cycle energy over the cycle time. Average power P = E/T = 14.0 kJ / 2.0 s = 7000 W, which is 7.00 kW. This is the rating the motor needs, ignoring a service factor. Without a flywheel the motor would have to supply the instantaneous peak demand during the working part of the cycle, which is E divided by 1.2 s = 11667 W, about 1.67 times larger. The flywheel is what allows a smaller motor to be selected, and the next parts size it.

Answer: 7.00 kW

(b)

During the 1.2 s working period the press demands 11667 W but the motor supplies only 7000 W. The deficit is 4667 W, so the flywheel must release ΔE = (P_w - P_avg) t_w = (11667 - 7000) × 1.2 = 5600 J = 5.60 kJ. Over the 0.8 s idle period the motor surplus of 7000 W × 0.8 s = 5600 J restores the same energy to the flywheel, which confirms the energy balance closes over the cycle. The speed is therefore at its minimum at the end of the working stroke and at its maximum at the end of the idle period, and ΔE is the energy swing between those two points.

Answer: 5.60 kJ

(c)

The energy swing is related to the speed fluctuation by ΔE = I ω_mean² Cs, since ΔE = ½ I (ω_max² - ω_min²) = I ω_mean (ω_max - ω_min). Mean speed ω = 240 × 2π/60 = 25.13 rad/s. Solving for I: I = ΔE/(Cs ω²) = 5600/(0.08 × 25.13²) = 110.8 kg·m². This is the total inertia of everything on the flywheel shaft, so any rotating parts that were neglected would reduce the inertia the added flywheel itself needs. A smaller allowed Cs would raise I in inverse proportion, which is the main design trade for a press that must hold speed tightly.

Answer: 110.8 kg·m²

(d)

For a solid disc of radius R and thickness t, the mass is m = ρπR²t and the moment of inertia is I = ½ m R² = ½ ρ π t R⁴. Solving for R: R⁴ = 2I/(ρ π t) = 2 × 110.8/(7850 × π × 0.15) = 0.0599 m⁴, so R = 0.4947 m = 495 mm. The disc mass is m = 7850 × π × 0.4947² × 0.15 = 905 kg and the diameter is about 0.99 m. A designer would check the rim speed against the material limit: v = ω R = 25.13 × 0.4947 = 12.4 m/s, which is very low compared with the strength-limited rim speed of cast or steel flywheels.

Answer: 495 mm

(e)

The speed varies by Cs × mean speed in total, symmetrically about the mean for the usual definition Cs = (ω_max - ω_min)/ω_mean. Therefore ω_max = ω_mean (1 + Cs/2) = 240 × (1 + 0.04) = 249.6 rpm and ω_min = 240 × (1 - 0.04) = 230.4 rpm. The maximum speed occurs at the end of the idle part of the cycle, when the flywheel has regained all of its energy. The minimum speed, 230.4 rpm, occurs at the end of the punching stroke and is the speed at which the punch actually finishes cutting.

Answer: 249.6 rpm

Problem 3 [A2-033] Balancing of rotating masses

A centrifuge rotor assembly for a laboratory has three eccentric masses on a rigid shaft. Measured from the left end of the rotor (plane L, axial position 0), mass A of 6.0 kg sits at 0.20 m axially, radius 100 mm, angular position 0°; mass B of 4.0 kg sits at 0.50 m, radius 120 mm, angular position 70°; mass C of 5.0 kg sits at 0.80 m, radius 80 mm, angular position 150°. Angles are measured in the same sense about the shaft from a common reference line. The rotor is to be balanced by adding one correction mass in each of two planes: plane L at axial position 0 and plane R at axial position 1.00 m, both at a radius of 150 mm. The rotor will run at 3000 rpm.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the resultant unbalanced centrifugal force of the three masses at 3000 rpm. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the correction mass required in plane R. [4]
  3. (c) Determine the angular position of the correction mass in plane R. [4]
  4. (d) Determine the correction mass required in plane L. [4]
  5. (e) Determine the angular position of the correction mass in plane L. [4]
(a)

Treat each mass as a vector m r at its angular position. The unbalanced forces sum as vectors: Σ m r cos θ = 6.0×0.10×cos 0° + 4.0×0.12×cos 70° + 5.0×0.08×cos 150° = 0.6000 + 0.1642 - 0.3464 = 0.4178 kg·m, and Σ m r sin θ = 0 + 0.48×sin 70° + 0.40×sin 150° = 0.4511 + 0.2000 = 0.6511 kg·m. The resultant has magnitude 0.7736 kg·m. At ω = 3000 × 2π/60 = 314.2 rad/s the rotating force is F = (Σ m r) ω² = 0.7736 × 314.2² = 76347 N = 76.35 kN. This force turns with the shaft and would be reacted by the bearings as a once-per-revolution load.

Answer: 76.35 kN

(b)

Balance requires both the force polygon and the couple polygon to close. Take moments of m r about plane L (z = 0), which removes the plane L correction mass from the couple equation. The couple vector of the three masses is Σ m r z: x-component = 0.6000×0.2 + 0.1642×0.5 - 0.3464×0.8 = -0.0750 kg·m², y-component = 0 + 0.4511×0.5 + 0.2000×0.8 = 0.3855 kg·m², magnitude 0.3928 kg·m². The plane R correction must cancel this couple, so (m r)_R × 1.00 = 0.3928 in the direction opposite to the couple vector. With r = 0.150 m, m_R = 0.3928/(1.00 × 0.150) = 2.618 kg.

Answer: 2.618 kg

(c)

The plane R correction mass vector must be opposite to the couple vector. The couple vector (Cx, Cy) = (-0.0750, 0.3855) points at atan2(0.3855, -0.0750) = 101.0°, so the plane R mass lies at 101.0° + 180° = 281.0°, measured in the same sense as the given angles. Check: the vector (m r)_R = 2.618 × 0.150 = 0.3928 kg·m at 281.0° gives x = 0.0750 and y = -0.3855, and multiplied by z_R = 1.00 these equal the negative of the couple components, so the couple polygon closes. A common mistake is to place the mass at the same angle as the couple vector, which doubles the couple instead of removing it.

Answer: 281.0 degrees

(d)

Now close the force polygon. The sum of all vectors must be zero, so (m r)_L = -(Σ m r) - (m r)_R. In components: x = -(0.4178) - (0.0750) = -0.4928 kg·m and y = -(0.6511) - (-0.3855) = -0.2655 kg·m. The magnitude is 0.5598 kg·m, so m_L = 0.5598/0.150 = 3.732 kg. Plane L carries the larger correction (3.732 kg versus 2.618 kg) because it must also cancel the net force residual left after plane R is set. Both correction masses are practical to add as bolt-on weights at 150 mm radius, and together they cancel the 76.35 kN resultant unbalanced force.

Answer: 3.732 kg

(e)

The plane L correction vector is (-0.4928, -0.2655) kg·m. Its angle is atan2(-0.2655, -0.4928), reduced to the range 0° to 360°, which is 208.3°. Verification of the complete solution: summing all five force vectors gives zero, and summing the moments of all five about plane L gives zero because only plane R has a non-zero lever arm, and it was set equal and opposite to the couple of the three original masses. A check on the arithmetic is to repeat the couple equation about plane R, which must also close and gives the same plane L answer.

Answer: 208.3 degrees

Problem 4 [A2-034] Gyroscopic effects

A marine steam turbine rotor of a coastal ferry has a polar moment of inertia of 620 kg·m² and spins at 3000 rpm about a horizontal axis parallel to the ship's centreline. The two journal bearings are 2.40 m apart. In rough water the ship pitches (rotates about a transverse horizontal axis) with simple harmonic motion: the angular displacement is θ = θ₀ sin(2πt/T), with amplitude θ₀ = 6.0° and period T = 14 s. Treat the rotor's spin speed as constant and neglect the rotor's weight and any centrifugal loads, so that only the gyroscopic effect loads the bearings. The designer must also set a limit on the pitching amplitude that the bearings can tolerate in service.

  1. (a) Find the maximum angular velocity of precession (the pitching rate) during the cycle. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum gyroscopic couple acting on the rotor. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum gyroscopic reaction force on each bearing, equal and opposite on the two bearings. [3]
  4. (d) The bearings can take no more than 3.0 kN of gyroscopic reaction. Find the largest pitching amplitude, at the same period, that meets this limit. [5]
  5. (e) State at what points in the pitching cycle the gyroscopic couple is a maximum and a minimum, and explain why, using the relation between the precession rate and the pitch angle. [3]
(a)

The precession rate is the rate of change of the pitch angle. With θ = θ₀ sin(ωt t), where ωt = 2π/T = 0.4488 rad/s, the angular velocity is dθ/dt = θ₀ ωt cos(ωt t). Its maximum is Ω_max = θ₀ ωt = (6.0° × π/180°) × 2π/14 = 0.10472 × 0.4488 = 0.04700 rad/s. This occurs when the ship passes through the mean (level) position. The pitch rate is small in absolute terms, about 2.69 degrees per second, but the rotor spin is fast and so the product that makes up the couple is substantial.

Answer: 0.0470 rad/s

(b)

The gyroscopic couple on a rotor with spin ω and precession Ω, where the two axes are perpendicular, is C = I ω Ω. The spin speed is ω = 3000 × 2π/60 = 314.16 rad/s. Then C_max = 620 × 314.16 × 0.04700 = 9154 N·m. The vector of the reaction couple that the hull and bearings exert on the rotor is perpendicular to both the spin and precession axes, so it acts about the vertical axis and tries to yaw the rotor in the horizontal plane. The direction reverses every half cycle as the pitch rate changes sign. This is the peak value, and the actual couple varies as the cosine of the pitch phase.

Answer: 9154 N·m

(c)

The bearings form a force couple that reacts the gyroscopic couple. For a bearing span L = 2.40 m, F × L = C, so F = C/L = 9154/2.40 = 3814 N = 3.81 kN at each bearing. The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction and act in the horizontal plane at right angles to the shaft axis, so they add to the static bearing loads from weight vectorially, not arithmetically. Because the force is inversely proportional to the span, a longer bearing span is a practical way to reduce the bearing loading without changing the rotor.

Answer: 3.81 kN

(d)

From F = I ω Ω/L, the limiting precession rate is Ω_lim = F_lim L/(I ω) = 3000 × 2.40/(620 × 314.16) = 0.03697 rad/s. Since Ω_max = θ₀ (2π/T), the limiting amplitude is θ₀ = Ω_lim T/(2π) = 0.03697 × 14/(2π) = 0.08236 rad = 4.72°. So the bearings are acceptable up to about 4.7° amplitude at a 14 s period; the 6° design condition exceeds the limit by a factor of 1.27. Options are a longer bearing span, bearings rated for the higher load, or a speed restriction in heavy seas, since the load is proportional to rotor speed.

Answer: 4.72 degrees

(e)

The couple is C = I ω Ω, and with constant spin ω the couple is proportional to the precession rate Ω = dθ/dt. For θ = θ₀ sin(ωt t), Ω = θ₀ ωt cos(ωt t). The couple is therefore a maximum when cos = ±1, which is when the pitch angle is zero (the ship passing through level, where the pitching is fastest). It is zero at the extremes of pitch, where θ = ±θ₀ and the ship momentarily stops before reversing, so there is no precession. The couple changes sign each time the pitching direction reverses, so the bearing reactions alternate at the pitching frequency of 1/14 Hz.

Answer: Maximum couple when the ship passes through level (pitch angle zero, pitch rate greatest); zero at the extremes of pitch.

Problem 5 [A2-035] Single degree of freedom free vibration

A vibration test rig for a small sensor module uses a horizontal steel cantilever strip to carry a 12.0 kg module at its free end. The strip is 40 mm wide and 0.600 m long, with Young's modulus 200 GPa and density 7850 kg/m³. The requirement is that the rig's first natural frequency be 18.0 Hz so that it excites the module in a band of interest. In the first design pass the strip's own mass is neglected and the module is treated as a point mass on a massless spring; the beam's tip stiffness is that of an end-loaded cantilever. The thickness of the strip is the free design variable. Take g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the tip stiffness the strip must have. [3]
  2. (b) Find the required thickness of the strip, taking the beam as massless. [5]
  3. (c) Find the static deflection of the tip under the module's weight. [3]
  4. (d) Now include the strip's own mass using the equivalent tip mass of a cantilever, 33/140 of the beam mass. Find the resulting natural frequency of the thickness found in part (b). [5]
  5. (e) The tip is pulled down 15 mm from equilibrium and released from rest, with the design frequency of 18.0 Hz assumed. Find the maximum velocity of the module in the resulting free vibration. [4]
(a)

For a single degree of freedom system the natural frequency is f = (1/2π) √(k/m), so k = m (2π f)². With ω_n = 2π × 18.0 = 113.10 rad/s, k = 12.0 × 113.10² = 153492 N/m = 153.5 kN/m. This is the stiffness the strip must provide at the tip. Because natural frequency depends on the stiffness-to-mass ratio, any error in estimating the mass, for example by neglecting the strip, shifts the frequency in proportion to the inverse square root of the effective mass. That is addressed in part (d).

Answer: 153.5 kN/m

(b)

For an end-loaded cantilever, tip stiffness k = 3EI/L³, with I = b h³/12 for a rectangular strip. Therefore I = k L³/(3E) = 153492 × 0.600³/(3 × 200×10⁹) = 5.5257 × 10⁻⁸ m⁴. Then h³ = 12 I/b = 12 × 5.5257 × 10⁻⁸/0.040 = 1.6577 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so h = 0.02550 m = 25.50 mm. The section is stocky, nearly as thick as it is wide, because a 12 kg module on a 0.6 m cantilever at 18 Hz needs a stiff beam. Since stiffness varies with h³, a 5 percent error in thickness produces about a 16 percent error in stiffness and an 8 percent error in frequency, so the strip should be ordered with a thickness tolerance in mind.

Answer: 25.50 mm

(c)

The static deflection is δ = W/k = m g/k = 12.0 × 9.81/153492 = 0.000767 m = 0.767 mm. A useful check is the relation f = (1/2π) √(g/δ), which gives (1/2π) √(9.81/0.000767) = 18.00 Hz, matching the design target of 18.0 Hz and confirming the stiffness. The static deflection of a fraction of a millimetre shows that the natural frequency of a stiff rig is high compared with the typical low-frequency excitations met in service, so the 18 Hz target is not a soft system. Marks are awarded for the equation, the substitution with consistent SI units, and the answer with its unit, so state each step.

Answer: 0.767 mm

(d)

The strip mass is m_b = ρ b h L = 7850 × 0.040 × 0.02550 × 0.600 = 4.804 kg. For a cantilever vibrating in its first mode, Rayleigh's method gives an equivalent tip mass of 33/140 of the distributed mass, so m_eff = 12.0 + (33/140) × 4.804 = 13.132 kg. The natural frequency becomes f = (1/2π) √(k/m_eff) = (1/2π) √(153492/13.132) = 17.21 Hz. The frequency is about 4.41 percent below the target, because the beam mass was neglected. To recover 18.0 Hz the thickness would have to be iterated upward slightly, since the stiffness rises faster with thickness than the added mass.

Answer: 17.21 Hz

(e)

For undamped free vibration released from rest, x(t) = x₀ cos(ω_n t), so the velocity is v(t) = -x₀ ω_n sin(ω_n t) and its maximum magnitude is v_max = x₀ ω_n. Using ω_n = 113.10 rad/s and x₀ = 0.015 m, v_max = 0.015 × 113.10 = 1.696 m/s. The maximum velocity occurs as the module passes through equilibrium, where the potential energy stored in the strip, ½ k x₀² = 17.27 J, has been fully converted to kinetic energy ½ m v² = 17.27 J. This energy equality is a useful independent check on the answer.

Answer: 1.696 m/s

A2 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A2-036] Damped free vibration and logarithmic decrement

An instrument platform of mass 45.0 kg rests on a spring of stiffness 2.10×10⁵ N/m in the vertical direction, with a linear viscous damper in parallel. After any knock, the platform must settle quickly so that readings can be taken. The specification is that the free-vibration amplitude falls to 5.0 percent of its initial value within 3 complete cycles of the damped motion. The damper is to be chosen as a single viscous element and the response treated as a single degree of freedom, with the platform constrained to move vertically only. After selecting the damper, the lab wants to know how long a disturbance takes to fall inside a 1.0 percent envelope.

  1. (a) Find the critical damping coefficient of the system. [4]
  2. (b) Find the damping ratio needed to meet the 3-cycle, 5 percent specification. [6]
  3. (c) Find the damping coefficient of the damper to be purchased. [3]
  4. (d) Find the period of the damped oscillation. [3]
  5. (e) Find the time for the amplitude envelope to fall to 1.0 percent of its initial value. [4]
(a)

Critical damping is the value at which the system just fails to oscillate, c_c = 2√(km) = 2 m ω_n. The undamped natural frequency is ω_n = √(k/m) = √(2.10×10⁵/45.0) = 68.31 rad/s (10.87 Hz). Then c_c = 2 × √(2.10×10⁵ × 45.0) = 2 × 3074.1 = 6148 N·s/m. Any damper below this value gives an underdamped, oscillatory response, which is what the specification assumes because it counts cycles. The damping ratio is later defined as ζ = c/c_c. The critical damping coefficient depends only on the stiffness and the mass, not on the damper, so it is a property of the structure that can be found before any damper is selected. Units of N·s/m confirm the result is a damping coefficient.

Answer: 6148 N·s/m

(b)

The logarithmic decrement relates successive peaks: δ = ln(x(n)/x(n+1)), and over N cycles ln(x₀/x_N) = N δ. Here the amplitude must fall to 0.05 of its initial value in N = 3 cycles, so δ = ln(1/0.05)/3 = ln(20)/3 = 0.9986. For viscous damping δ = 2πζ/√(1 - ζ²), which rearranges to ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²). Substituting: ζ = 0.9986/√(39.478 + 0.9972) = 0.9986/6.3620 = 0.1570. This is a lightly to moderately damped value, well below 1, so the system will still ring for a few cycles but decay quickly, and the result confirms the underdamped assumption.

Answer: 0.1570

(c)

The damping coefficient is c = ζ c_c = 0.1570 × 6148 = 965 N·s/m. The designer would buy the nearest standard damper size and then check the specification with the actual value, since the amplitude after 3 cycles scales roughly as exp(-2π ζ N), so a damper 10 percent weaker than this would leave about 6.8 percent of the amplitude after three cycles instead of 5.0 percent. Damper coefficients also vary with temperature and amplitude in real fluid dampers, so a margin is recommended. The damped natural frequency calculation in part (d) uses this chosen value.

Answer: 965 N·s/m

(d)

The damped angular frequency is ω_d = ω_n √(1 - ζ²) = 68.31 × √(1 - 0.1570²) = 68.31 × 0.9876 = 67.47 rad/s. The period of the damped oscillation is T_d = 2π/ω_d = 2π/67.47 = 0.09313 s = 93.1 ms. The damping lengthens the period by only about 1.3 percent compared with the undamped period of 92.0 ms, which is why the undamped frequency is often used for quick estimates when ζ is below about 0.2. Three cycles last 0.279 s, which is how long the platform needs to settle to 5 percent.

Answer: 93.1 ms

(e)

The envelope of the free response decays as x₀ e-ζ ω_n t. Setting this equal to 0.01 x₀ gives ζ ω_n t = ln(100) = 4.6052. With ζ ω_n = 0.1570 × 68.31 = 10.72 s⁻¹, t = 4.6052/10.72 = 0.429 s. This is 4.61 damped cycles. The time constant of the envelope is 1/(ζ ω_n) = 0.0933 s, so the platform reaches 1 percent after 4.6 time constants. A check on the specification is that 3 cycles (0.279 s) correspond to the 5 percent level, ln(20)/10.72 = 0.279 s, matching the cycle count.

Answer: 0.429 s

Problem 2 [A2-037] Forced vibration and resonance

A precision rotary table of mass 120 kg (including its payload) is supported by elastic mounts with a combined vertical stiffness of 3.00×10⁶ N/m. A nearby reciprocating compressor applies a harmonic vertical force of amplitude 650 N directly to the table through its structure, at a frequency of 22.0 Hz. The mounts have a damping ratio of 0.040. The table is modelled as a single degree of freedom system and only the steady-state response is of interest. The lab specification states that the vibration amplitude must not exceed 0.50 mm even if the excitation frequency drifts onto the table's resonance, so the designer must decide how much extra damping to add. After adding it, the transmitted force into the floor must be checked.

  1. (a) Find the natural frequency of the table on its mounts. [3]
  2. (b) Find the steady-state amplitude of the table at 22.0 Hz with the existing damping. [5]
  3. (c) Find the damping ratio that limits the amplitude to 0.50 mm at exact resonance. [5]
  4. (d) With that damping ratio, find the steady-state amplitude at 22.0 Hz. [3]
  5. (e) With that damping ratio, find the amplitude of force transmitted to the floor at 22.0 Hz. [4]
(a)

The undamped natural frequency is ω_n = √(k/m) = √(3.00×10⁶/120) = 158.11 rad/s, so f_n = ω_n/2π = 25.16 Hz. The excitation at 22.0 Hz lies below this, giving a frequency ratio r = 22.0/25.16 = 0.8742. That is only 12.6 percent below resonance, which signals that the response will be strongly amplified. The static deflection under the force amplitude is δ_st = F₀/k = 650/(3.00×10⁶) = 0.2167 mm, which sets the scale for all amplitudes below. Note that the force amplitude, not a base motion, drives this system, so the magnification factor applies directly to the static deflection. Keep the units consistent in newtons and metres before converting to millimetres for the final answer.

Answer: 25.16 Hz

(b)

For a steady-state harmonic force the amplitude is X = δ_st/√((1 - r²)² + (2ζ r)²). With r = 0.8742: 1 - r² = 0.2357, so (1 - r²)² = 0.05555; 2ζ r = 2 × 0.040 × 0.8742 = 0.0699, squared 0.00489. The sum is 0.06045 and the square root is 0.2459. Then X = 0.2167 mm/0.2459 = 0.881 mm. The dynamic magnification factor is 4.07, so the force at 22 Hz produces nearly 4.1 times the static deflection. At exact resonance with ζ = 0.040 the amplitude would be δ_st/(2ζ) = 2.708 mm, above the specified limit.

Answer: 0.881 mm

(c)

At resonance (r = 1) the amplitude is X = δ_st/(2ζ). The requirement X ≤ 0.50 mm gives ζ ≥ δ_st/(2 X_lim) = 2.1667 × 10⁻⁴/(2 × 5.0×10⁻⁴) = 0.2167. So the damping ratio must increase from 0.040 to at least 0.2167, about 5.4 times the existing value. This is a high damping ratio for elastomer mounts, so the designer would probably need a viscous damper or a tuned damper rather than simply a different rubber compound. The resonance case is the governing one because the specification says the frequency may drift; at 22 Hz the amplitude is already lower, as part (d) shows.

Answer: 0.2167

(d)

Using ζ = 0.2167 and r = 0.8742: 2ζ r = 0.3788, squared 0.14352; (1 - r²)² = 0.05555. The sum is 0.19907, with square root 0.4462. Then X = 0.2167 mm/0.4462 = 0.486 mm. The amplitude at 22 Hz is just inside the 0.50 mm limit and well below the 0.881 mm found with the original damping, showing that added damping helps strongly near resonance. Because r = 0.87 is close to 1, the response at 22 Hz is almost as large as at resonance itself, so the design meets the limit with very little margin.

Answer: 0.486 mm

(e)

Force transmitted through the mount spring and damper is F_T = k X √(1 + (2ζ r)²). Using X = 4.856088 × 10⁻⁴ m: k X = 3.00×10⁶ × 4.856088 × 10⁻⁴ = 1456.8 N, and √(1 + (2ζ r)²) = √(1 + 0.14352) = 1.0694. So F_T = 1456.8 × 1.0694 = 1557.9 N. The transmitted force is 240 percent of the applied 650 N, so the mounts amplify the load rather than isolate it. This is expected: a system excited below √2 times its natural frequency never isolates, and extra damping cannot change that. The floor should be checked for this larger force.

Answer: 1557.9 N

Problem 3 [A2-038] Base excitation and vibration isolation

A calibration instrument of mass 85.0 kg is to be mounted on elastomeric isolators on the floor of a mobile laboratory trailer. Measurements show that the floor vibrates vertically and harmonically at 35.0 Hz with an amplitude of 1.50 mm, due to the trailer's generator. The instrument manufacturer requires that the amplitude of the instrument's absolute motion be no more than 15 percent of the floor amplitude, that is a displacement transmissibility of 0.15 at 35.0 Hz. The chosen isolators have a damping ratio of 0.10. Treat the isolators as a single linear spring of combined stiffness k in parallel with viscous damping, and use the steady-state response. Take g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the frequency ratio r = ω/ω_n that gives a transmissibility of 0.15 (use the isolation region, r greater than √2). [5]
  2. (b) Find the combined stiffness of the isolators. [4]
  3. (c) Find the static deflection of the isolators under the instrument's weight. [3]
  4. (d) Find the amplitude of absolute acceleration of the instrument at 35.0 Hz. [4]
  5. (e) Find the amplitude of relative displacement across the isolators at 35.0 Hz. [4]
(a)

For base excitation of a damped single degree of freedom system the displacement transmissibility is T = X/Y = √[(1 + (2ζ r)²)/((1 - r²)² + (2ζ r)²)], with r = ω/ω_n. Isolation (T below 1) occurs only for r > √2 = 1.414, so the solution is sought there. The equation cannot be solved in closed form for r with ζ fixed, so it is solved by trial or by squaring and rearranging into a quadratic in r². Setting ζ = 0.10 and T = 0.15, the root above √2 is r = 2.953. Check: at r = 2.953, 2ζ r = 0.5906, the numerator is 1.3488, the denominator is 59.9466, and T = 0.1500, matching the requirement.

Answer: 2.953

(b)

From r = ω/ω_n the required natural frequency is f_n = f/r = 35.0/2.953 = 11.853 Hz, so ω_n = 2π f_n = 74.472 rad/s. For a mass m on a spring, k = m ω_n² = 85.0 × 74.472² = 471412 N/m = 471.4 kN/m. This is the total stiffness across all isolators combined. A designer would divide this among, say, four mounts and choose an elastomer hardness to match, noting that the dynamic stiffness of rubber is often 1.3 to 2 times its static value, which would need to be allowed for when selecting mounts.

Answer: 471.4 kN/m

(c)

The static deflection is δ_st = m g/k = 85.0 × 9.81/471412 = 0.00177 m = 1.77 mm. A check using δ_st = g/ω_n² gives 9.81/74.472² = 0.00177 m. A deflection of about 1.8 mm is typical of isolators for a 35 Hz disturbance, and it is practical because it is large enough to be reliably measured and small enough to avoid rocking problems. If the isolators were softer for greater isolation, the static deflection would rise as 1/f_n², so halving the natural frequency would quadruple the deflection. Keep units consistent in newtons and metres and state the final value in millimetres. Marks are given for the equation, the substitution and the interpretation.

Answer: 1.77 mm

(d)

The instrument's absolute displacement amplitude is X = T Y = 0.15 × 1.50 mm = 0.225 mm. For harmonic motion the acceleration amplitude is ω² X, with ω = 2π × 35.0 = 219.91 rad/s. Then a = 219.91² × 0.000225 = 10.881 m/s², which is 1.109 g. For comparison, the floor itself moves with acceleration amplitude ω² Y = 72.54 m/s², so the isolator reduces the acceleration at the instrument by the same factor T = 0.15. Acceleration is the quantity the instrument's internal sensors respond to, so it is the quantity in the manufacturer's requirement.

Answer: 10.881 m/s²

(e)

The relative displacement z = x - y of the mass with respect to the base has amplitude Z = Y r²/√[(1 - r²)² + (2ζ r)²]. With r = 2.953: r² = 8.7200, (1 - r²)² = 59.598, (2ζ r)² = 0.34880. The root is 7.7425, so Z = 1.50 × 8.7200/7.7425 = 1.689 mm. At high frequency ratio the relative motion approaches the base amplitude of 1.50 mm, because the mass is almost stationary in space and the isolator absorbs the whole floor motion. That is the mechanism of isolation: the isolator must have a stroke clearance of at least this amount plus the static deflection.

Answer: 1.689 mm

Problem 4 [A2-039] Rotating unbalance

A centrifugal blower of total mass 220 kg, including its motor, is to be mounted on a rigid frame that is supported by springs and constrained to move vertically only. The impeller has a residual unbalance equivalent to 0.45 kg at an eccentricity of 0.18 m, and the blower runs at 1450 rpm. The isolators contribute a damping ratio of 0.07. To protect nearby equipment, the vertical vibration amplitude of the blower at its running speed must not exceed 0.40 mm, and the designer must choose the combined spring stiffness. Once chosen, the force passed into the foundation at running speed and the peak amplitude as the blower runs up through resonance on starting must be reviewed.

  1. (a) Find the frequency ratio r = ω/ω_n that makes the amplitude exactly 0.40 mm at running speed, using the isolation region where r exceeds 1. [6]
  2. (b) Find the combined spring stiffness needed. [4]
  3. (c) Find the amplitude of the force transmitted to the foundation at running speed. [4]
  4. (d) Find the peak steady-state amplitude of the blower if it were to dwell at resonance. [3]
  5. (e) Find the natural frequency of the mounted blower and state whether starting the machine takes it through this natural frequency. [3]
(a)

For rotating unbalance the steady-state amplitude is X = (m₀e/M) r²/√[(1 - r²)² + (2ζ r)²], with r = ω/ω_n and m₀e = 0.45 × 0.18 = 0.0810 kg·m. The limit X ≤ 0.40 mm requires the magnification ratio R = r²/√[...] = X M/(m₀e) = 4.0×10⁻⁴ × 220/0.0810 = 1.0864. For r > 1 this ratio falls toward 1 from above as r grows, so a large enough r is needed. Solving R(r) = 1.0864 for r with ζ = 0.07 by trial gives r = 3.527. Check: r² = 12.4375; denominator = 11.4482; R = 1.0864, matching the requirement. A lower stiffness (larger r) is the only way to reduce the running amplitude below the 1.0 limit.

Answer: 3.527

(b)

The running speed is ω = 1450 × 2π/60 = 151.84 rad/s. The natural frequency required is ω_n = ω/r = 151.84/3.527 = 43.06 rad/s. The combined spring stiffness for the blower of mass 220 kg is k = M ω_n² = 220 × 43.06² = 407833 N/m = 407.8 kN/m. This is the total stiffness across all spring supports. The resulting static deflection of M g/k = 5.3 mm is large enough that the springs can be designed as coil springs with a modest travel. A designer would then split this stiffness among four or more corner mounts.

Answer: 407.8 kN/m

(c)

The transmitted force is the sum of the spring and damper forces: F_T = k X √(1 + (2ζ r)²). First X = (m₀e/M) R = (0.0810/220) × 1.0864 = 4.000000 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.400 mm. The spring force amplitude is k X = 407833 × 4.000000 × 10⁻⁴ = 163.1 N. The factor √(1 + (2ζ r)²) with 2ζ r = 0.4937 equals 1.1152. So F_T = 163.1 × 1.1152 = 182 N. For comparison, the unbalance force itself is m₀e ω² = 0.0810 × 151.84² = 1868 N, so the isolators transmit 10 percent of the exciting force. At r above √2 the transmitted force is less than the exciting force, confirming isolation is working.

Answer: 182 N

(d)

At resonance (r = 1) the amplitude is X = (m₀e/M)/(2ζ) because r² = 1 and the denominator reduces to 2ζ. Then X = (0.0810/220)/(2 × 0.07) = 3.681818 × 10⁻⁴/0.14 = 2.629870 × 10⁻³ m = 2.630 mm. This is 6.6 times the running amplitude of 0.400 mm. The blower will not dwell at resonance in normal service, but it passes through the resonance region on start-up and shut-down, so this value is the upper bound of the amplitude during the run-up, which is a short transient in practice. In reality the peak during acceleration is somewhat lower than the steady-state resonance amplitude because the response does not have time to build to its steady value.

Answer: 2.630 mm

(e)

The natural frequency is f_n = ω_n/(2π) = 43.06/(2π) = 6.85 Hz, compared with the running frequency of 1450/60 = 24.17 Hz. Since the running speed is above the natural frequency (r = 3.53 > 1), the blower must accelerate from rest through f_n = 6.85 Hz, where r = 1, before reaching its operating speed. It therefore does pass through resonance on every start and stop. The designer should accelerate quickly through this range, and the damping ratio of 0.07 limits the peak amplitude to the value found in part (d).

Answer: 6.85 Hz

Problem 5 [A2-040] Two degree of freedom systems and mode shapes

A small roof-mounted sensor pod is modelled as two lumped masses moving in one horizontal direction. Mass m₁ = 40.0 kg is the pod base, connected to the rigid roof by a mount of stiffness k₁ = 6.00×10⁵ N/m. Mass m₂ = 25.0 kg is the instrument carriage, connected to the base by a flexure of stiffness k₂ = 3.00×10⁵ N/m. Damping is negligible and motion is along a single line. The designer must first find the natural frequencies and mode shapes of this arrangement. A redesign then asks for the flexure stiffness k₂ that brings the lowest natural frequency of the system down to 12.0 Hz, to put it clear of a known 15 Hz disturbance from a rooftop fan.

  1. (a) Find the lowest natural frequency of the original system. [5]
  2. (b) Find the second natural frequency of the original system. [4]
  3. (c) Find the amplitude ratio x₂/x₁ in the first (lowest) mode. [3]
  4. (d) Find the flexure stiffness k₂ that makes the lowest natural frequency 12.0 Hz. [5]
  5. (e) With that redesigned stiffness, find the second natural frequency. [3]
(a)

Let x₁ and x₂ be the displacements of the masses. The equations of motion are m₁ẍ₁ + (k₁ + k₂)x₁ - k₂x₂ = 0 and m₂ẍ₂ - k₂x₁ + k₂x₂ = 0. For harmonic motion with frequency ω, the characteristic determinant gives m₁m₂ ω⁴ - [m₁k₂ + m₂(k₁ + k₂)] ω² + k₁k₂ = 0. Numerically, m₁m₂ = 1000, the bracket is 40.0×3.00×10⁵ + 25.0×9.00×10⁵ = 3.4500 × 10⁷, and k₁k₂ = 1.8000 × 10¹¹. Then ω² = [3.4500 × 10⁷ ± √(3.4500e+07² - 4 × 1000 × 1.8000 × 10¹¹)]/(2 × 1000). The smaller root is ω₁² = 6407.4, so ω₁ = 80.05 rad/s and f₁ = ω₁/2π = 12.74 Hz.

Answer: 12.74 Hz

(b)

The larger root of the same characteristic equation is ω₂² = 28092.6 (rad/s)², so ω₂ = 167.61 rad/s. The natural frequency is f₂ = ω₂/2π = 26.68 Hz. As a check, the sum of the two roots must equal the bracket divided by m₁m₂: 6407.4 + 28092.6 = 34500.0, and 3.4500 × 10⁷/1000 = 34500.0. The product of the roots equals k₁k₂/(m₁m₂) = 180000000.0, also matching. The ratio f₂/f₁ = 2.09, so the two modes are well separated, which means an excitation near either one would excite mostly that mode alone. Always check that the frequencies are real and positive and that the higher root is the larger, since a sign slip in the bracket gives a negative discriminant or swapped roots.

Answer: 26.68 Hz

(c)

The first row of the equation of motion gives the mode shape: (k₁ + k₂ - m₁ω²)x₁ = k₂x₂, so x₂/x₁ = (k₁ + k₂ - m₁ω₁²)/k₂. With ω₁² = 6407.4: m₁ω₁² = 256295 N/m equivalent, and the numerator is 9.00×10⁵ - 256295 = 643705. Dividing by k₂ = 3.00×10⁵ gives x₂/x₁ = 2.146. The ratio is positive, so in the lowest mode both masses move in phase, and the carriage swings further than the base. The mode has no node between the masses. The second row gives the same ratio, which provides a check: k₂/(k₂ - m₂ω₁²) = 2.146.

Answer: 2.146

(d)

For a target of 12.0 Hz, ω₁ = 2π × 12.0 = 75.398 rad/s, ω₁² = 5684.9. Substituting into the characteristic equation m₁m₂ ω⁴ - [m₁k₂ + m₂(k₁ + k₂)] ω² + k₁k₂ = 0 and collecting terms in k₂ gives a linear equation in k₂, since k₂ appears only to the first power: m₁m₂ω⁴ - (m₁k₂ + m₂k₁ + m₂k₂)ω² + k₁k₂ = 0, so k₂ [k₁ - (m₁ + m₂)ω²] = m₂k₁ω² - m₁m₂ω⁴. Numerically, the left bracket is 6.00×10⁵ - 65.0 × 5684.9 = 230482 and the right side is 25.0 × 6.00×10⁵ × 5684.9 - 1000 × 5684.9² = 5.2955 × 10¹⁰. So k₂ = 5.2955 × 10¹⁰/230482 = 229759 N/m = 229.8 kN/m. This is about 77 percent of the original flexure stiffness, a considerably softer flexure.

Answer: 229.8 kN/m

(e)

With k₂ = 229759 N/m the same characteristic equation now has coefficients m₁m₂ = 1000, bracket = 40.0 × 229759 + 25.0 × (6.00×10⁵ + 229759) = 2.9934 × 10⁷, and k₁k₂ = 1.3786 × 10¹¹. The sum of the two roots is 2.9934 × 10⁷/1000 = 29934.4 (rad/s)². The first root is 5684.9, so the second root is 24249.5, giving ω₂ = 155.72 rad/s and f₂ = 24.78 Hz. The lower mode moves to 12.0 Hz, clear of 15 Hz fan frequency by 3 Hz, but the second mode stays well above it. The mode shape ratio x₂/x₁ in the first mode is now 2.62, which shows that the carriage motion has become larger compared with the base, so the carriage amplitude under base shake will rise.

Answer: 24.78 Hz

A2 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A2-041] Vibration absorbers

A centrifugal blower of mass 450 kg is carried on springs of total vertical stiffness 1.8 MN/m, and damping can be neglected. The blower runs at a fixed 640 rpm and its unbalanced impeller produces a vertical harmonic force of amplitude 900 N at that speed. The plant engineer finds the vibration at the mounts unacceptable. A tuned vibration absorber will be fitted, with a mass equal to 10 percent of the blower mass and tuned to the running speed. Treat the blower as a single degree of freedom system with the absorber as a second spring and mass attached to it.

  1. (a) Find the steady-state amplitude of the blower, in mm, before any absorber is fitted. [4]
  2. (b) Find the absorber spring stiffness, in kN/m, that tunes it to the running speed. [4]
  3. (c) Find the steady-state amplitude of the absorber mass, in mm, at the running speed. [4]
  4. (d) Find the lower of the two natural frequencies of the blower plus absorber system, in rpm. [4]
  5. (e) Find by what percentage of the running speed the lower natural speed lies below it, and comment on the consequence for start-up. [4]
(a)

Assumptions: undamped single degree of freedom system under a harmonic force. Running speed ω = 2π(640)/60 = 67.02 rad/s. Natural frequency ωn = √(k/M) = √(1.8×10⁶/450) = 63.25 rad/s, so the machine runs about 6 percent above resonance. Steady-state amplitude X = F0/|k − Mω²|. Here Mω² = 450 × 67.02² = 2.021×10⁶ N/m, so k − Mω² = -2.213×10⁵ N/m. The negative sign only means the response is 180 degrees out of phase with the force; the magnitude is what matters. X = 900/2.213×10⁵ = 4.07 mm. A marker rewards noting that the operating point is close to resonance, which is why even a modest 900 N force gives a large amplitude.

Answer: 4.07 mm

(b)

Absorber mass ma = 0.10 × 450 = 45 kg. Tuning means the absorber alone has natural frequency equal to the forcing frequency, ka/ma = ω². Therefore ka = ma ω² = 45 × 67.02² = 2.0213×10⁵ N/m = 202.1 kN/m. Note that the tuning condition uses the running frequency, not the main system's natural frequency. For a machine running exactly at resonance the two are equal, but here the blower runs slightly above ωn, so using k/M would detune the absorber. With this stiffness the absorber spring force on the blower can cancel the applied force exactly, which makes the blower's steady-state amplitude zero at this speed. The ratio ka/k = 0.112 is small, so the absorber spring is much softer than the mounts, as expected for a 10 percent mass.

Answer: 202.1 kN/m

(c)

With the absorber tuned and the blower stationary in steady state (X = 0), the blower equation of motion reduces to a force balance: the spring force from the absorber must cancel the applied force, so ka Xa = F0 in magnitude. The absorber amplitude is therefore Xa = F0/ka = 900/2.0213×10⁵ = 4.45 mm, with the absorber moving 180 degrees out of phase with the force. Check with the absorber equation: −ma ω² Xa + ka Xa = ka X = 0, which holds since ka = ma ω². The dynamic force carried by the absorber spring is ka Xa = 900 N, equal to F0, which is a useful design check for the spring and its fatigue life. A stroke of about 4.5 mm each side of the mean is modest and easy to accommodate in the absorber housing.

Answer: 4.45 mm

(d)

Equations of motion with x1 for the blower and x2 for the absorber: M x1'' + (k + ka) x1 − ka x2 = F; ma x2'' − ka x1 + ka x2 = 0. The natural frequencies come from det(K − ω²M) = 0 with K = [[k + ka, −ka],[−ka, ka]] and M = diag(450, 45). Numerically k + ka = 2.0021×10⁶ N/m and ka = 2.0213×10⁵ N/m. Solving the resulting quadratic in ω² gives ω1² = 3049.9 and ω2² = 5891.1 rad²/s², so ω1 = 55.23 rad/s and ω2 = 76.75 rad/s. The lower natural speed is n1 = ω1 × 60/(2π) = 527.4 rpm and the upper is n2 = 732.9 rpm. The running speed of 640 rpm lies between the two, which is the standard result when a tuned absorber is added to a system running at its tuned frequency.

Answer: 527.4 rpm

(e)

Margin = (N − n1)/N × 100 = (640 − 527.4)/640 × 100 = 17.6 percent. The lower natural speed is therefore about 17 to 18 percent below the running speed, and the upper natural speed (732.9 rpm) is about 1.15 times the running speed. Because the blower must accelerate from rest to 640 rpm, it passes through the lower resonance at about 527.4 rpm on every start-up, and the undamped model predicts a very large amplitude there. In practice the passage is brief and real systems have some damping, but a designer would either accelerate quickly through that speed or add damping to the absorber. The absorber is therefore effective only over a narrow band around the tuned speed, a limitation a marker expects the candidate to state.

Answer: 17.6 percent

Problem 2 [A2-042] Torsional vibration of shafts

A 1800 rpm electric motor drives a water pump through a straight solid steel shaft of length 0.90 m. The motor rotor has polar mass moment of inertia 0.80 kg·m² and the pump impeller 0.30 kg·m². The shaft mass and the stiffness of the two rotors themselves are negligible, and the shear modulus of steel is 79 GPa. The specification requires that the first torsional natural frequency of the two-rotor system be at least 30 percent above the running speed, to keep clear of the torque pulsations at running speed. Shaft diameters are supplied in 5 mm steps. Treat the motor rotor and the pump impeller as rigid discs and ignore any coupling flexibility.

  1. (a) Find the minimum shaft torsional stiffness, in kN·m/rad, that satisfies the specification. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum shaft diameter, in mm, that gives this stiffness. [4]
  3. (c) Using the next standard diameter, find the first torsional natural frequency in Hz. [4]
  4. (d) Find the distance of the vibration node from the motor rotor, in metres. [4]
  5. (e) If a fluctuating torque of amplitude 1500 N·m is transmitted, find the maximum shear stress amplitude in the standard-diameter shaft, in MPa. [4]
(a)

Assumptions: two rigid rotors joined by a massless shaft, free torsional motion, no damping. Running speed ω = 2π(1800)/60 = 188.50 rad/s. The requirement is ωn ≥ 1.30 ω = 245.04 rad/s. For a two-rotor system the single non-zero natural frequency is ωn = √[kt (J1 + J2)/(J1 J2)]. Rearranging, kt = ωn² J1 J2/(J1 + J2). Substituting, kt = 245.04² × 0.80 × 0.30/(0.80 + 0.30) = 60047 × 0.21818 = 13101 N·m/rad, which is 13.1 kN·m/rad. This is the minimum stiffness: a stiffer shaft only raises the natural frequency further above the running speed, so the margin improves. The reduced inertia J1J2/(J1 + J2) = 0.2182 kg·m² is the value that controls the frequency.

Answer: 13.1 kN·m/rad

(b)

Torsional stiffness of a solid circular shaft is kt = G J/L with polar second moment of area J = πd⁴/32. Hence kt = πG d⁴/(32 L), and d = (32 kt L/(π G))1/4. Substituting, d = (32 × 13101 × 0.90/(π × 79×10⁹))1/4 = (1.5203×10⁻⁶ m⁴)1/4 = 0.03511 m = 35.11 mm. Since diameters come in 5 mm steps, a shaft of 40 mm is the smallest that passes. Using exactly the computed value would meet the specification with no margin, and any rounding down would fail it. The marker rewards the candidate who rounds up to the next size and who notes that stiffness varies as d⁴, so a small increase in diameter gives a large gain in frequency, here a gain of about 68 percent in kt.

Answer: 35.11 mm

(c)

For the 40 mm shaft, kt = πG d⁴/(32L) = π × 79×10⁹ × 0.040⁴/(32 × 0.90) = 22061 N·m/rad. The natural frequency is ωn = √[kt (J1 + J2)/(J1 J2)] = √[22061 × 1.10/(0.80 × 0.30)] = √1.0111×10⁵ = 317.98 rad/s. Convert to hertz, f = ωn/2π = 317.98/(2π) = 50.61 Hz, which corresponds to 3037 rpm. This is 1.69 times the running speed of 30 Hz. The requirement of at least 1.30 times is met with comfortable room, because the standard size is much stiffer than the minimum. A candidate should remark that with the margin this large the stiffer shaft is acceptable, but also that a stiffer shaft transmits larger torque peaks, which affects the coupling choice.

Answer: 50.61 Hz

(d)

For free torsional vibration of two rotors on a shaft, the shaft section at the node does not twist, and the two rotors oscillate in anti-phase. The condition is that the angular momentum is conserved: J1 θ1 = −J2 θ2, so the amplitudes are inversely proportional to the inertias. Equivalently, the node divides the shaft length in inverse proportion to the inertias. Let l1 be the distance from the motor to the node. Then l1 = L J2/(J1 + J2) = 0.90 × 0.30/(0.80 + 0.30) = 0.2455 m, and the distance to the pump is l2 = L J1/(J1 + J2) = 0.6545 m. The node lies closer to the heavier motor rotor, as expected, since the heavy rotor moves through a smaller angle. Check: each rotor with its own shaft length has the same natural frequency, ωn² = G J/(l1 J1) = G J/(l2 J2). Here l1 J1 = 0.1964 and l2 J2 = 0.1964, which are equal, confirming the result.

Answer: 0.2455 m

(e)

The shaft carries the full torque amplitude at every section (it is a torque member, with no distributed load), so the maximum shear stress occurs at the outer surface where τ = T r/J = 16 T/(π d³). Substituting, τ = 16 × 1500/(π × 0.040³) = 1.1937×10⁸ Pa = 119.4 MPa. This is a stress amplitude, so for fatigue it is compared with the endurance limit in shear after the usual modifying factors, not with the static yield strength. A typical shear endurance limit for a medium-carbon steel shaft is of the order of 100 to 150 MPa before stress concentration, so a keyway or shoulder here would be a concern. The marker would credit a comment that the node section has the largest relative twist per unit torque, but that the shaft torque is the same everywhere along its length, and that a larger diameter reduces stress as 1/d³.

Answer: 119.4 MPa

Problem 3 [A2-043] Critical speed of shafts

A mixing impeller of mass 35 kg is mounted at the midpoint of a horizontal solid steel shaft that is 1.20 m long between two self-aligning bearings, which may be treated as simple supports. Take E = 207 GPa and steel density 7850 kg/m³. The shaft turns at 3000 rpm. For safety the operating speed must not exceed 70 percent of the first lateral critical speed. Shaft diameters are supplied in 5 mm steps. The impeller may be treated as a point mass at midspan. In the first estimate neglect the mass of the shaft itself, and then account for it with Rayleigh's method using an equivalent midspan mass of 0.4857 times the shaft mass.

  1. (a) Find the lowest critical speed, in rpm, that the shaft must have to meet the 70 percent rule. [4]
  2. (b) Neglecting shaft mass, find the minimum shaft diameter in mm. [4]
  3. (c) For the next standard diameter above your answer to (b), find the first critical speed in rpm including the shaft mass. [4]
  4. (d) For that same standard diameter, find the static deflection of the shaft at midspan under the impeller weight alone, in mm. [4]
  5. (e) Including shaft mass, find the smallest diameter in 5 mm steps for which the 70 percent rule is satisfied, in mm. [4]
(a)

The first lateral critical speed is the natural frequency of the lateral vibration of the shaft carrying the impeller. The rule requires operating speed N ≤ 0.70 Nc, so Nc ≥ N/0.70. Operating speed ω = 2π(3000)/60 = 314.16 rad/s. The required critical angular speed is ωc = 314.16/0.70 = 448.80 rad/s, and in rpm Nc = 3000/0.70 = 4285.7 rpm. The required equivalent stiffness at midspan then follows as k = m ωc² = 35 × 448.80² = 7.05×10⁶ N/m. A marker looks for the clear statement that the operating speed is below the critical speed in this design (sub-critical operation), together with the use of rad/s in the stiffness formula.

Answer: 4285.7 rpm

(b)

A simply supported beam with a central point load has midspan stiffness k = 48 E I/L³. Therefore I = k L³/(48 E) = 7.05×10⁶ × 1.20³/(48 × 207×10⁹) = 1.226×10⁻⁶ m⁴. For a solid round section I = π d⁴/64, so d = (64 I/π)1/4 = (64 × 1.226×10⁻⁶/π)1/4 = 0.07069 m = 70.69 mm. This is the minimum diameter if the shaft mass is neglected. Because of rounding to a standard size and because the shaft mass will lower the critical speed, the real design will need a diameter above this value. The sensitivity is strong: stiffness is proportional to d⁴, so a 10 percent change in diameter changes the critical speed by roughly 21 percent. Assumptions: simple supports, no gyroscopic effect, no bearing flexibility, which are common simplifications.

Answer: 70.69 mm

(c)

The next standard size above 70.69 mm is 75 mm. Its second moment is I = π(0.075)⁴/64 = 1.553×10⁻⁶ m⁴, so the midspan stiffness is k = 48 E I/L³ = 48 × 207×10⁹ × 1.553×10⁻⁶/1.20³ = 8.931×10⁶ N/m. Shaft mass = ρ (π/4) d² L = 7850 × (π/4) × 0.075² × 1.20 = 41.62 kg, so the equivalent mass is m + 0.4857 ms = 35 + 0.4857 × 41.62 = 55.21 kg. Then ωc = √(k/me) = √(8.931×10⁶/55.21) = 402.18 rad/s, which is Nc = 402.18 × 60/(2π) = 3840.5 rpm. The shaft mass has reduced the speed noticeably compared with the mass-free estimate. The ratio of operating speed to this critical speed is 3000/3840.5 = 0.781, which exceeds 0.70.

Answer: 3840.5 rpm

(d)

Static deflection under the impeller weight alone: δ = W/k = m g/k = 35 × 9.81/8.931×10⁶ = 3.845×10⁻⁵ m = 0.03845 mm. This is very small, which is typical of a stiff shaft. A useful cross-check is the Rayleigh relation ωc = √(g/δ): √(9.81/3.845×10⁻⁵) = 505.1 rad/s, which corresponds to the critical speed of the same shaft with the impeller treated as the only mass, 4823.7 rpm. That figure is higher than the answer to (c) because the shaft mass was ignored in the check. The comparison shows that a mass-free estimate flatters the design. The marker also rewards recognising that the deflection is only a fraction of a millimetre, so the shaft is not close to bending-stress limits from the impeller weight alone.

Answer: 0.03845 mm

(e)

The 75 mm shaft gives a ratio of 0.781, so it fails the rule once the shaft mass is included, even though it passed the mass-free test. We repeat the calculation of part (c) for larger diameters. At 80 mm, I = π(0.080)⁴/64, k = 48 E I/L³ and the equivalent mass is 35 + 0.4857ρ(π/4)d²L; the resulting ratio is still above 0.70. At 85 mm the critical speed is 4694.6 rpm, and the ratio is 3000/4694.6 = 0.639, which is below 0.70. So 85 mm is the smallest 5 mm step that satisfies the rule. This shows that the answer to (b) was only a starting point, and that a design check with shaft mass included is required. The marker rewards a candidate who iterates and who states the sizing is limited by stiffness, not stress.

Answer: 85 mm

Problem 4 [A2-044] Rigid body planar kinetics with energy methods

A site hoist uses a winch drum, modelled as a uniform solid cylinder of mass 60 kg and radius 0.30 m, turning on frictionless bearings. An inextensible cable wrapped around the drum carries a 40 kg counterweight. The counterweight is released from rest and falls 3.0 m, the cable not slipping on the drum and having negligible mass. A brake applies a constant resisting torque to the drum during the fall. Safety rules for the hoist limit the speed of the counterweight to 4.0 m/s at the end of a 3.0 m drop. The hoist will be rated for repeated drops, so the brake duty must also be understood. Use g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the speed of the counterweight after 3.0 m of fall if no brake torque is applied, in m/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the constant brake torque, in N·m, needed to limit the speed to 4.0 m/s after the 3.0 m drop. [6]
  3. (c) With that brake torque, find the constant acceleration of the counterweight, in m/s². [3]
  4. (d) Find the cable tension during the drop, in N. [4]
  5. (e) Find the energy dissipated in the brake during the drop, in J. [3]
(a)

Assumptions: no friction in bearings, rigid drum, cable does not slip, so the weight speed v = rω. Apply work-energy to the system of weight plus drum. Moment of inertia of a solid cylinder I = ½ M r² = ½ × 60 × 0.30² = 2.70 kg·m². The drum kinetic energy ½ I ω² = ½ (I/r²) v² = ½ × 30.0 v², so the system behaves like a translating mass of m + I/r² = 40 + 30.0 = 70 kg. Energy: m g h = ½ meq v². Therefore v = √(2 m g h/meq) = √(2 × 40 × 9.81 × 3.0/70) = √33.63 = 5.8 m/s. That speed is higher than the allowed 4.0 m/s, so a brake is needed. A marker looks for a clear free-body statement that the cable tension does work on the drum and the weight in equal and opposite amounts and so does not appear in the system energy equation.

Answer: 5.8 m/s

(b)

Drum rotation during the drop θ = h/r = 3.0/0.30 = 10.0 rad. Work-energy for the system with the brake torque Tb doing negative work: m g h − Tb θ = ½ meq v². With v = 4.0 m/s, ½ meq v² = ½ × 70 × 16 = 560.0 J, and m g h = 40 × 9.81 × 3.0 = 1177.2 J. Then Tb θ = 1177.2 − 560.0 = 617.2 J, so Tb = 617.2/10.0 = 61.72 N·m. The brake is therefore absorbing about 52 percent of the available potential energy. Because the brake torque is constant, the drop is a constant-acceleration motion, which is why the work form of the equation with θ = h/r applies simply. A candidate should check units: N·m multiplied by radians gives joules, with the radian carrying no dimension in this product. Rounding Tb up slightly would give a small safety margin on the speed limit.

Answer: 61.72 N·m

(c)

Because the brake torque and weight are constant, the acceleration is constant. From v² = 2 a h with v = 4.0 m/s and h = 3.0 m: a = v²/(2h) = 16/(2 × 3.0) = 2.667 m/s². This is much smaller than g = 9.81 m/s² because both the drum inertia and the brake are resisting the fall. We can check this against Newton's laws using the angular acceleration α = a/r = 8.889 rad/s². The net torque on the drum is T r − Tb = I α, so T r = 61.72 + 2.70 × 8.889 = 61.72 + 24.000 = 85.720 N·m, and the cable tension then comes from this torque (part d). Alternatively, the energy approach and the force approach must give the same acceleration, and the check is satisfied by the tension result in part (d), which gives m(g − a) consistently.

Answer: 2.667 m/s²

(d)

Newton's second law for the counterweight, taking downward as positive: m g − T = m a, so T = m (g − a) = 40 × (9.81 − 2.667) = 285.7 N. Compare with the weight, m g = 392.4 N: the tension is 73 percent of the weight, since the counterweight accelerates downward at 2.667 m/s². Check with the drum: net torque on the drum T r − Tb = I α gives T = (Tb + I α)/r = (61.72 + 24.000)/0.30 = 285.7 N, which agrees with the first result. The agreement confirms both the brake torque and the acceleration. Design note: the cable must be rated for at least this tension times a safety factor, and the factor should account for the peak load at the instant the brake engages, which can exceed this steady value.

Answer: 285.7 N

(e)

The energy absorbed by the brake equals the work it does on the drum: Q = Tb θ = 61.72 × 10.0 = 617.2 J. This equals the potential energy released minus the kinetic energy gained, m g h − ½ meq v² = 1177.2 − 560.0 = 617.2 J, so the energy balance closes exactly. Almost all of this appears as heat in the brake lining and drum surface. If the drop repeats every minute, the average heating power would be about 10.3 W, a modest figure, but each single drop dissipates the full amount in about 1.50 s (time = 2h/v for constant acceleration from rest), so the peak heating rate is on the order of 411 W, which matters for brake fade. A marker rewards noting this distinction.

Answer: 617.2 J

Problem 5 [A2-045] Planar mechanism velocity analysis by instant centres

A pin-jointed four-bar linkage drives the rocking arm of a packaging machine. Link O2A is the crank, 80 mm long, turning at a constant 120 rad/s. The coupler AB is 260 mm long and the rocker O4B is 200 mm long. The fixed pivots O2 and O4 are 240 mm apart on a horizontal line, with O4 to the right of O2. Take O2 as the origin, and the x axis along O2O4. The linkage is assembled so that B lies above the line O2O4. With the crank at 60 degrees from the x axis, the mechanism is analysed.
