A redesign is then considered in which only the crank angle at the instant of interest changes, because the product is timed differently on the machine.

  1. (a) Find the angle of the rocker O4B measured from the positive x axis, in degrees. [3]
  2. (b) Find the distance from pin A to the instant centre of the coupler relative to the frame, in mm. [4]
  3. (c) Find the angular speed of the coupler, in rad/s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the angular speed of the rocker, in rad/s. [4]
  5. (e) If the crank is instead at 100 degrees, with the same crank speed, find the angular speed of the rocker in rad/s, and explain the change. [5]
(a)

Assumptions: rigid links, planar motion, frictionless pins. Place O2 at the origin; A = (80 cos 60°, 80 sin 60°) = (40.00, 69.28) mm and O4 = (240, 0). The distance AO4 is d = 211.66 mm. B lies on a circle of radius 260 mm about A and a circle of radius 200 mm about O4. The intersection above the line O2O4 gives B = (265.71, 198.34) mm. The rocker angle is θ4 = atan2(By − 0, Bx − 240) = atan2(198.34, 25.71) = 82.61 degrees, measured from the positive x axis. Check: the length of O4B from these coordinates is √(25.71² + 198.34²) = 200.00 mm, which equals 200 mm, and the length of AB comes out at 260 mm, confirming the position solution.

Answer: 82.61 degrees

(b)

The instant centre of the coupler relative to the frame is I13, which lies on the intersection of the line through O2 and A (the line of the crank, because the crank is pinned to the frame at O2) and the line through O4 and B (the rocker). Writing I13 = s·A for a point on line O2A and requiring it to lie on line O4B gives s = 7.7369, so I13 = (309.5, 536.0) mm. The distance from A to I13 is |A − I13| = 539 mm, and from B to I13 it is 340.5 mm. The instant centre lies well outside the linkage, about twice the coupler length from A, which signals that the coupler rotates slowly at this position, so its angular speed will be small compared with the crank speed. The marker rewards noting that I13 is found by the Kennedy theorem for three bodies, here links 1, 2 and 3, and that no velocity calculation is needed to place it.

Answer: 539 mm

(c)

The crank pin A has speed vA = ω2 × O2A = 120 × 0.080 = 9.60 m/s. Because the coupler turns about I13 at this instant, vA = ω3 × |A I13|, so ω3 = vA/|A I13| = 9.60/0.5390 = 17.81 rad/s. The loop-closure solution gives ω3 = -17.81 rad/s (negative means clockwise), so the sense is opposite to the crank; the magnitude is requested. For a check, the speed of B must satisfy vB = ω3 × |B I13| = 17.81 × 0.3405 = 6.065 m/s, and this is also the speed of the rocker end, which is perpendicular to O4B. The coupler angular speed is about 15 percent of the crank speed, which is modest for a coupler on a mechanism with a long coupler link.

Answer: 17.81 rad/s

(d)

Rocker end B has velocity vB = ω3 × |B I13| = 6.065 m/s and the same point lies on the rocker rotating about O4, so vB = ω4 × O4B. Therefore ω4 = vB/0.200 = 6.065/0.200 = 30.33 rad/s. An equivalent route uses the third instant centre I24, but we have already located I13, so the velocity ratio comes from the same data: ω4/ω2 = 0.2527. The rocker therefore turns at about 25 percent of the crank speed. Signs from the loop equation (counter-clockwise positive) of ω3 = -17.81 rad/s and ω4 = 30.33 rad/s. A marker should see the line of reasoning: crank speed gives vA, then I13 gives ω3, then ω3 and B I13 give vB, then ω4. Verification by the closed-loop velocity equation gives the same value, 30.33 rad/s, which confirms the result.

Answer: 30.33 rad/s

(e)

Repeat the construction with the crank at 100 degrees. A = (-13.89, 78.78) mm, and the position solution gives B = (216.83, 198.65) mm with the rocker at θ4 = 96.65 degrees. The instant centre I13 moves to (709.1, -4021.4) mm and |A I13| = 4163 mm, so ω3 = 9.60/4.1635 = 2.306 rad/s. Then ω4 = ω3 × |B I13|/0.200 = 48.98 rad/s. The rocker speed has risen from 30.33 to 48.98 rad/s, an increase of 62 percent. The explanation is that I13 has moved far away (about 4.2 m from A), so the coupler is almost in pure translation and B moves at nearly the speed of A: vB = ω4 × 0.200 = 9.80 m/s against vA = 9.60 m/s. The rocker speed is then close to vA/0.200. This shows how sensitive the velocity ratio is to the crank angle, and it is the reason a designer checks the whole cycle rather than one position. The coupler angular speed even changes sign when I13 passes through infinity, which happens when the crank and rocker lines become parallel.

Answer: 48.98 rad/s

A2 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A2-046] Relative velocity and acceleration of a four-bar linkage

A four-bar linkage operates the flap of a sorting gate. The crank O2A is 60 mm long and turns counter-clockwise at a constant 40 rad/s. The coupler AB is 180 mm, the rocker O4B is 150 mm, and the fixed pivots O2 and O4 are 200 mm apart on a horizontal line with O4 to the right of O2. Take O2 as origin with the x axis towards O4, and assemble the linkage with B above the line O2O4. The crank is at 45 degrees from the x axis. The gate controller will later be changed so that the crank runs faster, and the effect on the rocker's loading must be anticipated before the actuator is rated. Counter-clockwise rotation and acceleration are positive.

  1. (a) Find the angular velocity of the coupler AB, in rad/s, with sign. [4]
  2. (b) Find the angular velocity of the rocker O4B, in rad/s, with sign. [4]
  3. (c) Find the angular acceleration of the rocker, in rad/s², with sign. [5]
  4. (d) The crank speed is raised to 60 rad/s at the same crank angle, again constant. Find the new angular acceleration of the rocker, in rad/s². [4]
  5. (e) Explain the ratio between the two rocker accelerations in part (c) and part (d), and say what it means for the actuator and the pin loads. [3]
(a)

Position first: A = (60 cos 45°, 60 sin 45°) = (42.43, 42.43) mm and O4 = (200, 0). B is the intersection of a circle of radius 180 mm about A with a circle of radius 150 mm about O4, taking the upper solution. This gives θ3 = 36.48 degrees for AB and θ4 = 94.91 degrees for O4B, both from the positive x axis. The vector loop is r2 eiθ2 + r3 eiθ3 = r1 + r4 eiθ4. Differentiating, ω2 r2 eiθ2 + ω3 r3 eiθ3 − ω4 r4 eiθ4 = 0 (after dividing by i). The real and imaginary parts give two linear equations in ω3 and ω4. Solving them gives ω3 = -11.97 rad/s. The negative value means the coupler rotates clockwise at this instant, opposite to the counter-clockwise crank.

Answer: -11.97 rad/s

(b)

From the second equation of the same velocity loop, with ω3 = -11.97 rad/s: the x components give ω3 r3 cos θ3 − ω4 r4 cos θ4 = −ω2 r2 cos θ2, i.e. -11.97 × 0.180 × 0.8040 − ω4 × 0.150 × -0.0856 = −40 × 0.060 × 0.7071. The y components provide the same consistency check. Solving the pair gives ω4 = 2.782 rad/s, counter-clockwise. The rocker therefore turns slowly forward while the coupler rotates backward, which fits the picture of a rocker near the end of its swing. A check is the speed of B, vB = ω4 r4 = 0.417 m/s, which equals the vector sum of the speed of A (2.40 m/s at the crank) and the speed of B relative to A, ω3 r3 = 2.155 m/s; the vector triangle closes with these magnitudes.

Answer: 2.782 rad/s

(c)

Acceleration analysis with constant ω2 (α2 = 0). Differentiate the velocity loop equation once more: for each link the acceleration has a tangential part α r and a normal part ω² r towards the pivot. The loop gives α3 r3 eiθ3 − α4 r4 eiθ4 = −i[ω2² r2 eiθ2 + ω3² r3 eiθ3 − ω4² r4 eiθ4]. The normal accelerations are: crank 96.00 m/s², coupler 25.80 m/s², rocker 1.16 m/s². Putting the numbers into the two linear equations (same coefficient matrix as the velocity step) gives α3 = 483.6 rad/s² and α4 = 940 rad/s². The rocker angular acceleration is large, because the crank speed is high compared with the size of the mechanism. Direction check: a positive α4 means the rocker's speed is increasing counter-clockwise. The tangential acceleration of B is α4 r4 = 141.0 m/s², which is about 14 g, so the actuator must handle a very large inertia load.

Answer: 940 rad/s²

(d)

The new crank speed is 60 rad/s, so ω2 is 1.5 times larger. The mechanism position is unchanged, so θ3 and θ4 are unchanged. The velocities scale linearly with ω2: ω3 = -17.96 rad/s and ω4 = 4.172 rad/s. Every normal acceleration term depends on a velocity squared, so every term on the right of the acceleration loop equation scales with ω2². The angular accelerations, found from the same coefficient matrix, therefore scale by (60/40)² = 2.25. The rocker acceleration is α4 = 2.25 × 940 = 2115 rad/s². The tangential acceleration of B is now α4 r4 = 317.3 m/s², about 32 g. Note that the position has not changed so only the speed changes. The result matches the direct solution of the loop equations with ω2 = 60 rad/s.

Answer: 2115 rad/s²

(e)

Because the geometry is fixed, ω3, ω4, α3 and α4 are all proportional to ω2 or ω2² respectively, and the acceleration ratio is exactly (ω2'/ω2)² = (60/40)² = 2.25. Checking with the numbers: 2115/940 = 2.250. Increasing speed by 50 percent therefore multiplies the inertia loads by 2.25, which is why high-speed mechanisms are limited by acceleration, not velocity. The actuator torque required to produce the acceleration grows by the same factor, and so do the pin reactions from the inertia of the links, since F = m a. For a rating decision the designer should check at the worst crank angle over the whole cycle, not at one position, and may need to rebalance or lighten the rocker to hold the pin loads. The marker rewards identifying the speed-squared dependence and its design consequences.

Answer: Ratio (60/40)² = 2.25; see working

Problem 2 [A2-047] Slider-crank kinematics

A small reciprocating air compressor has a crank radius of 55 mm and a connecting rod 210 mm long between centres, and the piston pin lies on the cylinder axis, which passes through the crankshaft centre (no offset). The crank turns at a steady 3000 rpm. Measure the crank angle from top dead centre (TDC), where the piston is at its innermost position. The piston assembly has mass 1.8 kg. The manufacturer is considering a shorter connecting rod of 150 mm, with the same crank radius, to make the compressor more compact, and wants the effect on the piston inertia forces quantified.

  1. (a) Find the piston displacement from TDC, in mm, when the crank angle is 40 degrees, using the exact geometry. [4]
  2. (b) Find the piston velocity at 40 degrees using the exact derivative, in m/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the piston acceleration at TDC, in m/s². [4]
  4. (d) Find the piston acceleration at TDC with the 150 mm rod, in m/s². [4]
  5. (e) Find the increase in the peak piston inertia force at TDC caused by the shorter rod, in N. [4]
(a)

Assumptions: rigid crank and rod, no offset, constant crank speed ω = 2π(3000)/60 = 314.16 rad/s. With the crank angle θ from TDC, the piston position measured from TDC is x = r(1 − cos θ) + l − √(l² − r² sin² θ). At θ = 40°: sin θ = 0.64279, cos θ = 0.76604. The square-root term is √(0.210² − (0.055 × 0.64279)²) = √(0.042850) = 0.207003 m. Then x = 0.055 (1 − 0.76604) + 0.210 − 0.207003 = 0.015865 m = 15.86 mm. Check: at TDC the same expression gives x = 0. At θ = 90° it gives x = r + l − √(l² − r²) which is roughly r, confirming the usual stroke picture. A marker rewards using the exact expression rather than the first-order approximation x ≈ r(1 − cos θ) + r² sin²θ/(2l), though here they differ by only a fraction of a millimetre.

Answer: 15.86 mm

(b)

Differentiate the position with respect to time using v = (dx/dθ) ω. We get dx/dθ = r sin θ + r² sin θ cos θ/√(l² − r² sin²θ). Therefore v = r ω [sin θ + r sin θ cos θ/√(l² − r² sin² θ)] = 0.055 × 314.16 × [0.64279 + 0.055 × 0.64279 × 0.76604/0.207003] = 17.2788 × [0.64279 + 0.130830] = 13.37 m/s. The positive sign means the piston is moving away from TDC. The connecting-rod term adds about 20.4 percent to the velocity of a simple harmonic motion, which would give r ω sin θ = 11.11 m/s. The velocity is zero at TDC and bottom dead centre, and its peak occurs somewhat before the crank is perpendicular to the cylinder axis, with the exact angle depending on the ratio l/r, here 3.82.

Answer: 13.37 m/s

(c)

At TDC the piston is at its extreme position and its velocity is zero, so the acceleration is at a maximum. Differentiating the velocity expression once more and setting θ = 0, the exact result is a = r ω² (cos θ + (r/l) cos 2θ) to first order, and at θ = 0 the exact acceleration also equals r ω²(1 + r/l), because the higher-order terms vanish at the dead centre. With r ω² = 0.055 × 314.16² = 5428.282 m/s² and r/l = 0.055/0.210 = 0.2619, the acceleration is a = 5428.282 × (1 + 0.2619) = 6850 m/s². This is directed towards the crank centre, which means that at TDC the piston is decelerating as it comes to rest and reversing direction. The corresponding piston inertia force is m a = 1.8 × 6850 = 12330.0 N, which the crankpin and bearings must carry. For perspective that is about 698 g, which explains why piston mass is controlled tightly in high-speed machines.

Answer: 6850 m/s²

(d)

For the shorter rod the same expression applies, a = r ω² (1 + r/l) with l = 0.150 m. Now r/l = 0.055/0.150 = 0.3667, so a = 5428.282 × (1 + 0.3667) = 7418.7 m/s². The crank radius and speed are unchanged, so the first term r ω² is the same as before, and only the correction term differs. The acceleration at TDC is 8.3 percent higher with the 150 mm rod. At bottom dead centre the acceleration is r ω² (−1 + r/l), a smaller magnitude, so the shorter rod also increases the asymmetry between the two ends of the stroke. The marker rewards seeing that a short rod, with a larger r/l ratio, increases the second-harmonic component of the motion and the shaking force at twice crank speed.

Answer: 7418.7 m/s²

(e)

The peak piston inertia force at TDC is F = m a. For the original rod F = 1.8 × 6850 = 12330.0 N. For the shorter rod F = 1.8 × 7418.7 = 13353.6 N. The increase is ΔF = 13353.6 − 12330.0 = 1024 N, which is 8.3 percent more. This extra load acts on the piston pin, small end, crank pin and main bearings every revolution, so fatigue life is affected. The 1.8 kg mass and 3000 rpm make the inertia force very large compared with the weight of the piston (17.7 N). Offsetting the benefit of compactness, the shorter rod also increases the side thrust on the cylinder wall because the rod angle grows, with a maximum rod angle of asin(r/l) = 21.5 degrees against 15.2 degrees originally. A balanced answer weighs the size gain against these penalties.

Answer: 1024 N

Problem 3 [A2-048] Grashof and transmission angle

A four-bar linkage in a window-opening mechanism has a 70 mm crank, a 210 mm coupler, a 180 mm rocker and a fixed frame link (ground) of 240 mm between the two fixed pivots. The designer needs a full-rotation crank driving a rocking output. For smooth force transmission to the rocker, the transmission angle, the angle between the coupler and the rocker, should stay between 40 degrees and 140 degrees through the cycle. A revision proposes lengthening the crank from 70 mm to 120 mm to give a larger output swing. Consider the original design first and then the revision.

  1. (a) For the original design, find the Grashof margin, meaning the sum of the two intermediate links minus the sum of the shortest and longest links, in mm. [3]
  2. (b) Find the minimum transmission angle of the original design over a full crank revolution, in degrees. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum transmission angle with the 120 mm crank, in degrees. [5]
  4. (d) Find the longest crank length, in mm, for which the frame, coupler and rocker lengths still give a crank-rocker linkage (crank shortest). [3]
  5. (e) Say whether the revision is acceptable and what modification you would recommend. [4]
(a)

Assumptions: rigid links, pin joints. Grashof's condition says that a four-bar linkage has at least one fully rotating link if s + l ≤ p + q, where s is the shortest and l the longest link. Here the lengths are 70, 210, 180 and 240 mm. The shortest is the crank, s = 70, and the longest is the frame, l = 240. So s + l = 310 mm. The other two links give p + q = 210 + 180 = 390 mm. The linkage satisfies the condition with a margin of (p + q) − (s + l) = 390 − 310 = 80 mm. Because the shortest link is the crank, the crank can rotate fully relative to the frame, and the linkage is a crank-rocker with the rocker oscillating. The comfortable margin of 80 mm means a modest change in a link length will not destroy the full-rotation property.

Answer: 80 mm

(b)

The transmission angle μ between coupler and rocker satisfies the cosine rule on the triangle formed by the coupler, the rocker and the diagonal between the crank pin and the frame pivot. Writing the diagonal as the distance from the crank pin to the far frame pivot, cos μ = (b² + c² − e²)/(2bc), where b = 210, c = 180, and e is that diagonal. The diagonal is shortest when the crank lies along the frame towards the far pivot, e = d − a = 240 − 70 = 170 mm, and longest when it points away, e = d + a = 310 mm. For e = 170, cos μ = (44100 + 32400 − 28900)/(2 × 210 × 180) = 0.62963, giving μ = 50.98 degrees. For e = 310, cos μ = -0.25926, giving μ = 105 degrees, whose supplement is 74.97 degrees. The minimum transmission angle over the cycle is the smaller of 50.98 and 74.97, so it is 50.98 degrees. This exceeds the 40 degree limit.

Answer: 50.98 degrees

(c)

For the revised crank a = 120 mm the Grashof sum is s + l = 120 + 240 = 360 mm, which is still below 390 mm, so the crank still rotates fully. The diagonal ranges from d − a = 120 mm to d + a = 360 mm. At the short end, cos μ = (210² + 180² − 120²)/(2 × 210 × 180) = (44100 + 32400 − 14400)/75600 = 0.82143, so μ = 34.77 degrees. At the long end, cos μ = (44100 + 32400 − 129600)/75600 = -0.70238, so μ = 134.6 degrees, with a supplement of 45.38 degrees. The minimum transmission angle is therefore the smaller value, 34.77 degrees. The longer crank brings the minimum down by 16.2 degrees, because the diagonal swings over a wider range, which makes the coupler push at a shallower angle on the rocker at the near-dead-centre position.

Answer: 34.77 degrees

(d)

The Grashof condition with the crank as shortest link and the frame as longest is a + d ≤ b + c. Rearranging, the crank length must satisfy a ≤ b + c − d = 210 + 180 − 240 = 150 mm. At a = 150 mm the sum s + l equals p + q and the linkage becomes a change-point (or "folding") linkage, where the links can become collinear and the mechanism may jam or switch branches; so for a reliable crank-rocker the crank must be strictly less than 150 mm. The check that the crank is still the shortest link requires a ≤ 180 mm, which is automatically satisfied. Hence the revision to 120 mm is permitted by the Grashof limit with a margin of 30 mm, although this margin alone hides the transmission-angle problem found in part (c).

Answer: 150 mm

(e)

Limit: μmin ≥ 40 degrees. The original gives 51.0 degrees, which passes. The 120 mm crank gives 34.8 degrees, which falls below 40 degrees by 5.2 degrees, so the revision is not acceptable as it stands. A poor transmission angle means a large part of the coupler force acts along the rocker rather than across it, raising bearing loads and the risk of jamming under friction. Options: reduce the crank to about 90 mm so the minimum rises back above 40 degrees, shorten the frame so the diagonal range narrows, or lengthen the coupler. Another approach is to keep the 120 mm crank but restrict the working range of crank rotation to the part of the cycle in which μ is above 40 degrees, which is possible only if the output does not need the full cycle. The marker rewards the candidate who notes that Grashof alone does not guarantee a good mechanism, since transmission angle is a separate requirement.

Answer: Revision fails the 40 degree limit; see working

Problem 4 [A2-049] Cam profile and follower motion

A radial translating roller follower on a packaging cam must rise 24 mm with simple harmonic motion while the cam turns through 100 degrees, the cam turning at a constant 300 rpm. The prime circle (the circle through the roller centre at its lowest position) has radius 50 mm, and the follower axis passes through the cam centre. The machine builder asks what happens if the rise has to be completed in a shorter cam angle of 70 degrees, at the same speed and the same rise, because the dwell phase on the machine needs to be longer. The pressure angle, between the follower motion and the common normal at the roller contact, is a concern because it controls side thrust on the follower guide. Evaluate the original and the changed motion.

  1. (a) Find the maximum follower velocity during the rise, in m/s. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum follower acceleration during the rise, in m/s². [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum acceleration if the rise angle is cut to 70 degrees, in m/s². [4]
  4. (d) Find the pressure angle at mid-rise for the 100 degree rise, in degrees. [5]
  5. (e) Find the pressure angle at mid-rise for the 70 degree rise, in degrees. [4]
(a)

Assumptions: ideal rigid follower and cam, constant cam speed ω = 2π(300)/60 = 31.416 rad/s. Harmonic rise: s = (h/2)[1 − cos(πθ/β)], with h = 24 mm and β = 100° = 1.7453 rad. Velocity v = ds/dt = (π h ω/(2β)) sin(πθ/β), which peaks at mid-rise (θ = β/2) where the sine is 1. So vmax = π h ω/(2β) = π × 0.024 × 31.416/(2 × 1.7453) = 0.6786 m/s. The velocity is zero at the start and end of the rise, which is the useful property of harmonic motion at the dwells. The marker rewards correct conversion of β to radians before use, since using degrees in this formula gives an answer wrong by a factor of 57.3.

Answer: 0.6786 m/s

(b)

Acceleration a = dv/dt = (π² h ω²/(2β²)) cos(πθ/β). Its magnitude is greatest at the start and end of the rise (cosine = ±1). So amax = π² h ω²/(2β²) = π² × 0.024 × 31.416²/(2 × 1.7453²) = 233.8/6.092 = 38.37 m/s². Note that the acceleration does not fall to zero at the ends of the rise, but jumps from zero (in the dwell) to this value, so the acceleration is discontinuous and the jerk is theoretically infinite at the transition. Harmonic motion is therefore suitable for moderate speeds only. The corresponding inertial force on a follower of mass m is m × 38.37 N, which must be less than the spring preload to keep the roller in contact.

Answer: 38.37 m/s²

(c)

Maximum acceleration varies as 1/β². Reducing β from 100° to 70° gives amax2 = π² h ω²/(2β2²) with β2 = 70° = 1.2217 rad: amax2 = π² × 0.024 × 31.416²/(2 × 1.2217²) = 78.31 m/s². The ratio to the original is (100/70)² = 2.041, so 78.31/38.37 = 2.041 as expected. The acceleration roughly doubles, so the inertial force and the contact stress roughly double. The follower spring must be stiffer, with more preload to avoid jump at the end of the rise, and the cam shaft sees a larger torque pulsation. At the same speed, shortening the rise angle is thus an expensive change. A candidate who writes the ratio first and checks it against the direct calculation shows good method.

Answer: 78.31 m/s²

(d)

Pressure angle φ for an in-line translating roller follower satisfies tan φ = (ds/dθ)/(Rp + s), where Rp is the prime circle radius and ds/dθ is the follower speed per unit cam rotation (a length per radian). At mid-rise the speed is greatest, ds/dθ = π h/(2β) = π × 0.024/(2 × 1.7453) = 0.02160 m/rad, and the displacement is s = h/2 = 0.012 m. Therefore tan φ = 0.02160/(0.050 + 0.012) = 0.02160/0.062 = 0.3484, giving φ = 19.21 degrees. This is below the common guideline of about 30 degrees for translating followers, so the side thrust on the guide is acceptable. Note that the maximum pressure angle for harmonic motion does not occur exactly at mid-rise because the denominator Rp + s grows with s, but the mid-rise value is a good estimate and is the one asked.

Answer: 19.21 degrees

(e)

For the 70 degree rise the speed per radian is ds/dθ = π h/(2β2) = π × 0.024/(2 × 1.2217) = 0.03086 m/rad. At mid-rise s = 0.012 m again, so tan φ = 0.03086/0.062 = 0.4977, giving φ = 26.46 degrees. The pressure angle has increased from 19.21 to 26.46 degrees, which is closer to the guideline limit of about 30 degrees. The ratio of tangents is 100/70 = 1.429, so the increase is nearly proportional. If the designer wants to keep the angle down, the prime circle radius should be increased: for a limit of 30 degrees at this position the required Rp would be ds/dθ/tan 30° − s = 0.0414 m, i.e. 41 mm, which still fits here. Larger prime circle means a larger cam, so the saving in pressure angle is paid for in size and surface speed.

Answer: 26.46 degrees

Problem 5 [A2-050] Spur gear geometry and gear trains

A 4 mm module spur gear pair in a conveyor drive has a 19-tooth pinion meshing with a 47-tooth gear. Both gears are full-depth, with addendum equal to one module, and run on standard pitch radii at a 20 degree pressure angle. A designer asks whether raising the pressure angle to 25 degrees, with the same module, tooth numbers, addendum and centre distance, would be wise to gain tooth strength. Contact ratio, the average number of tooth pairs in contact, must stay above 1.2 for smooth running, and undercutting must be avoided on the pinion. Evaluate both options with the standard geometry relations.

  1. (a) Find the centre distance of the standard pair, in mm. [3]
  2. (b) Find the contact ratio at 20 degrees pressure angle. [5]
  3. (c) Find the contact ratio at 25 degrees with the same pitch radii and addendum. [5]
  4. (d) Find the theoretical minimum number of pinion teeth to avoid undercutting at 20 degrees, treating the result as a real number. [3]
  5. (e) Find the same minimum number at 25 degrees, and comment on the 19-tooth pinion in each case. [4]
(a)

Assumptions: standard involute gears, no backlash, standard pitch radii. The pitch radius of a gear is r = m z/2. Pinion: r1 = 4 × 19/2 = 38 mm. Gear: r2 = 4 × 47/2 = 94 mm. The centre distance is the sum of the pitch radii: C = r1 + r2 = 38 + 94 = 132 mm. The velocity ratio is z2/z1 = 47/19 = 2.474, so the gear turns at 0.404 times the pinion speed. Because the gears run on standard pitch circles, the operating pressure angle equals the cutting pressure angle, 20 degrees, which is a requirement for the contact ratio formula used next. If the centre distance were altered the operating pressure angle would change, and that must be remembered when judging changes later.

Answer: 132 mm

(b)

Base radii: rb = r cos φ. At 20°: rb1 = 38 × 0.93969 = 35.708 mm and rb2 = 94 × 0.93969 = 88.331 mm. Addendum radii: Ra1 = 38 + 4 = 42 mm and Ra2 = 94 + 4 = 98 mm. Lengths of the approach and recess paths: √(Ra1² − rb1²) = 22.111 mm and √(Ra2² − rb2²) = 42.445 mm. The path of contact is the sum minus C sin φ: 22.111 + 42.445 − 132 × 0.34202 = 19.410 mm. The base pitch is pb = π m cos φ = π × 4 × 0.93969 = 11.809 mm, so the contact ratio is mc = 19.410/11.809 = 1.644. This is well above the 1.2 requirement: on average between one and two pairs share the load; two pairs are in contact for about 64 percent of the mesh cycle and a single pair for about 36 percent.

Answer: 1.644

(c)

With a 25 degree pressure angle the pitch radii and addenda are unchanged (r1 = 38 mm, r2 = 94 mm, Ra1 = 42 mm, Ra2 = 98 mm), but the base radii shrink: rb1 = 38 × 0.90631 = 34.440 mm and rb2 = 94 × 0.90631 = 85.193 mm. Then √(Ra1² − rb1²) = 24.040 mm and √(Ra2² − rb2²) = 48.437 mm, and the path of contact is 24.040 + 48.437 − 132 × 0.42262 = 16.691 mm. Base pitch pb = π × 4 × 0.90631 = 11.389 mm. Contact ratio mc = 16.691/11.389 = 1.466. This is a fall of 10.8 percent from the 20 degree value, but still above the 1.2 minimum. A higher pressure angle thus gives shorter contact paths relative to the base pitch, a typical trade: stronger teeth, but less overlap and more noise sensitivity, and higher bearing loads because the normal force direction tilts more.

Answer: 1.466

(d)

To avoid undercutting a full-depth involute pinion cut with a rack whose addendum is one module, the number of teeth must satisfy z ≥ 2/sin² φ. At φ = 20°, sin φ = 0.34202, so sin² φ = 0.11698 and z_min = 2/0.11698 = 17.1. In practice the integer above this is used, 18 teeth. The 19-tooth pinion is just above the limit, so it avoids undercutting at 20 degrees, but only by one tooth. A pinion of fewer than 18 teeth would have its tooth root cut away by the generating tool, weakening the tooth and removing part of the involute near the base circle, the region that engages first. So the pair is safe, but with no margin for a smaller pinion.

Answer: 17.1

(e)

At φ = 25°, sin φ = 0.42262, sin² φ = 0.17861, so z_min = 2/0.17861 = 11.2. Rounded up this is 12 teeth. The 19-tooth pinion exceeds this by seven teeth, so it is comfortably free of undercutting at 25 degrees. The comparison is the useful part of the answer: increasing the pressure angle widens the tooth base, strengthens it, and allows smaller pinions, which is why 25 degree gears are used where compact drives are wanted. The cost is the lower contact ratio found in part (c) (1.466 against 1.644), and higher radial loads on the shafts. For this drive, with 19 teeth already clear of undercutting at 20 degrees, the strength gain is real but the contact ratio loss means the case for change rests only on tooth strength; if the bending stress at 20 degrees is acceptable, the standard 20 degree pair should be retained.

Answer: 11.2

A2 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A2-051] Planetary gear trains

A winch gearbox uses a simple planetary train with a 24 tooth sun gear, three identical planets of 18 teeth and an internal ring gear of 60 teeth. The sun gear is driven by a motor at 1800 rpm and the ring gear is bolted to the housing, so the carrier drives the drum. A technician proposes to re-plumb the unit so the sun is held and the ring is driven instead, hoping for a gentler start. All gears are standard, share one module and rotate in the same plane. Take rotation in the direction of the sun as positive. Use 100 percent efficiency in parts (a) to (c). In part (d) the sun carries 150 N·m input torque and the meshing efficiency of the whole train is 97 percent at steady speed.

  1. (a) Find the carrier speed with the ring fixed. [5]
  2. (b) Find the absolute angular speed of one planet gear about its own axis in the original arrangement, stating its direction relative to the sun. [5]
  3. (c) For the proposed re-plumbing (sun fixed, ring driven at 1800 rpm) find the carrier speed and comment on whether the start is gentler. [5]
  4. (d) For the original arrangement find the output torque on the carrier. [5]
(a)

Use the tabular or relative velocity method. With the ring fixed, the speed ratio between sun and ring relative to the carrier is (ωs - ωc)/(ωr - ωc) = -R/S, because the sun is external and the ring is internal (only the external sun-planet mesh reverses the direction of rotation; the internal planet-ring mesh keeps it, so the net effect is one reversal). Setting ωr = 0 gives ωs - ωc = (R/S) ωc, so ωc = ωs/(1 + R/S). Substituting, 1 + 60/24 = 3.5, so ωc = 1800/3.5 = 514.3 rpm. The reduction ratio is therefore 3.5:1, which is the usual result for a fixed ring planetary reducer. The planet teeth count does not enter the ratio because the planet is an idler between sun and ring.

Answer: 514.3 rpm

(b)

Fix the carrier momentarily and treat the train as an ordinary gear pair. Relative to the carrier the sun speed is ωs - ωc = 1800 - 514.3 = 1285.7 rpm. The planet meshes externally with the sun, so ωp/c = -(S/P)(ωs - ωc) = -(24/18)(1285.7) = -1714.3 rpm relative to the carrier. Add the carrier speed to convert to the ground frame: ωp = ωc + ωp/c = 514.3 + (-1714.3) = -1200.0 rpm. The negative sign means the planet spins opposite to the sun. Check using the ring: ωp/c = (R/P)(ωr - ωc) = (60/18)(0 - 514.3) = -1714.3 rpm, which agrees, so the planet speed is 1200 rpm.

Answer: -1200.0 rpm (opposite to the sun)

(c)

Now the sun is held (ωs = 0) and the ring is driven at ωr = 1800 rpm. Using (ωs - ωc)/(ωr - ωc) = -R/S, we get (0 - ωc)/(1800 - ωc) = -60/24 = -2.5. Then -ωc = -2.5(1800 - ωc), so ωc = 4500 - 2.5 ωc, which rearranges to ωc = ωr R/(R + S) = 1800 × 60/84 = 1285.7 rpm. The ratio is 84/60 = 1.4:1, a much smaller reduction than the 3.5:1 of the original unit. The drum would turn at 1286 rpm instead of 514 rpm, so the output torque drops to about 40 percent and the load will not start gently. The proposal gives a faster, weaker drive, not a gentler start.

Answer: 1285.7 rpm

(d)

With the ring fixed and the carrier as output, power balance with a mesh efficiency η gives Tout × ωc = η × Tin × ωs. Hence Tout = η Tin (ωs/ωc) = η Tin (1 + R/S). Substituting, Tout = 0.97 × 150 × 3.5 = 509.2 N·m. The ideal torque would be 525 N·m, so the losses account for about 15.75 N·m. The housing reaction supplies the difference between output and input torque: it must carry Tout - Tin = 359.2 N·m in the same sense as the input, which is the load the mounting bolts must resist. State that the efficiency was applied to power, not to the speed ratio, which is purely geometric.

Answer: 509.2 N·m

Problem 2 [A2-052] Static force analysis of a mechanism

A reciprocating pump has a crank of 80 mm radius and a connecting rod of 300 mm length driving a piston that slides in a fixed horizontal cylinder with no offset. At the instant studied the crank is 50 degrees past inner dead centre (the position at which the piston is furthest from the crankshaft) and the fluid pressure applies a force of 2.4 kN along the piston axis, towards the crank. Treat the mechanism as quasi-static and neglect the masses, friction and the weights of the links. The designer wants to know how sensitive the required drive torque is to the crank position, because a servo motor is proposed in place of the present induction motor.

  1. (a) Find the force in the connecting rod and state whether it is in tension or compression. [4]
  2. (b) Find the side thrust of the piston on the cylinder wall. [4]
  3. (c) Find the torque the motor must apply to the crank shaft to hold the mechanism in equilibrium at this position, using the principle of virtual work, and verify it by taking moments of the rod force about the crank centre. [6]
  4. (d) Repeat the torque calculation with the crank at 90 degrees and comment on which angle needs the larger torque for the same gas force. [6]
(a)

The rod angle φ from the cylinder axis follows from the geometry r sinθ = l sinφ. Then sinφ = 0.08 sin50°/0.30 = 0.2043, so φ = 11.79°. Isolate the piston: three forces act, the applied force F = 2400 N along the axis, the cylinder wall reaction normal to the axis and the rod force along the rod line. Resolving along the axis, Frod cosφ = F, so Frod = 2400/cos(11.79°) = 2452 N. The rod is a two force member pushing the piston away from the crank pin under the gas load, therefore it carries compression. The rod force is slightly larger than the gas force because of the rod obliquity.

Answer: 2452 N (compression)

(b)

From the same free body of the piston, the components normal to the cylinder axis must balance: the wall reaction N equals the transverse component of the rod force. N = Frod sinφ = F tanφ = 2400 × tan(11.79°) = 501 N. Its direction is such that the piston is pressed against the wall on the side away from the crank pin line. This thrust matters for wear and for the friction loss that was neglected: with a friction coefficient of 0.1 the extra axial resistance would be about 50 N, roughly 2.1 percent of the gas load. The result depends only on φ, so it grows when the rod is shortened for a fixed crank.

Answer: 501 N

(c)

Virtual work: let the crank turn through dθ, the piston moves dx where x = r cosθ + √(l² - r² sin²θ). Then dx/dθ = -[r sinθ + r² sinθ cosθ/√(l² - r² sin²θ)], magnitude 0.07201 m per radian at 50°. Equilibrium requires T dθ = F dx, so T = F|dx/dθ| = 2400 × 0.07201 = 172.8 N·m. Check by moments: the rod force acts on the crank pin along the rod line and its moment arm about the crank centre is r sin(θ + φ). Then T = Frod r sin(θ + φ) = 2452 × 0.08 × sin(61.79°) = 172.8 N·m, which agrees with the virtual work answer, so both methods are consistent.

Answer: 172.8 N·m

(d)

At θ = 90° the crank is perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Then sinφ = 0.08/0.30, and dx/dθ = r sin90° + 0 = 0.08 m/rad, because cosθ = 0 removes the second term. Therefore T = F × 0.08 = 2400 × 0.08 = 192.0 N·m. Compared with 172.8 N·m at 50°, this is larger by 11.1 percent. The torque is not greatest at 90°: it peaks at about 199 N·m near a crank angle of 76°, so the servo must be sized on the maximum of sin(θ + φ)/cosφ, which lies before 90°; 90° is still larger than 50°, and the moment arm is near zero at the dead centres.

Answer: 192.0 N·m

Problem 3 [A2-053] Dynamic force analysis of a slider-crank

A single cylinder air compressor has a crank radius of 60 mm, a connecting rod 240 mm long and a reciprocating mass (piston, gudgeon pin and a share of the rod) of 1.8 kg. At a crank angle of 30 degrees past top dead centre the gas pressure produces a force of 6.5 kN on the piston, acting along the cylinder axis towards the crank. The crank runs at a steady 3000 rpm. Measurements on a test rig show that the net force reaching the connecting rod at this crank angle changes sign when the speed is lowered, and the lab technician asks you to explain this numerically. Treat the crank speed as constant, neglect friction and use the standard approximate acceleration expression for the piston, keeping the second harmonic term.

  1. (a) Find the inertia force of the reciprocating mass at 30 degrees and 3000 rpm. [4]
  2. (b) Find the net force transmitted along the piston axis to the connecting rod at 3000 rpm, taking force towards the crank as positive. [4]
  3. (c) Find the torque on the crank shaft due to the net piston force at 3000 rpm. [6]
  4. (d) Find the net piston force when the speed is reduced to 2000 rpm and explain why the sign changes. [6]
(a)

The piston acceleration towards the crank is approximately a = ω² r (cosθ + (r/l) cos2θ), where r/l = 0.06/0.24 = 0.25. The angular speed is ω = 2π × 3000/60 = 314.16 rad/s, so ω² r = 5922 m/s². The bracket equals cos30° + 0.25 cos60° = 0.8660 + 0.125 = 0.9910. Hence a = 5868 m/s². The inertia force, the force required to accelerate the reciprocating mass, is Fi = m a = 1.8 × 5868 = 10564 N, directed towards the crank. It is large because it varies as the square of speed, and it is comparable to or larger than the gas load in many positions.

Answer: 10564 N

(b)

Apply Newton's second law to the reciprocating mass along the cylinder axis. The gas force Fg acts towards the crank and the rod force F acts on the piston in the opposite sense, so Fg - F = m a with a the acceleration towards the crank. The force the piston sends to the rod is the equal and opposite quantity, F = Fg - m a = Fg - Fi = 6500 - 10564 = -4064 N. A negative result shows the inertia of the piston exceeds the gas load, so the rod is pulled towards the piston, going into tension, and the crank pin and gudgeon pin must carry the reversal. This matters for bearing load reversal and for oil film support.

Answer: -4064 N (negative means the rod is pulled away from the crank)

(c)

First find the rod angle: sinφ = r sinθ/l = 0.06 sin30°/0.24 = 0.1250, so φ = 7.18°. The rod force is F/cosφ and its moment arm about the crank centre is r sin(θ + φ), so the torque is T = F r sin(θ + φ)/cosφ. Substituting, T = (-4064) × 0.06 × sin(37.18°)/cos(7.18°) = -148.5 N·m. The negative sign shows the inertia forces tend to drive the crank rather than resist it at this position. The mean torque over the cycle depends on the gas work, while inertia terms only redistribute torque within a revolution, so they smooth through the flywheel.

Answer: -148.5 N·m

(d)

At 2000 rpm, ω = 2π × 2000/60 = 209.44 rad/s, so ω² r = 2632 m/s². The inertia force becomes Fi = 1.8 × 2632 × 0.9910 = 4695 N. The net force is 6500 - 4695 = 1805 N, now positive. The inertia term falls with the square of speed: (2000/3000)² = 0.444, so it drops from 10564 N to 4695 N, below the constant 6500 N gas load. The sign change is therefore explained by the speed squared law, and the crossover speed at this angle is √(6500/(1.8 × 0.06 × 0.991)) = 2353 rpm.

Answer: 1805 N

Problem 4 [A2-054] Flywheel sizing

A punch press makes one stroke every 2.0 s. Each stroke needs 4.5 kJ delivered during a 0.25 s working interval, and the motor delivers constant power averaged over the full cycle. The flywheel must hold the coefficient of speed fluctuation to 0.10 (that is, (ωmax - ωmin)/ωmean) at a mean speed of 240 rpm. The workshop asks whether it would be cheaper to mount the flywheel on the faster intermediate shaft that runs at 480 rpm, since a smaller wheel could then be used. The wheel will be a solid steel disc of density 7850 kg/m³ and width 0.15 m. Neglect the inertia of the other rotating parts and any friction.

  1. (a) Find the maximum fluctuation of energy during a cycle. [5]
  2. (b) Find the required mass moment of inertia of the flywheel at 240 rpm. [5]
  3. (c) Find the radius and mass of the solid disc, and report the mass. [5]
  4. (d) Repeat the sizing for the 480 rpm shaft and report the new disc mass, then say what saving results. [5]
(a)

The motor supplies constant average power P = E/T = 4500/2.0 = 2250 W. During the 0.25 s working interval the motor supplies only 2250 × 0.25 = 562.5 J of the 4500 J demanded, so the flywheel must supply the remainder. The maximum energy fluctuation is ΔE = 4500 - 562.5 = 3937.5 J. During the remaining 1.75 s the motor delivers 2250 × 1.75 = 3937.5 J, of which the flywheel recovers all the energy it gave away, which confirms the cycle closes with zero net energy change. This ΔE is the energy that the flywheel speed swing must absorb and release.

Answer: 3938 J

(b)

For a flywheel, ΔE = I ω²mean Cs, where Cs = (ωmax - ωmin)/ωmean. The mean speed is ω = 2π × 240/60 = 25.133 rad/s, so ω² = 631.65 rad²/s². Rearranging, I = ΔE/(Cs ω²) = 3937.5/(0.10 × 631.65) = 62.34 kg·m². This is the total inertia required, which includes only the flywheel as inertia of other parts is neglected. A smaller Cs would raise I in direct proportion, so tightening the fluctuation to 0.05 would double the inertia required. Mean speed enters as the square, which is why the faster shaft looks attractive.

Answer: 62.34 kg·m²

(c)

For a solid disc of radius R and width b, I = ½ m R² with m = ρ π R² b, so I = ½ ρ π b R⁴. Solving, R⁴ = 2I/(ρ π b) = 2 × 62.34/(7850 × π × 0.15) = 0.03370, giving R = 0.4285 m, a diameter of 857 mm. The mass is m = ρ π R² b = 7850 × π × 0.1836 × 0.15 = 679 kg. Check: ½ m R² = 0.5 × 679 × 0.1836 = 62.34 kg·m², matching the required inertia. The rim speed is ωR = 10.8 m/s, well within the limits for cast steel.

Answer: 679 kg

(d)

At 480 rpm, ω = 50.27 rad/s so ω² is four times larger and the required inertia is I = 3937.5/(0.10 × 2526.6) = 15.58 kg·m², a quarter of the earlier value. Then R⁴ = 2I/(ρπb) scales by 1/4, so R = 0.3030 m. The mass is m = ρπR²b = 339.6 kg. Mass scales with R², hence it falls by a factor of 2 to about half, a saving of 340 kg. The gain has a cost: the gearbox between shafts must carry the full peak torque on its 480 rpm side with a lower torque but must transmit the fluctuating load, and the extra gear stage adds backlash and noise.

Answer: 339.6 kg

Problem 5 [A2-055] Balancing of rotating masses

A small turbine rotor has three blade segments modelled as point masses rotating in the same transverse plane: 2.0 kg at radius 0.15 m at angle 0 degrees, 3.0 kg at radius 0.12 m at 100 degrees and 1.5 kg at radius 0.20 m at 220 degrees, all angles measured counterclockwise from the datum. Following a rebuild the rotor is to be corrected by a single balancing mass bolted into the same plane at a radius of 0.10 m. The rotor runs at 6000 rpm. Maintenance also wants to know what happens in service if the 3.0 kg segment is shed after the rotor has been balanced, for instance by a blade failure. Neglect shaft flexibility and treat the rotor as rigid.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the resultant unbalance (the vector sum of m r) of the three masses. [5]
  2. (b) Find the balancing mass required at 0.10 m radius, and state its angular position. [5]
  3. (c) Find the unbalanced rotating force on the bearings before correction at 6000 rpm. [5]
  4. (d) After balancing, the 3.0 kg segment is lost. Find the force now transmitted to the bearings. [5]
(a)

Treat each unbalance as a vector m r at its angle. The x components are 2.0 × 0.15 cos0° = 0.3000, 3.0 × 0.12 cos100° = -0.0625 and 1.5 × 0.20 cos220° = -0.2298, summing to 0.0077 kg·m. The y components are 0, 0.3545 and -0.1928, summing to 0.1617 kg·m. The resultant magnitude is √(0.0077² + 0.1617²) = 0.1619 kg·m at 87.3° from the datum. This resultant is what the rotor would throw outwards per unit of ω². Writing the vectors in complex form and adding them is the quickest route on an exam, and a graphical polygon of vectors drawn to scale gives the same magnitude and angle as a check.

Answer: 0.1619 kg·m

(b)

For balance the added mass must produce a vector equal and opposite to the resultant, so mb rb = 0.1619 kg·m. With rb = 0.10 m the balancing mass is mb = 0.1619/0.10 = 1.619 kg. The mass must be placed 180° from the resultant, at 267.3° from the datum, so that its centrifugal pull cancels the sum. A larger radius would need a smaller mass, but the radius is limited by the clearance of the casing. Verify by adding vectors: the three original vectors plus the balance vector should sum to zero in both components, which is a check a marker rewards.

Answer: 1.619 kg

(c)

The centrifugal force from a rotating unbalance is F = (Σ m r) ω². The angular speed is ω = 2π × 6000/60 = 628.32 rad/s, so ω² = 394784 rad²/s². Then F = 0.1619 × 394784 = 63906 N. This force rotates with the shaft, so the bearings see a once per revolution sinusoidal load of this amplitude, shared between the two bearings according to the axial position of the plane. This force equals the weight of about 6.5 tonnes (63906/9.81), which shows how severe a resultant unbalance of 0.1619 kg·m is at 6000 rpm.

Answer: 63906 N

(d)

Once the rotor is balanced the vector sum of all m r terms is zero. When the 3.0 kg segment is lost, the remaining unbalance equals the negative of the lost vector: the residual is exactly the m r of the lost mass, 3.0 × 0.12 = 0.36 kg·m, directed opposite to where that segment was. The force is F = 0.36 × ω² = 0.36 × 394784 = 142122 N. Compare this with 63906 N for the original unbalance: the failure produces a load 2.22 times as large. The result is independent of the balancing mass details because the balanced state cancels everything except the lost piece, and it explains why a blade loss usually forces an immediate trip.

Answer: 142122 N

A2 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A2-056] Gyroscopic effects

A marine turbine rotor of mass 1200 kg has a radius of gyration of 0.35 m about its spin axis, which is aligned fore and aft in a ship. It spins at 3000 rpm. In a rough sea the ship pitches simple harmonically with an amplitude of 6 degrees and a period of 20 s. The two bearings that carry the rotor are 1.6 m apart. The ship's owner is considering a switch to a lower speed turbine running at 2000 rpm, because the sea state on the new route is worse and pitching would have a period of only 10 s with the same amplitude. The lower speed turbine has the same mass and radius of gyration as the present one. Neglect the change in angular momentum from the ship's roll and any torque from the rotor weight itself.

  1. (a) Find the maximum angular velocity of pitching (the precession rate) on the current route. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum gyroscopic couple acting on the ship structure through the rotor on the current route. [5]
  3. (c) Find the corresponding maximum additional reaction at each bearing. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum gyroscopic couple for the lower speed rotor on the new route and state which design gives the smaller couple. [6]
(a)

For simple harmonic pitching, θ = θ0 sin(2πt/T), so the angular velocity of the precession axis is dθ/dt = θ0 (2π/T) cos(2πt/T). Its maximum is ωp = θ0 (2π/T). With θ0 = 6° = 0.1047 rad and T = 20 s, ωp = 0.1047 × 2π/20 = 0.03290 rad/s. This maximum occurs when the ship passes through the level position moving fastest, and it is when the gyroscopic effect is greatest. At the extreme pitch angles the angular velocity is zero and so is the couple, so the effect is cyclic with the pitching period.

Answer: 0.03290 rad/s

(b)

The mass moment of inertia of the rotor about its spin axis is I = m k² = 1200 × 0.35² = 147.0 kg·m². The spin speed is ω = 2π × 3000/60 = 314.16 rad/s. The gyroscopic couple is C = I ω ωp for a spin axis perpendicular to the precession axis, which holds here because pitch is about a transverse axis while the spin axis is longitudinal. Thus C = 147.0 × 314.16 × 0.03290 = 1519 N·m. The couple acts about the third mutually perpendicular axis, tending to yaw the bow, and the bearings react it by a pair of equal and opposite forces.

Answer: 1519 N·m

(c)

The couple must be resisted by a pair of forces at the two bearings, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, separated by the bearing distance L = 1.6 m. Therefore Fb × L = C and Fb = C/L = 1519/1.6 = 950 N. One bearing is pushed in one direction horizontally and the other opposite, in the plane perpendicular to the spin axis. These reactions are in addition to the static weight support and they reverse sign every half pitch cycle, so they must be checked for bearing fatigue. Compare with the rotor weight 1200 × 9.81 = 11772 N: the gyroscopic reaction is 16.1 percent of the static load on one bearing.

Answer: 950 N

(d)

On the new route the pitching period is 10 s, so ωp = 0.10472 × 2π/10 = 0.06580 rad/s, double the earlier value. The spin speed falls to 2000 rpm, so ω = 209.44 rad/s, two thirds of before. If the rotor inertia were kept the same, C = I ω ωp = 147.0 × 209.44 × 0.06580 = 2026 N·m. This is 1.33 times the current couple, because the factor 2/3 from speed is outweighed by the factor 2 from precession rate. The existing 3000 rpm design with its smaller precession rate gives the smaller couple, so the lower speed turbine does not reduce the gyroscopic load on the new route.

Answer: 2026 N·m

Problem 2 [A2-057] Single degree of freedom free vibration

An instrument platform sits on four identical springs and its mass is not recorded. A technician taps it and records a natural frequency of 7.2 Hz. A 20 kg calibration block is then fixed to the platform and the test is repeated, giving a natural frequency of 6.4 Hz. Damping is small enough to be ignored. Treat the platform as a rigid body moving vertically on springs of constant total stiffness. Later the platform is displaced 5 mm downward from equilibrium and given a downward velocity of 0.20 m/s by a passing trolley. You must find the unknown platform properties from the two frequency tests, then predict the free response and check whether the spring clearance of 8 mm is adequate.

  1. (a) Find the mass of the platform. [5]
  2. (b) Find the total spring stiffness. [5]
  3. (c) Find the static deflection of the platform on its springs. [5]
  4. (d) Find the amplitude of the free vibration after the trolley disturbance and state whether the 8 mm clearance is adequate. [5]
(a)

For an undamped system ωn = √(k/m), so f ∝ 1/√m for a fixed k. Writing the two tests, (2π × 7.2)² = k/m and (2π × 6.4)² = k/(m + 20). Dividing the first by the second gives (7.2/6.4)² = (m + 20)/m = 1.265625. Hence 20/m = 0.265625 and m = 20/0.265625 = 75.3 kg. The method eliminates the unknown stiffness through the ratio of the squared frequencies. Check: adding 20 kg to 75.3 kg changes the frequency by the factor √(75.3/95.3) = 0.8889, and 6.4/7.2 = 0.8889, which agrees.

Answer: 75.3 kg

(b)

Using the first test, ωn = 2π × 7.2 = 45.239 rad/s, so the stiffness is k = m ωn² = 75.3 × 2046.6 = 154094 N/m = 154.1 kN/m. Since four identical springs share this load in parallel, each spring has stiffness k/4 = 38.52 kN/m. Cross check with the second test: √(k/(m + 20)) = √(154094/95.3) = 40.21 rad/s, which is 2π × 6.4 = 40.21 rad/s, so the two tests agree. The unit conversion from N/m to kN/m is the final step. Because the total stiffness is the sum of the four spring rates in parallel, a single damaged spring would lower both k and the natural frequency, which is how the test could also be used for diagnosis.

Answer: 154.1 kN/m

(c)

The static deflection is the compression of the springs under the platform's own weight, δst = m g/k = 75.3 × 9.81/154094 = 4.79 mm. A useful check uses the natural frequency formula fn = (1/2π)√(g/δst), giving √(9.81/0.00479) = 45.24 rad/s, which equals ωn. So the frequency and the static deflection carry the same information. The mid stroke deflection also tells the designer how much the platform settles when it is loaded, and it sets the vertical clearance that must be provided below the springs when the platform is first installed.

Answer: 4.79 mm

(d)

For free undamped motion x = x0 cos ωn t + (v0/ωn) sin ωn t, which has amplitude X = √(x0² + (v0/ωn)²). The velocity term gives v0/ωn = 0.20/45.239 = 4.421 mm. With x0 = 5 mm, X = √(5² + 4.421²) = 6.67 mm. The peak excursion from equilibrium is therefore 6.67 mm, below the 8 mm clearance, so the clearance is adequate with a margin of 1.33 mm. Since damping was neglected, this is a conservative estimate: any real damping would reduce the amplitude on later cycles, but the first peak is unaffected.

Answer: 6.67 mm (within the 8 mm clearance)

Problem 3 [A2-058] Damped free vibration and logarithmic decrement

A 220 kg trolley carrying a sensitive machine is suspended on a spring and a viscous damper, and its suspension properties are unknown. The trolley is pulled down and released, and a recorder traces the displacement. The first peak is 24 mm and the peak five complete cycles later is 6.2 mm. The time between successive peaks is 0.42 s. The designer suspects the damper has leaked fluid, since the vibration seems to persist longer than on the older identical trolley. Treat the system as a single degree of freedom with viscous damping, and use the recorded data to find the suspension constants so that you can compare them with the specification of the old trolley.

  1. (a) Find the logarithmic decrement from the recorded peaks. [4]
  2. (b) Find the damping ratio. [4]
  3. (c) Find the spring stiffness. [4]
  4. (d) Find the damping coefficient of the damper. [4]
  5. (e) Find the number of complete cycles needed for the amplitude to fall from 24 mm to below 1 mm. [4]
(a)

The logarithmic decrement is defined over successive peaks as δ = ln(xn/xn+1) and over n cycles as δ = (1/n) ln(x0/xn). With x0 = 24 mm, x5 = 6.2 mm and n = 5, δ = (1/5) ln(24/6.2) = (1/5)(1.3535) = 0.2707. Averaging over five cycles reduces the effect of reading error on any single peak, which is why the measurement used five cycles. The decrement is dimensionless and does not depend on the amplitude, as long as the damping is viscous and the system is linear. Using only the first and second peaks would give a noisier estimate, because a 0.2 mm reading error on a 6 mm peak is about 3 percent of the value and would feed straight into the decrement.

Answer: 0.2707

(b)

The exact relation is δ = 2πζ/√(1 - ζ²), which solves to ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²). Substituting, ζ = 0.2707/√(39.478 + 0.0733) = 0.2707/6.2890 = 0.0430. This is a lightly damped system, so the approximation ζ ≈ δ/2π = 0.0431 is also close, differing by under 1 percent. A damping ratio near 0.04 means the trolley will oscillate many times and indeed the observation of long lasting vibration is consistent with this value. The result also implies each cycle loses a fraction 1 - e-δ of its amplitude, so the logarithmic decrement is a direct and convenient measure of how quickly the vibration dies away in a suspension test.

Answer: 0.0430

(c)

The damped period is 0.42 s, so ωd = 2π/0.42 = 14.960 rad/s. The natural frequency follows from ωd = ωn √(1 - ζ²), giving ωn = 14.960/√(1 - 0.00185) = 14.974 rad/s. The correction for damping is only 0.09 percent. Then k = m ωn² = 220 × 224.22 = 49328 N/m = 49.3 kN/m. Using the damped frequency instead of the undamped one would have under-estimated the stiffness by about twice this percentage, because stiffness varies as the square of frequency. The result is the stiffness of the suspension alone and does not depend on the damper, so it can be compared directly with the spring rate quoted by the maker.

Answer: 49.3 kN/m

(d)

The damping coefficient is c = ζ cc, where the critical value is cc = 2 m ωn = 2 × 220 × 14.974 = 6588 N·s/m. Hence c = 0.0430 × 6588 = 284 N·s/m. Compare this with the specification of the old trolley: if the old damper gave ζ = 0.10 with the same mass and stiffness, it would have had c = 659 N·s/m, so the present damper delivers only 43 percent of that, supporting the suspicion of a leak. A marker expects the comparison to be stated with numbers and a recommendation to refill or replace the damper.

Answer: 284 N·s/m

(e)

The amplitude decays as xn = x0 e-nδ. Setting xn = 1 mm gives n = ln(x0/xn)/δ = ln(24/1)/0.2707 = 3.1781/0.2707 = 11.7 cycles. So 12 complete cycles are needed, which at 0.42 s per cycle is about 5.0 s. If the damper were restored to ζ = 0.10, δ = 2π(0.10)/√(1 - 0.01) = 0.631 and the number of cycles would drop to 5.0, which is about 5, more than halving the settling time. This estimate assumes the damping stays viscous at small amplitude, whereas dry friction in worn guides would remove amplitude linearly rather than exponentially, so the reading should be treated as a guide.

Answer: 11.7 cycles

Problem 4 [A2-059] Forced vibration and resonance

A centrifugal fan of 400 kg sits on a floor slab modelled as a spring of stiffness 1.6 MN/m with viscous damping equal to 6 percent of critical. A rotating imbalance and the blade pass effect produce a harmonic vertical force of amplitude 1800 N on the slab at the fan running frequency, which is currently 55 rad/s. The plant engineer proposes raising the running speed to 70 rad/s to increase the airflow and wants to know whether this moves the machine closer to or further from resonance. Treat the force amplitude as constant with frequency, which is a simplification, and model the slab and fan as a single degree of freedom system.

  1. (a) Find the undamped natural frequency of the fan and slab system. [3]
  2. (b) Find the steady state vibration amplitude at 55 rad/s. [5]
  3. (c) Find the phase lag of the displacement behind the force at 55 rad/s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the amplitude that would occur at resonance. [4]
  5. (e) Find the amplitude at the proposed 70 rad/s and say whether the change helps. [4]
(a)

The natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √(1.6 × 10⁶/400) = √4000 = 63.25 rad/s, equal to 10.07 Hz. The operating frequency of 55 rad/s gives a frequency ratio r = 55/63.25 = 0.8696, which is below resonance but close enough that the amplification is significant. The ratio is the key quantity for every following part. Keeping the running speed between about 0.7 and 1.3 times the natural frequency is generally avoided, and this fan at r = 0.87 sits inside the band that is normally avoided. The dynamic response in the later parts depends only on r and ζ, so computing ωn accurately here prevents errors from propagating into every other answer.

Answer: 63.25 rad/s

(b)

The steady state amplitude is X = (F0/k)/√[(1 - r²)² + (2ζr)²]. The static deflection is F0/k = 1800/1.6 × 10⁶ = 1.1250 mm. With r = 0.8696, 1 - r² = 0.2437 and 2ζr = 2(0.06)(0.8696) = 0.1044. The denominator is √(0.05941 + 0.01089) = 0.2651. Hence X = 1.1250/0.2651 = 4.243 mm. This is an amplification of 3.77 times the static deflection. The result is only a few times the static deflection, yet the force acts on a floor slab whose own strength must be checked against the dynamic load, which is the product of stiffness and amplitude.

Answer: 4.243 mm

(c)

The phase angle of the displacement behind the force is φ = tan⁻¹[2ζr/(1 - r²)], taken in the first or second quadrant. Here 2ζr = 0.1044 and 1 - r² = 0.2437 is positive because r < 1, so φ = tan⁻¹(0.4281) = 23.2°. Below resonance the displacement is nearly in phase with the force, and the phase lag rises to 90° at resonance and approaches 180° well above it. A phase of 23.2° confirms that the fan is still operating on the stiffness controlled side of the resonance curve.

Answer: 23.2 degrees

(d)

At resonance r = 1, so the first term in the denominator vanishes and X = (F0/k)/(2ζ) = 1.1250 mm/(2 × 0.06) = 9.375 mm. This is the quality factor Q = 1/(2ζ) = 8.33 times the static deflection. The true peak amplitude occurs very slightly below r = 1 at r = √(1 - 2ζ²) = 0.9964, but the difference is negligible at this low damping. The resonance amplitude is 2.21 times the amplitude at the present speed, which shows how sharp the resonance peak is and the danger of passing through it during run up.

Answer: 9.375 mm

(e)

At 70 rad/s the ratio is r = 70/63.25 = 1.1068, now above resonance. Then 1 - r² = -0.2250 and 2ζr = 0.1328, so the denominator is √(0.0506 + 0.0176) = 0.2613. The amplitude is X = 1.1250/0.2613 = 4.306 mm. This is slightly larger than the 4.243 mm at present, so raising the speed does not help; the fan must also pass through resonance at 63 rad/s during start up, and in practice the unbalance force grows as ω², so the real amplitude would be higher than this constant force estimate.

Answer: 4.306 mm

Problem 5 [A2-060] Base excitation and vibration isolation

A 45 kg laboratory instrument rests on four identical rubber mounts of total stiffness 220 kN/m and damping ratio 0.08. A compressor in the next room shakes the floor harmonically at 18 Hz with a displacement amplitude of 0.40 mm, and the instrument readings are noisy. A colleague suggests simply fitting softer mounts of half the stiffness, arguing that softer is always better for isolation. The mount damping coefficient would stay the same, so the damping ratio would change when the stiffness is halved. Treat the instrument as a rigid mass moving vertically only, and use the standard transmissibility relation for harmonic base motion.

  1. (a) Find the natural frequency of the instrument on its mounts in hertz. [4]
  2. (b) Find the displacement transmissibility at 18 Hz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the absolute vibration amplitude of the instrument. [5]
  4. (d) Find the transmissibility after the mounts are replaced by ones of half the stiffness at the same damping coefficient, and say whether the change helps. [6]
(a)

The natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √(220000/45) = 69.92 rad/s. Converting, fn = ωn/2π = 69.92/6.2832 = 11.13 Hz. The disturbing frequency of 18 Hz therefore gives a frequency ratio r = 18/11.13 = 1.618. Since r exceeds √2 = 1.414, the mounts are already in the isolation region, where the transmissibility falls below 1. This is the key observation for the later comparison: isolation only works when r > √2, and the damping that helps near resonance becomes slightly harmful above √2. Because the isolation formulae depend only on r and ζ, this single frequency calculation fixes the operating region for the remaining parts of the problem, so it deserves a check.

Answer: 11.13 Hz

(b)

The displacement transmissibility is T = √[1 + (2ζr)²]/√[(1 - r²)² + (2ζr)²]. With ζ = 0.08 and r = 1.618, 2ζr = 0.2588, so the numerator is √(1 + 0.0670) = 1.0329. The denominator uses 1 - r² = -1.6163, so it is √(2.6126 + 0.0670) = 1.6369. Therefore T = 1.0329/1.6369 = 0.631. About 63 percent of the floor motion reaches the instrument. The numerator term √(1 + (2ζr)²) shows the damping raises transmissibility above r = √2, which is why very lightly damped mounts isolate best in the high frequency region.

Answer: 0.631

(c)

The transmissibility is the ratio of the instrument's absolute displacement amplitude to the base amplitude, so X = T Y = 0.631 × 0.40 mm = 0.252 mm. This is a displacement amplitude at 18 Hz. The corresponding acceleration is ω² X = (2π × 18)² × 0.252 × 10⁻³ = 3.23 m/s², about 0.33 g, and may be the better measure of whether the readings are disturbed. The absolute amplitude, not the relative motion across the mounts, is what the instrument case actually feels. If the instrument manufacturer specifies a limit on floor acceleration, the acceleration form is the one to compare with the specification, because displacement can look harmless even where acceleration is not.

Answer: 0.252 mm

(d)

With the damping coefficient unchanged at c = 2ζ√(km) = 2(0.08)√(220000 × 45) = 503.4 N·s/m, halving the stiffness to k = 110 kN/m gives ωn = 49.44 rad/s and a new damping ratio ζ = c/(2√(km)) = 0.1131. The frequency ratio becomes r = 2π(18)/49.44 = 2.288. Then 2ζr = 0.5176 and 1 - r² = -4.2327, so T = √(1 + 0.2679)/√(17.9156 + 0.2679) = 0.264. This is lower than 0.631, so softer mounts do help here, as the machine is further beyond √2. The cost is a larger static deflection, 4.01 mm instead of 2.01 mm.

Answer: 0.264

A2 Practice Paper 13

Problem 1 [A2-061] Rotating unbalance

A centrifugal fan and motor set has a total mass of 240 kg, including a rotor with an unbalance product m·e = 0.25 kg·m (mass times eccentricity). The set is mounted on rubber-and-steel isolators whose combined vertical stiffness is 3.6 MN/m and whose damping ratio is 0.08. Motion is restricted to the vertical direction. The fan runs continuously at 1500 rpm. After a bearing was replaced, operators reported noticeable floor vibration, and the maintenance team is considering several modifications. Treat the isolators as a linear spring and viscous damper in parallel, and treat the unbalanced rotor as the only source of excitation. Gravity acts but only the dynamic response is of interest.

  1. (a) Determine the undamped natural frequency of the supported machine in rad/s. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the steady-state vibration amplitude at the running speed. [6]
  3. (c) The maintenance team proposes adding viscous dampers that raise the damping ratio to 0.20 without changing mass or stiffness. Find the new amplitude at the running speed and comment on the trend. [5]
  4. (d) For the original damping ratio, find the amplitude of the force transmitted to the floor at the running speed, in kN. [5]
(a)

The supported machine behaves as a single degree of freedom system with total mass M and spring stiffness k acting in parallel to the floor. The undamped natural frequency is ωn = √(k/M). Substituting, ωn = √(3.6×10⁶ / 240) = √15000 = 122.5 rad/s, which is 1170 rpm. Assumptions: the unbalance mass is part of the 240 kg, the motion is vertical only, damping is viscous and the supports are linear. This value is the reference against which the running speed is judged in the later parts, so state the frequency ratio before using it. Units: N/m divided by kg gives s⁻², hence rad/s after the root.

Answer: 122.5 rad/s

(b)

Running speed ω = 2π×1500/60 = 157.1 rad/s, so the frequency ratio r = ω/ωn = 157.1/122.5 = 1.283. For rotating unbalance the steady amplitude is X = (me/M) r² / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]. Here me/M = 0.25/240 = 0.001042 m. Numerator factor r² = 1.645. Denominator: (1 − r²)² = 0.4159 and (2ζr)² = (2×0.08×1.283)² = 0.04211, root = 0.6768. Therefore X = 2.532 mm. The machine runs above resonance, so the amplitude is controlled mainly by the mass ratio.

Answer: 2.532 mm

(c)

The same equation is used with ζ = 0.20, leaving r unchanged. Then (2ζr)² = (2×0.20×1.283)² = 0.2632, so the denominator is √(0.4159 + 0.2632) = 0.8241. X = (0.25/240)×1.645/0.8241 = 2.079 mm. The amplitude changes by only -17.9 percent. Well above resonance the (1 − r²) term dominates the denominator, so extra damping barely reduces the response, and the amplitude tends toward me/M. The trend is a lesson that dampers help mostly near resonance, and they raise force transmission at high r.

Answer: 2.079 mm

(d)

The force transmitted through the spring and damper is FT = X √(k² + (cω)²) = kX √(1 + (2ζr)²), with the original ζ = 0.08 and X = 2.532 mm. Evaluate 2ζr = 2×0.08×1.283 = 0.2052, so √(1 + 0.04211) = 1.021. Then FT = 3.6×10⁶ × 0.002532 × 1.021 = 9304 N = 9.304 kN. This is the dynamic load the floor must carry in addition to the 2.35 kN static weight of the machine. A marker expects the damper force to be added in quadrature with the spring force because the two are 90 degrees out of phase.

Answer: 9.304 kN

Problem 2 [A2-062] Two degree of freedom systems and mode shapes

A sampling hopper of mass m2 = 30 kg rides on a light horizontal rail carriage of mass m1 = 50 kg in a mineral-processing plant. The carriage is held to a fixed frame by a spring of stiffness k1 = 400 kN/m, and the hopper is connected to the carriage by a second spring of stiffness k2 = 250 kN/m. Both masses move only along the rail, with negligible friction and damping. Each mass has one coordinate, x1 for the carriage and x2 for the hopper, both measured from static equilibrium. Operators sometimes top up the hopper with extra ore, and the engineer wants to know how that changes the free vibration behaviour of the two-mass system.

  1. (a) Find the lower natural frequency of the system in Hz. [5]
  2. (b) Find the higher natural frequency of the system in Hz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the mode shape ratio X2/X1 for the lower mode. [5]
  4. (d) The sampling hopper is refilled so that m2 becomes 45 kg. Find the new lower natural frequency in Hz and say whether it rises or falls. [5]
(a)

Equations of motion: m1 x1'' + (k1 + k2) x1 − k2 x2 = 0 and m2 x2'' − k2 x1 + k2 x2 = 0. For harmonic motion, det(K − ω²M) = 0 gives m1m2 ω⁴ − [m2(k1 + k2) + m1k2] ω² + k1k2 = 0. Numbers: 1500 ω⁴ − [30×6.5×10⁵ + 50×2.5×10⁵] ω² + 4×10⁵×2.5×10⁵ = 0, that is 1500 ω⁴ − 3.2×10⁷ ω² + 1×10¹¹ = 0. The roots are ω² = 3803 and 1.753 × 10⁴ s⁻². Lower ω1 = 61.67 rad/s, so f1 = ω1/2π = 9.815 Hz. Assumptions: small linear motion, massless springs, no damping, and both masses move horizontally on a frictionless guide.

Answer: 9.815 Hz

(b)

Using the same characteristic equation, the larger root is ω² = 1.753 × 10⁴ s⁻², so ω2 = 132.4 rad/s. Convert to hertz: f2 = 132.4/(2π) = 21.07 Hz. A useful check is that the sum of the two roots equals the trace term (k1 + k2)/m1 + k2/m2 = 2.133 × 10⁴ s⁻², and the product equals k1k2/(m1m2) = 6.667 × 10⁷ s⁻⁴. Here 3803 + 1.753 × 10⁴ = 2.133 × 10⁴, which matches. The frequency ratio f2/f1 = 2.147 shows how widely spaced the modes are, which matters when the excitation frequency lies between them.

Answer: 21.07 Hz

(c)

Take the first row of (K − ω1²M)X = 0: (k1 + k2 − m1ω1²) X1 − k2 X2 = 0, so X2/X1 = (k1 + k2 − m1ω1²)/k2. Substituting, X2/X1 = (6.5×10⁵ − 50×3803)/2.5×10⁵ = (4.599 × 10⁵)/2.5×10⁵ = 1.839. The ratio is positive and greater than 1, so in the lower mode both masses move in phase with the outer mass m2 having the larger amplitude, and there is no node. In the upper mode the ratio is negative (the masses move in opposition), which is the usual pattern for a chain with one end fixed.

Answer: 1.839

(d)

With m2 = 45 kg the characteristic equation becomes m1m2 ω⁴ − [m2(k1 + k2) + m1k2] ω² + k1k2 = 0, i.e. 2250 ω⁴ − [45×6.5×10⁵ + 1.25×10⁷] ω² + 1×10¹¹ = 0, or 2250 ω⁴ − 4.175×10⁷ ω² + 1×10¹¹ = 0. The lower root is ω² = 2825 s⁻², giving ω1 = 53.15 rad/s and f1 = 8.46 Hz. This is a fall of 13.8 percent from the original 9.815 Hz. Adding mass to a vibrating system with unchanged stiffness always lowers every natural frequency (Rayleigh's monotonicity), so the lower mode moves toward the likely excitation band, which should be checked.

Answer: 8.46 Hz, lower

Problem 3 [A2-063] Vibration absorbers

A reciprocating compressor of mass 800 kg is supported on a rigid frame that behaves as a spring of stiffness 3.2 MN/m in the vertical direction. It experiences a harmonic vertical force of amplitude 1200 N at a fixed running frequency that, by coincidence, equals the natural frequency of the supported machine, giving a resonance problem. The plant engineer proposes an undamped dynamic vibration absorber (a small mass on a spring attached to the machine) with a mass equal to 10 percent of the machine mass. Neglect damping in both the support and the absorber, and treat the motion as one-dimensional in the vertical direction.

  1. (a) Find the absorber stiffness, in kN/m, that tunes the absorber to the machine natural frequency. [4]
  2. (b) Find the lower natural frequency of the combined two-mass system, in Hz. [4]
  3. (c) Find the higher natural frequency of the combined system, in Hz. [4]
  4. (d) At exactly the original forcing frequency, find the absorber mass amplitude in mm. [4]
  5. (e) Wear causes the forcing frequency to drift upward by 6 percent. Find the machine amplitude in mm and state whether the absorber still protects the machine. [4]
(a)

The machine natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √(3.2×10⁶/800) = 63.25 rad/s (10.07 Hz), and the forcing frequency is equal to this value. The absorber mass is ma = μm = 0.10×800 = 80 kg. Tuning requires √(ka/ma) = ωn, so ka = ma ωn² = 80×4000 = 3.2 × 10⁵ N/m = 320 kN/m. At this tuning the absorber force on the machine exactly cancels the applied force, which is the principle of the undamped dynamic vibration absorber. Equivalent check: ka/k = μ = 0.10 because the two natural frequencies are equal.

Answer: 320 kN/m

(b)

Combined system: [m 0; 0 ma]{x''} + [k + ka, −ka; −ka, ka]{x} = {F0 sin ωt; 0}. With ωa = ωn and μ = 0.10, the frequency equation in β = ω/ωn is β⁴ − (2 + μ) β² + 1 = 0, so β² = 1 + μ/2 ∓ √(μ + μ²/4) = 1.05 ∓ 0.3202. The lower root is β1² = 0.7298, β1 = 0.8543. Then ω1 = 0.8543×63.25 = 54.03 rad/s and f1 = 8.599 Hz. The original resonance at 10.07 Hz has been replaced by two resonances either side of it.

Answer: 8.599 Hz

(c)

The upper root is β2² = 1.05 + 0.3202 = 1.37, so β2 = 1.171. Then ω2 = 1.171×63.25 = 74.03 rad/s and f2 = ω2/2π = 11.78 Hz. The usable band for the absorber lies between f1 = 8.599 Hz and f2 = 11.78 Hz, a window of about ±15.8 percent of the operating frequency. A larger μ widens this window but needs a heavier absorber and a stiffer spring. The check β1²β2² = 1 confirms the tuned case: 1.

Answer: 11.78 Hz

(d)

At ω = ωn the machine amplitude is zero, so the absorber spring force must balance the applied force: ka X2 = F0 (in magnitude). Thus X2 = F0/ka = 1200/3.2 × 10⁵ = 0.00375 m = 3.75 mm, with the absorber moving 180 degrees out of phase with the applied force. This is also the amplitude the absorber spring must be designed for, since the fatigue stress in the spring follows ka X2 = F0 = 1200 N. If this amplitude were too large for the available space, a larger mass ratio (with a stiffer ka) would be required.

Answer: 3.75 mm

(e)

With ω = 1.06 ωn = 67.04 rad/s, solve the 2×2 dynamic stiffness equations: X1 = F0 (ka − maω²)/Δ, where Δ = (k + ka − mω²)(ka − maω²) − ka². Compute ka − maω² = -3.955 × 10⁴ N/m and k + ka − mω² = -7.552 × 10⁴ N/m. Then Δ = -9.941 × 10¹⁰ N²/m², so |X1| = 0.4774 mm. This is small compared with the unprotected resonant response, but no longer zero. At 1.06 ωn the frequency is still between f1 and f2, so the absorber still protects the machine, though with only a small margin to the upper resonance.

Answer: 0.4774 mm, still protects

Problem 4 [A2-064] Torsional vibration of shafts

A motor drives a slurry pump through a solid steel shaft of diameter 60 mm and length 1.2 m. The shear modulus of the steel is 79 GPa. The motor rotor has a mass moment of inertia of 1.8 kg·m² and the pump impeller 0.6 kg·m². The shaft itself and the couplings can be treated as massless, and the bearings do not restrain twisting, so the pair behaves as a free-free two-inertia torsional system. A variable-frequency drive produces a small pulsating torque, and the commissioning engineer must confirm that the torsional natural frequency is clear of it. The plant layout is under review, which may force a longer shaft of the same diameter.

  1. (a) Find the torsional stiffness of the shaft, in kN·m/rad. [4]
  2. (b) Find the fundamental torsional natural frequency of the two-rotor system in Hz. [6]
  3. (c) Find the distance from the motor rotor to the vibration node. [4]
  4. (d) Layout changes require a shaft of the same diameter but length 1.5 m. Find the new natural frequency in Hz and the percentage change. [6]
(a)

For a solid circular shaft the polar second moment of area is J = πd⁴/32 = π(0.060)⁴/32 = 1.272 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. The torsional stiffness of a uniform shaft between two rotors is kt = GJ/L = 79×10⁹ × 1.272 × 10⁻⁶/1.2 = 8.376 × 10⁴ N·m/rad = 83.76 kN·m/rad. Assumptions: the shaft is uniform with negligible inertia, the rotors are rigid discs with the stated mass moments of inertia, there is no damping, and the elastic behaviour is linear. The result is the spring rate used in the two-inertia model in the next part. Check units: Pa × m⁴ / m = N·m, per radian.

Answer: 83.76 kN·m/rad

(b)

A two-rotor shaft system free at both ends has one rigid-body mode at zero frequency and one torsional mode, with the rotors twisting in opposition. Equations: J1 θ1'' + kt(θ1 − θ2) = 0 and J2 θ2'' + kt(θ2 − θ1) = 0. Subtracting leads to ωn = √[kt (J1 + J2)/(J1 J2)]. With kt = 8.376 × 10⁴ N·m/rad, J1 + J2 = 2.4 kg·m² and J1J2 = 1.08 kg²·m⁴, ωn = √(8.376 × 10⁴×2.4/1.08) = 431.4 rad/s. Therefore f = ωn/2π = 68.67 Hz. The rotors swing against each other, and this frequency should be compared with any torque harmonics from the drive.

Answer: 68.67 Hz

(c)

At the natural frequency the node is the section of the shaft that does not twist. Since the inertias oscillate in opposition, the angular amplitudes are inversely proportional to the inertias: J1 Θ1 = −J2 Θ2, so Θ1/Θ2 = −J2/J1 = −0.6/1.8. The node lies along the shaft at distance l1 from J1, where l1/(L − l1) = Θ1/Θ2 in magnitude. Hence l1 = L J2/(J1 + J2) = 1.2×0.6/2.4 = 0.3 m from the motor rotor. The heavier rotor moves less, so the node lies close to it. Each half behaves like a single-rotor shaft with the node as a fixed end, and each half gives the same ωn, which is a good check.

Answer: 0.3 m

(d)

Changing the length alters only the stiffness, kt ∝ 1/L. New stiffness kt = GJ/L = 79×10⁹×1.272 × 10⁻⁶/1.5 = 6.701 × 10⁴ N·m/rad. New frequency ωn = √(kt (J1 + J2)/(J1J2)) = √(6.701 × 10⁴×2.4/1.08) = 385.9 rad/s, so f = 61.42 Hz. The percentage change from 68.67 Hz is -10.6 percent, which equals √(1.2/1.5) − 1, since frequency scales with 1/√L. Mass moments of inertia are unchanged, so the node position stays at 0.3 m from the motor rotor because it depends only on the ratio of inertias.

Answer: 61.42 Hz, -10.6 percent

Problem 5 [A2-065] Critical speed of shafts

A pump shaft in a municipal water plant is a solid steel shaft of diameter 40 mm and length 1.4 m, resting in two self-aligning bearings that act as simple supports. Young's modulus is 207 GPa. Two impellers are keyed to the shaft: a 30 kg impeller located 0.5 m from the left bearing and an 18 kg impeller located 1.0 m from the left bearing. The shaft mass is small compared with the impellers and may be neglected. The pump is to be run up through a range of speeds, and the engineer needs to estimate the first lateral critical speed and judge a possible shaft upgrade. Use g = 9.81 m/s². Treat the supports as having no flexibility.
