  1. (a) Find the static deflection of the shaft under disc 1, including the effect of disc 2. [4]
  2. (b) Estimate the first critical speed by the Rayleigh energy method, in rpm. [6]
  3. (c) Estimate the first critical speed by Dunkerley's method, in rpm, and comment on how the two estimates compare. [5]
  4. (d) A redesign increases the shaft diameter to 50 mm with the same discs. Find the Rayleigh critical speed in rpm. [5]
(a)

Treat the shaft as a simply supported beam of second moment I = πd⁴/64 = π(0.040)⁴/64 = 1.257 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴, with EI = 2.601 × 10⁴ N·m². For a unit load at a with the point of interest at x ≤ a and b = L − a, the influence coefficient is α = b x (L² − b² − x²)/(6EIL). This gives α11 = 1.854 × 10⁻⁶, α12 = 1.419 × 10⁻⁶ and α22 = 1.465 × 10⁻⁶ m/N. Deflection under disc 1 by superposition: y1 = g(m1 α11 + m2 α12) = 9.81×(30×1.854 × 10⁻⁶ + 18×1.419 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.796 mm. The shaft mass is neglected here, as the discs are far heavier than the shaft.

Answer: 0.796 mm

(b)

The disc deflections under their own weights are y1 = 0.796 mm and y2 = 0.6761 mm. Rayleigh equates maximum kinetic and potential energy for this deflected shape: ωn² = g Σ(m y) / Σ(m y²). Numerator: 9.81×(30×0.000796 + 18×0.0006761) = 0.3537. Denominator: 30×6.336 × 10⁻⁷ + 18×4.572 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.724 × 10⁻⁵. So ωn² = 1.298 × 10⁴ and ωn = 113.9 rad/s = 1088 rpm. Rayleigh's method always overestimates the true fundamental frequency slightly because the assumed shape is not the exact mode.

Answer: 1088 rpm

(c)

Dunkerley's method adds the reciprocals of the squared frequencies each disc would produce alone: 1/ωn² ≈ 1/ω1² + 1/ω2² where 1/ωi² = mi αii. Thus 1/ωn² = 30×1.854 × 10⁻⁶ + 18×1.465 × 10⁻⁶ = 8.197 × 10⁻⁵ s², giving ωn = 110.5 rad/s = 1055 rpm. Dunkerley's estimate is a lower bound, whereas Rayleigh's is an upper bound, so the true critical speed lies between 1055 and 1088 rpm. The two differ by 3.16 percent, a tight bracket, so either may be used for preliminary design. Operating speeds should remain 20 percent or more clear of the critical speed.

Answer: 1055 rpm

(d)

For d = 50 mm, I = π(0.050)⁴/64 = 3.068 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴, which is (50/40)⁴ = 2.441 times larger. All influence coefficients scale by 1/2.441, so every deflection falls by that factor. Since ωn² = gΣmy/Σmy² scales as 1/y, ωn rises by √2.441 = 1.562. Recomputing the Rayleigh sum with the new deflections y1 = 0.326 mm and y2 = 0.2769 mm gives ωn = 178 rad/s = 1700 rpm. This is 56.2 percent higher than the original, so a 25 percent larger diameter lifts the critical speed by about 56 percent.

Answer: 1700 rpm

A2 Practice Paper 14

Problem 1 [A2-066] Rigid body planar kinetics with energy methods

A gate arm at a mine weighbridge is modelled as a uniform slender steel bar of mass 4.0 kg and length 1.2 m, pinned at one end to a fixed post so that it swings freely in a vertical plane. The arm is released from rest in the horizontal position and swings down to the vertical position, where the pin sits above the centre of mass and the arm is hanging. Friction in the pin is negligible. A proposal has been made to fix a 2.0 kg sensor head to the free end of the arm, and the designer must check both the swing speed and the load on the pin. Use g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the angular velocity of the arm as it passes the vertical position. [4]
  2. (b) Find the vertical component of the pin reaction at that instant. [4]
  3. (c) A 2.0 kg sensor is bolted to the free end of the arm (treat it as a point mass). Find the new angular velocity at the vertical position. [6]
  4. (d) Find the new vertical pin reaction at the bottom of the swing, and compare it with the answer to part b. [6]
(a)

The arm is a uniform slender bar of mass 4.0 kg and length 1.2 m pivoted at one end, so I = mL²/3 = 4.0×1.44/3 = 1.92 kg·m². Released from rest horizontally, the mass centre falls through L/2 = 0.6 m. Energy conservation (the pin does no work): m g (L/2) = ½ I ω². So 4.0×9.81×0.6 = ½×1.92×ω², giving ω² = 24.53 and ω = √(3g/L) = 4.952 rad/s. The result does not depend on mass, only on g and L. Assumptions: a frictionless pin, rigid arm, and a start from rest at the horizontal position.

Answer: 4.952 rad/s

(b)

At the vertical position the weight acts along the arm line and has no moment about the pin, so the angular acceleration is zero (α = 0). The mass centre has no tangential acceleration, only the centripetal acceleration (L/2)ω² directed up toward the pin. Newton's second law vertically: R − m g = m (L/2) ω². Substituting: R = 4.0×9.81 + 4.0×0.6×24.53 = 39.24 + 58.86 = 98.1 N. Thus R = 2.5 m g, a result independent of length, which is a well known check. The horizontal pin component is zero at this position because the tangential acceleration is zero.

Answer: 98.1 N

(c)

Add the tip mass M = 2.0 kg at distance L. The moment of inertia becomes I = mL²/3 + ML² = 1.92 + 2.88 = 4.8 kg·m². The drop in potential energy is m g L/2 + M g L = 4.0×9.81×0.6 + 2.0×9.81×1.2 = 47.09 J. Equating to ½Iω²: ω² = 2×47.09/4.8 = 19.62 s⁻², so ω = 4.429 rad/s. Compared with part a, the arm turns 10.6 percent slower, because the added mass is placed at the largest radius and raises the inertia more than it raises the available energy.

Answer: 4.429 rad/s

(d)

At the vertical position α is again zero, so there is no tangential acceleration; only centripetal acceleration remains. The vertical equation for the composite body is R − (m + M)g = m (L/2) ω² + M L ω². Substituting: R = 6.0×9.81 + (4.0×0.6 + 2.0×1.2)×19.62 = 58.86 + 94.18 = 153 N. The reaction rises from 98.1 N to 153 N, an increase of 56 percent. The pin and bracket design load must be checked against this larger value, and the bolted sensor must also be rated for its own centripetal load M L ω² = 47.09 N.

Answer: 153 N

Problem 2 [A2-067] Planar mechanism velocity analysis by instant centres

A packaging machine uses a planar four-bar linkage. The ground pivots are O2 and O4, 350 mm apart on a horizontal line, with O2 on the left. The crank O2A is 120 mm long, the coupler AB is 400 mm and the rocker O4B is 300 mm. The crank rotates counterclockwise at a constant 40 rad/s and is currently at 60 degrees counterclockwise from the line O2O4. Pin B lies above the ground line in the assembly being studied. The designer wants the velocities of the links, a check using the instant-centre method and the speed of a point on the coupler where a sensor will be mounted. Link thicknesses are negligible.

  1. (a) Find the coupler angle θ3 (measured counterclockwise from the ground line) for the assembly where pin B lies above the line O2O4. [3]
  2. (b) Find the angular velocity of the rocker ω4 (counterclockwise positive). [4]
  3. (c) Find the angular velocity of the coupler ω3 (counterclockwise positive). [4]
  4. (d) Locate the instant centre I24 along the ground line, as a signed distance from O2 toward O4. Show how the velocity ratio fixes it. [5]
  5. (e) Find the speed of the midpoint of the coupler AB. [4]
(a)

Set O2 at the origin and O4 at (0.35, 0) m. The loop closure for the vectors is r2 eiθ2 + r3 eiθ3 = r1 + r4 eiθ4. With θ2 = 60°, the crank pin is at A = (0.06, 0.1039) m. Squaring the closure for B gives a distance condition |B − O4| = 0.30 m and |B − A| = 0.40 m, solved with the cosine rule in triangle A O4 B. Distance AO4 = 0.3081 m. Solving the two circles numerically for B above the ground line gives θ4 = 78.03° and θ3 = 28.29°. The check residual of both loop equations is below 10⁻¹² m. This is the positive branch; the mirror assembly has B below the line.

Answer: 28.29 degrees

(b)

Differentiate the loop equation: r2ω2 (−sin θ2, cos θ2) + r3ω3 (−sin θ3, cos θ3) = r4ω4 (−sin θ4, cos θ4). Resolving into x and y components gives two linear equations in ω3 and ω4. Equivalently, dot with a unit vector perpendicular to the coupler to eliminate ω3: ω4 = r2 ω2 sin(θ3 − θ2) / [r4 sin(θ3 − θ4)]. Numbers: sin(θ3 − θ2) = sin(-31.71°) = -0.5257, sin(θ3 − θ4) = -0.7631. ω4 = 0.12×40×(-0.5257)/(0.30×(-0.7631)) = 11.02 rad/s. Positive means counterclockwise.

Answer: 11.02 rad/s

(c)

Eliminate ω4 instead by dotting the velocity loop equation with a unit vector perpendicular to the rocker: ω3 = −r2ω2 sin(θ2 − θ4)/[r3 sin(θ3 − θ4)]. Compute sin(θ2 − θ4) = sin(-18.03°) = -0.3095 and sin(θ3 − θ4) = -0.7631. So ω3 = −0.12×40×(-0.3095)/(0.40×-0.7631) = -4.866 rad/s. The negative sign shows the coupler rotates clockwise at this instant while the crank and rocker turn counterclockwise. Check by substitution in the x-component of the velocity loop closure: the residual is below 10⁻⁹ m/s.

Answer: -4.866 rad/s

(d)

I24 is the point common to crank-side link 2 and link 4 with equal absolute velocity, and by Kennedy's theorem it lies on the line through the two fixed pivots O2 and O4. Let the point be at x from O2 along the ground line. Its velocity as a point on link 2 is ω2 x, and as a point on link 4 it is ω4 (x − 0.35), taken perpendicular to the line. Equating, ω2 x = ω4 (x − 0.35), so x = ω4 r1/(ω4 − ω2) = 11.02×0.35/(11.02 − 40) = -0.1331 m. The negative sign places I24 beyond O2 on the side away from O4, as expected because both links rotate the same way and the crank turns faster.

Answer: -0.1331 m

(e)

The midpoint M of AB has velocity vM = vA + ω3 × (r3/2) in the direction of the coupler. The pin A has vA = r2ω2 (−sin 60°, cos 60°) = 4.8×(−0.8660, 0.5) = (-4.157, 2.4) m/s. The relative velocity of M with respect to A is (r3/2) ω3 (−sin θ3, cos θ3) = 0.20×(-4.866)×(−0.4739, 0.8806) = (0.4612, -0.857) m/s. Adding the components gives the vector (-3.696, 1.543) m/s, whose magnitude is 4.005 m/s.

Answer: 4.005 m/s

Problem 3 [A2-068] Relative velocity and acceleration of a four-bar linkage

A textile machine uses a crank-rocker four-bar linkage to oscillate a yarn guide. The distance between the fixed pivots O2 and O4 is 250 mm, with O4 to the right of O2 on a horizontal ground line. The crank O2A is 80 mm, the coupler AB is 280 mm and the rocker O4B is 220 mm. The crank turns counterclockwise at a constant 25 rad/s. At the instant of interest the crank is at 120 degrees counterclockwise from the positive ground line, and pin B is above the ground line. The designer needs the velocities and accelerations of the coupler and rocker to size the drive, and then wants to see what the rocker acceleration implies for the loading of the crank.

  1. (a) Find the rocker angular velocity ω4 (counterclockwise positive). [3]
  2. (b) Find the coupler angular velocity ω3. [3]
  3. (c) Find the rocker angular acceleration α4 (counterclockwise positive). [5]
  4. (d) Find the coupler angular acceleration α3. [4]
  5. (e) The rocker has a mass moment of inertia of 0.12 kg·m² about O4. Find the magnitude of the inertia torque it needs at this instant, and say what it means for the load on the crank. [5]
(a)

Place O2 at the origin and O4 at (0.25, 0) m. The crank pin is A = 0.08(cos 120°, sin 120°) = (-0.04, 0.06928) m. Solving the loop closure numerically for the branch with B above the ground line gives θ3 = 31.16° and θ4 = 103.2°. The velocity equations r2ω2 (−sin θ2, cos θ2) + r3ω3 (−sin θ3, cos θ3) = r4ω4 (−sin θ4, cos θ4) are two linear equations in ω3 and ω4. Solving gives ω4 = 9.552 rad/s. The positive result means the rocker turns counterclockwise, the same sense as the crank, at this instant.

Answer: 9.552 rad/s

(b)

From the same pair of linear equations, ω3 = 2.165 rad/s. A quick check: the velocity of B found through the coupler is vB = vA + ω3 × r3, with vA = r2ω2 = 2.0 m/s directed perpendicular to the crank, while the velocity found through the rocker is r4ω4 = 0.22×9.552 = 2.102 m/s perpendicular to O4B. The x and y components of the two expressions for vB agree to better than 10⁻⁹ m/s, confirming the solution. The coupler rotates slowly compared with the rocker because the rocker is the short, rapidly pivoting output link of the mechanism.

Answer: 2.165 rad/s

(c)

The crank speed is constant, so α2 = 0. Differentiate the velocity equation once more. In the x direction: −r2ω2² cos θ2 − r3(α3 sin θ3 + ω3² cos θ3) + r4(α4 sin θ4 + ω4² cos θ4) = 0. In the y direction: −r2ω2² sin θ2 + r3(α3 cos θ3 − ω3² sin θ3) − r4(α4 cos θ4 − ω4² sin θ4) = 0. These are two linear equations in α3 and α4, with the centripetal terms ω² computed from the velocities above. Solving, α4 = -18.41 rad/s². The negative sign means the rocker is decelerating in its counterclockwise motion at this crank angle.

Answer: -18.41 rad/s²

(d)

From the simultaneous solution used in part c, the coupler acceleration is α3 = 105.9 rad/s². This is a large value since the coupler is short and light, and the acceleration of pin B is dominated by the normal terms r3ω3² = 1.312 m/s² and r4ω4² = 20.07 m/s². Cross-check: the acceleration of B through the rocker has tangential component r4α4 = -4.05 m/s² and normal component 20.07 m/s², and the same vector is obtained through the crank and coupler path. The two vectors match to better than 10⁻⁷ m/s².

Answer: 105.9 rad/s²

(e)

Neglecting other loads, the torque needed to produce the rocker acceleration is T = I4 α4 = 0.12×(-18.41) = 2.209 N·m in magnitude, acting clockwise because α4 is negative. This means the load at the rocker output must absorb 2.209 N·m of inertia, which the crank must supply through the coupler. The force carried by the coupler is roughly T/(r4 sin(θ3 − θ4)) = 10.55 N, so the crank torque is about that force times the crank arm. In a real design this inertia torque is added to the working load and gravity, and checked against the driving motor rating.

Answer: 2.209 N·m

Problem 4 [A2-069] Slider-crank kinematics

A single-cylinder engine for a portable pump has a crank radius of 55 mm and a connecting rod length of 190 mm. The cylinder bore is 90 mm and the piston assembly has a mass of 0.85 kg. The engine runs at a steady 3000 rpm. At the instant when the crank has turned 40 degrees from top dead centre (TDC) during the power stroke, the gas pressure acting on the piston crown is 2.4 MPa. The designer needs the exact kinematics of the piston at this angle and wants to see how the piston inertia modifies the force delivered to the connecting rod. Gudgeon-pin friction and the weight of the piston are neglected, and the cylinder is vertical.

  1. (a) Find the piston displacement from top dead centre, in mm. [4]
  2. (b) Find the exact piston velocity in m/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the exact piston acceleration in m/s² (positive toward the crankshaft). [4]
  4. (d) Find the net force delivered along the cylinder axis to the connecting rod, after allowing for the inertia of the piston, in kN. [4]
  5. (e) Find the force in the connecting rod at this crank angle, in kN. [4]
(a)

Measure the displacement x from top dead centre (TDC) toward the crank. The exact slider-crank relationship is x = r(1 − cos θ) + l(1 − √(1 − (r/l)² sin² θ)). With r = 55 mm, l = 190 mm and θ = 40°: sin θ = 0.6428, (r/l) sin θ = 0.1861, √(1 − 0.03462) = 0.9825. So x = 55(1 − 0.766) + 190(1 − 0.9825) = 16.19 mm. Rod ratio l/r = 3.455, a typical value for a mid-size engine.

Answer: 16.19 mm

(b)

Crank speed ω = 2π×3000/60 = 314.2 rad/s. Differentiate x with respect to time at constant ω: v = rω [sin θ + (r/(2l)) sin 2θ / √(1 − (r/l)² sin² θ)] (the exact derivative is evaluated). Using n = r/l = 0.2895: sin θ = 0.6428, sin 2θ = 0.9848, root = 0.9825. The bracket is 0.7879, and rω = 17.28 m/s, so v = 13.61 m/s toward the crankshaft. The exact derivative is used rather than the approximate expression with the n² term neglected.

Answer: 13.61 m/s

(c)

Differentiating again, the acceleration is a = rω² [cos θ + n cos 2θ + corrections in n³]. A first estimate using the common approximation a ≈ rω²(cos θ + n cos 2θ) = 5428×(0.766 + 0.2895×0.1736) = 4431 m/s². The exact derivative of the displacement function, which includes the higher-order terms, gives a = 4470 m/s². The sign is positive, so the piston is still accelerating toward the crankshaft. Peak acceleration occurs at TDC, where a = rω²(1 + n) = 7000 m/s², so the piston here is at 63.9 percent of the maximum.

Answer: 4470 m/s²

(d)

The cylinder gas force is Fg = p A with A = πD²/4 = π(0.090)²/4 = 0.006362 m², so Fg = 2.4×10⁶ × 0.006362 = 15.27 kN acting toward the crank. The piston inertia force m a opposes the acceleration, so the net force delivered to the rod along the cylinder axis is F = Fg − m a = 1.527 × 10⁴ − 0.85×4470 = 1.527 × 10⁴ − 3799 = 1.147 × 10⁴ N = 11.47 kN. The inertia correction is 24.9 percent of the gas load here. At 3000 rpm the inertia term grows, and near TDC it can remove several percent of the gas force. Friction is neglected.

Answer: 11.47 kN

(e)

The connecting rod makes angle φ with the cylinder axis where sin φ = (r/l) sin θ = 0.1861, so φ = 10.72° and cos φ = 0.9825. The rod is a two-force member in line with itself and carries compression Frod = F/cos φ, because the axial component must equal the net axial force. Frod = 11.47/0.9825 = 11.67 kN. The remaining lateral component is F tan φ = 2.172 kN, carried by the cylinder wall as side thrust on the piston. Friction on the wall is neglected, so the rod force is a slight underestimate.

Answer: 11.67 kN

Problem 5 [A2-070] Grashof and transmission angle

A sorting arm on a conveyor is driven by a four-bar linkage. The ground link between fixed pivots is 300 mm. The driving crank is 70 mm, the coupler 260 mm and the output rocker 200 mm. The crank is driven by a constant-speed gearmotor. The designer must confirm the linkage can be driven by a continuously rotating crank, check that force transmission to the rocker is acceptable throughout the cycle and determine how much quicker the return stroke is than the working stroke. Treat all links as rigid, joints as frictionless and the mechanism as planar. The crank speed is constant, and the arm is expected to dwell briefly between loads.

  1. (a) Show that the linkage satisfies the Grashof condition by finding the margin pq − (s + l) in mm, and classify the mechanism. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum transmission angle over a full crank revolution, in degrees, and state at which crank position it occurs. [6]
  3. (c) Find the quick-return angle β, the amount by which the crank angle between the two toggle (dead-centre) positions differs from 180°. [5]
  4. (d) Find the time ratio (forward stroke time to return stroke time) of the rocker at constant crank speed, and comment on suitability for a sorting arm that must rest between loads. [5]
(a)

Let the links be: crank a = 70 mm, coupler b = 260 mm, rocker c = 200 mm, ground d = 300 mm. The shortest link s = 70 mm and the longest l = 300 mm; the other two are p = 200 mm and q = 260 mm. Grashof's criterion: s + l ≤ p + q. Here s + l = 370 mm and p + q = 460 mm, so the margin is 460 − 370 = 90 mm, which is positive. The shortest link is the crank, adjacent to the fixed link, so the crank can rotate fully while the rocker oscillates: a crank-rocker. Had the margin been negative, no link could make a full revolution (a triple rocker), and had it been zero the mechanism would be a change-point type.

Answer: 90 mm, crank-rocker

(b)

The transmission angle μ is the angle between the coupler and rocker. By the cosine rule on the diagonal joining A to O4: cos μ = (b² + c² − a² − d² + 2ad cos θ)/(2bc), where θ is the crank angle from the ground line. With b² + c² − a² − d² = 0.0127 m² and 2ad = 0.042 m², cos μ = (0.0127 + 0.042 cos θ)/0.104. At θ = 0, cos μ = 0.526, so μ = 58.27°. At θ = 180°, μ = 106.4°. The minimum (confirmed by a 0.05° sweep over a full turn) occurs when the crank lies along the ground line on the near side. A common design rule keeps μ above about 40°, which is met by 18.27 degrees.

Answer: 58.27 degrees

(c)

At the toggle positions the crank and coupler are collinear. In the extended position the combined length is b + a = 330 mm, giving triangle O2, O4 and B with sides d = 300, c = 200 and 330 mm. By the cosine rule the angle at O2 is φ1 = acos[(d² + (b + a)² − c²)/(2d(b + a))] = acos[(0.1589)/(0.198)] = 36.63°. In the folded position the length is b − a = 190 mm, so φ2 = acos[(d² + 0.19² − c²)/(2d×0.19)] = acos[(0.0861)/(0.114)] = 40.95°. The offset angle is β = |φ2 − φ1| = 4.324°.

Answer: 4.324 degrees

(d)

For a crank-rocker the crank turns through 180° + β on the forward stroke and 180° − β on the return, with β = 4.324° from part c. At constant crank speed the times are in proportion to these angles. Time ratio = (180 + β)/(180 − β) = 184.3/175.7 = 1.049. The quick return is modest, because the forward stroke takes only about 4.92 percent longer than the return. For a sorting arm that must rest between loads, such a small ratio is not very helpful, and a larger offset, or an added dwell mechanism, would be needed to create a clear working stroke and a fast return.

Answer: 1.049

A2 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A2-071] Cam profile and follower motion

A radial plate cam drives a roller follower that slides horizontally in a guide, so gravity and friction may be ignored. The follower assembly has mass 0.35 kg. During 90° of cam rotation the follower rises 18 mm with cycloidal motion, and the cam turns at a constant 600 rpm. A return spring with a preload of 20 N at zero lift and an unknown stiffness k keeps the roller on the cam. Design rule: the spring force must be at least 1.25 times the follower inertia force at the position of maximum follower deceleration during the rise, which for cycloidal motion occurs at three quarters of the rise angle. Determine the follower and spring requirements.

  1. (a) Find the maximum follower velocity during the rise. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum follower acceleration magnitude during the rise. [4]
  3. (c) Find the spring stiffness k needed to satisfy the design rule at 600 rpm. [6]
  4. (d) The cam speed is raised to 800 rpm. Keeping the stiffness from part c and the same design rule, find the new preload. [6]
(a)

Cycloidal motion: s = h(φ - sin2πφ/2π) with φ = θ/β, so v = (hω/β)(1 - cos2πφ) and the peak occurs at φ = 0.5, giving v_max = 2hω/β. The cam speed is ω = 600×2π/60 = 62.83 rad/s and the rise angle is β = π/2 = 1.5708 rad. Substitute: v_max = 2×0.018×62.83/1.5708 = 1.440 m/s. Because the cam turns at constant speed, time derivatives follow directly from derivatives with respect to cam angle multiplied by ω, and no other term appears in the velocity. The velocity is zero at the start and end of the rise, which is the property that makes cycloidal motion free of jerk spikes at the dwell junctions.

Answer: 1.44 m/s

(b)

Differentiating again, a = (2πhω²/β²) sin2πφ, so the peak magnitude is a_max = 2πhω²/β² at φ = 0.25 (acceleration) and φ = 0.75 (deceleration). Substitute the data: ω² = 3947.8 rad²/s² and β² = 2.4674 rad², so a_max = 2π×0.018×3947.8/2.4674 = 181.0 m/s². The inertia force at that instant is therefore m a_max = 0.35×181.0 = 63.3 N. Acceleration scales with the square of cam speed, which is why high speed cams are limited by contact loss rather than by stress alone.

Answer: 181 m/s²

(c)

At φ = 0.75 the lift is s = h(0.75 - sin(1.5π)/2π) = 0.018×(0.75 + 0.15915) = 16.365 mm, or 0.01636 m. The required spring force is 1.25 × m × a_max = 1.25×63.33 = 79.17 N. The spring force at that lift is F0 + k s, so k = (F_required - F0)/s = (79.17 - 20)/0.01636 = 3616 N/m. This value keeps the roller in contact at the worst point, because 0.75 of the rise angle is the check point specified by the design rule. The spring force also rises with lift, so the true minimum margin lies slightly earlier in the rise (near φ = 0.73, where the ratio is about 1.24); applying the rule at 0.75 is a design simplification.

Answer: 3616 N/m

(d)

Acceleration is proportional to ω², so a_max at 800 rpm is 181.0×(800/600)² = 321.7 m/s². The required spring force at φ = 0.75 becomes 1.25×0.35×321.7 = 140.74 N. The stiffness stays at 3616 N/m and the lift at that position is unchanged at 0.01636 m, so the spring contributes k s = 59.17 N. The new preload is F0 = 140.74 - 59.17 = 81.6 N. A larger preload raises the contact force at the dwell and rise start, so the designer should also check roller contact stress and the pressure angle at the new loading.

Answer: 81.58 N

Problem 2 [A2-072] Spur gear geometry and gear trains

A 7.5 kW electric motor running at 1450 rpm drives a conveyor reducer through a single stage of standard full-depth involute spur gears: a 20 tooth pinion on the motor shaft meshing with a 52 tooth gear. The module is 4 mm, the pressure angle is 20°, and the addendum equals one module. Treat the load as a steady transmitted power with the pinion rotating at motor speed. Mesh efficiency is 98 percent. The designer must check the geometry of the pair, the contact ratio for smooth operation, and the tooth loads that the shafts and bearings will carry, then state the speed and torque delivered to the conveyor shaft.

  1. (a) Find the centre distance of the gear pair. [3]
  2. (b) Find the contact ratio of the pair. [5]
  3. (c) Find the tangential force transmitted at the pitch circle. [4]
  4. (d) Find the radial (separating) force on the gears. [3]
  5. (e) Find the torque delivered to the conveyor shaft, including the mesh efficiency. [5]
(a)

The pitch radius of a gear is mz/2. For the pinion r1 = 4×20/2 = 40 mm and for the gear r2 = 4×52/2 = 104 mm. Standard gears run with their pitch circles tangent, so the centre distance is C = r1 + r2 = 40 + 104 = 144 mm. Equivalently C = m(z1 + z2)/2 = 4×72/2 = 144 mm. The velocity ratio is z2/z1 = 2.6, and the pitch circle diameters are 80 mm and 208 mm. Any shift of the centre distance away from this value would change the operating pressure angle and the backlash, which is why the housing bores are machined to this dimension with a close tolerance.

Answer: 144 mm

(b)

The contact ratio is the length of the path of contact divided by the base pitch. Base radii are rb = r cos20°, giving rb1 = 37.59 mm and rb2 = 97.73 mm. Addendum radii are ra1 = 44 mm and ra2 = 108 mm. The path of contact length is √(ra1² - rb1²) + √(ra2² - rb2²) - C sin20°, which is 22.87 + 45.97 - 49.25 = 19.59 mm. The base pitch is p_b = πm cos20° = 11.809 mm. So the contact ratio is 1.659. A value above 1.2 means at least one tooth pair is always sharing the load, with two pairs engaged for about 66 percent of the mesh cycle.

Answer: 1.659

(c)

The pinion angular speed is ω1 = 1450×2π/60 = 151.84 rad/s. The motor torque on the pinion shaft is T1 = P/ω1 = 7500/151.84 = 49.39 N·m. The tangential force acts at the pitch radius, so W_t = T1/r1 = 49.39/0.040 = 1235 N. Check with pitch line velocity: v = ω1 r1 = 6.074 m/s and P/v = 7500/6.074 = 1235 N, which agrees. This force is the basis for the bending stress in the Lewis equation and for the shaft bending moment.

Answer: 1235 N

(d)

For an involute pair with no friction the resultant tooth force acts along the line of action inclined at the pressure angle to the common tangent. The radial component is W_r = W_t tanφ, with W_t = 1235 N from part c and φ = 20°. Then W_r = 1235×tan20° = 449 N, directed toward the centre of each gear. The total normal force is W_t/cos20° = 1314 N. Both shafts must be designed for the combined action of this radial load, the tangential load and the torque, and the bearings see the vector sum of the two components.

Answer: 449.4 N

(e)

Ideal speed and torque follow the tooth ratio. Output speed is n2 = 1450×20/52 = 557.7 rpm. With no losses the torque would multiply by z2/z1 = 2.6, giving 128.4 N·m. Mesh efficiency of 98 percent means the output power is 0.98×7500 = 7350 W. Output torque is therefore T2 = 0.98×T1×z2/z1 = 0.98×49.39×2.6 = 125.9 N·m. Check: P_out/ω2 = 7350/(557.7×2π/60) = 125.9 N·m. The 2 percent loss of 150 W appears as heat in the oil, which the gearbox casing must reject.

Answer: 125.9 N·m

Problem 3 [A2-073] Planetary gear trains

A simple epicyclic reduction stage has a 24 tooth sun gear, three identical 18 tooth planet gears carried on a single arm (the carrier), and an internal ring gear with 60 teeth. The module is 3 mm. The ring gear is bolted to the housing. The sun gear is the input, turning at 1200 rpm and carrying 15 kW, and the carrier is the output. Take the three planets to share the load equally. Analyse the stage to give the carrier speed, the planet spin, and the torques and tooth forces, first with ideal gears and then with a stage efficiency of 97 percent.

  1. (a) Find the carrier speed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the speed of rotation of each planet gear about its own axis, relative to the housing. [4]
  3. (c) Find the ideal output torque on the carrier. [4]
  4. (d) Find the tangential force at each sun-planet mesh. [4]
  5. (e) With a stage efficiency of 97 percent, find the output torque on the carrier. [4]
(a)

Use the tabular relation for the train with the carrier as the reference arm: (ω_r - ω_c)/(ω_s - ω_c) = -N_s/N_r, the negative sign arising because the external sun-planet mesh reverses direction once while the internal planet-ring mesh does not. With the ring fixed, ω_r = 0, so -ω_c/(ω_s - ω_c) = -24/60, giving 60 ω_c = 24 ω_s - 24 ω_c. Hence ω_c = ω_s N_s/(N_s + N_r) = 1200×24/84 = 342.9 rpm in the same direction as the sun. The overall ratio is 1 + N_r/N_s = 3.5. Check geometry: N_r = N_s + 2N_p = 24 + 36 = 60, so the gears fit around a common centre.

Answer: 342.9 rpm

(b)

The planet meshes internally with the ring and externally with the sun. Using the ring-planet mesh: (ω_r - ω_c)/(ω_p - ω_c) = +N_p/N_r (internal mesh, same direction). With ω_r = 0: -ω_c/(ω_p - ω_c) = 18/60, so ω_p - ω_c = -ω_c×60/18 = -1142.9 rpm. Then ω_p = 342.9 - 1142.9 = -800.0 rpm. Check with the sun-planet mesh: (ω_p - ω_c)/(ω_s - ω_c) = -N_s/N_p = -1.3333, giving ω_p - ω_c = -1.3333×(857.1) = -1142.9 rpm, which agrees. The magnitude is 800.0 rpm, turning opposite to the sun.

Answer: 800 rpm (magnitude)

(c)

The sun angular speed is 125.66 rad/s, so the input torque is T_in = P/ω = 15000/125.66 = 119.4 N·m. With the ring fixed, the housing supplies a reaction torque on the ring. Torque balance on the whole train gives T_s + T_c + T_r = 0, and with no losses power in equals power out, T_s ω_s = -T_c ω_c. So the carrier torque has magnitude T_c = T_in ω_s/ω_c = T_in×(1 + N_r/N_s) = 119.4×3.5 = 417.8 N·m. The ring reaction torque is T_c - T_in = 298.4 N·m, carried by the housing bolts.

Answer: 417.8 N·m

(d)

The sun pitch radius is r_s = m N_s/2 = 3×24/2 = 36 mm. The input torque 119.4 N·m is shared equally by three planets, so each mesh carries a tangential force F_t = T_in/(3 r_s) = 119.4/(3×0.036) = 1105 N. The sun gear sees three equal radial forces 120° apart that cancel, so the sun shaft carries no net bearing load from the mesh. This self-centring is one of the main advantages of epicyclic gearing. Load sharing is only equal if the carrier and planets are made accurately or the sun is allowed to float, so real designs derate by a load-share factor.

Answer: 1105 N

(e)

The carrier speed 342.9 rpm equals 35.90 rad/s. Output power is P_out = 0.97×15000 = 14550 W. The carrier torque is T_c = P_out/ω_c = 14550/35.90 = 405.2 N·m. This is lower than the ideal 417.8 N·m by the factor 0.97, because the speed ratio is fixed by the tooth counts and the whole power loss of 450 W must show up as reduced torque. The lost power appears as heat in the meshes and bearings.

Answer: 405.2 N·m

Problem 4 [A2-074] Static force analysis of a mechanism

A single-cylinder compressor has a slider-crank mechanism with a crank of length 50 mm, a connecting rod of length 200 mm and a piston that slides in a fixed cylinder aligned with the crank axis. At one instant the crank angle measured from the inner dead centre is 50° and the gas pressure produces a net force of 12 kN on the piston along the cylinder axis. The inertia of the moving parts is negligible at this slow speed, so a static force analysis applies. First neglect friction. Then include Coulomb friction between the piston and cylinder wall, with coefficient 0.10. Find the rod and wall forces and the crank torque that holds the mechanism in equilibrium.

  1. (a) Find the angle between the connecting rod and the cylinder axis. [3]
  2. (b) With friction neglected, find the force in the connecting rod. [4]
  3. (c) With friction neglected, find the torque that must be applied to the crank to hold equilibrium. [5]
  4. (d) With friction neglected, find the side thrust of the piston on the cylinder wall. [3]
  5. (e) Now include piston-wall friction with μ = 0.10 for the piston moving outward under the gas force. Find the crank torque required. [5]
(a)

The crank pin and the piston pin must have the same height above the axis offsets, so r sinθ = l sinφ. Then sinφ = (r/l) sinθ = (50/200)×sin50° = 0.25×0.76604 = 0.19151. The rod angle is φ = arcsin(0.19151) = 11.04°. The rod leans in the opposite sense to the crank. The ratio n = l/r = 4 sets the severity of the obliquity, and the maximum possible rod angle in this mechanism is arcsin(1/4) = 14.48° at θ = 90°. At 50° the rod is therefore close to its largest tilt, which is why the side thrust is sizeable here.

Answer: 11.04 degrees

(b)

The piston is a three force body when friction is ignored: the gas force F along the axis, the wall reaction N normal to the axis, and the rod force F_AB along the rod. Resolve along the cylinder axis: F_AB cosφ = F. So F_AB = F/cosφ = 12000/cos(11.04°) = 12000/0.9815 = 12226 N (compression). The rod force exceeds the gas force only by about 1.9 percent. The same force acts at the crank pin, so the crankpin bearing and the rod's compressive strength are sized on this value.

Answer: 12230 N

(c)

The rod force acts at the crank pin with a moment arm equal to the perpendicular distance from the crank centre to the rod's line of action. The rod makes an angle θ + φ = 61.04° with the crank direction, so the arm is r sin(θ + φ). T = F_AB r sin(θ + φ) = F r sin(θ + φ)/cosφ = 12000×0.05×sin(61.04°)/0.9815 = 534.9 N·m. Equivalent virtual work check: torque equals force times piston velocity per crank speed, T = F (dx/dθ) = F r (sinθ + cosθ tanφ) = 534.9 N·m, which agrees.

Answer: 534.9 N·m

(d)

The wall reaction balances the lateral component of the rod force: N = F_AB sinφ = F tanφ. Substituting: N = 12000×tan(11.04°) = 12000×0.1951 = 2341 N. This force presses the piston skirt against the cylinder wall and is the origin of piston slap and cylinder wear. It is largest when sinφ is largest, near a crank angle of 90°, and it reverses direction through the cycle as the rod swings, which is why the thrust faces on the piston are designated major and minor.

Answer: 2341 N

(e)

Friction opposes the piston's motion, so the friction force μN acts against the gas force and the force reaching the rod along the axis is F - μN. The wall reaction is produced by the rod's lateral component: N = (F - μN) tanφ, so N = F tanφ/(1 + μ tanφ) = 2341/(1 + 0.10×0.1951) = 2297 N. The net axial force on the rod is F_eff = 12000 - 0.10×2297 = 11770 N. Torque at the crank is T = F_eff r sin(θ + φ)/cosφ = 11770×0.05×0.8750/0.9815 = 524.6 N·m, about 1.9 percent less than the frictionless value.

Answer: 524.6 N·m

Problem 5 [A2-075] Dynamic force analysis of a slider-crank

A four-stroke petrol engine runs at a steady 3000 rpm. Its crank radius is 45 mm and its connecting rod length is 160 mm. The piston has mass 0.45 kg and the rod has mass 0.62 kg, of which one third may be treated as reciprocating at the piston pin and two thirds as rotating at the crank pin. The bore is 80 mm. Use the standard approximate piston acceleration a = rω²(cosθ + cos2θ/n), where n is the ratio of rod length to crank radius and θ is measured from the inner dead centre. Gravity and friction may be ignored. During the power stroke the cylinder gas pressure is 3.5 MPa when the crank is at 60° after inner dead centre. Find the inertia and torque quantities.

  1. (a) Find the piston acceleration at inner dead centre. [4]
  2. (b) Find the inertia force of the reciprocating mass at inner dead centre. [4]
  3. (c) Find the net force transmitted by the piston to the connecting rod, along the cylinder axis, at θ = 60° on the power stroke. [6]
  4. (d) Find the engine torque delivered at the crankshaft at θ = 60°. [6]
(a)

The crank speed is ω = 3000×2π/60 = 314.16 rad/s and the rod to crank ratio is n = 160/45 = 3.556. At θ = 0 the approximate acceleration is a = rω²(1 + 1/n) = 0.045×98696×(1 + 0.2812) = 5690 m/s². This is the largest acceleration of the cycle and is about 580 g. It is directed toward the crankshaft, which means the piston is being pulled back from the dead centre. The term 1/n comes from the finite rod length; an infinitely long rod would give simple harmonic motion with a = rω² only, so the finite rod raises the peak by 28.1 percent.

Answer: 5690 m/s²

(b)

The equivalent reciprocating mass is the piston plus one third of the rod: m_rec = 0.45 + 0.62/3 = 0.6567 kg. The rotating two thirds of the rod belongs at the crank pin and produces a constant centripetal force that does not enter the piston-axis balance. The inertia force on the reciprocating mass is F_i = m_rec a = 0.6567×5690 = 3737 N. At inner dead centre this force acts away from the crank on the structure through the piston pin, which is why engine mounts and the cylinder head studs must resist a primary shaking force of this order every revolution.

Answer: 3737 N

(c)

First the acceleration at 60°: a = rω²(cos60° + cos120°/n) = 0.045×98696×(0.5 + (-0.5)/3.556) = 1596 m/s². The piston area is A = π×0.08²/4 = 50.27 cm², so the gas force is F_g = pA = 3.5×10⁶×0.005027 = 17593 N. The piston is moving away from inner dead centre with positive acceleration along its motion, so part of the gas force goes into accelerating the reciprocating mass. Net force: F = F_g - m_rec a = 17593 - 0.6567×1596 = 16545 N. This is the force that reaches the rod.

Answer: 16540 N

(d)

The rod angle follows from sinφ = sinθ/n = 0.8660/3.556 = 0.2436, so φ = 14.10°. The piston force F along the axis acts through the rod at the crank pin with the torque arm r sin(θ + φ)/cosφ. T = F r sin(θ + φ)/cosφ = 16545×0.045×sin(74.10°)/cos(14.10°) = 16545×0.045×0.9617/0.9699 = 738.3 N·m. The rotating rod mass produces no torque about the shaft in steady running, so only the net piston force contributes.

Answer: 738.3 N·m

A2 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A2-076] Flywheel sizing

A punch press cuts a 40 mm diameter hole through steel plate 10 mm thick. The ultimate shear strength of the plate is 350 MPa. During cutting the shear force falls off linearly, so the average force over the 10 mm punch travel is half the peak force. The press makes 20 strokes per minute, and the cutting takes 0.25 s of each stroke. A motor delivers constant power throughout the cycle and its losses may be ignored. The flywheel runs at a mean speed of 300 rpm and the coefficient of speed fluctuation must not exceed 0.08. The flywheel is to be a solid steel disc of density 7800 kg/m³ and width 120 mm. Size it.

  1. (a) Find the peak punching force. [3]
  2. (b) Find the energy required for one punching stroke. [3]
  3. (c) Find the motor power needed, taking the motor to run at constant power over the whole cycle. [4]
  4. (d) Find the mass moment of inertia required of the flywheel. [5]
  5. (e) Find the outer radius of the solid steel disc flywheel. [5]
(a)

The sheared area is the hole perimeter times the plate thickness: A = π d t = π×0.040×0.010 = 1256.6 mm². The peak force is the ultimate shear strength times that area: F_p = τ A = 350×10⁶×0.001257 = 439823 N, or 439.8 kN. This is the force the press frame, ram and punch must resist at the instant of break-through, and is why a heavy press needs a large flywheel even though the energy per stroke is small: the peak force does not affect the energy balance directly, but it sets the structural size.

Answer: 439.8 kN

(b)

With the force decreasing linearly, the mean force is half the peak. The work done over the punch travel t = 0.010 m is E = (F_p/2) t = 0.5×439823×0.010 = 2199 J. This is the energy that must be supplied during the cut. It is a modest amount compared with the energy the flywheel can store, but it is delivered in a quarter of a second, so the motor alone would have to supply it at a power of 8.8 kW, far above the average demand. This mismatch between the instantaneous and the average power is what the flywheel evens out.

Answer: 2199 J

(c)

At 20 strokes per minute the cycle time is 60/20 = 3 s. The energy per stroke is 2199 J, and the motor must replace it in each cycle. The required constant power is P = E/cycle time = 2199/3 = 733 W. This is the average power; the motor does not need the 8.8 kW peak because the flywheel supplies the shortfall during the cut. In practice, a motor of about 1 kW would be selected to cover losses and the overload margin. The calculation assumes a perfectly stiff constant-power characteristic, which a real induction motor approximates through its speed slip.

Answer: 733 W

(d)

During the 0.25 s cut the motor still delivers P×t = 733×0.25 = 183 J. The flywheel must supply the rest: ΔE = E - P t = 2199 - 183 = 2016 J. The speed fluctuation relation is ΔE = I ω² C_s, with mean speed ω = 300×2π/60 = 31.416 rad/s. Then I = ΔE/(C_s ω²) = 2016/(0.08×987.0) = 25.53 kg·m². The result takes the full energy swing as occurring in the cutting interval; it also assumes that the rest of the cycle restores the energy at a steady rate, which is consistent with a constant-power motor.

Answer: 25.53 kg·m²

(e)

For a solid disc of width b and radius R the mass is m = πR² b ρ and the inertia is I = ½ m R² = ½ π ρ b R⁴. Solving: R = (2I/(π ρ b))¼ = (2×25.53/(π×7800×0.12))0.25 = (0.01736)0.25 = 0.3630 m, or 363 mm. The diameter is 726 mm and the mass is π R² b ρ = 387 kg. The rim speed is ωR = 11.4 m/s, which is far below the bursting limit of cast iron or steel, so the speed stress is not critical.

Answer: 363 mm

Problem 2 [A2-077] Balancing of rotating masses

A rigid shaft of length 600 mm carries three out-of-balance masses in separate planes. Take plane L at the left-hand end of the shaft (axial position 0) and plane M at the right-hand end (600 mm). Mass 1 is 5 kg at radius 80 mm and axial position 150 mm. Mass 2 is 7 kg at radius 60 mm, 75° ahead of mass 1 in the direction of rotation, at 300 mm. Mass 3 is 4 kg at radius 100 mm, 200° ahead of mass 1, at 450 mm. The shaft is to be balanced completely by one correction mass in plane L and one in plane M, each fitted at a radius of 100 mm. The bearings sit at planes L and M and the speed is 1500 rpm.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the correction mass required in plane M. [5]
  2. (b) Find the angular position of the correction mass in plane M, measured from mass 1 in the direction of rotation. [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the correction mass required in plane L. [6]
  4. (d) Before balancing, find the dynamic bearing reaction at plane M caused by the unbalanced masses at 1500 rpm. [5]
(a)

Treat each product m r as a vector at its angle. Reference the moments to plane L, so the correction in plane L drops out of the couple equation. The unbalanced couple is the sum of m r x with phase: C = Σ m r x ejθ = -0.0765 + j0.0601 kg·m². The correction in plane M must cancel it: m_M r_M L ejθM = -C. Magnitude: m_M = |C|/(r_M L) = 0.0973/(0.100×0.600) = 1.622 kg. The force vector Σ m r = 0.1328 + j0.2689 kg·m is not zero, so the single plane M mass alone could not balance the shaft; a second correction mass in plane L is needed.

Answer: 1.622 kg

(b)

The balancing vector in plane M is the negative of C/L. With the real and imaginary parts of -C/L equal to 0.1276 and -0.1002 kg·m, the angle is θ_M = arctan2(-0.1002, 0.1276) = 321.8° after bringing it into the range 0 to 360°. The angle is measured from the position of mass 1 in the direction of rotation, the same convention used for the given 75° and 200°. The correction mass sits roughly opposite the net couple direction, as expected. A mistake of sign here moves the correction to the same side as the couple and doubles the unbalance.

Answer: 321.8 degrees

(c)

Now the force balance. The sum of all vectors m r must be zero: F + m_L r_L ejθL + m_M r_M ejθM = 0. The plane M contribution is 1.622×0.100 = 0.1622 kg·m at 321.8°, giving the vector 0.1276 + j-0.1002. Then the plane L vector is -(F + vB2) = -0.2604 + j-0.1686 kg·m. Magnitude 0.3102 kg·m. Dividing by the radius: m_L = 0.3102/0.100 = 3.102 kg, placed at 212.9° from mass 1. Both correction masses are within normal bolt-on balance weight practice for a shaft of this size.

Answer: 3.102 kg

(d)

Take moments about the bearing at plane L. The rotating unbalance produces a centrifugal force ω² Σ m r ejθ whose moment about L is ω² C. The reaction at M balances this couple over the span 0.600 m: R_M = ω² |C|/L. The speed is ω = 1500×2π/60 = 157.08 rad/s, so ω² = 24674. R_M = 24674×0.0973/0.600 = 4003 N. This reaction rotates with the shaft, producing a once per revolution force on the bearing housing and foundation of 408 kgf. Adding the two correction masses removes both the net force and the couple, so this reaction falls to zero in the ideal case.

Answer: 4003 N

Problem 3 [A2-078] Gyroscopic effects

The turbine rotor of a ship's propulsion set has mass 900 kg and a radius of gyration of 0.25 m. It spins at 3000 rpm about a longitudinal axis, and its two bearings are 1.8 m apart. In heavy seas the ship pitches with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 6° and a period of 14 s about a transverse axis. Separately, in calm water the ship steers around a circular turn of radius 250 m at a steady speed of 15 m/s. Treat the rotor as a rigid gyroscope with a constant spin speed and ignore its other inertia. Determine the gyroscopic loads on the bearings in both cases.

  1. (a) Find the spin speed of the rotor in rad/s. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum angular velocity of pitching, which is the maximum precession rate. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum gyroscopic couple due to pitching. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum gyroscopic reaction force at each bearing from pitching. [4]
  5. (e) In the circular turn at 15 m/s on a 250 m radius, find the gyroscopic couple on the rotor. [4]
(a)

The rotor mass moment of inertia about its spin axis is I = m k² = 900×0.25² = 56.25 kg·m². The spin angular velocity is ω = 2πN/60 = 2π×3000/60 = 314.16 rad/s. The spin angular momentum is H = Iω = 56.25×314.16 = 17671 kg·m²/s. All gyroscopic couples in this problem are proportional to H, so a change in rotor speed changes the loads in direct proportion, and a change in radius of gyration changes them with its square. This is the starting point, and its value does not change while the rotor turns at a constant 3000 rpm.

Answer: 314.2 rad/s

(b)

The pitch angle varies as θ = θ0 sin(2πt/T), where θ0 = 6° = 0.1047 rad and T = 14 s. The angular velocity is the derivative, θ̇ = θ0 (2π/T) cos(2πt/T), whose maximum magnitude is θ0 × 2π/T = 0.1047×0.4488 = 0.0470 rad/s. This occurs as the ship passes through the level position. The precession rate is greatest there, so the largest gyroscopic couple acts as the bow swings fastest, not at the extreme pitch angles where the angular velocity is zero.

Answer: 0.047 rad/s

(c)

When a spinning body is turned about an axis perpendicular to its spin axis, it exerts a reaction couple C = I ω ω_p on its supports, acting about the third mutually perpendicular axis (a vertical axis here, which tends to swing the ship's bow sideways, a yawing effect). Substituting: C = 56.25×314.16×0.0470 = 830.5 N·m. Sense: the spin axis tends to move toward the precession axis, so when the bow rises, the reaction on the hull pushes the bow toward one side depending on the direction of spin. The couple varies sinusoidally in time at the pitching frequency, with this value as its amplitude.

Answer: 830.5 N·m

(d)

The gyroscopic couple of 830.5 N·m must be resisted by a couple formed by equal and opposite horizontal (athwartships) reaction forces at the two bearings, which are 1.8 m apart. The force at each bearing is R = C/L = 830.5/1.8 = 461.4 N. One bearing is pushed to port and the other to starboard, the sense reversing every half period of the pitching. These forces add to the static bearing load from the rotor weight of 4414 N per bearing, so the gyroscopic effect is 10.5 percent of the static load, minor in this case.

Answer: 461.4 N

(e)

In a steady turn the ship, and so the rotor's spin axis, rotates about a vertical axis at ω_t = v/R = 15/250 = 0.060 rad/s. The precession is constant, so the gyroscopic couple is constant: C = I ω ω_t = 56.25×314.16×0.060 = 1060 N·m. It acts about a transverse horizontal axis, tending to raise or lower the bow depending on the direction of the turn and the spin. The corresponding bearing force is 589 N at each bearing. This steady couple exceeds the sea-induced peak of 831 N·m because a steady turn is a larger constant precession than the pitching peak.

Answer: 1060 N·m

Problem 4 [A2-079] Single degree of freedom free vibration

A 120 kg motor is mounted at the mid-span of a simply supported steel beam of length 2.4 m. The beam has flexural rigidity given by Young's modulus 200 GPa and second moment of area 8.5×10⁻⁶ m⁴, and a mass of 30 kg per metre of length. First treat the beam as massless and model the system as an undamped single degree of freedom oscillator. Then consider the effect of the beam's own mass, using the Rayleigh method with the static deflection shape of a centrally loaded simply supported beam, for which the effective mass at mid-span is 17/35 of the beam mass. Assume vertical vibration only and use g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the stiffness of the beam at mid-span. [4]
  2. (b) Find the natural frequency with the beam mass neglected. [4]
  3. (c) Find the static deflection of the beam under the motor weight. [3]
  4. (d) Find the natural frequency when the beam's own mass is included by the Rayleigh method. [5]
  5. (e) A hammer blow gives the motor, at rest in equilibrium, an impulse of 30 N·s. Using the massless-beam model, find the maximum vertical displacement. [4]
(a)

For a simply supported beam with a central point load the mid-span deflection is δ = P L³/(48 E I), so the stiffness is k = P/δ = 48 E I/L³. Substitute: E I = 200×10⁹×8.5×10⁻⁶ = 1700000 N·m². L³ = 2.4³ = 13.824 m³. Then k = 48×1700000/13.824 = 5902778 N/m, or 5.903 MN/m. This is a rigid supporting beam by machinery standards. Because the beam is the only elastic member carrying the motor, the system has a single stiffness and, for vertical motion at the centre, a single degree of freedom.

Answer: 5.903 × 10⁶ N/m

(b)

For an undamped single degree of freedom system the natural circular frequency is ω_n = √(k/m) = √(5902778/120) = √49190 = 221.8 rad/s. The cyclic frequency is f_n = ω_n/2π = 221.8/6.2832 = 35.30 Hz, with a period of 28.3 ms. The motor running speed that would excite this resonance is 2118 rpm. A designer would therefore keep the operating speed well away from this value, typically outside a band of ±20 percent.

Answer: 35.3 Hz

(c)

The static deflection at mid-span is δ_st = m g/k = 120×9.81/5902778 = 0.000199 m = 0.199 mm. It links to the natural frequency by ω_n = √(g/δ_st) = √(9.81/0.000199) = 221.8 rad/s, which matches the result of the previous part. This relation is a quick check that is often used when a static deflection has been measured instead of a stiffness. The vibration oscillates about the statically deflected position, and the gravity force does not change the frequency.

Answer: 0.1994 mm

(d)

The beam mass is m_b = 30×2.4 = 72 kg. The Rayleigh kinetic energy equivalence, using the static deflection shape, gives an effective mass at mid-span of (17/35) m_b = 0.4857×72 = 34.97 kg. This adds to the motor mass in the inertia term: m_total = 120 + 34.97 = 154.97 kg. The stiffness is unchanged. Then f_n = (1/2π)√(k/m_total) = (1/2π)√(5902778/154.97) = 31.06 Hz. Including the beam lowers the frequency by 12.0 percent, a result that is conservative with respect to resonance with higher speed excitation.

Answer: 31.06 Hz

(e)

The impulse changes the motor momentum, so the initial velocity is v0 = J/m = 30/120 = 0.250 m/s with zero initial displacement. The response of an undamped system is x(t) = (v0/ω_n) sin ω_n t, so the amplitude is x_max = v0/ω_n = J/(m ω_n) = 30/(120×221.8) = 0.001127 m = 1.127 mm. The 1.127 mm amplitude is about 5.7 times the static deflection of 0.199 mm, but it is still small relative to the 2.4 m span (under 0.05 percent), so the linear small-deflection model remains valid. With no damping the oscillation would continue indefinitely; real structures decay over time due to material and joint damping.

Answer: 1.127 mm

Problem 5 [A2-080] Damped free vibration and logarithmic decrement

A 180 kg machine-tool slide is supported on a flexure suspension that behaves as a single degree of freedom viscously damped oscillator. In a tap test the displacement is recorded. The peak displacement of the first cycle is 12.0 mm. After six further complete cycles the peak is 2.1 mm. The time between successive peaks, the damped period, is measured as 0.080 s. Assume linear viscous damping and treat the slide as moving in one direction only. Use the measurements to identify the damping and the stiffness of the suspension, and then size an additional damper that would make the slide critically damped.

  1. (a) Find the logarithmic decrement. [4]
  2. (b) Find the damping ratio. [4]
  3. (c) Find the stiffness of the suspension. [4]
  4. (d) Find the viscous damping coefficient of the suspension. [4]
  5. (e) Find the extra damping coefficient to be added by a parallel damper so that the slide becomes critically damped. [4]
(a)

The logarithmic decrement is the natural logarithm of the ratio of successive peaks, and it is the same for every cycle in a linear viscous system. Over six cycles the amplitude ratio is x0/x6 = 12.0/2.1 = 5.7143, so six times the decrement is ln(5.7143) = 1.7430. Then δ = (1/6) ln(x0/x6) = 0.2905. Using the whole span of six cycles averages out reading error on any one pair of peaks, which is the reason that this form of the measurement is preferred in practice. Each cycle therefore loses 25.2 percent of its amplitude.

Answer: 0.2905

(b)

The logarithmic decrement relates to the damping ratio by δ = 2πζ/√(1 - ζ²), which inverts to ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²). Substitute: ζ = 0.2905/√(39.478 + 0.0844) = 0.2905/6.2899 = 0.0462. The small-damping approximation ζ ≈ δ/2π would give 0.0462, differing by only 0.1 percent, so for lightly damped systems either form is acceptable. The slide is lightly damped, with a damping ratio below five percent, which is typical of a flexure with no added dampers.

Answer: 0.04618

(c)

The measured period gives the damped frequency ω_d = 2π/T_d = 2π/0.080 = 78.54 rad/s. The undamped natural frequency is ω_n = ω_d/√(1 - ζ²) = 78.54/√(1 - 0.00213) = 78.62 rad/s. The stiffness follows from ω_n² = k/m: k = m ω_n² = 180×6181.7 = 1112704 N/m, or 1.113 MN/m. The correction from damped to undamped frequency is only 0.11 percent here, so neglecting it would not matter at this damping level, but it must be kept for higher damping.

Answer: 1.113 × 10⁶ N/m

(d)

The damping ratio is ζ = c/c_cr with critical damping c_cr = 2 m ω_n = 2×180×78.62 = 28305 N·s/m. So the damping coefficient is c = ζ c_cr = 0.0462×28305 = 1307 N·s/m. Equivalent check: c = 2 ζ √(k m) = 2×0.0462×√(1112704×180) = 1307 N·s/m. This is the inherent damping of the flexure and the surrounding joints, and it is the quantity that governs how quickly a disturbance dies out after a cut.

Answer: 1307 N·s/m

(e)

Critical damping is reached when c_total = c_cr = 2 m ω_n = 28305 N·s/m, since the stiffness and mass are unchanged. The damper acts in parallel with the existing suspension, so the coefficients add. The added coefficient is c_extra = c_cr - c = 28305 - 1307 = 26997 N·s/m. At critical damping the slide returns to rest in the shortest time without overshoot, but a slightly underdamped design with ζ near 0.7 usually settles faster to within a small tolerance band, and is often the practical target.

Answer: 27000 N·s/m

A2 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A2-081] Forced vibration and resonance

A vibrating screen deck used to grade crushed aggregate has a total moving mass of 240 kg. It is carried on four identical steel coil springs acting in parallel with a combined stiffness of 3.6 × 10⁵ N/m, and two viscous dampers give a combined damping coefficient of 1800 N·s/m. Motion is vertical only and may be treated as a single degree of freedom system. An eccentric-shaft exciter applies a harmonic vertical force of amplitude 900 N at 11 Hz to the deck. The plant engineer wants to know how hard the damper works and whether the deck is operating above or below resonance. Analyse the steady-state response of the deck.

  1. (a) Determine the damping ratio of the system. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the steady-state displacement amplitude of the deck, in millimetres. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the phase angle by which the displacement lags the exciting force, in degrees. [4]
  4. (d) Determine the average power dissipated in the dampers, and confirm it equals the average power delivered by the exciting force. [6]
(a)

Treat the deck as a mass-spring-damper. Critical damping coefficient c_cr = 2√(km) = 2√(3.6 × 10⁵ × 240) = 1.859 × 10⁴ N·s/m. Damping ratio ζ = c/c_cr = 1800/1.859 × 10⁴ = 0.0968. The natural frequency is ω_n = √(k/m) = 38.73 rad/s, or 6.16 Hz, so the system is lightly damped (ζ is well below 0.3). This value is needed for the frequency-response formulas in the later parts and tells us the resonant peak would be sharp if the exciter ran near 6.16 Hz.

Answer: 0.0968

(b)

Forcing frequency ω = 2π × 11 = 69.12 rad/s. Frequency ratio r = ω/ω_n = 1.785, so the deck runs above resonance. Steady-state amplitude X = F0 / √[(k − mω²)² + (cω)²]. k − mω² = 3.6 × 10⁵ − 240 × 4777 = -7.865 × 10⁵ N/m. cω = 1.244 × 10⁵ N/m. Denominator = 7.962 × 10⁵ N/m. X = 900/7.962 × 10⁵ = 0.00113 m = 1.13 mm. The inertia term dominates, as expected above resonance.

Answer: 1.13 mm

(c)

The phase lag of displacement behind force is φ = tan⁻¹[cω/(k − mω²)], taken in the correct quadrant. Here k − mω² is negative (-7.865 × 10⁵ N/m) and cω = 1.244 × 10⁵ N/m, so φ = atan2(1.244 × 10⁵, -7.865 × 10⁵) = 171°. A value greater than 90° confirms operation above resonance, where the deck moves nearly in antiphase with the force. A calculator giving a negative arctangent must have 180° added.

Answer: 171 degrees

(d)

Only the damper dissipates energy. Average power P = ½ c ω² X² = 0.5 × 1800 × 4777 × (0.00113)² = 5.49 W. Check against the input power: P_in = ½ F0 ω X sin φ = 0.5 × 900 × 69.12 × 0.00113 × sin(171°) = 5.49 W. The two agree, as they must in steady state because the spring and mass store and return energy each cycle with zero net average work. This power appears as heat in the dampers and must be rejected by their design.

Answer: 5.49 W

Problem 2 [A2-082] Base excitation and vibration isolation

A calibrated gas analyser of mass 18 kg is carried in the cargo bay of a survey vehicle on a single elastic mount of equivalent stiffness 7.2 × 10⁴ N/m and damping ratio 0.12. Engine and road vibration make the floor move vertically in simple harmonic motion with amplitude 3 mm at 25 Hz. Treat the analyser as a rigid mass with one vertical degree of freedom. The manufacturer limits the force passed into the analyser frame through the mount, and the technician also wants to know the mount deflection so that the travel of the mount is not exceeded. Using the steady-state response, answer the following.

  1. (a) Determine the displacement transmissibility of the mount. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the absolute displacement amplitude of the analyser, in millimetres. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the amplitude of relative motion across the mount (floor to analyser), in millimetres. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the amplitude of the force transmitted through the mount to the analyser frame. [5]
(a)

Natural frequency ω_n = √(k/m) = √(7.2 × 10⁴/18) = 63.25 rad/s. Forcing ω = 2π × 25 = 157.1 rad/s, so r = ω/ω_n = 2.484. Since r > √2 the mount isolates. Transmissibility TR = √[1 + (2ζr)²] / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]. 2ζr = 0.5961; 1 − r² = -5.169. Numerator = 1.164, denominator = 5.203. TR = 0.224. The floor motion is cut to roughly 22.4 percent.

Answer: 0.224

(b)

The absolute amplitude is the transmissibility times the base amplitude: X = TR × Y = 0.2238 × 3 mm = 0.671 mm. This is the motion the analyser frame actually experiences. It is smaller than the floor motion because the frequency ratio is well above √2, the isolation region. Had the mount been stiffer such that r approached 1, the analyser would instead have moved more than the floor.

Answer: 0.671 mm

(c)

Relative motion z = x − y obeys the equation of motion with an inertial forcing term mω²Y, giving Z = Y r² / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]. r² = 6.169. Denominator = 5.203. Z = 3 × 6.169 / 5.203 = 3.56 mm. Above resonance the relative amplitude approaches Y, since the mass stays nearly still and the floor moves under it. The mount must be able to accommodate this travel.

Answer: 3.56 mm

(d)

The mount force is the spring plus damper force, and it equals the inertia force on the analyser, so F_T = m ω² X = 18 × 2.467 × 10⁴ × 0.0006713 = 298 N. Cross-check using the mount elements: F_T = Z √(k² + (cω)²) = 0.003557 × √((7.2 × 10⁴)² + (4.292 × 10⁴)²) = 298 N. Both routes agree, so the force limit can be compared directly with this value.

Answer: 298 N

Problem 3 [A2-083] Rotating unbalance

A centrifugal blower set, total mass 520 kg including the rotor, sits on four identical spring-damper isolators whose combined vertical stiffness is 2.1 × 10⁶ N/m with an overall damping ratio of 0.08. The rotor carries a residual unbalance equivalent to a 0.35 kg mass at a radius of 60 mm. Only vertical motion of the whole set is to be considered. In normal service the rotor runs at 1200 rpm, but during start-up and run-down it must pass through lower speeds. The designer needs the vibration amplitude, the force that reaches the floor, and the danger posed by the resonance during run-up.

  1. (a) Determine the steady-state vertical amplitude of the set at the service speed, in millimetres. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the amplitude of the force transmitted to the floor through the isolators at the service speed. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the rotor speed, in rpm, at which resonance occurs (frequency ratio of 1). [5]
  4. (d) Determine the amplitude of vibration at resonance, in millimetres, and state whether it is acceptable for a case with 5 mm of clearance around the base. [5]
(a)

Rotating unbalance gives an excitation force m_e e ω². The amplitude is X = (m_e e/M) r² / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]. ω = 2π × 1200/60 = 125.7 rad/s. ω_n = √(k/M) = 63.55 rad/s. r = 1.977. The denominator is √[(-2.91)² + (0.3164)²] = 2.927. m_e e/M = 4.038 × 10⁻⁵ m. X = 4.038 × 10⁻⁵ × 3.91 / 2.927 = 0.0539 mm.

Answer: 0.0539 mm

(b)

The force through spring and damper is F_T = X √(k² + (cω)²) = kX √[1 + (2ζr)²]. 2ζr = 0.3164, so the root factor is 1.049. F_T = 2.1 × 10⁶ × 5.394 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.049 = 119 N. Compare with the raw unbalance force m_e e ω² = 331.6 N: the transmitted force of 119 N is about 36 percent of the raw unbalance force, so the isolators help, but modestly because the running speed ratio is only 1.98. A softer mount would reduce it further.

Answer: 119 N

(c)

Resonance occurs when ω = ω_n, so the rotor speed is N_res = 60 ω_n/(2π) = 60 × 63.55/(2π) = 606.8 rpm. This is 50.6 percent of the service speed, so the blower passes through resonance on every start and stop. With damping ζ = 0.08, the transit should be rapid, and the speed should never be held near this value. The true peak of the amplitude curve is at r slightly above 1 for rotating unbalance, but r = 1 is the standard design check.

Answer: 606.8 rpm

(d)

At r = 1 the amplitude simplifies to X = (m_e e/M)/(2ζ) = 4.038 × 10⁻⁵/(2 × 0.08) = 0.252 mm. The available clearance is 5 mm, so 0.252 mm is acceptable on the amplitude alone, and the margin is 4.75 mm. Steady running at resonance is still bad practice because of fatigue in the springs. Since the set only passes through, the transient peak will be lower than this steady value.

Answer: 0.252 mm

Problem 4 [A2-084] Two degree of freedom systems and mode shapes

A laboratory test fixture consists of two blocks that slide on a frictionless horizontal air track. Block 1, of mass 40 kg, is joined to a rigid wall by a spring of stiffness 2 × 10⁵ N/m. Block 2, of mass 25 kg, is joined to Block 1 by a spring of stiffness 1.5 × 10⁵ N/m. There is no other spring and damping is negligible. Both blocks move along the track only. A harmonic force will later be applied to Block 1 only, and the technician wants to know both natural frequencies, the mode shapes, and the forcing frequency at which Block 1 would stay still while Block 2 oscillates.

  1. (a) Determine the lower natural frequency of the system, in hertz. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the higher natural frequency of the system, in hertz. [4]
  3. (c) Determine the amplitude ratio X2/X1 in the first (lower frequency) mode. [4]
  4. (d) Determine the amplitude ratio X2/X1 in the second (higher frequency) mode, and describe the motion of the two blocks in each mode in words. [4]
  5. (e) If a harmonic force is applied to Block 1, determine the frequency, in hertz, at which Block 1 has zero steady-state amplitude. [4]
(a)

Equations of motion: m1 x1'' + (k1 + k2) x1 − k2 x2 = 0 and m2 x2'' − k2 x1 + k2 x2 = 0. Assuming x = X cos ωt gives det(K − ω²M) = 0, i.e. (m1 m2) ω⁴ − [m2(k1 + k2) + m1 k2] ω² + k1 k2 = 0. Coefficients: m1 m2 = 1000; m2(k1 + k2) + m1 k2 = 1.475 × 10⁷; k1 k2 = 3 × 10¹⁰. Roots in ω²: 2436 and 1.231 × 10⁴ rad²/s². The lower is ω1 = 49.36 rad/s, so f1 = ω1/2π = 7.856 Hz.

Answer: 7.856 Hz

(b)

The larger root of the same characteristic equation is ω² = 1.231 × 10⁴ rad²/s². Then ω2 = √1.231 × 10⁴ = 111 rad/s. Converting, f2 = ω2/2π = 17.66 Hz. The sum of the roots equals [m2(k1 + k2) + m1 k2]/(m1 m2) = 1.475 × 10⁴, and ω1² + ω2² = 1.475 × 10⁴, which confirms the pair. The product of the roots equals k1 k2/(m1 m2), another check on the arithmetic.

Answer: 17.66 Hz

(c)

From the first equation of motion with x = X cos ωt: (k1 + k2 − m1 ω²) X1 = k2 X2, so X2/X1 = (k1 + k2 − m1 ω²)/k2. For the first mode, ω² = 2436: X2/X1 = (3.5 × 10⁵ − 40 × 2436)/1.5 × 10⁵ = 1.68. The ratio is positive and above 1, so the blocks move in phase and Block 2 swings further than Block 1.

Answer: 1.68

(d)

For the second mode, ω² = 1.231 × 10⁴: X2/X1 = (3.5 × 10⁵ − 40 × 1.231 × 10⁴)/1.5 × 10⁵ = -0.95. The negative sign means the blocks move in opposite directions (antiphase), with a node in the middle spring between them. In mode 1 both blocks move together, the spring k2 stretching only a little. In mode 2 the spring k2 is stretched and compressed strongly, so this mode has the higher frequency.

Answer: -0.95

(e)

With a force F0 sin ωt on Block 1 the steady response is X1 = F0 (k2 − m2 ω²)/Δ(ω), where Δ is the determinant of the dynamic stiffness matrix. X1 is zero when k2 − m2 ω² = 0, giving ω = √(k2/m2) = √(1.5 × 10⁵/25) = 6000½ = 77.46 rad/s, i.e. f = 12.33 Hz. Block 2 then acts as an undamped absorber on Block 1 and its spring force exactly cancels the applied force. This frequency lies between f1 and f2.

Answer: 12.33 Hz

Problem 5 [A2-085] Vibration absorbers

A reciprocating pump of effective mass 320 kg is bolted to a steel support frame whose vertical stiffness is 1.4 × 10⁶ N/m. The pump runs at a fixed speed of 640 rpm and produces an unbalanced vertical force of amplitude 1500 N at that speed. The running frequency is close to the natural frequency of the pump on its frame, so vibration is severe. The maintenance team proposes to bolt on an undamped tuned absorber of mass 32 kg, tuned exactly to the running speed. Damping in the original system may be neglected. Assess the absorber design.

  1. (a) Determine the absorber spring stiffness needed to tune it to the running speed. [4]
  2. (b) With the absorber fitted, determine the lower natural frequency of the combined two degree of freedom system, in hertz. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the higher natural frequency of the combined system, in hertz, and state whether the running speed lies safely between the two. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the steady-state amplitude of the absorber mass at the running speed, in millimetres. [6]
(a)

Running angular frequency ω = 2π × 640/60 = 67.02 rad/s. For the absorber to cancel the motion of the pump at this speed, its own natural frequency must equal ω: √(k_a/m_a) = ω, so k_a = m_a ω² = 32 × 4492 = 1.437 × 10⁵ N/m. For reference, the original pump-on-frame natural frequency is ω_n = √(k/M) = 66.14 rad/s, i.e. 10.5 Hz, only 1.3 percent from the running speed, which explains the heavy vibration.

Answer: 1.437 × 10⁵ N/m

(b)

Combined equations: M x'' + (k + k_a) x − k_a y = F0 sin ωt and m_a y'' + k_a (y − x) = 0. The free-vibration frequencies come from det[[k + k_a − Mω², −k_a], [−k_a, k_a − m_a ω²]] = 0. That is M m_a ω⁴ − [m_a (k + k_a) + M k_a] ω² + k k_a = 0. Using M m_a = 1.024 × 10⁴, bracket = 9.54 × 10⁷, k k_a = 2.012 × 10¹¹, the roots are ω² = 3228 and 6088. The lower gives ω = 56.81 rad/s, f = 9.042 Hz.

Answer: 9.042 Hz

(c)

The higher root is ω² = 6088, so ω = 78.03 rad/s and f = 12.42 Hz. The running frequency is 10.67 Hz. Its distance from the lower resonance is 15.2 percent of itself, and from the higher resonance 16.4 percent. The running speed sits between the two resonances, but with a mass ratio of only 0.1 the margin is modest, so the speed must be held steady and the run-up passes through the lower resonance.

Answer: 12.42 Hz

(d)

At the tuned frequency the pump mass amplitude is zero, because the absorber spring force on the pump equals −F0. For the absorber mass, the force on the pump from the absorber spring is k_a (y − x) with x = 0, so k_a Y = F0 in magnitude. Y = F0/k_a = 1500/1.437 × 10⁵ = 0.01044 m = 10.4 mm. The absorber spring must be designed for this travel and the stress at this amplitude, and the force it carries is F0 = 1500 N, equal and opposite to the exciting force.

Answer: 10.4 mm

A2 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A2-086] Torsional vibration of shafts

A steam turbine rotor of polar moment of inertia 4.2 kg·m² drives a generator rotor of 1.8 kg·m² through a solid circular steel shaft of diameter 60 mm and length 1.4 m between the two rotors. The shear modulus of the shaft is 80 GPa. The shaft mass and the supporting bearings are negligible, and both rotors are free to twist about the shaft axis, so the system is a free-free two-disc torsional system. During commissioning, a torsional oscillation is excited with an amplitude of 0.8 degrees at the turbine rotor. Analyse the torsional vibration.

  1. (a) Determine the torsional stiffness of the shaft. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the natural frequency of the two-rotor torsional mode, in hertz. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the distance of the vibration node from the turbine rotor, in metres. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the maximum shear stress in the shaft, in MPa, when the turbine rotor oscillates with the stated amplitude. [6]
(a)

Polar second moment of area J = πd⁴/32 = π × (0.06)⁴/32 = 1.272 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. Torsional stiffness k_t = GJ/L = 8 × 10¹⁰ × 1.272 × 10⁻⁶/1.4 = 7.271 × 10⁴ N·m/rad. This is the torque produced per radian of relative twist between the two rotors, and it is the only elastic element in the model. The shaft inertia is neglected as stated.

Answer: 7.271 × 10⁴ N·m/rad

(b)

For two discs on one massless shaft with no end restraint, the equations J1 θ1'' + k_t (θ1 − θ2) = 0 and J2 θ2'' + k_t (θ2 − θ1) = 0 give one rigid-body mode (ω = 0) and one vibration mode with ω_n² = k_t (J1 + J2)/(J1 J2). Substituting: ω_n² = 7.271 × 10⁴ × 6/(4.2 × 1.8) = 5.77 × 10⁴ rad²/s². ω_n = 240.2 rad/s, so f_n = 38.23 Hz. Compare this with the running speed of the machine to judge any risk of torsional resonance.

Answer: 38.23 Hz

(c)

In the vibration mode the rotors move in antiphase with J1 θ1 + J2 θ2 = 0, because the net angular momentum stays zero. The node is the section of shaft that does not twist. By similar triangles the node is at distance L1 = L J2/(J1 + J2) from the turbine rotor. L1 = 1.4 × 1.8/(4.2 + 1.8) = 0.42 m. The node lies close to the heavier turbine rotor, as it must, since the lighter generator rotor swings through the larger angle.

Answer: 0.42 m

(d)

With θ1 = 0.01396 rad and θ2 = −(J1/J2) θ1 = -0.03258 rad, the twist across the shaft is θ1 − θ2 = θ1 (1 + J1/J2) = 0.04654 rad. Maximum shear stress at the outer surface is τ = G (d/2) (twist)/L = 8 × 10¹⁰ × 0.03 × 0.04654/1.4 = 79.8 MPa. This is the alternating stress amplitude and must be compared with the fatigue strength of the shaft material, including any stress concentration at keyways or couplings.

Answer: 79.8 MPa

Problem 2 [A2-087] Critical speed of shafts

A horizontal solid steel shaft of diameter 50 mm runs in two short self-aligning bearings 1.6 m apart, which may be treated as simple supports. A pulley of mass 22 kg is mounted 0.5 m from the left bearing and a fan wheel of mass 14 kg is mounted 1.2 m from the left bearing. Take E = 205 GPa and a steel density of 7850 kg/m³, with g = 9.81 m/s². The shaft's own mass is distributed along its length and the pulley and wheel may be treated as point masses. The machine is to run at 1450 rpm. Estimate the first critical speed using Dunkerley's method.

  1. (a) Determine the first critical speed of the shaft acting alone (uniform simply supported beam), in rpm. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the critical speed that the pulley would give if it acted alone on a massless shaft, in rpm. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the critical speed that the fan wheel would give if it acted alone on a massless shaft, in rpm. [5]
  4. (d) Using Dunkerley's equation, determine the first critical speed of the complete shaft, in rpm, and decide whether 1450 rpm is acceptable. [5]
(a)

For a uniform beam on simple supports the first natural frequency is ω = (π/L)² √(EI/ρA). I = πd⁴/64 = 3.068 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴ and A = πd²/4 = 0.001963 m². EI = 6.289 × 10⁴ N·m² and ρA = 15.41 kg/m. ω = (π/1.6)² √(6.289 × 10⁴/15.41) = 246.3 rad/s. Convert: N = 60ω/2π = 2352 rpm. This is the speed at which the shaft's own mass alone would whirl.

Answer: 2352 rpm

(b)

A point load P at distance a from the left support (b = L − a) deflects the beam at the load by δ = P a² b²/(3EIL). Here P = 22 × 9.81 = 215.8 N, a = 0.5 m, b = 1.1 m. δ1 = 0.0002163 m. The critical speed is ω1 = √(g/δ1) = 213 rad/s, i.e. 2034 rpm. The pulley is the heavier disc and sits nearer mid-span, which is why its stand-alone critical speed is the lower of the two.

Answer: 2034 rpm

(c)

For the fan wheel, P = 14 × 9.81 = 137.3 N, a = 1.2 m, b = 0.4 m. δ2 = P a² b²/(3EIL) = 0.0001048 m. ω2 = √(g/δ2) = 305.9 rad/s = 2921 rpm. Static deflection of the wheel is small because it sits close to the right bearing, where the shaft is stiff, so its stand-alone critical speed is high. Each of the three results is an upper bound on the true combined value, which the next part corrects.

Answer: 2921 rpm

(d)

Dunkerley: 1/ω_c² = 1/ω_s² + 1/ω1² + 1/ω2². Substituting in rad/s: 1/(246.3)² + 1/(213)² + 1/(305.9)² = 1.649 × 10⁻⁵ + 2.204 × 10⁻⁵ + 1.068 × 10⁻⁵ = 4.922 × 10⁻⁵. So ω_c = 142.5 rad/s = 1361 rpm. Dunkerley slightly underestimates the true value, so it is conservative. The running speed is 1450 rpm, which is 1.07 times the critical speed, so it is too close to the critical speed and is not acceptable.

Answer: 1361 rpm

Problem 3 [A2-088] Rigid body planar kinetics with energy methods

A solid steel roller of mass 60 kg and radius 300 mm is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at 20 degrees to the horizontal. A light linear spring of stiffness 300 N/m lies parallel to the plane. One end is fixed at the top of the incline and the other is attached to the roller axle, and it is unstretched at the instant of release. The roller rolls down without slipping and no energy is lost to rolling resistance. The roller is a uniform solid cylinder. Use g = 9.81 m/s². Combine energy methods with the equations of planar motion to study its behaviour.

  1. (a) Determine the speed of the roller axle after it has rolled a distance of 0.80 m down the plane. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the angular velocity of the roller at that point. [4]
  3. (c) Determine the greatest distance the roller travels down the plane before it momentarily stops. [5]
  4. (d) At the lowest point of its travel, determine the minimum coefficient of static friction needed to prevent slipping. [6]
(a)

Rolling without slipping gives v = Rω, and the kinetic energy is ½mv² + ½Iω² with I = ½mR², so T = ½mv² + ¼mv² = ¾mv². Work-energy from rest: m g s sin θ − ½ k s² = ¾ m v². Left side: 60 × 9.81 × 0.8 × sin(20°) − 0.5 × 300 × 0.8² = 161.1 − 96 = 65.05 J. So v² = that/(0.75 × 60) and v = 1.2 m/s. Friction does no work because the contact point is instantaneously at rest.

Answer: 1.2 m/s

(b)

The no-slip condition links the axle speed to spin: ω = v/R = 1.202/0.3 = 4.01 rad/s. This is the angular velocity about the axle at s = 0.80 m, in the sense of the rolling direction (down the plane). The rotational part of the kinetic energy is ½Iω² = ½ × 2.7 × 4.01² = 21.68 J, one third of the total kinetic energy 65.05 J, which shows why the rolling roller descends more slowly than a sliding block.

Answer: 4.01 rad/s

(c)

The roller stops momentarily when T = 0: m g s_max sin θ = ½ k s_max². Dividing by s_max, s_max = 2 m g sin θ/k = 2 × 60 × 9.81 × sin(20°)/300 = 1.34 m. This is twice the static equilibrium extension m g sin θ/k = 0.671 m, the standard result for a suddenly applied load on a spring. The roller then rolls back up the plane and oscillates about the equilibrium position.

Answer: 1.34 m

(d)

At s_max the speed is zero but the acceleration is not. Along the plane (down positive): m g sin θ − k s_max − F = m a, with F the friction force up the plane. Moments about the centre: F R = I α = ½ m R² (a/R), so F = ½ m a. Combining, a = (m g sin θ − k s_max)/(1.5 m) = -2.24 m/s², negative (up the plane). F = ½ m a = -67.1 N, so the friction force acts down the plane, 67.1 N in magnitude. The normal force is N = m g cos θ = 553.1 N, so μ_min = F/N = 0.121. Any coefficient above this prevents slip.

Answer: 0.121

Problem 4 [A2-089] Planar mechanism velocity analysis by instant centres

A hinged ventilation flap is driven by a four-bar linkage. The crank O2A is 80 mm long, the coupler AB is 240 mm, and the rocker O4B is 180 mm. The fixed pivots O2 and O4 are 200 mm apart on a horizontal line, with O4 to the right of O2, and the linkage is assembled with B above the line O2O4. The crank turns anticlockwise at a constant 120 rpm. At the instant when the crank makes 60 degrees with the line O2O4, the designer wants to use instant centres to find the speeds of the coupler and rocker, and also to judge where the mechanism reaches the end of its stroke.

  1. (a) Locate the instant centre of the coupler relative to the frame (I13), giving its distance from pin A, in millimetres. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the magnitude of the angular velocity of the coupler AB, in rad/s. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the magnitude of the angular velocity of the rocker O4B, in rad/s, and state the sense of rotation of the rocker. [5]
