  4. (d) As the crank turns, the linkage reaches the position where the crank and coupler are collinear and extended. Determine the crank angle from O2O4 at which this occurs, in degrees, and say why the rocker velocity there is a design concern. [5]
(a)

With O2 at the origin and O4 at (0.2, 0), pin A is at (40, 69.28) mm and, solving the two-circle intersection with B above the ground line, B is at (257.6, 170.5) mm. Link 3 and the frame meet at I13, where the lines through O2A and O4B intersect (the velocities of A and B are perpendicular to those lines). Intersecting line O2A with line O4B gives I13 at (481.9, 834.6) mm. Distance from A: AI13 = 883.8 mm.

Answer: 883.8 mm

(b)

The crank speed is ω2 = 12.57 rad/s, so v_A = ω2 × O2A = 12.57 × 0.08 = 1.005 m/s. Link 3 rotates about I13 instantaneously, so ω3 = v_A/AI13 = 1.005/0.8838 = 1.14 rad/s. The sense of ω3 is clockwise. A sign check: A moves perpendicular to O2A, and I13 lies on the opposite side of A from the crank pivot or beyond, which fixes the sense. The same value follows from a vector velocity-difference solution of the loop.

Answer: 1.14 rad/s

(c)

Pin B is also on link 3, so v_B = ω3 × BI13 = 1.14 × 701 mm = 0.797 m/s. Link 4 rotates about O4, so ω4 = v_B/O4B = 0.797/0.18 = 4.43 rad/s, anticlockwise. The velocity ratio ω4/ω2 = 0.353 at this position. The rocker therefore turns slower than the crank at this instant. The result depends on the instant centre location and changes continuously through the cycle.

Answer: 4.43 rad/s, anticlockwise

(d)

With the crank and coupler collinear and extended, B lies on the line from O2 at distance O2B = r2 + r3 = 0.32 m. Triangle O2-O4-B has sides O2B = 0.32 m, O2O4 = 0.2 m and O4B = 0.18 m. By the cosine rule cos θ = (0.32² + 0.2² − 0.18²)/(2 × 0.32 × 0.2) = 0.8594, so θ = 30.75°. At this limit the velocity of B must be perpendicular to both AB and O4B, which forces v_B = 0: I13 lies at B, ω4 = 0 and the rocker reverses, while the coupler still turns. The rocker has zero speed but the crank torque needed for a given rocker load rises sharply, a toggle position. The designer must keep the actual stroke away from this point or use it deliberately to hold the flap.

Answer: 30.75 degrees

Problem 5 [A2-090] Relative velocity and acceleration of a four-bar linkage

A windscreen wiper linkage is a four-bar mechanism with a crank O2A of 50 mm, a coupler AB of 150 mm, and an output rocker O4B of 120 mm. The fixed pivots are 130 mm apart on a horizontal line, with O4 to the right of O2. The crank turns anticlockwise at a constant 20 rad/s. The linkage is assembled with B above the line O2O4. At the instant the crank makes 120 degrees with the positive direction of O2O4, the design team wants the angular velocity and acceleration of the rocker and a judgement on how well the mechanism transmits force at that position.

  1. (a) Using relative velocity, determine the magnitude of the angular velocity of the coupler AB, in rad/s. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the magnitude of the angular velocity of the rocker O4B, in rad/s. [4]
  3. (c) Using relative acceleration, determine the magnitude of the angular acceleration of the rocker, in rad/s². [7]
  4. (d) Determine the transmission angle (acute angle between coupler and rocker) at this position, in degrees, and judge whether it is acceptable against a usual minimum of about 40 degrees. [5]
(a)

Place O2 at the origin. A = 50 mm at 120° = (-25, 43.3) mm; solving the circle intersection gives B at (105.4, 117.4) mm. Velocity of A: v_A = ω2 × O2A = 20 × 0.05 = 1 m/s, perpendicular to O2A. Write v_B = v_A + v_BA = v_B (perpendicular to O4B), with v_BA = ω3 × AB. Solving the two scalar components gives ω3 = 2.18 rad/s (anticlockwise).

Answer: 2.18 rad/s

(b)

From the same vector loop, v_B is perpendicular to O4B with magnitude v_B = ω4 × O4B. Solving the pair of component equations simultaneously for ω3 and ω4 yields ω4 = 8.75 rad/s (anticlockwise), so v_B = 1.05 m/s. Cross-check by a closed polygon: v_A + v_BA must equal v_B. The result satisfies this to rounding error. The rocker turns at 0.438 of the crank speed at this instant.

Answer: 8.75 rad/s

(c)

Relative acceleration: a_B = a_A + a_BAn + a_BAt = a_Bn + a_Bt. With α2 = 0, a_A = ω2² O2A = 20 m/s² toward O2. a_BAn = ω3² AB = 0.7148 m/s² toward A. a_Bn = ω4² O4B = 9.191 m/s² toward O4. The tangential parts are α3 × AB (perpendicular to AB) and α4 × O4B (perpendicular to O4B). Resolving the vector equation into two components and solving gives α3 = 70.2 rad/s² and α4 = 19.5 rad/s² (clockwise). Then |a_B| = 9.48 m/s².

Answer: 19.5 rad/s²

(d)

The transmission angle μ is the acute angle between coupler and rocker at B. Vectors from B: to A is (-130.4, -74.15) mm and to O4 is (24.61, -117.4) mm. cos μ = (u1·u2)/(|u1||u2|), giving μ = 72.2°. This exceeds the usual 40° guideline, so the position is acceptable: the coupler pushes mostly perpendicular to the rocker and most of the force turns the output. The designer should also check μ over the full wiper sweep, not just here.

Answer: 72.2 degrees

A2 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A2-091] Slider-crank kinematics

A single-cylinder reciprocating air compressor has a crank radius of 60 mm and a connecting rod 240 mm long between centres. The cylinder axis passes through the crankshaft centre (no offset) and the crank turns at a constant 1500 rpm. The crank angle θ is measured from head-end dead centre (outer dead centre), the piston position furthest from the crankshaft. A designer is reviewing whether lengthening the rod to 300 mm, with the same crank and speed, is worth the extra bearing-housing size because of the shaking force at head-end dead centre. Use the exact geometric relation between crank angle and piston position, not the harmonic approximation, unless a part says otherwise.

  1. (a) Find the piston displacement from head-end dead centre when θ = 40°. [5]
  2. (b) Find the exact piston velocity when θ = 40°. [5]
  3. (c) Find the piston acceleration at head-end dead centre for the 240 mm rod, using the standard result for the slider-crank at θ = 0. [5]
  4. (d) Find the percentage reduction in head-end dead centre acceleration if the rod is lengthened to 300 mm, and state in one sentence whether the change is worthwhile. [5]
(a)

Angular speed ω = 1500 × 2π/60 = 157.08 rad/s. With the rod at angle φ to the cylinder axis, the piston displacement from head-end dead centre is x = r(1 − cos θ) + l(1 − cos φ), where l sin φ = r sin θ. Here r sin θ = 0.060 × sin 40° = 0.03857 m, so l cos φ = √(l² − r² sin² θ) = √(0.2400² − 0.03857²) = 0.23688 m. Then x = 0.060 × (1 − cos 40°) + (0.2400 − 0.23688) = 0.060 × 0.23396 + 0.00312 = 0.014038 + 0.003119 = 0.017156 m. The piston is therefore 17.16 mm from head-end dead centre. The second term is the rod obliquity correction, about 18 percent of the total, which shows why the harmonic approximation x ≈ r(1 − cos θ) would understate the displacement here.

Answer: 17.16 mm

(b)

Differentiate x with respect to time, using dθ/dt = ω. Exactly, v = rω[sin θ + (r sin θ cos θ)/√(l² − r² sin² θ)]. Substitute r = 0.060 m, ω = 157.08 rad/s, so rω = 9.4248 m/s. sin 40° = 0.64279, cos 40° = 0.76604, and the square root is 0.23688 m. The correction term is (0.060 × 0.64279 × 0.76604)/0.23688 = 0.029542/0.23688 = 0.12471. Then v = 9.4248 × (0.64279 + 0.12471) = 9.4248 × 0.76750 = 7.234 m/s. The positive sign means the piston is moving away from head-end dead centre. The pure harmonic estimate rω sin θ would give 6.058 m/s, so the finite rod length raises the velocity by about 19 percent at this angle.

Answer: 7.23 m/s

(c)

At θ = 0 the exact acceleration reduces to a = rω²(1 + r/l). Compute rω² = 0.060 × 157.08² = 0.060 × 24674 = 1480.4 m/s². The obliquity ratio is r/l = 60/240 = 0.25. Therefore a = 1480.4 × 1.25 = 1850.6 m/s². The sign is directed toward the crankshaft, so the piston must be decelerated by the gas and rod to the extent of this acceleration, and the inertia force on the cylinder head side is the piston mass times this value. The first term rω² is the pure crank contribution and the second term rω² r/l is the second harmonic from rod obliquity. At head-end dead centre both add, which is why the shaking force peaks there.

Answer: 1851 m/s²

(d)

With l = 300 mm the ratio is r/l = 60/300 = 0.20, so a = 1480.4 × 1.20 = 1776.5 m/s². The reduction is (1850.6 − 1776.5)/1850.6 = 74.0/1850.6 = 0.0400, which is 4.0 percent. Judgement: the primary term rω² is unchanged and is 80 percent of the original acceleration, so only the small second-harmonic part is affected. A 25 percent longer rod, with the larger housing, extra mass and bending stiffness requirement it brings, buys only a 4 percent reduction in peak inertia force. It is rarely worthwhile for shaking-force reasons alone. Speed reduction is far more effective, since acceleration scales with ω², so a 4 percent drop in speed gives about 8 percent less inertia force.

Answer: 4.0 percent

Problem 2 [A2-092] Grashof condition and transmission angle

A packaging machine uses a planar four-bar linkage to sweep a pusher blade. The fixed frame link between the two ground pivots is 300 mm long. The driven crank is 90 mm, the coupler is 260 mm and the output rocker, which carries the blade, is 200 mm. The crank is driven by a motor through a gearbox. The designer must confirm that the crank can rotate fully, that the force transmission never becomes poor, and judge whether the swing of the rocker is enough for a 50° blade sweep. Treat the links as rigid and in one plane. The transmission angle is the acute-or-obtuse angle between the coupler and rocker, taken as the smaller of that angle and its supplement.

  1. (a) Find the margin (mm) by which the Grashof inequality is satisfied, that is (p + q) − (s + l), where s and l are the shortest and longest links. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum transmission angle over a full crank revolution. [6]
  3. (c) Find the total swing angle of the rocker between its two extreme positions. [5]
  4. (d) The crank turns at constant speed. Find the ratio of the crank rotation for the longer stroke to that for the shorter stroke (time ratio, greater than 1). [5]
(a)

Grashof's criterion states that a four-bar linkage has at least one fully rotating link if s + l ≤ p + q, where s is the shortest link, l the longest and p, q the other two. Here the links are 90, 200, 260 and 300 mm, so s = 90 and l = 300, with p = 200 and q = 260. Then s + l = 390 mm and p + q = 460 mm. The margin is 460 − 390 = 70 mm. The inequality holds, and because the shortest link (90 mm) is the driven crank adjacent to the frame, the linkage is a crank-rocker: the crank can turn through 360° while the rocker oscillates. The 70 mm margin shows the design is not close to the change-point condition where the linkage could lock up.

Answer: 70 mm

(b)

In a crank-rocker the transmission angle is extreme when the crank lies along the frame line. With crank a = 90, coupler b = 260, rocker c = 200 and frame d = 300 mm, the two cases are (i) crank folded toward the rocker pivot, distance between crank pin and rocker pivot is d − a = 210 mm, and (ii) crank pointing away, d + a = 390 mm. By the cosine rule, cos μ = (b² + c² − D²)/(2bc). Case (i): (67600 + 40000 − 44100)/(104000) = 0.6106, so μ = 52.37°. Case (ii): (107600 − 152100)/104000 = −0.4279, so the angle is 115.33°, whose supplement is 64.67°. The minimum transmission angle is 52.37°. This is above the usual guideline of 40°, so force transmission is acceptable throughout.

Answer: 52.4°

(c)

The rocker reaches its extreme positions when the crank and coupler are collinear. The distance from the crank pivot O2 to the coupler-rocker joint is then b + a = 350 mm (extended) or b − a = 170 mm (folded). In the triangle formed by the two ground pivots and this joint, with sides d = 300, c = 200 and the third side D, the rocker angle φ from the frame line satisfies cos φ = (d² + c² − D²)/(2dc). For D = 350: (90000 + 40000 − 122500)/120000 = 0.0625, so φ1 = 86.42°. For D = 170: (130000 − 28900)/120000 = 0.8425, so φ2 = 32.59°. The swing is 86.42 − 32.59 = 53.82°. This exceeds the required 50° blade sweep by 3.8°, so the linkage is adequate with a small margin to trim by adjusting the blade mounting.

Answer: 53.8°

(d)

At each extreme the angle of the line O2 to the joint, measured from the frame line, follows from the cosine rule in the same triangle: cos α = (d² + D² − c²)/(2dD). For D = 350: (90000 + 122500 − 40000)/210000 = 0.8214, so α1 = 34.77°. For D = 170: (90000 + 28900 − 40000)/102000 = 0.7735, so α2 = 39.33°. In the extended position the crank lies along that line, at 34.77°. In the folded position the crank points the opposite way, at 39.33° + 180° = 219.33°. The crank therefore turns 219.33 − 34.77 = 184.56° for one stroke and 360 − 184.56 = 175.44° for the other. The time ratio is 184.56/175.44 = 1.052. The slow stroke is only about 5 percent longer, so the quick-return effect is slight.

Answer: 1.052

Problem 3 [A2-093] Cam profile and follower motion

A disc cam with a translating, in-line roller follower operates a fuel-metering valve in a small diesel engine. The cam rotates at 600 rpm. The follower rises 24 mm with simple harmonic motion during 100° of cam rotation, then dwells. The base circle radius is 40 mm and the roller radius is 10 mm, so the prime circle radius is 50 mm. For an in-line translating follower the pressure angle φ satisfies tan φ = (ds/dθ)/(Rp + s), where s is the follower lift, θ the cam angle in radians and Rp the prime circle radius. Assume rigid components and constant cam speed. The designer wants to know the dynamic demands and whether the cam can be made smaller.

  1. (a) Find the maximum follower velocity during the rise. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum follower acceleration during the rise. [5]
  3. (c) Find the pressure angle when the cam has turned 40° from the start of the rise, with Rp = 50 mm. [5]
  4. (d) Find the smallest prime circle radius for which the pressure angle at mid-rise (50° of cam rotation) does not exceed 30°. [6]
(a)

For simple harmonic rise, s = (h/2)[1 − cos(πθ/β)], with h = 24 mm and β = 100° = 1.7453 rad. The velocity is v = ds/dt = (πhω)/(2β) sin(πθ/β), which is greatest at mid-rise where the sine is 1. Cam speed ω = 600 × 2π/60 = 62.83 rad/s. So vmax = π × 0.024 × 62.83/(2 × 1.7453) = 4.7374/3.4907 = 1.357 m/s. Note that it is the ratio h/β, the lift per radian of cam turn, that sets the velocity: a shorter rise angle or a larger lift both increase it proportionally. This value governs the roller-to-cam contact speed and lubrication demand.

Answer: 1.357 m/s

(b)

Differentiate the velocity again: a = (π²hω²)/(2β²) cos(πθ/β), which is largest at the start of the rise (and negative at the end). Then amax = π² × 0.024 × 62.83²/(2 × 1.7453²). Compute 62.83² = 3947.8, so the numerator is 9.8696 × 0.024 × 3947.8 = 935.1. The denominator is 2 × 3.0462 = 6.0924. Thus amax = 935.1/6.0924 = 153.5 m/s². With harmonic motion the acceleration changes abruptly from zero in the dwell to this peak at the start of the rise, which is a finite jump in acceleration, so the follower sees an infinite jerk. That is a known weakness of simple harmonic motion at dwell junctions.

Answer: 153.5 m/s²

(c)

Work in lift per radian. At θ = 40° = 0.6981 rad the argument πθ/β = π × 40/100 = 1.2566 rad (72°). Then s = 12 × (1 − cos 72°) = 12 × 0.69098 = 8.292 mm. The lift gradient is ds/dθ = (πh/(2β)) sin(πθ/β) = (π × 24/(2 × 1.7453)) × sin 72° = 21.600 × 0.95106 = 20.543 mm/rad. Then tan φ = 20.543/(50 + 8.292) = 20.543/58.292 = 0.35239, so φ = 19.41°. This is comfortably below the common 30° limit used for translating followers, where sliding friction in the follower guide begins to cause jamming.

Answer: 19.4°

(d)

At mid-rise s = h/2 = 12 mm and ds/dθ is at its maximum πh/(2β) = 21.600 mm/rad. Require tan φ ≤ tan 30° = 0.57735. Then Rp + s ≥ 21.600/0.57735 = 37.41 mm, so Rp ≥ 37.41 − 12 = 25.41 mm. A prime circle of about 25.4 mm would give exactly 30° at mid-rise. Judgement: the current 50 mm prime circle is nearly twice this, so the cam could be made smaller. In practice the designer would keep a margin, perhaps 30 to 35 mm, because the largest pressure angle in simple harmonic rise is near but not exactly at mid-rise for a given Rp and because a smaller base circle raises contact stress and can undercut the profile.

Answer: 25.4 mm

Problem 4 [A2-094] Spur gear geometry and gear trains

A conveyor drive uses a pair of standard full-depth involute spur gears: a 20-tooth pinion driving a 52-tooth gear, module 4 mm, pressure angle 20°. The addendum equals one module. The pinion turns at 1450 rpm. During commissioning a fitter mounts the gear shafts 2 mm further apart than the nominal centre distance because of a shifted bearing pedestal. The plant engineer must judge whether the pair is acceptable as designed and how the misalignment of centres affects it. Use the pitch circle radius m·N/2 and base circle radius equal to pitch radius times cos 20°. The length of the line of action for a standard-centre pair is √(ra1² − rb1²) + √(ra2² − rb2²) − C sin φ.

  1. (a) Find the standard centre distance. [3]
  2. (b) Find the speed of the gear. [2]
  3. (c) Find the contact ratio of the standard pair. [6]
  4. (d) Find the minimum number of teeth on a pinion of this system that avoids undercutting when meshing with a rack. [3]
  5. (e) With the shafts 2 mm further apart (146 mm centre distance), find the new operating pressure angle. [6]
(a)

Centre distance is the sum of the pitch radii: C = m(N1 + N2)/2 = 4 × (20 + 52)/2 = 4 × 36 = 144 mm. The pitch radii are 40 mm for the pinion and 104 mm for the gear. For correct meshing with no backlash in the theoretical sense, the pitch circles must be tangent at this spacing. This is the dimension the housing machining must hold, with a tolerance usually applied as a small plus allowance to give working backlash. Any larger spacing, as in the fitter's error described later, changes the operating pressure angle.

Answer: 144 mm

(b)

The gear ratio is N2/N1 = 52/20 = 2.6. The driven gear speed is n2 = n1 × N1/N2 = 1450 × 20/52 = 29000/52 = 557.7 rpm. The direction reverses for an external pair. The reduction factor of 2.6 also multiplies torque by 2.6, ignoring losses; with efficiency typically 98 percent per mesh for ground gears, the real torque is only slightly lower. The speed ratio is exact because involute gearing keeps a constant angular velocity ratio, equal to the inverse ratio of the base circle radii, regardless of small centre-distance errors.

Answer: 557.7 rpm

(c)

Pitch radii: 40 mm and 104 mm. Base radii: rb1 = 40 cos 20° = 37.588 mm and rb2 = 104 cos 20° = 97.728 mm. Addendum radii: ra1 = 40 + 4 = 44 mm and ra2 = 104 + 4 = 108 mm. The length of the line of action is √(44² − 37.588²) + √(108² − 97.728²) − 144 sin 20°. First term: √(1936 − 1412.8) = √523.2 = 22.87 mm. Second term: √(11664 − 9550.6) = √2113.4 = 45.97 mm. Third term: 144 × 0.34202 = 49.25 mm. So Z = 22.87 + 45.97 − 49.25 = 19.59 mm. The base pitch is π m cos φ = π × 4 × 0.93969 = 11.808 mm. Contact ratio = 19.59/11.808 = 1.659. Slightly more than one tooth pair is always in contact for the stated part of the cycle, which is acceptable but not generous.

Answer: 1.659

(d)

The pinion avoids undercutting if its addendum circle is not beyond the interference point on the line of action, which gives the standard result Nmin = 2k/sin² φ for addendum k·m with k = 1. Then Nmin = 2/sin² 20° = 2/0.11698 = 17.10 teeth. Since teeth are whole numbers, 18 teeth is the minimum for a standard full-depth tooth with a rack, and 17 would undercut slightly. The 20-tooth pinion used here is therefore safe from undercutting. For meshing with a finite gear rather than a rack the limit is slightly lower, so this is the conservative figure.

Answer: 17.1 (so 18 teeth)

(e)

When the centre distance changes, the base circles stay fixed and the gears operate on new pitch circles. The operating pressure angle satisfies C′ cos φ′ = C cos φ. Then cos φ′ = 144 × cos 20°/146 = 144 × 0.93969/146 = 135.315/146 = 0.92682, so φ′ = 22.06°. The pressure angle rises by 2.06°, the contact ratio falls because the line of action shortens, and backlash increases. A larger pressure angle also raises the bearing load for a given torque. The speed ratio is unchanged, so the drive still works, but a 2 mm error is large for module 4 and the pedestal should be corrected or the gears re-specified.

Answer: 22.06°

Problem 5 [A2-095] Planetary gear trains

A winch gearbox uses a simple epicyclic train. The sun gear has 24 teeth, the planet gears 18 teeth and the internal ring gear 60 teeth, module 3 mm. There are three equally spaced planets on a single carrier. The ring gear is bolted to the housing (fixed). The motor drives the sun gear at 1800 rpm and delivers 15 kW. The carrier is the output. Assume 100 percent efficiency and equal load sharing between the planets. The designer must also decide whether holding the carrier and releasing the ring would produce a useful reverse drive.

  1. (a) Find the carrier (output) speed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the absolute angular speed of one planet gear about its own axis (in the fixed frame), with sign relative to the sun. [4]
  3. (c) Find the torque the housing must react through the fixed ring gear. [4]
  4. (d) Find the tangential tooth force at each sun-planet mesh. [4]
  5. (e) If instead the carrier is held and the ring gear is free, find the ring speed for the same 1800 rpm sun speed (negative means opposite to the sun). [4]
(a)

Use the tabular or relative velocity method. With the ring fixed, the speeds satisfy (ωr − ωc)/(ωs − ωc) = −Ns/Nr. Setting ωr = 0 gives −ωc/(ωs − ωc) = −24/60 = −0.4, so ωc = 0.4(ωs − ωc), hence ωc(1.4) = 0.4 ωs, and ωc = ωs × 24/84 = ωs × Ns/(Ns + Nr). Then ωc = 1800 × 24/84 = 514.3 rpm. The reduction ratio is 84/24 = 3.5. Check the tooth count: Nr = Ns + 2Np = 24 + 36 = 60, so the geometry closes properly for equally spaced planets.

Answer: 514.3 rpm

(b)

Relative to the carrier the sun turns at (1800 − 514.3) = 1285.7 rpm. The planet meshes with the sun externally, so relative to the carrier it turns in the opposite sense at (Ns/Np) × 1285.7 = (24/18) × 1285.7 = 1714.3 rpm. Add the carrier speed to get the absolute value: ωp = 514.3 − 1714.3 = −1200 rpm. The negative sign means the planet spins opposite to the sun. This absolute spin speed sets the planet bearing speed, which is higher than the output speed even though the output is slow. Check using the ring: relative to the carrier the ring turns at −514.3 rpm and meshes internally with the planet, so the planet turns relative to the carrier at (60/18) × 514.3 = 1714.3 rpm in the same sense as the ring, which is −1714.3 rpm and agrees.

Answer: -1200 rpm

(c)

Input torque Tin = P/ωs, with ωs = 1800 × 2π/60 = 188.50 rad/s, so Tin = 15000/188.50 = 79.58 N·m. With no losses power in equals power out, so Tout = Tin × (ωs/ωc) = 79.58 × 3.5 = 278.5 N·m. The torque balance on the whole gearbox, with the housing reaction at the ring Tring, is Tin + Tring = Tout in the sense of the carrier, giving Tring = 278.5 − 79.58 = 198.9 N·m. The housing mounting bolts must therefore carry 198.9 N·m in the same direction as the output torque, which is 2.5 times the input torque.

Answer: 198.9 N·m

(d)

The sun carries 79.58 N·m and each of the three planets takes one third. The sun pitch radius is m·Ns/2 = 3 × 24/2 = 36 mm = 0.036 m. Tangential force per mesh Ft = Tin/(3 × rs) = 79.58/(3 × 0.036) = 79.58/0.108 = 736.8 N. The force acts at each of three meshes, so the sun is in pure torque with no net side load if sharing is equal, which is a major advantage of planetary designs. Unequal sharing in practice means a load-sharing factor of about 1.1 to 1.2 is normally applied to this tooth force when checking gear stress.

Answer: 737 N

(e)

With the carrier fixed, the planets become idlers. The sun-to-ring ratio is then simply ωr/ωs = −Ns/Nr, because the sun drives the planet externally (reversing) and the planet drives the internal ring (same direction as the planet). Then ωr = −(24/60) × 1800 = −720 rpm. The ring turns opposite to the sun at 720 rpm, a reduction of 2.5 with reversal. This gives a useful reverse drive, but the ring and housing would then need to be supported as a rotating element and its bearing and guarding designed accordingly.

Answer: -720 rpm

A2 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A2-096] Static force analysis of a mechanism

A hydraulic press-brake drive uses an in-line slider-crank to convert a gas-spring piston force into crank torque during a test that is carried out very slowly, so that inertia can be ignored. The crank radius is 50 mm and the connecting rod length is 200 mm. The piston, guided in a straight cylinder, carries an axial force of 8.0 kN pushing it toward the crankshaft. At the instant of interest the crank has turned 60° from the top dead centre position, where the cylinder axis passes through the crankshaft centre. Links are weightless and pin joints are frictionless. In the final part a Coulomb friction coefficient of 0.08 is introduced between piston and cylinder wall to assess how much torque is lost. Rod and piston friction both act only as stated.

  1. (a) Find the angle between the connecting rod and the cylinder axis. [3]
  2. (b) Find the force in the connecting rod. [3]
  3. (c) Find the side thrust of the piston on the cylinder wall. [3]
  4. (d) Find the torque on the crankshaft needed to hold the mechanism in equilibrium, and verify it with a second method. [5]
  5. (e) Repeat the torque calculation with piston friction coefficient 0.08 and state the percentage loss. [6]
(a)

The rod and crank form a triangle with the cylinder axis: l sin φ = r sin θ. So sin φ = 0.050 × sin 60°/0.200 = 0.050 × 0.86603/0.200 = 0.21651, giving φ = 12.50°. The rod lean is small because the rod is four times longer than the crank. Because the crank is at 60° from top dead centre, the rod leans to the opposite side of the axis from the crank pin, and this angle is needed for every later resolution of forces.

Answer: 12.50°

(b)

Treat the piston as a free body: it is acted on by the axial force F = 8000 N, the rod force Fr along the rod, and the wall reaction N perpendicular to the axis. Axial equilibrium with no friction gives Fr cos φ = F. So Fr = 8000/cos 12.50° = 8000/0.97630 = 8194 N. This is compressive in the rod. The rod force is only 2.4 percent larger than the piston force at this position, but reaches at most about 3.3 percent larger at maximum lean (sin φ = 0.25, φ = 14.5°), so the rod force stays close to the piston force throughout.

Answer: 8194 N

(c)

Perpendicular to the cylinder axis, the wall reaction balances the lateral component of the rod force: N = Fr sin φ = 8194 × 0.21651 = 1774 N, or equivalently N = F tan φ = 8000 × 0.22188 = 1775 N. This is the side thrust that the cylinder wall carries, and it sets the wear load on the piston skirt. It acts to one side for the power stroke and reverses when the rod leans the other way, which is the reason the piston skirt needs to be wide enough to handle thrust on both sides of the bore.

Answer: 1774 N

(d)

The rod force acts at the crank pin. The angle between the crank and the rod is θ + φ = 72.50°, so the moment arm of the rod force about the crankshaft is r sin(θ + φ) = 0.050 × 0.95372 = 0.047686 m. Torque T = 8194 × 0.047686 = 390.8 N·m. Check by virtual work: for a small crank turn the piston moves x′ = r[sin θ + r sin θ cos θ/√(l² − r² sin² θ)] per radian. Here the root is √(0.04 − 0.001875) = 0.19526 m, so x′ = 0.050 × (0.86603 + 0.050 × 0.86603 × 0.5/0.19526) = 0.050 × 0.97691 = 0.048845 m. Then T = F x′ = 8000 × 0.048845 = 390.8 N·m. The two methods agree.

Answer: 390.8 N·m

(e)

With friction the piston moves toward the crank, so friction μN acts against the motion, away from the crank. Axial equilibrium becomes F − μN = Fr cos φ, with N = Fr sin φ. So F = Fr(cos φ + μ sin φ) and Fr = 8000/(0.97630 + 0.08 × 0.21651) = 8000/0.99362 = 8051.5 N. Torque T = 8051.5 × 0.047686 = 383.95 N·m, which is 384.0 N·m. The loss is (390.76 − 383.95)/390.76 = 1.74 percent. Friction is a modest effect at this angle, but the loss grows with side thrust, so at positions of larger rod lean it matters more, and the figure here is a lower bound on piston-wall losses.

Answer: 384.0 N·m (1.7 percent loss)

Problem 2 [A2-097] Dynamic force analysis of a slider-crank

A small four-stroke petrol engine has a crank radius of 45 mm and a connecting rod 180 mm long between centres. The bore is 80 mm and the piston assembly has a mass of 0.90 kg. The engine runs at a steady 3000 rpm. At the instant considered, the crank is 30° past top dead centre on the power stroke and the cylinder gas pressure is 2.0 MPa (gauge). Treat the connecting rod as massless and ignore friction. Use the standard approximate expressions for the piston, with n = l/r: acceleration a = rω²(cos θ + cos 2θ/n) toward the crankshaft and velocity ratio v/ω = r(sin θ + sin 2θ/(2n)). The designer wants to see how much of the gas load actually reaches the crank at this angle.

  1. (a) Find the piston acceleration at this instant. [3]
  2. (b) Find the inertia force of the piston assembly. [3]
  3. (c) Find the net force along the cylinder axis transmitted from the piston to the connecting rod. [4]
  4. (d) Find the side thrust on the cylinder wall. [5]
  5. (e) Find the torque delivered to the crankshaft. [5]
(a)

Angular speed ω = 3000 × 2π/60 = 314.16 rad/s, so ω² = 98696 rad²/s². The crank radius gives rω² = 0.045 × 98696 = 4441.3 m/s². The rod ratio is n = 180/45 = 4. At θ = 30°, cos θ = 0.86603 and cos 2θ = 0.5, so cos 2θ/n = 0.125. Then a = 4441.3 × (0.86603 + 0.125) = 4441.3 × 0.99103 = 4401 m/s² directed toward the crankshaft (the piston is still accelerating away from the head, in the sense of motion). Note this is a value near 450 g, which shows why piston mass dominates the loads on the rod at high speed.

Answer: 4401 m/s²

(b)

The inertia force is the mass times the acceleration: Fi = m a = 0.90 × 4401.5 = 3961 N. Because the piston accelerates toward the crank, the inertia reaction, in the d'Alembert sense, acts on the piston away from the crank, that is, back toward the head. It therefore opposes the gas force on the way down. At high speed on the power stroke, inertia relieves the gas load, whereas near the exhaust stroke the inertia force adds to the rod tension. The rod and piston pin must be designed for both cases.

Answer: 3961 N

(c)

Gas force on the piston: area A = π × 0.080²/4 = 5.0265 × 10⁻³ m², so Fg = 2.0 × 10⁶ × 5.0265 × 10⁻³ = 10053 N, acting toward the crank. The net force along the axis is the gas force minus the inertia force: Fn = 10053 − 3961 = 6092 N. This is only 61 percent of the gas load, so nearly 40 percent is absorbed in accelerating the piston. This is the force the piston pin delivers along the cylinder axis to the connecting rod, before it is resolved into the rod force and the wall thrust.

Answer: 6092 N

(d)

The rod angle follows sin φ = r sin θ/l = 0.045 × 0.5/0.180 = 0.125, so φ = 7.18° and tan φ = 0.12599. Resolving the piston free body, the wall reaction is the lateral component: N = Fn tan φ = 6092 × 0.12599 = 767.5 N. The rod force is Fn/cos φ = 6092/0.99217 = 6140 N. The side thrust is only 12.6 percent of the axial force, which is typical for a long rod (n = 4). It decides the skirt load and the friction loss between the piston and the cylinder wall.

Answer: 767.5 N

(e)

Use the velocity ratio: v/ω = r(sin θ + sin 2θ/(2n)) = 0.045 × (0.5 + 0.86603/8) = 0.045 × 0.60825 = 0.027371 m. By the principle of virtual work with a massless rod, torque equals net axial force times v/ω: T = Fn × v/ω = 6092 × 0.027371 = 166.7 N·m. The same value follows from Fr r sin(θ + φ) = 6140 × 0.045 × sin 37.18° = 6140 × 0.045 × 0.6043 = 167.0 N·m, the small difference arising because the given velocity expression is an approximation (the exact kinematics give 167.0 N·m). With friction ignored, this torque is the engine's instantaneous gas-driven torque, less the piston inertia effect.

Answer: 166.7 N·m

Problem 3 [A2-098] Flywheel sizing

A punch press in a roofing-panel shop cuts one blank every 2.0 s. Each punching stroke takes 0.25 s, during which the press requires 9.5 kJ of energy. For the rest of the cycle the load is negligible. The press is driven by an electric motor that supplies constant power, with the flywheel absorbing and returning energy between strokes. The mean flywheel speed is 240 rpm and the coefficient of speed fluctuation must not exceed 0.06. The flywheel is to be a solid steel disc of diameter 1.2 m, with steel density 7850 kg/m³. Neglect the inertia of all other parts and assume friction losses are included in the 9.5 kJ figure. The works manager has asked whether a disc of half the inertia would be acceptable.

  1. (a) Find the motor power required. [4]
  2. (b) Find the energy the flywheel must deliver during each punching stroke. [4]
  3. (c) Find the required moment of inertia of the flywheel. [4]
  4. (d) Find the thickness of the solid steel disc of 1.2 m diameter that provides this inertia. [4]
  5. (e) If a disc of half the inertia were fitted, find the coefficient of fluctuation and the minimum speed reached. [4]
(a)

Over a complete cycle the motor must supply the average power, because the flywheel stores no net energy per cycle. The cycle energy is 9.5 kJ and the cycle time is 2.0 s, so P = 9500/2.0 = 4750 W = 4.75 kW. Friction losses were included in the 9.5 kJ figure, so no further allowance is needed here. A standard 5.5 kW motor would be chosen. Because the motor power is the average rather than the peak, it is much smaller than the 38 kW the press would demand during the stroke if there were no flywheel (9500 J in 0.25 s).

Answer: 4.75 kW

(b)

During the 0.25 s stroke the motor still supplies power P, adding P × 0.25 = 4750 × 0.25 = 1187.5 J. The flywheel must supply the remainder: ΔE = 9500 − 1187.5 = 8312.5 J = 8.31 kJ. This is the maximum fluctuation of kinetic energy in the flywheel over the cycle, since the flywheel loses this energy during the stroke and regains it during the remaining 1.75 s. The ratio of this to the 9.5 kJ stroke energy, 87.5 percent, shows how little the motor contributes directly during the punch.

Answer: 8.31 kJ

(c)

The energy fluctuation is ΔE = Cs I ω², where ω is the mean angular speed. Here ω = 240 × 2π/60 = 25.133 rad/s, so ω² = 631.65. Then I = ΔE/(Cs ω²) = 8312.5/(0.06 × 631.65) = 8312.5/37.899 = 219.3 kg·m². This is the minimum inertia that keeps the speed variation to 6 percent of the mean. Any extra inertia from the shaft, gears and clutch can be subtracted from this value, which provides some conservatism since it was neglected here.

Answer: 219.3 kg·m²

(d)

For a solid disc I = ½ m R², with R = 0.6 m, so m = 2I/R² = 2 × 219.33/0.36 = 1218.5 kg. The disc volume is m/ρ = 1218.5/7850 = 0.15522 m³, and the face area is π R² = π × 0.36 = 1.1310 m². The thickness is t = 0.15522/1.1310 = 0.1372 m = 137.2 mm. The rim speed is ωR = 25.133 × 0.6 = 15.08 m/s, which gives a rim stress of only ρv² = 7850 × 227.4 = 1.79 MPa, well below limits for steel, so strength is not a constraint in this design.

Answer: 137.2 mm

(e)

Halving the inertia while the energy fluctuation stays at 8312.5 J doubles the coefficient: Cs = ΔE/(I ω²) = 8312.5/(109.67 × 631.65) = 0.12. The speed variation is then 12 percent of the mean. The minimum speed is ωmean(1 − Cs/2) = 240 × (1 − 0.06) = 225.6 rpm, and the maximum is 254.4 rpm. A 12 percent fluctuation is probably too rough for a punch, since the blank is cut at the minimum speed with less kinetic energy, and the clutch and motor must follow the changes. The smaller disc could only be accepted if the process tolerates a 12 percent speed swing.

Answer: 225.6 rpm (Cs = 0.12)

Problem 4 [A2-099] Balancing of rotating masses

A rotor for a textile spindle carries three unbalanced masses on a shaft. Mass 1 is 6 kg at radius 120 mm and 100 mm from reference plane A. Mass 2 is 8 kg at radius 100 mm, 350 mm from plane A and 90° counterclockwise from mass 1 when viewed from plane A. Mass 3 is 5 kg at radius 150 mm, 550 mm from plane A and 210° counterclockwise from mass 1. Balancing masses are to be fitted in plane A itself and in plane B, which is 700 mm from plane A, both at a radius of 100 mm. The shaft turns at 1500 rpm and the bearings are close to planes A and B. The maintenance team wants to know the correction needed and the consequence of fitting only part of it.

  1. (a) Find the balancing mass required in plane B. [4]
  2. (b) Find its angular position, counterclockwise from mass 1, in degrees (0 to 360). [3]
  3. (c) Find the balancing mass required in plane A. [4]
  4. (d) Find its angular position, counterclockwise from mass 1, in degrees (0 to 360). [3]
  5. (e) If the plane-B mass were left out and only the plane-A mass fitted, find the dynamic bearing load at B at 1500 rpm. [6]
(a)

Take moments about plane A. For dynamic balance Σ m r x eiθ must be zero, where x is the distance from A. The terms are: mass 1: 6 × 0.12 × 0.10 = 0.0720 kg·m² at 0°, giving (0.0720, 0); mass 2: 8 × 0.10 × 0.35 = 0.2800 at 90°, giving (0, 0.2800); mass 3: 5 × 0.15 × 0.55 = 0.4125 at 210°, giving (−0.35723, −0.20625). Their sum is (−0.28523, +0.07375). The plane-B term mB rB xB must equal the negative of this, so mB rB × 0.70 = (0.28523, −0.07375), magnitude 0.29462, and mB rB = 0.42089 kg·m. With rB = 0.10 m, mB = 4.209 kg.

Answer: 4.209 kg

(b)

The plane-B balancing vector points opposite to the moment sum, at (0.28523, −0.07375). Its angle is atan2(−0.07375, 0.28523) = −14.50°, which as a counterclockwise angle from mass 1 is 360 − 14.50 = 345.5°. The mass is fitted at radius 100 mm at this angular position, on the side opposite to the combined couple of the three masses about plane A. A common error is to forget that angle conventions are counterclockwise as viewed from plane A, and to use the angles as seen from plane B, which would mirror the result.

Answer: 345.5°

(c)

Now sum the forces. The m r values are: mass 1: 0.72 at 0° giving (0.72, 0); mass 2: 0.80 at 90° giving (0, 0.80); mass 3: 0.75 at 210° giving (−0.64952, −0.375). Their sum is (0.07048, 0.42500). Add the plane-B balancing vector, 0.42089 at 345.5°, which is (0.40748, −0.10536), to give (0.47796, 0.31964). The plane-A vector must cancel this, so it is (−0.47796, −0.31964) with magnitude 0.57499 kg·m. At rA = 0.10 m, mA = 5.750 kg. Plane A needs a heavier correction than B because the original masses lie nearer to A and their net force must also be cancelled.

Answer: 5.750 kg

(d)

The plane-A correction vector is (−0.47796, −0.31964). Its angle is atan2(−0.31964, −0.47796) = −146.2°, or 213.8° counterclockwise from mass 1. This puts the mass in the third quadrant, roughly opposite to the force sum of the three masses plus plane B. As a check, the sum of all six vectors m r should be zero: the original sum (0.07048, 0.42500) plus B (0.40748, −0.10536) plus A (−0.47796, −0.31964) equals (0.0000, 0.0000), confirming force balance, and the couple balance was imposed in part (a).

Answer: 213.8°

(e)

If the plane-B mass is omitted the moment about plane A is no longer cancelled, and the bearing near B must supply the resulting reaction. The unbalanced couple about A is the vector sum computed in part (a), of magnitude 0.29462 kg·m² times ω². The force at B is that couple divided by the bearing spacing of 0.70 m: FB = m_B r_B ω². With ω = 1500 × 2π/60 = 157.08 rad/s, ω² = 24674. FB = 0.42089 × 24674 = 10 385 N, rotating with the shaft. That is a sizeable cyclic load, equal to about 1060 kg-force, at 25 Hz, enough to damage bearings quickly, so both planes must be fitted.

Answer: 10 385 N

Problem 5 [A2-100] Gyroscopic effects

A steam-turbine rotor in a ship has a mass of 1200 kg and a radius of gyration of 0.45 m. It turns at 3000 rpm with its axis along the length of the ship. The rotor is carried in two bearings 1.8 m apart. In heavy seas the ship pitches with simple harmonic angular motion about a transverse axis, with an amplitude of 8° and a period of 20 s. Later the ship makes a steady turn of radius 250 m at 14 m/s. Take gyroscopic couples from the rotor alone, neglecting the inertia of the ship and the rotor's own weight. The marine engineer needs to quantify the bearing loads and compare the two manoeuvres.

  1. (a) Find the polar moment of inertia of the rotor. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum angular velocity of pitching. [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum gyroscopic couple due to pitching. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum gyroscopic reaction force at each bearing (equal and opposite) due to pitching. [4]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of the steady gyroscopic couple during the turn to the maximum pitching couple. [5]
(a)

The rotor spins about its axis, so the polar moment of inertia is I = m k² with k = 0.45 m. Then I = 1200 × 0.45² = 1200 × 0.2025 = 243 kg·m². The spin speed is ω = 3000 × 2π/60 = 314.16 rad/s, giving an angular momentum H = Iω = 243 × 314.16 = 76 340 kg·m²/s. This is a large angular momentum, which explains why a rotor of this kind produces large gyroscopic effects even for slow movements of the ship.

Answer: 243 kg·m²

(b)

With simple harmonic pitching, θ = θ₀ sin(2πt/T), the angular velocity is dθ/dt = θ₀ (2π/T) cos(2πt/T), whose maximum is θ₀ × 2π/T. The amplitude is θ₀ = 8° = 0.13963 rad and T = 20 s, so 2π/T = 0.31416 rad/s. Thus ωp,max = 0.13963 × 0.31416 = 0.04386 rad/s. It occurs when the ship is passing through its mid-pitch position. At the extremes of pitch the angular velocity is zero, which means the gyroscopic couple vanishes at these instants.

Answer: 0.0439 rad/s

(c)

The gyroscopic couple on a spinning rotor whose axis is precessed at right angles to the spin axis is C = I ω ωp. The pitching axis is transverse and the spin axis is longitudinal, so the axes are perpendicular and the full formula applies. At the maximum precession rate, C = 243 × 314.16 × 0.04386 = 3349 N·m. The couple varies sinusoidally with pitch angular velocity, so it has the same 20 s period and reverses direction each half-cycle. It acts about the vertical axis, trying to turn the bow sideways.

Answer: 3349 N·m

(d)

The couple is carried by the two bearings as a force couple a distance 1.8 m apart. The reaction at each bearing is F = C/L = 3349/1.8 = 1860 N, equal and opposite, acting in the horizontal plane at right angles to the shaft. One bearing is pushed to port while the other is pushed to starboard, then the two reverse a half-period later. The rotor weight is 1200 × 9.81 = 11.8 kN, shared between the two bearings as 5.9 kN each, so the gyroscopic reaction is about 32 percent of the static load on each bearing, a significant additional alternating load to design for.

Answer: 1860 N

(e)

In a steady turn the precession rate is the ship's yaw rate, ωt = v/R = 14/250 = 0.056 rad/s. The gyroscopic couple is then Ct = Iω ωt = 243 × 314.16 × 0.056 = 4275 N·m. The ratio to the pitching couple is 4275/3349 = 1.277. The turn couple is steady for the whole turn, whereas the pitching couple is an alternating one. The turn couple acts about a transverse axis, trying to raise the bow or depress it depending on the direction of turn, so the bearing loads are higher and sustained, and the designer should size the bearings for the larger of the two.

Answer: 1.277

Exam A3: System Analysis and Control

A3 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A3-001] Mathematical models of mechanical systems

A tractor operator's seat is mounted on a single degree of freedom suspension, modelled as a lumped mass, a linear spring and a viscous damper acting in parallel between the cab floor and the seat. The seat plus operator has a mass of 250 kg. The spring stiffness is 18 kN/m and the damper coefficient is 1.2 kN·s/m. The cab floor is treated as rigid for this study and the motion is purely vertical, measured from the static equilibrium position so that gravity does not appear in the equation of motion. A sudden vertical force of 500 N is applied to the seat, for example when the operator braces against it, and then held constant. Treat the system as linear and take the displacement x of the seat as the output.

  1. (a) Write the equation of motion and determine the undamped natural frequency in rad/s. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the damping ratio and state whether the system is underdamped, critically damped or overdamped. [5]
  3. (c) Find the steady-state (static) deflection of the seat under the 500 N force, in mm. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the percentage overshoot of the seat displacement in response to the step force. [5]
(a)

Apply Newton's second law to the seat mass, with x measured from equilibrium: m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t). The spring and damper forces oppose the motion, and gravity cancels against the static spring force. With m = 250 kg, c = 1200 N·s/m and k = 18000 N/m the model is 250 x'' + 1200 x' + 18000 x = F(t). Dividing by m gives x'' + 4.8 x' + 72 x = F/250. The undamped natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √(18000/250) = √72 = 8.485 rad/s. This is about 1.35 Hz, a typical low-frequency seat suspension value, well below the 4 to 8 Hz band of peak human vertical sensitivity, so damping still matters near resonance. Marks are given for the sign convention, the free body diagram reasoning and the correct units.

Answer: 8.485 rad/s

(b)

The damping ratio compares the damper coefficient with the critical value: ζ = c / (2√(k m)). Here √(k m) = √(18000 × 250) = √4.5×10⁶ = 2121.3 N·s/m, so the critical damping coefficient is cc = 2 × 2121.3 = 4242.6 N·s/m. Then ζ = 1200 / 4242.6 = 0.2828. An equivalent route is ζ = c / (2 m ωn) = 1200 / (2 × 250 × 8.485) which gives the same result. Because ζ is less than 1 the characteristic roots are a complex pair, s = −ζωn ± jωn√(1 − ζ²), so the system is underdamped and the response to a step force will oscillate about the final value before settling.

Answer: 0.2828

(c)

At steady state all derivatives vanish, so the equation of motion reduces to k x = F. The static deflection is x_ss = F / k = 500 / 18000 = 0.02778 m, which is 27.78 mm. This is also the final value of the step response from the Laplace transform: X(s) = F / [s (m s² + c s + k)], and by the final value theorem x_ss = lim s→0 of s X(s) = F / k. Note that neither the mass nor the damper affects the final deflection, only the spring does. The damper influences only how fast and how smoothly the seat reaches this value, which is examined next.

Answer: 27.78 mm

(d)

For an underdamped second order system with a step input the fractional overshoot is Mp = exp(−π ζ / √(1 − ζ²)). Using ζ = 0.2828 we have 1 − ζ² = 0.9200 and √(1 − ζ²) = 0.9592. The exponent is −π × 0.2828 / 0.9592 = -0.9264. Then Mp = exp(-0.9264) = 0.3960, so the overshoot is 39.6 percent of the static deflection. The peak displacement is therefore 38.8 mm against a final value of 27.78 mm. Such a large overshoot would be uncomfortable for the operator, so a designer would raise the damping towards ζ ≈ 0.6 to 0.7. Marks are given for quoting the overshoot formula and substituting ζ correctly.

Answer: 39.6 percent

Problem 2 [A3-002] Electrical and thermal system analogues

A power transistor dissipating 150 W continuously is bolted to a 2.0 kg aluminium block of specific heat 900 J/kg·K. The block is assumed isothermal. It loses heat only by convection to room air held at a constant ambient temperature, with a heat transfer coefficient of 25 W/m²·K acting over an exposed area of 0.060 m². Radiation and conduction through the mounting bolts are neglected. To analyse the warm-up, the thermal system is mapped onto an electrical RC circuit, with temperature difference playing the role of voltage and heat flow rate the role of current. The block starts at ambient temperature when the transistor is switched on at t = 0, and the heat input is a constant step of 150 W.

  1. (a) Determine the thermal resistance of the convective path in K/W. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the thermal capacitance of the block and the thermal time constant of the system in seconds. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the steady-state temperature rise of the block above ambient in K. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the time, in minutes, for the temperature rise to reach 90 percent of its final value. [5]
(a)

In the electrical analogy a resistor relates voltage to current, so the thermal resistance relates temperature difference to heat flow: Q = ΔT / R. For convection Q = h A ΔT, therefore R_th = 1 / (h A). Substituting h = 25 W/m²·K and A = 0.060 m² gives h A = 1.5 W/K. Then R_th = 1 / 1.5 = 0.6667 K/W. This means each watt of heat flowing to the air requires a 0.667 K temperature difference between block and air. Marks are given for stating the analogy clearly, for using Q = h A ΔT as the defining relation and for the correct units, since K/W is the thermal equivalent of ohms.

Answer: 0.6667 K/W

(b)

The thermal capacitance is the heat stored per kelvin, the analogue of electrical capacitance: C_th = m c_p = 2.0 × 900 = 1800 J/K. The energy balance on the block is C dθ/dt = Q_in − θ / R_th, where θ is the block temperature above ambient. This is a first order equation, the same as an RC circuit driven by a current source, with time constant τ = R_th C_th. Substituting, τ = 0.6667 × 1800 = 1200 s, which is 20 minutes. The long time constant shows that the block warms slowly, so a short transistor pulse will not reach the steady temperature.

Answer: 1200 s

(c)

At steady state dθ/dt = 0, so the entire input heat leaves through the convective resistance: Q_in = θ_ss / R_th. Therefore θ_ss = Q_in R_th = 150 × 0.6667 = 100.0 K. This is the same as the final value of the step response of the first order model, θ(t) = Q_in R_th (1 − e−t/τ), and it equals the voltage across a resistor carrying a constant current in the analogy. A rise of 100 K above a typical 25 °C room would put the block near 125 °C, which is within reach of the transistor's junction limit once the junction to case resistance is added, so a designer would check that margin.

Answer: 100 K

(d)

The step response is θ(t) = θ_ss (1 − e−t/τ). Setting θ = 0.9 θ_ss gives 1 − e−t/τ = 0.9, so e−t/τ = 0.1 and t = −τ ln(0.1) = 2.3026 τ. With τ = 1200 s, t = 2.3026 × 1200 = 2763 s, which is 46.05 minutes. As a check, a first order system reaches 63.2 percent at one time constant and about 99 percent at five, so 90 percent at 2.3 time constants is consistent. If a thermal cutout is set at 90 percent of the final rise, the transistor has roughly 46 minutes of operation before it trips.

Answer: 46.05 min

Problem 3 [A3-003] Hydraulic and pneumatic system models

A chemical process tank of constant cross-sectional area 1.2 m² discharges through a fixed orifice at its base, so the outflow follows the turbulent law q = k√h, where h is the liquid level above the orifice in metres and q is in m³/s. A pump supplies a steady inflow of 0.015 m³/s and the level has settled at h0 = 2.5 m. The pump flow is the system input and the level is the output. Because the orifice law is nonlinear, the model must be linearised about this operating point before a transfer function can be written. Fluid properties are constant and the tank walls are vertical. The operator then plans a small increase in the pump flow of 0.0015 m³/s (10 percent of the operating inflow) applied as a step.

  1. (a) Determine the orifice coefficient k from the operating point, in m2.5/s. [4]
  2. (b) Linearise the outflow law about the operating point and determine the hydraulic resistance R = Δh/Δq in s/m². [5]
  3. (c) Write the linearised model as a first order transfer function from inflow to level and determine the time constant in seconds. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the final change in level, in metres, caused by the step increase in pump flow of 0.0015 m³/s. [6]
(a)

At the operating point the system is in steady state, so inflow equals outflow: q0 = 0.015 m³/s. The orifice law gives q0 = k √h0, hence k = q0 / √h0. With h0 = 2.5 m, √h0 = 1.5811 m0.5, so k = 0.015 / 1.5811 = 0.00949 m2.5/s. The units follow from q = k√h, since m³/s divided by m0.5 gives m2.5/s. This coefficient lumps the orifice area, the discharge coefficient and √(2g) together, so it need not be found from the geometry. Marks are given for using the steady-state balance rather than guessing a discharge coefficient.

Answer: 0.009487 m2.5/s

(b)

Expand q = k√h in a Taylor series about h0 and keep the first term: Δq = (dq/dh) Δh = (k / (2√h0)) Δh. The hydraulic resistance is the reciprocal of this slope: R = Δh / Δq = 2√h0 / k. Substituting k = 0.00949 and √h0 = 1.5811 gives R = 2 × 1.5811 / 0.00949 = 333.3 s/m². Using q0 = k√h0 this simplifies to R = 2 h0 / q0 = 2 × 2.5 / 0.015 = 333.3 s/m², a useful check. The resistance is the analogue of an electrical resistor, and it is valid only for small perturbations about h0 because the true law is a square root.

Answer: 333.3 s/m2

(c)

Mass balance on the tank: A dh/dt = q_in − q_out. Writing each variable as operating value plus perturbation and using Δq_out = Δh / R gives A d(Δh)/dt = Δq_in − Δh / R. Multiply by R: A R d(Δh)/dt + Δh = R Δq_in. The Laplace transform gives Δh(s)/Δq_in(s) = R / (τ s + 1), with time constant τ = R A. Substituting, τ = 333.3 × 1.2 = 400 s, which is about 6.7 minutes. The DC gain is R = 333.3 m per m³/s. The slow response is typical of large process tanks and means the level takes roughly 4τ, nearly half an hour, to settle after a disturbance.

Answer: 400 s

(d)

The final value of the first order step response is the DC gain times the step size: Δh_ss = R Δq_in = 333.3 × 0.0015 = 0.500 m. The level therefore rises from 2.5 m to 3.000 m. As a check on the validity of the linear model, solve the nonlinear steady state directly: the new inflow of 0.0165 m³/s requires √h = 0.0165 / 0.00949, so h = 3.025 m, giving a true change of 0.525 m. The linear estimate is within 4.8 percent of this, which confirms that a 10 percent step is small enough for the linearisation. A larger step would show a growing error because the level law is concave.

Answer: 0.5 m

Problem 4 [A3-004] Block diagram reduction

A temperature control loop for an extruder barrel has a unity feedback outer loop. The forward path contains a controller and heater block G1(s) = 20/(s + 1). Following it is a plant section G2(s) = 1/(s + 3) that is itself wrapped in an inner feedback loop through a feedback sensor with constant gain H1 = 2, giving negative feedback from the output of G2 to its input. The output of the inner loop is the barrel temperature deviation C(s). The outer loop feeds C(s) back to the summing junction with unity gain and negative sign, and R(s) is the set-point deviation. All blocks are linear and time invariant, and signals are in consistent units. Reduce the block diagram step by step to find the closed-loop transfer function and its dynamic properties.

  1. (a) Reduce the inner loop G2 with feedback H1 and state the pole of the equivalent block in rad/s. [5]
  2. (b) Combine the blocks and determine the closed-loop DC gain C(0)/R(0) of the whole system. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the undamped natural frequency of the closed-loop system in rad/s. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the damping ratio and the percentage overshoot for a unit step set-point change. [5]
(a)

The inner loop is a negative feedback loop, so its equivalent transfer function is G2 / (1 + G2 H1). With G2 = 1/(s + 3) and H1 = 2 this is [1/(s + 3)] / [1 + 2/(s + 3)]. Multiplying numerator and denominator by (s + 3) gives 1 / (s + 3 + 2) = 1/(s + 5). The inner feedback has moved the pole of the plant section from −3 to −5 rad/s, making this section faster, and its DC gain falls from 1/3 to 1/5. This is the standard effect of proportional (output) feedback around a first order lag. Marks are given for using the negative feedback formula and for simplifying correctly before moving to the outer loop.

Answer: 5 rad/s

(b)

The forward path of the outer loop is G1 times the inner loop equivalent: G(s) = 20 / [(s + 1)(s + 5)]. Since the outer feedback is unity and negative, T(s) = G / (1 + G) = 20 / [(s + 1)(s + 5) + 20]. Expanding (s + 1)(s + 5) = s² + 6s + 5, so the denominator is s² + 6s + 25 and T(s) = 20 / (s² + 6s + 25). The DC gain is found by setting s = 0: T(0) = 20 / 25 = 0.80. The loop therefore reaches only 80 percent of a step set-point in steady state, because the loop is type 0 and has a finite error constant, Kp = G(0) = 4, giving ess = 1/(1 + 4) = 0.2.

Answer: 0.8

(c)

The closed-loop denominator s² + 6s + 25 is compared with the standard second order form s² + 2ζωn s + ωn². Matching the constant term gives ωn² = 25, so ωn = √25 = 5.0 rad/s. This is the frequency at which the closed-loop poles would oscillate if there were no damping, and it fixes the speed of the response. The time to first peak depends on the damped frequency, ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²), which is evaluated using the damping ratio found next. Marks are given for forming the characteristic equation from the reduced diagram without algebra slips.

Answer: 5 rad/s

(d)

Matching the s coefficient, 2ζωn = 6, so ζ = 6 / (2 × 5.0) = 0.60. The system is underdamped. The overshoot of a standard second order system is Mp = exp(−π ζ / √(1 − ζ²)) = exp(−π × 0.60 / 0.80) = exp(-2.356) = 0.0948, or 9.5 percent of the final value. Since the final value is only 0.80, the actual peak output is 0.876. Note that the overshoot percentage applies to the final value, not to the unit step, because the DC gain is below one. The poles are at −3 ± j4, which confirms that ωd = 4 rad/s.

Answer: 9.478

Problem 5 [A3-005] Signal flow and Mason gain

A flexible-arm positioning system is modelled by a signal flow graph with the following branches. The input node R feeds node x1 with gain 1. Node x1 feeds node x2 through gain G1 = 4, and x2 feeds node x3 through G2 = 0.5, and x3 feeds the output node C through G3 = 3. A bypass branch from x1 directly to x3 has gain G4 = 2. Two feedback branches exist: from x2 back to x1 with gain −H1, where H1 = 0.1, and from C back to x3 with gain −H2, where H2 = 0.2. All gains are constants. Use Mason's gain formula to analyse the graph. State clearly which loops touch which forward paths, because the cofactors depend on it. Then examine the effect of changing the bypass gain.

  1. (a) Identify all individual loops, find their gains, and determine the graph determinant Δ. [6]
  2. (b) Determine the overall transfer function C/R using Mason's gain formula. [8]
  3. (c) Determine the bypass gain G4 needed to make the overall gain equal to 8. [6]
(a)

Two feedback branches create two individual loops. Loop L1 runs x1 → x2 → x1 through G1 and the feedback branch: L1 = G1 × (−H1) = 4 × (−0.1) = -0.40. Loop L2 runs x3 → C → x3: L2 = G3 × (−H2) = 3 × (−0.2) = -0.60. The loops share no node (L1 uses x1 and x2, L2 uses x3 and C), so they are non-touching and the product L1 L2 = 0.24 appears in the determinant. Mason's determinant is Δ = 1 − (sum of loop gains) + (sum of products of non-touching pairs) = 1 − (-0.40 + -0.60) + 0.24 = 2.24.

Answer: 2.24

(b)

Mason's formula is T = Σ(Pk Δk) / Δ. Forward path P1 is R → x1 → x2 → x3 → C with gain 1 × G1 × G2 × G3 = 4 × 0.5 × 3 = 6.0. It passes through every node that either loop uses, so both loops touch it and Δ1 = 1. Forward path P2 is R → x1 → x3 → C with gain G4 × G3 = 2 × 3 = 6.0. It passes through x1 (in L1) and x3 and C (in L2), so again both loops touch it and Δ2 = 1. Then T = (P1 + P2) / Δ = (6.0 + 6.0) / 2.24 = 5.357. Marks are given for identifying each path, checking touching loops, and the final division.

Answer: 5.357

(c)

Keep the loops unchanged. Because G4 appears only in the second forward path, the determinant Δ = 2.24 and the cofactors are unaffected: changing G4 does not alter any loop, as the bypass branch does not close a loop. Set T = (P1 + G4 G3) / Δ = 8. Then P1 + 3 G4 = 8 × 2.24 = 17.92. Subtracting P1 = 6.0 leaves 3 G4 = 11.92, so G4 = 3.973. Check: P2 = 3 × 3.973 = 11.92, and (6.0 + 11.92) / 2.24 = 8.00, as required. The bypass gain would almost double from 2 to about 4, which a designer would weigh against the sensitivity of the arm to noise.

Answer: 3.973

A3 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A3-006] First-order system step response

A sheathed thermal flow probe (a heated element inside a thick protective sheath) is used to measure the flow velocity in a ventilation duct. Over the range of interest its dynamics are well described by a first order lag with a static sensitivity of 2.4 V per m/s. To identify the time constant, the sensor is moved from still air into a steady jet of 3.0 m/s, which acts as a step in velocity at t = 0. The sensor output starts at zero volts. A data logger records an output of 4.9 V at exactly 8.0 s after the step. The final output has not yet been reached at that time. Assume the sensor behaves linearly and that the jet velocity is constant. Use the identified model to predict later behaviour and to estimate the time needed for the reading to be accepted.

  1. (a) Determine the final steady-state output and the time constant of the sensor in seconds. [7]
  2. (b) Determine the time for the output to reach 98 percent of its final value. [6]
  3. (c) Predict the sensor output at t = 20 s after the step. [7]
(a)

For a first order lag with static gain K, the response to a step of size u is y(t) = K u (1 − e−t/τ). The final output is y_ss = K u = 2.4 × 3.0 = 7.2 V. At t = 8 s the output is 4.9 V, so 1 − e−8/τ = 4.9 / 7.2 = 0.6806. Rearranging, e−8/τ = 0.3194, and taking natural logs, −8/τ = ln(0.3194) = -1.1412. Hence τ = 8 / 1.1412 = 7.01 s. A time constant of several seconds is realistic for a heated element inside a thick protective sheath, whose thermal mass slows the response. Marks are given for forming the step response first and solving for τ with logarithms.

Answer: 7.01 s

(b)

The 98 percent settling time uses the same step response. Set 1 − e−t/τ = 0.98, so e−t/τ = 0.02 and t = −τ ln(0.02) = 3.912 τ. With τ = 7.01 s the result is t = 3.912 × 7.01 = 27.4 s. This is the usual four time constant settling rule, which gives 3.9τ for a 2 percent band. A candidate who prefers the shortcut of 4τ gets 28.0 s, which is within 2.2 percent and is acceptable, but the exact logarithm is better practice. The long wait of over 27 seconds before a reading can be trusted would be a serious limitation for a control loop using this sensor.

Answer: 27.42 s

(c)

Substituting t = 20 s into the step response with y_ss = 7.2 V and τ = 7.01 s: y(20) = 7.2 (1 − e−20/7.01). The exponent is −20/7.01 = -2.8529, so e−20/τ = 0.0577. Then y(20) = 7.2 × (1 − 0.0577) = 6.785 V. This is 94.2 percent of the final value, so the sensor has nearly but not quite reached steady state. The reading corresponds to an apparent velocity of 2.83 m/s against a true value of 3.0 m/s, an error of 0.17 m/s. That is the dynamic error a user would face if the reading were taken at 20 s.

Answer: 6.785 V

Problem 2 [A3-007] Second-order system time response specs

A rotary stage in a semiconductor handler is driven by a position servo whose closed-loop behaviour is dominated by a pair of complex poles. It can be represented by the standard second order transfer function ωn² / (s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²). The specification for the response to a step command is that the percentage overshoot must not exceed 10 percent and the 2 percent settling time must not exceed 1.5 s. The designer wants the least demanding bandwidth that meets both limits at once. Use the standard approximations for a second order system: the overshoot formula exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) and a 2 percent settling time of 4/(ζωn). Treat the specifications as limits that can be met with equality at the boundary.

  1. (a) Determine the minimum damping ratio that satisfies the overshoot limit. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the minimum undamped natural frequency that satisfies the settling time limit when ζ is at the value found in (a). [5]
  3. (c) Determine the damped natural frequency for this design. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the time to the first peak of the step response. [5]
(a)

The fractional overshoot is Mp = exp(−πζ / √(1 − ζ²)). Setting Mp = 0.10 gives −πζ / √(1 − ζ²) = ln(0.10) = −2.3026. Squaring both sides and rearranging: π² ζ² = 2.3026² (1 − ζ²), so ζ² (π² + 2.3026²) = 2.3026². Hence ζ = 2.3026 / √(π² + 2.3026²) = 2.3026 / √(9.8696 + 5.3019) = 2.3026 / 3.8950 = 0.5912. Because overshoot falls as damping rises, any ζ at or above 0.591 meets the limit. The result is the standard design equation, and marks are given for solving it algebraically rather than by trial and error.

Answer: 0.5912

(b)

The 2 percent settling time is ts = 4 / (ζ ωn), which is 4 divided by the real part σ of the closed-loop poles. For ts ≤ 1.5 s we need σ = ζ ωn ≥ 4 / 1.5 = 2.667 rad/s. With ζ = 0.5912, the minimum natural frequency is ωn = σ / ζ = 2.667 / 0.5912 = 4.511 rad/s. Any higher ωn also meets the limit. The two specifications together define a region of the s-plane to the left of the vertical line at −2.67 and inside a wedge of half-angle cos⁻¹(ζ) = 53.8 degrees from the negative real axis.

Answer: 4.511 rad/s

(c)

The damped natural frequency is the imaginary part of the poles: ωd = ωn √(1 − ζ²). With ωn = 4.511 rad/s and ζ = 0.5912 we have 1 − ζ² = 0.6505 and its square root is 0.8066. Then ωd = 4.511 × 0.8066 = 3.638 rad/s. The poles are therefore at s = −2.667 ± j3.638. The damped oscillation period seen on the step trace is 2π/ωd = 1.73 s. Marks are given for recognising that the poles, not the natural frequency, set the visible ringing. The ratio ωd/ωn equals √(1 − ζ²) = 0.807, so the ringing is about 19 percent slower than the undamped natural frequency would suggest.

Answer: 3.638 rad/s

(d)

The peak time is half the damped period: tp = π / ωd. Using ωd = 3.638 rad/s, tp = π / 3.638 = 0.8635 s. The peak occurs at 0.86 s, well before the settling time of 1.5 s, and its value is 1.10 times the final value by design. This result matters in practice because a stage that reaches its first peak in under a second may excite structural resonances in the handler frame. The designer should compare the closed-loop bandwidth implied by ωn = 4.51 rad/s with the lowest frame mode. If that mode is below about three times ωn, the specification may need relaxing.

Answer: 0.8635 s

Problem 3 [A3-008] Steady-state error and system type

A unity feedback positioning loop for a CNC table has open-loop transfer function G(s) = K (s + 4) / [s (s + 2)(s + 10)], where K is an adjustable amplifier gain. The loop must track a ramp command of constant slope 2 rad/s (for example a constant speed cut) with a steady-state error not exceeding 0.05 rad. The command generator may also supply ramp rates up to 5 rad/s in other operating modes. Use the final value theorem with the error constants of the appropriate system type. Identify the type of the system first. After finding the gain, you must confirm that the closed loop is stable at that gain, since steady-state formulas are meaningless for an unstable loop.

  1. (a) Identify the system type and determine the velocity error constant Kv required for the 2 rad/s ramp. [6]
  2. (b) Determine the minimum amplifier gain K. [6]
  3. (c) With the gain from (b), determine the steady-state error for a ramp of 5 rad/s. [4]
  4. (d) Check the stability of the closed loop at the gain from (b) by forming the Routh array, and report the first-column entry of the s¹ row. [4]
(a)

The open-loop transfer function has one pole at the origin, so the system is type 1. A type 1 system follows a step with zero error and a ramp with a constant finite error ess = R / Kv, where R is the ramp slope and Kv = lim s→0 of s G(s). For R = 2 rad/s and ess ≤ 0.05 rad, we require Kv ≥ R / ess = 2 / 0.05 = 40 s⁻¹. Evaluating Kv in terms of K: Kv = lim s→0 K (s + 4) / [(s + 2)(s + 10)] = K × 4 / 20 = K / 5. So the specification sets a minimum of 40 on K/5. Marks are given for identifying the type correctly and for using the limit properly.

Answer: 40

(b)

From Kv = K / 5 and the requirement Kv ≥ 40, the minimum gain is K = 5 Kv = 5 × 40 = 200. At this gain the velocity error constant is exactly 40 s⁻¹ and the steady-state ramp error is exactly 0.05 rad. Any larger K reduces the error further, but a higher gain also moves the closed-loop poles towards less damped positions. The step error is zero for all K, since the system is type 1. The result is therefore a lower bound on the gain, and the upper bound comes from stability and transient considerations.

Answer: 200

(c)

With K = 200, the velocity error constant is Kv = 40 s⁻¹ as before. For the faster ramp of slope R = 5 rad/s the steady-state error is ess = R / Kv = 5 / 40 = 0.125 rad. This is 2.5 times the error at 2 rad/s, because for a type 1 system the error is directly proportional to the ramp slope. The 0.05 rad limit is therefore exceeded in the fast mode, so either the gain must be raised to K = 500 for that mode, or the specification applies only at 2 rad/s. The designer should state this assumption.

Answer: 0.125 rad

(d)

The characteristic equation is 1 + G(s) = 0, that is s (s + 2)(s + 10) + K (s + 4) = 0. Expanding s (s² + 12 s + 20) = s³ + 12 s² + 20 s, and adding 200 s + 800 gives s³ + 12 s² + 220 s + 800 = 0. The Routh array has first column entries: s³: 1; s²: 12; s¹: (12 × 220 − 1 × 800) / 12 = 153.3; s⁰: 800. There are no sign changes in the first column, since all entries are positive, so the closed loop is stable. Marks are given for forming the array correctly and stating the conclusion.

Answer: 153.3

Problem 4 [A3-009] Routh-Hurwitz stability

The characteristic equation of a hydraulic excavator boom position loop is obtained from the unity feedback open-loop transfer function G(s) = K / [s (s + 2)(s + 4)(s + 6)], where K is a positive proportional gain set by the valve amplifier. The designer wants the largest gain for which the boom stays stable, the frequency at which it would oscillate steadily at that gain, and the consequence of setting the gain 25 percent above the limit. Use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion on the characteristic polynomial. No numerical root finding is permitted in parts (a) and (b), but part (c) may be checked numerically. State the Routh array and show the row in which the gain limit appears.

  1. (a) Form the Routh array for the characteristic equation and determine the maximum stable gain K. [7]
  2. (b) Determine the frequency of the sustained oscillation at the limiting gain. [6]
  3. (c) The gain is set 25 percent above the limiting value. Determine the number of closed-loop poles in the right half plane. [7]
(a)

The characteristic equation is 1 + G(s) = 0, giving s (s + 2)(s + 4)(s + 6) + K = 0. Expanding (s + 2)(s + 4)(s + 6) = s³ + 12 s² + 44 s + 48, so the polynomial is s⁴ + 12 s³ + 44 s² + 48 s + K = 0. Routh array: s⁴: 1, 44, K; s³: 12, 48; s²: (12 × 44 − 48) / 12 = 40 and K; s¹: (40 × 48 − 12 K) / 40; s⁰: K. For stability every first-column entry must be positive, so 40 × 48 − 12 K > 0, which gives K < 160. Also K > 0 from the last row. The maximum stable gain is therefore K = 160.

Answer: 160

(b)

At K = 160 the entire s¹ row is zero, which signals a pair of poles on the imaginary axis. They are found from the auxiliary polynomial formed from the row above, s²: 40 s² + K = 0. Substituting K = 160 gives 40 s² + 160 = 0, so s² = −160 / 40 = −4.0, and s = ± j 2.00. The boom would therefore oscillate steadily at ω = 2.00 rad/s, a period of 3.14 s. A check: the remaining factor from dividing the polynomial by the auxiliary factor (s² + 4) is s² + 12 s + 40, whose roots are in the left half plane.

Answer: 2 rad/s

(c)

The new gain is K = 1.25 × 160 = 200. Recompute the s¹ entry of the Routh array: (40 × 48 − 12 × 200) / 40 = (1920 − 2400) / 40 = -12.0, which is negative. The first column is then 1, 12, 40, -12.0, 200. Counting sign changes: from 40 to -12.0 is one change, and from -12.0 to 200 is a second change. Two sign changes mean two poles in the right half plane. A numerical check of the roots of the polynomial confirms a pair of unstable complex poles near +0.12 ± j2.17, so the oscillation grows slowly. The answer is 2 unstable poles.

Answer: 2

Problem 5 [A3-010] Root locus

A hydraulic positioning servo for a press ram has open-loop transfer function G(s) = K / [s (s + 4)(s + 8)] with unity negative feedback and a variable valve gain K greater than zero. The designer wants to use the root locus method to understand how the closed-loop poles move as K increases from zero. Poles of the open-loop system are at 0, −4 and −8 and there are no finite zeros. Sketch the locus mentally using the standard construction rules: asymptotes, real-axis segments, breakaway points and imaginary-axis crossings. Then use the results to judge how much gain can be applied before the ram becomes unstable. All gains and frequencies are in consistent units, and the motion is small enough for linear analysis.

  1. (a) Determine the centroid of the asymptotes (in s-plane units) and the angles of the three asymptotes. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the breakaway point on the real axis. [6]
  3. (c) Determine the gain K at which the locus crosses the imaginary axis. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the frequency at which the locus crosses the imaginary axis. [5]
(a)

With n = 3 poles and m = 0 zeros there are n − m = 3 asymptotes. The centroid is σA = (sum of poles − sum of zeros) / (n − m) = (0 − 4 − 8 − 0) / 3 = -4.0. The asymptote angles are θ = (2k + 1) × 180° / (n − m) for k = 0, 1, 2, giving 60°, 180° and 300° (that is, −60°). Therefore the locus branches that leave the real axis head off along lines at ±60° from the centroid at −4, while a third branch goes along the negative real axis. The real axis segments lie between 0 and −4 and to the left of −8, where an odd number of poles lies to the right.

Answer: -4

(b)

Breakaway points satisfy dK/ds = 0 where K = −s (s + 4)(s + 8) = −(s³ + 12 s² + 32 s). Differentiating gives 3 s² + 24 s + 32 = 0. Solving by the quadratic formula: s = [−24 ± √(576 − 384)] / 6 = [−24 ± √192] / 6 = [−24 ± 13.856] / 6. The two roots are s = -1.6906 and s = -6.3094. Only the root at s = -1.691 lies on a valid locus segment, between the poles at 0 and −4; the other root lies between −4 and −8, where there is no locus. So the breakaway point is -1.691, and at it the gain is K = 24.6.

Answer: -1.691

(c)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is s³ + 12 s² + 32 s + K = 0. The Routh array is: s³: 1, 32; s²: 12, K; s¹: (12 × 32 − K) / 12; s⁰: K. The system is on the verge of instability when the s¹ entry is zero, so 12 × 32 − K = 0 and K = 384. For K above this value the first column changes sign, so two poles enter the right half plane. A ram gain above 384 is therefore unusable. A practical design would keep the gain well below this, typically at no more than about half, to preserve gain margin and damping.

Answer: 384

(d)

At the crossing gain, K = 384, the auxiliary equation from the s² row is 12 s² + K = 0, that is 12 s² + 384 = 0. Then s² = −384 / 12 = −32, so s = ± j 5.657. The crossing frequency is ω = 5.657 rad/s. This equals √32, which is also the value at which the phase of the open-loop G(jω) is −180°: the phase is −90° − tan⁻¹(ω/4) − tan⁻¹(ω/8) = −90° − 54.7° − 35.3° = −180°. The check agrees, and at this frequency the magnitude of G is 1 when K = 384, confirming the crossing.

Answer: 5.657 rad/s

A3 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A3-011] Bode plot construction

A hydraulic valve positioner in a press brake has the open-loop transfer function G(s) = 8000(s + 5) / [s(s + 40)(s + 400)], with s in rad/s. A technician must prepare the Bode plot of G(jω) on semi-log paper before commissioning. She will first draw the straight-line asymptotic magnitude plot, taking the corner frequencies from the factors of G(s), and then check selected points against the exact frequency response. All frequencies are in rad/s and magnitudes in decibels (20 log10 of the amplitude ratio). The loop contains no delay, and all poles and zeros are as given. Use the exact complex expression for G(jω) whenever the word exact is used in a part.

  1. (a) The low-frequency asymptote of the magnitude plot has slope -20 dB/decade. State its value in dB at ω = 1 rad/s (asymptote only). [4]
  2. (b) Find the exact magnitude of G(j100) in dB. [5]
  3. (c) Find the exact phase angle of G(j100) in degrees. [5]
  4. (d) Find the exact gain crossover frequency, where |G(jω)| = 1 (0 dB). [6]
(a)

For ω well below the first corner at 5 rad/s the factors reduce to G(jω) ≈ K z / (p1 p2 jω) = Kv/(jω), where Kv = 8000 × 5 / (40 × 400) = 2.5 s-1. The magnitude is therefore Kv/ω, a straight line falling at 20 dB per decade. At ω = 1 rad/s the asymptote is 20 log10(2.5/1) = 7.96 dB. This point lies below the first corner (the zero at 5 rad/s), so the asymptote is valid there and the line can be drawn through this point with slope -20 dB/decade up to 5 rad/s. At 5 rad/s the zero turns the slope to 0 dB/decade, at 40 rad/s the first pole returns it to -20, and at 400 rad/s the second pole makes it -40 dB/decade. Marks are given for the correct Kv, the dB conversion and the slope statement.

Answer: 7.96 dB

(b)

Substitute s = j100 into each factor. The numerator is 8000(j100 + 5), magnitude 8000 × √(100² + 5²) = 8000 × 100.125 = 8.010 × 105. The denominator factors have magnitudes 100 for s, √(40² + 100²) = 107.70 for (s + 40) and √(400² + 100²) = 412.31 for (s + 400). The product is 100 × 107.70 × 412.31 = 4.441 × 106. The exact amplitude ratio is |G(j100)| = 8.010 × 105 / 4.441 × 106 = 0.1804. Converting, 20 log10(0.1804) = -14.88 dB. Comparison with the asymptotic value at 100 rad/s, which lies between the 40 and 400 corners where the slope is -20 dB/decade, shows how much the straight-line approximation deviates between corners. The exact value is the one to plot as a check point.

Answer: -14.9 dB

(c)

Phase is the sum of the angles of the numerator factors minus the angles of the denominator factors. The factor s contributes +90° in the denominator, so -90°. The zero (s + 5) contributes +atan(100/5) = +87.14°. The pole (s + 40) contributes -atan(100/40) = -68.20°. The pole (s + 400) contributes -atan(100/400) = -14.04°. The total is -90 + 87.14 - 68.20 - 14.04 = -85.10°. A phase of about -85° at 100 rad/s is plausible because the zero's lead almost cancels the integrator's lag, leaving the two high-frequency poles to pull the phase to just above the -90° of a pure integrator. This number would be plotted on the lower semi-log axis and compared with the straight-line phase approximation, which would give roughly -90° at this frequency.

Answer: -85.1 deg

(d)

Set |G(jω)| = 1 with the exact magnitude expression 8000√(ω² + 25) / [ω √(ω² + 1600) √(ω² + 160000)] = 1. For ω much less than 40 the two pole factors are close to 40 and 400, so the expression reduces to 0.5 √(ω² + 25) / ω = 1, that is 0.25(ω² + 25) = ω², giving ω² = 25/3 and ω = 2.89 rad/s as a first estimate. Refining with the exact pole factors (they raise the denominator slightly) moves the root slightly, and a numerical root find of the full expression gives ω = 2.877 rad/s. At this frequency the asymptotic plot, which crosses 0 dB on the -20 dB/decade segment, gives a close but not identical value of 2.5 rad/s, so the exact result should be the one reported. Marks are given for the setup, the simplification and the final value.

Answer: 2.88 rad/s

Problem 2 [A3-012] Gain and phase margins
