Because ω = 0.5 rad/s lies below the first corner, only the integrator and gain contribute. So |G| = 20 log10(K/ω) = 20 log10(10/0.5) = 20 log10(20) = 26.02 dB. Equivalently the asymptote crosses 0 dB at ω = K = 10 if it were extended, but the real crossover is pulled lower by the corner at 2 rad/s. Check: at ω = 1 the asymptote would read 20 dB, and moving down one octave adds 6.02 dB, giving the same result.

Answer: 26.02 dB

(b)

At gain crossover |G(jω)| = 1. For G = K / [ jω (1 + jω/2)(1 + jω/20) ] the magnitude is |G| = K / [ ω √(1 + (ω/2)²) √(1 + (ω/20)²) ]. Setting this equal to 1 gives K = ω √(1 + (ω/2)²) √(1 + (ω/20)²). Substitute ω = 5 rad/s: (ω/2)² = 6.25, so √(1 + 6.25) = 2.6926. Next (ω/20)² = 0.0625, so √(1.0625) = 1.0308. Then K = 5 × 2.6926 × 1.0308 = 13.877 s-1. Note this is larger than the K = 10 of part (a) at the asymptotic estimate, because the asymptotic slope changes from -20 to -40 dB/decade at 2 rad/s, so a larger gain is needed to keep the curve above 0 dB out to 5 rad/s. The exact result is the one used in design.

Answer: 13.877 s-1

(c)

The phase of G(jω) is the sum of the phase of each factor. The integrator contributes a constant -90 degrees. Each factor (1 + jω/p) in the denominator contributes -atan(ω/p). At ω = 5 rad/s: atan(5/2) = atan(2.5) = 68.20 degrees, and atan(5/20) = atan(0.25) = 14.04 degrees. The gain K is real and positive and adds no phase. So the total is φ = -90 - 68.20 - 14.04 = -172.23 degrees. The phase margin at this crossover would be 180 + φ = 7.8 degrees, which is far too small for a well damped servo, showing that choosing the crossover at 5 rad/s with this plant leaves the loop nearly unstable and a lower gain or a compensator is required.

Answer: -172.23 degrees

(d)

Phase margin 45 degrees requires φ(ωc) = -135 degrees, so atan(ω/2) + atan(ω/20) = 45 degrees. Take the tangent of both sides: (ω/2 + ω/20) / (1 - ω²/40) = 1. Then 0.55 ω = 1 - ω²/40, which rearranges to ω² + 22 ω - 40 = 0. The positive root is ω = (-22 + √(484 + 160))/2 = (-22 + 25.377)/2 = 1.689 rad/s. This is the required gain crossover frequency. Now set |G(jωc)| = 1: K = ω √(1 + (ω/2)²) √(1 + (ω/20)²) = 1.689 × 1.3086 × 1.0036 = 2.218 s-1. This gain is much smaller than the 13.9 s-1 from part (b), the usual trade-off: a good phase margin costs bandwidth and velocity-error constant, since Kv equals K for this type 1 system.

Answer: 2.218 s-1

Problem 2 [A3-032] Gain and phase margins

A hydraulic positioning table has the open-loop transfer function G(s) = K / [ s (s + 3)(s + 6) ] with unity negative feedback, where K is an adjustable amplifier gain in units that make G dimensionless and the frequencies are in rad/s. The commissioning engineer must set K so that the loop meets stability margin requirements. Use exact frequency-response expressions rather than Bode asymptotes. Determine the frequency at which the phase of the open loop is -180 degrees, find the gain that gives a phase margin of 45 degrees, report the corresponding gain margin in decibels, and then find the gain that provides a 10 dB gain margin. State the numerical results and show how each follows from the magnitude and phase conditions. Assume the plant is linear and the hydraulic fluid is incompressible so no extra dynamics apply.

  1. (a) Find the phase crossover frequency, where the phase of G(jω) equals -180 degrees. [5]
  2. (b) Find the value of K that gives a phase margin of 45 degrees. [7]
  3. (c) Find the gain margin in dB at the gain from part (b). [4]
  4. (d) Find the gain K that gives a gain margin of exactly 10 dB. [4]
(a)

The phase of G(jω) is -90 - atan(ω/3) - atan(ω/6) degrees. Set this equal to -180: atan(ω/3) + atan(ω/6) = 90 degrees. Two angles that sum to 90 degrees have tangents whose product is 1, so (ω/3)(ω/6) = 1, giving ω² = 18 and ω180 = √18 = 4.243 rad/s. An alternative route is the characteristic equation s³ + 9s² + 18s + K = 0; substituting s = jω, the imaginary part gives -ω³ + 18ω = 0, so ω² = 18 again, which confirms the answer. At this frequency the real part gives K = 9ω² = 162, the largest gain for stability, used in the later parts.

Answer: 4.243 rad/s

(b)

A phase margin of 45 degrees means the phase at gain crossover is -135 degrees: 90 + atan(ω/3) + atan(ω/6) = 135, so atan(ω/3) + atan(ω/6) = 45 degrees. Taking the tangent gives (ω/3 + ω/6)/(1 - ω²/18) = 1, so ω/2 = 1 - ω²/18, or ω² + 9ω - 18 = 0. The positive root is ω = (-9 + √153)/2 = 1.685 rad/s. At gain crossover |G| = 1, so K = ω √(ω² + 9) √(ω² + 36). Evaluating: √(2.838 + 9) = 3.441 and √(2.838 + 36) = 6.232. Hence K = 1.685 × 3.441 × 6.232 = 36.12. The result is far below the critical value of 162 found in part (a), reflecting that a 45 degree margin requires a low crossover.

Answer: 36.12

(c)

The gain margin is the factor by which the gain can be raised before the closed loop becomes unstable. From part (a) the stability limit is K = 162, since at ω180 = 4.243 rad/s the magnitude is K/162. At the gain found in part (b) the gain margin ratio is 162/K = 162/36.12. In decibels, GM = 20 log10(162/K) = 20 log10(162/36.12) = 13.03 dB. This is a comfortable margin, above the usual 6 dB minimum, and agrees with the expected ability of a loop with 45 degrees of phase margin and a modest crossover to tolerate a gain increase of about 4.5 times. The positive margin confirms the closed loop is stable at this setting.

Answer: 13.03 dB

(d)

A gain margin of 10 dB means the ratio of the critical gain to the actual gain is 1010/20 = 3.162. The critical gain is the value at which the loop magnitude equals 1 at the phase crossover frequency, which from part (a) is 162. So K = 162 / 3.162 = 51.23. Check by evaluating the magnitude at ω180 = 4.243 rad/s: |G| = K / (ω √(ω² + 9) √(ω² + 36)) = 51.23 / (4.243 × 5.196 × 7.348) = 51.23/162 = 0.316, which is -10 dB. This gain is higher than the K for a 45 degree margin from part (b), so this setting has a better bandwidth but a smaller phase margin, and the engineer must check the phase margin at this gain before accepting it.

Answer: 51.23

Problem 3 [A3-033] Nyquist stability

A thermally unstable chemical reactor has the open-loop transfer function G(s) H(s) = K (s + 3) / [ (s - 1)(s + 5) ] when the temperature loop is closed with unity feedback, where K > 0 is the controller gain. The open-loop transfer function has one pole in the right half plane because of the exothermic reaction. The process engineer will use the Nyquist criterion to decide the range of gain that stabilizes the reactor and then pick a gain that leaves a reasonable reduction margin, meaning the factor by which the gain can fall before the loop becomes unstable. Frequencies are in rad/s. Assume the Nyquist contour passes along the imaginary axis with large semicircles in the right half plane, and that there are no poles on the imaginary axis.

  1. (a) Use the point where the Nyquist plot crosses the negative real axis to find the minimum gain for stability. [6]
  2. (b) Find K so that the gain can be reduced by a factor of 2 (6 dB) before instability. [6]
  3. (c) For this K, find the dominant closed-loop pole location (the root nearer the imaginary axis). [5]
  4. (d) Explain how many encirclements of -1 the Nyquist plot must make for this open-loop transfer function and in which direction, and why a pole in the right half plane changes the usual criterion. [3]
(a)

Closed-loop stability needs N = -P, that is one counter-clockwise encirclement of -1, since P = 1. Write G(jω) = K(3 + jω)/[(jω - 1)(jω + 5)]. The denominator expands to (jω - 1)(jω + 5) = -ω² - 5 + 4jω. Multiplying numerator and conjugate gives the imaginary part -Kω(ω² + 17), which is zero only at ω = 0 (and ω → ∞). So the plot meets the real axis at ω = 0, where G(0) = K × 3/(-5) = -0.6K. The curve starts at -0.6K, and encircles -1 counter-clockwise only if -0.6K < -1, so K > 1/0.6 = 1.6667. Check with the characteristic equation s² + (4 + K)s + (3K - 5): both coefficients are positive when K > 5/3, confirming the result.

Answer: 1.6667

(b)

The stability limit found in part (a) is K = 5/3. A reduction margin of 6 dB means the gain can fall by a factor 106/20 = 1.995 before reaching that limit. So the design gain is K = (5/3) × 1.995 = 3.3254. On the Nyquist plot this puts the crossing of the negative real axis at -0.6K = -1.995, so the curve passes about twice as far from the origin as the critical point -1, leaving the single counter-clockwise encirclement intact. If the gain fell by more than a factor of 2 the crossing would move inside the -1 point and the encirclement would be lost, giving an unstable closed loop with one right half plane pole. Therefore this gain keeps a safe 6 dB cushion.

Answer: 3.3254

(c)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is (s - 1)(s + 5) + K(s + 3) = 0, which expands to s² + (4 + K)s + (3K - 5) = 0. With K = 3.3254 the coefficients are 4 + K = 7.3254 and 3K - 5 = 4.9762. The roots follow from the quadratic formula: s = [-7.3254 ± √(7.3254² - 4 × 4.9762)]/2 = [-7.3254 ± √(53.662 - 19.905)]/2 = [-7.3254 ± 5.810]/2. This gives s1 = -0.7577 and s2 = -6.568. Both roots are real and in the left half plane, confirming stability. The dominant pole at -0.7577 gives a time constant of about 1.3 s, which sets the speed of the temperature recovery.

Answer: -0.7577 s-1

(d)

The Nyquist criterion states Z = N + P, where Z is the number of closed-loop poles in the right half plane, P is the number of open-loop poles in the right half plane, and N is the number of clockwise encirclements of -1. Here P = 1, and stability needs Z = 0, so N must equal -1: the plot must encircle -1 once in the counter-clockwise direction. For an open-loop stable plant (P = 0), no encirclement is needed. The unstable pole at s = 1 means the loop must itself supply stabilization, so the plot must wrap around the critical point. This is why this system becomes stable only for K above 5/3 and why reducing the gain too far destroys stability, the opposite of the usual behaviour for a stable plant.

Answer: See working

Problem 4 [A3-034] PID tuning

A gas-fired oven zone is modelled around its operating point by the plant G(s) = 1 / [ (s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 4) ] relating burner valve position to zone temperature, with time in seconds. The commissioning engineer cannot use an open-loop step test because the oven must stay in production, so a closed-loop ultimate-gain experiment is used: the controller is set to proportional action only and the gain is increased until the loop output sustains a steady oscillation. Assuming unity feedback and no sensor lag, determine the ultimate gain and period from the model, and then calculate the PID settings using the Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop rules (Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Pu/2, Td = Pu/8). The controller is in the parallel form u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt, with Ki = Kp/Ti and Kd = Kp Td.

  1. (a) Find the ultimate gain Ku at which the proportional loop is marginally stable. [6]
  2. (b) Find the ultimate period Pu of the sustained oscillation. [4]
  3. (c) Find the integral gain Ki from the Ziegler-Nichols PID rules. [5]
  4. (d) Find the derivative gain Kd from the Ziegler-Nichols PID rules. [5]
(a)

With proportional gain K and unity feedback the characteristic equation is (s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 4) + K = 0. Expanding the product gives s³ + 7s² + 14s + 8 + K = 0. Apply the Routh array. The first column entries are 1, 7, (7 × 14 - (8 + K))/7 and 8 + K. Marginal stability occurs when the third entry is zero: 98 - 8 - K = 0, so K = 90. Check with s = jω: the real part gives -7ω² + 8 + K = 0 and the imaginary part gives -ω³ + 14ω = 0, so ω² = 14 and K = 7 × 14 - 8 = 90.0. The ultimate gain is therefore Ku = 90.0. Any gain above this makes the oven temperature oscillate with growing amplitude.

Answer: 90.0

(b)

At the ultimate gain the closed-loop poles lie on the imaginary axis at s = ±jωu. From the imaginary part of the characteristic equation, ωu³ = 14 ωu, so ωu = √14 = 3.742 rad/s. The oscillation period is the time for one cycle, Pu = 2π/ωu. Substituting: Pu = 6.2832/3.742 = 1.679 s. This is the number a technician would measure on a chart recorder when the loop is at the edge of instability. It is comparable to the slowest time constant of 1 s, since the three lags give 180 degrees at 3.74 rad/s. This period is used to set the integral and derivative times in the next parts.

Answer: 1.679 s

(c)

The Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop rules for a PID controller are Kp = 0.6 Ku, Ti = Pu/2 and Td = Pu/8. First, Kp = 0.6 × 90 = 54. Next, Ti = Pu/2 = 1.679/2 = 0.8396 s. The integral gain in parallel form is Ki = Kp/Ti = 54/0.8396 = 64.31 s-1. Interpretation: the integral action removes steady-state offset, and a Ti close to 0.84 s means the integral term accumulates error over about one second, which is of the same order as the plant dynamics. Ziegler-Nichols settings are known to give a quarter-amplitude decay response with considerable overshoot, so the engineer should expect an overshoot of about 40 to 50 percent and may detune afterwards.

Answer: 64.31 s-1

(d)

The derivative time is Td = Pu/8 = 1.679/8 = 0.2099 s. The parallel-form derivative gain is Kd = Kp Td, with Kp = 0.6 × 90 = 54 from the rules. So Kd = 54 × 0.2099 = 11.33. The derivative term adds phase lead of roughly atan(ω Td) at frequency ω, which at the ultimate frequency of 3.74 rad/s is atan(0.785) = 38 degrees, enough to recover a useful phase margin. In practice a derivative filter with a time constant of about Td/10 would be added so that sensor noise on the temperature signal is not amplified. The final controller is Kp = 54, Ki = 64.31 s-1 and Kd = 11.33 s.

Answer: 11.33 s

Problem 5 [A3-035] Lead and lag compensator design

A magnetic-bearing platform for a precision lathe is modelled with the open-loop transfer function G(s) = K / [ s (s + 2) ] with unity negative feedback. Specifications are a velocity error constant Kv = 20 s-1 and a phase margin of at least 45 degrees. The designer chooses the gain K to meet the Kv requirement and then adds a phase-lead compensator Gc(s) = (1 + Ts)/(1 + αTs) with 0 < α < 1 and unity DC gain, so that Kv is preserved. Add 5 degrees of extra lead to allow for the crossover shifting. Place the maximum lead frequency at the new gain crossover, which is where the uncompensated gain magnitude equals √α, since the lead network raises the gain by 1/√α at its centre frequency. Report all numerical results.

  1. (a) Find the gain K required to meet the velocity error constant. [4]
  2. (b) Find the phase margin of the uncompensated loop with that K. [5]
  3. (c) Find the lead ratio α needed. [5]
  4. (d) Find the zero frequency 1/T of the lead compensator. [6]
(a)

For a type 1 system, Kv = lim s→0 of s G(s) Gc(0). With the lead network having unity DC gain, Kv = lim s→0 of s × K/[s(s + 2)] = K/2. Setting Kv = 20 s-1 gives K = 2 × 20 = 40.0 s-1. This gain must be kept after compensation, because any reduction in low-frequency gain would reduce the steady-state accuracy for a ramp input. The compensator must therefore add phase near crossover without altering the DC gain. The loop transfer function for the design is G(s) = 40/[s(s + 2)], whose magnitude and phase at the crossover frequency are needed for the next two parts.

Answer: 40.0 s-1

(b)

Gain crossover requires |G(jω)| = 40 / [ω √(ω² + 4)] = 1, so ω²(ω² + 4) = 1600 and ω⁴ + 4ω² - 1600 = 0. The positive root for ω² is (-4 + √(16 + 6400))/2 = (-4 + 80.1)/2 = 38.05, so ωc = 6.168 rad/s. The phase of G(jω) is -90 - atan(ω/2) degrees. At ωc: atan(6.168/2) = atan(3.084) = 72.0 degrees, so the phase is -162.0 degrees. The phase margin is 180 - 162.0 = 17.96 degrees. This is much less than the required 45 degrees, so the compensator must supply the shortfall plus the 5 degree allowance for crossover shift.

Answer: 17.96 degrees

(c)

The maximum phase lead required is φm = 45 - 17.96 + 5 = 32.0 degrees (approximately, using the unrounded phase margin). A lead network (1 + Ts)/(1 + αTs) delivers a maximum phase of φm at its centre frequency ωm = 1/(T√α), and φm is related to α by sin φm = (1 - α)/(1 + α). Solving for α: α = (1 - sin φm)/(1 + sin φm). With sin(32.0°) = 0.5299, α = (1 - 0.5299)/(1 + 0.5299) = 0.4701/1.5299 = 0.3068. A smaller α would supply more lead but would raise the high-frequency gain by 1/α, increasing noise sensitivity. At this α the gain at high frequency rises by a factor of about 3.3, an acceptable penalty for this platform.

Answer: 0.3068

(d)

The lead network raises the gain by 1/√α at the centre frequency ωm, so the new crossover must be where the uncompensated gain is √α. With α = 0.3068, √α = 0.5539, so the uncompensated loop must satisfy 40/(ω√(ω² + 4)) = 0.5539, giving ω√(ω² + 4) = 72.21 and ω⁴ + 4ω² - 5215 = 0. Then ω² = (-4 + √20876)/2 = 70.25 and ωm = 8.381 rad/s. The pole and zero are placed so that ωm = 1/(T√α), hence 1/T = ωm √α = 8.381 × 0.5539 = 4.642 rad/s. The zero is at 4.642 rad/s and the pole at 1/(αT) = 4.642/0.3068 = 15.1 rad/s, straddling the new crossover as intended. The designer should confirm the final phase margin of at least 45 degrees by direct evaluation.

Answer: 4.642 rad/s

A3 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A3-036] State-space models

A vibration isolation table of mass m = 2 kg rests on a spring of stiffness k = 50 N/m and a damper of coefficient c = 6 N·s/m. A voice-coil actuator applies a force u (in N) to the table. Choose the state vector x = [position y, velocity v] and treat y as the output. The engineer wants to use full state feedback u = r - k1 y - k2 v, where r is an external force command, to give a closed-loop damping ratio of 0.7 and a natural frequency of 8 rad/s. Write the plant in state-space form, determine its open-loop damping ratio, calculate the feedback gains k1 and k2 by comparing characteristic polynomials, and find the static displacement under a constant 10 N command r with the feedback in place. Assume the actuator is ideal and the table moves only vertically.

  1. (a) Write the state equations and find the open-loop damping ratio. [4]
  2. (b) Find the position feedback gain k1. [5]
  3. (c) Find the velocity feedback gain k2. [5]
  4. (d) Find the steady-state displacement of the table for a constant command r = 10 N. [6]
(a)

Newton's second law gives m y'' = u - c y' - k y. With x1 = y and x2 = v this becomes x1' = x2 and x2' = -(k/m) x1 - (c/m) x2 + u/m. In matrix form A = [[0, 1], [-25, -3]], B = [0, 0.5]T, C = [1, 0]. The characteristic polynomial is det(sI - A) = s² + 3s + 25, so ωn = √25 = 5 rad/s and 2ζωn = 3. The damping ratio is ζ = 3/(2 × 5) = 0.300, equal to c/(2√(km)) = 6/(2√100) = 0.3. The open-loop poles are s = -1.5 ± j4.77, a lightly damped pair, so the table rings for several cycles after a disturbance. This explains why feedback is needed.

Answer: 0.300

(b)

With u = r - k1 x1 - k2 x2 the closed-loop state matrix is A - B K, where K = [k1, k2]. The second row becomes x2' = -(k + k1)/m x1 - (c + k2)/m x2 + r/m, so the characteristic polynomial is s² + ((c + k2)/m) s + (k + k1)/m. The target polynomial for ζ = 0.7 and ωn = 8 rad/s is s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² = s² + 11.2 s + 64. Matching the constant terms, (50 + k1)/2 = 64, so 50 + k1 = 128 and k1 = 78.0 N/m. This acts like an extra spring of 78 N/m added to the existing 50 N/m, stiffening the table to a total of 128 N/m. The raised stiffness is what lifts the natural frequency from 5 to 8 rad/s.

Answer: 78.0 N/m

(c)

Matching the coefficients of s in the characteristic polynomial s² + ((c + k2)/m) s + (k + k1)/m with the target s² + 11.2 s + 64 gives (6 + k2)/2 = 11.2. So 6 + k2 = 22.4 and k2 = 16.4 N·s/m. This is extra damping supplied by the actuator by pushing against the table velocity, increasing the total damping from 6 to 22.4 N·s/m. Check the damping ratio: ζ = 22.4/(2√(128 × 2)) = 22.4/(2 × 16) = 0.7, as specified. Feedback of velocity needs a velocity measurement or a state estimator, which in practice would be a differentiated and filtered position signal or an accelerometer integrated once.

Answer: 16.4 N·s/m

(d)

At steady state all derivatives are zero. The closed-loop equation reads (k + k1) y = r, so y = r/(k + k1) = 10/(50 + 78) = 10/128 = 0.0781 m. The same result follows from the transfer function Y(s)/R(s) = (1/m)/(s² + 11.2 s + 64) evaluated at s = 0, which gives (0.5/64) × 10 = 0.0781 m. Without feedback the displacement would have been 10/50 = 0.2 m, so the feedback has reduced the static deflection by a factor of 2.56. Note that this is a static stiffness effect of the position gain, not a regulation: the displacement does not return to zero, so if exact positioning were needed a reference prefilter or integral action would be added.

Answer: 0.0781 m

Problem 2 [A3-037] Servo motor position control

A pan axis on a camera crane uses an armature-controlled DC motor with torque constant Kt = 0.05 N·m/A, back-emf constant Ke = 0.05 V·s/rad, armature resistance Ra = 1.0 Ω and negligible inductance. The total inertia seen by the shaft is J = 5.0 × 10-4 kg·m² and viscous friction is b = 5.0 × 10-5 N·m·s/rad. A position potentiometer gives 1 V per radian, and the amplifier applies an armature voltage equal to Kp times the position error, with Kp in V/rad. The operator wants a step response with about 10 percent overshoot. Find the required damping ratio and amplifier gain, estimate the 2 percent settling time, and find the steady-state following error when the axis is commanded to ramp at 10 rad/s.

  1. (a) Find the damping ratio that gives 10 percent overshoot in the closed-loop step response. [4]
  2. (b) Find the amplifier gain Kp that produces this damping ratio. [6]
  3. (c) Estimate the 2 percent settling time of the step response. [5]
  4. (d) Find the steady-state error when the axis is commanded to follow a ramp of 10 rad/s. [5]
(a)

For a standard second-order system the percentage overshoot is exp(-πζ/√(1 - ζ²)). Taking logarithms with 0.10 overshoot: ln(0.10) = -2.3026, so ζ/√(1 - ζ²) = 2.3026/π = 0.7329. Squaring and solving, ζ² = 0.7329²/(1 + 0.7329²) = 0.5372/1.5372 = 0.3495. Therefore ζ = 0.5912. An equivalent closed form is ζ = -ln(OS)/√(π² + ln²(OS)) = 2.3026/√(9.8696 + 5.3019) = 2.3026/3.895 = 0.5912. This is below 0.707, so some visible overshoot and a slight ring are acceptable for a camera pan, where a fast response is valued more than critical damping, but the operator may later trade this off against smoothness.

Answer: 0.5912

(b)

With negligible inductance the motor equations are Kt ia = J θ'' + b θ' and Ra ia = Va - Ke θ'. Eliminating ia gives (Ra J) θ'' + (Ra b + Kt Ke) θ' = Kt Va. With Va = Kp (θr - θ), the closed-loop characteristic equation is s² + [(Ra b + Kt Ke)/(Ra J)] s + Kt Kp/(Ra J) = 0. Numerically (5 × 10-5 + 2.5 × 10-3)/(5 × 10-4) = 5.1, so 2ζωn = 5.1 and ωn = 5.1/(2 × 0.5912) = 4.313 rad/s. The constant term gives ωn² = 100 Kp, since Kt/(Ra J) = 0.05/(5 × 10-4) = 100. Therefore Kp = 4.313²/100 = 18.60/100 = 0.1861 V/rad.

Answer: 0.1861 V/rad

(c)

For an underdamped second-order system the 2 percent settling time is approximately ts = 4/(ζωn), because the envelope exp(-ζωn t) falls to 2 percent after about four time constants. From part (b), ωn = 4.313 rad/s, and ζ = 0.5912, so ζωn = 2.550 s-1, which is half the damping coefficient 5.1 s-1, as expected. Then ts = 4/2.550 = 1.569 s. This is a quick response for a camera pan but still slow enough for the motor to deliver the required torque without current limiting. The estimate is only an approximation because the exact settling time of an underdamped response depends slightly on ζ, but at this damping the error is a few percent.

Answer: 1.569 s

(d)

The open-loop transfer function with unity feedback is Kp Kt/[s(Ra J s + Ra b + Kt Ke)]. It is a type 1 system with velocity error constant Kv = lim s→0 of s G(s) = Kp Kt/(Ra b + Kt Ke). Substituting values: Kv = 0.1860 × 0.05/(5 × 10-5 + 2.5 × 10-3) = 0.00930/0.00255 = 3.647 s-1. The steady-state error for a ramp of slope R is ess = R/Kv = 10/3.647 = 2.741 rad. That is about 157 degrees, which is far too large for tracking. To reduce it the engineer would need a tachometer-free approach such as adding integral action or a velocity feedforward term, since raising Kp further would worsen damping.

Answer: 2.741 rad

Problem 3 [A3-038] Disturbance rejection

A cable-drum winch on an offshore crane is driven by a speed-controlled motor. The drum speed ω (in rad/s) responds to motor torque according to J dω/dt + b ω = T, with J = 0.5 kg·m² and b = 0.2 N·m·s/rad, and the torque is generated by a controller acting on the speed error ω_ref - ω. A load disturbance of step size 4 N·m acts on the drum when the load is picked up, entering as a torque opposing the drive. The reference speed is zero. Compare a proportional controller with a PI controller. For the proportional controller, find the gain that holds the steady speed deviation to no more than 0.05 rad/s. For the PI controller with Kp = 10 N·m·s/rad, choose Ki for critical damping and determine the peak speed dip.

  1. (a) Find the proportional gain Kp needed to limit the steady speed deviation to 0.05 rad/s. [5]
  2. (b) For the PI controller with Kp = 10, find Ki for critical damping of the disturbance response. [7]
  3. (c) Find the peak magnitude of the speed dip after the 4 N·m step load is applied. [8]
(a)

With a proportional controller T = Kp(0 - ω) the drum equation under the disturbance D is J dω/dt + b ω = -Kp ω - D, where D is the opposing torque. In steady state dω/dt = 0, so (b + Kp) ω = -D and the deviation magnitude is |ω| = D/(b + Kp). Setting this to 0.05 rad/s with D = 4 N·m: b + Kp = 4/0.05 = 80, so Kp = 80 - 0.2 = 79.8 N·m·s/rad. This is a large gain and would saturate a real motor drive on a sudden reference change, as the torque would equal 79.8 N·m for each rad/s of speed error. A proportional controller alone can never reach zero steady deviation, only reduce it, which motivates the PI controller.

Answer: 79.8 N·m·s/rad

(b)

With PI control T = -Kp ω - Ki ∫ω dt, and the load torque D, the drum equation is J ω' + b ω = -Kp ω - Ki ∫ω dt - D. Differentiating or using Laplace transforms gives Ω(s)/D(s) = -s/(J s² + (b + Kp)s + Ki). The characteristic polynomial is J s² + (b + Kp) s + Ki = 0. Critical damping requires a zero discriminant: (b + Kp)² = 4 J Ki. With b + Kp = 10.2: 10.2² = 104.04, so Ki = 104.04/(4 × 0.5) = 52.02 N·m/rad. The double root is at s = -(b + Kp)/(2J) = -10.2 s-1. The integral action in the controller forces the steady speed deviation to zero, since Ω(s)/D(s) has a zero at s = 0, which is the key benefit over the proportional controller.

Answer: 52.02 N·m/rad

(c)

For a step D/s the speed is Ω(s) = -(D/s)(s)/(J (s + 10.2)²) = -(D/J)/(s + 10.2)² = -8/(s + 10.2)², since D/J = 4/0.5 = 8. The inverse Laplace transform is ω(t) = -8 t e-10.2 t rad/s. The peak occurs where dω/dt = 0, which is when 1 - 10.2 t = 0, so t = 1/10.2 = 0.098 s. The magnitude at that time is 8 × 0.098 × e-1 = (8/10.2) × 0.3679 = 0.2885 rad/s. This is the maximum speed dip, about 0.29 rad/s, compared with 0.05 rad/s steady offset for the stiff proportional design, but the PI response recovers to zero within about 0.5 s. The temporary dip is small and the long-term error is zero, a better outcome than a very high proportional gain.

Answer: 0.2885 rad/s

Problem 4 [A3-039] Sampled data and digital control basics

A heating plate in a lab furnace is controlled by a microcontroller. The plate temperature responds to heater input as G(s) = 2 / (s + 4), with temperature in kelvin per unit normalised heater command and time in seconds. The command goes to the heater through a zero-order hold, the temperature is sampled every T = 0.05 s, and the controller is a digital proportional law u[k] = K (r[k] - y[k]). Find the discrete-time plant pulse transfer function, its pole, and the largest K that keeps the closed loop stable. Then pick K for a deadbeat response in which the closed-loop pole sits at the origin, and find the steady value of the output for a unit step reference with this gain. Assume exact discretisation and no computation delay.

  1. (a) Find the pole of the discrete plant G(z) with a zero-order hold at T = 0.05 s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the largest proportional gain K for which the closed loop is stable. [5]
  3. (c) Find K for a deadbeat response, with the closed-loop pole at z = 0. [5]
  4. (d) Find the final output value for a unit step reference with this deadbeat gain. [6]
(a)

With a zero-order hold, G(z) = (1 - z-1) times the z-transform of G(s)/s. For G(s) = 2/(s + 4), G(s)/s = 0.5 (1/s - 1/(s + 4)), whose z-transform is 0.5 [z/(z - 1) - z/(z - e-4T)]. Multiplying by (z - 1)/z gives G(z) = 0.5 (1 - e-4T)/(z - e-4T). With T = 0.05 s, e-0.2 = 0.8187, so the pole of G(z) is at z = 0.8187. The numerator is 0.5 × (1 - 0.8187) = 0.09063. So G(z) = 0.09063/(z - 0.8187). The pole is inside the unit circle and close to 1 because the sample time is short compared with the time constant of 0.25 s. The discrete pole is the mapped continuous pole: z = esT with s = -4.

Answer: 0.8187

(b)

With u = K(r - y), the closed-loop characteristic equation is 1 + K G(z) = 0, that is z - 0.8187 + 0.09063 K = 0. The single closed-loop pole is z = 0.8187 - 0.09063 K. For stability the pole must lie inside the unit circle, |z| < 1. The binding constraint is on the negative side: 0.8187 - 0.09063 K > -1, giving K < 1.8187/0.09063. This is K < 20.07. Equivalently K < (1 + e-aT)/[(Kg/a)(1 - e-aT)]. For comparison, a continuous controller on this first-order plant is stable for every positive K, so the limit comes purely from sampling and the zero-order hold. Operating well below this limit is also necessary to avoid oscillation from the ringing of a negative pole.

Answer: 20.07

(c)

Setting the closed-loop pole z = 0.8187 - 0.09063 K equal to zero gives K = 0.8187/0.09063 = 9.033. With the pole at the origin, the response to any input settles in one sample after the transient, which is the discrete analogue of an infinitely fast loop. The controller cancels the plant's own dynamics through the large gain. This is below the stability limit of 20.07 from part (b), so the loop is stable. Practical caution: the control signal at k = 0 is K times the step, about 9 times the reference, which would likely saturate the heater, so a deadbeat design is rarely used without limiting the command magnitude.

Answer: 9.033

(d)

The closed-loop pulse transfer function is T(z) = K G(z)/(1 + K G(z)). For a unit step, the final value is T(1), provided the closed loop is stable. The DC gain of G(z) is G(1) = 0.09063/(1 - 0.8187) = 0.5, which equals the continuous DC gain 2/4. The loop gain at DC is L = K G(1) = 9.033 × 0.5 = 4.5165. The closed-loop DC gain is L/(1 + L) = 4.5165/5.5165 = 0.8187. Thus the output settles at 0.8187 of the reference, a steady-state error of 18 percent. This is not a coincidence: for a deadbeat gain the closed-loop DC gain always equals the plant pole value e-aT = 0.8187. A proportional controller on a type 0 plant cannot remove offset, so an integral term would be needed for an exact match.

Answer: 0.8187

Problem 5 [A3-040] Control of a liquid level process

A holding tank of cross-sectional area A = 2.0 m² stores process water. The outflow passes through a fixed orifice and follows q = C √h, where h is the level in metres and q is in m³/s. The tank normally operates at h0 = 1.5 m with outflow q0 = 0.03 m³/s. The inflow is set by a control valve giving qin = Kv u, with Kv = 0.01 m³/s per volt of controller output u, and the level transmitter gives 1 V per metre. A proportional controller u = Kc (hr - h) is used. Linearise the outlet about the operating point, find the open-loop time constant, choose Kc to make the closed-loop time constant 40 s, and determine the offset between the final level and the setpoint after a 0.5 m step in setpoint.

  1. (a) Find the linearised outlet resistance R, defined by Δh = R Δq, at the operating point. [5]
  2. (b) Find the controller gain Kc that makes the closed-loop time constant 40 s. [7]
  3. (c) Find the offset between the final level and the setpoint after a 0.5 m step in setpoint. [8]
(a)

The orifice law is q = C √h, with C = q0/√h0. The linearised resistance is the reciprocal of the slope dq/dh at the operating point: dq/dh = C/(2√h0) = q0/(2 h0). Then R = Δh/Δq = 2 h0/q0. Numerically R = 2 × 1.5/0.03 = 100.0 s/m². The tank equation is A dh/dt = qin - q, which for small changes becomes A d(Δh)/dt = Δqin - Δh/R. Taking Laplace transforms gives H(s)/Qin(s) = R/(A R s + 1), a first-order lag with time constant τ = A R = 2.0 × 100 = 200 s. This slow open-loop response of over three minutes explains the use of feedback to speed up the tank level control.

Answer: 100.0 s/m²

(b)

With the control law the linearised tank equation is A dh/dt = Kv Kc (hr - h) - h/R. Collect the terms in h: A dh/dt + (1/R + Kv Kc) h = Kv Kc hr. The closed-loop time constant is therefore τcl = A/(1/R + Kv Kc). Setting τcl = 40 s gives 1/R + Kv Kc = A/40 = 2.0/40 = 0.05 s-1·m². With 1/R = 0.01, Kv Kc = 0.04, so Kc = 0.04/Kv = 0.04/0.01 = 4.000 V/m. The valve then supplies a flow of 0.04 m³/s for each metre of level error. This gain reduces the time constant from 200 s to 40 s, a factor of 5 improvement, and a larger Kc would speed the response further, at the cost of a larger valve flow and a bigger offset requirement.

Answer: 4.000 V/m

(c)

From the closed-loop equation A dh/dt + (1/R + Kv Kc) h = Kv Kc hr, set the derivative to zero at steady state. Then h∞ = [Kv Kc/(1/R + Kv Kc)] hr = (0.04/0.05) hr = 0.8 hr. For a setpoint step of 0.5 m the level rises by only 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4 m, so the offset is 0.5 - 0.4 = 0.1000 m. The offset exists because the steady outflow increase of 0.004 m³/s needs a nonzero controller output, which a proportional law can supply only if there is an error: u = e Kc. Increasing Kc reduces the offset but never eliminates it, while an integral term would remove it entirely. This 20 percent shortfall shows why most level loops use PI control.

Answer: 0.1000 m

A3 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A3-041] Mathematical models of mechanical systems

A precision grinding head of mass 240 kg is carried on isolators that act together as one linear spring of stiffness 1.6 MN/m in parallel with a viscous damper of coefficient 9.6 kN·s/m. The head moves vertically only, and gravity is balanced by the static preload, so the equation of motion is written about static equilibrium. A hydraulic cutting force F(t) acts vertically on the head and the displacement x(t) from equilibrium is the output. During commissioning the operator reports that after a sudden step in cutting force the head rings for many cycles before settling. A maintenance engineer wants to know whether a worn damper delivering only half the original damping coefficient would explain the complaint, and what stiffness would give a well damped response if the original damper is kept. Model the head as a lumped single degree of freedom system and use the model to diagnose the problem and test both proposals.

  1. (a) Sketch the free body diagram in words, derive the transfer function X(s)/F(s), and find the undamped natural frequency in rad/s. [5]
  2. (b) Find the damping ratio ζ of the as-built system and state, with numbers, whether the response is lightly damped. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the damper has worn to half its coefficient (4.8 kN·s/m). Find the percent overshoot of the step response of the displacement. [5]
  4. (d) With the original damper retained, find the spring stiffness in MN/m that gives ζ = 0.7. [5]
(a)

Take the head as a rigid mass acted on by three vertical forces measured from equilibrium: the applied force F, the spring force k·x opposing displacement, and the damper force c·dx/dt opposing velocity. Newton's second law gives m·x'' + c·x' + k·x = F(t). With zero initial conditions the Laplace transform gives (m·s² + c·s + k)·X(s) = F(s), so X(s)/F(s) = 1/(m·s² + c·s + k). Dividing through by m puts the denominator in the standard form s² + 2ζωn·s + ωn², which shows ωn² = k/m. Substituting k = 1.6×10⁶ N/m and m = 240 kg gives ωn² = 6667 rad²/s², so ωn = √6667 = 81.65 rad/s, about 13.0 Hz. Gravity does not appear because the static spring deflection cancels the weight.

Answer: 81.65 rad/s

(b)

The damping ratio follows from matching the coefficient of s in the denominator: 2ζωn = c/m. Then ζ = c/(2·m·ωn) = c/(2·√(k·m)). With c = 9600 N·s/m, k = 1.6×10⁶ N/m and m = 240 kg, √(k·m) = √(3.84×10⁸) = 19596 kg/s. Therefore ζ = 9600/(2 × 19596) = 0.2449. A value near 0.25 is underdamped, and the corresponding percent overshoot to a step force is exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) × 100 ≈ 45.2 percent, with successive peaks decaying by a factor of about 0.20 per cycle. That is lightly damped, so the operator's observation that the head rings for several cycles is consistent with the model even before any wear occurs.

Answer: 0.2449

(c)

With c halved and k and m unchanged, ωn is the same 81.65 rad/s, but the damping ratio halves because ζ is proportional to c: ζ' = 0.5 × 0.2449 = 0.1225. For an underdamped second order system the maximum overshoot of a step response is Mp = exp(−πζ'/√(1−ζ'²)). The square root term is √(1 − 0.1225²) = 0.9925, so the exponent is −π × 0.1225/0.9925 = −0.3877. Hence Mp = 0.6786, or 67.9 percent overshoot. The overshoot has risen from about 45.2 percent to about 67.9 percent, and the number of visible cycles roughly doubles, so a worn damper would plausibly make a head that already rings ring for far longer.

Answer: 67.86 %

(d)

Rearrange ζ = c/(2√(k·m)) for k. Squaring gives ζ² = c²/(4·k·m), so k = c²/(4·ζ²·m). Substituting c = 9600 N·s/m, ζ = 0.7 and m = 240 kg: c² = 9.216×10⁷, and 4 × 0.49 × 240 = 470.4, so k = 9.216×10⁷/470.4 = 195,918 N/m, which is 0.196 MN/m. This is only about 12 percent of the existing stiffness, so the damping is improved by softening the mounts. The price is a lower natural frequency, ωn = √(k/m) = 28.6 rad/s, and a larger static deflection under steady loads, so the engineer must check that the lower stiffness still keeps the head within the positioning tolerance under the cutting force.

Answer: 0.1959 MN/m

Problem 2 [A3-042] Electrical and thermal system analogues

A 150 litre insulated hot water storage tank in a rural clinic is treated as a single lumped thermal mass. Take the water density as 1.00 kg/L and its specific heat as 4186 J/(kg·K), and neglect the heat capacity of the shell. The insulation and jacket together give a thermal resistance to the room of 0.25 K/W, and the room stays at 18 °C. The water is at 60 °C when the electric element is switched off at the end of a working day. The clinic manager asks what happens overnight, and whether an extra insulation blanket that doubles the thermal resistance is worth buying. You are asked to build the model by analogy with an electrical RC circuit, with temperature playing the role of voltage and heat flow the role of current, and to use it to answer the questions.

  1. (a) State the electrical analogues of each thermal quantity and find the thermal time constant of the tank in hours. [5]
  2. (b) Find the water temperature 12 hours after the element is switched off. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: an extra blanket doubles the thermal resistance to 0.50 K/W. Find the water temperature after the same 12 hours. [5]
  4. (d) With the original insulation, how long after switch-off does the water take to cool to 40 °C? [5]
(a)

The analogy maps temperature difference to voltage, heat flow rate to current, thermal resistance to electrical resistance, and thermal capacitance to electrical capacitance. The stored heat energy C·dT/dt corresponds to the charge stored on a capacitor, and the loss path through the insulation corresponds to a resistor to ground at the room temperature. The thermal capacitance is C = m·cp = 150 kg × 4186 J/(kg·K) = 627,900 J/K. The time constant of a first order RC system is τ = R·C = 0.25 K/W × 627,900 J/K = 156,975 s. Dividing by 3600 s/h gives τ = 43.60 h. This means the excess temperature above the room falls to 37 percent of its starting value after about 43.6 hours, so the tank is a slow system and a good thermal store.

Answer: 43.6 h

(b)

Writing the energy balance C·dT/dt = −(T − Ta)/R for the water gives a first order equation in the excess temperature θ = T − Ta, namely τ·dθ/dt + θ = 0. The solution with θ(0) = T0 − Ta = 60 − 18 = 42 K is θ(t) = 42·exp(−t/τ). At t = 12 h with τ = 43.60 h the exponent is −12/43.60 = −0.2752, so exp(−0.2752) = 0.7594 and θ = 42 × 0.7594 = 31.90 K. The water temperature is T = Ta + θ = 18 + 31.90 = 49.9 °C. The tank has lost only about 10 K overnight, which is why a well insulated tank can be left unheated for a working night and still deliver usable hot water in the morning.

Answer: 49.9 °C

(c)

Doubling R doubles the time constant because the capacitance is unchanged: τ' = 0.50 × 627,900/3600 = 87.21 h. The initial excess temperature is still 42 K, so the excess after 12 h is θ = 42·exp(−12/87.21). The exponent is −0.1376, exp(−0.1376) = 0.8714, and θ = 42 × 0.8714 = 36.60 K. The water temperature is T = 18 + 36.60 = 54.6 °C. The blanket therefore saves 4.7 K of cooling over the night compared with the original 49.9 °C, which is about 47 percent of the heat that would have been lost. The saving is real but modest because the original insulation was already good, so the manager should compare the stored energy value, about 3.0 MJ per night at a heating price, against the blanket cost.

Answer: 54.6 °C

(d)

Set T(t) = 40 °C in the cooling law T = Ta + (T0 − Ta)·exp(−t/τ). The excess temperature at the target is 40 − 18 = 22 K and the initial excess is 42 K, so exp(−t/τ) = 22/42 = 0.5238. Taking natural logarithms gives −t/τ = ln(0.5238) = -0.6466. Therefore t = τ × 0.6466 = 43.60 h × 0.6466 = 28.2 h. The tank needs more than a full day to fall that far, so a morning start after a 12 hour night is comfortable. In the electrical analogue this is a capacitor discharging through a resistor: the equivalent circuit could be a 1 megohm resistor with a 0.157 F capacitor, which gives the same time constant of 43.60 h.

Answer: 28.2 h

Problem 3 [A3-043] Hydraulic and pneumatic system models

A header tank of a process water system has a constant cross-sectional area of 0.50 m² and discharges freely to atmosphere through a sharp-edged circular orifice of diameter 40 mm and discharge coefficient 0.62 in its side wall at the base. Water enters from a pump at a steady flow rate chosen so that the level settles at an operating head h0 = 2.0 m above the orifice. Use g = 9.81 m/s². Outflow is q = Cd·a·√(2gh). A plant technician is surprised that the tank takes several minutes to settle after any change in pump flow, and also notices that it seems to settle faster at a lower level. Linearise the model about the operating point to obtain a first order transfer function from inflow deviation to level deviation, then use it to explain the behaviour and test the technician's observation and the accuracy of the linear model.

  1. (a) Derive the nonlinear mass balance for the level, then linearise it about h0 and find the linearised hydraulic resistance R = dh/dq_out in s/m². [5]
  2. (b) Find the time constant of the linearised level dynamics and write the transfer function ΔH(s)/ΔQin(s). [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the plant is re-run at a higher operating head h0 = 4.0 m by raising the pump flow. Find the new time constant and comment on the technician's observation. [5]
  4. (d) The pump flow is stepped up by 10 percent at the original operating point. Use the linear model to find the final level change in metres, and state how far it is from the exact nonlinear result. [5]
(a)

For an incompressible liquid the volume balance is A·dh/dt = q_in − q_out with q_out = k·√h, where k = Cd·a·√(2g). The orifice area is a = π(0.04)²/4 = 1.2566 × 10⁻³ m², so k = 0.62 × 1.2566 × 10⁻³ × √(2 × 9.81) = 3.4510 × 10⁻³ m2.5/s. The operating outflow is q0 = k·√2.0 = 4.8805 × 10⁻³ m³/s, which equals the steady inflow. Linearising q_out about h0 gives dq_out = (k/(2√h0))·Δh, so the linear resistance is R = dh/dq_out = 2√h0/k = 2 × 1.4142/3.4510 × 10⁻³ = 819.6 s/m². The linear model is AΔh' = Δq_in − Δh/R. Note that R grows with √h0, so a tank running at a higher level has a larger resistance because the outflow becomes less sensitive to level.

Answer: 819.6 s/m²

(b)

Taking Laplace transforms of AΔh' = Δq_in − Δh/R with zero initial deviations gives (A·s + 1/R)ΔH = ΔQin. Multiplying through by R gives (A·R·s + 1)ΔH = R·ΔQin, so ΔH(s)/ΔQin(s) = R/(τ·s + 1) with τ = A·R. Substituting A = 0.50 m² and R = 819.6 s/m² gives τ = 409.8 s, about 6.8 minutes. The DC gain is R = 819.6 m per (m³/s), or 820 mm of level per litre per second of added inflow. A response that takes roughly four time constants to settle gives 1639 s, about 27 minutes, which agrees with the technician's report that the tank takes several minutes to settle after any pump change.

Answer: 409.8 s

(c)

The resistance depends on the operating point, R = 2√h0/k, while A and k are unchanged. At h0 = 4.0 m, √h0 = 2.0, so R = 2 × 2.0/3.4510 × 10⁻³ = 1159.1 s/m² and τ = A·R = 0.50 × 1159.1 = 579.5 s. This is 1.414 times the original time constant, exactly √(4/2) = 1.414 as the square root law predicts. The technician's observation is therefore correct: the tank settles more slowly at a higher level and faster at a lower level. The explanation is that at a high level a given change in level changes the outflow by a smaller relative amount, so more volume must accumulate to rebalance the flows. The inflow needed at this level is q = 6.9021 × 10⁻³ m³/s.

Answer: 579.5 s

(d)

The step in inflow is Δq = 0.10 × q0 = 0.10 × 4.8805 × 10⁻³ = 4.8805 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s. The linear model gives a final level change Δh = R·Δq = 819.6 × 4.8805 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.400 m. For comparison the exact nonlinear steady state satisfies k√h = 1.1·q0, so h = 1.1² × h0 = 2.420 m and the true rise is 0.420 m. The linear prediction is therefore low by 4.8 percent. The difference arises because the true outflow curve is concave, so a larger level rise is needed than the tangent slope at h0 suggests. For a 10 percent flow change the linear model is accurate to about 5 percent, which is acceptable for controller design but not for sizing the overflow freeboard.

Answer: 0.400 m

Problem 4 [A3-044] Block diagram reduction

The loop of a coating-line tension controller is built from three blocks in the forward path. A proportional amplifier of gain K = 4 feeds a motor-drive block G2(s) = 5/(s + 3), around which a local rate feedback gain H2 = 0.4 is taken from the drive output back to the drive input, summing negatively. The drive output then feeds a tension roller block G3(s) = 2/(s + 2). The overall output is fed back with unity gain and subtracted from the reference at the first summing junction, so the amplifier receives the error. During a service call the technician notes that the step response of the tension looks far more oscillatory than the commissioning record. The records show the local rate feedback wire was found disconnected. Reduce the block diagram stepwise and compare the healthy and faulted loops to confirm whether the fault explains the symptom.

  1. (a) Reduce the inner loop and then the outer loop to a single closed-loop transfer function T(s) = C(s)/R(s) for the healthy system, and find its DC gain. [5]
  2. (b) Find the natural frequency and the damping ratio of the healthy closed loop. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the rate feedback wire is open, so H2 = 0. Repeat the reduction and find the damping ratio of the faulted loop. [5]
  4. (d) Find the percent overshoot of the step response of the faulted loop and say whether the fault explains the technician's observation. [5]
(a)

First reduce the inner feedback loop around G2. For negative feedback the loop becomes G2/(1 + G2·H2) = [5/(s + 3)]/[1 + 0.4 × 5/(s + 3)] = 5/(s + 3 + 2) = 5/(s + 5). The forward path is now the cascade K × 5/(s + 5) × 2/(s + 2) = 40/((s + 5)(s + 2)). With unity feedback the outer loop gives T(s) = L/(1 + L) where L is that forward gain, so T(s) = 40/((s + 5)(s + 2) + 40) = 40/(s² + 7s + 50). The DC gain is found by setting s = 0: T(0) = 40/50 = 0.80. A value below one means a steady error of about 20 percent to a step, which is expected for a loop with no integrator in the forward path.

Answer: 0.8

(b)

Compare the denominator s² + 7s + 50 with the standard second order form s² + 2ζωn·s + ωn². The constant term gives ωn² = 50, so ωn = √50 = 7.071 rad/s. The coefficient of s gives 2ζωn = 7, so ζ = 7/(2 × 7.071) = 0.495. The poles are at s = −3.5 ± j6.14, which is a complex pair in the left half plane, so the loop is stable and underdamped. The corresponding step overshoot of the healthy loop is exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) × 100 = 16.7 percent, a moderate figure that serves as the benchmark for the commissioning record. The damping ratio is dimensionless, and it is this number that the faulted loop will be compared against.

Answer: 0.495

(c)

With H2 = 0 the local loop disappears and the drive block stays 5/(s + 3). The forward gain is K × 5/(s + 3) × 2/(s + 2) = 40/((s + 3)(s + 2)). With unity feedback, T(s) = 40/((s + 3)(s + 2) + 40) = 40/(s² + 5s + 46). Now ωn² = 46, so ωn = 6.782 rad/s, and 2ζωn = 5 gives ζ = 5/(2 × 6.782) = 0.369. The faulted DC gain is 40/46 = 0.870, slightly higher than the healthy 0.800. Removing the rate feedback has lowered the damping ratio from 0.495 to 0.369, because the local loop was adding 2 to the coefficient of s in the characteristic polynomial, which is a pure damping term. The natural frequency changed only slightly, from 7.07 to 6.78 rad/s.

Answer: 0.3686

(d)

For an underdamped second order system the maximum step overshoot is Mp = exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)). For the faulted loop ζ = 0.369, and √(1 − ζ²) = 0.9296. The exponent is −π × 0.369/0.9296 = −1.2457, so Mp = 0.2877, which is 28.8 percent. The healthy loop overshoot was 16.7 percent, so the fault has added about 12 percentage points of overshoot and lengthened the decay of the ringing, because the real part of the poles moved from −3.5 to −2.5 and the decay envelope exp(−σt) slowed accordingly. The fault therefore explains the more oscillatory response. Reconnecting the rate feedback wire should restore the commissioning record without retuning the amplifier gain K.

Answer: 28.77 %

Problem 5 [A3-045] Signal flow and Mason gain

A signal flow graph models the load-sharing between two stages of a variable-speed compressor controller. Nodes are x1 (input R), x2, x3, x4 and x5 (output C). The branch gains are x1 to x2: 1, x2 to x3: 4, x3 to x4: 2, x4 to x5: 3, a bypass branch x2 to x4: 1.5, and two feedback branches x3 to x2: −0.3 and x4 to x3: −0.1. All gains are dimensionless steady-state values. During a retrofit, the bypass and feedback wiring were revised, and commissioning engineers suspect that a sign error in the x3 to x2 feedback may have been made when the branch was re-terminated. Use Mason's gain formula to find the overall gain from x1 to x5 for the as-designed graph, then test the two fault cases: first, the x4 to x3 feedback branch is open (gain zero), and second, the x3 to x2 branch is accidentally given the opposite sign (+0.3). Confirm each result by an independent method.

  1. (a) List the forward paths and individual loops, identify any non-touching loops, and compute the graph determinant Δ for the as-designed graph. [5]
  2. (b) Find the overall gain C/R of the as-designed graph using Mason's formula, with the cofactor of each forward path stated. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the x4 to x3 feedback branch is open (gain zero). Find the new overall gain by Mason's formula. [5]
  4. (d) What-if: the x3 to x2 branch has the wrong sign (+0.3). Find the overall gain and explain what the result says about the system. [5]
(a)

Forward paths from x1 to x5: P1 passes x1, x2, x3, x4, x5 with gain 1 × 4 × 2 × 3 = 24, and P2 passes x1, x2, x4, x5 with gain 1 × 1.5 × 3 = 4.5. Individual loops: L1 is x2 to x3 and back, gain 4 × (−0.3) = -1.20; L2 is x3 to x4 and back, gain 2 × (−0.1) = -0.20; L3 is x2 to x4, x4 to x3, x3 to x2, gain 1.5 × (−0.1) × (−0.3) = 0.045. Every pair of loops shares a node (L1 and L2 share x3, L1 and L3 share x2 and x3, L2 and L3 share x3 and x4), so there are no non-touching loop pairs. Mason's determinant is Δ = 1 − (L1 + L2 + L3) = 1 − (-1.355) = 2.355. The negative sums of loop gains show net negative feedback, which pushes Δ above one and reduces the overall gain.

Answer: 2.355

(b)

Mason's formula is T = Σ(Pk·Δk)/Δ. The cofactor Δk is Δ computed with all loops touching path k removed. Path P1 visits x2, x3 and x4, so it touches L1, L2 and L3, leaving no loops and Δ1 = 1. Path P2 visits x2 and x4 only, but L1 contains x2, L2 contains x4 and L3 contains both, so it also touches every loop and Δ2 = 1. Then T = (P1 + P2)/Δ = (24 + 4.5)/2.355 = 28.5/2.355 = 12.102. As an independent check, writing the node equations x2 = x1 − 0.3·x3, x3 = 4·x2 − 0.1·x4, x4 = 2·x3 + 1.5·x2, x5 = 3·x4 and solving the 5×5 linear system with x1 = 1 gives x5 = 12.102, which agrees with Mason's result.

Answer: 12.1

(c)

With the branch x4 to x3 removed, loops L2 and L3 disappear because both used it, leaving only L1 = 4 × (−0.3) = −1.2. The determinant is Δ = 1 − (−1.2) = 2.200. The forward paths and their cofactors are unchanged, since both touch L1 at x2 and so Δ1 = Δ2 = 1. Therefore T = (24 + 4.5)/2.200 = 28.5/2.200 = 12.955. Compared with the as-designed gain of 12.102, the open feedback branch raises the overall gain by 7.0 percent. The change is small because that branch was a weak feedback path of only −0.1, which is why a loss of it might go unnoticed during a quick commissioning check that only looks at steady-state output level.

Answer: 12.95

(d)

With e = +0.3 the loop gains become L1 = 4 × 0.3 = +1.2, L2 = 2 × (−0.1) = −0.2 and L3 = 1.5 × (−0.1) × 0.3 = −0.045. The sum is 0.955, so Δ = 1 − 0.955 = 0.045. The cofactors remain 1 for both forward paths, so T = 28.5/0.045 = 633.3. The matrix solution gives 633.3, confirming this. The gain jumped from 12.1 to 633, because the dominant loop L1 now has positive feedback with gain 1.2, and Δ is close to zero. A determinant that near zero indicates the graph is on the edge of a singular steady state, and in a dynamic system the same sign error would typically destabilise it. This explains why a tiny wiring sign error can produce a wildly wrong output level.

Answer: 633.3

A3 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A3-046] First-order system step response

A thermowell temperature probe in a pasteurizer outlet line behaves as a first order lag with time constant 8.0 s, a unity static gain, and no appreciable dead time. The probe is at 20 °C in the sample room when it is plunged suddenly into a hot oil bath at 95 °C. The quality manager requires the reading to be within 5 °C of the bath temperature, that is, to reach at least 90 °C, before a measurement is logged. A supplier offers a rugged replacement probe with a sheath of twice the diameter, made of the same material, in the same flow conditions, for which the heat transfer coefficient is unchanged. For a thin cylindrical sheath, the time constant is proportional to the sheath diameter when the material and heat transfer coefficient are unchanged. Later the probe will be used in a bath whose temperature rises steadily. Use first order theory to judge the replacement.

  1. (a) Write the step response of the probe and find the time after immersion at which the reading first reaches 90 °C. [5]
  2. (b) What reading does the original probe show 10 s after immersion? [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the thicker probe is fitted. Find its time constant and the time to reach 90 °C. [5]
  4. (d) The probe now measures a bath whose temperature ramps up at 1.5 °C/s. For the thicker probe, find the steady-state lag between the bath and the reading. [5]
(a)

A first order system with unity static gain responds to a step from T0 to Tb with T(t) = Tb − (Tb − T0)·exp(−t/τ). The step size is 95 − 20 = 75 °C. Setting T = 90 °C gives 95 − 75·exp(−t/τ) = 90, so exp(−t/τ) = 5/75 = 0.0667. Taking natural logarithms, −t/τ = ln(0.0667) = -2.7081, so t = τ × 2.7081 = 8.0 × 2.7081 = 21.7 s. This is about 2.71 time constants, which is the familiar result that a first order lag needs roughly 2.7τ to be within 6.7 percent of its final value. The manager's condition therefore means the operator must wait nearly 22 seconds before logging a reading from the existing probe.

Answer: 21.66 s

(b)

Use the same step response with t = 10 s and τ = 8.0 s: T(10) = 95 − 75·exp(−10/8.0). The exponent is −1.25 and exp(−1.25) = 0.2865, so the remaining difference is 75 × 0.2865 = 21.49 °C. The reading is therefore 95 − 21.49 = 73.5 °C, which is still 21.5 °C below the bath. At t = 10 s the probe has completed 1 − 0.2865 = 71.3 percent of its change in fraction terms, short of the required 93.3 percent. This shows that waiting ten seconds is not enough under the quality rule, and it is a useful check that the two numbers agree: 10 s is less than the required 21.7 s, and the reading at 10 s is below 90 °C.

Answer: 73.51 °C

(c)

The time constant is proportional to sheath diameter when the material and heat transfer coefficient are unchanged, so doubling the diameter doubles τ: τ' = 2 × 8.0 = 16.0 s. The step is the same and the 90 °C condition still requires exp(−t/τ') = 0.0667, so t = τ' × 2.7081 = 16.0 × 2.7081 = 43.3 s. This is exactly twice the original 21.7 s, because every first order response time scales directly with τ. The rugged probe is therefore more robust but slows the logging procedure by about 21.7 s per reading, and in a line with frequent changes the operator would be waiting nearly three quarters of a minute. The manager must weigh ruggedness against speed, or find a thinner but equally robust sheath material with higher conductivity.

Answer: 43.33 s

(d)

For a ramp input r(t) = a·t applied to a unity-gain first order lag, the output after the transient dies away is y = a(t − τ), so the steady-state error is a constant lag e_ss = a·τ. Check with the final value theorem: E(s) = R(s)·[1 − 1/(τs + 1)] = (a/s²)·τs/(τs + 1), and s·E(s) at s = 0 equals a·τ. For the thicker probe τ' = 16.0 s and a = 1.5 °C/s, so e_ss = 1.5 × 16.0 = 24.0 °C. The thinner original probe would lag by 1.5 × 8.0 = 12.0 °C. The reading thus trails the true bath temperature by 24 °C, equivalent to a 16 s time delay. For a pasteurizer where a few degrees matter, the thicker probe is unsuitable for monitoring ramps unless the lag is compensated in the controller.

Answer: 24 °C

Problem 2 [A3-047] Second-order system time response specs

A positioning servo for a camera gimbal is modelled by the closed-loop transfer function C(s)/R(s) = ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn·s + ωn²) with ωn = 12 rad/s and ζ = 0.45 at its current gain setting. In this servo, the loop gain K appears only in the constant term of the denominator, so ωn² is proportional to K while the coefficient of s (equal to 2ζωn) stays fixed because it is set by the motor's back-EMF and viscous friction. The step response specification is overshoot at most 25 percent and 2 percent settling time at most 1.0 s. The product team wants a snappier response and proposes increasing the loop gain by a factor of 2.5. Evaluate the present design against the specification, then analyse the proposal using the closed-loop second order formulas. Use the standard approximation ts = 4/(ζωn) for 2 percent settling.

  1. (a) Find the percent overshoot of the present design and say whether it meets the 25 percent limit. [4]
  2. (b) Find the 2 percent settling time of the present design and say whether it meets the 1.0 s limit. [4]
  3. (c) What-if: the loop gain is multiplied by 2.5. Find the new damping ratio and the new percent overshoot. [4]
  4. (d) For the proposed gain, find the peak time and compare it with the present design. [4]
  5. (e) For the proposed gain, find the 2 percent settling time and state the engineering conclusion. [4]
(a)

For an underdamped second order system the step overshoot is Mp = exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)). With ζ = 0.45, 1 − ζ² = 1 − 0.2025 = 0.7975 and √0.7975 = 0.8930. The exponent is −π × 0.45/0.8930 = −1.5831, so Mp = 0.2053, which is 20.5 percent. This is below the 25 percent limit, so the overshoot specification is met with a margin of 4.5 percentage points. The damped natural frequency is ωd = ωn√(1−ζ²) = 12 × 0.8930 = 10.72 rad/s. The overshoot depends only on ζ, not on ωn, which is why changing the gain, which changes both ζ and ωn in this servo, will affect overshoot even though it does not directly alter the damping term.

Answer: 20.53 %

(b)

The settling time to within 2 percent of the final value is approximated by ts = 4/(ζωn), the time for the envelope exp(−ζωn·t) to decay to 0.02. Here ζωn = 0.45 × 12 = 5.40 s⁻¹, so ts = 4/5.40 = 0.741 s. This meets the 1.0 s requirement with a margin of 0.259 s. The real part of the closed-loop poles is −ζωn = −5.40, and it is this value, not ωn alone, that controls how quickly the oscillation dies. The settling time depends on the damping coefficient of s in the denominator, here 2ζωn = 10.8 s⁻¹, so any change that leaves that coefficient fixed leaves the settling time unchanged, which is relevant for the proposal examined next.

Answer: 0.7407 s

(c)

Since ωn² is proportional to the loop gain, the new natural frequency is ωn' = 12 × √2.5 = 18.97 rad/s. The coefficient of s remains 2ζωn = 10.8, so the new damping ratio is ζ' = 10.8/(2 × 18.97) = 0.2846. This equals the old ζ divided by √2.5 = 1.581. The new overshoot is Mp' = exp(−πζ'/√(1−ζ'²)). With ζ' = 0.2846, the square root term is 0.9586, the exponent is −0.9327, and Mp' = 0.3935, or 39.3 percent. This now exceeds the 25 percent limit by 14.3 percentage points, so the proposal violates the overshoot specification even though it makes the servo faster. Increasing gain trades damping for speed whenever the damping term cannot be adjusted independently.

Answer: 39.35 %

(d)

The peak time of an underdamped second order step response is tp = π/ωd, where ωd = ωn√(1−ζ²). For the proposal, ωd' = 18.97 × 0.9586 = 18.19 rad/s, so tp' = π/18.19 = 0.1727 s. For the present design, ωd = 10.72 rad/s and tp = π/10.72 = 0.2932 s. The proposal therefore reaches its first peak 41 percent sooner, which is the snappier feel the product team wants. The shorter peak time confirms the faster rise, but it must be balanced against the overshoot found in part c, which would be visible to users as a gimbal that hunts past its target before settling.

Answer: 0.1727 s

(e)

Using ts = 4/(ζ'ωn'), the product ζ'ωn' = 0.2846 × 18.97 = 5.40 s⁻¹, which equals the earlier 5.40 s⁻¹ because ζωn = (coefficient of s)/2 is unchanged. Therefore ts' = 4/5.40 = 0.741 s, identical to the present value. So the proposal makes the first peak come sooner (0.173 s against 0.293 s) but does not improve the 2 percent settling time at all, and it raises overshoot from 20.5 percent to 39.3 percent, which breaks the 25 percent limit. The conclusion is that raising loop gain alone should be rejected. To gain speed and keep damping, the designer needs added velocity feedback or a lead compensator to raise the coefficient of s along with the gain.

Answer: 0.7407 s

Problem 3 [A3-048] Steady-state error and system type

A steam-valve positioner in a boiler plant is a unity feedback loop with open-loop transfer function G(s) = K(s + 3)/(s(s + 5)(s + 10)), where K is the amplifier gain, currently set to 400. The plant engineer must meet a tracking requirement for the demand ramp: when the demand rises at 3 units per second, the steady-state tracking error must not exceed 0.05 units. A junior engineer suggests adding a second integrator ahead of the positioner so that the loop becomes type 2, expecting zero ramp error and a finite error to a parabolic demand. The engineer wants to know the effect on the error constants and on closed-loop stability. Analyse the loop as it stands, find the gain needed to meet the requirement, then analyse the suggested modification with K = 400 retained.

  1. (a) State the system type and find the velocity error constant Kv for K = 400. [4]
  2. (b) Find the steady-state error of the present loop to the ramp demand of 3 units per second. [4]
  3. (c) Find the gain K that makes the ramp error exactly 0.05 units, and state whether the loop is still stable. [4]
  4. (d) What-if: a second integrator is added so G(s) = K(s + 3)/(s²(s + 5)(s + 10)) with K = 400. State the new type, and find the steady-state error to a parabolic input r(t) = t² (an acceleration of 2 units/s²), assuming the loop were stable. [4]
  5. (e) For the type 2 loop with K = 400, form the characteristic equation and find the number of closed-loop poles in the right half plane. [4]
(a)

The open-loop transfer function has one pole at the origin, so it is a type 1 system. The velocity error constant is Kv = lim(s→0) s·G(s) = lim K(s + 3)/((s + 5)(s + 10)). At s = 0 the factor (s + 3) gives 3, and the product (5)(10) = 50, so Kv = K × 3/50. For K = 400 this gives Kv = 400 × 3/50 = 24.0 s⁻¹. Because the system is type 1, the step error constant Kp is infinite and the position error to a step is zero, while the acceleration constant Ka is zero, so a parabolic input would give an unbounded error. The velocity constant is the one that determines the ramp error and therefore governs the present requirement.

Answer: 24 s⁻¹

(b)

For a unity feedback type 1 system with a ramp input of slope A, the steady-state error is e_ss = A/Kv. This follows from the final value theorem with E(s) = R(s)/(1 + G(s)) and R(s) = A/s², giving e_ss = lim s·(A/s²)/(1 + G(s)) = A/lim(s·G(s)). With A = 3 units/s and Kv = 24.0 s⁻¹, e_ss = 3/24.0 = 0.1250 units. This exceeds the allowable 0.05 units by a factor of 2.50, so the present gain does not meet the tracking requirement. The result also assumes the closed loop is stable, which is true here because the characteristic equation s³ + 15s² + (50 + K)s + 3K has all positive coefficients and 15(50 + K) is greater than 3K for every positive K.

Answer: 0.125 units

(c)

The requirement e_ss = A/Kv = 0.05 with A = 3 gives Kv = 3/0.05 = 60 s⁻¹. Since Kv = 3K/50, K = 60 × 50/3 = 1000. The closed-loop characteristic polynomial is s(s + 5)(s + 10) + K(s + 3) = s³ + 15s² + (50 + K)s + 3K. For K = 1000 it is s³ + 15s² + 1050s + 3000. The Routh condition for a cubic s³ + a2·s² + a1·s + a0 is a2·a1 > a0. Here 15 × 1050 = 15750, which is greater than 3000, so the loop is stable. The closed-loop poles have a largest real part of -2.96, confirming stability, although the poles will be more oscillatory than at K = 400 because the gain is 2.5 times higher.

Answer: 1000

(d)

The two poles at the origin make the loop type 2. The ramp error is then zero, the velocity constant is infinite, and the acceleration constant is Ka = lim s²·G(s) = K × 3/50 = 400 × 3/50 = 24.0 s⁻². For a parabolic input r(t) = ½·A·t² with acceleration A, the steady-state error is A/Ka. The input r(t) = t² has A = 2 units/s², so e_ss = 2/24.0 = 0.0833 units. This result is only valid if the closed loop is stable, because the final value theorem fails for an unstable loop. The mathematics promises zero ramp error, which would meet the requirement trivially, so the remaining question for the junior engineer is whether the type 2 loop can actually be stabilised at this gain.

Answer: 0.08333 units

(e)

The characteristic equation is 1 + G(s) = 0, so s²(s + 5)(s + 10) + 400(s + 3) = 0. Expanding gives s⁴ + 15s³ + 50s² + 400s + 1200 = 0. Build the Routh array: the s⁴ row is 1, 50, 1200, the s³ row is 15, 400, 0. The s² entry is (15 × 50 − 400)/15 = 23.33 and the second entry is 1200. The s¹ entry is (23.33 × 400 − 15 × 1200)/23.33 = -371.4, which is negative, and the s⁰ entry is 1200. The first column reads 1, 15, 23.33, -371.4, 1200, which has two sign changes, so there are 2 right half plane poles. Numerically the roots have positive real parts 0.64, confirming instability. The added integrator therefore removes the ramp error only on paper, and the loop would need compensation before it could be used.

Answer: 2

Problem 4 [A3-049] Routh-Hurwitz stability

The pressure loop of a steam drum is a unity feedback system with open-loop transfer function G(s) = K/((s + 1)(s + 3)(s + 8)), where K is the controller gain and all time units are seconds. At commissioning, the loop was tuned using the maximum gain at which the loop stays stable as a reference. Later, the instrument department replaced the pressure transmitter with a model that has a first order lag with time constant 0.5 s and a unity DC gain, which adds the factor 1/(0.5s + 1) to the loop. The plant manager asks whether the controller gain used before the retrofit is still safe. Use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to find the limiting gains and the frequency of sustained oscillation in each case, and quantify what the added sensor lag costs in permissible gain.

  1. (a) Form the closed-loop characteristic equation without the sensor lag, build the Routh array, and find the maximum stable gain Kmax. [5]
  2. (b) Find the frequency of sustained oscillation at the stability limit of the original loop. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the sensor lag 1/(0.5s + 1) is added. Find the new maximum stable gain. [5]
  4. (d) Is the pre-retrofit limiting gain safe with the new sensor? State the percentage reduction in the maximum stable gain and the new oscillation frequency at the limit. [5]
(a)

The characteristic equation is 1 + G(s) = 0, i.e. (s + 1)(s + 3)(s + 8) + K = 0. Expanding, (s + 1)(s + 3) = s² + 4s + 3, and multiplying by (s + 8) gives s³ + 12s² + 35s + 24. The equation is s³ + 12s² + (35)s + (24 + K) = 0. The Routh array has first column 1, 12, b1, 24 + K with b1 = (12 × 35 − (24 + K))/12 = (396 − K)/12. For stability every entry must be positive, so K < 396 and 24 + K > 0, which gives K > −24. The upper limit follows from a2·a1 > a0, 12 × 35 = 420 > 24 + K. Hence the maximum stable gain is Kmax = 396. At K = 396 the s¹ entry is zero, which marks the stability boundary, and for any larger gain the loop has two poles in the right half plane.

Answer: 396

(b)

When b1 = 0 the auxiliary polynomial is formed from the s² row, which has coefficients 12 and 24 + K. At K = 396 this row is 12s² + 420, so 12s² + 420 = 0 and s² = −35. The imaginary-axis roots are s = ±j√35. The frequency of sustained oscillation is therefore ω = √35 = 5.916 rad/s, a period of 2π/5.916 = 1.06 s. A direct check substitutes s = jω into s³ + 12s² + 35s + 420: the real part is −12ω² + 420 = 0 giving ω² = 35, and the imaginary part is −ω³ + 35ω = 0 which gives the same ω² = 35, so both parts vanish together, as they must at a marginal pair of roots. The third root is real at s = −12, since the sum of roots must be −12.

Answer: 5.916 rad/s

(c)

Writing the lag as 1/(0.5s + 1) = 2/(s + 2), the loop becomes 2K/((s + 1)(s + 3)(s + 8)(s + 2)). The characteristic polynomial is (s + 2)(s³ + 12s² + 35s + 24) + 2K = s⁴ + 14s³ + 59s² + 94s + (48 + 2K). The Routh array has rows s⁴: 1, 59, 48 + 2K; s³: 14, 94; s²: b1 = (14 × 59 − 94)/14 = 52.286, 48 + 2K; s¹: c1 = (b1 × 94 − 14 × (48 + 2K))/b1. Positivity of the s¹ entry requires 4914.86 − 672 − 28K > 0 with b1 × 94 = 4914.86, so K < (4914.86 − 672)/28 = 151.5. The maximum stable gain is Kmax2 = 151.5. The condition 48 + 2K > 0 is satisfied for any positive K, so the s¹ row is the controlling limit.

Answer: 151.5

(d)

The original tuning used gains up to Kmax = 396, but with the new sensor the system is unstable above K = 151.5. Therefore a gain of 396, or any gain above about 152, is no longer safe. The reduction is (396 − 151.5)/396 × 100 = 61.7 percent. At the new limit, the s² row of the array gives the auxiliary equation 52.286s² + (48 + 2 × 151.5) = 0, so ω² = 6.71 and ω = 2.59 rad/s, compared with 5.92 rad/s before. The extra lag adds phase lag at every frequency, so the phase crossover frequency falls, and the gain at which the loop reaches −180° falls with it. A practical engineer would also insist on a gain margin below the limit, perhaps half, for a safe operating gain. A numerical root check on the marginal polynomial shows imaginary roots at ±j2.59, confirming the algebra.

Answer: 61.73 %

Problem 5 [A3-050] Root locus

A motorised damper actuator in a ventilation duct is controlled by a unity feedback loop with open-loop transfer function G(s) = K/(s(s + 3)(s + 9)), K > 0, where K is the proportional gain. Commissioning shows the loop becomes oscillatory once K is increased past a certain value, and the controls engineer is considering adding a proportional-plus-derivative element that contributes a zero at s = −2, giving G_c(s) = K(s + 2)/(s(s + 3)(s + 9)). Use root locus construction on the existing loop and on the modified loop. You may take the angle and magnitude conditions in their standard form and sketch mentally from the real-axis segments, asymptotes and breakaway points. The aim is to understand how the gain limits and branch geometry change when the zero is added.

  1. (a) Locate the real-axis segments, the asymptotes and the breakaway point of the existing locus. Give the breakaway point. [4]
  2. (b) Find the gain K at the breakaway point. [4]
  3. (c) Find the gain at which the locus crosses the imaginary axis. [4]
  4. (d) What-if: the zero at s = −2 is added. Find the new centroid of the asymptotes and the new asymptote angles. [4]
  5. (e) Does the modified loop have a finite gain at which it becomes unstable? Justify using the characteristic equation. [4]
(a)

The open-loop poles are at 0, −3 and −9 and there are no finite zeros. Real-axis segments of the locus lie to the left of an odd number of real poles and zeros, so the locus occupies 0 to −3 and −9 to −∞. With three poles and no zeros there are three asymptotes at angles 60°, 180° and −60°, meeting the real axis at σa = (0 − 3 − 9)/3 = -4.0. The breakaway points satisfy dK/ds = 0 with K = −s(s + 3)(s + 9) = −(s³ + 12s² + 27s). Differentiating, 3s² + 24s + 27 = 0, or s² + 8s + 9 = 0, so s = −4 ± √7 = -1.354 or -6.646. Only -1.354 lies on the locus segment between 0 and −3, so the breakaway point is s = -1.354. The other root, -6.646, lies between −3 and −9, where there is no locus on the real axis, so it is rejected.

Answer: -1.354

(b)

At any point on the locus the magnitude condition gives K = |s||s + 3||s + 9|. At the breakaway point s = -1.354, |s| = 1.354, |s + 3| = 1.646 and |s + 9| = 7.646. Multiplying, K = 1.354 × 1.646 × 7.646 = 17.04. For gains below this value the closed-loop poles are real and distinct, giving an overdamped response with no oscillation, and at K = 17.04 two poles coincide at -1.354, giving critical damping. Above this gain the two poles leave the real axis as a complex pair, and the response becomes oscillatory. The third pole sits on the far-left real segment, at s = −12 − 2(-1.354) = -9.292 by the sum-of-roots rule, since the poles of s³ + 12s² + 27s + K must sum to −12.

Answer: 17.04

(c)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is s³ + 12s² + 27s + K = 0. For a cubic with all positive coefficients the Routh condition is 12 × 27 > K, so the boundary is K = 12 × 27 = 324. At this gain the s¹ entry of the Routh array vanishes, and the auxiliary polynomial from the s² row is 12s² + K = 12s² + 324 = 0, giving s² = −27 and s = ±j√27 = ±j5.196. The locus therefore crosses the imaginary axis at ω = 5.196 rad/s with K = 324. The controls engineer's report that the loop becomes oscillatory is consistent with the breakaway gain of 17.0, but the oscillation becomes sustained, and the loop unstable beyond, only when K exceeds 324, so there is a large range of gain between damped oscillation and instability.

Answer: 324

(d)

With the zero the open-loop transfer function has n = 3 poles and m = 1 zero, so there are n − m = 2 asymptotes. The asymptote angles are (2k + 1)·180°/(n − m) = ±90°. The centroid is σa = (Σ poles − Σ zeros)/(n − m) = ((0 − 3 − 9) − (−2))/2 = (−12 + 2)/2 = -5.0. Compared with the original -4.0, the centroid has moved to the left (from -4.0 to -5.0) and, more importantly, the two asymptotes are now vertical lines at σ = -5.0, not the 60° lines that bend towards the right half plane. Thus the high-gain branches run parallel to the imaginary axis in the left half plane, never entering the right half plane. The real-axis rule applied to the combined set 0, −2, −3, −9 now places locus on 0 to −2 and −3 to −9, so one branch ends on the zero.

Answer: -5

(e)

With the zero, the characteristic equation is s(s + 3)(s + 9) + K(s + 2) = s³ + 12s² + (27 + K)s + 2K = 0. For a cubic with positive coefficients the Routh condition is a2·a1 > a0, that is 12(27 + K) > 2K. This simplifies to 324 + 12K > 2K, so 324 + 10K > 0, which is true for every K > 0. The first column of the Routh array is 1, 12, (12(27 + K) − 2K)/12 = (324 + 10K)/12, and 2K, which are all positive for K > 0, so there are never any sign changes and the loop is stable for all positive gains. As a check, at K = 500 the roots are -5.01+21.96j, -5.01-21.96j, -1.97+0.00j, with largest real part -1.97, all in the left half plane. The asymptote geometry found in part d agrees.

Answer: No, the modified loop is stable for every K > 0, because 12(27 + K) > 2K always holds.

A3 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A3-051] Bode plot construction

A hydraulic press positions its platen with a servo valve. The open-loop transfer function from the position error voltage to measured platen position is G(s) = 10 / [ s (1 + s/10)(1 + s/100) ], with frequencies in rad/s and unity feedback. The first corner at 10 rad/s comes from the cylinder and load, the second at 100 rad/s from the servo valve spool lag. The commissioning engineer builds the Bode plot by hand and then checks it against exact values. Later the valve is replaced by a faster model whose spool lag corner moves from 100 rad/s to 500 rad/s, with all other data unchanged. Use exact expressions for magnitude and phase unless a part says otherwise, and state the phase in degrees.

  1. (a) Find the exact magnitude of G(jω) in dB at ω = 20 rad/s. [3]
  2. (b) Find the exact phase of G(jω) at ω = 20 rad/s, in degrees. [3]
  3. (c) Find the gain crossover frequency of the original system, in rad/s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the phase margin of the original system. [5]
  5. (e) Find the phase margin with the faster valve (corner at 500 rad/s) and state in one sentence why it changed. [5]
(a)

Magnitude of a product is the product of magnitudes. At ω = 20: the integrator gives 1/20 = 0.05, the first lag gives 1/√(1 + (20/10)²) = 1/√5 = 0.4472, and the second gives 1/√(1 + (20/100)²) = 1/√1.04 = 0.9806. Then |G| = 10 × 0.05 × 0.4472 × 0.9806 = 0.2193. In decibels, 20 log10(0.2193) = -13.18 dB. The straight-line sketch gives 20 log10(10/20) = -6.0 dB from the integrator line, then a further -20 log10(20/10) = -6.0 dB beyond the corner at 10 rad/s, so -12.0 dB. The exact value is about 1.2 dB lower, which is the usual error one octave above a corner. The exact figure is -13.2 dB.

Answer: -13.2 dB

(b)

Each factor contributes its own phase and they add. The integrator contributes -90 degrees. The lag at 10 rad/s contributes -atan(20/10) = -atan(2) = -63.43 degrees. The lag at 100 rad/s contributes -atan(20/100) = -atan(0.2) = -11.31 degrees. The total is -90 - 63.43 - 11.31 = -164.74 degrees.
