A hand sketch would use the straight-line phase approximation, which would place the first lag near -63 degrees only roughly; the exact arctangent value is better here, and it shows the loop already has less than 15 degrees of extra lag from the valve at this frequency. The phase at 20 rad/s is -164.7 degrees.

Answer: -164.7 degrees

(c)

The gain crossover is where |G(jω)| = 1. Write the condition as 10 = ω √(1 + (ω/10)²) √(1 + (ω/100)²). The left side is constant and the right side increases monotonically with ω, so there is exactly one root. Because no simple closed form exists for the product of the two square roots, solve numerically by bisection or Newton iteration. At ω = 8 the right side is 8 × 1.2806 × 1.0032 = 10.28, slightly above 10, and at ω = 7.5 it is 7.5 × 1.2500 × 1.0028 = 9.40, so the root lies just under 8. The converged value is ω_gc = 7.84 rad/s. This is the frequency at which phase margin must be read.

Answer: 7.8 rad/s

(d)

Phase margin is PM = 180 degrees + phase of G(jω_gc). At ω_gc = 7.84 rad/s the integrator gives -90 degrees, the first lag gives -atan(7.84/10) = -38.11 degrees, and the second lag gives -atan(7.84/100) = -4.49 degrees. The sum is -132.60 degrees. Therefore PM = 180 + (-132.60) = 47.40 degrees. A phase margin near 47 degrees corresponds, by the usual second-order rule of thumb PM ≈ 100ζ, to a damping ratio around 0.45, so a step response overshoot of about 20 percent would be expected, a sensible result for a press that must settle quickly without hammering the stops. The phase margin is 47.4 degrees.

Answer: 47.4 degrees

(e)

Moving the valve corner to 500 rad/s changes only the second factor. The new crossover solves 10 = ω √(1 + (ω/10)²) √(1 + (ω/500)²). The second root is almost unity at these frequencies, so the crossover rises slightly to 7.86 rad/s, since the second lag removes less magnitude. The phase at that frequency is -90 - atan(7.86/10) - atan(7.86/500) = -129.07 degrees, so PM = 180 + (-129.07) = 50.93 degrees. The margin improves by 3.5 degrees because a faster valve adds less phase lag near crossover: the delay of the spool is pushed well above the crossover frequency. The new phase margin is 50.9 degrees, which also improves the overshoot estimate and shortens the settling time.

Answer: 50.9 degrees

Problem 2 [A3-052] Gain and phase margins

A thickness control loop on a rolling mill has the open-loop transfer function L(s) = K / [ (s + 1)(s + 3)(s + 6) ] with unity negative feedback. The three real poles represent the hydraulic gap actuator, the strip transport and the thickness gauge filter, in rad/s. The controller is a simple proportional gain, currently set to K = 60. Operators report that the loop becomes sluggish and rings when the strip alloy changes, and maintenance suspects that the effective loop gain drifts upward by about 40 percent with the harder alloy. A reviewer asks for the stability margins at the present setting, for the gain that would give a conventional 10 dB gain margin, and for an estimate of what the drift does to the margin. Give frequencies in rad/s, margins in dB or degrees.

  1. (a) Find the phase crossover frequency, where the phase of L(jω) equals -180 degrees. [4]
  2. (b) Find the gain margin at K = 60, in dB. [4]
  3. (c) Find the gain crossover frequency at K = 60, in rad/s, and the phase margin in degrees. Give the phase margin as your answer. [6]
  4. (d) Find the new gain margin in dB if the effective gain drifts 40 percent upward from K = 60, and say what it implies. [6]
(a)

At the phase crossover the three lags add to -180 degrees: atan(ω) + atan(ω/3) + atan(ω/6) = 180 degrees (π rad). No static gain affects phase, so K plays no role. Solve numerically, or use the tangent addition formula. A neat route is the cubic that results from setting the imaginary part of the denominator (s+1)(s+3)(s+6) = s³ + 10s² + 27s + 18 to zero at s = jω: the imaginary part is -ω³ + 27ω, which vanishes when ω² = 27. Hence ω_pc = √27 = 5.196 rad/s. Check: atan(5.196) + atan(1.732) + atan(0.866) = 79.1 + 60.0 + 40.9 = 180 degrees, as required. The phase crossover is 5.20 rad/s.

Answer: 5.20 rad/s

(b)

The gain margin is the factor by which K can rise before |L(jω_pc)| reaches 1. At ω_pc = √27 the real part of the denominator is 10(−27) + 18 = −252, and the imaginary part is zero, so |denominator| = 252 and |L| = K/252. Thus the limiting gain is K_max = 252. At K = 60 the margin as a ratio is 252/60 = 4.20. In decibels GM = 20 log10(252/60) = 20 log10(4.20) = 12.46 dB. A conventional design asks for at least 6 dB and ideally 10 dB, so this setting is acceptable but not generous: the loop becomes unstable if the gain rises by a factor 4.20. The gain margin is 12.5 dB.

Answer: 12.5 dB

(c)

First locate the gain crossover by solving 60 / √[(1+ω²)(9+ω²)(36+ω²)] = 1, which is (1+ω²)(9+ω²)(36+ω²) = 3600. Let u = ω². The product is increasing in u, so there is one root; numerical solution gives ω_gc = 2.274 rad/s. Then the phase there is -[atan(2.274) + atan(2.274/3) + atan(2.274/6)] = -124.18 degrees. Phase margin = 180 + (-124.18) = 55.82 degrees. A margin of this size indicates a well damped transient response, though the type-0 loop has a steady-state error of 1/(1 + 60/18) = 0.231 of the setpoint, which the supervisor must accept or remove with integral action. The phase margin is 55.8 degrees.

Answer: 55.8 degrees

(d)

A 40 percent drift gives an effective gain of 60 × 1.4 = 84. The limiting gain is still 252, because the phase crossover does not depend on K. The gain margin ratio becomes 252/84 = 3.00, and in decibels GM = 20 log10(3.00) = 9.54 dB. That is a drop of 2.92 dB from the 12.5 dB at the nominal setting, since 20 log10(1.4) = 2.92 dB. The margin falls below the 10 dB target but stays above 6 dB, so the loop remains stable and only mildly more oscillatory. The remedy is either to reduce K by about 1.4 or to schedule the gain by alloy. The new gain margin is 9.5 dB.

Answer: 9.5 dB

Problem 3 [A3-053] Nyquist stability

A kiln heating zone is controlled with a proportional controller of gain K. The open-loop transfer function, including the thermocouple transport delay, is L(s) = K e-0.5 s / (2 s + 1), with time in seconds and unity negative feedback. The plant has no right-half-plane poles, so the Nyquist criterion requires that the locus of L(jω) not encircle the point -1. The plant manager wants to know how large the proportional gain can be, how much margin the present setting K = 3 has, and what happens if the thermocouple is relocated farther from the burner so that the delay doubles to 1.0 s. Use radians for angles inside the exponential and give frequencies in rad/s.

  1. (a) Find the frequency at which the Nyquist locus crosses the negative real axis. [5]
  2. (b) Find the largest K for which the closed loop remains stable. [5]
  3. (c) Find the gain margin in dB at K = 3. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest stable K if the delay doubles to 1.0 s, and compare with part (b). [6]
(a)

The delay contributes phase -ωT without changing magnitude, and the first-order lag contributes -atan(2ω). The locus crosses the negative real axis when the total phase is -π: 0.5ω + atan(2ω) = π. Define f(ω) = 0.5ω + atan(2ω) - π. At ω = 3, f = 1.5 + 1.4056 - 3.1416 = -0.236, and at ω = 4, f = 2.0 + 1.4464 - 3.1416 = 0.305, so the root lies between them. A few Newton or bisection steps give ω_pc = 3.4310 rad/s. At this frequency the phase is exactly -180 degrees, so L(jω) is real and negative. Because the delay is a pure phase term, the crossing occurs at a frequency far above the plant corner at 0.5 rad/s, where the lag contributes nearly -90 degrees. The crossing frequency is 3.431 rad/s.

Answer: 3.431 rad/s

(b)

At the crossing, L is real and negative, with magnitude |L| = K/√(1 + (2ω)²) because the delay has unit magnitude. Stability needs this crossing to lie to the right of -1, that is |L(jω_pc)| < 1. At ω_pc = 3.431: 2ω = 6.862, √(1 + 47.087) = 6.935. Therefore |L| = K/6.935 and the limit is K_max = 6.935. For K above this value the full locus (both frequency signs) encircles -1 clockwise twice, so Z = N + P = 2 + 0 = 2 and the closed loop has a right-half-plane pole pair. The largest stable gain is 6.93. Notice that a plain first-order plant with no delay would be stable for any K, so all of the limit is caused by the delay.

Answer: 6.93

(c)

The gain margin is the ratio of the critical gain to the operating gain. With K_max = 6.935 and K = 3 the ratio is 6.935/3 = 2.312. In decibels, GM = 20 log10(2.312) = 7.28 dB. This is the amount by which the loop gain could be increased before the Nyquist curve touches -1. A margin of about 7.3 dB is slightly above the 6 dB commonly requested for process loops, so the present setting is acceptable, but a rise in plant gain of 2.31 times, from a burner change for instance, would destabilize the zone. The result is 7.28 dB.

Answer: 7.28 dB

(d)

With T = 1.0 the phase equation becomes ω + atan(2ω) = π. At ω = 1.5 the left side is 1.5 + 1.249 = 2.749, below π, and at ω = 2.0 it is 2.0 + 1.326 = 3.326, above π, so the root lies between. Solving numerically gives ω_pc = 1.8366 rad/s. The critical gain is K_max = √(1 + (2ω_pc)²) = √(1 + 13.492) = 3.807. Compared with 6.935 before, the limit drops by a factor 1.82. At the present K = 3 the loop is now only 3.807/3 = 1.27 times from instability (2.07 dB), so relocating the thermocouple eats most of the margin and K would need to be reduced. The new maximum gain is 3.81.

Answer: 3.81

Problem 4 [A3-054] PID controller tuning

A reflow oven conveyor drive has a measured velocity-loop plant G(s) = 3 / [ (s + 1)(2 s + 1)(0.5 s + 1) ] with time in seconds. A technician applies the closed-loop (ultimate sensitivity) Ziegler-Nichols method: with only proportional control, raise the gain until the loop oscillates steadily at constant amplitude, record the ultimate gain K_u and ultimate period P_u, and then set Kp = 0.6 K_u, Ti = P_u/2 and Td = P_u/8 for a PID controller in standard form. Later the drive is rebuilt so that the plant gain becomes 6 instead of 3, with the same dynamics, and the technician wonders whether the previously tuned proportional gain can be reused. Use radians in the phase calculations and give times in seconds.

  1. (a) Find the ultimate gain K_u for the original plant. [5]
  2. (b) Find the ultimate period P_u, in seconds. [4]
  3. (c) Find the Ziegler-Nichols integral time Ti, in seconds. [3]
  4. (d) With the plant gain doubled and the old Kp kept, find the gain margin of the proportional part alone, in dB, and state whether the loop is stable. [8]
(a)

Steady oscillation occurs when the loop with proportional gain K has L(jω) = -1, so the phase must equal -180 degrees. The phase of the plant is -[atan(ω) + atan(2ω) + atan(0.5ω)]. Setting the sum to π and solving numerically gives the ultimate frequency ω_u = 1.8708 rad/s. There the magnitude of the plant without gain is 3/√[(1 + ω²)(1 + 4ω²)(1 + 0.25ω²)] = 0.2667. For the loop gain to equal 1, K_u = 1/0.2667 = 3.750. A gain below this gives a damped response, above it an unstable, growing oscillation. In practice the technician would find this by raising K slowly, but the model gives it directly. The ultimate gain is K_u = 3.750.

Answer: 3.750

(b)

The ultimate period follows from the ultimate frequency found in part (a). With ω_u = 1.8708 rad/s the period is P_u = 2π/ω_u = 6.2832/1.8708 = 3.359 s. This is the period of the sustained oscillation the technician would measure on the strip chart, and it carries the information about the dominant dynamics. It is longer than the largest plant time constant of 2 s by a factor about 1.7, which is typical of third-order plants whose combined lags push the phase crossover well above the slowest corner. The ultimate period is 3.359 s.

Answer: 3.359 s

(c)

The Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop rule for a PID controller sets the integral time to half the ultimate period: Ti = P_u/2. Using P_u = 3.359 s from part (b), Ti = 3.359/2 = 1.679 s. The remaining settings for completeness are Kp = 0.6 K_u = 0.6 × 3.750 = 2.250 and Td = P_u/8 = 0.420 s. The integral time sets how fast the controller removes the steady-state offset; the rule places the integral corner well below the oscillation frequency, which keeps the added phase lag modest. The integral time is 1.679 s.

Answer: 1.679 s

(d)

Doubling the plant gain doubles the loop gain at every frequency, so the new ultimate gain is half the old one: K_u,new = 3.750/2 = 1.875. The old proportional gain was Kp = 0.6 K_u = 2.250, which is now 1.200 times the new ultimate gain. The gain margin of the P part alone is the ratio of ultimate gain to operating gain: GM = 20 log10(1.875/2.250) = 20 log10(0.8333) = -1.58 dB. A negative margin means the loop is unstable, since the gain exceeds the critical value. The old tuning cannot be reused, and Kp must be cut by at least a factor of about 1.2 and preferably to 0.3 K_u,old. The margin is -1.58 dB, so the loop is unstable.

Answer: -1.58 dB

Problem 5 [A3-055] Lead and lag compensator design

A pan-tilt camera mount on a patrol vessel has the open-loop transfer function G(s) = 20 / [ s (0.2 s + 1) ] with unity negative feedback, with time in seconds. The designer wants a phase margin of at least 50 degrees and decides on a lead compensator C(s) = (1 + aTs)/(1 + Ts), with a = 1/α and α < 1, placed so that its maximum phase lead occurs at the new gain crossover. A 5 degree allowance is added to the required lead to cover the crossover shift caused by the compensator. After a first design review, a second proposal asks what would happen if the allowance were 15 degrees instead of 5 degrees, to leave more room for sensor lag that was neglected. Use the standard relationships for a lead network and give angles in degrees.

  1. (a) Find the gain crossover frequency of the uncompensated system, in rad/s, and its phase margin. Give the phase margin. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum phase lead required, in degrees, with the 5 degree allowance. [3]
  3. (c) Find the lead ratio α = (1 - sin φm)/(1 + sin φm) for that lead. [4]
  4. (d) Find the frequency, in rad/s, at which the compensator's maximum lead should be placed (the new crossover). [5]
  5. (e) Find α if the allowance is 15 degrees rather than 5 degrees, and state the consequence for noise amplification. [4]
(a)

The gain crossover satisfies 20 = ω √(1 + 0.04ω²). Squaring gives 400 = ω² + 0.04ω⁴. With u = ω², 0.04u² + u - 400 = 0, so u = [-1 + √(1 + 64)]/0.08 = 88.28 and ω_gc = 9.396 rad/s. The phase there is -90 - atan(0.2 × 9.396) = -90 - 61.98 = -151.98 degrees. The phase margin is 180 + (-151.98) = 28.02 degrees. This is well below the 50 degrees demanded, so the system would respond with strong overshoot, and a lead network is needed to supply the missing phase. The uncompensated phase margin is 28.0 degrees.

Answer: 28.0 degrees

(b)

The compensator must raise the phase margin from 28.0 to 50 degrees, which requires 22.0 degrees. The lead network also raises the crossover frequency, where the plant phase is more negative, so an allowance of 5 degrees is added to compensate for this shift. The required maximum lead is φm = 50 - 28.0 + 5 = 27.0 degrees. This is within the practical range of a single lead stage, which can give up to about 60 degrees before the pole-zero separation becomes impractically large and the high-frequency gain amplifies sensor noise. The required maximum lead is 27.0 degrees.

Answer: 27.0 degrees

(c)

For a lead network the maximum phase occurs at the geometric mean of the zero and pole and has magnitude sin φm = (1 - α)/(1 + α). Solving for α gives α = (1 - sin φm)/(1 + sin φm). With φm = 27.0 degrees, sin φm = 0.4537. So α = (1 - 0.4537)/(1 + 0.4537) = 0.5463/1.4537 = 0.3758. With this form the zero is at α/T and the pole at 1/T, so the pole is 1/α = 2.66 times the zero frequency. The high-frequency gain of the lead network is 1/α = 2.66, equal to 8.5 dB, so this is how much extra loop gain appears at high frequency. The ratio is α = 0.376.

Answer: 0.376

(d)

At its centre frequency the lead network has gain 1/√α, so the loop magnitude with compensation equals 1 at the frequency where the uncompensated magnitude equals √α. Hence solve 20/[ω√(1 + 0.04ω²)] = √0.3758 = 0.6130. Squaring and rearranging: ω²(1 + 0.04ω²) = 400/0.3758 = 1064.3. With u = ω², 0.04u² + u - 1064.3 = 0, giving u = 151.1 and ω = 12.29 rad/s. The lead zero is then at ω_m√α = 7.54 rad/s and the pole at ω_m/√α = 20.05 rad/s. Place the maximum lead at 12.29 rad/s, which becomes the new gain crossover.

Answer: 12.29 rad/s

(e)

With a 15 degree allowance the required lead is φm = 50 - 28.0 + 15 = 37.0 degrees, so sin φm = 0.6015 and α = (1 - 0.6015)/(1 + 0.6015) = 0.2488. Compared with the earlier ratio of 0.3758, the pole is pushed to a higher frequency and the high-frequency gain increases from 2.66 to 4.02, that is from 8.5 dB to 12.1 dB. The extra 10 degrees of lead buys a safer margin against neglected sensor lag, but the compensated loop amplifies high-frequency noise about 1.5 times more, so encoder noise and quantization would be more visible in the torque command. The ratio is α = 0.249.

Answer: 0.249

A3 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A3-056] State-space models

An engine mounted on a rubber isolator is modelled as a mass-spring-damper. The engine and bracket have mass m = 15 kg, the isolator has stiffness k = 24 000 N/m and viscous damping c = 300 N·s/m. Define the state vector x = [position; velocity] of the mass relative to the frame, with the input u being a force in newtons, so that ẋ = A x + B u with A = [[0, 1], [-k/m, -c/m]] and B = [0; 1/m]. The workshop wants to understand the free response, then asks what happens if ageing halves the isolator damping to c = 150 N·s/m while stiffness and mass are unchanged. Use the characteristic equation of A to answer, and give the overshoot of the unit-step response as a percentage using the standard second-order relationship.

  1. (a) Find the real part of the eigenvalues of A (the decay rate σ) for the original isolator, in 1/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the damped natural frequency ω_d of the original system, in rad/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the damping ratio ζ of the original system. [4]
  4. (d) Find the step-response percent overshoot after the damping is halved to c = 150 N·s/m. [8]
(a)

The eigenvalues satisfy det(sI - A) = s² + (c/m)s + k/m = 0. With c/m = 300/15 = 20 and k/m = 24 000/15 = 1600, the characteristic equation is s² + 20s + 1600 = 0. The roots are s = -10 ± j√(1600 - 100) = -10 ± j38.73. The real part is therefore σ = -c/(2m) = -10 1/s, which is half the trace of A. The envelope of the free motion decays as e-10t, giving a time constant of 0.1 s and a settling time within 2 percent of about 4/10 = 0.4 s. The eigenvalue real part is -10.00 1/s.

Answer: -10.00 1/s

(b)

The imaginary parts of the eigenvalues give the damped frequency. From s² + 20s + 1600 = 0 the discriminant is 20² - 4 × 1600 = -6000, so the roots are s = [-20 ± j√6000]/2 = -10 ± j38.7298. Therefore ω_d = 38.73 rad/s, which corresponds to a damped frequency of 6.16 Hz. Check with ω_d = ω_n√(1 - ζ²) = 40 × √(1 - 0.0625) = 38.73 rad/s, using ω_n = √(k/m) = √1600 = 40 rad/s and ζ = 0.25. The damped frequency is only about 3 percent below the undamped value, as is typical for lightly damped isolators. The damped frequency is 38.73 rad/s.

Answer: 38.73 rad/s

(c)

The damping ratio compares actual damping with the critical value. Critical damping is c_c = 2√(km) = 2√(24 000 × 15) = 2 × 600 = 1200 N·s/m. Therefore ζ = c/c_c = 300/1200 = 0.250. The same value follows from the characteristic polynomial s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n², where 2ζω_n = 20 and ω_n = 40, so ζ = 20/(2 × 40) = 0.250. A damping ratio of 0.25 is quite light: the transient oscillates for several cycles, and rubber mounts of this kind are usually chosen between 0.1 and 0.3 as a compromise between isolation at high frequency and resonance peak. The damping ratio is 0.250.

Answer: 0.250

(d)

Halving the damper gives c = 150 N·s/m. The natural frequency is unchanged at 40 rad/s but the damping ratio halves: ζ = 150/1200 = 0.1250. The percent overshoot for the unit step of a standard second-order system is %OS = 100 exp(-πζ/√(1 - ζ²)). With ζ = 0.1250, √(1 - ζ²) = 0.9922, and the exponent is -π × 0.1250/0.9922 = -0.3958, so %OS = 100 × e-0.3958 = 67.3 percent. Before the change, ζ = 0.25 would have given about 44.4 percent, so ageing raises overshoot by roughly 23 percentage points. Check the mount: the real part of the eigenvalues moves to -5 1/s, doubling the ring-down time. The overshoot is 67.3 percent.

Answer: 67.3 percent

Problem 2 [A3-057] Servo motor position control

A DC servo motor drives a camera focus ring through a stiff gear train. The armature resistance is R = 1.2 Ω, torque constant K_t = 0.05 N·m/A, back-emf constant K_b = 0.05 V·s/rad, viscous friction b = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ N·m·s/rad and the total inertia reflected to the motor shaft is J = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m². Armature inductance is negligible. The motor is driven by an amplifier of voltage gain K_a, in a unity feedback position loop where the position error in radians is multiplied by K_a. The designer will first obtain the plant parameters, then set K_a for a damping ratio of 0.7, and finally check what happens when a heavier lens triples the load inertia to 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m² with the amplifier gain unchanged. Neglect backlash.

  1. (a) Find the motor gain K_m = Θ(s)/V(s) low-frequency constant in rad/s per volt, where the plant is K_m / [ s (τ s + 1) ]. [4]
  2. (b) Find the mechanical time constant τ, in seconds. [4]
  3. (c) Find the amplifier gain K_a that gives ζ = 0.7 in the original system, in V/rad. [6]
  4. (d) With the load inertia tripled and K_a unchanged, find the percent overshoot of the step response. [6]
(a)

With negligible inductance, the armature equation is V = R i + K_b ω and the torque balance is K_t i = J dω/dt + b ω. Eliminating the current gives (R J) dω/dt + (R b + K_t K_b) ω = K_t V. In the Laplace domain, Ω/V = K_t / [R J s + (R b + K_t K_b)], and Θ/V = Ω/(V s). The denominator constant is R b + K_t K_b = 1.2 × 1.0×10⁻⁴ + 0.05 × 0.05 = 1.2×10⁻⁴ + 2.5×10⁻³ = 0.00262. Dividing numerator and denominator by this constant gives the standard form with K_m = K_t/0.00262 = 19.08 rad/(s·V). Note that the back-emf term dominates the friction, which is typical of small permanent magnet motors. The motor gain is 19.08 rad/(s·V).

Answer: 19.08 rad/(s·V)

(b)

From the same transfer function, the denominator is R J s + (R b + K_t K_b). Dividing by the constant term gives (τ s + 1) with τ = R J/(R b + K_t K_b). The numerator R J = 1.2 × 2.0×10⁻⁴ = 2.4×10⁻⁴ and the denominator constant is 0.00262, so τ = 2.4×10⁻⁴/0.00262 = 0.0916 s. This is the time the unloaded speed takes to reach 63 percent of its final value for a voltage step, about 92 ms. The time constant would be longer without the back-emf term, which acts like a strong electrical damper, so electrical damping dominates the mechanical friction here. The mechanical time constant is 0.0916 s.

Answer: 0.0916 s

(c)

With unity feedback and an amplifier gain K_a, the closed-loop characteristic equation is τ s² + s + K_a K_m = 0, or s² + (1/τ)s + K_a K_m/τ = 0. Compare with s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n². Then ω_n² = K_a K_m/τ and 2ζω_n = 1/τ. Eliminating ω_n gives ζ = 1/(2√(K_a K_m τ)), so K_a = 1/(4ζ² K_m τ). With ζ = 0.7, 4ζ² = 1.96 and K_m τ = 19.08 × 0.0916 = 1.7481. Thus K_a = 1/(1.96 × 1.7481) = 0.292 V/rad. The corresponding natural frequency is ω_n = √(K_a K_m/τ) = 7.8 rad/s. The amplifier gain is 0.292 V/rad.

Answer: 0.292 V/rad

(d)

Tripling the inertia triples the time constant, since τ = RJ/(R b + K_t K_b) and the denominator is unchanged: τ' = 3 × 0.0916 = 0.2748 s. The motor gain K_m is unchanged because it does not depend on J. With K_a = 0.292 V/rad, the new damping ratio is ζ' = 1/(2√(K_a K_m τ')) = 1/(2√(1.531)) = 0.4041. The percent overshoot is 100 exp(-πζ'/√(1 - ζ'²)) = 100 exp(-π × 0.4041/0.9147) = 25.0 percent. The original design at ζ = 0.7 gives about 4.6 percent, so the heavier lens raises overshoot by 20.4 points, because ζ falls by a factor √3. The overshoot is 25.0 percent, so the gain should be retuned or a rate feedback added.

Answer: 25.0 percent

Problem 3 [A3-058] Disturbance rejection

A conveyor belt carries aggregate to a crusher. Its speed y (m/s) responds to the controller output u (volts) through G_p(s) = 2/(5 s + 1), and to the load torque disturbance d (N·m) through G_d(s) = -0.5/(5 s + 1), so that Y = G_p U + G_d D. A proportional controller U = K_p (R - Y) is used with the speed set-point R held constant at zero deviation for this analysis. When a heavy load arrives, the disturbance steps by 4 N·m. The plant manager wants to know the steady speed drop with K_p = 10, then what happens if the gain is cut to K_p = 5 to reduce motor noise, and what gain would keep the steady deviation below 0.05 m/s. Finally, ask how fast the loop recovers at the original gain.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the steady-state speed deviation (speed drop) caused by the 4 N·m disturbance step with K_p = 10, in m/s. [5]
  2. (b) Find the steady-state deviation if the gain is cut to K_p = 5, in m/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the smallest K_p that keeps the steady deviation at or below 0.05 m/s. [5]
  4. (d) Find the closed-loop time constant with K_p = 10, in seconds. [6]
(a)

With R = 0, the output depends on the disturbance through Y = G_d D/(1 + K_p G_p). In the steady state after a step, the final value theorem requires only the DC gains: G_d(0) = -0.5 and G_p(0) = 2. The disturbance step is D = 4 N·m. The deviation is Y_ss = -0.5 × 4/(1 + K_p × 2) = -2/(1 + 2 K_p), so the magnitude of the speed drop is 2/(1 + 2 K_p). With K_p = 10, the drop is 2/21 = 0.0952 m/s. This is the speed drop of the belt under load, about 4.8 percent of an assumed 2 m/s nominal speed. A proportional controller cannot remove it fully because a non-zero error is needed to produce the compensating control signal. The steady deviation is 0.0952 m/s.

Answer: 0.0952 m/s

(b)

The same expression applies with the new gain: Y_ss = 2/(1 + 2K_p). For K_p = 5, the denominator is 1 + 10 = 11, so Y_ss = 2/11 = 0.1818 m/s. Halving the gain increases the deviation from 0.0952 to 0.1818, a rise of 1.91 times, which is a smaller increase than the factor of 2 in gain might suggest because the 1 in the denominator is the open-loop (uncontrolled) part. The reduction in motor noise is therefore paid for with a clearly larger speed sag when the heavy load arrives. Without feedback at all (K_p = 0), the drop would be 2 m/s, which shows how much the loop helps. The deviation at K_p = 5 is 0.1818 m/s.

Answer: 0.1818 m/s

(c)

Set the deviation limit: 2/(1 + 2K_p) ≤ 0.05. Rearranging, 1 + 2K_p ≥ 2/0.05 = 40, so 2K_p ≥ 39 and K_p ≥ 19.5. The smallest acceptable proportional gain is therefore K_p = 19.5. At that gain the loop gain at DC is 2K_p = 39, and the closed-loop DC gain from reference to output is 39/40 = 0.975, so the set-point tracking error is 2.5 percent as well. Higher gain reduces the sag but increases the amplifier noise passed to the motor and tightens limits from actuator saturation, so an integral term would normally be preferred over simply raising K_p. The required gain is 19.5.

Answer: 19.5

(d)

The closed loop is Y = [G_p K_p/(1 + K_p G_p)]R + [G_d/(1 + K_p G_p)]D. The characteristic equation is 1 + K_p × 2/(5s + 1) = 0, i.e. 5s + 1 + 2K_p = 0. The pole is at s = -(1 + 2K_p)/5. For K_p = 10, s = -21/5 = -4.2 1/s, so the closed-loop time constant is τ_cl = 5/21 = 0.238 s. Compared with the open-loop 5 s, the speed loop recovers about 21 times faster, and the response reaches 95 percent of the final deviation after about 3τ_cl = 0.71 s. Feedback has therefore shrunk both the size and the duration of the disturbance effect. The time constant is 0.238 s.

Answer: 0.238 s

Problem 4 [A3-059] Sampled data and digital control basics

An oven heater element behaves as the first-order plant G(s) = 2/(s + 2), unit DC gain, with time in seconds. A digital controller samples the temperature and updates the heater through a zero-order hold at sample period T. The pulse transfer function of the hold and plant is G(z) = (1 - p)/(z - p) with p = e-2T. The controller is a discrete proportional gain K with unity negative feedback, so the closed-loop characteristic equation is z - p + K(1 - p) = 0. The engineer first uses T = 0.25 s, then considers lengthening T to 1.0 s to relieve the processor load. Give closed-loop poles as real numbers in the z-plane and state stability using the unit-circle criterion |z| < 1.

  1. (a) Find the plant pole p in the z-plane for T = 0.25 s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the largest K for which the closed loop is stable at T = 0.25 s. [5]
  3. (c) Find the closed-loop pole at K = 2 with T = 0.25 s. [5]
  4. (d) Find the largest stable K when the sample period is lengthened to T = 1.0 s, and comment on the change. [6]
(a)

Exact discretization of a first-order plant with a zero-order hold maps the continuous pole s = -2 to z = esT. For T = 0.25 s: p = e-2 × 0.25 = e-0.5 = 0.6065. The pole lies inside the unit circle, so the open-loop sampled plant is stable, as expected for a stable continuous plant. The numerator (1 - p) = 0.3935 keeps the DC gain at 1, since G(1) = (1 - p)/(1 - p) = 1. A slower sampling rate moves p closer to the origin, while a faster rate moves it towards 1, because the plant changes only slightly during one short sample interval. The pole is at 0.6065.

Answer: 0.6065

(b)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is z - p + K(1 - p) = 0, giving the single pole z = p - K(1 - p). Stability requires |z| < 1. The positive limit is no problem for small K; the negative limit is reached when p - K(1 - p) = -1, so K = (1 + p)/(1 - p). With p = 0.6065, K_max = (1 + 0.6065)/(1 - 0.6065) = 1.6065/0.3935 = 4.083. Beyond this the pole leaves the unit circle through -1 and the loop oscillates with alternating sign each sample. The corresponding continuous design would be stable for every K, so the limit is entirely a result of sampling. The maximum stable gain is 4.083.

Answer: 4.083

(c)

Insert K = 2 and p = 0.6065 into z = p - K(1 - p). Then 1 - p = 0.3935 and K(1 - p) = 0.7869. The pole is z = 0.6065 - 0.7869 = -0.1804. Its magnitude 0.1804 is below 1, so the loop is stable, and since it is negative the response alternates in sign from sample to sample while decaying, a ringing at half the sampling frequency. A pole near zero would be a deadbeat design, and at K = 1/(1 - p) × p, i.e. K = 1.541, the pole would be exactly at the origin. The closed-loop pole at K = 2 is -0.1804.

Answer: -0.1804

(d)

For T = 1.0 s the plant pole is p = e-2 = 0.1353. The same stability limit applies: K_max = (1 + p)/(1 - p) = (1 + 0.1353)/(1 - 0.1353) = 1.1353/0.8647 = 1.313. Compared with 4.083 at T = 0.25 s, the allowable gain has dropped by a factor of 3.11. So the longer sample period is cheaper for the processor but cuts the gain margin: the K = 2 setting that worked at 4 Hz would now be unstable, since 2 exceeds 1.313. Lengthening T cuts the available gain because more time passes between corrections; the sampled loop sees the plant as having a delay of about half a sample. The maximum stable gain is 1.313.

Answer: 1.313

Problem 5 [A3-060] Control of a liquid level or temperature process

A cylindrical storage tank of cross-sectional area A = 0.8 m² drains through a fixed valve whose outflow follows q_out = 0.004 √h in m³/s, with the liquid height h in metres. Inflow q_in is the manipulated variable. At the operating point the level is h0 = 1.6 m and the system is at equilibrium. For small deviations the plant is linearized as H(s)/Q(s) = R/(R A s + 1), where R is the incremental resistance dh/dq_out evaluated at the operating point. The inflow is then stepped up by Δq = 0.0005 m³/s. The plant supervisor also wants to know how the dynamics change if the nominal operating level is raised to h0 = 3.6 m with the same valve. Give times in seconds and heights in metres.

  1. (a) Find the incremental resistance R at h0 = 1.6 m, in s/m². [4]
  2. (b) Find the time constant τ = R A at h0 = 1.6 m, in seconds. [3]
  3. (c) Find the final steady rise in level caused by the 0.0005 m³/s step, in metres. [4]
  4. (d) Find the time for the level to complete 90 percent of that rise, in seconds. [4]
  5. (e) Find the new time constant when the operating level is raised to h0 = 3.6 m, in seconds. [5]
(a)

The outflow is q_out = C√h with C = 0.004. Linearizing about h0 gives the incremental slope dq_out/dh = C/(2√h0), and the resistance is its reciprocal: R = 2√h0/C. At h0 = 1.6 m, √1.6 = 1.2649, so R = 2 × 1.2649/0.004 = 632.5 s/m². As a check, the equilibrium outflow is q0 = 0.004 × 1.2649 = 0.00506 m³/s, and R = 2h0/q0 = 3.2/0.00506 = 632.5 s/m², the same. A bigger R means a small change in flow produces a bigger level change, which is why a nearly closed valve gives a slow, sensitive tank. The resistance is 632.5 s/m².

Answer: 632.5 s/m²

(b)

For a tank with linearized outlet, the mass balance A dh/dt = q_in - q_out gives A dh/dt = Δq_in - Δh/R. In Laplace form, H/Q = R/(RAs + 1), so the time constant is τ = R A. With R = 632.5 s/m² and A = 0.8 m², τ = 632.5 × 0.8 = 506.0 s, about 8.4 minutes. The level therefore reacts slowly: a plant with this time constant needs more than half an hour to settle completely after a disturbance, since five time constants are about 2530 s. The time constant is 506.0 s.

Answer: 506.0 s

(c)

After a step in inflow, the linearized level approaches h = Δq R (1 - e-t/τ). The final value is the DC gain times the step: Δh = R Δq = 632.5 × 0.0005 = 0.3162 m. This is a rise of 0.316 m on a base level of 1.6 m, about 20 percent, so the linearization remains plausible. Check by outflow balance: at the new equilibrium the outflow must rise by 0.0005 m³/s, from 0.00506 to 0.00556 m³/s, which needs √h = 0.00556/0.004, h = 1.9319 m. The exact nonlinear rise is 0.3319 m, within a few percent of the linear result. The rise is 0.3162 m.

Answer: 0.3162 m

(d)

The step response is Δh(t) = Δh_final (1 - e-t/τ). To complete 90 percent of the rise, 1 - e-t/τ = 0.9, so e-t/τ = 0.1 and t = τ ln 10 = 2.3026 τ. With τ = 506.0 s, t90 = 2.3026 × 506.0 = 1165 s, which is about 19.4 minutes (2.3 time constants). If the process were controlled by a proportional controller the loop would speed this up, but the open-loop tank takes this long on its own. The same factor 2.3 applies to every first-order lag, which is a convenient rule. The 90 percent time is 1165 s.

Answer: 1165 s

(e)

The valve is the same but the operating level rises to h0 = 3.6 m. The incremental resistance changes because the outflow depends on the square root of the level: R = 2√h0/C. With √3.6 = 1.8974, R = 2 × 1.8974/0.004 = 948.7 s/m². The time constant becomes τ = R A = 948.7 × 0.8 = 758.9 s. Compared with 506.0 s, this is 1.50 times larger, which equals √(3.6/1.6) = 1.5, as the formula predicts since τ is proportional to √h0. The tank is therefore slower at high level, and a controller tuned at 1.6 m would be more sluggish at 3.6 m, a case for gain scheduling. The new time constant is 758.9 s.

Answer: 758.9 s

A3 Practice Paper 13

Problem 1 [A3-061] Mathematical models of mechanical systems

A packaging line indexing table is driven by a permanent-magnet DC motor through a speed-reducing gear train. The motor armature resistance is 2.0 Ω and its inductance is small enough to neglect. The torque constant and the back-emf constant are both 0.050 (N·m/A and V·s/rad). The rotor inertia is 2.0×10⁻⁵ kg·m² and motor friction is negligible. The gear ratio is 10:1, so the motor turns ten times for each turn of the table. The table and its tooling have a moment of inertia of 0.020 kg·m² about the table axis and a viscous friction coefficient of 0.050 N·m·s/rad at the table shaft. The gears are rigid and lossless. Armature voltage is the input and table angle is the output. You are building a lumped-parameter model of the drive and checking it against sizing data.

  1. (a) Find the equivalent inertia of the drive referred to the table shaft, in kg·m². [5]
  2. (b) Find the steady table speed in rad/s when a constant 12 V is applied to the armature. [6]
  3. (c) Find the time constant of the table speed response in seconds. [5]
  4. (d) Find the stall torque available at the table shaft with 12 V applied, in N·m. [4]
(a)

Treat the motor, gear train and table as one rigid assembly and refer every inertia to the table shaft. With gear ratio N = 10 the motor speed is N times the table speed, so equating kinetic energy gives the equivalent inertia J_eq = J_L + N²J_m. Substituting the data, N² = 100 and N²J_m = 100 × 2.0×10⁻⁵ = 0.0020 kg·m². Then J_eq = 0.020 + 0.0020 = 0.0220 kg·m². Assumptions: rigid shafts, lossless gears with no backlash, and negligible motor friction, all as stated. The rotor supplies about 9.1 percent of the total even though its own inertia is tiny, which is why the N² factor must be shown explicitly rather than quoted in drive sizing work.

Answer: 0.022 kg·m²

(b)

With inductance neglected the armature equation is V = R_a i + K_b ω_m, and the motor torque is T_m = K_t i. Referred to the table, the torque is N T_m and ω_m = N ω. Eliminating the current gives J_eq dω/dt + [b_L + N²K_tK_b/R_a] ω = (N K_t/R_a) V. The back-emf term acts as electrical damping: N²K_tK_b/R_a = 100 × 0.0025 / 2.0 = 0.1250 N·m·s/rad, so the total damping is b_eq = 0.050 + 0.1250 = 0.1750 N·m·s/rad. The gain is K = N K_t/R_a = 10 × 0.050/2.0 = 0.250. At steady state dω/dt = 0, so ω = K V / b_eq = 0.250 × 12 / 0.1750 = 17.143 rad/s, about 163.7 rev/min. Assumption: constant supply voltage and negligible Coulomb friction.

Answer: 17.14 rad/s

(c)

The speed equation obtained in part (b) is first order, J_eq dω/dt + b_eq ω = K V, with the transfer function from voltage to speed K/(J_eq s + b_eq). Dividing through by b_eq gives the standard form with time constant τ = J_eq / b_eq. Using J_eq = 0.0220 kg·m² from part (a) and b_eq = 0.1750 N·m·s/rad from part (b), τ = 0.0220 / 0.1750 = 0.1257 s. Since the table reaches about 63 percent of its final speed after one time constant and effectively full speed after four, the table settles in about 0.50 s. The model assumes constant parameters; the electrical damping from back-emf also dominates the shaft friction and therefore sets the response speed.

Answer: 0.1257 s

(d)

At stall the table speed is zero, so there is no back-emf and the armature current is limited only by resistance: i_stall = V/R_a = 12/2.0 = 6.0 A. The motor torque is T_m = K_t i_stall = 0.050 × 6.0 = 0.300 N·m. The gear train multiplies torque by N for the same power with lossless gears, so the torque at the table shaft is T = N K_t V / R_a = 10 × 0.300 = 3.000 N·m. This agrees with setting ω = 0 in the speed equation of part (b), where the steady torque balance gives b_eq ω = K V minus the load. In practice the supply current limit and thermal rating of the armature would cap this value, so it is an upper bound rather than a continuous rating.

Answer: 3 N·m

Problem 2 [A3-062] Electrical and thermal system analogues

A copper billet of mass 8.0 kg is heated for forging in an electric furnace whose gas temperature is held constant at 800 °C. The billet starts at 20 °C and must reach 600 °C. Its specific heat is 385 J/kg·K. The combined convective and radiative heat transfer coefficient is 25 W/m²·K over a surface area of 0.12 m². Treat the billet as a lumped body at uniform temperature, so conduction inside the copper is ignored. A colleague wants to study the heating process on an analogue computer built from a resistor and a capacitor connected to ground. The analogue is scaled so that 1 K of temperature is represented by 1 V and a heat flow of 1 W is represented by a current of 1 mA. You are asked to model the billet and build the analogue.

  1. (a) Find the thermal capacitance of the billet in J/K. [4]
  2. (b) Find the thermal time constant of the heating process in seconds. [3]
  3. (c) Find the time for the billet to reach 600 °C, in seconds. [6]
  4. (d) Find the resistor value for the electrical analogue in Ω. [3]
  5. (e) Find the capacitor value for the electrical analogue in F, keeping the analogue in real time. [4]
(a)

The thermal capacitance of a lumped body is the energy needed to raise its temperature by one kelvin, C_th = m c, the thermal equivalent of a capacitor storing charge. Substituting, C_th = 8.0 kg × 385 J/kg·K = 3080 J/K. The assumption of uniform temperature is reasonable when the Biot number is small; for copper, whose conductivity is near 400 W/m·K, the internal resistance is tiny compared with the surface film, so the lumped model holds. Only the temperature difference matters in the energy balance, so the absolute reference temperature does not affect C_th. The result will be combined with the film resistance in part (b) to give the process time constant, and it also sets the scaled capacitor needed in part (e).

Answer: 3080 J/K

(b)

The film resistance between furnace gas and billet surface is R_th = 1/(hA), analogous to an electrical resistor, with units K/W. Then R_th = 1/(25 × 0.12) = 0.3333 K/W. An energy balance on the billet gives C_th dT/dt = (T_∞ − T)/R_th, which is the equation of an RC circuit charging toward a source voltage. The time constant is the product of the resistance and the capacitance: τ = R_th C_th = 0.3333 × 3080 = 1026.7 s, about 17.1 minutes. Assumptions are a constant furnace temperature, a constant coefficient h and negligible internal gradients. The long time constant shows why large forgings need long soak times.

Answer: 1026.7 s

(c)

The solution of the first-order balance for a constant furnace temperature T_∞ is T(t) = T_∞ − (T_∞ − T_i) e−t/τ, the same as a capacitor charging through a resistor. Solving for time, t = τ ln[(T_∞ − T_i)/(T_∞ − T)]. Substituting, the initial driving difference is 800 − 20 = 780 K and the final difference is 800 − 600 = 200 K, so the ratio is 3.900 and its natural logarithm is 1.3610. Then t = 1026.7 × 1.3610 = 1397 s, about 23.3 minutes. Because the billet approaches the furnace temperature asymptotically, the last few degrees take disproportionately long, so reaching 800 °C would take infinite time on this model.

Answer: 1397.3 s

(d)

In the analogue, temperature maps to voltage and heat flow to current, so thermal resistance maps to electrical resistance through the scale factors. A temperature difference of 1 K is 1 V and a heat flow of 1 W is 1 mA, so the resistor is R_e = R_th × (1 V per K) / (1 mA per W). Substituting, R_e = 0.3333 K/W × 1 V/K ÷ 0.001 A/W = 333.3 Ω. Check by ohm's law: a 1 K difference gives 1 V, and the heat flow it drives is 1/0.3333 = 3.00 W, which the analogue represents as 3.00 mA through 333.3 Ω, giving back 1 V. The scaling is arbitrary; the product R_eC_e must equal the real time constant to keep real time.

Answer: 333.3 Ω

(e)

To keep the analogue in real time the electrical time constant must equal the thermal one, τ = R_eC_e. Equivalently, charge maps to energy: a capacitor holding charge Q at voltage V stores C_e = Q/V, and with 1 W mapped to 1 mA and 1 K to 1 V, one joule maps to one millicoulomb. Using the scale factors, C_e = C_th × (1 mA per W) / (1 V per K), where C_th is in J/K. Then C_e = 3080 × 0.001 = 3.080 F. Check the time constant: R_e C_e = 333.3 × 3.080 = 1026.7 s, which matches the thermal value of 1026.7 s. A capacitor this large is unrealistic as a single component, so in practice the analogue would be speeded up by scaling time, but this shows how an energy store maps to a capacitor.

Answer: 3.08 F

Problem 3 [A3-063] Hydraulic and pneumatic system models

A process-water buffer tank has a constant plan area of 0.50 m². Water leaves through a fixed valve so that the outflow follows q_out = k√h, where h is the water level in metres, q_out is in m³/s and k = 0.0040 m2.5/s. A metering pump supplies a constant inflow, and the tank is currently in equilibrium at a level of 1.60 m. The plant engineer wants a linear model for a level controller and also wants to know how far the linear model can be trusted. The pump flow is about to be increased by 10 percent from its present value, and the tank is allowed to settle completely. Assume incompressible flow, a vertical-walled tank and a valve coefficient that does not change with level or time.

  1. (a) Find the equilibrium outflow, equal to the present pump flow, in litres per second. [4]
  2. (b) Linearise the outflow about the operating point and find the hydraulic resistance R = dh/dq_out in s/m². [5]
  3. (c) Find the time constant of the linearised level response in seconds. [4]
  4. (d) After the 10 percent inflow increase, find the exact new equilibrium level using the nonlinear outflow law, in m. [4]
  5. (e) Find the percentage by which the linear model underestimates the true level rise, as a percentage of the true rise. [3]
(a)

At equilibrium the pump inflow equals the valve outflow, so q_0 = k√h_0. Substituting the data, √1.60 = 1.2649 m0.5 and q_0 = 0.0040 × 1.2649 = 0.005060 m³/s. Converting, 1 m³/s is 1000 L/s, so q_0 = 5.060 L/s. The tank is a mass-conservation device: dh/dt = (q_in − q_out)/A, which is zero at the operating point. Assumptions are incompressible liquid and a constant area, as stated. This operating flow is also the reference against which the 10 percent increase in the later parts is measured, so keep the unrounded value in later arithmetic to avoid compounding rounding error.

Answer: 5.06 L/s

(b)

The outflow is nonlinear in level, so expand about (h_0, q_0) with a first-order Taylor series: Δq_out = (dq/dh) Δh, where dq/dh = k/(2√h_0). The hydraulic resistance, the analogue of electrical resistance, is the reciprocal slope, R = dh/dq = 2√h_0 / k. Substituting, R = 2 × 1.2649 / 0.0040 = 632.5 s/m². Then the linear model is Δh = R Δq_out. The linearisation is valid only for small deviations, because the true curve is a square root whose slope changes with level: at lower levels the slope dq/dh is larger and the resistance smaller. Part (e) quantifies the resulting error for a 10 percent flow change.

Answer: 632.5 s/m²

(c)

Combine mass conservation with the linearised outflow. With deviation variables, A dΔh/dt = Δq_in − Δq_out and Δq_out = Δh/R. Then A R dΔh/dt + Δh = R Δq_in, a first-order system with gain R in m per m³/s and time constant τ = A R. Substituting, τ = 0.50 × 632.5 = 316.2 s, about 5.3 minutes. This is the hydraulic capacitance times the hydraulic resistance, exactly as an RC circuit, with the tank area acting as the capacitance in m². The slow response means a level controller can use a modest gain, and for a small disturbance the level settles to within 2 percent after about four time constants, near 1265 s.

Answer: 316.2 s

(d)

The new steady inflow is 1.10 q_0 = 1.10 × 0.005060 = 0.005566 m³/s. At the new equilibrium the outflow equals this inflow, so k√h_n = q_n and h_n = (q_n/k)². Substituting, q_n/k = 1.3914 and squaring gives h_n = 1.9360 m. As a check, since level goes with the square of flow, a 10 percent flow increase raises the level by a factor 1.10² = 1.21, so h_n = 1.21 × 1.60 = 1.9360 m, the same result. The level rises by 0.3360 m. This uses the full nonlinear law with no approximation, so it is the benchmark for the linear prediction in the next part.

Answer: 1.936 m

(e)

The linear model predicts Δh_lin = R Δq, where Δq = 0.10 q_0 = 0.000506 m³/s. Substituting, Δh_lin = 632.5 × 0.000506 = 0.3200 m. The true rise from part (d) is 0.3360 m. The difference is 0.0160 m, so the linear model underestimates the rise by 0.0160 / 0.3360 × 100 = 4.76 percent. The linear model is a tangent to a curve that bends upward in level against flow, so it underpredicts for increases and would overpredict for decreases. A 5 percent error from a 10 percent flow change is acceptable for a controller design, but the error grows roughly with the square of the step size.

Answer: 4.76 percent

Problem 4 [A3-064] Block diagram reduction

A concentration control loop for a chemical mixing tank has the following block structure. The error signal, formed by comparing the setpoint with the measured concentration through a unity feedback path, drives a proportional controller of gain 12. The controller output drives an actuator valve with transfer function 1/(s + 1). The valve is wrapped in its own inner negative feedback loop through a constant rate-feedback gain of 2. The inner loop output drives the tank, whose transfer function is 1/(s + 5). The tank output is the measured concentration, and there are no other dynamics in the sensor. You are asked to reduce the diagram step by step and to describe the closed-loop behaviour that results for a unit step in setpoint.

  1. (a) Reduce the inner loop and find its transfer function value at s = 0, that is, its steady-state gain. [3]
  2. (b) Find the closed-loop steady-state gain of the full system, C/R at s = 0. [4]
  3. (c) Find the undamped natural frequency of the closed loop, in rad/s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the damping ratio of the closed loop. [4]
  5. (e) Find the percentage overshoot of the unit step response. [5]
(a)

The inner loop has forward block G_2 = 1/(s + 1) and negative feedback H_1 = 2. The standard reduction for a negative feedback loop is G_2/(1 + G_2H_1). Multiplying numerator and denominator by (s + 1), this becomes 1/(s + 1 + 2) = 1/(s + 3). At s = 0 the steady-state gain is 1/3 = 0.3333. Rate feedback has therefore moved the valve pole from −1 to −3, making the valve faster but reducing its gain by the same factor of 3. Assumptions are linear blocks and no loading between the blocks. The reduced inner block is combined in series with the controller and the tank in the next part.

Answer: 0.3333

(b)

Multiply the series blocks to get the forward path: G(s) = 12 × [1/(s + 3)] × [1/(s + 5)] = 12/[(s + 3)(s + 5)]. The outer loop has unity negative feedback, so the closed loop is T(s) = G/(1 + G) = 12/[(s + 3)(s + 5) + 12]. Expanding the product (s + 3)(s + 5) = s² + 8s + 15 and adding 12 gives the denominator s² + 8s + 27. So T(s) = 12/(s² + 8s + 27). At s = 0 the gain is 12/27 = 0.4444. The steady-state gain is below one, which means a unit step in setpoint leaves a steady offset of 0.5556 because the loop is type zero, as there is no integrator in the forward path.

Answer: 0.4444

(c)

The closed-loop denominator is s² + 8s + 27, which is compared with the standard second-order form s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n². Matching the constant term, ω_n² = 27, so ω_n = √27 = 5.1962 rad/s. This frequency is the rate at which the system would oscillate if there were no damping. It is set by the controller gain and by both pole locations: raising the controller gain from 12 would raise ω_n and speed the response, but it would also reduce the damping ratio found in the next part. The assumptions are the linear model and the reduction in part (a), which is exact for these blocks.

Answer: 5.196 rad/s

(d)

Matching the s coefficient of the closed-loop denominator, 2ζω_n = 8. With ω_n = 5.1962 rad/s from part (c), ζ = 8/(2 × 5.1962) = 0.7698. Since ζ is less than 1 the response is underdamped, with complex conjugate poles at s = −ζω_n ± jω_d, where −ζω_n = −4.000 and ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²) = 3.3166 rad/s. The poles therefore lie at −4 ± j3.317. A damping ratio near 0.77 is close to the value, 0.707, usually taken as a good compromise between speed and overshoot, so the rate-feedback design is sensible. The check on the poles is that their sum equals −8, the negative of the s coefficient.

Answer: 0.7698

(e)

For a standard second-order system with no zeros, the fractional overshoot of the step response beyond its final value is M_p = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)). Using ζ = 0.7698, √(1 − ζ²) = 0.6383, so the exponent is −π × 0.7698 / 0.6383 = −3.7889. Then M_p = e−3.7889 = 0.02262, so the overshoot is 2.26 percent. This is measured relative to the final value, which is 0.4444 for a unit step, so the peak output is 0.4545. The steady offset from part (b) is the more serious performance problem than the small overshoot, and adding integral action would remove the offset at some cost in damping.

Answer: 2.26 percent

Problem 5 [A3-065] Signal flow and Mason gain

A multistage fluid-power amplifier is described by a signal flow graph with five nodes: input R, internal nodes x1, x2 and x3, and output C. The branch gains are R to x1: 2; x1 to x2: 3; x2 to x3: 4; x3 to C: 1; and a bypass branch x1 to x3: 5. Two feedback branches return signals: x2 to x1 with gain −0.10 and x3 to x2 with gain −0.050. All gains are constants, so the graph is evaluated at a fixed operating condition. You are asked to apply Mason's gain formula, checking for touching and non-touching loops, and then to consider what happens if one feedback path is removed by a maintenance change that disables the second feedback branch.

  1. (a) Find the sum of all individual loop gains in the graph. [4]
  2. (b) Find the graph determinant Δ, after checking which pairs of loops do not touch. [3]
  3. (c) Find the overall gain C/R using Mason's formula. [5]
  4. (d) The second feedback branch (x3 to x2) is disabled. Find the new overall gain C/R. [4]
  5. (e) Find the percentage change in overall gain caused by the fault in part (d). [4]
(a)

List every closed path that visits no node twice. Loop 1 runs x1 to x2 and back to x1: gain 3 × (−0.10) = -0.300. Loop 2 runs x2 to x3 and back to x2: gain 4 × (−0.050) = -0.200. Loop 3 runs x1 to x3 by the bypass, back to x2 by the second feedback branch, and back to x1 by the first feedback branch: gain 5 × (−0.050) × (−0.10) = 0.025. These are the only loops, since the feedback branches can only be used in these combinations. The sum is -0.300 + -0.200 + 0.025 = -0.475. Two negative loops and one positive loop is typical when a bypass path is combined with two negative feedbacks.

Answer: -0.475

(b)

Two loops are non-touching if they share no node. Loop 1 uses nodes x1 and x2, loop 2 uses x2 and x3, and loop 3 uses x1, x2 and x3. Loops 1 and 2 share x2, loop 1 and loop 3 share x1 and x2, and loops 2 and 3 share x2 and x3, so every pair touches and there are no products of non-touching loops. Mason's determinant is therefore Δ = 1 − (sum of loop gains) with no higher-order terms: Δ = 1 − (-0.475) = 1.475. Since Δ = 1.475 is greater than 1, it reduces the overall gain relative to the plain sum of the forward-path gains.

Answer: 1.475

(c)

Mason's formula is T = Σ P_k Δ_k / Δ. Find the forward paths from R to C. Path 1 is R, x1, x2, x3, C with gain P_1 = 2 × 3 × 4 × 1 = 24. Path 2 uses the bypass: R, x1, x3, C with gain P_2 = 2 × 5 × 1 = 10. Each path touches every loop because it visits x1 and x3, which are in all three loops, so each cofactor is Δ_k = 1 (the determinant with all touching loops removed). Then T = (P_1 + P_2)/Δ = (24 + 10) / 1.475 = 23.051. The bypass contributes 29.4 percent of the numerator, so a fault in the bypass would change the overall gain noticeably.

Answer: 23.05

(d)

Set the gain of the second feedback branch to zero. Loop 2 and loop 3 both contain that branch, so both vanish. Only loop 1 remains, with gain -0.300, and the new determinant is Δ' = 1 − (-0.300) = 1.300. The forward paths are unchanged, since they do not use the removed feedback branch, so P_1 = 24 and P_2 = 10 still apply, and both still touch loop 1 because they pass through x1, so the cofactors remain 1. Then T' = (24 + 10) / 1.300 = 26.154. Removing the branch lowers Δ from 1.475 to 1.300 and raises C/R by 13.46 percent.

Answer: 26.15

(e)

The percentage change relative to the healthy gain is (T' − T)/T × 100. From part (c) T = 23.051 and from part (d) T' = 26.154. The difference is 3.103, so the change is 3.103 / 23.051 × 100 = 13.46 percent. The gain rises by about 13.5 percent when feedback is lost. This is a measure of the sensitivity of the amplifier to the feedback path: the closed-loop gain depends on the feedback only through Δ, so S = d(ln T)/d(ln Δ) = −1. A candidate who answers with a negative sign has the direction wrong, because the gain increases when feedback is removed.

Answer: 13.46 percent

A3 Practice Paper 14

Problem 1 [A3-066] First-order system step response

A thermocouple in a furnace exhaust duct is modelled as a first-order instrument. The gas temperature is suddenly stepped from 20 °C to 120 °C, and the thermocouple, initially at 20 °C, is observed to read 71.0 °C exactly 4.0 s after the step. The reading comes from a bead whose response is assumed to be a single time constant with no delay or higher-order lag. Later the same thermocouple will be used in a heating transient in which the gas temperature rises steadily with time. The plant technicians need the dynamic performance figures to decide whether the instrument is fast enough to feed a trip alarm with limited tolerance on indication error. Use the model for all four parts below.

  1. (a) Find the time constant of the thermocouple in seconds. [6]
  2. (b) Find the time after the step for the reading to settle within 1 percent of the final step value, in seconds. [5]
  3. (c) The gas temperature now rises as a steady ramp of 2.0 °C/s. Find the steady-state lag between the gas temperature and the indicated temperature, in °C. [5]
  4. (d) The alarm can tolerate a steady ramp-lag error of at most 3.0 °C. Find the largest ramp rate for which the instrument can be used, in °C/s. [4]
(a)

A first-order system with initial value T_i and final value T_g responds to a step as T(t) = T_g − (T_g − T_i) e−t/τ. At t = 4.0 s the reading is 71.0 °C, so the fraction of the step completed is (71.0 − 20)/(120 − 20) = 0.510. Rearranging, e−t/τ = 1 − 0.510 = 0.490. Take natural logarithms: −t/τ = ln(0.490) = -0.7133, so τ = 4.0 / 0.7133 = 5.607 s. Assumptions: a single time constant, constant gas temperature after the step, and an initial reading equal to the initial gas temperature. Since 4.0 s is below τ, the reading at that instant is correctly below the 63.2 percent level reached at t = τ.

Answer: 5.607 s

(b)

Within 1 percent of the final value means the remaining error is 1 percent of the step, so e−t/τ = 0.01. Take logarithms: t = −τ ln(0.01) = τ × 4.605. With τ = 5.607 s from part (a), t = 5.607 × 4.605 = 25.82 s. Conventionally the 2 percent settling time is about 4τ = 22.43 s, so tightening the band from 2 percent to 1 percent costs only about 3.39 s extra. The exponential tail means the final approach is slow, which is why alarm logic should not wait for the reading to settle. Assumption: the gas temperature stays at 120 °C during the whole settling time, which may not hold in a real duct.

Answer: 25.82 s

(c)

For a first-order instrument G(s) = 1/(τs + 1) driven by a ramp input r(t) = a t with a = 2.0 °C/s, the output eventually follows the ramp with a constant lag. Using the final value theorem on the error, E(s) = R(s)[1 − G(s)] = (a/s²) × τs/(τs + 1), and e_ss = lim s E(s) = lim aτ/(τs + 1) = aτ. Substituting, e_ss = 2.0 × 5.607 = 11.215 °C. The instrument therefore reads 11.2 °C below the true gas temperature at all times once the transient has died away, which is equivalent to a time delay of τ. This only holds after about 4τ, near 22.4 s, so the indication error during the first seconds is smaller than the final lag.

Answer: 11.21 °C

(d)

The steady-state lag for a ramp of rate a is e_ss = aτ, from part (c). Setting the limit e_ss ≤ 3.0 °C gives a_max = 3.0/τ. Substituting τ = 5.607 s, a_max = 3.0 / 5.607 = 0.535 °C/s. The 2.0 °C/s ramp of part (c) therefore exceeds the allowable rate by a factor of 3.74. To use the thermocouple at 2.0 °C/s the time constant would have to be at most 3.0/2.0 = 1.5 s, which would call for a finer bead or a faster flow past it. Assumptions are a single-lag instrument and a constant ramp lasting several time constants, so that the transient has decayed.

Answer: 0.535 °C/s

Problem 2 [A3-067] Second-order system time response specs

A robotic joint positioner is controlled with a unity-feedback loop around the plant G(s) = K/[s(s + 6)], where K is an adjustable gain set in the servo amplifier. The joint angle is measured without lag. The customer specification calls for no more than 10 percent overshoot for a step command. As the design engineer you are to choose K, then to verify the main time-domain figures of merit that the specification refers to and compute the error constant that governs tracking of a steadily moving command. Use the standard second-order step response formulas, which apply because the closed loop has no zeros and only two poles.

  1. (a) Find the minimum damping ratio that meets the 10 percent overshoot limit. [5]
  2. (b) Find the gain K that gives this damping ratio. [4]
  3. (c) Find the peak time of the step response in seconds. [4]
  4. (d) Find the 2 percent settling time using the 4/(ζω_n) approximation, in seconds. [3]
  5. (e) Find the velocity error constant K_v of the loop, in s⁻¹. [4]
(a)

The step overshoot of a standard second-order system is M_p = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)). Setting M_p = 0.10 and taking logarithms gives −πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = ln 0.10 = -2.3026. Squaring both sides: π²ζ² = ln² (1 − ζ²), so ζ²(π² + ln²) = ln², and ζ = |ln| / √(π² + ln²). Substituting, π² = 9.8696 and ln² = 5.3019, so ζ = 2.3026 / √15.1715 = 0.5912. Any damping ratio above this value gives overshoot below 10 percent, so this is the minimum acceptable ζ. Assumption: the closed-loop response is dominated by the second-order pair and has no zeros, which holds for this unity-feedback loop with a single integrator in the plant.

Answer: 0.5912

(b)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is 1 + K/[s(s + 6)] = 0, which gives s² + 6s + K = 0. Compare with s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n². Matching coefficients, 2ζω_n = 6 so ω_n = 6/(2ζ) = 3/ζ = 3 / 0.5912 = 5.0748 rad/s, and K = ω_n² = 5.0748² = 25.75. The s coefficient is fixed at 6 by the plant pole, so ζ = 3/ω_n falls as K raises ω_n. The result is the largest gain for the overshoot limit, because raising K further would reduce ζ below the minimum. In a real amplifier K would be set slightly below this value to leave a margin.

Answer: 25.75

(c)

The step response reaches its first peak at the time when the sinusoidal component has advanced by half a period of the damped oscillation: t_p = π/ω_d, where ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²). Substituting, √(1 − ζ²) = 0.8066 and ω_d = 5.0748 × 0.8066 = 4.0931 rad/s. Then t_p = π / 4.0931 = 0.7675 s. This is a bit less than a second, so the joint reaches its overshoot peak quickly, in line with the 10 percent overshoot specified. Assumptions are the underdamped second-order form with no zeros. The peak time is independent of the amplitude of the step, a property of linear systems.

Answer: 0.7675 s

(d)

The envelope of the step response decays as exp(−ζω_n t). The 2 percent band is entered when exp(−ζω_n t) ≈ 0.02, which gives ζω_n t ≈ 3.9, usually rounded to 4. So t_s = 4/(ζω_n). Using ζω_n = 3.000 s⁻¹ (half the s coefficient 6, independent of K), t_s = 4/3.000 = 1.333 s. This is the real part of the closed-loop poles, −3, so the settling time depends only on the plant pole and not on the gain; changing K moves the poles vertically, not horizontally. The approximation is accurate to a few percent for damping ratios near 0.6, which is the case here.

Answer: 1.333 s

(e)

The velocity error constant is K_v = lim as s tends to 0 of s G(s) for a unity-feedback loop. With G(s) = K/[s(s + 6)], sG(s) = K/(s + 6), so K_v = K/6. Substituting K = 25.75, K_v = 25.75 / 6 = 4.292 s⁻¹. The steady-state error of the loop for a ramp command of slope r is e_ss = r/K_v, so for a command moving at 0.5 rad/s the error would be 0.1165 rad. The loop is type one, giving zero error for a step and a finite error for a ramp. The overshoot-limited gain therefore sets the tracking accuracy and the two requirements trade against each other.

Answer: 4.292 s⁻¹

Problem 3 [A3-068] Steady-state error and system type

The position loop of a gantry machine-tool feed drive has unity feedback and the open-loop transfer function G(s) = K(s + 5)/[s²(s + 10)]. Position is measured in millimetres. At present the gain is K = 200. The machine will cut a profile that requires the tool to follow a parabolic command r(t) = ½ A t² with A = 2.0 mm/s², and the customer allows a steady-state following error of no more than 0.005 mm. Before raising the gain, the controls engineer must also confirm that the loop stays stable. Assume the closed loop is stable when the error constants are used and verify the assumption at the end.

  1. (a) Find the static acceleration error constant K_a at the present gain K = 200, in s⁻². [4]
  2. (b) Find the steady-state error for the parabolic command at K = 200, in mm. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum gain K that meets the 0.005 mm error limit. [5]
  4. (d) State the steady-state error of this loop for a ramp command (a constant velocity of 30 mm/s) and explain why in terms of system type. This part has no numerical answer. [3]
  5. (e) Using the Routh array, find the first-column element of the s¹ row at K = 800, and state whether the loop is stable. [3]
(a)

For a unity-feedback loop the acceleration error constant is K_a = lim as s tends to 0 of s²G(s). Here s²G(s) = K(s + 5)/(s + 10), and setting s = 0 gives K_a = 5K/10 = K/2. Substituting K = 200, K_a = 100.0 s⁻². The double pole at the origin makes this a type two system: it has a finite K_a, and the position and velocity constants K_p and K_v are infinite. The constant K_a is the quantity that governs tracking of a parabolic command and it depends on the zero at −5 and the pole at −10 only through their ratio. Assumption: the closed loop is stable, which is verified in part (e).

Answer: 100 s⁻²

(b)

For a unity-feedback system the steady-state error to a parabolic input r(t) = ½ A t² is e_ss = A/K_a. This follows from the final value theorem: E(s) = R(s)/(1 + G(s)) with R(s) = A/s³, and e_ss = lim s E(s) = A / lim s²G(s) = A/K_a. Substituting A = 2.0 mm/s² and K_a = 100.0 s⁻² from part (a), e_ss = 2.0 / 100.0 = 0.0200 mm. This is above the allowed 0.005 mm limit by a factor of 4.0, so the present gain is not high enough. The error is a constant lag behind the moving command, not a growing one, because the loop is type two. The next part finds the gain needed.

Answer: 0.02 mm

(c)

The requirement is e_ss = A/K_a ≤ 0.005 mm, so K_a ≥ A/0.005 = 2.0/0.005 = 400 s⁻². Since K_a = K/2 from part (a), K ≥ 2K_a = 2 × 400 = 800. Therefore K must be at least 800, which is 4 times the present value. This is a large increase, and a gain increase of that size normally degrades relative stability and would raise noise sensitivity in a real drive. The calculation shows that a type two loop trades its accuracy directly against gain; an alternative would be to add a velocity feedforward term instead of simply raising K.

Answer: 800

(d)

The loop has two poles at the origin, so it is a type two system. For a unity-feedback system the velocity error constant is K_v = lim as s tends to 0 of sG(s) = K(s + 5)/[s(s + 10)], and this tends to infinity because of the remaining factor of 1/s. The steady-state error for a ramp of slope 30 mm/s is e_ss = 30/K_v, which is therefore zero. This is true at any gain, provided the loop is stable, and it is independent of the ramp slope. Two integrators in the forward path mean that the controller can hold a nonzero constant output with zero input error, which is what is needed to follow a constant velocity command exactly. The answer is zero error, and only a parabolic command gives a finite nonzero error.

Answer: Zero steady-state error (type two system)

(e)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is 1 + G(s) = 0, giving s²(s + 10) + K(s + 5) = 0, that is, s³ + 10s² + Ks + 5K = 0. Form the Routh array with rows s³: 1, K; s²: 10, 5K; s¹: (10K − 5K)/10 = K/2; s⁰: 5K. For K = 800 the s¹ element is 400.0 and the s⁰ element is 4000. All first-column entries (1, 10, 400.0, 4000) are positive, so there is no sign change and the loop is stable. In fact the first column stays positive for every K > 0, so the stability assumption made in parts (a) to (c) is justified, though the damping becomes poor at high K and must be checked separately.

Answer: 400

Problem 4 [A3-069] Routh-Hurwitz stability

A web-tension control loop on a paper winding line has a unity-feedback arrangement with open-loop transfer function G(s) = K/[(s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 3)], where K is the adjustable gain of the tension controller. The plant poles come from the roller inertia, the web elasticity and the drive. The commissioning engineer wants the maximum gain before the loop becomes unstable, the frequency of the resulting sustained oscillation, and a feel for the safety margin at the intended operating gain of K = 15. A further specification demands that every closed-loop pole lie to the left of s = −0.5, so that disturbances decay with a minimum rate, and the engineer also wants to confirm what goes wrong if the gain is set to 80 by mistake.

  1. (a) Find the largest gain K for which the closed loop is stable. [5]
  2. (b) Find the frequency of the sustained oscillation at the stability limit, in rad/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the gain margin at the operating gain K = 15, in dB. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest gain K for which all closed-loop poles lie to the left of s = −0.5. [4]
  5. (e) The gain is mistakenly set to K = 80. Find the number of closed-loop poles in the right half-plane. [3]
(a)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is 1 + G(s) = 0, so (s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 3) + K = 0. Expanding the product, (s + 1)(s + 2) = s² + 3s + 2, and multiplying by (s + 3) gives s³ + 6s² + 11s + 6, so the equation is s³ + 6s² + 11s + (6 + K) = 0. The Routh array has rows s³: 1, 11; s²: 6, 6 + K; s¹: (6 × 11 − 1 × (6 + K))/6 = (60 − K)/6; s⁰: 6 + K. For stability every first-column entry must be positive, requiring (60 − K)/6 > 0, so K < 60, and 6 + K > 0, so K > −6. For positive gain the stability limit is K_max = 60. At this value the s¹ entry vanishes and the loop is marginally stable.

Answer: 60

(b)

At K = 60 the s¹ row of the Routh array is zero, which signals a pair of poles on the imaginary axis. They are found from the auxiliary polynomial formed from the s² row: 6s² + (6 + K) = 0, that is, 6s² + 66 = 0. Solving, s² = −66/6 = −11.0, so s = ±j√11.0 = ±j3.3166. The sustained oscillation therefore has angular frequency ω = 3.317 rad/s, a period of 1.894 s. As a check, the same result comes from setting s = jω in the characteristic equation: the real part gives −6ω² + 6 + K = 0 and the imaginary part gives ω(11 − ω²) = 0, so ω² = 11, which agrees.

Answer: 3.317 rad/s

(c)

The gain margin is the factor by which the loop gain can be increased before instability, here K_max/K, since the stability limit is K = 60 and the stable region starts at zero. At the intended gain of 15, the factor is 60/15 = 4.00. Expressed in decibels, GM = 20 log10(60/15) = 20 log10(4.00) = 12.04 dB. A margin of this size, roughly 12 dB, is comfortable: common practice asks for at least 6 dB, and a factor of four allows for plant gain variations from web tension and roll diameter changes during winding. The result assumes the plant gain varies only as a multiplier, with no change in the pole locations.

Answer: 12.04 dB

(d)

Shift the axis by substituting s = z − 0.5, so that Re(z) < 0 corresponds to Re(s) < −0.5. The shifted polynomial for the plant part is (z − 0.5)³ + 6(z − 0.5)² + 11(z − 0.5) + 6 = z³ + 4.50z² + 5.75z + 1.875, and K adds to the constant term. The Routh array now has rows z³: 1, 5.75; z²: 4.50, 1.875 + K; z¹: (4.50 × 5.75 − 1.875 − K)/4.50. For the z¹ entry to be positive we need K < 4.50 × 5.75 − 1.875 = 24.00. So the gain must stay below 24.0 to guarantee a decay rate of at least 0.5 per second, much stricter than the simple stability limit of 60.

Answer: 24

(e)

With K = 80 the characteristic equation is s³ + 6s² + 11s + 86 = 0. The Routh array is s³: 1, 11; s²: 6, 86; s¹: (6 × 11 − 86)/6 = -3.33; s⁰: 86. The first column is therefore 1, 6, -3.33, 86, with signs +, +, −, +. The number of sign changes in the first column equals the number of roots in the right half-plane. There are two sign changes, one from 6 to -3.33 and one back to 86, so there are 2 right-half-plane poles. A numerical root finder confirms a complex pair with a positive real part, so the loop would oscillate with a growing amplitude until the actuator saturates.

Answer: 2

Problem 5 [A3-070] Root locus

A vibration-isolation platform carrying a sensitive instrument uses an active actuator. With a unity-feedback position loop the open-loop transfer function is G(s) = K/[s(s + 4)(s + 8)], where K > 0 is the controller gain. The designer wants to plot the root locus and to use it to read off several gains: the gain where the locus first leaves the real axis, the gain at which the platform becomes unstable, and the gain that gives a well-damped dominant pair with damping ratio 0.5. The designer should also locate the point where the asymptotes meet the real axis and relate the locus to the Routh stability limit. Assume ideal sensors and a rigid platform so that the three-pole model holds.

  1. (a) Find the centroid of the root-locus asymptotes (the point where they meet the real axis). [3]
  2. (b) Find the location of the breakaway point on the real axis. [5]
  3. (c) Find the gain K at the breakaway point. [3]
  4. (d) Find the gain K at which the locus crosses the imaginary axis. [4]
  5. (e) Find the gain K that gives a dominant complex pair with damping ratio 0.5. [5]
(a)

The open-loop transfer function has n = 3 poles, at s = 0, −4 and −8, and no finite zeros, so the locus has three branches that go to infinity along asymptotes. The asymptote centroid is σ_a = (Σ poles − Σ zeros)/(n − m), with m = 0. Substituting, σ_a = (0 − 4 − 8 − 0)/3 = -4.000. The asymptote angles are (2k + 1) × 180°/3, that is, 60°, 180° and 300°. This tells us the locus bends toward the right-half plane along the 60° and 300° rays, which meet the real axis at −4, so the closed-loop system must become unstable at some finite gain. The assumption is that all three open-loop poles are real and simple.

Answer: -4

(b)

On the real axis, the locus exists between the poles at 0 and −4 and to the left of −8. The two branches starting at 0 and −4 meet and leave the axis at a breakaway point. Breakaway points are found from dK/ds = 0, where K = −s(s + 4)(s + 8) = −(s³ + 12s² + 32s). Differentiating gives 3s² + 24s + 32 = 0, with roots s = [−24 ± √(576 − 384)]/6 = [−24 ± 13.856]/6, that is, -1.691 and -6.309. Only -1.691 lies on the locus, between −4 and 0, so the breakaway point is s = -1.691. The other root, -6.309, lies between −8 and −4 where no locus exists for positive K, so it is rejected.

Answer: -1.691

(c)

The gain at any point on the locus is K = |s| |s + 4| |s + 8|, which is the product of the distances from the point to the open-loop poles. At the breakaway point s = -1.691 the distances are |s| = 1.691, |s + 4| = 2.309 and |s + 8| = 6.309. Then K = 1.691 × 2.309 × 6.309 = 24.63. For gains below this value the closed-loop poles are all real and the platform response is overdamped, while above this value two poles become a complex pair and oscillation begins. The gain at the breakaway point is the highest gain that gives a purely non-oscillatory response.

Answer: 24.63

(d)

The characteristic equation is s³ + 12s² + 32s + K = 0. Using the Routh array, rows s³: 1, 32; s²: 12, K; s¹: (12 × 32 − K)/12. The loop is marginally stable when the s¹ entry is zero, so K = 12 × 32 = 384. The crossing frequency follows from the auxiliary polynomial 12s² + K = 0, giving s² = −384/12 = −32.0, so ω = 5.657 rad/s. Check by the angle condition: at s = j5.657 the angles from the poles at 0, −4 and −8 are 90°, 54.7° and 35.3°, which sum to 180°. For any gain above 384 two poles move into the right-half plane and the platform becomes unstable.

Answer: 384

(e)

A damping ratio of 0.5 corresponds to a pole at an angle of arccos(0.5) = 60° from the negative real axis, that is, s = r(−0.5 + j0.866). Substitute into the characteristic equation s³ + 12s² + 32s + K = 0. Because 3 × 120° = 360°, s³ is real and equals r³. The imaginary part of 12s² + 32s must be zero: 12 × (−0.866 r²) + 32 × 0.866 r = 0, so r = 32/12 = 2.6667. The real part gives K = −[r³ + 12 r²(−0.5) + 32 r(−0.5)]. With r = 2.6667: r³ = 18.963, 6r² = 42.667, 16r = 42.667, so K = −(18.963 − 42.667 − 42.667) = 66.37. The pair is at -1.333 ± j2.309, and the third pole follows from the sum of poles being −12.

Answer: 66.37

A3 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A3-071] Bode plot construction

A hydraulic positioning table has a measured open-loop transfer function with unity negative feedback, G(s) = 25(1 + s/2) / [s(1 + s/10)(1 + s/50)], where s is in rad/s and the input and output are table position in radians of the lead screw. The design office wants to read the main loop properties from a Bode plot built from straight-line asymptotes, then check them against exact calculations. The table is expected to follow a ramp command of 0.8 rad/s during a slow traverse. Treat the phase of each factor exactly (arctangent) when asked for exact quantities, and use asymptotic magnitude only where stated. Answer the following in order, showing the break frequencies and slopes you use.

  1. (a) Using straight-line asymptotes, find the magnitude of G in dB at ω = 20 rad/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the exact gain crossover frequency ω_gc where |G(jω)| = 1. [5]
  3. (c) Find the exact phase margin of the loop. [6]
  4. (d) Find the steady-state following error for the 0.8 rad/s ramp command. [5]
(a)

Break frequencies are 2 rad/s (zero), 10 rad/s (pole) and 50 rad/s (pole). Below 2 rad/s the integrator gives a -20 dB/decade line, and its value at ω = 2 is 20 log10(K/ω) = 20 log10(25/2) = 21.94 dB. At 2 rad/s the zero adds +20 dB/decade, cancelling the integrator slope, so the asymptote is flat at 21.94 dB from 2 to 10 rad/s. At 10 rad/s the first pole restores a slope of -20 dB/decade, which continues until 50 rad/s. Since 20 rad/s lies in that last segment, the drop from 10 to 20 rad/s is 20 log10(20/10) = 6.02 dB. The asymptotic magnitude is therefore 21.94 - 6.02 = 15.92 dB. This straight-line value is slightly different from the exact gain at 20 rad/s because the corner corrections are ignored, which is acceptable for a sketch.

Answer: 15.92 dB

(b)

The exact magnitude is |G(jω)| = 25 √(1 + (ω/2)²) / [ω √(1 + (ω/10)²) √(1 + (ω/50)²)]. The asymptotic plot shows the magnitude is above 0 dB (value 21.94 dB) up to 10 rad/s and then falls at 20 dB/decade, so the crossing lies beyond 50 rad/s, where the net slope becomes -40 dB/decade (integrator -20, zero +20, two poles -40). A first estimate comes from the high-frequency form |G| ≈ 25(ω/2)/(ω (ω/10)(ω/50)) = 6250/ω², giving ω ≈ 79 rad/s. Solving the exact expression numerically (bisection on |G| - 1 = 0) refines this to ω_gc = 71.2 rad/s. At this frequency the zero and the pole at 10 are well inside their asymptotic regions, but 71.2 is only 1.4 times the corner at 50, which is why the asymptotic estimate of 79 rad/s is about 10 percent high. This is the frequency at which the phase margin must be read.

Answer: 71.2 rad/s

(c)

The phase of G(jω) is φ = arctan(ω/2) - 90° - arctan(ω/10) - arctan(ω/50). At the crossover ω_gc = 71.2 rad/s the terms are arctan(71.2/2) = 88.4°, arctan(71.2/10) = 82.0° and arctan(71.2/50) = 54.9°. Substituting, φ = 88.4° - 90° - 82.0° - 54.9° = -138.5°.
