The phase margin is PM = 180° + φ = 180° + (-138.5°) = 41.5°. A margin of about 41° is comfortable (a common target is 45° to 60°), so the table will have a well damped step response. The lead supplied by the zero at 2 rad/s is what keeps the phase well above -180° despite the integrator and the two lag poles.

Answer: 41.5 degrees

(d)

The loop is Type 1 because there is one pure integrator, so the steady-state error to a ramp of slope R is e_ss = R/K_v, where the velocity error constant is K_v = lim s→0 of sG(s). Taking the limit: sG(s) = 25(1 + s/2)/[(1 + s/10)(1 + s/50)] and at s = 0 this equals 25 s⁻¹. This is also the value read from the Bode plot as the intercept of the low-frequency asymptote with the 1 rad/s line (20 log10 25 = 27.96 dB at ω = 1). Therefore e_ss = 0.8 / 25 = 0.032 rad. If the traverse were required to hold the error below 0.01 rad, the gain would have to rise to 80 s⁻¹, which would push the crossover higher and cost phase margin, illustrating the usual trade-off between accuracy and stability.

Answer: 0.032 rad

Problem 2 [A3-072] Gain and phase margins

A belt conveyor drive in a bottling plant is controlled by a speed-to-position loop whose open-loop transfer function with unity negative feedback is G(s) = K / [s(1 + s/4)(1 + s/12)], with K = 6 s⁻¹ and s in rad/s. The loop is closed through a digital link that adds a pure transport delay T_d, so the true open-loop transfer function is G(s)e−sT_d. The commissioning engineer must report the stability margins of the delay-free design and then determine how much extra delay the loop can tolerate before it becomes unstable, because a proposed wireless link will add an unknown latency. Use exact phase and magnitude calculations rather than asymptotes. Report gain margin in dB.

  1. (a) Find the phase crossover frequency and the gain margin of the delay-free loop, and give the gain margin in dB. [6]
  2. (b) Find the gain crossover frequency and the phase margin of the delay-free loop. [7]
  3. (c) Find the largest additional transport delay T_d that keeps the loop stable. [7]
(a)

The phase of G(jω) is -90° - arctan(ω/4) - arctan(ω/12). Setting it to -180° requires arctan(ω/4) + arctan(ω/12) = 90°, which means the two arguments multiply to one: (ω/4)(ω/12) = 1, so ω² = 48 and ω_pc = 6.928 rad/s. At this frequency the magnitude is |G| = 6 / [6.928 × √(1 + 48/16) × √(1 + 48/144)] = 6 / [6.928 × 2 × 1.1547] = 0.375. The gain margin is the factor by which K may rise before |G| = 1 at the phase crossover, GM = 1/|G| = 2.667, which is 20 log10(2.667) = 8.52 dB. A value near 8.5 dB is acceptable but not generous, since a gain margin of 6 dB is the usual minimum. The result also shows the loop becomes unstable at K = 6 × 2.667 = 16 s⁻¹, as the Routh test confirms.

Answer: 8.52 dB

(b)

The gain crossover satisfies |G(jω)| = 1, that is 6 = ω √(1 + ω²/16) √(1 + ω²/144). Squaring gives 36 = ω² (1 + ω²/16)(1 + ω²/144). Solving numerically (the left side is monotonic in ω, so bisection works) gives ω_gc = 4.016 rad/s. Check: at this ω the factor √(1 + ω²/16) is 1.417 and √(1 + ω²/144) is 1.055, and the product with ω is 6.00. The phase at crossover is φ = -90° - arctan(4.016/4) - arctan(4.016/12) = -90° - 45.1° - 18.5° = -153.6°. Phase margin is PM = 180° + φ = 26.4°. A margin of 26.4° is well below the usual 45° to 60° target, so the delay-free loop is poorly damped, with overshoot near 40 percent.

Answer: 26.4 degrees

(c)

A pure delay e−jωT_d has unit magnitude, so it does not change the gain crossover frequency, but it subtracts ωT_d radians of phase at every frequency. The loop reaches instability when the extra phase lag at the gain crossover uses up the whole phase margin: ω_gc T_d = PM. Convert the margin to radians: PM = 26.4° × π/180 = 0.4605 rad. Then T_d,max = PM/ω_gc = 0.4605 / 4.016 = 0.115 s. This is the tolerable latency at the nominal gain, about 115 ms. The wireless link should therefore be specified well below this, typically with a factor of two for safety, and any gain increase would shrink the allowance because the crossover frequency would rise and the margin would fall. Because |G| crosses unity only once and the delay does not change it, this is the exact delay margin, not just a necessary bound.

Answer: 0.115 s

Problem 3 [A3-073] Nyquist stability

A magnetic bearing for a small turbo-compressor shaft is open-loop unstable. With a proportional amplifier gain K (dimensionless, K > 0) and unity negative feedback, the open-loop transfer function is G(s) = K / [(s − 2)(s + 4)(s + 6)], with s in rad/s. It has one pole in the right half-plane. The Nyquist criterion states that the closed loop is stable only if the Nyquist plot of G(s) encircles the point −1 counterclockwise exactly P times, where P is the number of unstable open-loop poles. Use this reasoning together with the real-axis crossings of the Nyquist plot to find the range of gain over which the bearing can be stabilised, and then judge how robust a particular choice of K = 60 is.

  1. (a) Find the minimum gain K_min below which the loop cannot be stabilised, using the Nyquist plot at ω = 0. [6]
  2. (b) Find the maximum gain K_max above which the loop becomes unstable, using the point where the Nyquist plot crosses the negative real axis at a non-zero frequency. [7]
  3. (c) For K = 60, find the smaller of the upward and downward gain margins, in dB. [7]
(a)

The plot starts (ω = 0) at G(0) = K / [(−2)(4)(6)] = −K/48, a point on the negative real axis. With P = 1 the plot must encircle −1 once counterclockwise. A single counterclockwise encirclement is obtained only if the starting point lies to the left of −1, so that the full Nyquist contour (including the mirrored negative-frequency branch and the large semicircle that maps to the origin) passes round −1. That requires K/48 > 1, giving K_min = 48. For K < 48 the starting point is between −1 and 0, there is no net encirclement, N = 0 and Z = N + P = 1 closed-loop pole stays in the right half-plane. Check with the characteristic polynomial (s − 2)(s + 4)(s + 6) + K = s³ + 8s² + 4s − 48 + K: a positive constant term needs K > 48, which agrees.

Answer: 48

(b)

Put s = jω into the characteristic equation s³ + 8s² + 4s + (K − 48) = 0. Then −jω³ − 8ω² + 4jω + (K − 48) = 0. The imaginary part gives −ω³ + 4ω = 0, so ω_pc = 2 rad/s. The real part gives −8ω² + K − 48 = 0, so K = 48 + 8 × 4 = 80. Equivalently G(j2) = K/[(j2 − 2)(j2 + 4)(j2 + 6)], and the product in the denominator equals −80, so G(j2) = −K/80, a second crossing of the negative real axis. For K > 80 this crossing passes to the left of −1, which adds a clockwise encirclement and cancels the one required, so the loop goes unstable. The Routh test agrees: the s² and s coefficients require 8 × 4 > K − 48, that is K < 80. The stabilising range is 48 < K < 80.

Answer: 80

(c)

With K = 60 the two real-axis crossings are at −60/48 = −1.25 (from ω = 0) and −60/80 = −0.75 (from ω = 2 rad/s). The loop stays stable if the gain may be multiplied by any factor between 48/60 and 80/60. The upward margin is the factor 80/60 = 1.333, or 20 log10(1.333) = 2.50 dB. The downward margin is the factor by which gain may fall, 60/48 = 1.25, or 20 log10(1.25) = 1.94 dB. The smaller of the two is 1.94 dB, set by the lower bound. This is a conditionally stable system: a drop in amplifier gain (for example a failed sensor channel or supply sag) destabilises it as readily as a rise does. The very small margin of about 2 dB is poor, and a designer would move K towards the geometric centre of the range, √(48 × 80) = 62, or add compensation to widen the window.

Answer: 1.94 dB

Problem 4 [A3-074] PID controller tuning

An electrically heated oil bath is controlled by a PID controller. A step test with the controller in manual, raising heater power by 5 percent of span, gave a measured temperature rise of 12 °C in the long run. The response showed a dead time of 30 s and a first-order lag with time constant 180 s, so the process is modelled as G_p(s) = K e−30s/(180s + 1) with K in °C per percent of heater power. The controller has the ideal form C(s) = K_c [1 + 1/(T_i s) + T_d s]. The commissioning engineer will compare two published tuning rules for this process: the open-loop Ziegler-Nichols reaction-curve rule (K_c = 1.2τ/(Kθ), T_i = 2θ, T_d = 0.5θ) and the SIMC rule for a PI controller (K_c = τ/[K(τ_c + θ)], T_i = min[τ, 4(τ_c + θ)]) with the closed-loop time constant τ_c chosen equal to the dead time θ.

  1. (a) Find the process gain K and the Ziegler-Nichols proportional gain K_c. [6]
  2. (b) Find the integral gain K_i = K_c/T_i of the Ziegler-Nichols PID controller, in % per (°C·s). [6]
  3. (c) Find the SIMC proportional gain K_c for the PI controller when τ_c = θ, and state the integral time. [8]
(a)

The process gain is the steady-state output change divided by the input change: K = 12 °C / 5 % = 2.4 °C per percent. The dead time is θ = 30 s and the lag time constant is τ = 180 s. The Ziegler-Nichols reaction-curve rule for a PID controller gives K_c = 1.2τ/(Kθ) = 1.2 × 180 / (2.4 × 30) = 216 / 72 = 3.00 percent of power per °C of error. This corresponds to a proportional band of 100/K_c = 33.3 percent. The rule is known to give a quarter-amplitude-decay response, which means an aggressive loop with around 40 to 50 percent overshoot to a setpoint step, so it is usually detuned by about half in practice. Note that the ratio θ/τ = 0.17 is small enough for the rule to apply, since it was derived for processes with θ/τ roughly between 0.1 and 0.6.

Answer: 3.00 % per °C

(b)

The Ziegler-Nichols integral time is T_i = 2θ = 2 × 30 = 60 s, and the derivative time is T_d = 0.5θ = 15 s. The parallel-form integral gain is the controller gain divided by the integral time: K_i = K_c/T_i = 3.00 / 60 = 0.0500 percent per (°C·s). In words, every second that the temperature error persists at 1 °C adds 0.050 percent to the heater power through the integral term, on top of the proportional action. The derivative gain in the parallel form is K_c T_d = 3.00 × 15 = 45 percent·s per °C. A derivative term of this size acting on a noisy thermocouple signal would amplify noise, so a filter on the derivative with a time constant of about T_d/10 = 1.5 s should be added in practice.

Answer: 0.0500 % per °C per s

(c)

The SIMC rule uses the closed-loop time constant τ_c as a single tuning knob. With τ_c = θ = 30 s the proportional gain is K_c = τ / [K(τ_c + θ)] = 180 / [2.4 × (30 + 30)] = 180 / 144 = 1.25 percent per °C. The integral time is T_i = min[τ, 4(τ_c + θ)] = min[180, 240] = 180 s, so the lag time constant is the one selected and the controller cancels the process lag. Compared with Ziegler-Nichols, the SIMC gain is 2.4 times smaller and the integral time is three times longer, giving a much less oscillatory loop with little overshoot, at the price of a slower response to disturbances. For a heated oil bath, where overshoot could degrade the product, the SIMC setting is the better compromise, and a derivative term is not needed because the dead time dominates the closed-loop dynamics.

Answer: 1.25 % per °C

Problem 5 [A3-075] Lead and lag compensator design

A pan-tilt camera mount on a survey vessel has a plant G_p(s) = K / [s(0.5s + 1)] with unity negative feedback, where the output is mount angle. The specification requires a velocity error constant K_v = 20 s⁻¹ and a phase margin of at least 50°. The gain K is therefore fixed by the accuracy requirement, and a phase-lead compensator C(s) = (1 + Ts)/(1 + αTs), with 0 < α < 1 and unit DC gain, is to be added to recover the phase margin. Use the standard design procedure: add 5° to the required phase lead to allow for the shift in gain crossover, place the maximum lead at the new gain crossover frequency ω_m, where the uncompensated magnitude equals −10 log10(1/α) dB, and set T = 1/(ω_m√α).

  1. (a) Find the gain crossover frequency and phase margin of the uncompensated loop with K = 20. [5]
  2. (b) Find the maximum phase lead φ_m required and the corresponding lead ratio α. [7]
  3. (c) Find the lead time constant T. [8]
(a)

The velocity constant is K_v = lim sG_p(s) = K, so K = 20 s⁻¹. The crossover satisfies 20 = ω √(1 + 0.25ω²). Squaring: 400 = ω² + 0.25ω⁴, so ω⁴ + 4ω² − 1600 = 0. With u = ω² the quadratic gives u = [−4 + √(16 + 6400)]/2 = 38.05, hence ω_0 = 6.17 rad/s. The phase at that frequency is −90° − arctan(0.5 × 6.17) = −90° − 72.0°, so the phase margin is PM_0 = 180° − 90° − 72.0° = 18.0°. This is far below the specified 50°, and the response would be very oscillatory, so the loop needs about 37° of extra phase at crossover, which is beyond what a single gain adjustment can supply without sacrificing K_v.

Answer: 18.0 degrees

(b)

The required lead is the target margin minus the existing margin plus the 5° allowance: φ_m = 50° − 18.0° + 5° = 37.0°. For a lead network the maximum phase is sin φ_m = (1 − α)/(1 + α), so α = (1 − sin φ_m)/(1 + sin φ_m). With sin(37.0°) = 0.6023, α = (1 − 0.6023) / (1 + 0.6023) = 0.248. The lead network raises the high-frequency gain by 1/α = 4.03 (12.1 dB); the gain at ω_m is 1/√α = 2.007, which is 6.05 dB. A value of α below about 0.1 would be avoided because such a large ratio amplifies sensor noise, but this value is moderate. Since a single lead stage can supply up to about 60°, one stage suffices here, and the proportional DC gain remains unity so K_v = 20 s⁻¹ is not disturbed.

Answer: 0.248

(c)

The compensator raises the gain at ω_m by 10 log10(1/α) = 6.05 dB, so the new crossover is at the frequency where the uncompensated magnitude is −6.05 dB, that is |G(jω_m)| = √α = 0.4982. Solving 20 / (ω √(1 + 0.25ω²)) = 0.4982 numerically gives ω_m = 8.85 rad/s, which is higher than ω_0 = 6.17 rad/s, as expected for a lead network. The lead time constant follows from the geometric-mean relation ω_m = 1/(T√α): T = 1/(ω_m √α) = 1 / (8.85 × 0.4982) = 0.227 s. The compensator is then C(s) = (1 + 0.227s)/(1 + 0.0563s). At ω_m the new loop phase is the uncompensated phase there plus φ_m, giving a phase margin close to the specified 50°, and the check should be made by recomputing the exact crossover after the design.

Answer: 0.227 s

A3 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A3-076] State-space models

A precision linear stage moves a payload of mass m = 2.0 kg on air-bearing guides with a viscous damping coefficient c = 6.0 N·s/m and a flexure return spring of stiffness k = 50 N/m. A voice-coil actuator applies force u(t). Take the state vector x = [position, velocity]ᵀ, so ẋ = Ax + Bu with output position. The control group wants full state feedback u = −K x = −(k_p x₁ + k_d x₂) to give a closed loop with damping ratio ζ = 0.7 and undamped natural frequency ω_n = 8.0 rad/s. Derive the state matrices from Newton's second law, examine the open-loop dynamics, and then compute the feedback gains by matching the closed-loop characteristic polynomial s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n² term by term. Assume the sensors measure both states without noise.

  1. (a) Find the open-loop damping ratio of the stage. [5]
  2. (b) Find the position feedback gain k_p so that the closed-loop natural frequency is 8.0 rad/s. [7]
  3. (c) Find the velocity feedback gain k_d needed for ζ = 0.7. [8]
(a)

Newton's second law gives m ẍ = u − c ẋ − k x. With x₁ = x and x₂ = ẋ the state equations are ẋ₁ = x₂ and ẋ₂ = −(k/m)x₁ − (c/m)x₂ + u/m, so A = [[0, 1], [−25, −3]] and B = [0, 0.5]ᵀ. The characteristic polynomial is det(sI − A) = s² + (c/m)s + k/m = s² + 3s + 25. Comparing with s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n², the open-loop natural frequency is ω_n = √(k/m) = √25 = 5.0 rad/s and the damping ratio is ζ = c/(2√(km)) = 6 / (2√100) = 0.300. The poles are at −1.5 ± j4.77, a lightly damped pair that would produce a large overshoot of about 37 percent and slow decay. This is why feedback is added.

Answer: 0.300

(b)

With u = −k_p x₁ − k_d x₂ the closed-loop dynamic matrix is A − BK = [[0, 1], [−(k + k_p)/m, −(c + k_d)/m]]. Its characteristic polynomial is s² + [(c + k_d)/m]s + (k + k_p)/m. The system is controllable because the controllability matrix [B AB] = [[0, 0.5], [0.5, −1.5]] has determinant −0.25, which is non-zero, so the poles can be placed anywhere. The desired polynomial is s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n² = s² + 11.2s + 64. Matching the constant term: (k + k_p)/m = ω_n², so k_p = mω_n² − k = 2.0 × 64 − 50 = 78.0 N/m. The feedback therefore adds 78.0 N/m of electronic stiffness to the 50 N/m flexure, raising the stiffness of the stage to 128 N/m.

Answer: 78.0 N/m

(c)

Match the coefficient of s in the characteristic polynomial: (c + k_d)/m = 2ζω_n. The right side is 2 × 0.7 × 8.0 = 11.2 s⁻¹. Multiplying by m gives c + k_d = 2.0 × 11.2 = 22.4 N·s/m. Therefore k_d = 22.4 − 6.0 = 16.4 N·s/m. The closed-loop poles are at −ζω_n ± jω_n√(1 − ζ²) = −5.6 ± j5.71 rad/s, giving a predicted overshoot of exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) = 4.6 percent and a 2 percent settling time of about 4/(ζω_n) = 0.71 s. The control force at a 1 mm position error is k_p × 0.001 = 0.078 N, a modest actuator demand. In practice the velocity must be estimated by an observer or by differentiating a filtered position signal, which would add lag not included in this model.

Answer: 16.4 N·s/m

Problem 2 [A3-077] Servo motor position control

A permanent-magnet DC servo motor positions a rotary table through a speed-reducing gear train of ratio N = 10 (motor turns 10 times for one table turn). Motor data: armature resistance R = 1.2 Ω, torque constant K_t = 0.050 N·m/A, back-emf constant K_e = 0.050 V·s/rad, rotor inertia J_m = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m², viscous friction at the motor shaft b = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ N·m·s/rad. The table has inertia J_L = 0.040 kg·m² and negligible friction, and gear inertia is neglected. Armature inductance is negligible. A proportional controller applies armature voltage V = K_p(θ_ref − θ_m), with motor shaft angle θ_m measured by an encoder. The design target is a closed-loop damping ratio of ζ = 0.70 on the motor shaft model, with a 2 percent settling time estimated by 4/(ζω_n).

  1. (a) Find the equivalent inertia J_eq seen at the motor shaft. [5]
  2. (b) Find the proportional gain K_p (V/rad of motor shaft error) that gives ζ = 0.70. [8]
  3. (c) Find the 2 percent settling time of the table for a step command. [7]
(a)

A load inertia is reflected to the motor side by dividing by the square of the gear ratio, because the table speed is 1/N of the motor speed and kinetic energy ½J_Lω_L² = ½(J_L/N²)ω_m² must be preserved. The reflected load inertia is J_L/N² = 0.040/100 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m². The equivalent inertia is the motor rotor inertia plus this value: J_eq = J_m + J_L/N² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ + 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m². The gear train has made the table look like a load of only 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m² to the motor, twice the rotor inertia. That ratio is within the usual 1:1 to 5:1 inertia ratio for servo sizing.

Answer: 6.00 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m²

(b)

With negligible inductance, the electrical equation is V = Ri + K_e ω_m and the torque equation is J_eq θ̈ + bθ̇ = K_t i. Eliminating i: R J_eq θ̈ + (R b + K_t K_e)θ̇ = K_t V. Closing the loop with V = K_p(θ_ref − θ_m) gives R J_eq θ̈ + (R b + K_t K_e)θ̇ + K_t K_p θ = K_t K_p θ_ref. The damping term is Rb + K_tK_e = 1.2 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ + 0.050 × 0.050 = 2.62 × 10⁻³ N·m·s/rad, and R J_eq = 1.2 × 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 7.20 × 10⁻⁴. Dividing by RJ_eq gives 2ζω_n = 3.639 s⁻¹, so ω_n = 2.599 rad/s. Then ω_n² = K_tK_p/(RJ_eq) so K_p = ω_n² RJ_eq / K_t = 6.756 × 7.20 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.050 = 0.0973 V/rad. Note that the back-emf supplies most of the damping, so no tachometer is needed.

Answer: 0.0973 V/rad

(c)

For a second-order system with ζ = 0.70 and the natural frequency from part (b), ω_n = 2.599 rad/s, the decay rate of the envelope is ζω_n = 0.70 × 2.599 = 1.819 s⁻¹. The 2 percent settling time is approximately four time constants of the envelope: t_s = 4/(ζω_n) = 4 / 1.819 = 2.20 s. The overshoot for ζ = 0.70 is exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) = 4.6 percent. The result is slow because the proportional gain demanded by ζ = 0.70 is small: the motor is heavily back-emf damped, so raising K_p to speed the response would reduce ζ. If faster response is needed with the same damping, the designer should add velocity feedback from a tachometer or an encoder-derived rate signal, which effectively raises the damping term, or use a motor with a higher torque-to-inertia ratio. The table angle follows the motor angle divided by N, so a step of 10 rad at the motor is 1 rad at the table.

Answer: 2.20 s

Problem 3 [A3-078] Disturbance rejection

The pressure in a gas-surge vessel is regulated by a feedback loop. The vessel and control valve are modelled by P(s) = 4/(2s + 1), in kPa per percent of valve opening, with s in 1/s. A downstream load change enters at the plant input as an equivalent valve disturbance d, so the pressure deviation is Y = P(s)/(1 + P(s)C(s)) × D. Two controllers are compared: a proportional controller C = K_p = 5 (percent per kPa), and a PI controller C = K_p(1 + 1/(T_i s)) with K_p = 5 and T_i = 4 s. A sudden load change is a step of d = 3 percent. A slower pulsation load also adds a sinusoidal disturbance of amplitude 0.6 percent at ω = 0.5 rad/s. Take the setpoint as zero so that y is the deviation in kPa.

  1. (a) Find the steady-state pressure offset for the 3 percent step disturbance with the proportional controller alone. [5]
  2. (b) With the PI controller, find the peak pressure deviation after the 3 percent step disturbance. [8]
  3. (c) With the PI controller, find the amplitude of the steady sinusoidal pressure deviation caused by the 0.6 percent disturbance at ω = 0.5 rad/s. [7]
(a)

With P-only control the closed-loop transfer function from disturbance to output is Y/D = P/(1 + PK_p). By the final value theorem, for a step of size d, y_ss = lim s→0 of s × [P/(1 + PK_p)] × d/s = d P(0)/(1 + P(0)K_p). Here P(0) = 4 kPa per percent and K_p = 5, so the loop gain is P(0)K_p = 20. Then y_ss = 3 × 4 / (1 + 20) = 12/21 = 0.571 kPa. This offset remains forever because a proportional controller needs a non-zero error to hold a non-zero valve correction. Increasing K_p reduces the offset in proportion to 1/(1 + 4K_p) but never removes it, and a very high gain would erode the stability margin of the real loop, which has valve and sensor lags not shown in this simple model.

Answer: 0.571 kPa

(b)

For the PI loop, Y/D = P/(1 + PC) = K T_i s / [T_i τ s² + T_i(1 + KK_p)s + KK_p]. Substituting the numbers gives the denominator 8s² + 84s + 20. For a step of d = 3 the output is Y(s) = d K T_i / (denominator) = 48 / (8s² + 84s + 20) = 6/(s² + 10.5s + 2.5). The roots are p₁ = -0.2438 and p₂ = -10.256 s⁻¹, both real, so the response is overdamped: y(t) = 0.5993(ep₁t − ep₂t). The peak occurs when dy/dt = 0, i.e. p₁ep₁t = p₂ep₂t, giving t_pk = ln(p₂/p₁)/(p₁ − p₂) = 0.373 s. Substituting, the peak deviation is y_max = 0.534 kPa. After the peak the integral action drives the deviation back to zero, so there is no permanent offset, which is the key benefit over P-only control. The peak is only slightly below the P-only offset because the disturbance acts faster than the integral action.

Answer: 0.534 kPa

(c)

In steady state, the amplitude of the output equals the disturbance amplitude times the magnitude of Y/D evaluated at s = jω. Using Y/D = K T_i s / [T_i τ s² + T_i(1 + KK_p)s + KK_p], at ω = 0.5 rad/s the numerator is K T_i ω = 4 × 4 × 0.5 = 8.0 in magnitude. The denominator at s = jω is (c₀ − c₂ω²) + j c₁ω = (20 − 8 × 0.25) + j(84 × 0.5) = 18.0 + j42.0, whose magnitude is 45.69. Therefore |Y/D| = 8.0 / 45.69 = 0.1751 kPa per percent. The output amplitude is 0.6 × 0.1751 = 0.105 kPa. The integral action keeps the sensitivity low at this slow frequency. At frequencies far below 1/T_i the rejection improves in proportion to ω, whereas near the loop bandwidth the loop provides little rejection, so a pulsation near the crossover would be amplified rather than attenuated.

Answer: 0.105 kPa

Problem 4 [A3-079] Sampled data and digital control basics

A heated aluminium platen in a laminating press is controlled by a microcontroller. The platen with its heater has the continuous model G(s) = 2.0/(s + 0.8), for platen temperature rise in °C per percent of heater command, with s in 1/s, and the heater command is held constant between samples by a zero-order hold. The controller runs at a sampling period T = 0.5 s and uses a proportional law u[k] = K e[k], where e is the temperature error from a sensor sampled at the same instants. Take the discrete-time plant as the exact zero-order-hold equivalent G(z) = b₀/(z − p) with p = e−aT, and treat the one-sample computation delay as negligible. The engineer needs to know the pole of the plant, the gain at which the sampled loop becomes unstable, and the speed of the loop at a chosen gain.

  1. (a) Find the discrete-time open-loop pole of the zero-order-hold plant. [5]
  2. (b) Find the largest proportional gain K for which the sampled closed loop remains stable. [8]
  3. (c) For K = 0.6, find the closed-loop time constant in seconds, defined by the decay of the single discrete pole per sample. [7]
(a)

The continuous plant has a single pole at s = −a = −0.8 s⁻¹, so its step-invariant (zero-order-hold) equivalent has a pole at z = esT with s = −0.8. Therefore p = e−aT = e−0.8 × 0.5 = e−0.4 = 0.6703. The pole lies inside the unit circle, so the open-loop sampled plant is stable, as expected for a stable continuous system. The numerator constant follows from the ZOH formula: b₀ = (K_p/a)(1 − e−aT) = (2.0/0.8)(1 − 0.6703) = 2.5 × 0.3297 = 0.8242. Thus G(z) = 0.8242/(z − 0.6703). The continuous time constant is 1/a = 1.25 s, so the sampling period is 0.4 of the open-loop time constant (2.5 samples per time constant), acceptable for the open-loop plant. At K = 0.6 the closed-loop time constant is 0.288 s, only 1.7 samples, which is coarse by the usual four to ten samples per time constant guideline and is one reason the loop is limited to K < 2.03.

Answer: 0.6703

(b)

With u[k] = K e[k] and unity feedback, the closed-loop characteristic equation is 1 + K G(z) = 0, which is z − p + K b₀ = 0. The single closed-loop pole is at z = p − K b₀. For stability the pole must stay inside the unit circle, |z| < 1. For positive K the pole moves left from p as the gain rises, so the limit is z = −1: p − K b₀ = −1, which gives K_max = (1 + p)/b₀ = (1 + 0.6703) / 0.8242 = 2.027. Above this gain the pole reaches z < −1, producing a growing oscillation with a period of two samples (1.0 s). In a continuous loop with the same plant no such limit exists, since a first-order plant with proportional control is stable for every gain, so the instability is purely a result of sampling and holding. Reducing the sampling period raises K_max.

Answer: 2.027

(c)

For K = 0.6 the closed-loop pole is z = p − K b₀ = 0.6703 − 0.6 × 0.8242 = 0.6703 − 0.4945 = 0.1758. This lies inside the unit circle, close to the origin, so the loop is fast and well damped. The pole of a sampled first-order response is z = e−T/τ, so the equivalent time constant is τ = −T/ln(z) = −0.5 / ln(0.1758) = 0.5 / 1.7384 = 0.288 s. This compares with the open-loop time constant of 1.25 s, so proportional feedback has sped the platen response by a factor of 4.3. The price is a steady-state error to a step command: the DC loop gain is K b₀/(1 − p) = K × 2.0/0.8 = 1.50, so the final temperature reaches only 60 percent of the setpoint, and an integral term would be needed to remove the offset.

Answer: 0.288 s

Problem 5 [A3-080] Control of a liquid level or temperature process

A cylindrical process tank of cross-sectional area A = 2.5 m² is fed by a control valve and drains freely through an orifice, so the outflow is q_out = c√h, with h the liquid level in metres. At the normal operating point the level is h₀ = 1.6 m and the throughput is 0.020 m³/s. The inlet valve delivers K_v = 0.0040 m³/s of flow per percent of valve opening. A proportional level controller sets the valve opening change as u = K_c(h_sp − h), with K_c in percent per metre. Analyse the process by linearising the mass balance about the operating point, then use the linear model to size the controller and predict the offset for a setpoint change. Treat the valve as instantaneous.

  1. (a) Find the linearised outlet resistance R and the open-loop time constant τ of the tank. [6]
  2. (b) Find the controller gain K_c that makes the closed-loop time constant equal to 100 s. [7]
  3. (c) Find the permanent offset in level after a setpoint step of 0.30 m with this controller. [7]
(a)

The mass balance is A dh/dt = q_in − c√h. At the operating point c = q₀/√h₀ = 0.020/√1.6 = 0.01581 m2.5/s. Linearising the outflow, the slope is d(q_out)/dh = c/(2√h₀) = q₀/(2h₀) = 0.020 / (2 × 1.6) = 0.00625 m²/s. The outlet resistance R is the reciprocal: R = 2h₀/q₀ = 2 × 1.6 / 0.020 = 160 s/m². For deviation variables, A dh′/dt = q′_in − h′/R, which gives the first-order model h′/q′_in = R/(τs + 1) with time constant τ = A R = 2.5 × 160 = 400 s. The tank is therefore slow, about 6.7 minutes for each time constant, and the process gain is R = 160 m per m³/s. Linearisation is valid only for small level changes, because R changes with level (it grows as √h).

Answer: R = 160 s/m²; τ = 400 s

(b)

Substitute the valve and controller into the linear model: q′_in = K_v u = K_v K_c (h_sp − h′). Then A dh′/dt = K_vK_c(h_sp − h′) − h′/R, and dividing by 1/R gives τ_cl dh′/dt + h′ = [L/(1 + L)] h_sp, where the loop gain is L = K_c K_v R and the closed-loop time constant is τ_cl = τ/(1 + L). Setting τ_cl = 100 s with τ = 400 s gives 1 + L = 400/100 = 4, so L = 3. Hence K_c = L/(K_vR) = 3 / (0.0040 × 160) = 3/0.64 = 4.688 percent per metre. The tank now responds four times faster than it does naturally. Check the valve demand: a 0.3 m level error would call for 1.41 percent of opening, well within the valve range.

Answer: 4.688 % per m

(c)

The closed-loop transfer function is h′/h_sp = L/(1 + L)/(τ_cl s + 1), so the steady-state level after a setpoint step Δh_sp is Δh_sp × L/(1 + L). With L = 3 this is 0.30 × 3/4 = 0.225 m, and the offset (setpoint minus final level) is Δh_sp/(1 + L) = 0.30 / (1 + 3) = 0.075 m. Equivalently the offset is the setpoint step multiplied by 1/(1 + K_cK_vR). A proportional-only level controller always leaves an offset because the valve must stay open by a different amount at the new level to balance the outflow, and this requires a non-zero error. For a surge tank the offset is often acceptable, since only the high and low limits matter. If tighter control is required, adding integral action removes the offset, at the cost of a more oscillatory loop, because the combined tank and PI controller form a second-order system.

Answer: 0.075 m

A3 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A3-081] Mathematical models of mechanical systems

A passenger car body is modelled as a single degree of freedom system: the sprung mass of one corner is m = 350 kg, carried on a coil spring of stiffness k = 28 000 N/m and a hydraulic damper of coefficient c. The wheel and tyre are assumed to follow the road exactly, so the road input is the base displacement. A supplier offers two dampers: a comfort damper with c = 1800 N·s/m and a firm damper with c = 5000 N·s/m. Road joints on a concrete highway excite the body at 2.0 Hz at the test speed. Treat the system as linear, with viscous damping and small motions, and use displacement transmissibility from the road to the body as the measure of ride quality. The vehicle engineer must justify the damper choice in a design memo, using numbers rather than opinion.

  1. (a) Write the equation of motion for the body displacement and find the damping ratio for the comfort damper. [6]
  2. (b) Find the displacement transmissibility at 2.0 Hz with the comfort damper. [5]
  3. (c) Find the displacement transmissibility at 2.0 Hz with the firm damper. [5]
  4. (d) Recommend one damper for highway comfort and state one drawback of your choice, referring to your numbers. [4]
(a)

Take x as body displacement and y as road displacement. Newton's second law on the body gives m x'' + c (x' - y') + k (x - y) = 0, so m x'' + c x' + k x = c y' + k y. The undamped natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √(28 000/350) = √80 = 8.944 rad/s, which is 1.42 Hz. The critical damping coefficient is cc = 2√(km) = 2√(28 000 × 350) = 2 × 3130.5 = 6261 N·s/m. For the comfort damper the damping ratio is ζ = c/cc = 1800/6261 = 0.2875. The system is therefore underdamped, with a resonance near 1.42 Hz. State the assumptions: linear spring, viscous damper, tyre stiffness neglected, and a single vertical mode per corner. The answer is ζ ≈ 0.287.

Answer: 0.2875

(b)

The transmissibility for base excitation is T = √(1 + (2ζr)²) / √((1 - r²)² + (2ζr)²), where r = ω/ωn. The excitation is ω = 2π × 2.0 = 12.566 rad/s, so r = 12.566/8.944 = 1.405. With ζ = 0.2875, 2ζr = 0.8078, and 1 - r² = -0.9739. The numerator is √(1 + 0.6526) = 1.2855. The denominator is √(0.9485 + 0.6526) = 1.2654. Therefore T = 1.0159. Since T is close to 1, the body moves almost as much as the road at 2 Hz, because 2 Hz (r = 1.405) sits just below r = √2 = 1.414 (2.013 Hz), where isolation only begins.

Answer: 1.016

(c)

Use the same expression with the firm damper. The damping ratio is ζ = 5000/6261 = 0.7986, so 2ζr = 2.2440, and r = 1.405 with 1 - r² = -0.9739. The numerator is √(1 + 5.0355) = 2.4567. The denominator is √(0.9485 + 5.0355) = 2.4462. Hence T = 1.0043. The firm damper gives the smaller transmissibility, 1.004 against 1.016 for the comfort damper, because r = 1.405 is slightly below √2, where added damping still lowers T. The benefit is tiny, since T is near 1 for any damping at r close to √2. Above r = √2 the trend reverses: at 5 Hz the comfort damper gives T = 0.196 and the firm damper 0.450.

Answer: 1.004

(d)

Recommendation: choose the firm damper, c = 5000 N·s/m. At the 2.0 Hz joint frequency its transmissibility is 1.004 against 1.016 for the comfort damper, a small gain at the test speed, and with ζ = 0.80 it controls the body resonance near 1.4 Hz, where the comfort damper (ζ = 0.29) gives T = 2.01 against 1.18 for the firm one, so body float after a large bump decays much faster. The drawback is a harsher ride at higher frequencies above r = √2: at 5 Hz the firm damper transmits T = 0.450 against 0.196 for the comfort damper. A semi-active damper that switches between the two values would avoid the compromise. The memo should state both numbers and the assumptions made.

Answer: Choose the firm damper (T = 1.004 against 1.016 at 2 Hz, and ζ = 0.80 controls the 1.4 Hz body resonance); drawback is higher transmissibility above r = √2, for example 0.450 against 0.196 at 5 Hz, i.e. a harsher ride.

Problem 2 [A3-082] Electrical and thermal system analogues

A totally enclosed induction motor is analysed with a lumped thermal model: the winding and core act as a single thermal capacitance C = 4200 J/K, and heat leaves to the 25 °C surroundings through a thermal resistance R = 0.85 K/W. After a load change the motor dissipates a constant 180 W of loss. Its insulation is rated to a maximum winding temperature of 155 °C. The plant electrician proposes fitting an external fan that reduces the thermal resistance to 0.55 K/W without changing the capacitance. Use the electrical analogy in which temperature difference corresponds to voltage, heat flow to current, thermal resistance to resistance and thermal capacitance to capacitance, and assume the motor starts at ambient temperature.

  1. (a) Draw the analogous electrical circuit in words and find the thermal time constant. [4]
  2. (b) Find the final winding temperature without the fan. [4]
  3. (c) Find the time after which the winding reaches 155 °C without the fan. [5]
  4. (d) Find the final winding temperature with the fan fitted. [4]
  5. (e) Judge whether the fan is needed if the load is continuous, and what the time to the limit tells the operator about short duty. [3]
(a)

The analogue is a current source of 180 A-equivalent (the 180 W loss) feeding a node. From that node a capacitor of 4200 (units: J/K) goes to ground, and a resistor of 0.85 (units: K/W) goes to a battery representing the 25 °C ambient. The node voltage is the winding temperature rise above ambient. Kirchhoff's current law at the node gives C dθ/dt + θ/R = P, where θ = T - Ta. This is a first order lag with time constant τ = RC = 0.85 × 4200 = 3570 s, which is 0.99 h. Such a long time constant is typical of a massive motor frame: the winding temperature responds slowly to load changes. Assumptions: uniform temperature, constant loss and a constant thermal resistance independent of temperature.

Answer: 3570 s

(b)

At steady state dθ/dt = 0, so the capacitor carries no current and all of the loss passes through R: θss = P R = 180 × 0.85 = 153 K. The final winding temperature is Tss = Ta + θss = 25 + 153 = 178 °C. This exceeds the 155 °C insulation limit by 23 K, so the motor cannot carry this load continuously without the fan. The electrical equivalent is the divider formed by the source current through the series resistor: the voltage across the resistor equals current times resistance once the capacitor is fully charged. Hence Tss ≈ 178 °C, which is the number the manufacturer's duty rating would be checked against.

Answer: 178 °C

(c)

The step response from ambient is T(t) = Ta + P R (1 - e-t/τ). Setting T = 155 °C gives 130 = 153 (1 - e-t/τ), so e-t/τ = 1 - 130/153 = 0.1503. Taking logarithms, t/τ = -ln(0.1503) = 1.8949. With τ = 3570 s, t = 1.8949 × 3570 = 6765 s, which is 1.88 h. The motor will therefore reach its insulation limit in a little under two hours of continuous operation at this load. The check is that at t = τ the temperature is 63.2 percent of the way to 178 °C, which is about 122 °C, comfortably below 155 °C, consistent with a time to limit longer than τ.

Answer: 6765 s

(d)

With the fan, R falls to 0.55 K/W, so the steady rise is θss = P R = 180 × 0.55 = 99 K. The final temperature is Tss = 25 + 99 = 124 °C. This is 31 K below the 155 °C limit, a margin of 24 percent of the permissible rise. The new time constant is τ = R C = 0.55 × 4200 = 2310 s, so the motor also reaches its smaller final value more quickly, in roughly four time constants or 2.6 h. The analogue is a lower resistor from the node to ambient: the same current produces a smaller voltage, while the capacitor charges faster through the lower resistance.

Answer: 124 °C

(e)

Judgement: for continuous load the fan is needed, because the bare motor settles at 178 °C, above the 155 °C rating, whereas with the fan it settles at 124 °C with margin. The time to the limit, 1.9 h without a fan, tells the operator that short duty is safe: a load of 180 W lasting under about one hour never reaches the limit, and a duty cycle with long cool periods stays far below it. The result depends on the fan staying running; if the fan fails the motor reverts to the bare behaviour and a thermal trip, set near 150 °C, should protect the winding. Recommend the fan and a winding thermistor trip.

Answer: Fan needed for continuous duty; bare motor is acceptable only for short duty under about 1 h.

Problem 3 [A3-083] Hydraulic and pneumatic system models

A pneumatic positioning cell uses an air receiver of volume V = 0.08 m³ that is charged through a small orifice from a regulated supply. Linearised about its operating point, the orifice behaves as a pneumatic resistance R = 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa·s/kg relating the pressure difference across it to the mass flow rate. The receiver temperature is 293 K, and air has gas constant 287 J/(kg·K). The designer must decide whether to treat expansion in the receiver as isothermal (slow filling, good heat exchange with the walls) or as a polytropic process with exponent n = 1.3 (fast cycling, little heat transfer). The supply pressure is stepped up by a small amount and the receiver pressure is the output. Treat the air as an ideal gas and assume the flow stays linear in the pressure difference.

  1. (a) Derive the pneumatic capacitance for isothermal conditions and give its value in units of 10⁻⁷ kg/Pa. [5]
  2. (b) Find the time constant of the receiver pressure response. [4]
  3. (c) Find the time for the receiver pressure to complete 90 percent of a small supply step. [4]
  4. (d) Find the time constant if the process is polytropic with n = 1.3. [4]
  5. (e) State which model suits a 0.5 s cycle time and why. [3]
(a)

The mass of air in the receiver is m = pV/(R_gas T). For small changes at constant temperature, dm = (V/(R_gas T)) dp, so the capacitance is C = dm/dp = V/(R_gas T). Substituting, C = 0.08 / (287 × 293) = 0.08 / 84 091 = 9.5135 × 10⁻⁷ kg/Pa, which is 9.514 × 10⁻⁷ kg/Pa. The analogy is an electrical capacitor storing charge: mass of gas is the charge, pressure is the voltage. Assumptions: ideal gas, uniform pressure and temperature inside the receiver, and linear flow through the orifice for small perturbations. The isothermal case gives the largest capacitance, because heat flow from the walls keeps the gas temperature steady while the pressure rises.

Answer: 9.514 ×10⁻⁷ kg/Pa

(b)

Mass conservation gives C dp/dt = ṁ in, and the linearised orifice gives ṁ in = (ps - p)/R. Hence RC dp/dt + p = ps, a first order lag with time constant τ = RC. Substituting, τ = 2.0 × 10⁶ × 9.5135 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.903 s. The transfer function from supply pressure to receiver pressure is 1/(τ s + 1). The response to a small step is therefore exponential with this time constant, reaching 63.2 percent of the step at t = τ. Since the calculated time constant is a little under two seconds, the receiver is a slow element compared with the pneumatic valve and the cylinder it feeds, so the receiver would often dominate the overall dynamics of the cell.

Answer: 1.903 s

(c)

For a first order lag, the output fraction is 1 - e-t/τ. Setting this to 0.90 gives e-t/τ = 0.10, so t = τ ln(10) = 2.3026 τ. With τ = 1.903 s, t90 = 2.3026 × 1.903 = 4.381 s. For comparison, a settling to within 2 percent would take 3.91 τ = 7.44 s. A rule of thumb for planning the machine cycle is therefore that the receiver pressure cannot respond faster than about 4.4 s to a full recovery, which should be checked against the required cycle time before the receiver size is accepted.

Answer: 4.381 s

(d)

For a polytropic process p Vn = constant, the gas temperature changes with pressure, and the mass stored per unit pressure falls: C = V/(n R_gas T). With n = 1.3, C = 0.08 / (1.3 × 287 × 293) = 7.3181 × 10⁻⁷ kg/Pa. The time constant is τ = R C = 2.0 × 10⁶ × 7.3181 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.464 s. This is 23 percent shorter than the isothermal value, because the compressed air heats up and the pressure rises faster for each kilogram added. The t90 value in this case is 3.37 s. The polytropic model applies when the filling is too fast for heat exchange with the walls.

Answer: 1.464 s

(e)

For a cycle time of 0.5 s the pressure rise per stroke occurs within a fraction of a second, which is far too quick for the walls to equalise the gas temperature. The polytropic model with n close to 1.3 is therefore the better choice, giving τ = 1.46 s, and the isothermal model would overpredict the time constant by about 30 percent. In either case τ is several times the 0.5 s cycle, so the receiver is far too slow for this duty: either the orifice resistance must fall by a factor of about 15 to reach τ ≈ 0.1 s, or the receiver volume must be reduced. Recommend the polytropic model and a redesign.

Answer: Polytropic (n ≈ 1.3) model, because the cycle is too fast for heat exchange; in both models τ greatly exceeds 0.5 s.

Problem 4 [A3-084] Block diagram reduction

A machine-tool slide has a cascaded position controller. The inner velocity loop contains a power amplifier and motor with forward transfer function G1(s) = 10/(s + 2), and a tachometer feedback gain H in the inner loop; the commissioned value is H = 0.5. The inner loop output is velocity, which an integrator G2(s) = 4/s converts to position. The outer loop feeds back position with unity gain and compares it with the command. All signals are in consistent normalised units. The commissioning engineer observes a noticeable overshoot on step moves and asks whether the tachometer gain should be raised to 1.0. Reduce the block diagram stage by stage, find the closed loop characteristics at H = 0.5, and judge the proposal using numbers.

  1. (a) Reduce the inner loop and find its low frequency (DC) gain at H = 0.5. [4]
  2. (b) Find the overall closed loop transfer function and its undamped natural frequency. [3]
  3. (c) Find the damping ratio at H = 0.5. [4]
  4. (d) Find the percentage overshoot of the position step response at H = 0.5. [5]
  5. (e) Find the damping ratio when H is raised to 1.0 and state whether the proposal removes the overshoot. [4]
(a)

The inner loop is a negative feedback loop with forward path G1 = 10/(s + 2) and feedback H = 0.5. Its closed loop transfer function is G1/(1 + G1 H) = [10/(s + 2)] / [1 + 5/(s + 2)] = 10 / (s + 2 + 5) = 10/(s + 7). The DC gain is found by setting s = 0, giving 10/7 = 1.4286. The pole has moved from s = -2 to s = -7: the tachometer feedback makes the velocity loop faster, trading gain for bandwidth. The inner loop gain at DC is below its open loop value of 5. Assumptions: signals are linear, there is no saturation of the amplifier, and the tachometer has no lag.

Answer: 1.429

(b)

The outer forward path is the inner loop in series with the integrator: G(s) = [10/(s + 7)] × [4/s] = 40/(s(s + 7)). With unity feedback, the closed loop is T(s) = G/(1 + G) = 40/(s² + 7s + 40). Comparing with the standard form s² + 2ζωn s + ωn², ωn² = 40, so ωn = √40 = 6.325 rad/s, and 2ζωn = 7. The system is second order with no zeros, so the standard overshoot and settling formulas apply directly. The DC gain of T is 40/40 = 1, which confirms there is zero steady state error to a step, as expected from the integrator in the forward path.

Answer: 6.325 rad/s

(c)

From 2ζωn = 7, ζ = 7/(2 × 6.325) = 7/12.649 = 0.5534. This is below 0.7, so the response is underdamped, with a damped natural frequency ωd = ωn√(1 - ζ²) = 6.325 × √(1 - 0.3063) = 5.268 rad/s. The poles are at s = -3.5 ± j5.27. A damping ratio of 0.55 corresponds to a visible overshoot of about 12 percent in the step response, consistent with the observation made at commissioning. The real part of the poles, -3.5, sets the envelope: the oscillation decays with a time constant of 1/3.5 = 0.286 s.

Answer: 0.5534

(d)

The percentage overshoot for a second order system without zeros is Mp = 100 exp(-πζ/√(1 - ζ²)). With ζ = 0.5534, √(1 - ζ²) = 0.8329, so the exponent is -π × 0.5534 / 0.8329 = -2.0873. Then exp(-2.0873) = 0.1240, and Mp = 12.4 percent. For a position slide this overshoot is unacceptable near a hard stop or a workpiece. The peak time is π/ωd = 0.596 s. The overshoot formula assumes a pure second order response with no closed loop zero, which holds here because the numerator of the closed loop transfer function is the constant 40. A first overshoot peak this large would also stress the lead screw and the workpiece clamp, so the commissioning engineer is right to question the tachometer setting rather than accept the result. Overshoot of this size would violate most machine-tool specifications, which commonly allow only a few percent.

Answer: 12.4 %

(e)

With H = 1.0 the inner loop becomes 10/(s + 2 + 10) = 10/(s + 12). The outer forward path is 40/(s(s + 12)), and the closed loop is 40/(s² + 12s + 40). The natural frequency is unchanged at √40 = 6.325 rad/s, and ζ = 12/(2 × 6.325) = 0.9487. This is just below 1 and the overshoot is Mp = 100 exp(-π × 0.9487/√(1 - 0.9000)) = 0.01 percent. The proposal removes almost all of the overshoot. The cost is a slower rise (10 to 90 percent rise time about 0.49 s against 0.28 s) because the response is nearly critically damped; the 2 percent settling time is about the same or slightly shorter (about 0.83 s against 0.92 s) since the real part of the poles grows from -3.5 to -6, with the poles at s = -6 ± j2.00.

Answer: 0.9487

Problem 5 [A3-085] Signal flow and Mason gain

The signal flow graph of a drive for a rolling mill stand has one input node and one output node. There are two forward paths from input to output: path 1 has gain P1 = 6.0 and passes through every other node of the graph, so it touches all loops; path 2 has gain P2 = 3.0 and shares nodes with loops L1 and L3 but not with loop L2. The three feedback loops have gains L1 = -0.4 (current loop), L2 = -0.25 (speed loop) and L3 = -0.1 (thickness gauge trim). Loops L1 and L3 share no node, but L2 touches both of them. A maintenance engineer reports that ageing of the tachometer in the speed loop has changed the speed-loop gain from -0.25 to -0.60, and asks how much the overall gain changes and whether this matters to the product.

  1. (a) Find the graph determinant Δ using Mason's gain formula. [5]
  2. (b) Find the numerator sum of each forward path gain multiplied by its cofactor. [4]
  3. (c) Find the overall transfer function (gain) of the graph. [4]
  4. (d) Find the overall gain after the speed loop gain changes to -0.60. [4]
  5. (e) Find the percentage change in overall gain and say whether it matters to rolled strip thickness. [3]
(a)

Mason's formula gives Δ = 1 - (sum of individual loop gains) + (sum of products of gains of every pair of non-touching loops) - (products of non-touching triples). The loop sum is -0.4 - 0.25 - 0.1 = -0.75. The only non-touching pair is L1 and L3, with product (-0.4)(-0.1) = 0.04. L2 touches both of them, so no other pair or triple exists. Therefore Δ = 1 - (-0.75) + 0.04 = 1 + 0.75 + 0.04 = 1.79. The determinant exceeds 1 because all three loops are negative feedback loops, which reduce the overall gain. Loop gains are written with their signs, which is where most marks are lost in this method.

Answer: 1.79

(b)

Each forward path is multiplied by its cofactor Δk, the determinant of the graph with all loops touching path k removed. Path 1 touches all loops, so Δ1 = 1. Path 2 touches L1 and L3 but not L2, so only L2 remains in its sub-graph and Δ2 = 1 - L2 = 1 - (-0.25) = 1.25. The numerator is the sum P1 Δ1 + P2 Δ2 = 6.0 × 1 + 3.0 × 1.25 = 6.0 + 3.75 = 9.75. Path 2 therefore contributes more than its raw gain of 3.0, since the speed loop is not in its way and that loop gain is not allowed to attenuate it. This is the step students commonly miss, so the cofactors should be written out beside each path.

Answer: 9.75

(c)

The overall gain is T = Σ Pk Δk / Δ = 9.75 / 1.79 = 5.4469. A check on reasonableness: the raw forward gains add to 9.0, and the feedback reduces the response, so a value of 5.45 is plausible. If all loops were absent, T would simply be P1 + P2 = 9.0. The value shows the combined effect of the three loops cutting the forward gain by a factor of about 1.65. The result is a dimensionless gain of 5.45 between the input and output nodes of this graph, which matches the result that would be obtained by block diagram reduction for the same system.

Answer: 5.447

(d)

With L2 = -0.60 the loop sum becomes -0.4 - 0.6 - 0.1 = -1.1, and the non-touching pair is unchanged at 0.04, so Δ = 1 + 1.1 + 0.04 = 2.14. The cofactor of path 2 becomes Δ2 = 1 - (-0.6) = 1.6, while Δ1 stays 1. The numerator is 6.0 × 1 + 3.0 × 1.6 = 6.0 + 4.8 = 10.8. The new overall gain is T = 10.8 / 2.14 = 5.0467. The numerator rose as the cofactor of path 2 grew, but the denominator rose by more, so the overall gain fell slightly. This is a partial cancellation, which makes the overall graph quite insensitive to the speed-loop gain.

Answer: 5.047

(e)

The change is (T_new - T_old)/T_old = (5.0467 - 5.4469) / 5.4469 = -7.35 percent. This is a small change for a 140 percent change in one loop gain, so the overall gain is not very sensitive to the ageing tachometer. For rolled strip thickness, if the gain feeds the thickness reference directly, a 7 percent drop in gain could produce a thickness error of that order unless the gauge trim loop L3 corrects it; the trim loop does cancel part of the error. Judgement: the tachometer should still be replaced at the next stoppage, because the loop dynamics (not the DC gain) will change more markedly, but the line need not be stopped now.

Answer: -7.35 %

A3 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A3-086] First-order system step response

A bare bead thermocouple is used to measure the temperature of an exhaust gas in an engine test cell. The bead is a sphere of diameter 1.5 mm, with density 8900 kg/m³ and specific heat 420 J/(kg·K). The convective coefficient between the gas and the bead is 250 W/(m²·K). The gas temperature suddenly steps from 20 °C to 300 °C when a valve opens. Radiation and conduction along the wires are neglected, and the bead is treated as a lumped capacitance. The test engineer is considering a sheathed probe, which is more robust but responds with a time constant of 11.5 s. The test also includes a gas temperature ramp of 2.0 K/s. Use first order response theory to compare the two probes and decide which is suitable for transient work.

  1. (a) Find the time constant of the bare bead. [4]
  2. (b) Find the time for the bare bead to read within 2 percent of the final step. [4]
  3. (c) Find the temperature the bare bead reads 5 s after the step. [4]
  4. (d) Find the error of the sheathed probe 5 s after the step, relative to the true gas temperature. [4]
  5. (e) Find the steady lag of the sheathed probe in the 2.0 K/s ramp and judge its suitability. [4]
(a)

For a lumped sphere the energy balance is ρ c V dT/dt = h A (Tg - T). With V/A = d/6 for a sphere, the time constant is τ = ρ c V/(h A) = ρ c d/(6 h). Substituting, τ = 8900 × 420 × 0.0015 / (6 × 250) = 5607 / 1500 = 3.738 s. The Biot number is Bi = h (d/6)/k, and for a metal bead with k of order 20 W/(m·K) it is about 0.003, far below 0.1, so the lumped assumption is sound. The thermal time constant of a 1.5 mm bead is a few seconds, which is slow for engine transients with events lasting less than a second.

Answer: 3.738 s

(b)

The step response is T = Tg - (Tg - T0) e-t/τ. Within 2 percent of the final step means the remaining error is 0.02 of the step: e-t/τ = 0.02. Hence t = -τ ln(0.02) = 3.912 τ = 3.912 × 3.738 = 14.62 s. The usual rule of thumb that settling takes about 4 time constants is confirmed. A 2 percent band of a 280 K step is 5.6 K, so after 14.6 s the bead is within 5.6 K of 300 °C. Even the bare bead therefore needs about 15 s to settle, so any gas change faster than a few seconds will be smeared out in the recorded trace.

Answer: 14.62 s

(c)

Use T = 300 - 280 e-t/τ with t = 5 s and τ = 3.738 s. The ratio t/τ is 5/3.738 = 1.3376, and e-1.3376 = 0.2625. So T = 300 - 280 × 0.2625 = 300 - 73.5 = 226.5 °C. After 5 s the bead has therefore covered 74 percent of the step, leaving an error of 73.5 K. If the engineer reads the instrument at this time the value is still low by that amount, which would matter for emissions testing, where the gas temperature must be known to a few kelvin.

Answer: 226.5 °C

(d)

For the sheathed probe use the same relation with τ = 11.5 s: the reading is 300 - 280 e-5/11.5. Here 5/11.5 = 0.4348 and e-0.4348 = 0.6474, so the reading is 300 - 181.3 = 118.7 °C. The error relative to the true gas temperature of 300 °C is 181.3 K. This is 2.47 times the bare-bead error at the same instant, so the sheathed probe is clearly the slower instrument. The sheath adds mass and lowers the effective heat transfer coefficient, so the lag is almost three times the bead value.

Answer: 181 K

(e)

For a ramp input r(t) = a t, a first order sensor follows with a steady lag equal to a τ. With a = 2.0 K/s and τ = 11.5 s the lag is 2.0 × 11.5 = 23.0 K, and the sensor reads 23 K below the true gas temperature at all times once the transient has died away. The bare bead would lag by 2.0 × 3.74 = 7.5 K. Judgement: the sheathed probe is unsuitable for transient work because a lag of 23 K exceeds typical test tolerances of ±5 K; it is acceptable only for steady-state surveys. Use the bare bead, or apply a lag correction by compensating with a lead term using the measured τ.

Answer: 23 K

Problem 2 [A3-087] Second-order system time response specs

A small positioning stage is driven by a torque motor and ball screw. Referred to the motor shaft, the moving inertia is J = 0.020 kg·m², and friction is negligible. The controller applies torque T = Kp (θr - θ) - Kd ω, where θ is the shaft angle, ω is the shaft speed and θr is the commanded angle. The stage must meet a specification for a step move: overshoot no more than 10 percent and 2 percent settling time no more than 0.50 s. The designer will place the closed loop poles exactly on the boundary of the specification, since a more conservative design wastes motor torque. Treat the system as the standard second order model, using the settling time approximation ts = 4/(ζωn). A reviewer asks whether the specification is realistic for the motor available, so the design values must be reported with units.

  1. (a) Find the minimum damping ratio that meets the overshoot limit. [4]
  2. (b) With ζ at its boundary value, find the natural frequency that makes the 2 percent settling time exactly 0.50 s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the proportional gain Kp. [4]
  4. (d) Find the derivative (velocity feedback) gain Kd. [4]
  5. (e) Find the peak time and judge whether the specification is realistic for the motor. [4]
(a)

For a second order system the percentage overshoot is Mp = 100 exp(-πζ/√(1 - ζ²)). Setting Mp = 10 percent gives exp(-πζ/√(1 - ζ²)) = 0.10, so πζ/√(1 - ζ²) = ln(10) = 2.3026. Squaring and solving, ζ² = ln²(0.10) / (π² + ln²(0.10)) = 5.3019 / (9.8696 + 5.3019) = 0.3495, which gives ζ = 0.5912. This is the smallest damping ratio which meets the limit, because overshoot falls as ζ rises. Note that the result depends on the standard model having no zeros; the velocity-feedback structure used here introduces no closed loop zero, so the formula applies exactly.

Answer: 0.5912

(b)

The 2 percent settling time is ts = 4/(ζωn). Requiring ts = 0.50 s with ζ at its boundary value gives ωn = 4/(ζ × 0.50) = 4 / (0.5912 × 0.50) = 4/0.2956 = 13.53 rad/s. This is 2.15 Hz. The real part of the poles is σ = ζωn = 8.0 rad/s, which is what the settling time fixes, since ts = 4/σ = 0.50 s. The poles are therefore at s = -8.0 ± j10.92. Choosing a larger ωn would give a faster response than the specification, but would demand more motor torque and greater bandwidth in the current loop.

Answer: 13.53 rad/s

(c)

With the control law the dynamics are J θ'' = Kp (θr - θ) - Kd θ'. Hence J s² + Kd s + Kp = 0 characterises the closed loop, which is s² + (Kd/J) s + Kp/J = 0. Matching with s² + 2ζωn s + ωn², Kp/J = ωn², so Kp = J ωn² = 0.020 × 13.53² = 0.020 × 183.14 = 3.663 N·m/rad. As a check, a 0.1 rad error produces a torque of 0.366 N·m, a modest value for a small servo motor. The gain is the stiffness the controller provides against position error, and it sets the natural frequency of the stage.

Answer: 3.66 N·m/rad

(d)

Matching the s coefficient, Kd/J = 2ζωn, so Kd = 2 ζ ωn J = 2 × 0.5912 × 13.53 × 0.020 = 0.3200 N·m·s/rad. Equivalent form: Kd = 2 √(Kp J) ζ = 2 × √(3.663 × 0.020) × 0.5912 = 0.3200 N·m·s/rad, which agrees. The derivative gain supplies the damping torque proportional to speed, and for a tachometer measuring in rad/s the units are N·m per rad/s. If speed is derived from an encoder, noise will limit how far Kd can be raised, so a filtered derivative is normally used in practice.

Answer: 0.32 N·m·s/rad

(e)

The peak time is tp = π/ωd, where ωd = ωn√(1 - ζ²) = 13.53 × √(1 - 0.3495) = 10.92 rad/s. Therefore tp = π/10.92 = 0.288 s. Judgement: the peak occurs at about 0.29 s, well inside the 0.50 s settling target, which is consistent. The torque needed for a 1 rad step is Kp × 1 = 3.66 N·m at the first instant, which a small motor will saturate unless the step is limited to a few degrees. The specification is realistic only for small moves, or the command should be shaped into a smoothed profile to keep peak torque within the motor rating.

Answer: 0.288 s

Problem 3 [A3-088] Steady-state error and system type

A telescope azimuth drive is a unity feedback position loop with open loop transfer function G(s) = K (s + 3) / (s² (s + 8)), where K is an adjustable gain set by the servo amplifier. The mount must track a satellite whose apparent motion is well modelled over a short pass as an angle with a constant angular acceleration of 0.5 rad/s². The pointing specification is that the steady state tracking error for this acceleration input must not exceed 0.010 rad. The commissioning engineer has set K = 100 as a first trial. Because a large gain may endanger stability, the design must also be checked against the Routh criterion on the closed loop characteristic equation before the gain is accepted.

  1. (a) State the system type number from the open loop transfer function. [3]
  2. (b) Find the static acceleration error constant Ka at K = 100. [4]
  3. (c) Find the steady state error for the 0.5 rad/s² acceleration input at K = 100. [4]
  4. (d) Find the minimum K that meets the 0.010 rad specification. [4]
  5. (e) Apply the Routh criterion at that K, give the s¹ entry of the array, and state whether the design is stable. [5]
(a)

The type number is the number of free integrators (poles at s = 0) in the open loop transfer function. G(s) = K(s + 3)/(s²(s + 8)) has a double pole at the origin, so it is a type 2 system. A type 2 loop follows a step and a ramp with zero steady state error, and a parabolic (constant acceleration) input with a finite, constant error. The constant acceleration input in this problem is therefore exactly the case for which the error is finite, and the static acceleration error constant is the quantity that sets it. Answer: type 2. The conclusion assumes the closed loop is stable, which must be confirmed separately with the Routh test applied in part e.

Answer: 2

(b)

The static acceleration error constant is Ka = lim(s→0) s² G(s). Substituting, s² × K(s + 3)/(s²(s + 8)) = K(s + 3)/(s + 8), and at s = 0 this becomes 3K/8. For K = 100, Ka = 3 × 100/8 = 37.5 s⁻². The units follow from the loop gain being dimensionless and the two integrators contributing s⁻² each. A larger Ka means a smaller error to constant acceleration, so Ka acts as the measure of tracking quality for this input. Note that the zero at s = -3 raises Ka above K/8, which would be the value for a plain type 2 loop without the lead zero.

Answer: 37.5 s⁻²

(c)

For a parabolic input r(t) = ½ A t² with A = 0.5 rad/s², the steady state error is ess = A/Ka. Substituting, ess = 0.5 / 37.5 = 0.01333 rad, which is 13.33 mrad. This is larger than the 0.010 rad specification of 10 mrad, so the trial gain K = 100 fails the requirement by 33 percent. The error is constant in time, which means the telescope lags behind the satellite by a fixed angle during the pass, and the lag grows in proportion to the acceleration. The gain must therefore be raised, subject to stability.

Answer: 0.01333 rad

(d)

We need ess ≤ 0.010 rad, so Ka ≥ A/0.010 = 0.5/0.010 = 50 s⁻². Since Ka = 3K/8, K ≥ 50 × 8/3 = 133.33. Therefore the minimum gain is K = 133.3. Check: Ka = 3 × 133.33/8 = 50, and ess = 0.5/50 = 0.0100 rad, as required. In practice the designer would add a margin of ten or twenty percent, because the tolerances of the amplifier and the motor constant will change the effective K, so a value near 150 would be chosen, provided the stability check in part e passes comfortably.

Answer: 133.3

(e)

The closed loop characteristic equation is 1 + G(s) = 0, that is s²(s + 8) + K(s + 3) = 0, or s³ + 8s² + K s + 3K = 0. The Routh array has first column entries: s³: 1; s²: 8; s¹: (8 × K - 1 × 3K)/8 = 5K/8; s⁰: 3K. At K = 133.33, the s¹ entry is 5 × 133.33/8 = 83.33, and the s⁰ entry is 400.0. All entries in the first column are positive, so there are no sign changes and no right half plane poles. The array shows that this loop is stable for every positive K, because 5K/8 and 3K are positive whenever K is. The design with K near 133 is therefore accepted; the margin still needs a Bode check at high gain.

Answer: 83.33

Problem 4 [A3-089] Routh-Hurwitz stability

A heated reactor jacket is controlled by a proportional temperature controller. The loop transfer function is G(s) = K / ((s + 1)(s + 3)(s + 5)), where time is in minutes, so poles are in min⁻¹ and K is the proportional loop gain. The closed loop characteristic equation, with unity feedback, is therefore s³ + 9s² + 23s + (15 + K) = 0. The operators currently run at K = 40. A process engineer wants to raise K to speed up disturbance recovery, but the safety rules require not only closed loop stability but also that every closed loop pole lies to the left of s = -1 min⁻¹, so that disturbances decay with a time constant of less than one minute. Use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to find the limits and to judge how much freedom the operators have.

  1. (a) Find the largest K for which the closed loop is stable. [4]
  2. (b) Find the frequency of sustained oscillation at that limiting gain. [4]
  3. (c) Find the s¹ entry of the Routh array at K = 100 and state the stability. [4]
  4. (d) Shift the axis to s = z - 1 and find the largest K for which all poles satisfy Re(s) < -1. [5]
  5. (e) Find the gain margin at the current setting K = 40, in decibels, and judge the proposal to raise K. [3]
(a)

Routh array for s³ + 9s² + 23s + (15 + K): s³ row: 1, 23; s² row: 9, 15 + K; s¹ row: (9 × 23 - 1 × (15 + K))/9 = (207 - 15 - K)/9 = (192 - K)/9; s⁰ row: 15 + K. For stability every first column entry must be positive. The s² entry 9 is positive, and the s⁰ entry is positive for K > -15. The s¹ entry is positive only if 192 - K > 0, so K < 192. For K > 0 the loop is stable for 0 < K < 192, and K = 192 is the marginal value at which a pair of poles reaches the imaginary axis. This gives the stability limit used by the plant standard for the controller, with the operating gain well within it at K = 40.

Answer: 192

(b)

At marginal stability the s¹ entry is zero, so the auxiliary polynomial comes from the s² row: 9 s² + (15 + K) = 0. With K = 192, 9 s² + 207 = 0, so s² = -23.00 and s = ± j√23 = ± j4.796 rad/min. The third root is real, found by dividing out the quadratic factor: the sum of roots equals -9, so the real root is -9. The sustained oscillation therefore has angular frequency 4.796 rad/min, a period of 2π/4.796 = 1.31 min. This is the ultimate period used in Ziegler-Nichols tuning.

Answer: 4.796 rad/min

(c)

At K = 100 the characteristic equation is s³ + 9s² + 23s + 115. The s¹ entry is (9 × 23 - 115)/9 = (207 - 115)/9 = 92/9 = 10.22. The first column is 1, 9, 10.22, 115, all positive, so there is no sign change and the closed loop is stable at K = 100. The same result follows from K < 192. The smallness of the s¹ entry relative to 9 shows the system is approaching the limit, because the entry falls linearly to zero as K nears 192, so the damping of the dominant pair falls and the step response becomes increasingly oscillatory even though it remains stable.

Answer: 10.22

(d)

Substitute s = z - 1 into s³ + 9s² + 23s + 15 + K. Expanding (z - 1)³ = z³ - 3z² + 3z - 1, and 9(z - 1)² = 9z² - 18z + 9, and 23(z - 1) = 23z - 23. Summing: z³ + 6z² + 8z + (-1 + 9 - 23 + 15 + K) = z³ + 6z² + 8z + K. The Routh s¹ entry is (6 × 8 - K)/6 > 0, so K < 48. The s⁰ entry K is positive for K > 0. Hence all poles lie to the left of s = -1 only when 0 < K < 48. That is a far tighter limit than the stability bound of 192.

Answer: 48

(e)

The gain margin is the factor by which K can rise before instability, GM = 192/40 = 4.8, or 20 log10(4.8) = 13.62 dB. That is ample for the plain stability test. But the relative stability requirement fixes K < 48, so at K = 40 only 20 percent increase is available: 48/40 = 1.2, or 1.58 dB. Judgement: the proposal to raise K is acceptable only up to about 45, giving a small improvement; beyond 48 some pole moves to the right of s = -1 and disturbances decay slower than the one-minute safety rule requires. The stability margin is large, but the performance rule is already almost binding.

Answer: 13.62 dB

Problem 5 [A3-090] Root locus

A telescope focus drive has open loop transfer function G(s) = K / (s (s + 4)(s + 6)) in a unity feedback loop, where K is the amplifier gain that the technician can set. The designer sketches the root locus for K from 0 to infinity, and must then select K to give a well damped dominant pair. The step response must show a dominant damping ratio of 0.5, a compromise between speed and overshoot, but the pair must not be allowed to approach instability. The technician also needs to know the gain at which the focus drive will break into sustained oscillation, so that a safety cut-out can be set well below it. Poles are in rad/s. Use root locus rules and the characteristic equation s³ + 10s² + 24s + K = 0 to answer the questions.

  1. (a) Find the centroid of the asymptotes (the number and angles of the asymptotes are 3 and ±60°, 180°). [3]
  2. (b) Find the breakaway point on the real axis. [4]
  3. (c) Find the gain K at the breakaway point. [3]
  4. (d) Find the gain at which the locus crosses the imaginary axis, and the oscillation frequency there. [5]
  5. (e) Find K giving a dominant pole pair of damping ratio 0.5 and judge the margin to instability. [5]
(a)

With three open loop poles at 0, -4 and -6 and no finite zeros, there are n - m = 3 asymptotes. Their angles are (2k + 1) × 180°/3 = 60°, 180° and 300° (that is, ±60° and 180°). The centroid is σa = (sum of poles - sum of zeros)/(n - m) = (0 - 4 - 6)/3 = -10/3 = -3.333. All three asymptotes leave the real axis at this point. The locus begins at the poles; the segments on the real axis lie between 0 and -4 and to the left of -6, since the test point must have an odd number of poles and zeros to its right. These facts fix the overall shape: two branches bend into the complex plane and head to ±60° asymptotes.

Answer: -3.333

(b)

Breakaway points satisfy dK/ds = 0, where K = -s(s + 4)(s + 6) = -(s³ + 10s² + 24s). Differentiating, 3s² + 20s + 24 = 0. The roots are s = (-20 ± √(400 - 288))/6 = (-20 ± √112)/6 = (-20 ± 10.583)/6, which gives s = -1.5695 and s = -5.0972. The second value lies between -4 and -6, which is not on the locus (that segment has an even number of poles to its right), so it is rejected. The valid breakaway point is s = -1.569, between 0 and -4. Here the two branches leave the real axis and move into the complex plane toward the asymptotes.

Answer: -1.569

(c)

The magnitude condition gives K = |s| |s + 4| |s + 6| at the breakaway point s = -1.5695. The factors are |s| = 1.5695, |s + 4| = 2.4305 and |s + 6| = 4.4305. Multiplying, K = 1.5695 × 2.4305 × 4.4305 = 16.90. For gains below 16.9 all three closed loop poles are real and the step response is overdamped; above this value, a complex pair appears. This gain is the largest at which the drive responds without any overshoot, and it is often chosen for backlash-sensitive focus drives.

Answer: 16.9

(d)

Use the Routh array on s³ + 10s² + 24s + K. The s¹ entry is (10 × 24 - K)/10, which is zero at K = 240. The auxiliary polynomial 10 s² + K = 0 gives s² = -240/10 = -24, so s = ± j√24 = ± j4.899 rad/s. Alternatively, substitute s = jω: -jω³ - 10ω² + 24jω + K = 0, so the real part gives K = 10ω² and the imaginary part gives ω² = 24. Both methods give K = 240 and ω = 4.899 rad/s. The gain at which the drive oscillates continuously is 240, so the safety cut-out should be set at a small fraction of this.

Answer: 240

(e)

A damping ratio of 0.5 means the dominant poles lie on a line at 120° from the positive real axis, s = -σ ± jσ√3. Solving the cubic numerically for the gain at which the complex pair has -Re/|s| = 0.5 gives K = 43.8; the roots at that gain are -7.600+0.000j, -1.200+2.078j and -1.200-2.078j. Check by the sum of poles: 2 × (-σ) + p3 = -10, which is satisfied. The margin to the instability gain of 240 is a factor of 5.48, or 14.8 dB. Judgement: set K near 44, with the cut-out set at no more than 120, which keeps a factor of two to the oscillation limit, and then confirm the real third pole is faster than the dominant pair.

Answer: 43.8

A3 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A3-091] Bode plot construction

A vibration-isolation table for an electron microscope uses a voice-coil actuator driven by a servo amplifier. The measured open-loop transfer function of the position loop is G(s) = 1000(s + 5) / [s(s + 50)(s + 200)], with s in rad/s and unity feedback. Before running any simulation, the control engineer wants to sketch the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot by hand, check it against exact values at selected frequencies, and judge how far the straight-line approximation can be trusted near a corner frequency. Use 20 log10 for decibels and take phase angles in degrees from the exact transfer function. The frequency ω = 50 rad/s sits exactly on one of the corners, so the difference between the asymptote and the exact curve there is of particular interest to the reviewing engineer.

  1. (a) Write G(s) in standard (Bode) form and find the velocity error constant Kv. [4]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the low-frequency asymptote at ω = 0.1 rad/s, in dB. [4]
  3. (c) State the slope of the asymptotic magnitude plot above 200 rad/s, in dB per decade. [4]
  4. (d) Find the exact magnitude of G(jω) at ω = 50 rad/s, in dB. [4]
  5. (e) Find the exact phase angle of G(jω) at ω = 50 rad/s, in degrees. [4]
(a)

Assumptions: linear, time-invariant loop with unity feedback. Divide each factor by its constant term so that every factor has the form (1 + s/ωc). The numerator (s + 5) becomes 5(1 + s/5), the factor (s + 50) becomes 50(1 + s/50), and (s + 200) becomes 200(1 + s/200). Then G(s) = Kv(1 + s/5) / [s(1 + s/50)(1 + s/200)] with Kv = lim s→0 of sG(s) = 1000 × 5 / (50 × 200) = 0.5 s⁻¹. The corner frequencies are read directly as 5, 50 and 200 rad/s. The loop is type 1 because of the single integrator, so a unit ramp leaves a steady error of 1/Kv = 2 units. Markers reward the standard form, the correct limit and the corner list.

Answer: 0.5 s⁻¹

(b)

Below the first corner at 5 rad/s only the constant Kv and the integrator matter, so the asymptote is |G| ≈ Kv/ω, a line falling at -20 dB/decade. At ω = 0.1 rad/s: 20 log10(Kv/ω) = 20 log10(0.5/0.1) = 20 log10(5) = 13.98 dB. This is an asymptote, not the exact curve, but ω = 0.1 is fifty times below the first corner, so the exact magnitude differs by less than 0.01 dB. The check is useful because the low-frequency intercept is how a hand sketch is anchored: the asymptote crosses 0 dB at ω = Kv = 0.5 rad/s if extended. The anchor then carries forward as slopes change at each corner.

Answer: 13.98 dB

(c)

Each pole adds -20 dB/decade beyond its corner and each zero adds +20 dB/decade. Starting at -20 dB/decade from the integrator (below 5 rad/s), the zero at 5 rad/s raises the slope to 0 dB/decade between 5 and 50 rad/s. The pole at 50 rad/s drops it to -20 dB/decade between 50 and 200 rad/s. The pole at 200 rad/s drops it to -40 dB/decade above 200 rad/s. Equivalently, the slope at high frequency is -20 × (number of poles - number of zeros) = -20 × (3 - 1) = -40 dB/decade. This matches the relative degree of 2, which also means the high-frequency phase tends to -180 degrees.

Answer: -40 dB/decade

(d)

Evaluate the exact magnitude: |G(j50)| = 1000 |j50 + 5| / [50 × |j50 + 50| × |j50 + 200|]. The factors are |j50 + 5| = √(2500 + 25) = 50.25, |j50 + 50| = 70.71 and |j50 + 200| = √(2500 + 40000) = 206.2. So |G| = 1000 × 50.25 / (50 × 70.71 × 206.2) = 0.06894, and 20 log10(0.06894) = -23.23 dB. The asymptote at 50 rad/s is 20 log10(0.5/5) + 20 = -20 dB. The asymptote there is the straight-line value at the corner, and the exact curve lies about 3 dB below it at the pole corner at 50 rad/s, as expected for a simple pole.

Answer: -23.23 dB

(e)

Add the phase contribution of each factor at ω = 50 rad/s. The integrator contributes -90 degrees. The zero (s + 5) contributes +arctan(50/5) = +84.29 degrees. The pole (s + 50) contributes -arctan(50/50) = -45.00 degrees. The pole (s + 200) contributes -arctan(50/200) = -14.04 degrees. The sum is -90 + 84.29 - 45.00 - 14.04 = -64.75 degrees. A straight-line phase sketch (the pole at 200 contributing about -18 degrees at 0.25 of its corner) gives -90 + 90 - 45 - 18 = -63 degrees, within 2 degrees of the exact value; the larger errors in phase sketches occur within a decade of each corner, which is why exact evaluation is used before judging margins.

Answer: -64.75 degrees

Problem 2 [A3-092] Gain and phase margins

The pitch axis of a camera gimbal on an inspection drone is controlled with unity feedback and an open-loop transfer function L(s) = K / [s(0.1s + 1)(0.02s + 1)], where the time constants are in seconds and K is the loop gain in s⁻¹. The supplier set K = 40 s⁻¹. A flight-test engineer sees a lightly damped wobble and asks whether the loop was left with enough stability margin. Assume the plant is modelled well in the region of the crossover and that no other dynamics (delay, saturation) act. Use radians per second for frequency and decibels as 20 log10 for gain. The design target for the revised loop is a phase margin of 45 degrees. The engineer wants numbers on how much gain was left in reserve and how much it must be reduced to reach the target, not only a qualitative statement.

  1. (a) Find the gain crossover frequency for K = 40. [4]
  2. (b) Find the phase margin for K = 40. [4]
  3. (c) Find the phase crossover frequency (where the phase is -180 degrees). [4]
  4. (d) Find the gain margin for K = 40, in dB. [4]
  5. (e) Find the value of K that gives a phase margin of exactly 45 degrees. [4]
(a)

The gain crossover is where |L(jω)| = 1. With the magnitude |L| = K / [ω √(1 + (0.1ω)²) √(1 + (0.02ω)²)] and K = 40, set |L| = 1 and solve numerically, since the equation is a quartic in ω². Try ω = 17: |L| = 40 / (17 × 1.97 × 1.056) = 1.13. Try ω = 20: |L| = 40 / (20 × 2.236 × 1.077) = 0.83. Interpolating and refining with a root finder gives ω_gc = 18.15 rad/s. This is the frequency at which the margins are judged. A crossover this high relative to the 10 rad/s corner of the first lag is already a warning sign that the phase will be eroding quickly, which part (b) quantifies.

Answer: 18.15 rad/s

(b)

The phase at the gain crossover is φ = -90 - arctan(0.1ω) - arctan(0.02ω) with ω = 18.15 rad/s. This gives arctan(1.815) = 61.14 degrees and arctan(0.3629) = 19.95 degrees, so φ = -90 - 61.14 - 19.95 = -171.1 degrees. The phase margin is PM = 180 + φ = 8.909 degrees. A value near 8 degrees is far below the usual target of 45 to 60 degrees, and it corresponds to a closed loop with damping ratio of only about 0.08. That explains the lightly damped wobble the flight-test engineer saw: the step response will ring for many cycles at about the crossover frequency.

Answer: 8.909 degrees

(c)

The phase crossover is where the phase equals -180 degrees. The integrator gives -90 degrees, so the two lags together must supply -90 degrees: arctan(0.1ω) + arctan(0.02ω) = 90 degrees. This holds when the product of the arguments equals one, because arctan(x) + arctan(y) = 90 degrees when xy = 1. So (0.1ω)(0.02ω) = 1, which gives 0.002ω² = 1 and ω² = 500. Therefore ω_180 = √500 = 22.36 rad/s. Note that this frequency does not depend on K, since K changes only the magnitude. It is a property of the dynamics, and any gain increase pushes the gain crossover toward it.

Answer: 22.36 rad/s

(d)
