At the phase crossover ω = 22.36 rad/s the magnitude is |L| = K / [ω √(1 + (0.1ω)²) √(1 + (0.02ω)²)]. Here (0.1ω)² = 5 and (0.02ω)² = 0.2, so the square roots are √6 = 2.449 and √1.2 = 1.095. Then |L| = 40 / (22.36 × 2.449 × 1.095) = 0.6667. The gain margin is GM = -20 log10(|L|) = 3.522 dB, or a factor of 1.5. The loop is stable (the margin is positive) but the gain could rise by only about 50 percent before the closed loop oscillates continuously. A margin under 6 dB is generally judged inadequate for a loop that will see gain tolerance in the amplifier or motor constant.

Answer: 3.522 dB

(e)

For a 45 degree phase margin the phase at the new crossover must be -135 degrees. Then arctan(0.1ω) + arctan(0.02ω) = 45 degrees, so tan of the sum is one: (0.12ω) / (1 - 0.002ω²) = 1. Rearranged, 0.002ω² + 0.12ω - 1 = 0, with positive root ω = 7.417 rad/s. K is set so that |L| = 1 at that frequency: K = ω √(1 + (0.1ω)²) √(1 + (0.02ω)²) = 7.417 × 1.245 × 1.011 = 9.335 s⁻¹. The gain must therefore be cut by a factor of 4.285, to roughly one quarter of the supplier setting. The price is a lower crossover and slower response; if that is unacceptable, a lead compensator is the next step.

Answer: 9.335 s⁻¹

Problem 3 [A3-093] Nyquist stability

A pressure regulator on a natural-gas metering skid has an open-loop transfer function L(s) = K / [(s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 5)] with unity feedback, where K is the loop gain, s is in rad/s and all open-loop poles lie in the left half-plane. The commissioning crew sets K = 60 and a second site proposes K = 200 to speed up the response. Before either setting is accepted, the supervising engineer wants the Nyquist plot interpreted directly: where it crosses the negative real axis, how close it passes to the critical point -1 + j0, and how many closed-loop poles would sit in the right half-plane for the higher gain. Use the Nyquist criterion, with Z = N + P, N counted as clockwise encirclements of -1, and cross-check the result against the closed-loop characteristic equation. State any assumptions about the plant being minimum phase.

  1. (a) Find the frequency at which the Nyquist plot of L(jω) crosses the negative real axis. [4]
  2. (b) For K = 60, find the real-axis crossing value of L(jω). [4]
  3. (c) Find the critical gain K at which the plot passes through -1 + j0. [4]
  4. (d) Find the gain margin at K = 60, in dB. [4]
  5. (e) For K = 200, find the number of closed-loop poles in the right half-plane. [4]
(a)

Write the denominator as the cubic s³ + 8s² + 17s + 10, since (s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 5) expands to that. At s = jω the denominator is (10 - 8ω²) + j(17ω - ω³). The plot crosses the negative real axis where the imaginary part of the denominator is zero (and the real part is negative), so 17ω - ω³ = 0, giving ω² = 17 and ω = √17 = 4.123 rad/s. The root ω = 0 corresponds to the start of the plot on the positive real axis. At the crossing frequency the real part of the denominator is 10 - 8 × 17 = -126, which is negative, so the crossing is indeed on the negative real axis, as required for a stability test.

Answer: 4.123 rad/s

(b)

At ω = √17 the denominator equals 10 - 8(17) = -126, and the imaginary part is zero, so L(jω) = K / (-126). For K = 60: L = 60 / (-126) = -0.4762. The plot therefore crosses the negative real axis at -0.476, which lies between the origin and the critical point at -1, so it does not encircle -1. With no open-loop right-half-plane poles (P = 0) and N = 0 encirclements, Z = N + P = 0 and the closed loop is stable. The distance from -0.476 to -1 is the visual form of the gain margin, and it is the quantity the supervising engineer should quote, not simply that the plot looks safe.

Answer: -0.4762 (dimensionless)

(c)

The plot passes through the critical point when the crossing value equals -1: -K / 126 = -1, so K_crit = 126. This agrees with the Routh array for the closed-loop characteristic polynomial s³ + 8s² + 17s + (10 + K): the array requires 8 × 17 > 10 + K, which gives K < 126. At exactly K = 126 the closed loop has a pair of poles on the imaginary axis at ± j√17 and sustains oscillation at 4.123 rad/s. Two independent methods agreeing is the reason this check is worth doing: the Nyquist plot gives the margin graphically, Routh gives it algebraically.

Answer: 126 (dimensionless)

(d)

The gain margin is the factor by which the gain can increase before the plot reaches -1. GM = K_crit / K = 126 / 60 = 2.1. In decibels GM = 20 log10(126/60) = 6.444 dB. This margin is the reciprocal of the magnitude of the crossing, since the crossing magnitude is 60/126 = 0.476 and 1/0.476 = 2.1. A margin of 6.4 dB is acceptable but not generous: a 2.1 times gain error from valve tolerance or a supply-pressure change would drive the regulator unstable, and the margin is below the 10 dB some operators specify for pressure control on a metering skid.

Answer: 6.444 dB

(e)

For K = 200 the crossing is at -200/126 = -1.587, which lies to the left of -1, so the plot encircles the critical point. With P = 0, the Nyquist criterion gives Z = N + P, and N = 2 clockwise encirclements (the plot together with its mirror image encircles -1 twice). So Z = 2 closed-loop poles lie in the right half-plane. This is confirmed by the closed-loop characteristic polynomial s³ + 8s² + 17s + 210, whose roots are numerically a real pole near -8.8 and a complex pair with positive real part near +0.4 ± j4.9. The faster setting proposed by the second site is therefore unstable, and the response would grow in oscillation.

Answer: 2 poles

Problem 4 [A3-094] PID tuning

A jacketed fermenter holds a batch of broth at a set temperature. An open-loop step test on the steam valve opening gives a first-order-plus-dead-time response. For a 10 percent step in valve position the temperature rose, after an initial delay of 8 s, along a first-order curve to a final change of 25 K. The process time constant was 40 s. The process gain is therefore Kp = 2.5 K per percent of valve position (25 K for a 10 percent step). The plant engineer proposes the Ziegler-Nichols open-loop (reaction curve) tuning rules for a PID controller in the ideal form C(s) = Kc[1 + 1/(Ti s) + Td s]: Kc = 1.2τ/(Kp θ), Ti = 2θ and Td = 0.5θ. The engineer is concerned that the dead time may be underestimated and wants a second set of numbers if the true dead time is larger. All values are in the units stated.

  1. (a) Find the controller gain Kc, in percent of valve position per kelvin. [4]
  2. (b) Find the integral time Ti. [4]
  3. (c) Find the derivative time Td. [4]
  4. (d) Find the derivative gain Kc·Td. [4]
  5. (e) If the dead time proves to be 12 s instead of 8 s, find the revised Kc. [4]
(a)

The process gain is the final change divided by the step: Kp = 25 K / 10 percent = 2.5 K per percent. The process is first-order with time constant τ = 40 s and dead time θ = 8 s, so θ/τ = 0.2, which is in the range where the reaction-curve rules apply. Assume the response approximates a first-order plus dead-time model and that the valve is linear. The Ziegler-Nichols rule gives Kc = 1.2τ / (Kp θ) = 1.2 × 40 / (2.5 × 8) = 48 / 20 = 2.4 percent of valve per kelvin of error. The sign convention is that a positive error (temperature below set point) opens the steam valve. The gain is proportional to τ/θ, so it rises as the dead time falls.

Answer: 2.4 % per K

(b)

Ziegler-Nichols open-loop tuning sets the integral time to twice the dead time: Ti = 2θ = 2 × 8 = 16 s. This is much shorter than the process time constant of 40 s, so the integral action is quick relative to the process dynamics and the loop will overshoot on a set-point change, which is a known property of the method (it is tuned for quarter-amplitude decay, not for minimal overshoot). The integral gain Ki = Kc/Ti = 0.15 percent per kelvin per second. If overshoot above the batch temperature could harm the culture, the engineer should lengthen Ti or reduce Kc, trading disturbance-rejection speed for a gentler set-point response.

Answer: 16 s

(c)

The derivative time is half the dead time: Td = 0.5θ = 0.5 × 8 = 4 s. Derivative action anticipates the trend of the error, which helps with a process whose output is delayed, but it amplifies measurement noise. With Td = 4 s and Kc = 2.4, the derivative term has gain Kc Td s at high frequency, so a noisy thermocouple would drive the steam valve visibly. Practical implementations filter the derivative with a time constant of about Td/10 = 0.4 s. The assumption here is that the temperature signal is clean; if it is not, a PI controller with Td = 0 is a reasonable fallback for a process with θ/τ as small as 0.2.

Answer: 4 s

(d)

The derivative gain in the parallel form C(s) = Kc + Kc/(Ti s) + Kc Td s is Kd = Kc Td. With Kc = 2.4 percent per kelvin and Td = 4 s, Kd = 2.4 × 4 = 9.6 percent seconds per kelvin. Likewise the integral gain is Ki = Kc/Ti = 0.15 percent per kelvin per second, and the proportional gain is Kp,c = 2.4. Engineers need this conversion because many industrial controllers are configured in the parallel form, with separate P, I and D gains, rather than the ideal form with Ti and Td. Entering Ti and Td into a parallel-form block would give a very different controller, so the form must be confirmed.

Answer: 9.6 % s per K

(e)

If the true dead time is θ = 12 s, the reaction-curve rule gives Kc = 1.2τ / (Kp θ) = 1.2 × 40 / (2.5 × 12) = 48 / 30 = 1.6 percent per kelvin. The revised integral time is 2θ = 24 s and the revised derivative time is 6 s. The gain falls by a factor of 1.5 compared with the original setting, because Kc is inversely proportional to the dead time. Judgement: if the controller were left at Kc = 2.4 while the dead time was really 12 s, the loop gain would be 50 percent too high for that process, so the margins would shrink and the response would ring, which supports retesting the dead time before commissioning.

Answer: 1.6 % per K

Problem 5 [A3-095] Lead and lag compensator design

An azimuth drive for a radio-telescope dish has the unity-feedback open-loop transfer function G(s) = 20 / [s(s + 2)], with s in rad/s. The specification requires a velocity error constant Kv of 10 s⁻¹, which the existing loop already meets, and a phase margin of at least 50 degrees. The design engineer will use a phase-lead compensator of the form Gc(s) = (1 + s/z) / (1 + s/p) with p > z, with unity DC gain so that Kv is preserved. Use the frequency-response method: place the maximum phase lead at the new gain crossover, and add 5 degrees to the required lead to allow for the shift of the crossover frequency. The lead compensator provides a gain of 1/√α at the frequency of maximum lead, where α = z/p. State the assumption that the actuator is linear and not saturating.

  1. (a) Find the phase margin of the uncompensated loop. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum phase lead φm that the compensator must supply, including the 5 degree allowance. [4]
  3. (c) Find the ratio α = z/p. [4]
  4. (d) Find the frequency ωm at which the lead is placed (the new gain crossover). [4]
  5. (e) Find the compensator zero location z. [4]
(a)

Find the gain crossover of G(s) = 20 / [s(s + 2)], where |G| = 1: 20 / (ω √(ω² + 4)) = 1. Squaring gives ω²(ω² + 4) = 400, so ω⁴ + 4ω² - 400 = 0 and ω² = (-4 + √(16 + 1600)) / 2 = 18.1, giving ω_c = 4.254 rad/s. The phase there is -90 - arctan(ω/2) = -90 - arctan(2.127) = -154.8 degrees. The phase margin is 180 + φ = 25.18 degrees. This is well under the required 50 degrees, so the unsatisfactory margin must be corrected, and since lead compensation adds phase near crossover without disturbing Kv, it is the natural tool (a lag would instead cut crossover and slow the response).

Answer: 25.18 degrees

(b)

The required phase margin is 50 degrees and the existing margin is 25.18 degrees, so the shortfall is 50 - 25.18 = 24.82 degrees. Adding the 5 degree allowance for the fact that the lead network raises the gain near crossover, which moves the crossover to a higher frequency where the plant has less phase, the compensator must supply φm = 24.82 + 5 = 29.82 degrees at its centre frequency. A single lead stage can reasonably supply up to about 60 degrees, so this requirement is comfortable. If the requirement exceeded 60 degrees the engineer would have to cascade two stages, since α becomes impractically small and amplifies sensor noise.

Answer: 29.82 degrees

(c)

For a lead network Gc = (1 + s/z)/(1 + s/p), the maximum phase lead is sin φm = (p - z)/(p + z) = (1 - α)/(1 + α), where α = z/p. Solving for α gives α = (1 - sin φm)/(1 + sin φm). With φm = 29.82 degrees, sin φm = 0.4973, so α = (1 - 0.4973)/(1 + 0.4973) = 0.3357. The pole is therefore 2.979 times the zero frequency. The high-frequency gain of the compensator is 1/α = 2.979, i.e. 9.48 dB, so sensor noise is amplified by that factor, which is the cost of using lead and must be checked against the noise level.

Answer: 0.3357 (dimensionless)

(d)

The lead network has magnitude 1/√α = 1.726 at its centre frequency ωm. For the compensated loop to cross 0 dB at ωm, the plant magnitude there must be |G(jωm)| = √α = 0.5794. Solve 20 / (ω √(ω² + 4)) = 0.5794, i.e. ω²(ω² + 4) = (20/0.5794)² = 1191.4. This gives ω² = (-4 + √(16 + 4 × 1191.4)) / 2 and ωm = 5.707 rad/s. The new crossover is higher than the original 4.254 rad/s, which means a faster response, and the plant phase there is -90 - arctan(5.707/2) = -160.7 degrees, so the actual phase margin is 180 - 160.7 + 29.82 = 49.1 degrees, marginally short of 50 degrees. A slightly larger allowance (about 7 degrees instead of 5) or one design iteration is needed to reach the specification exactly.

Answer: 5.707 rad/s

(e)

The lead is centred at ωm, the geometric mean of the zero and pole: ωm = √(z p) = z/√α. So z = ωm √α = 5.707 × 0.5794 = 3.307 rad/s, and the pole is p = ωm/√α = 9.85 rad/s. The compensator is Gc(s) = (1 + s/3.307) / (1 + s/9.85), with DC gain 1 so that Kv = 10 s⁻¹ is unchanged. Check: at ωm the lead phase is arctan(ωm/z) - arctan(ωm/p) = arctan(1.726) - arctan(0.5794) = 29.82 degrees, matching φm. A simulation of the step response should be run to confirm the overshoot is acceptable.

Answer: 3.307 rad/s

A3 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A3-096] State-space models

A permanent-magnet DC motor drives a small conveyor roller. The armature resistance is R = 1.2 Ω and the armature inductance is L = 8 mH. The torque constant is Kt = 0.06 N·m/A and the back-emf constant is Ke = 0.06 V·s/rad. The rotor and roller together have inertia J = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m² and viscous friction b = 1 × 10⁻⁴ N·m·s/rad. Take the state vector as x = [i, ω]ᵀ, with armature current i in A and angular speed ω in rad/s, the input as the applied voltage v in V and the output as ω. The designer will use the model to judge whether the electrical or the mechanical dynamics dominate the response, and whether the state vector can be steered by the voltage alone. No load torque acts, and the model is linear.

  1. (a) Find the steady-state speed per volt, ω/v, in rad/s per V. [4]
  2. (b) Find the undamped natural frequency of the second-order model. [4]
  3. (c) Find the damping ratio. [4]
  4. (d) Find the time constant of the slower closed-loop-free (open-loop) pole. [4]
  5. (e) Find the determinant of the controllability matrix [B AB]. [4]
(a)

Write the equations: L di/dt = v - R i - Ke ω and J dω/dt = Kt i - b ω. In matrix form A = [[-R/L, -Ke/L], [Kt/J, -b/J]] and B = [1/L, 0]ᵀ, with C = [0, 1]. At steady state both derivatives are zero. From the second equation i = bω/Kt. Substituting into the first: v = R(bω/Kt) + Keω = ω(Rb + KtKe)/Kt. So ω/v = Kt / (Rb + KtKe) = 0.06 / (1.2 × 1 × 10⁻⁴ + 0.06 × 0.06) = 0.06 / 3.72 × 10⁻³ = 16.13 rad/s per V. The friction contributes only 3 percent of the denominator, so the speed is set almost entirely by the back-emf, as expected for a well-made motor.

Answer: 16.13 rad/s per V

(b)

The characteristic polynomial is det(sI - A) = s² + (R/L + b/J)s + (Rb + KtKe)/(LJ). Here R/L = 1.2 / 0.008 = 150 s⁻¹ and b/J = 1 × 10⁻⁴ / 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.4 s⁻¹, so the s coefficient is 150.4. The constant term is 3.72 × 10⁻³ / (0.008 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.72 × 10⁻³ / 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 1860. Comparing with s² + 2ζωn s + ωn², the undamped natural frequency is ωn = √1860 = 43.13 rad/s. This is only a comparison form: because the system is overdamped (part c), the poles are real and ωn is the geometric mean of the two pole magnitudes.

Answer: 43.13 rad/s

(c)

From the coefficient of s, 2ζωn = R/L + b/J = 150.4. So ζ = 150.4 / (2 × 43.13) = 1.744. A damping ratio above 1 means the two poles are real and distinct, the response to a voltage step has no overshoot, and the motor speed rises smoothly. The poles are s = -ζωn ± ωn √(ζ² - 1) = -13.6 and -136.8 rad/s. The ratio of the pole magnitudes is about 10.06, so the dynamics are well separated: the fast pole is close to the electrical R/L (150 rad/s); the slow pole is the electromechanical pole, approximately Kt Ke/(R J) = 12 rad/s, set mainly by the back-emf and not by the unloaded mechanical J/b = 0.4 rad/s.

Answer: 1.744 (dimensionless)

(d)

The two real poles from the characteristic polynomial are -13.6 and -136.8 rad/s. The slower pole has magnitude 13.6 rad/s, so its time constant is 1/13.6 = 0.07355 s = 73.55 ms. The faster pole has time constant 7.31 ms. After a voltage step the speed reaches 63 percent of its final value after about 73.55 ms, and about 95 percent after three time constants, roughly 220.7 ms. This tells the designer that the mechanical dynamics dominate the speed response: the electrical time constant L/R of 6.7 ms is about 11 times shorter, and the fast pole could be neglected for a speed-control loop slower than about 30 rad/s.

Answer: 73.55 ms

(e)

The controllability matrix is [B AB]. B = [1/L, 0]ᵀ = [125, 0]ᵀ. A B = [-R/L² , Kt/(J L)]ᵀ = [-1.2/(6.4 × 10⁻⁵), 0.06/(2.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.008)]ᵀ = [-18750, 30000]ᵀ. The matrix is [[125, -18750], [0, 30000]], and its determinant is 125 × 30000 - (-18750 × 0) = 3.75 × 10⁶. Algebraically this equals Kt/(J L²). A non-zero determinant means the matrix has full rank 2, so the voltage input can steer both the current and the speed to any values, and the pair (A, B) is completely controllable. Full state feedback could therefore place both poles anywhere, which is the basis for pole-placement design.

Answer: 3.75 × 10⁶ SI units

Problem 2 [A3-097] Servo motor position control

A wafer-handling robot joint is driven by a servo motor and gearbox. From the voltage input to the joint angle the plant is G(s) = Km / [s(τm s + 1)], with motor-gear gain Km = 12 rad/s per V and mechanical time constant τm = 0.08 s. The controller is a proportional position loop: u = Kp (θref - θ), with Kp in V per rad, and the angle is measured by an encoder with unity gain. The designer must choose Kp for a well-damped response, find the corresponding time-domain figures, and check the tracking error when the joint follows a constant-velocity ramp of 2 rad/s. The assumptions are that the amplifier is ideal, the gearbox has no backlash, and the voltage does not saturate. Use the standard second-order formulas for percent overshoot and the 2 percent settling time.

  1. (a) Find Kp for a closed-loop damping ratio ζ = 0.7. [4]
  2. (b) Find the percent overshoot of the step response at that gain. [4]
  3. (c) Find the 2 percent settling time at that gain. [4]
  4. (d) Find the steady-state error to the 2 rad/s ramp at that gain. [4]
  5. (e) Find the Kp needed to hold the ramp error to 0.1 rad, and the resulting damping ratio. [4]
(a)

The closed-loop characteristic equation is 1 + Kp Km / [s(τm s + 1)] = 0, which becomes τm s² + s + Km Kp = 0, or s² + (1/τm)s + Km Kp/τm = 0. Comparing with s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² = 0 gives 2ζωn = 1/τm, so ωn = 1/(2ζτm) = 1 / (2 × 0.7 × 0.08) = 8.929 rad/s. Also ωn² = Km Kp/τm, so Kp = ωn² τm / Km = (8.929)² × 0.08 / 12 = 0.5315 V/rad. Assumes the plant is exactly second order in closed loop and there is no zero. Note that ζ is set by 1/τm and Km Kp together, so choosing ζ fixes Kp; the designer cannot choose speed and damping independently with proportional gain alone.

Answer: 0.5315 V/rad

(b)

For a standard second-order system without zeros, the percent overshoot is OS = 100 exp(-πζ / √(1 - ζ²)). With ζ = 0.7, √(1 - ζ²) = √(0.51) = 0.7141, so the exponent is -π × 0.7 / 0.7141 = -3.079 and exp(-3.079) = 0.04604. Therefore OS = 4.599 percent. This is the textbook figure for ζ = 0.7, a common compromise between speed and overshoot. For a wafer handler, an overshoot of 4.6 percent of a move is likely acceptable in free travel but might not be near a wafer cassette slot, where clearances of a few millimetres would drive a lower overshoot target.

Answer: 4.599 percent

(c)

The 2 percent settling time of an underdamped second-order system is approximately ts = 4 / (ζ ωn). With ζ = 0.7 and ωn = 8.929 rad/s, ζωn = 6.25 s⁻¹ (equal to 1/(2τm) = 6.25 s⁻¹ exactly, independent of Kp), so ts = 4 / 6.25 = 0.64 s. The envelope of the response is governed by the real part of the closed-loop poles, -1/(2τm), which depends only on the motor time constant. This is a useful insight: with a proportional position loop, the settling time cannot be reduced by raising Kp. Only the oscillation frequency and damping change, so a velocity (derivative) feedback or a larger-torque motor is needed for a faster settling.

Answer: 0.64 s

(d)

The loop has one integrator, so it is type 1 and the velocity error constant is Kv = lim s→0 of sG(s)Kp = Km Kp = 12 × 0.5315 = 6.378 s⁻¹. For a ramp input of rate R = 2 rad/s the steady-state error is ess = R / Kv = 2 / 6.378 = 0.3136 rad, or 17.97 degrees. This lag of the joint behind the commanded ramp would translate into a following error at the end effector of several millimetres for a long arm. This is why a position servo for a moving target usually adds velocity feedforward or integral action: the error is intrinsic to a type 1 loop under proportional control and cannot be removed by gain tuning alone without hurting damping.

Answer: 0.3136 rad

(e)

For a ramp error of 0.1 rad at 2 rad/s, the required Kv is R/ess = 2 / 0.1 = 20 s⁻¹. Since Kv = Km Kp, Kp = 20 / 12 = 1.667 V/rad. The damping ratio follows from ζ = 1/(2√(τm Km Kp)) because 2ζωn = 1/τm and ωn² = Km Kp/τm: ζ = 1 / (2 √(0.08 × 12 × 1.667)) = 1 / (2 × 1.265) = 0.3953. The damping ratio falls from 0.7 to 0.3953, giving an overshoot of 25.87 percent, so the tighter ramp tracking is bought at the expense of a much more oscillatory step response. A compromise would add a tachometer (velocity) feedback to restore damping.

Answer: 0.3953 (damping ratio)

Problem 3 [A3-098] Disturbance rejection

A conveyor drive in a bulk-material terminal is a speed loop with plant ω/T = 1/(J s + b), where J = 0.8 kg·m² is the total inertia, b = 0.4 N·m·s/rad is the viscous friction and T is the motor torque in N·m. The controller is a PI law, C(s) = Kp + Ki/s, with Kp = 6 N·m·s/rad and Ki = 3 N·m/rad. A sudden load torque disturbance Td, a step of 5 N·m, acts at the plant input, for example when a heavy load of material lands on the belt. The speed reference is held constant. The plant engineer wants to compare the disturbance rejection of this controller with a proportional-only controller and with no feedback, and to find the gain that would make the disturbance response critically damped. Ignore actuator saturation and sensor dynamics, and treat the loop as linear.

  1. (a) Find the steady-state speed deviation with proportional-only control (Ki = 0), in rad/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the factor by which proportional feedback reduces the steady deviation compared with no feedback. [4]
  3. (c) With the PI controller, find the peak speed deviation caused by the disturbance. [4]
  4. (d) Find the time at which that peak occurs. [4]
  5. (e) Find the integral gain Ki that makes the disturbance response critically damped (Kp = 6). [4]
(a)

With the disturbance entering at the plant input, the deviation of speed from the reference is ω(s) = -G/(1 + G C) Td(s). For proportional-only control, G/(1 + GC) = 1/(Js + b + Kp). For a step Td/s the final value is ω(∞) = -Td/(b + Kp) = -5 / (0.4 + 6) = 0.7812 rad/s in magnitude. The sign is negative, meaning the belt slows when the load lands. Assumptions: linear friction, no saturation. The deviation is small compared with the open-loop value but it is not zero, because a proportional law needs a persistent error to generate the extra torque that balances the disturbance. This is the offset that integral action removes.

Answer: 0.7812 rad/s

(b)

With no feedback the steady deviation is found from b ω = -Td, i.e. ω = Td/b = 5 / 0.4 = 12.5 rad/s in magnitude. With proportional feedback it is Td/(b + Kp) = 0.7812 rad/s. The ratio is (b + Kp)/b = (0.4 + 6)/0.4 = 16. So the proportional loop reduces the steady deviation by a factor of 16, which is the same as the factor 1 + Kp/b, the loop gain at DC. This shows that disturbance rejection in the steady state is set by the loop gain: a high DC gain at the point where the disturbance enters gives a small deviation. This is why integral action, which has infinite DC gain, gives zero steady error.

Answer: 16 (dimensionless)

(c)

With the PI controller the deviation transfer function is ω/Td = -s / (J s² + (b + Kp)s + Ki). For a step Td/s this becomes -Td / (J s² + 6.4 s + 3). Dividing by J, the poles solve s² + 8s + 3.75 = 0, giving s = -0.5 and -7.5 rad/s (overdamped). The time response is -Td h(t) with h(t) = (ep1 t - ep2 t) / (J (p1 - p2)). Its maximum occurs at t = ln(p2/p1)/(p1 - p2) (see part d). Evaluating there gives a peak deviation of 0.6868 rad/s. This is slightly below the proportional-only offset of 0.781 rad/s, and the PI loop then returns the speed to zero error, which is why the integral term is used.

Answer: 0.6868 rad/s

(d)

The peak of h(t) occurs where its derivative is zero: p1 ep1 t = p2 ep2 t, so e(p1 - p2) t = p2/p1 and t = ln(p2/p1) / (p1 - p2). With p1 = -0.5 and p2 = -7.5, p2/p1 = 15, ln(p2/p1) = 2.708, and p1 - p2 = 7, giving t_peak = 2.708 / 7 = 0.3869 s. The deviation therefore peaks within about 0.4 s of the load landing, and then decays with a time constant of about 1/0.5 = 2 s, set by the slow pole. The operator would see the belt dip and recover over several seconds, which a speed-recovery requirement can be checked against.

Answer: 0.3869 s

(e)

The disturbance response is critically damped when the characteristic polynomial J s² + (b + Kp)s + Ki has a repeated root, i.e. when the discriminant is zero: (b + Kp)² = 4 J Ki. Therefore Ki = (b + Kp)² / (4J) = (6.4)² / (4 × 0.8) = 40.96 / 3.2 = 12.8 N·m/rad. This is more than four times the present Ki = 3, so the integral action would clear the error faster (the slow pole moves from -0.5 to -4 rad/s) but there is a danger: a larger Ki reduces the phase margin of the speed loop against any sensor lag or delay that has been neglected here. The result is only a bound on the model used, and Ki should be checked against the neglected dynamics.

Answer: 12.8 N·m/rad

Problem 4 [A3-099] Sampled data and digital control basics

A dosing pump in a water-treatment plant controls chlorine flow with a digital controller. The flow dynamics are a first-order lag, G(s) = K / (τs + 1) with K = 3 (flow units per unit command) and τ = 2.5 s, preceded by a zero-order hold and sampled at T = 0.5 s. The controller is a pure digital proportional law, u[k] = Kd (r[k] - y[k]), with unity feedback of the sampled output. The engineer needs the pulse transfer function, the closed-loop pole for Kd = 2, and the largest Kd that keeps the loop stable. In addition, the pump's motor produces a 6.4 Hz vibration that leaks into the flow sensor, and a separate data acquisition channel logs the flow sensor at 10 Hz. Assume exact zero-order-hold discretisation, no computational delay and a linear plant. The z-domain stability test is that all closed-loop poles lie inside the unit circle.

  1. (a) Find the discrete pole a of the zero-order-hold equivalent G(z) = b/(z - a). [4]
  2. (b) Find the numerator constant b of G(z). [4]
  3. (c) Find the closed-loop pole for Kd = 2. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest Kd for which the closed loop is stable. [4]
  5. (e) Find the apparent (aliased) frequency of the 6.4 Hz vibration when logged at 10 Hz. [4]
(a)

The zero-order-hold equivalent of G(s) = K/(τs + 1) is G(z) = (1 - z⁻¹) times the z-transform of G(s)/s. Expanding G(s)/s = K/s - Kτ/(τs + 1) and transforming gives G(z) = K(1 - a)/(z - a), where a = e-T/τ. Here T/τ = 0.5/2.5 = 0.2, so a = e-0.2 = 0.8187. The discrete pole lies inside the unit circle and close to 1, which is typical when the sampling period is short compared with the time constant. The mapping z = esT takes the continuous pole at s = -1/τ = -0.4 s⁻¹ to the discrete pole at z = 0.8187. Assumptions: the hold is ideal and the input is constant between samples.

Answer: 0.8187 (dimensionless)

(b)

From the derivation in part (a), the numerator constant is b = K(1 - a) = 3 × (1 - 0.8187) = 3 × 0.1813 = 0.5438. Therefore the pulse transfer function is G(z) = 0.5438/(z - 0.8187). A useful check is the DC gain: G(1) = b/(1 - a) = K(1 - a)/(1 - a) = K = 3, which equals the continuous DC gain G(0) = 3, as it must for a zero-order-hold equivalent. This check catches the common error of forgetting the (1 - a) factor, which would give b = K = 3 and a DC gain of K/(1 - a) = 16.5, about 5.5 times too large, and the DC check catches it. Matching DC gain is how engineers verify a discretisation before simulating.

Answer: 0.5438 (dimensionless)

(c)

With u[k] = Kd e[k], the closed-loop pulse transfer function is Kd G(z)/(1 + Kd G(z)). The characteristic equation is 1 + Kd b/(z - a) = 0, so z - a + Kd b = 0 and the single closed-loop pole is z = a - Kd b. For Kd = 2: z = 0.8187 - 2 × 0.5438 = 0.8187 - 1.088 = -0.2689. This pole is inside the unit circle but negative, which means the closed-loop step response alternates in sign from sample to sample (a ringing, oscillatory response at the Nyquist rate) even though the continuous plant is a smooth first-order lag. The response decays by a factor of 0.2689 each step. This behaviour has no continuous-time analogue and is why digital loops are checked in the z-plane.

Answer: -0.2689 (dimensionless)

(d)

Stability requires the closed-loop pole z = a - Kd b to satisfy |z| < 1, i.e. -1 < a - Kd b < 1. The upper limit gives Kd b > a - 1, which holds for any positive Kd. The lower limit gives a - Kd b > -1, so Kd < (1 + a)/b = (1 + 0.8187) / 0.5438 = 3.344. At exactly this gain the pole is at z = -1 and the output oscillates at half the sampling rate. In continuous time the same first-order loop would be stable for every positive gain, so the digital loop has a finite gain limit caused by the sample and hold lag. A design gain of Kd = 2 leaves a margin of 1.672 on gain, which is acceptable but not generous.

Answer: 3.344 (dimensionless)

(e)

Sampling at fs = 10 Hz folds any frequency above fs/2 = 5 Hz back into the band 0 to 5 Hz. A 6.4 Hz sinusoid is above the 5 Hz Nyquist limit, so it appears at |f - fs| = |6.4 - 10| = 3.6 Hz. The 10 Hz record therefore shows a 3.6 Hz ripple in the measured flow that does not exist in the real flow at that frequency, and anyone acting on that record could chase it needlessly. To avoid the problem the sensor signal should be low-pass filtered before sampling (an anti-aliasing filter with a corner well below 5 Hz), or the sampling rate raised to at least 2 × 6.4 = 12.8 Hz, with a margin above that in practice.

Answer: 3.6 Hz

Problem 5 [A3-100] Control of a liquid level or temperature process

A cylindrical storage tank of cross-sectional area A = 3.2 m² is fed through a control valve and drains through a fixed outlet whose flow is linearly proportional to the level, q_out = h/R, with R = 40 s/m² (q in m³/s, h in m). The inlet flow comes from a proportional level controller: q_in = q_b + Kc(h_sp - h), where q_b = 0.02 m³/s is the bias flow set at commissioning, h_sp = 1.0 m is the set point and Kc is the controller gain in m³/s per m. A first design uses Kc = 0.05 m³/s per m. The operator notes that the level settles below the set point and asks whether a higher gain will fix it, since the valve can pass at most 0.1 m³/s. Assume constant density, a linear outlet and an ideal valve and level transmitter.

  1. (a) Find the open-loop (outlet-only) tank time constant. [4]
  2. (b) Find the steady level with the valve fixed at the bias flow, no feedback. [4]
  3. (c) Find the steady level and offset with Kc = 0.05 m³/s per m. [4]
  4. (d) Find the closed-loop time constant with Kc = 0.05 m³/s per m. [4]
  5. (e) Find the Kc needed to hold the offset to 0.02 m or less. [4]
(a)

Mass balance on the tank: A dh/dt = q_in - h/R. With q_in held fixed, this is a first-order system A dh/dt + h/R = q_in. Multiply by R: AR dh/dt + h = R q_in, so the time constant is τ = A R = 3.2 × 40 = 128 s, about 2.1 minutes. The steady-state gain from inlet flow to level is R = 40 m per (m³/s). Assumptions: constant density, outlet flow linear in level (a real orifice gives q ∝ √h, which would need linearisation at the operating point), and no dead time in the valve. The time constant tells the operator how slowly the tank responds to an upset when left uncontrolled.

Answer: 128 s

(b)

With the valve fixed at the bias flow, the steady level satisfies q_b = h/R, so h = R q_b = 40 × 0.02 = 0.8 m. This is 0.2 m below the set point of 1.0 m, so the bias flow is not enough to hold the set point and the controller must supply the extra inlet flow of (1.0/40) - 0.02 = 0.005 m³/s. The set point can only be held if the controller makes up this shortfall, which a proportional controller can do only by running with a persistent error. This is the origin of the offset in part (c), and it would vanish if the bias were set to exactly 0.025 m³/s, matching the demand at the set point.

Answer: 0.8 m

(c)

With feedback, the steady balance is q_b + Kc(h_sp - h) = h/R. Solving for h: h(1/R + Kc) = q_b + Kc h_sp, so h = (R q_b + R Kc h_sp)/(1 + R Kc). Here R Kc = 40 × 0.05 = 2, so h = (0.8 + 2 × 1.0) / 3 = 0.9333 m. The offset is h_sp - h = 0.06667 m, i.e. the level settles about 6.7 cm below the set point. A general form of the offset is (h_sp - R q_b)/(1 + R Kc) = 0.2/3, which shows the offset is the open-loop shortfall (0.2 m) divided by one plus the loop gain R Kc. A higher gain reduces the offset but never eliminates it.

Answer: 0.06667 m (offset)

(d)

Substituting the control law into the mass balance: A dh/dt = q_b + Kc(h_sp - h) - h/R, so A dh/dt + (Kc + 1/R) h = q_b + Kc h_sp. The coefficient of h is (1/R)(1 + R Kc), so the time constant is τ_cl = A / (Kc + 1/R) = AR / (1 + R Kc) = 128 / 3 = 42.67 s. Feedback has made the tank respond three times faster, to about 43 s, because the controller adds inflow whenever the level drops and removes it when the level rises. The speed-up factor equals 1 + R Kc, the same factor that reduces the offset, so faster response and smaller offset both come from a higher gain.

Answer: 42.67 s

(e)

The offset is (h_sp - R q_b)/(1 + R Kc) = 0.2/(1 + 40 Kc). For the offset to be at most 0.02 m: 1 + 40 Kc ≥ 0.2/0.02 = 10, so Kc ≥ 9/40 = 0.225 m³/s per m. At that gain the closed-loop time constant is 128/10 = 12.8 s. Judgement: a gain of 0.225 means a level error of 0.36 m would demand 0.1 m³/s, the full valve capacity (q_in = 0.02 + 0.225 e reaches 0.1 m³/s at e = 0.356 m), so for a start-up from a low level the valve would saturate, and the linear analysis would no longer hold. The alternative is a PI controller, which removes the offset at a moderate gain without saturating in normal operation.

Answer: 0.225 m³/s per m

Exam A4: Design and Manufacture of Machine Elements

A4 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A4-001] Static failure theories for ductile materials

A bracket on an excavator boom is machined from hot-rolled low-carbon steel with a yield strength of 350 MPa and is treated as ductile. Strain gauges and a stress analysis give the following plane stress state at a free surface point where a crack-like defect is of concern: normal stress σx = 140 MPa in tension, normal stress σy = 60 MPa in compression, and shear stress τxy = 50 MPa. There is no stress normal to the free surface. The designer must decide whether the bracket is safe against yielding under this loading and compare two failure criteria, since the company standard allows the more conservative of the two to govern. Treat the loading as static and neglect residual stresses and stress concentration beyond the values given.

  1. (a) Find the larger principal stress σ1 at the point. [5]
  2. (b) Find the smaller in-plane principal stress σ2 at the point. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the factor of safety against yielding using the distortion energy (von Mises) criterion. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the factor of safety using the maximum shear stress (Tresca) criterion, and state which criterion governs the design. [5]
(a)

Assume plane stress and a ductile material. The centre of Mohr's circle is σc = (σx + σy)/2 = (140 - 60)/2 = 40.0 MPa. The radius is R = √[((σx - σy)/2)² + τxy²] = √[(100)² + (50)²] = √(10000 + 2500) = 111.8 MPa. The larger principal stress is σ1 = σc + R = 40.0 + 111.8 = 151.8 MPa. Because the free surface carries no normal stress, the through-thickness principal stress is σ3 = 0, so the three ordered principal stresses are 151.8, 0 and -71.8 MPa. Marker note: always state that the third principal stress is zero before applying a failure criterion, because it affects the Tresca result when both in-plane principal stresses have the same sign.

Answer: 151.8 MPa

(b)

The smaller in-plane principal stress is the other end of the Mohr's circle diameter: σ2 = σc - R = 40.0 - 111.8 = -71.8 MPa (compressive). Check: the sum σ1 + σ2 must equal σx + σy, the first stress invariant. 151.8 + (-71.8) = 80.0 MPa, and 140 - 60 = 80 MPa, so the result is consistent. The principal angle follows from tan 2θp = 2τxy/(σx - σy) = 100/200, giving 2θp = 26.6°, so θp = 13.3° from the x axis. Since σ1 is positive and σ2 negative, the point is in a tension and compression combination, and the maximum in-plane shear stress equals R = 111.8 MPa. The ordered principal stresses are therefore σ1 = 151.8, σ2 = 0 (surface) and σ3 = -71.8 MPa.

Answer: -71.8 MPa

(c)

The distortion energy criterion predicts yielding when the von Mises equivalent stress reaches Sy. For plane stress, σ' = √(σ1² - σ1σ2 + σ2²). Substitute σ1 = 151.8 and σ2 = -71.8 MPa: σ1² = 23044, σ1σ2 = -10900, σ2² = 5156. So σ' = √(23044 + 10900 + 5156) = 197.7 MPa. The factor of safety is n = Sy/σ' = 350/197.7 = 1.77. This is above 1, so the bracket does not yield at this point under the criterion that best matches experimental data for ductile steels. Marker note: the cross term -σ1σ2 is positive when the principal stresses have opposite signs, which is why the equivalent stress here is large relative to the larger principal stress.

Answer: 1.77

(d)

The Tresca criterion says yielding begins when the maximum shear stress equals Sy/2, which for principal stresses is σmax - σmin. The ordered principal stresses are σ1 = 151.8 MPa, σ3 = -71.8 MPa (the smallest, since σ2 = 0 lies between them). Therefore σ1 - σ3 = 223.6 MPa. The factor of safety is n = Sy/(σ1 - σ3) = 350/223.6 = 1.57. Comparing: von Mises gives 1.77 and Tresca gives 1.57. Tresca is the lower value and is the more conservative, so it governs under the company standard. Tresca typically predicts yielding up to about 15 percent earlier than von Mises, and the difference is greatest in pure shear and for opposite-sign principal stresses like this one. Final answer: governing n = 1.57.

Answer: 1.57

Problem 2 [A4-002] Fatigue: endurance limit and Marin factors

A rotating countershaft in a conveyor drive is machined from cold-drawn alloy steel with an ultimate tensile strength Sut = 900 MPa. The shaft diameter at the bearing seat is 32 mm and the seat is a machined surface. The shaft carries a steady bending load from a belt pull, so any point on the surface sees fully reversed bending stress as the shaft turns. The shaft operates at 250 °C in an oven enclosure, where the temperature factor is taken as kd = 0.975, and the design reliability is 99 percent, for which ke = 0.814. For the surface factor use ka = a·Sutb with a = 4.51 MPa1-b and b = -0.265 for machined surfaces, and for size use kb = 1.24·d-0.107 with d in millimetres. Take the load factor as kc = 1 and ignore stress concentration.

  1. (a) Determine the surface factor ka. [3]
  2. (b) Determine the size factor kb. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the corrected endurance limit Se at the bearing seat, starting from the rotating-beam specimen value Se' = 0.5·Sut. [7]
  4. (d) The shaft must have infinite life with a factor of safety of 1.8 against the endurance limit. Find the largest fully reversed bending moment it may carry. [7]
(a)

The corrected endurance limit follows Se = ka·kb·kc·kd·ke·Se'. The surface factor accounts for the machined finish. Using the given relation with Sut in MPa: ka = 4.51 × 900-0.265. Take the natural log: ln 900 = 6.802, times -0.265 gives -1.8025, and e-1.8025 = 0.1649. So ka = 4.51 × 0.1649 = 0.744. A ka below 1 reflects that a machined surface is rougher than the polished test specimen, and the effect grows with strength because high-strength steels are more notch sensitive. Marker note: give ka to three figures and state that Sut is entered in MPa because the constants a and b were given for that unit. The size factor is computed in the next part from the shaft diameter.

Answer: 0.744

(b)

The size factor reflects the larger volume of highly stressed material in a bigger shaft compared with the 7.62 mm test specimen. For 2.79 ≤ d ≤ 51 mm the given relation applies and d = 32 mm lies inside this range. kb = 1.24 × 32-0.107. ln 32 = 3.466, multiplied by -0.107 gives -0.3709, and e-0.3709 = 0.690. So kb = 1.24 × 0.690 = 0.856. The load factor kc = 1 is correct for bending, and the temperature and reliability factors are already given as kd = 0.975 and ke = 0.814. All the Marin modifiers are below 1, and together they will cut the specimen value by roughly half, which is typical for a real shaft compared with a polished laboratory bar. Marker note: confirm the diameter range before using the size relation.

Answer: 0.856

(c)

First the specimen limit: Se' = 0.5 Sut = 0.5 × 900 = 450 MPa, valid because Sut is below about 1400 MPa. Then apply the Marin factors in sequence: Se = ka·kb·kc·kd·ke·Se' = 0.744 × 0.856 × 1 × 0.975 × 0.814 × 450. Multiplying the first two gives 0.6363; times 0.975 gives 0.6204; times 0.814 gives 0.5050; times 450 gives Se = 227.3 MPa. This is about 51 percent of the specimen value. The result is the stress amplitude the shaft surface can sustain for infinite life if the loading is fully reversed and there are no stress raisers, which is the baseline for the design check in the next part. Always state the units of Se in MPa.

Answer: 227.3 MPa

(d)

The design condition is σa ≤ Se/nf. Fully reversed bending at the surface of a solid round shaft has σ = 32M/(πd³). With nf = 1.8, the allowable amplitude is Se/nf = 227.3/1.8 = 126.3 MPa. Solve for the moment: M = σ·πd³/32. With d = 0.032 m, d³ = 3.277×10⁻⁵ m³, so πd³/32 = 3.2170 × 10⁻⁶ m³. Then M = 126.3×10⁶ Pa × 3.2170 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 406.2 N·m. This is the maximum bending moment that the shaft section can carry indefinitely with the required margin. If the actual belt pull produces a larger moment, the designer must increase the diameter, improve the finish, or use a stronger material. Note that the section modulus carries a cubic dependence on the diameter, so a modest diameter increase pays off strongly.

Answer: 406.2 N·m

Problem 3 [A4-003] Fatigue design with Goodman or Gerber

A tie bar in a hydraulic press frame is a flat bar of rectangular section 40 mm wide by 8 mm thick, machined from medium-carbon steel with ultimate strength Sut = 620 MPa and yield strength Sy = 450 MPa. The bar carries a tensile load that cycles between a minimum of 5 kN and a maximum of 35 kN on every press stroke. After applying surface, size, loading, temperature and reliability factors, the corrected axial endurance limit of the bar is Se = 190 MPa. Neglect stress concentration and buckling. The designer wants to compare two fatigue failure criteria, a straight Goodman line and a Gerber parabola, and also check against first-cycle yielding using the conservative Langer line. Assume the load ratio stays constant as the load level changes.

  1. (a) Find the stress amplitude σa in the bar. [3]
  2. (b) Find the mean stress σm in the bar. [3]
  3. (c) Find the factor of safety against fatigue failure using the Goodman criterion. [5]
  4. (d) Find the factor of safety against yielding using the Langer line. [4]
  5. (e) Find the fatigue factor of safety using the Gerber criterion, and comment on which criterion the designer should trust. [5]
(a)

The section area is A = 40 × 8 = 320 mm². The load cycles between Fmin = 5 kN and Fmax = 35 kN, so the alternating force is Fa = (Fmax - Fmin)/2 = (35 000 - 5000)/2 = 15 000 N. The stress amplitude is σa = Fa/A = 15 000/320 = 46.88 MPa. Assumptions: uniform axial stress over the section, no bending from misalignment, and no stress concentration, as the problem states. The stress amplitude is the half-range of the stress cycle, not the full range, which is a common marking error. The full stress range would be 93.75 MPa. The result will be plotted on the vertical axis of the Goodman diagram and compared with the corrected endurance limit of 190 MPa.

Answer: 46.88 MPa

(b)

The mean force is Fm = (Fmax + Fmin)/2 = (35 000 + 5000)/2 = 20 000 N. The mean stress is σm = Fm/A = 20 000/320 = 62.50 MPa. As a check, the maximum stress is σm + σa = 62.50 + 46.88 = 109.38 MPa, which equals 35 000/320 = 109.38 MPa, and the minimum stress is 15.62 MPa. The load ratio R = σmin/σmax = 0.143, so this is a pulsating tension with a substantial mean load. The ratio σa/σm = 0.750 is the slope of the load line from the origin in the σm-σa plane, and this slope stays fixed when the load is scaled up. Marker note: a tension mean stress reduces the fatigue strength, so ignoring σm would overestimate the safety.

Answer: 62.50 MPa

(c)

The Goodman line joins Se on the stress-amplitude axis to Sut on the mean-stress axis. For a load line of constant slope the factor of safety satisfies 1/n = σa/Se + σm/Sut. Substituting: σa/Se = 46.88/190 = 0.2467 and σm/Sut = 62.50/620 = 0.1008. Sum = 0.3475, so n = 1/0.3475 = 2.88. A value above 1 means the bar survives to infinite life under this criterion, but the margin is only about 188 percent. The Goodman line is straight and conservative: most experimental points for ductile steels lie above it. Assumption: the endurance limit Se already contains all the Marin modifiers, as given. Always state the criterion used when quoting a factor of safety.

Answer: 2.88

(d)

The Langer line is the straight line of static yielding on the σm-σa plane, running from Sy on both axes. It guards against yielding in the first cycle, and it is checked even when the fatigue criterion is satisfied. The condition for failure along a constant-slope load line is σa + σm = Sy, so n = Sy/(σa + σm) = 450/(46.88 + 62.50) = 450/109.38 = 4.11. Since this equals the ratio of Sy to the maximum stress, it is simply the yield factor of safety at peak load. Compare: Goodman gives 2.88 and Langer gives 4.11. Yielding gives the higher margin, so fatigue is the governing mode. Marker note: check both lines, because a high-strength, low-ductility material can be limited by the Langer line.

Answer: 4.11

(e)

For the Gerber parabola, σa/Se + (σm/Sut)² = 1 at failure, and for a load line of slope σa/σm the factor of safety is n = (1/2)(Sut/σm)²(σa/Se)[-1 + √(1 + (2σmSe/(Sutσa))²)]. Evaluate the pieces: Sut/σm = 9.920, squared = 98.406; σa/Se = 0.2467; 2σmSe/(Sutσa) = 0.817, squared = 0.668; the square root of (1 + 0.668) is 1.291. Then n = 0.5 × 98.406 × 0.2467 × (1.291 - 1) = 3.54. Gerber is less conservative, giving 3.54 against Goodman 2.88. A designer who wants a safe design should trust Goodman, because scatter in tension data lies below the Gerber curve.

Answer: 3.54

Problem 4 [A4-004] Stress concentration

A stepped shaft in a food-processing mixer gearbox is turned from a steel bar. The larger diameter is D = 50 mm, the smaller is d = 40 mm, and the shoulder fillet radius is r = 4 mm. A bending moment of 600 N·m acts at the shoulder and the shaft rotates, so the stress at the fillet is fully reversed. The theoretical stress concentration factor for bending from published charts is Kt = 1.78 for these ratios. The notch sensitivity is to be found from the Neuber relation q = 1/(1 + √a/√r), where the Neuber constant for this steel is √a = 0.55 √mm and r is in millimetres. The corrected endurance limit of the shaft material, with all Marin factors applied, is Se = 210 MPa. Neglect axial and torsional loads.

  1. (a) Determine the notch sensitivity q of the fillet. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the fatigue stress concentration factor Kf. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the nominal bending stress at the smaller diameter, and hence the stress amplitude at the fillet corrected for fatigue. [6]
  4. (d) Find the factor of safety against infinite fatigue life, and explain why using Kt instead of Kf would be over-conservative here. [6]
(a)

The notch sensitivity measures how much of the theoretical stress concentration actually reduces fatigue strength. Given q = 1/(1 + √a/√r). The radius is r = 4 mm, so √r = 2.000 √mm. The ratio √a/√r = 0.55/2.000 = 0.275. Then q = 1/(1 + 0.275) = 0.784. A value of q = 1 would mean the notch acts at full theoretical strength, and q = 0 would mean no effect. Here q is 0.784, which means a little more than three quarters of the geometric effect is felt. Assumptions: the Neuber relation applies with the given constant, and r is substituted in millimetres because √a was given in √mm. Notch sensitivity increases with both fillet radius and material strength, so a sharper fillet gives a smaller q and a harder steel gives a larger q.

Answer: 0.784

(b)

The fatigue stress concentration factor is the effective multiplier on the nominal stress for a fatigue life calculation. Kf = 1 + q(Kt - 1). Substitute q = 0.784 and Kt = 1.78: Kf = 1 + 0.784 × (1.78 - 1) = 1 + 0.784 × 0.78 = 1 + 0.612 = 1.612. The value of Kf is below the theoretical Kt = 1.78, because notch sensitivity is less than unity. Kf is always between 1 and Kt. This factor applies to the stress amplitude, since the load is fully reversed with no mean stress. Marker note: for ductile steel under static load the stress concentration is normally ignored, but under fatigue it must be applied. If a candidate multiplies the mean stress by Kf in a Goodman calculation, only the stress amplitude is multiplied for ductile materials with no local yielding.

Answer: 1.612

(c)

The nominal bending stress uses the section at the smaller diameter, because the fillet stress is referenced to the net section d = 40 mm. σnom = 32M/(πd³). With d = 0.040 m, d³ = 6.4×10⁻⁵ m³, so πd³/32 = 6.2832 × 10⁻⁶ m³. σnom = 600/6.2832 × 10⁻⁶ = 95.49 MPa. Now apply the fatigue factor: σa = Kf × σnom = 1.612 × 95.49 = 153.9 MPa. Since the stress is fully reversed, the mean stress is zero and this value is the full stress amplitude at the root of the fillet. Marker note: state clearly which diameter the nominal stress is based on, because the published Kt values are defined relative to the smaller section. Using D = 50 mm would give an unconservative answer, about half the real stress.

Answer: 153.9 MPa

(d)

With zero mean stress the factor of safety is the ratio of the endurance limit to the stress amplitude: n = Se/σa = 210/153.9 = 1.36. This is above 1, so infinite life is predicted with a modest margin. If the designer used the theoretical Kt = 1.78 instead, the stress would be 170.0 MPa and n = 1.24, which is 9 percent lower than the proper value. That is over-conservative because real materials are not fully sensitive to the notch: local yielding, the finite grain size, and the stress gradient near a small fillet all reduce the effective peak stress. The Kf approach, using notch sensitivity, is the accepted method for fatigue. Increasing the fillet radius lowers Kt while q rises only slightly (r = 8 mm gives q = 0.836), so Kf falls and the margin improves.

Answer: 1.36

Problem 5 [A4-005] Bolted joints preload and joint stiffness

A pressure-vessel cover plate is clamped to a flange by M16 × 2 bolts of property class 8.8, with a tensile stress area At = 157 mm² and a proof strength Sp = 600 MPa. The clamped members are two steel plates of total grip 40 mm. Take the bolt as a uniform rod of effective length 44 mm (grip plus allowance for the nut and thread run-out) with E = 207 GPa, and take the compressed member material as an equivalent cylinder of area 1350 mm², length equal to the grip, same E. The bolts are tightened to a preload Fi = 0.75 Sp At. In service each bolt carries a steady external tensile load P = 12 kN shared through the joint. Assume the joint is reused and the members are rigid in bending.

  1. (a) Find the bolt stiffness kb in kN/mm. [3]
  2. (b) Find the member stiffness km in kN/mm. [3]
  3. (c) Find the joint constant C = kb/(kb + km). [4]
  4. (d) Find the factor of safety against exceeding the proof strength of the bolt in service. [5]
  5. (e) Find the factor of safety against joint separation, and state the clamping force remaining in the joint under the load. [5]
(a)

The bolt is a spring in tension of stiffness kb = At·E/lb, where At is the tensile stress area and lb the effective bolt length. Substitute: At = 157 mm², E = 207 000 N/mm², lb = 44 mm. kb = 157 × 207 000/44 = 32 499 000/44 = 738614 N/mm = 738.6 kN/mm. Assumption: the bolt behaves as a uniform rod with the stress area acting over the entire length, which is slightly less stiff than the real bolt, because the unthreaded shank has a larger area than At, so kb is a lower-bound simplification. This is a standard simplification at this level. A stiff bolt carries a larger share of any external load, so the value of kb is compared with the member stiffness in the next part to decide how the external load splits between the two.

Answer: 738.6 kN/mm

(b)

The clamped members behave as a compression spring in parallel with the bolt, with stiffness km = Am·E/lm for the stated equivalent cylinder. Substitute Am = 1350 mm², E = 207 000 N/mm², lm = 40 mm: km = 1350 × 207 000/40 = 279 450 000/40 = 6986250 N/mm = 6986.2 kN/mm. The members are about 9.5 times as stiff as the bolt, which is typical of a well-designed joint where the clamped material is much stiffer than the fastener. In a real joint the compressed region is a pressure frustum with a half-angle of about 30°, but the problem supplies an equivalent area so the calculation stays direct. Marker note: both stiffnesses are in the same unit system, and the ratio is what matters in the next part, not the absolute values.

Answer: 6986.2 kN/mm

(c)

The joint constant gives the fraction of the external load that goes into the bolt. C = kb/(kb + km) = 738.6/(738.6 + 6986.2) = 738.6/7724.9 = 0.096. So only 9.6 percent of the external load increases the bolt tension, and the remaining 90.4 percent comes off the clamping force in the members. A small C is desirable: it means the bolt tension changes little when the external load is applied, which also helps fatigue life. A designer can reduce C by using a longer, more flexible bolt, or by increasing member stiffness with a larger clamped area. The preload does not affect C. This relationship holds only while the joint stays closed.

Answer: 0.096

(d)

The preload is Fi = 0.75 Sp At = 0.75 × 600 × 157 = 70650 N. The bolt tension under load is Fb = Fi + C·P = 70650 + 0.096 × 12 000 = 70650 + 1147 = 71797 N. The proof load is Sp·At = 600 × 157 = 94200 N. The factor of safety against exceeding proof strength is np = Sp·At/Fb = 94200/71797 = 1.31. The bolt stays elastic with a margin, because the preload alone already uses 75 percent of the proof load and the external load adds only a small amount. Marker note: the proof strength is the limit for a reusable joint, so np is the correct yielding measure here rather than tensile strength.

Answer: 1.31

(e)

Separation occurs when the external load reduces the member compression to zero. The clamping force in the members under load is Fm = Fi - (1 - C)·P = 70650 - 0.904 × 12 000 = 70650 - 10853 = 59797 N, which is positive, so the joint stays closed. The load that would cause separation is P0 = Fi/(1 - C) = 70650/0.904 = 78119 N. The factor of safety against separation is n0 = P0/P = Fi/(P(1 - C)) = 6.51. Comment: the margin against separation is large, and a leaking joint is unlikely. The remaining clamping force of 59797 N must also be enough to hold a gasket seal, which would need checking against the gasket manufacturer's requirement.

Answer: 6.51

A4 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A4-006] Bolted joints under fatigue loading

The head of a reciprocating air compressor is held to the cylinder block by M12 × 1.75 bolts of class 8.8 steel with tensile stress area At = 84.3 mm², proof strength Sp = 600 MPa and ultimate strength Sut = 830 MPa. The threads are rolled, and the corrected completely reversed endurance limit of the bolt, including the thread stress concentration, is Se = 129 MPa. Each bolt is tightened to a preload Fi = 36 kN. The joint constant is C = 0.25. Each compression stroke applies an external tensile load that cycles from zero to P = 14 kN per bolt. Use the fatigue line that starts at the preload stress on the mean-stress axis, joining it to the endurance limit, and treat the bolt stress as uniform over At.

  1. (a) Find the bolt stress amplitude σa. [4]
  2. (b) Find the mean bolt stress σm. [4]
  3. (c) Find the fatigue factor of safety using the preload-referenced Goodman line. [5]
  4. (d) Find the factor of safety against reaching the proof strength under peak load. [4]
  5. (e) Find the factor of safety against joint separation, and say what it implies for the fatigue loading seen by the bolts. [3]
(a)

The external load cycles between 0 and 14 kN, and only a fraction C of it passes into the bolt; the rest reduces the clamping force. The bolt force therefore varies between Fi and Fi + C·P. The alternating bolt force is Fa = C·P/2 = 0.25 × 14 000/2 = 1750 N. The stress amplitude is σa = Fa/At = 1750/84.3 = 20.8 MPa. Assumptions: the joint stays closed during the whole cycle, so the bolt force follows the linear joint relation, and the stress is uniform over the tensile stress area. This amplitude is small relative to the endurance limit of 129 MPa, which is why preloaded bolted joints with a low C perform well in fatigue. Marker note: the amplitude does not depend on the preload, only on C and P.

Answer: 20.8 MPa

(b)

The bolt stress is never below the preload stress. First the preload stress: σi = Fi/At = 36 000/84.3 = 427.0 MPa. The mean bolt stress is the preload stress plus half the load-induced increase: σm = σa + σi = 20.8 + 427.0 = 447.8 MPa. Check: the peak stress is σi + 2σa = 468.6 MPa, which equals (Fi + C·P)/At = 39500/84.3 = 468.6 MPa. The bolt therefore sees a stress cycle that swings between 427.0 and 468.6 MPa on a large tensile mean. A high mean stress shortens fatigue life, but the cycle is narrow. The preload stress is 71 percent of the proof strength, a typical value for a permanent joint.

Answer: 447.8 MPa

(c)

The fatigue line is the Goodman line that starts at the preload stress σi on the mean axis (because the stress can never fall below σi) and ends at Se on the amplitude axis, with the other end at Sut. The factor of safety is nf = Se(Sut - σi)/[Sut·σa + Se(σm - σi)]. Numerator: 129 × (830 - 427.0) = 51981. Denominator: 830 × 20.8 + 129 × (447.8 - 427.0) = 17230 + 2678 = 19908. So nf = 51981/19908 = 2.61. This is a comfortable margin against fatigue. The result is high because the joint constant is small and the preload takes up most of the load swing. Marker note: if the preload were lost, the full 14 kN would act on the bolt and the margin would fall sharply.

Answer: 2.61

(d)

The peak bolt force is Fb = Fi + C·P = 36 000 + 0.25 × 14 000 = 36 000 + 3500 = 39500 N, giving a peak stress of 468.6 MPa. The proof load is Sp·At = 600 × 84.3 = 50580 N. The factor of safety against proof strength is np = Sp·At/(Fi + C·P) = 50580/39500 = 1.28. The bolt stays elastic, though the margin is only 28 percent, because the preload alone is 71 percent of the proof load. A designer who wanted extra margin could trim the preload slightly, since fatigue has room to spare. The proof check is made at the peak of the cycle because yielding of a preloaded bolt would relax the clamping force and ruin the joint.

Answer: 1.28

(e)

The joint separates when the external load drives the member compression to zero, which occurs at P0 = Fi/(1 - C) = 36 000/0.75 = 48000 N. The factor of safety against separation is n0 = P0/P = 48000/14 000 = 3.43. Since n0 is well above 1, the joint stays closed throughout every stroke, which is what makes the linear bolt-force relation used in parts (a) to (c) valid. If the factor of safety were below 1, the bolt would take the whole external load, the amplitude would be much larger, and the fatigue calculation would have to be repeated. Separation margin and fatigue margin must both be checked, and the preload is the main design lever for the first.

Answer: 3.43

Problem 2 [A4-007] Welded joints

A cantilever lifting bracket for a workshop gantry is attached to a steel column by two parallel vertical fillet welds. Each weld is 120 mm long and the welds are 80 mm apart, measured between weld centrelines. The leg size of each fillet is h = 6 mm. A vertical load of 20 kN hangs from the bracket at a horizontal distance of 150 mm from the centroid of the weld group, in the plane of the welds. Treat the welds as lines for the purpose of finding the unit second polar moment, then multiply by the throat thickness t = 0.707 h. Take the allowable shear stress on the throat as 120 MPa and neglect any stress concentration at the weld ends and bending of the column.

  1. (a) Find the primary shear stress in the weld group due to the direct load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the second polar moment of area J of the weld throat group about its centroid, in millions of mm⁴. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum resultant shear stress on the throat, including the torsional stress at the critical corner. [6]
  4. (d) Find the largest vertical load the bracket may carry before the allowable shear stress is reached, assuming the same load position. [5]
(a)

Assume the throat of each fillet is a plane inclined at 45° with thickness t = 0.707h = 0.707 × 6 = 4.242 mm. The throat area of the two welds is A = 2 × t × L = 2 × 4.242 × 120 = 1018 mm². The direct load is shared equally in shear over the throat area: τ' = F/A = 20 000/1018 = 19.6 MPa. This primary shear acts vertically, in the direction of the load, at every point of the weld group. Marker note: the primary shear must be added vectorially, not numerically, to the torsional shear, because its direction differs from the torsional component except at one corner. The weld lines are treated as having unit width for the geometry calculation in the next part, and the throat thickness is introduced afterwards.

Answer: 19.6 MPa

(b)

The load is eccentric, so the weld group is twisted about its centroid, which lies at the geometric centre of the two welds. For line welds, the unit second polar moment is the sum of the polar moments of each line about the centroid: for each vertical line of length L at a horizontal offset b/2 from the centroid, Ju = L³/12 + L(b/2)² (parallel axis theorem). One weld: 120³/12 + 120 × 40² = 144 000 + 192 000 = 336000 mm³. Two welds: Ju = 672000 mm³. Multiply by the throat thickness: J = t·Ju = 4.242 × 672000 = 2850624 mm⁴, which equals 2.851 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The units are mm⁴ because Ju is mm³ and t is mm. Bending of the throat is not used here.

Answer: 2.85 10⁶ mm⁴

(c)

The torque about the centroid is M = F·e = 20 000 × 150 = 3000000 N·mm. The critical points are the four corners of the group, at a radius r = √[(b/2)² + (L/2)²] = √(40² + 60²) = 72.1 mm. The torsional shear there is τ'' = M·r/J = 3000000 × 72.1/2850624 = 75.9 MPa, perpendicular to the radius. Components: horizontal τ''x = τ''·(L/2)/r = 63.1 MPa, vertical τ''y = τ''·(b/2)/r = 42.1 MPa. At the worst corner the vertical torsional component acts in the same direction as the primary shear, so the vertical total is 42.1 + 19.6 = 61.7 MPa. The resultant is τ = √(63.1² + 61.7²) = 88.3 MPa. The factor of safety against the allowable stress is 1.36.

Answer: 88.3 MPa

(d)

The stresses scale linearly with the load, because both the primary and the torsional shear are proportional to F at a fixed eccentricity and geometry. At F = 20 kN the maximum throat shear stress is 88.3 MPa and the allowable stress is 120 MPa. The ratio is n = 120/88.3 = 1.359. The largest load is therefore F_max = n × F = 1.359 × 20 000 = 27176 N = 27.2 kN. Check: the stress at that load equals the allowable value, so there is no margin left, and the designer would apply a further safety factor and consider the weld ends. A larger leg size would raise the capacity in proportion to h, because both A and J are proportional to t. Increasing the weld length L raises J faster than increasing the spacing b for this geometry (Ju rises about 20 percent for a 10 percent increase in L, against about 12 percent for a 10 percent increase in b), because the L³/12 term is large.

Answer: 27.2 kN

Problem 3 [A4-008] Helical compression springs

A cam-follower return spring in a packaging machine is a helical compression spring wound from 3.0 mm music wire with a mean coil diameter D = 24 mm and 8 active coils. The ends are squared and ground, and the spring is assumed to be fixed at both ends for surge purposes. The shear modulus is G = 79.3 GPa and the wire density is 7850 kg/m³. During operation the spring carries a maximum force of 180 N. The cam cycles at 25 Hz, and for surge safety the first natural frequency of the spring should be at least 13 times the cycling frequency. Neglect pitch angle effects and use the Wahl correction factor for the maximum shear stress.

  1. (a) Find the spring rate k in N/mm. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum shear stress in the wire at 180 N using the Wahl factor. [6]
  3. (c) Find the deflection of the spring at 180 N. [3]
  4. (d) Find the first natural frequency of the spring, and decide whether the surge requirement of 13 times the cycling frequency is met. [7]
(a)

For a helical compression spring made from round wire, the spring rate is k = G·d⁴/(8D³Na), from the torsion of the wire. Substitute G = 79 300 N/mm², d = 3.0 mm, D = 24 mm and Na = 8. d⁴ = 81 mm⁴, and D³ = 13824 mm³. The numerator is 79 300 × 81 = 6423300 and the denominator is 8 × 13824 × 8 = 884736. So k = 6423300/884736 = 7.26 N/mm. Assumptions: only the active coils deflect, the end coils are dead, and the wire stays in the linear elastic range. The spring index is C = D/d = 8, which lies in the usual 4 to 12 range for good manufacturing and moderate stress, so the formula is applicable. A larger index would give a softer spring for the same wire diameter.

Answer: 7.26 N/mm

(b)

The Wahl factor accounts for the curvature of the coil and the direct shear: Kw = (4C - 1)/(4C - 4) + 0.615/C. With C = 8: (4 × 8 - 1)/(4 × 8 - 4) = 31/28 = 1.1071, and 0.615/8 = 0.0769. So Kw = 1.1840. The maximum shear stress at the inside of the coil is τ = Kw·8FD/(πd³). Substitute F = 180 N, D = 24 mm, d = 3.0 mm: 8FD = 8 × 180 × 24 = 34560 N·mm and πd³ = 84.82 mm³. τ = 1.1840 × 34560/84.82 = 482 MPa. For music wire of this size the ultimate strength is roughly 2000 MPa, so the stress is about 24 percent of the tensile strength, which is well inside the usual limit of about 45 percent for a spring under repeated loading. Marker note: compare with static allowable values before accepting.

Answer: 482 MPa

(c)

The deflection follows directly from the spring rate and the load, using the linear force-deflection relation F = k·y. With k = 7.26 N/mm and F = 180 N, the deflection is y = F/k = 180/7.26 = 24.8 mm. The spring is therefore compressed by about 24.8 mm under the maximum load, so the solid height and free length must be chosen to allow this travel with a margin against going solid. Marker note: always check that the spring does not close up fully, usually allowing a clash allowance of about 10 to 15 percent of the working deflection. The force at the solid length would also have to be checked against the stress limit, since that stress is the worst case for an overload or a jam.

Answer: 24.8 mm

(d)

For a spring fixed at both ends, the fundamental natural frequency is fn = (1/2)√(k/m), where m is the mass of the active coils. The wire cross-section is A = π(0.003)²/4 = 7.069 × 10⁻⁶ m². The active wire length is π·D·Na = π × 0.024 × 8 = 0.6032 m. The mass is m = ρ·A·L = 7850 × 7.069 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.6032 = 0.0335 kg. Convert the rate: k = 7.26 N/mm = 7260 N/m. Then fn = 0.5 × √(7260/0.0335) = 0.5 × 465.7 = 233 Hz. The ratio to the operating frequency is 9.3. The requirement is 13, so the surge requirement is not met. If it fails, the designer should increase the wire diameter or reduce the active coils.

Answer: 233 Hz

Problem 4 [A4-009] Shaft design under combined loading

A solid steel intermediate shaft in a mine hoist gearbox transmits 30 kW at 900 rpm. At the critical shoulder next to the pinion, the shaft carries a bending moment of 520 N·m from the gear forces. The shaft rotates, so the bending stress is fully reversed, while the torque is steady. The material has Sut = 640 MPa and Sy = 420 MPa, and the corrected endurance limit at this section is Se = 240 MPa. The fatigue stress concentration factors at the shoulder are Kf = 1.6 for bending and Kfs = 1.3 for torsion. The design factor of safety is nf = 2.0. Use the distortion energy-Goodman criterion for the fatigue sizing and the von Mises stress with the same stress concentration factors for a conservative yield check.

  1. (a) Find the steady torque transmitted by the shaft. [3]
  2. (b) Find the minimum shaft diameter at the shoulder for infinite life using the distortion energy-Goodman criterion. [7]
  3. (c) A standard 45 mm shaft is chosen. Find the actual fatigue factor of safety at the shoulder. [5]
  4. (d) For the 45 mm shaft, find the factor of safety against yielding using the von Mises stress with the stress concentration factors included. [5]
(a)

The shaft rotates at ω = 2πn/60 = 2π × 900/60 = 94.25 rad/s. Power equals torque times angular speed, so T = P/ω = 30 000/94.25 = 318.3 N·m. Assumption: the full 30 kW passes through this section at steady speed, so the torque is constant, and there is no start-up or shock multiplier (a service factor would be applied in practice). This torque produces a steady torsional shear stress at the surface, τ = 16T/(πd³), which is a mean stress with no alternating component. The bending moment is fully reversed because the shaft turns once per cycle under a stationary load, so the bending stress is purely alternating. These two stress components are the inputs to the combined fatigue criterion.

Answer: 318.3 N·m

(b)

The distortion energy-Goodman design equation for a solid round shaft with alternating bending Ma and steady torque Tm is d = {(16n/π)[(1/Se)√(4(Kf·Ma)²) + (1/Sut)√(3(Kfs·Tm)²)]}1/3. First term: (1/Se) × 2 × Kf × Ma = 2 × 1.6 × 520/(240×10⁶) = 6.9333 × 10⁻⁶ m⁻². Second term: (1/Sut) × √3 × Kfs × Tm = 1.732 × 1.3 × 318.3/(640×10⁶) = 1.1199 × 10⁻⁶. The sum is 8.0532 × 10⁻⁶. Multiply by 16 × 2.0/π = 10.186 to get d³ = 8.2029 × 10⁻⁵ m³. Then d = 43.5 mm. A diameter at or above this value achieves nf = 2.0 for infinite life. Marker note: the bending term dominates because the bending stress is fully alternating and Se is much lower than Sut; round up to a standard size.

Answer: 43.5 mm

(c)

With d = 45 mm, the section modulus is πd³/32 = 8.9462 × 10⁻⁶ m³. The alternating bending stress at the shoulder is σa = Kf·M/(πd³/32) = 1.6 × 520/8.9462 × 10⁻⁶ = 93.0 MPa. The mean torsional shear is τm = Kfs·16T/(πd³) = 1.3 × 16 × 318.3/(π × 0.045³) = 23.1 MPa. The distortion energy-Goodman line gives 1/nf = σa/Se + √3·τm/Sut = 93.0/240 + 1.732 × 23.1/640 = 0.3875 + 0.0626 = 0.4501. So nf = 2.22. This is above the design value of 2.0 because the standard diameter is bigger than the 43.5 mm minimum. The extra size is a sound margin, and the larger diameter also reduces deflection at the pinion.

Answer: 2.22

(d)

For the yield check, take the maximum stresses with the stress concentration factors included, which is conservative. The von Mises stress combines the bending stress and the shear stress: σ' = √(σ² + 3τ²). With σ = 93.0 MPa (the peak bending stress) and τ = 23.1 MPa, σ' = √(93.0² + 3 × 23.1²) = √(8649 + 1605) = 101.3 MPa. The factor of safety against yield is ny = Sy/σ' = 420/101.3 = 4.15. Since ny is above 1 and also above nf = 2.0 in magnitude, the shaft will not yield on the first application of the peak load. In practice the bending peak is evaluated as the alternating amplitude added to the mean, which for fully reversed bending equals σa. Fatigue governs here by a small margin.

Answer: 4.15

Problem 5 [A4-010] Rolling bearing selection and life

A deep-groove ball bearing supports the output shaft of a helical gearbox driving a belt conveyor. The shaft turns at 1450 rpm, the inner ring rotates, and the bearing carries a steady radial load of 3.2 kN and an axial thrust of 1.1 kN. The manufacturer lists a basic dynamic load rating C = 29.5 kN. For the load ratio in this case, the manufacturer gives the equivalent load factors e = 0.28, and for Fa/(V·Fr) greater than e, X = 0.56 and Y = 1.6. The rotation factor is V = 1.0. The life is defined as a number of revolutions at 90 percent reliability for a ball bearing, with the load-life exponent of 3, and the 95 percent reliability life adjustment factor is a1 = 0.64.

  1. (a) Find the equivalent dynamic radial load P on the bearing. [4]
  2. (b) Find the basic rating life L10 in millions of revolutions. [4]
  3. (c) Convert the basic rating life to hours of operation at 1450 rpm. [4]
  4. (d) Find the life in hours at 95 percent reliability. [3]
  5. (e) If the same bearing must reach an L10 life of 20 000 h at 1450 rpm, find the largest equivalent radial load it can carry. [5]
(a)

First decide which branch of the equivalent-load rule applies. The ratio of thrust to radial load is Fa/(V·Fr) = 1.1/(1.0 × 3.2) = 0.344. This is greater than e = 0.28, so the axial load must be included with X = 0.56 and Y = 1.6. The equivalent dynamic load is P = X·V·Fr + Y·Fa = 0.56 × 1.0 × 3.2 + 1.6 × 1.1 = 1.792 + 1.760 = 3.55 kN. Compare this with using the radial load alone: 3.2 kN, so the thrust increases the equivalent load by 11 percent. Marker note: a candidate who forgets to compare the ratio with e, or who adds Fa directly to Fr, loses the method marks. The equivalent load is a single radial load that would give the same life as the combined loading.

Answer: 3.55 kN

(b)

The basic rating life for a ball bearing follows L10 = (C/P)3 million revolutions, where the exponent 3 holds for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. Substitute C = 29.5 kN and P = 3.55 kN: C/P = 8.305. Cubing, L10 = 8.305³ = 573 million revolutions. This is the life that 90 percent of a large group of identical bearings would reach or exceed under the same conditions, so it is not a mean life. The cubic dependence means a 10 percent increase in load cuts the life by about 25 percent, which is why accurate load estimates are critical in bearing selection. Assumptions: steady load, no shock factor, normal lubrication and operation within the temperature range.

Answer: 573 10⁶ rev

(c)

Hours of operation equal the revolutions divided by the revolutions per hour. The shaft turns at 1450 rpm, so 1450 × 60 = 87000 rev/h. The life is L10h = L10 × 10⁶/(60n) = 573 × 10⁶/87000 = 6585 h. This is about 0.8 years of continuous running, or roughly 3.3 years at eight hours per day for 250 days per year. Compare this with a typical gearbox design life of 20 000 to 30 000 h: 6585 h falls well short, which motivates the check in part (e). Marker note: state that the figure is a 90 percent reliability life; a bearing that fails earlier than L10h is not a design error, it is expected for 10 percent of units.

Answer: 6585 h

(d)

A higher reliability reduces the allowed life. The life adjustment factor a1 multiplies the basic rating life: L95 = a1 × L10h = 0.64 × 6585 = 4214 h. For a reliability of 95 percent, only 5 percent of bearings are expected to fail before this time. Reliability factors are less than 1 for any value above 90 percent. They come from a Weibull distribution of fatigue life, with the characteristic that failures are widely scattered even under identical conditions. The 95 percent life of 4214 h is well below 20 000 h, so the bearing is unsuitable at 95 percent reliability. At 99 percent reliability the factor would drop to about 0.25 and the life would be shorter still.

Answer: 4214 h

(e)

Work backwards from the required life. The required number of revolutions is 20 000 h × 60 × 1450 rev/h = 1740 million revolutions. From L10 = (C/P)3, the maximum equivalent load is P = C/L101/3. The cube root of 1740 is 12.028. So P = 29.5/12.028 = 2.45 kN. The actual equivalent load of 3.55 kN exceeds this limit by 45 percent, so the bearing does not reach 20 000 h. A larger rating C (about 42.7 kN at the present load) or a lower load is required. This calculation is a quick selection check: the bearing is acceptable only for equivalent loads up to 2.45 kN at this speed, and the check is easily repeated if the thrust load changes.

Answer: 2.45 kN

A4 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A4-011] Journal bearing basics

A full hydrodynamic journal bearing supports the shaft of a centrifugal pump in a municipal water plant. The journal diameter is 80 mm and the bearing length is 80 mm. The radial clearance is 0.050 mm and the shaft turns at 1500 rpm under a steady radial load of 4.0 kN. The lubricating oil has a dynamic viscosity of 0.025 Pa·s at its operating temperature. Treat the journal as concentric with the bush and neglect side leakage, so that the Petroff equation for the coefficient of friction f = 2π² (μN/P)(r/c) applies, where N is the speed in revolutions per second, P is the projected bearing pressure, r is the journal radius and c is the radial clearance. The bearing is cooled by an oil circulation system that must remove all frictional heating.

  1. (a) Determine the projected bearing pressure in MPa. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the Petroff coefficient of friction. [6]
  3. (c) Determine the friction torque on the journal. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the power lost to friction in the bearing, in watts, which the oil system must remove. [5]
(a)

The projected area of a journal bearing is the diameter multiplied by the length, which gives the average pressure the oil film must carry. Here D = 0.080 m and L = 0.080 m, so the projected area is 0.080 × 0.080 = 0.0064 m². The radial load is W = 4000 N. The average pressure is P = W/(D L) = 4000 / 0.0064 = 625000 Pa = 0.625 MPa. This is a moderate value for a pump bearing running on a hydrodynamic film, well below the few MPa often allowed for white-metal bushes.
