The stress amplitude is that load divided by the stress area: σa = 1739 / 115 = 15.12 MPa. The value is small compared with the endurance limit of 162 MPa, because the bolt is much more flexible than the clamped members and takes only about one quarter of the external load. This is the main reason a correctly preloaded bolt survives a pulsating load.

Answer: 15.12 MPa

(c)

For a preloaded bolt the mean stress is the preload stress plus the stress amplitude, σm = σi + σa, so the difference σm − σi is simply σa. The Goodman expression reduces to nf = Se (Sut − σi) / [σa (Sut + Se)]. The numbers are Se = 162 MPa, Sut = 1040 MPa, σi = 622.5 MPa and σa = 15.12 MPa. The numerator is 162 × (1040 − 622.5) = 67635 and the denominator is 15.12 × (1040 + 162) = 18180. Therefore nf = 67635/18180 = 3.72. Compared with the target of 5.0, the result is below 5.0, so the target is not met. The joint is safe in fatigue, but the margin is smaller than the low stress amplitude suggests, because the high mean stress from the preload eats into the available fatigue strength.

Answer: 3.72

(d)

The factor of safety falls as the preload stress σi rises, since a larger σi reduces the numerator Sut − σi while σa stays fixed. Setting nf = 5.0 and solving for σi: 5.0 = Se (Sut − σi)/[σa (Sut + Se)], so σi = Sut − 5.0 σa (Sut + Se)/Se. Substituting, σi = 1040 − 5.0 × 15.12 × 1202 / 162 = 1040 − 561.1 = 478.9 MPa. As a percentage of the proof strength of 830 MPa this is 57.7 percent. The required preload is therefore 55.1 kN. Any preload at or below this value meets the fatigue target. However a lower preload makes separation of the cap more likely, so a compromise must be found. The result also shows that higher preload is not always better for fatigue, in contrast to a common belief.

Answer: 57.7 percent

(e)

The separation factor is the ratio of the preload to the portion of the external load that unloads the clamped members. The members relieve a fraction (1 − C) of the external load, so at the maximum load the relief is (1 − C) Pmax = (1 − 0.2485) × 14000 = 10521 N. The preload from part (d) is Fi = 478.9 × 115 = 55074 N. Therefore n0 = 55074 / 10521 = 5.23. A value above 1 means the cap stays clamped on every cycle, and here the margin of 423 percent is comfortable for a bearing cap. If the preload had to be reduced further for fatigue, the separation factor would be the limiting criterion. The designer should also remember that gasket creep and thermal effects relax the preload over time.

Answer: 5.23

A4 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A4-031] Welded joints

A bracket plate carries a vertical load of 24 kN applied 200 mm horizontally from the centroid of its weld group. The bracket is attached to a steel column by two vertical fillet welds, each 150 mm long, with their centrelines 100 mm apart. The welds are made with an E70 electrode and the designer may use an allowable shear stress of 144 MPa on the weld throat. Treat the welds as lines, with throat thickness 0.707 h for leg size h, and combine the direct shear with the torsional shear about the centroid of the group. Standard leg sizes available from the weld shop are 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 mm. The designer must choose the smallest standard leg size that carries the load, and then check how sensitive the choice is to a larger load eccentricity.

  1. (a) Find the unit polar moment of area Ju of the two-weld group about its centroid. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum leg size h required for an allowable shear stress of 144 MPa. [6]
  3. (c) Select the smallest standard leg size and find the maximum shear stress it develops. [5]
  4. (d) The load eccentricity is increased to 300 mm. Find the new minimum leg size. [5]
(a)

Treat each weld as a line of unit throat. For two parallel welds of length d = 150 mm whose centrelines are b = 100 mm apart, the unit second polar moment about the group centroid is the sum of each line's own inertia and its parallel-axis term: Ju = 2 × (d³/12 + d(b/2)²) = d³/6 + d b²/2. Substituting, Ju = 150³/6 + 150 × 100²/2 = 562 500 + 750 000 = 1312500 mm³. The actual polar moment of the throats is then J = 0.707 h Ju, with h the leg size. Working in unit lines first lets the leg size be found afterwards from the stress limit, so the same Ju can be reused for every trial leg size and every new eccentricity.

Answer: 1312500 mm³

(b)

The critical point is the corner farthest from the centroid, at horizontal offset b/2 = 50 mm and vertical offset d/2 = 75 mm. Direct shear per unit leg: F/(2d) = 24 000/300 = 80 N/mm, vertical. Torque M = F e = 24 000 × 200 = 4.8×10⁶ N·mm. The torsional shear components per unit leg are M(b/2)/Ju = 182.9 N/mm vertical and M(d/2)/Ju = 274.3 N/mm horizontal. Add the vertical parts: 80 + 182.9 = 262.9 N/mm. The resultant is k = √(262.9² + 274.3²) = 379.9 N/mm of leg. The throat stress is k/(0.707 h), so setting it equal to 144 MPa gives h = 379.9/(0.707 × 144) = 3.73 mm. Any leg smaller than this overstresses the corner weld.

Answer: 3.73 mm

(c)

Standard sizes are 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 mm, so the smallest size not below the required 3.73 mm is 4 mm. At this size the throat is 0.707 × 4 = 2.83 mm. The maximum shear stress follows from the unit-line resultant: τ = k/(0.707 h) = 379.9/(0.707 × 4) = 134.3 MPa. This is below the allowable 144 MPa, so the factor of margin on allowable stress is 144/134.3 = 1.07, which is thin. A designer would normally accept this only because the load is quasi-static; for a fluctuating load the 5 mm leg would be the sensible choice, and the weld shop cost difference between the two sizes is small.

Answer: 134.3 MPa

(d)

With e = 300 mm the torque becomes M = 24 000 × 300 = 7.2×10⁶ N·mm, and Ju is unchanged at 1 312 500 mm³. The torsional components per unit leg are 7.2×10⁶ × 50/1 312 500 = 274.3 N/mm vertical and 7.2×10⁶ × 75/1 312 500 = 411.4 N/mm horizontal. The vertical sum is 80 + 274.3 = 354.3 N/mm, so k = √(354.3² + 411.4²) = 542.9 N/mm. Then h = 542.9/(0.707 × 144) = 5.33 mm, which rounds up to a 6 mm standard leg. A 50 percent increase in eccentricity therefore raises the required leg size by about 43 percent, because the torsion term dominates the direct shear.

Answer: 5.33 mm

Problem 2 [A4-032] Helical compression springs

A relief valve uses a helical compression spring of music wire to hold the poppet closed. The wire diameter is 3.0 mm, the mean coil diameter is 24 mm and the shear modulus is 79.3 GPa. The spring has squared and ground ends, so the total number of coils is the active number plus two. The valve designer needs a spring rate close to 12 N/mm, then a spring that works at a service force of 150 N without exceeding a corrected shear stress limit of 800 MPa when compressed solid. Use the Wahl correction factor for shear stress. A clash allowance of 15 percent of the maximum working deflection must be added to the solid height when finding the free length. The designer rounds the active coil count to the nearest whole number.

  1. (a) Find the number of active coils needed for a rate of 12 N/mm. [4]
  2. (b) Find the actual spring rate with the rounded coil count. [4]
  3. (c) Find the Wahl-corrected maximum shear stress at the 150 N service force. [6]
  4. (d) Find the free length so that solid stress does not exceed 800 MPa, including the 15 percent clash allowance. [6]
(a)

The rate of a helical compression spring is k = d⁴G/(8D³N), where N is the number of active coils. Rearranging, N = d⁴G/(8D³k). Use millimetres and N/mm², with G = 79 300 N/mm². The wire diameter to the fourth power is 3⁴ = 81 mm⁴ and the mean diameter cubed is 24³ = 13 824 mm³. Then N = 81 × 79 300/(8 × 13 824 × 12) = 6 423 300/1 327 104 = 4.84 coils. Active coils are normally a whole number or a half, so the designer rounds to 5. With squared and ground ends two more coils are inactive, giving seven coils in total, which matters for the solid height later in the problem.

Answer: 4.84 coils (use 5)

(b)

With N = 5 active coils the rate is recalculated from k = d⁴G/(8D³N). Substituting, k = 81 × 79 300/(8 × 13 824 × 5) = 6 423 300/552 960 = 11.62 N/mm. This is about 3 percent below the 12 N/mm target, which is acceptable because the target was approximate and the coil count must be an integer. Using four coils would give 14.5 N/mm, a 21 percent overshoot, so five is the better choice. A lower rate means a given deflection produces a smaller force, so the valve cracking pressure will be slightly more sensitive to spring length tolerance than the designer first wanted.

Answer: 11.62 N/mm

(c)

The spring index is C = D/d = 24/3 = 8. The Wahl factor is Kw = (4C - 1)/(4C - 4) + 0.615/C = 31/28 + 0.0769 = 1.1838. This factor accounts for both the direct shear and the curvature of the wire, which raises the stress on the inside of the coil. The maximum shear stress is τ = Kw × 8FD/(πd³) = 1.1838 × 8 × 150 × 24/(π × 27) = 1.1838 × 339.5 = 402 MPa. This sits at roughly half the 800 MPa limit, which leaves ample room for the valve to open further and for the fatigue loading that a relief valve spring will see over its life.

Answer: 402 MPa

(d)

At the stress limit, the limiting force follows from τ = Kw 8FD/(πd³): Fs = 800 × π × 27/(8 × 24 × 1.1838) = 67 858/227.3 = 298.5 N. The deflection to reach that force is ys = Fs/k = 298.5/11.62 = 25.7 mm. The solid height of seven coils is Hs = 7 × 3 = 21 mm. The free length must cover the solid height, the maximum deflection and the clash allowance of 15 percent of that deflection: L0 = 21 + 1.15 × 25.7 = 50.6 mm. A free length of about 50 mm therefore lets the spring travel to its design limit without the coils clashing, and the stress is exactly 800 MPa at that deflection. Note that the 15 percent clash allowance adds extra travel before the coils actually touch, so if the spring were driven fully solid (29.55 mm, 343 N) the stress would reach about 920 MPa, above the limit; 800 MPa is the working limit, not the solid-height stress.

Answer: 50.6 mm

Problem 3 [A4-033] Shaft design under combined loading

A solid steel shaft in a gearbox carries a helical gear at mid-span. At the critical section the bending moment is 620 N·m and, because the shaft rotates, the bending stress is fully reversed. The transmitted torque is a steady 480 N·m. The shaft material has an ultimate strength of 620 MPa and a yield strength of 420 MPa. The corrected endurance limit at the critical section, with all Marin factors already applied, is 210 MPa. The shoulder fillet gives fatigue stress concentration factors of 1.8 in bending and 1.4 in torsion. The design must have a fatigue factor of safety of 2.0 using the DE-Goodman criterion. The designer will then choose a standard 55 mm shaft and check both fatigue and first-cycle yielding at that size.

  1. (a) Find the minimum shaft diameter for a DE-Goodman fatigue factor of 2.0. [6]
  2. (b) For the 55 mm shaft, find the alternating von Mises stress at the critical section. [4]
  3. (c) Find the fatigue factor of safety of the 55 mm shaft by DE-Goodman. [5]
  4. (d) Find the first-cycle yield factor of safety of the 55 mm shaft using the maximum von Mises stress. [5]
(a)

For fully reversed bending and steady torsion, the alternating von Mises stress comes from bending only and the midrange von Mises stress from torsion only. The DE-Goodman diameter equation is d = {(16n/π) [ (1/Se)(4(Kf Ma)²)½ + (1/Sut)(3(Kfs Tm)²)½ ]}⅓. Here Kf Ma = 1.8 × 620 = 1116 N·m and Kfs Tm = 1.4 × 480 = 672 N·m. In N·mm the first term is 2 × 1.116×10⁶/210 = 10 629 and the second is √3 × 672 000/620 = 1877. Their sum is 12 506. Multiplying by 16 × 2/π = 10.186 gives 127 390 mm³, whose cube root is d = 50.3 mm. The next standard size above is 55 mm.

Answer: 50.3 mm

(b)

The alternating stress comes from the fully reversed bending moment, increased by the fatigue stress concentration factor. For a solid round shaft, σa = 32 Kf Ma/(π d³). With d = 55 mm, d³ = 166 375 mm³, so σa = 32 × 1.8 × 620 000/(π × 166 375) = 35.71×10⁶/522 680 = 68.3 MPa. There is no alternating torsion, so the alternating von Mises stress equals this bending value: σa' = √(σa² + 3 × 0²). Because the shaft rotates once per cycle in a fixed bending plane, each fibre sees this stress reversing in sign every revolution, which is why it enters the endurance check with zero mean.

Answer: 68.3 MPa

(c)

The midrange stress arises only from the steady torque. The torsional shear is τm = 16 Kfs Tm/(π d³) = 16 × 1.4 × 480 000/(π × 166 375) = 10.752×10⁶/522 680 = 20.57 MPa. The midrange von Mises stress is σm' = √3 × 20.57 = 35.6 MPa. The DE-Goodman criterion gives 1/n = σa'/Se + σm'/Sut = 68.3/210 + 35.6/620 = 0.325 + 0.057 = 0.382 using σa' = 68.3 MPa from bending, so n = 2.61. This exceeds the required 2.0, which is expected because 55 mm is larger than the 50.3 mm minimum diameter. The fatigue term from bending dominates the sum.

Answer: 2.61

(d)

To guard against yielding on the first load cycle, take the worst case where the alternating and steady stresses act together. The maximum von Mises stress at the critical fibre is σmax' = √(σa² + 3τm²) with σa = 68.3 MPa and τm = 20.57 MPa. Then σmax' = √(68.3² + 3 × 20.57²) = √(4665 + 1269) = 77.0 MPa. The yield factor of safety is ny = Sy/σmax' = 420/77.0 = 5.45. This is much larger than the fatigue factor, which confirms that fatigue, not yielding, governs the design. This treatment is conservative because it adds the peak bending stress to the full torsion without allowing for load phasing.

Answer: 5.45

Problem 4 [A4-034] Rolling bearing selection and life

A deep-groove ball bearing supports the head shaft of a belt conveyor pulley. The bearing carries a steady radial load of 4.2 kN and a steady axial load of 1.5 kN while the shaft turns at 900 rpm. The design life is 25 000 hours. For this bearing family the catalogue gives a limiting axial-to-radial load ratio e = 0.30; when Fa/Fr exceeds e, use X = 0.56 and Y = 1.55 in the equivalent load, otherwise use X = 1 and Y = 0. The rated basic dynamic load C is based on a life of one million revolutions at 90 percent reliability. Use a life exponent of 3 for ball bearings. The owner wants 95 percent reliability, for which the reliability life factor a1 is 0.62. A catalogue bearing with C = 55.9 kN is available for purchase.

  1. (a) Find the equivalent dynamic radial load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the required basic dynamic load rating for 25 000 hours at 90 percent reliability. [5]
  3. (c) Find the required rating for 25 000 hours at 95 percent reliability. [5]
  4. (d) Find the 95 percent reliability life, in hours, of the bearing with C = 55.9 kN. [6]
(a)

The ratio Fa/Fr = 1500/4200 = 0.357 exceeds the catalogue limit e = 0.30, so the axial load influences the bearing and the factors X = 0.56 and Y = 1.55 apply. The equivalent dynamic radial load is P = X Fr + Y Fa = 0.56 × 4200 + 1.55 × 1500 = 2352 + 2325 = 4.68 kN after converting from 4677 N. Note that although the axial load is only 36 percent of the radial load, it contributes almost as much to P as the radial load itself, because Y is large for a deep-groove ball bearing. A designer who ignored the thrust would size the bearing about 10 percent too small (4200 N instead of 4677 N).

Answer: 4.68 kN

(b)

First convert the design life to millions of revolutions: L10 = 60 n Lh/10⁶ = 60 × 900 × 25 000/10⁶ = 1350 million revolutions. The basic life equation for a ball bearing is L10 = (C/P)³, so the required rating is C = P × L101/3. The cube root of 1350 is 11.05, so C = 4677 × 11.05 = 51 680 N, which is 51.7 kN. This is the rating at 90 percent reliability, meaning ten bearings in a hundred could fail before 25 000 hours. A catalogue bearing must have at least this basic dynamic rating, and in practice the designer picks the next size up from the table.

Answer: 51.7 kN

(c)

At 95 percent reliability the life is derated by a1 = 0.62, so L = a1 (C/P)³. To meet the same 1350 million revolutions, the basic rating must satisfy (C/P)³ = 1350/0.62 = 2177.4. The cube root is 12.96, so C = 4677 × 12.96 = 60 610 N, which is 60.6 kN. Compared with the 90 percent case, the rating requirement rises by 17 percent. Because bearing rating grows roughly with the cube of bore for similar series, this usually means one size step larger, with higher cost, so the owner should decide whether the extra reliability is justified for a conveyor head pulley.

Answer: 60.6 kN

(d)

For the bearing with C = 55.9 kN, the 95 percent life is L = a1 (C/P)³ = 0.62 × (55 900/4677)³. The ratio is 11.952, and its cube is 1707.4, so L = 0.62 × 1707.4 = 1058.6 million revolutions. Convert to hours using Lh = L × 10⁶/(60 n) = 1058.6×10⁶/(60 × 900) = 19603 h. This is about 22 percent short of the 25 000 hours required, which agrees with part (c), since 55.9 kN is below the 60.6 kN needed. The bearing would meet the 90 percent target, giving 31 600 hours, but not the 95 percent target.

Answer: 19603 h

Problem 5 [A4-035] Journal bearing basics

A lightly loaded full journal bearing supports a pump shaft. The journal diameter is 60 mm, the bearing length is 60 mm and the radial clearance is 0.050 mm. The shaft turns at 1800 rpm and the bearing carries a steady radial load of 3000 N. The oil has an effective viscosity of 0.025 Pa·s at the operating temperature. Assume a concentric journal so that Petroff's equation applies, with friction coefficient f = 2π² (μN/P)(r/c), where N is in revolutions per second, P is the projected bearing pressure and r and c are the journal radius and radial clearance. The designer must keep the frictional power loss below 120 W to stay within the oil cooling capacity. Calculate the bearing pressure, check the friction, and decide on the lubricant viscosity needed.

  1. (a) Find the projected bearing pressure. [4]
  2. (b) Find the coefficient of friction by Petroff's equation. [5]
  3. (c) Find the friction power loss. [5]
  4. (d) Find the oil viscosity that limits the power loss to 120 W. [6]
(a)

The projected bearing area is the journal diameter times the bearing length: A = D L = 0.060 × 0.060 = 0.0036 m². The mean pressure on this projected area is P = W/(D L) = 3000/0.0036 = 833 333 Pa = 0.833 MPa. This is a modest value; for oil-lubricated bearings in pumps, projected pressures up to a few megapascals are common. The length-to-diameter ratio here is 1.0, which is a standard compromise: a longer bearing carries more load but is harder to align, and a shorter one loses oil from its ends. Petroff's equation will be used with this pressure.

Answer: 0.833 MPa

(b)

Work in SI units. The speed is N = 1800/60 = 30 rev/s, the journal radius is r = 0.030 m, the clearance is c = 5×10⁻⁵ m, so r/c = 600. The viscosity term is μN/P = 0.025 × 30/833 333 = 9.0×10⁻⁷. Petroff's equation gives f = 2π² (μN/P)(r/c) = 19.739 × 9.0×10⁻⁷ × 600 = 0.0107. This value assumes a concentric journal and a fully developed film, so it represents the friction in the lightly loaded limit. Heavily loaded journals run eccentrically and show larger friction, so Petroff gives a lower estimate than the true value would be for heavy duty.

Answer: 0.0107

(c)

The friction torque is the friction force times the journal radius: T = f W r = 0.01066 × 3000 × 0.030 = 0.959 N·m. The angular speed is ω = 2π N = 2π × 30 = 188.5 rad/s. The power dissipated as heat in the oil film is H = T ω = 0.959 × 188.5 = 181 W. This exceeds the 120 W cooling limit by about 51 percent, so the bearing as specified would run hotter than the design allows. The designer has two choices: increase the clearance, which also raises the flow of oil carrying heat away, or choose a thinner oil as the next part explores.

Answer: 181 W

(d)

In Petroff's equation, friction coefficient, torque and power are all directly proportional to viscosity when load, speed and geometry are fixed. The power loss therefore scales with μ, so the allowed viscosity is μ2 = 0.025 × 120/180.8 = 0.0166 Pa·s. A lighter oil with about two thirds of the original viscosity meets the limit. The designer must then verify that the minimum film thickness is still adequate, because a thinner oil reduces load capacity and raises the risk of metal contact at start-up and under shock loads. This trade-off between friction and film strength is the central decision in journal bearing lubrication.

Answer: 0.0166 Pa·s

A4 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A4-036] Spur and helical gear stress

A 20-tooth spur pinion with module 4 mm, 20 degree pressure angle and 40 mm face width transmits 15 kW at 1500 rpm in a conveyor reducer. The pinion is made of through-hardened steel. For a first design check use the Lewis bending equation with a form factor Y = 0.32 for 20 teeth, written in module form as σ = Kv Wt/(b m Y). The velocity factor for cut teeth is Kv = (6.1 + V)/6.1, with V the pitch-line velocity in m/s. The allowable bending stress in the pinion tooth for this duty is 70 MPa. The designer needs to know the minimum face width, and whether an increase in speed to 2500 rpm at the same power makes the original 40 mm face width acceptable.

  1. (a) Find the pitch-line velocity and the tangential load, giving the load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Lewis bending stress in the pinion at 1500 rpm. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum face width for an allowable stress of 70 MPa. [5]
  4. (d) Find the bending stress with the 40 mm face width at 2500 rpm and the same power. [6]
(a)

The pitch diameter is d = m Z = 4 × 20 = 80 mm = 0.080 m. The pitch-line velocity is V = π d n/60 = π × 0.080 × 1500/60 = 6.283 m/s. The tangential load transmits the power at the pitch line: Wt = P/V = 15 000/6.283 = 2387 N. This is the force that bends the tooth as a cantilever, and it acts at the pitch circle in the Lewis model. The radial separating force would be Wt tan 20° = 869 N, but this does not enter the bending stress in this simple approach, which assumes the load is carried at the tooth tip for safety and is spread evenly across the face width.

Answer: 2387 N

(b)

First find the velocity factor for cut teeth: Kv = (6.1 + V)/6.1 = (6.1 + 6.283)/6.1 = 2.030. The Lewis equation in module form gives the bending stress as σ = Kv Wt/(b m Y). Substituting, σ = 2.030 × 2387/(40 × 4 × 0.32) = 4846/51.2 = 94.7 MPa. This is 35 percent above the allowable 70 MPa for the duty, so the 40 mm face width is too narrow. The velocity factor roughly doubles the nominal load; it accounts for the dynamic effects of tooth errors, which grow with speed, so even a modest speed increase raises the stress in the tooth root.

Answer: 94.7 MPa

(c)

Rearranging the Lewis equation for face width gives b = Kv Wt/(m Y σall). With Kv = 2.030, Wt = 2387 N, m = 4 mm, Y = 0.32 and σall = 70 MPa, b = 2.030 × 2387/(4 × 0.32 × 70) = 4846/89.6 = 54.1 mm. A face width of about 54 mm is therefore needed, and the designer would round up to 55 mm. The face width is commonly limited to about 3 to 5 times the circular pitch, here 12.57 mm, so 54 mm is 4.3 pitches and sits within the usual range. Beyond that, misalignment would concentrate the load on one end of the tooth.

Answer: 54.1 mm

(d)

At 2500 rpm the pitch-line velocity is V = π × 0.080 × 2500/60 = 10.47 m/s. The same 15 kW is now transmitted with a lower tangential load: Wt = 15 000/10.47 = 1433 N. The velocity factor rises to Kv = (6.1 + 10.47)/6.1 = 2.716. The stress is σ = Kv Wt/(b m Y) = 2.716 × 1433/(40 × 4 × 0.32) = 3892/51.2 = 76.0 MPa. This is lower than at 1500 rpm, 94.6 MPa, because the load fell faster than the velocity factor rose, but it is still above the 70 MPa allowable. Raising the speed alone does not rescue the 40 mm face width.

Answer: 76.0 MPa

Problem 2 [A4-037] Clutches

A wet multi-plate clutch couples the engine to a tractor power take-off. Each friction surface has an outside radius of 110 mm and an inside radius of 70 mm. The friction material is paper-based, with a coefficient of friction of 0.08 in oil, and the maximum allowable pressure is 1.2 MPa. Assume uniform wear. The clutch must transmit a torque of 400 N·m, and the designer rounds the number of friction interfaces up to the next whole number. On engagement the driving side has an inertia of 2.5 kg·m² spinning at 150 rad/s, and the driven side has an inertia of 8.0 kg·m² initially at rest. Assume the clutch slips at its constant torque capacity and neglect any load torque during the slip period.

  1. (a) Find the axial clamping force from the uniform-wear model. [4]
  2. (b) Find the torque capacity of one friction interface. [4]
  3. (c) Find the number of friction interfaces required. [4]
  4. (d) Find the energy dissipated in the clutch during one engagement. [4]
  5. (e) Find the slip time at the actual clutch capacity. [4]
(a)

Under uniform wear, the pressure varies inversely with radius, so p r is constant and the maximum pressure occurs at the inside radius: p ri = pmax ri. The axial force is the integral of the pressure over the annulus: F = 2π pmax ri (ro - ri). Substituting in millimetres and megapascals, F = 2π × 1.2 × 70 × (110 - 70) = 2π × 1.2 × 70 × 40 = 21112 N. This is the force the clutch springs or hydraulic piston must supply. The same force acts through every interface in the stack, since the plates are clamped in series, so the total clamp load does not rise with the number of discs.

Answer: 21112 N

(b)

With uniform wear the effective friction radius is the mean of the inner and outer radii: reff = (ro + ri)/2 = (110 + 70)/2 = 90 mm. The torque of one interface is T = μ F reff = 0.08 × 21 112 × 90 = 152 003 N·mm = 152.0 N·m. Compare this with a uniform-pressure assumption, which would give a slightly larger torque for the same peak pressure; the uniform-wear result is the safer one for design, because it applies after the surfaces have bedded in and the pressure has redistributed toward the inside radius. Oil lowers the friction coefficient to 0.08 but also keeps the surfaces cool.

Answer: 152.0 N·m

(c)

The required torque is 400 N·m and each friction interface supplies 152.0 N·m. The number of interfaces is N = 400/152.0 = 2.63, which is rounded up to 3. With three interfaces the capacity is 3 × 152.0 = 456.0 N·m, which gives a margin of 14 percent over the required torque. This margin is useful because the oil film and wear reduce friction with time. A three-interface clutch needs four plates, for instance two driving plates and two driven plates arranged to give three working faces, and the plate stack is clamped at a force of 21.1 kN throughout.

Answer: 3 interfaces

(d)

The energy lost in a slipping engagement of two inertias is the loss of kinetic energy when they reach a common speed. For a driver J1 = 2.5 kg·m² at ω1 = 150 rad/s and a driven J2 = 8.0 kg·m² at rest, the lost energy is E = ½ [J1 J2/(J1 + J2)] ω1². The reduced inertia is 2.5 × 8.0/10.5 = 1.905 kg·m². Then E = 0.5 × 1.905 × 150² = 21429 J. This heat appears at the interfaces and is carried away by the oil. It does not depend on the clutch torque, only on the inertias and speed difference, so a stronger clutch engages faster but heats the plates the same amount.

Answer: 21429 J

(e)

During slip the clutch torque acts on both sides: it decelerates J1 and accelerates J2. The relative acceleration is T(1/J1 + 1/J2), so the time to equalise speeds is t = ω1/[T (1/J1 + 1/J2)]. With the actual capacity T = 456.0 N·m, 1/J1 + 1/J2 = 0.4 + 0.125 = 0.525 kg⁻¹·m⁻², so t = 150/(456.0 × 0.525) = 0.627 s. The common final speed is J1 ω1/(J1 + J2) = 35.7 rad/s. A slip time of about 0.63 s is a firm engagement for a tractor PTO; a lower pedal force would extend this time and put more heat into the discs per second of operation.

Answer: 0.627 s

Problem 3 [A4-038] Brakes

A simple band brake slows a hoist drum of 500 mm diameter. The steel band wraps the drum through 270 degrees, the band-drum friction coefficient is 0.30 and the band width is 60 mm. The brake must exert a torque of 1.2 kN·m. The slack end of the band is attached to an actuating lever at 80 mm from the lever pivot, while the tight end is fixed to the frame, and the operator pushes at the end of the lever 600 mm from the pivot. For band life the maximum band pressure should not exceed 0.35 MPa. The drum and load have an equivalent inertia of 60 kg·m², turning at 300 rpm at the instant the brake is applied. Find the brake design quantities for the specified torque, and the energy to be absorbed in a stop at this torque.

  1. (a) Find the tight-side band tension. [4]
  2. (b) Find the operating force at the lever end. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum band pressure with the 60 mm band. [4]
  4. (d) Find the minimum band width for a pressure of 0.35 MPa. [4]
  5. (e) Find the kinetic energy absorbed in stopping the drum from 300 rpm. [4]
(a)

For a flexible band on a drum, the tension ratio is T1/T2 = eμθ, where θ is the angle of wrap in radians. Here θ = 270° = 4.712 rad, so μθ = 0.30 × 4.712 = 1.4137 and the ratio is e1.4137 = 4.111. The braking torque is T = (T1 - T2) r, so T1 - T2 = 1200/0.25 = 4800 N. With T1 = 4.111 T2, 3.111 T2 = 4800 and T2 = 1543 N. Then T1 = 4.111 × 1543 = 6343 N. The tight side carries most of the load and sets the maximum pressure. The friction force on the drum is the 4800 N difference between the two tensions acting at the drum surface.

Answer: 6343 N

(b)

Take moments about the lever pivot. The tight end is fixed to the frame and so applies no moment. The slack end, carrying T2 = 1543 N, acts at 80 mm from the pivot, and the operator force F acts at 600 mm. Moment balance gives F × 600 = T2 × 80, so F = 1543 × 80/600 = 205.7 N. A hand force of about 206 N is reasonable for a manual brake, and could be reduced further by lengthening the lever or attaching the slack end closer to the pivot. The lever position matters: if the band were attached so that the tension acted on the other side of the pivot, the brake would be self-locking.

Answer: 205.7 N

(c)

The pressure on the band is largest at the tight end, where the tension is highest, because the pressure along the contact is p = T/(b r) for a thin band. At the tight end, p = T1/(b r) = 6343/(60 × 250) = 0.423 MPa, using the band width b = 60 mm and the drum radius r = 250 mm, both in millimetres. This is 21 percent above the 0.35 MPa limit set for band life, so the 60 mm band would wear faster than specified and may glaze with heat. The designer can reduce the pressure by widening the band or by increasing the angle of wrap, which would also reduce the tensions needed.

Answer: 0.423 MPa

(d)

Setting the tight-side pressure equal to the allowable value, pmax = T1/(b r), and solving for the width gives b = T1/(pmax r) = 6343/(0.35 × 250) = 72.5 mm. A 75 mm standard band would therefore be selected, and with it the maximum pressure becomes 6343/(75 × 250) = 0.338 MPa. A wider band also lowers the heat flux per unit area at the drum surface, which helps the lining survive repeated stops. The operating force and tensions are unchanged by the width, because they depend only on the torque, the friction coefficient and the angle of wrap.

Answer: 72.5 mm

(e)

The drum turns at 300 rpm, so ω = 300 × 2π/60 = 31.42 rad/s. The kinetic energy of the equivalent inertia is E = ½ J ω² = 0.5 × 60 × 31.42² = 29609 J. This is all converted to heat at the band-drum interface. At the 1.2 kN·m braking torque the stop takes t = J ω/T = 60 × 31.42/1200 = 1.57 s, so the mean heat flow is about 18.8 kW. Such a heat rate is large for a band brake, and repeated stops would drive the drum temperature up quickly, so the duty cycle matters as much as the torque.

Answer: 29609 J

Problem 4 [A4-039] Belt and chain drives

A flat-belt drive connects a 7.5 kW induction motor running at 1450 rpm to a fan shaft. The motor pulley has a diameter of 200 mm and the fan pulley has a diameter of 500 mm. The open belt runs on a centre distance of 900 mm, with a coefficient of friction of 0.35 between the belt and the pulleys. The belt has a mass per unit length of 0.45 kg/m. The belt manufacturer specifies an allowable tight-side tension of 9 N per millimetre of width. Find the quantities needed to size the belt, taking into account the centrifugal tension. The designer also needs to know how much power the same belt can carry if the pulleys get oily and the friction coefficient falls to 0.25.

  1. (a) Find the angle of wrap on the small pulley. [3]
  2. (b) Find the effective pull on the belt. [4]
  3. (c) Find the tight-side tension including centrifugal tension. [5]
  4. (d) Find the belt width needed for 9 N per millimetre. [4]
  5. (e) Find the power the belt can carry at the same tight-side tension when μ = 0.25. [4]
(a)

For an open belt the angle of wrap on the small pulley is θ = π - 2 arcsin[(D - d)/(2C)], where D and d are the large and small pulley diameters and C is the centre distance. Here (D - d)/(2C) = 300/1800 = 0.16667, whose arcsine is 0.16745 rad. Then θ = 3.1416 - 2 × 0.16745 = 2.807 rad, which is about 160.8 degrees. The small pulley always has the smaller wrap angle, so it governs the grip: slip would start there first. The large pulley wraps 3.1416 + 0.3349 = 3.476 rad and so has spare grip. The wrap angle will be used with the friction coefficient in the belt tension ratio.

Answer: 2.807 rad

(b)

The belt speed is V = π d n/60 = π × 0.200 × 1450/60 = 15.18 m/s. The power transmitted equals the effective pull times the belt speed, so the effective pull is Fe = P/V = 7500/15.18 = 494 N. This is the difference between the tight-side and slack-side tensions, T1 - T2. The velocity is moderate for a flat belt, which commonly runs at 10 to 25 m/s, and the centrifugal effects are not yet dominant. The effective pull determines how much drive torque reaches the fan shaft; once it is known, the individual tensions can be fixed from the friction condition at the point of impending slip.

Answer: 494 N

(c)

The centrifugal tension is Tc = m V² = 0.45 × 15.18² = 103.7 N. The friction condition at impending slip is (T1 - Tc)/(T2 - Tc) = eμθ = e0.35 × 2.8067 = e0.9823 = 2.671. Combined with T1 - T2 = 494 N, the slack-side excess is T2 - Tc = 494/(2.671 - 1) = 295.6 N. Then T2 = 295.6 + 103.7 = 399.3 N and the tight-side tension is T1 = 399.3 + 494 = 893 N. Without the centrifugal correction the tight side would be 790 N, so ignoring it would understate the belt load by about 12 percent at this speed. The correction grows with the square of the belt speed.

Answer: 893 N

(d)

The allowable tight-side tension is 9 N per millimetre of width. The required width is the tight-side tension divided by this allowable value: b = T1/9 = 893.3/9 = 99.3 mm. A standard 100 mm belt would be selected, which gives an allowable tension of 900 N and a small margin of less than 1 percent over the calculated 893 N. That margin is thin, so the designer may prefer a 125 mm belt for a fan drive with starting surges. The belt width does not change the friction condition, which depends only on the wrap angle and the friction coefficient, so the tensions are unchanged by the selection.

Answer: 99.3 mm

(e)

With oily pulleys the friction coefficient falls to 0.25, so eμθ = e0.25 × 2.8067 = e0.7017 = 2.017. Keep the tight-side tension at 893.3 N, so T1 - Tc = 789.6 N. At impending slip, T2 - Tc = 789.6/2.017 = 391.4 N, and the effective pull is Fe = (T1 - Tc)(1 - 1/2.017) = 789.6 × 0.5042 = 398.1 N. The transmitted power is P = Fe V = 398.1 × 15.18 = 6.05 kW. This is 19 percent below the 7.5 kW load, so the belt would slip and overheat in oily conditions. Cleaning or a higher initial tension would be required.

Answer: 6.05 kW

Problem 5 [A4-040] Power screws

A bench-mounted screw jack lifts a steady load of 50 kN. The screw has a single-start square thread with a mean diameter of 44 mm and a lead of 8 mm. The coefficient of friction in the threads is 0.12. A thrust collar of mean diameter 70 mm carries the axial load against a bearing surface with a coefficient of friction of 0.10. The operator turns a handle and can apply a steady force of 350 N. Find the torque needed to raise and to lower the load, and the efficiency of the jack. Decide whether the jack will hold the load by itself when the handle is released, and size the handle so that one operator can raise the full load.

  1. (a) Find the torque to raise the load, including collar friction. [5]
  2. (b) Find the overall efficiency in raising the load. [4]
  3. (c) Find the torque to lower the load, including collar friction. [4]
  4. (d) Find the handle length needed for a 350 N hand force when raising the load. [4]
  5. (e) State, with reasons based on your numbers, whether the jack is self-locking. [3]
(a)

The raising torque has a thread part and a collar part. For a square thread the thread torque is Tt = (F dm/2)(l + π μ dm)/(π dm - μ l). With dm = 44 mm, l = 8 mm, μ = 0.12: π μ dm = 16.59, π dm = 138.2 and μ l = 0.96. So Tt = (50 000 × 22)(24.59/137.27) = 1.1×10⁶ × 0.1791 = 197 060 N·mm. The collar torque is Tc = F μc dc/2 = 50 000 × 0.10 × 35 = 175 000 N·mm. The total is T = 372 060 N·mm = 372.0 N·m. Nearly half of the input torque is lost to collar friction, which is why a thrust bearing is often worth its cost in a heavy jack.

Answer: 372.0 N·m

(b)

Efficiency is the useful work done divided by the work put in. In one revolution the load rises by the lead, l = 8 mm, so the useful work is F l = 50 000 × 8 = 400 000 N·mm. The input work is 2π T = 2π × 372 060 = 2.338×10⁶ N·mm. The efficiency is e = F l/(2π T) = 400 000/2 337 700 = 0.171, or about 17 percent. Such a low efficiency is the price of a self-locking screw. The thread alone, without collar friction, would have e = 400 000/(2π × 197 060) = 0.32. The collar loss therefore cuts the efficiency to roughly half the thread-only value.

Answer: 0.171

(c)

When lowering, the thread friction acts to resist the motion and the thread torque becomes Tt = (F dm/2)(π μ dm - l)/(π dm + μ l). Substituting, Tt = 1.1×10⁶ × (16.59 - 8)/(138.2 + 0.96) = 1.1×10⁶ × 0.0617 = 67 900 N·mm. The collar friction still resists, so Tc = 175 000 N·mm as before. The total lowering torque is 242 900 N·mm = 242.9 N·m. Because this torque is positive, the operator must actively turn the handle to lower the load; the load will not descend by itself. If the thread part had come out negative, a holding torque would have been required to restrain the screw from running down.

Answer: 242.9 N·m

(d)

The operator can apply 350 N at a steady rate, so the handle length must give at least the raising torque of 372.1 N·m. Then L = T/F = 372.06/350 = 1.06 m. A handle of about 1.1 m is long for a bench jack but workable if the jack is floor-mounted. Options for shortening it include a larger thrust bearing with a lower collar friction coefficient, which would cut the collar torque from 175 N·m, or a smaller lead. Lowering the lead raises the mechanical advantage, but it also lowers the speed of lift per turn, which makes the jack slower to operate.

Answer: 1.06 m

(e)

A screw is self-locking when the friction angle exceeds the lead angle, which for a square thread means μ > l/(π dm). Here l/(π dm) = 8/138.2 = 0.0579, and the thread friction coefficient is 0.12, which is about twice as large, so the thread is self-locking. The same conclusion comes from the lowering torque: it is positive at 242.9 N·m, so a torque must be applied to lower the load, and the load will not overhaul the screw and run down when the handle is released. This holds even without the collar, since the thread part alone is 67.9 N·m. Vibration can still cause creep, so a brake or pawl is wise for long holds.

Answer: Yes: the thread is self-locking since μ exceeds l/(π dm), and the lowering torque is positive.

A4 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A4-041] Material removal: cutting force and power

A 4140 steel shaft of 80 mm diameter is to be rough turned on a CNC lathe in a single pass. The cutting speed is 220 m/min, the depth of cut is 3.0 mm and the feed is 0.30 mm/rev. For this work material and a carbide insert the specific cutting energy is taken as 2.4 J/mm³ (equivalently 2400 N/mm²), and it may be assumed constant over the range of feed used. The overall efficiency from motor to cutting edge is 0.82. The shop is considering a 15 kW motor and must decide whether the machine can run this cut, and by how much the feed could be raised, at the same speed and depth, before the motor is fully loaded. Ignore the power used by the feed motion and by idling losses.

  1. (a) Find the spindle speed in rev/min. [4]
  2. (b) Find the tangential cutting force. [4]
  3. (c) Find the power required at the motor, in kW, for this cut. [6]
  4. (d) Find the largest feed, in mm/rev, at which the 15 kW motor is just fully loaded, at the same speed and depth. [6]
(a)

The cutting speed is the surface speed of the work, V = π D N, so the spindle speed is N = V/(π D). Work in consistent units: V = 220 m/min = 220 000 mm/min and D = 80 mm. Substituting, N = 220 000/(π × 80) = 220 000/251.33 = 875.4 rev/min. The result is rounded to a practical setting of about 875 rev/min when programming the lathe, since controllers accept whole-number speeds. This speed will be held constant for the pass, and the cutting speed at the surface is then 220 m/min as specified. Note that the cutting speed is based on the starting diameter, because the depth of cut removes only 3.0 mm from the radius and the surface speed at the finished 74 mm diameter is about 7.5 percent lower, which does not affect the force estimate used in later parts.

Answer: 875 rev/min

(b)

With a constant specific cutting energy u, the cutting force is the energy per unit volume multiplied by the uncut chip cross-section. The chip area is A = f d = 0.30 × 3.0 = 0.90 mm². The specific energy in force units is u = 2.4 J/mm³ = 2.4 N·m/mm³ = 2400 N/mm². Hence Fc = u f d = 2400 × 0.90 = 2160 N. This is the main component acting tangentially to the work surface in the direction of the cutting velocity, and it is the only component that consumes significant power. The radial and feed components act at right angles to the cutting velocity or at low speed, so their power contribution is negligible, which is why the problem instructs us to ignore it.

Answer: 2160 N

(c)

Power at the cutting edge equals the cutting force multiplied by the cutting speed. With V = 220 m/min = 220/60 = 3.667 m/s, Pc = Fc V = 2160 × 3.667 = 7920 W = 7.92 kW. As a check, Pc also equals u times the material removal rate; the removal rate is f d V = 0.30 × 3.0 × 220 000 = 198000 mm³/min = 3300 mm³/s, and 2.4 J/mm³ × 3300 mm³/s gives the same 7.92 kW. The drive losses must be supplied by the motor, so the motor power is Pm = Pc/η = 7.92/0.82 = 9.66 kW. This is 64 percent of the 15 kW rating, so the cut can be run with margin.

Answer: 9.66 kW

(d)

Power is proportional to feed at constant speed and depth, because the force is u f d. Set the usable power at the cutting edge equal to the motor rating times the efficiency: Pc,max = 15 000 × 0.82 = 12300 W. Then Fc,max = Pc,max/V = 12300/3.667 = 3355 N. Solving Fc = u f d for the feed, f = Fc,max/(u d) = 3355/(2400 × 3.0) = 0.4659 mm/rev. That is a 55 percent increase over the present 0.30 mm/rev. In practice the feed would be limited below this by insert strength, surface finish and shaft deflection, and the motor should not be run at 100 percent continuously, so a feed near 0.40 mm/rev is a sensible working limit.

Answer: 0.466 mm/rev

Problem 2 [A4-042] Machining: tool life and cost

A batch of 60 mm diameter, 150 mm long alloy-steel bars is turned in one pass at a feed of 0.25 mm/rev. The tool follows the Taylor equation V Tn = C with n = 0.25 and C = 300 when V is in m/min and T in minutes. The machine and operator rate is 75 dollars per hour. Each carbide edge costs 8.00 dollars, and changing an edge takes 1.5 minutes of machine time. Non-cutting handling time is the same for all conditions and is excluded. The planner is presently running at 180 m/min because that is the speed the tooling supplier recommended, and wants to know whether a different speed would lower the cutting-related cost per part, and by how much.

  1. (a) Find the tool life at 180 m/min. [3]
  2. (b) Find the tool life that gives minimum cost per part. [5]
  3. (c) Find the cutting speed that gives this tool life. [4]
  4. (d) Find the cutting-related cost saved per part by running at the economic speed rather than at 180 m/min. [8]
(a)

Rearrange the Taylor equation V Tn = C for the tool life: T = (C/V)1/n. With C = 300, V = 180 and n = 0.25, the exponent 1/n is 4. So T = (300/180)4 = (1.6667)4 = 7.72 min. This means one edge will cut for about 7.7 minutes before it must be replaced. Since the cutting time per bar is under one minute at this speed, an edge produces roughly 12 bars before it wears out. The strong sensitivity of life to speed, with life proportional to V to the power minus four, is the key feature the later parts exploit, because a modest drop in speed lengthens the life by a large factor.

Answer: 7.72 min

(b)

For minimum cost per part the economic tool life is T = (1/n − 1)(Tc + Ct/Co), where Tc is the tool-change time, Ct the cost of one edge and Co the machine rate per minute. The rate is Co = 75/60 = 1.25 dollars/min. The edge cost expressed as machine minutes is Ct/Co = 8.00/1.25 = 6.40 min. Adding the change time, Tc + Ct/Co = 1.5 + 6.40 = 7.90 min. The factor (1/n − 1) = 4 − 1 = 3. Therefore T_opt = 3 × 7.90 = 23.7 min. This is about 3.1 times the life obtained at 180 m/min, which already tells us the planner is running too fast for minimum cost.

Answer: 23.7 min

(c)

Apply the Taylor equation again with the economic life: V = C/Tn. With T = 23.70 min and n = 0.25, T0.25 = 2.2064. So V_opt = 300/2.2064 = 136.0 m/min. This is 24 percent lower than 180 m/min. The lower speed lengthens the cutting time per bar, which raises the machine cost, but the edge is used far more fully, so the tooling and tool-change cost per bar fall faster than the machining cost rises. The balance between those two opposing trends is exactly what the economic-life formula captures, and the optimum is fairly flat, so a speed within a few percent of this value costs almost the same.

Answer: 136.0 m/min

(d)

Cutting time per part is Tm = π D L/(1000 V f) with D and L in mm. The area term π D L = π × 60 × 150 = 28274 mm². At 180 m/min, Tm = 28274/(1000 × 180 × 0.25) = 0.6283 min. Cost per part is Co Tm + (Tm/T)(Co Tc + Ct), where the second term is the tooling share. At 180 m/min this is 1.25 × 0.6283 + (0.6283/7.716) × 9.875 = 1.5895 dollars. At 136.0 m/min, Tm = 0.8318 min and the cost is 1.25 × 0.8318 + (0.8318/23.70) × 9.875 = 1.3863 dollars. The saving is 1.5895 − 1.3863 = 0.203 dollars per part, about 12.8 percent, which is worth 406 dollars on a batch of 2000 bars.

Answer: 0.203 dollars

Problem 3 [A4-043] Casting and solidification time

A foundry casts a steel plate 300 mm × 200 mm × 40 mm in a green-sand mould. To calibrate the mould, a trial sphere of 120 mm diameter poured in the same sand and at the same superheat took 5.4 min to solidify. Chvorinov's rule, t = B (V/A)², is assumed to apply with the same constant B for all shapes cast in this mould. The plate is to be fed by one cylindrical top riser with height equal to 1.5 times its diameter, cooling through its side and top face, while its base is attached to the casting and loses no heat. The riser must freeze 25 percent later than the casting. The steel suffers 6 percent volumetric solidification shrinkage, and only 14 percent of the riser volume can be delivered as feed metal before the riser freezes.

  1. (a) Find the mould constant B from the sphere trial, in min/cm². [3]
  2. (b) Find the solidification time of the plate. [4]
  3. (c) Find the riser diameter needed so that it freezes 25 percent later than the plate. [7]
  4. (d) Check whether this riser has enough feed metal, and find the smallest riser diameter that supplies the required feed volume. [6]
(a)

For a sphere of diameter D the volume is π D³/6 and the surface area is π D², so the volume-to-area ratio is V/A = D/6. For D = 120 mm = 12 cm, V/A = 2.0 cm. Chvorinov's rule gives t = B (V/A)², so B = t/(V/A)². Substituting, B = 5.4/(2.0)² = 5.4/4.0 = 1.350 min/cm². Using centimetres here keeps B in a convenient size and the same units must then be used for every later calculation. The constant depends on the mould material, the metal and its superheat, so it holds for the plate and the riser only because the problem states the same sand and pouring conditions.

Answer: 1.350 min/cm²

(b)

Compute the plate volume and cooling surface in centimetres. V = 30 × 20 × 4 = 2400 cm³. The plate is surrounded by the mould on all six faces, so A = 2(30 × 20 + 30 × 4 + 20 × 4) = 2(600 + 120 + 80) = 1600 cm². Then V/A = 2400/1600 = 1.50 cm, and the solidification time is t = B (V/A)² = 1.350 × 1.50² = 3.04 min. This is the time the riser must outlast. The result shows that the thickness dominates: for a flat plate V/A is close to half the thickness minus a small edge correction (1.5 cm against 2.0 cm), so thin sections freeze quickly even when their area is large.

Answer: 3.04 min

(c)

The riser requirement is t_r = 1.25 t_c. Because both follow the same B, (V/A)_r² = 1.25 (V/A)_c², so (V/A)_r = √1.25 × 1.50 = 1.677 cm. For the riser, with H = 1.5 D, the volume is π D² H/4 = 0.375 π D³. The cooling area is the side plus the top, π D H + π D²/4 = π D² (1.5 + 0.25) = 1.75 π D², since the base loses no heat. Thus V/A = 0.375 D/1.75 = 0.2143 D. Setting 0.2143 D = 1.677 gives D = 7.83 cm and H = 11.74 cm. The riser volume is 565 cm³, which is 0.24 times the casting volume.

Answer: 7.83 cm

(d)

The metal needed to replace the shrinkage is 6 percent of the casting volume: 0.06 × 2400 = 144 cm³. Only 14 percent of the riser volume can be delivered, so the riser from part (c) supplies 0.14 × 565 = 79 cm³, which is less than the 144 cm³ required. The riser satisfies the freezing-time rule but fails the volume rule, so it would leave a shrinkage cavity. The volume rule controls the design: the riser volume must be at least 144/0.14 = 1029 cm³. With V = 0.375 π D³, D = (Vneed/(0.375π))1/3 = 9.56 cm. Because this is larger than the diameter in part (c), it also freezes later than required, so it governs.

Answer: 9.56 cm

Problem 4 [A4-044] Forming: rolling and forging forces

A cold-forging plant upsets cylindrical billets of low-carbon steel between flat dies. Each billet is 60 mm in diameter and 90 mm high and is to be reduced to a height of 30 mm in one stroke. The flow curve is σ_f = K εn with K = 600 MPa and n = 0.15, where ε is true strain. Friction at the die interface is described by a Coulomb coefficient of 0.12, and the forging force at the end of the stroke is estimated from F = σ_f A (1 + 2 μ r/(3 h)), with σ_f the flow stress at the final strain, A the final contact area, r the final radius and h the final height. Volume is constant and the billet barrels are neglected. The press under consideration has a rated capacity of 6.0 MN, and the plant is considering a lubricant that lowers the friction coefficient to 0.05.

  1. (a) Find the final diameter of the billet and the true strain. [4]
  2. (b) Find the ideal (frictionless) deformation work for the stroke. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum forging force at the end of the stroke. [6]
  4. (d) Find the maximum forging force if the lubricant brings the friction coefficient to 0.05, and the percentage reduction in force. [5]
(a)

Constancy of volume gives A0 h0 = A h, so the final area is A = A0 h0/h. The initial area is A0 = π × 60²/4 = 2827.4 mm². Then A = 2827.4 × 90/30 = 8482.3 mm². The final radius follows from A = π r²: r = √(8482.3/π) = 51.96 mm, so the final diameter is 103.9 mm. The true strain for compression is ε = ln(h0/h) = ln(90/30) = ln 3 = 1.0986. The final diameter is 103.9 mm, an increase of 73 percent, which is a large lateral spread, so the real billet will barrel and friction will matter noticeably. Both results are needed for the force calculation that follows.

Answer: 103.9 mm

(b)

The work with no friction is the volume times the area under the true stress-strain curve, W = V × ∫σ dε. For the power-law flow curve the average flow stress over the strain range is Y_f = K εn/(1 + n). Evaluating, Y_f = 600 × 1.09860.15/1.15 = 529.2 MPa. The volume is V = A0 h0 = 2827.4 × 90 = 254469 mm³ = 2.5447 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Hence W = Y_f ε V = 529.2 × 10⁶ × 1.0986 × 2.5447 × 10⁻⁴ = 147931 J, which is 147.9 kJ. This is the minimum energy the press must supply for the deformation; friction, die deflection and press losses add to it. The figure is useful for sizing the flywheel or the energy rating of a hammer or screw press.

Answer: 147.9 kJ

(c)

At the end of the stroke the strain is the full 1.0986, so the flow stress there is σ_f = K εn = 600 × 1.09860.15 = 608.5 MPa. The friction multiplier is 1 + 2 μ r/(3 h) = 1 + 2 × 0.12 × 51.96/(3 × 30) = 1 + 0.1386 = 1.1386. The contact area is 8482.3 mm². Therefore F = 608.5 × 8482.3 × 1.1386 = 5876910 N = 5.877 MN. The force rises steeply near the end of the stroke because the contact area is largest and the aspect ratio is smallest there, which is why the maximum, not the average, sets the press capacity. The 6.0 MN press carries this load with about 2 percent in hand.

Answer: 5.877 MN

(d)

The flow stress and area are unchanged, so only the friction multiplier alters. With μ = 0.05, 1 + 2 × 0.05 × 51.96/(3 × 30) = 1 + 0.0577 = 1.0577. The force is F = 608.5 × 8482.3 × 1.0577 = 5459696 N = 5.460 MN. The reduction relative to the unlubricated case is (5.877 − 5.460)/5.877 = 7.1 percent. Better lubrication therefore trims the load, but by a modest amount here because the friction term is a minor part of the total for this squat reduction. The main benefits are lower die wear, less barrelling and a more uniform grain flow, rather than a large press-capacity saving.

Answer: 5.460 MN

Problem 5 [A4-045] Sheet metal forming and bending

A brake-formed bracket is made from 3.0 mm thick mild steel strip, 800 mm wide, with one 90 degree bend. The finished part is to have an inside bend radius of 6.0 mm. The outside dimensions of the two legs, measured to the virtual sharp of the outside corner, are 50 mm and 70 mm. Use a bend allowance based on a neutral-axis position K t from the inside surface, with K = 0.40. The bending force for air bending in a V-die with opening W = 24 mm is F = k UTS w t²/W, with k = 1.33 and UTS = 420 MPa. The yield strength is 250 MPa and the elastic modulus 205 GPa. The designer needs the blank length, the press force, and the punch radius that will give the required inside radius after springback. Springback follows R_i/R_f = 4(R_i Y/(E t))³ − 3(R_i Y/(E t)) + 1.

  1. (a) Find the flat blank length. [5]
  2. (b) Find the bending force required. [5]
  3. (c) Find the punch (tool) radius that gives a final inside radius of 6.0 mm after springback. [5]
  4. (d) Find the bend angle the brake must form to allow for springback, assuming the bend length at the neutral axis is unchanged. [5]
(a)

The flat length is the sum of the straight legs plus the bend allowance. For a bend of angle α = π/2 radians, the bend allowance is BA = α (R + K t) = 1.5708 × (6.0 + 0.40 × 3.0) = 1.5708 × 7.20 = 11.31 mm. Outside dimensions run to the virtual sharp, so each leg loses the outside setback, which for a 90 degree bend equals R + t = 6.0 + 3.0 = 9.0 mm. The straight lengths are therefore 50 − 9.0 = 41.0 mm and 70 − 9.0 = 61.0 mm. The blank length is 41.0 + 61.0 + 11.31 = 113.31 mm. Equivalently, outside sum of legs 120 minus 2 × 9.0 plus 11.31. The blank should be cut to this length and a trial bend checked, because the K factor is an estimate.

Answer: 113.31 mm

(b)

For air bending the force is F = k UTS w t²/W. Substituting k = 1.33, UTS = 420 MPa (N/mm²), w = 800 mm, t = 3.0 mm and W = 24 mm: t² = 9.0 mm², so F = 1.33 × 420 × 800 × 9.0/24. The numerator is 1.33 × 420 = 558.6, times 800 = 446880, times 9.0 = 4021920; dividing by 24 gives F = 167580 N = 167.6 kN, about 17.1 tonnes-force. A brake with at least this capacity over an 800 mm length is needed, and a margin is normally taken since the true tensile strength varies from coil to coil. The die opening of 24 mm equals eight times the thickness, which is a common choice; a narrower opening would raise the force considerably.

Answer: 167.6 kN

(c)

The required final radius is R_f = 6.0 mm, and the unknown tool radius R_i appears on both sides of the springback relation R_i/R_f = 4(R_i Y/(E t))³ − 3(R_i Y/(E t)) + 1. Define x = R_i Y/(E t) = R_i × 250/(205 000 × 3.0) = R_i × 4.065 × 10⁻⁴. For an initial guess R_i ≈ 6, x = 0.00244, and the cubic term is negligible, so R_i/6 ≈ 1 − 3x = 0.99268 giving R_i ≈ 5.956 mm. Solving the full relation numerically converges to R_i = 5.956 mm. So the punch should be ground about 0.044 mm under the required radius. This small value reflects the low yield-to-modulus ratio of mild steel.

Answer: 5.956 mm

(d)

Springback keeps the neutral-axis arc length fixed, so (R_i + t/2) α_i = (R_f + t/2) α_f. The final angle is α_f = 90 degrees and t/2 = 1.5 mm. The final neutral radius is R_f + t/2 = 6.0 + 1.5 = 7.5 mm, and the tool-side neutral radius is R_i + t/2 = 5.956 + 1.5 = 7.456 mm. Hence α_i = 90 × 7.5/7.456 = 90.53 degrees. The brake must therefore close the strip to about 90.53 degrees of bend, and the material relaxes back to 90 degrees. The overbend is only about 0.53 degrees because the ratio of radius to thickness is small; thin, large-radius bends spring back much more.

Answer: 90.53 degrees

A4 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A4-046] Welding heat input and joining processes

A pressure-vessel fabricator welds 25 mm thick quenched-and-tempered steel plate with gas metal arc welding. The arc voltage is 26 V, the current 280 A, and the travel speed 6.0 mm/s. The arc efficiency is 0.80. The steel is hardenable, and the welding procedure requires the cooling rate through 550 degrees C to stay at or below 20 K/s to avoid a brittle martensitic heat-affected zone. Treat the plate as thick, so that the Rosenthal thick-plate relation applies: R = 2π k (T_c − T_0)²/H, with R the cooling rate in K/s, k = 0.028 W/(mm·K) the thermal conductivity, T_c = 550 degrees C, T_0 the initial plate temperature and H the net heat input per unit length in J/mm. The welder can either preheat the plate or slow the travel speed. A single seam is 2.4 m long.

  1. (a) Find the net heat input per unit length of weld. [4]
  2. (b) Find the cooling rate at 550 degrees C for a plate initially at 20 degrees C. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum preheat temperature that brings the cooling rate to 20 K/s at the same heat input. [6]
  4. (d) Without preheat, find the travel speed at which the cooling rate falls to 20 K/s, and the time to weld the 2.4 m seam at that speed compared with the 6.0 mm/s case. [5]
(a)

The net heat input per unit length is H = η V I/v, where η is the arc efficiency, V the arc voltage, I the current and v the travel speed. The arc power is V I = 26 × 280 = 7280 W. Applying the efficiency, the net power into the plate is 0.80 × 7280 = 5824 W. Dividing by the travel speed of 6.0 mm/s gives H = 5824/6.0 = 971 W·s/mm = 971 J/mm, which is 0.97 kJ/mm. This is a moderate heat input for GMAW on thick plate. Note that the units work because 1 W is 1 J/s, so dividing power by speed in mm/s leaves joules per millimetre. The gross figure without the efficiency would be 1213 J/mm, and quoting that value would overstate the energy actually reaching the workpiece.

Answer: 971 J/mm

(b)

Use the thick-plate relation R = 2π k (T_c − T_0)²/H. The temperature difference is 550 − 20 = 530 K, so its square is 280900 K². The factor 2π k = 2π × 0.028 = 0.17593 W/(mm·K). The numerator is 0.17593 × 280900 = 49419. Dividing by H = 971 J/mm gives R = 49419/971 = 50.9 K/s. This is 2.5 times the limit of 20 K/s, so the procedure as written would give a hard, crack-prone heat-affected zone. The cooling rate is high because thick plate carries heat away in three dimensions and the bead is relatively small. Either the cooling rate must be cut by preheating, or the heat input must go up.

Answer: 50.9 K/s

(c)

Solve the thick-plate relation for the initial temperature at the limiting rate R = 20 K/s. Rearranging, (T_c − T_0)² = R H/(2π k) = 20 × 971/0.17593 = 110347 K². Then T_c − T_0 = √110347 = 332.2 K, and T_0 = 550 − 332.2 = 217.8 degrees C. The plate must therefore be preheated to at least about 218 degrees C over the full weld zone and held there between passes. This is a typical figure for a hardenable plate, and it should be checked with a contact pyrometer or temperature-indicating crayons at several points on the joint. A margin of 20 to 30 degrees is usually added in practice, so a working preheat near 243 degrees C would be specified.

Answer: 218 degrees C

(d)

With the plate at 20 degrees C, the limiting heat input is H_req = 2π k (T_c − T_0)²/R = 49419/20 = 2471 J/mm. The net power is unchanged at 5824 W, so the required travel speed is v = P/H_req = 5824/2471 = 2.357 mm/s. The weld time for 2400 mm at this speed is 2400/2.357 = 1018 s, compared with 2400/6.0 = 400 s at the original speed, a factor of 2.55 longer. Slowing down also produces a wider bead and a larger distorted region, and the single-pass heat input of 2471 J/mm may exceed the toughness limit of the steel. Preheating is therefore the practical remedy.

Answer: 2.357 mm/s

Problem 2 [A4-047] Quality control: process capability and control charts

A shaft diameter is specified as 24.000 ± 0.040 mm. The finishing operation is monitored with X-bar and R charts using subgroups of n = 5 consecutive parts. After 25 subgroups the grand mean of the subgroup means is 24.012 mm and the mean subgroup range is 0.036 mm, with all points in control. Use the constants A2 = 0.577, D3 = 0, D4 = 2.114 and d2 = 2.326 for n = 5, and assume individual diameters are normally distributed. The quality manager is concerned that the process is off-centre, and wants to know how many parts are being scrapped or reworked, and what the process would have to achieve to reach a Cpk of 1.33. Report capability using the short-term standard deviation estimated from the mean range.

  1. (a) Find the upper control limit for the X-bar chart, and state the R-chart upper control limit. [5]
  2. (b) Estimate the process standard deviation and calculate Cp and Cpk. [5]
  3. (c) Find the expected percentage of parts outside the specification limits. [5]
  4. (d) Find the process standard deviation needed to reach Cpk = 1.33 after the process is centred on 24.000 mm, and the Cpk obtained by centring alone. [5]
(a)

For the X-bar chart based on the mean range the limits are the grand mean plus or minus A2 times the mean range. With A2 = 0.577 and a mean range of 0.036 mm, A2 R-bar = 0.577 × 0.036 = 0.02077 mm. The upper limit is UCL = 24.012 + 0.02077 = 24.0328 mm and the lower limit is LCL = 24.012 − 0.02077 = 23.9912 mm. For the R chart, UCL = D4 R-bar = 2.114 × 0.036 = 0.0761 mm, and the lower limit is D3 R-bar = 0 because D3 = 0 for n = 5. These control limits describe what the process does, not what the drawing demands, so they should not be confused with the tolerance limits of 23.960 and 24.040 mm.

Answer: 24.0328 mm

(b)

The short-term standard deviation is estimated from the mean range as σ = R-bar/d2 = 0.036/2.326 = 0.01548 mm. The tolerance width is 0.080 mm, so Cp = (USL − LSL)/(6σ) = 0.080/(6 × 0.01548) = 0.861. This measures potential capability if the process were centred. For Cpk we take the smaller distance from the mean to a specification limit: the upper side gives (24.040 − 24.012)/(3σ) = 0.028/0.04643 = 0.603, and the lower side gives (24.012 − 23.960)/(3σ) = 0.052/0.04643 = 1.120. Cpk is the lower of the two, 0.603. Cp is below 1.0 and Cpk is lower again, so the process is both too wide and off-centre toward the upper limit. The reported value is Cpk.

Answer: 0.603

(c)

With a normal distribution of mean 24.012 mm and standard deviation 0.01548 mm, the fraction above the upper limit corresponds to z_u = (24.040 − 24.012)/0.01548 = 1.809. The upper tail area is Φ(−1.809) = 0.03522. Below the lower limit, z_l = (24.012 − 23.960)/0.01548 = 3.360, and the lower tail is 0.000390. The total outside tolerance is 0.03522 + 0.000390 = 0.03561, which is 3.56 percent, or about 35607 parts per million. Almost all of the loss is oversize, and since oversize shafts can often be reworked while undersize ones cannot, the cost depends on which side the defect lies. Centring alone would remove most of the loss.

Answer: 3.56 percent

(d)

If the mean is set to 24.000 mm, both distances to the limits equal 0.040 mm, so Cpk = Cp = 0.040/(3σ). With the present σ = 0.01548 mm, centring alone gives Cpk = 0.040/0.04643 = 0.861, which is still below 1.0. To reach Cpk = 1.33 the standard deviation must satisfy 0.040/(3σ) = 1.33, so σ = 0.040/(3 × 1.33) = 0.01003 mm. That is a reduction of 35 percent from the present value, which requires better spindle, fixturing or tool control rather than adjustment. The corresponding mean range for n = 5 would be 2.326 × 0.01003 = 0.0233 mm, giving a target for the R chart.

Answer: 0.01003 mm

Problem 3 [A4-048] Process selection and production line balancing

An assembly line for a small gearbox is to produce 300 units per shift. The shift is 8 hours long, with 30 minutes of scheduled breaks and downtime, so 450 minutes are productive. The work has eight tasks with these times in minutes: A 0.8, B 0.6, C 0.7, D 0.5, E 0.9, F 0.4, G 0.6 and H 0.5. Precedence: A precedes B and C; B and C both precede D; D precedes E and F; E and F both precede G; G precedes H. Each task must be done at one station, one worker per station. The planner will first use the largest-candidate rule (assign the available task with the longest time that fits in the remaining station time), and will then examine the best that any assignment could do with four stations.

  1. (a) Find the cycle time required, in minutes. [3]
  2. (b) Find the theoretical minimum number of stations. [3]
  3. (c) Apply the largest-candidate rule. State the stations formed and find the line efficiency. [7]
  4. (d) If the line may be rebalanced freely using four stations, find the smallest possible cycle time and the corresponding hourly output. [7]
(a)

The cycle time is the productive time available divided by the required output. Productive time per shift is 480 − 30 = 450 min. The demand is 300 units. So c = 450/300 = 1.50 min per unit. Every station must complete its assigned work within this period, otherwise the line cannot meet the target. A line operating at this rate delivers one unit every 1.50 minutes, or 40 units each hour. The cycle time is also the upper limit on the work content of any single station, and no individual task may exceed it. The longest task is E at 0.9 min, which fits easily, so no task needs to be split or duplicated.

Answer: 1.50 min

(b)

The minimum number of stations is the total task time divided by the cycle time, rounded up to the next whole number. The sum of the task times is 0.8 + 0.6 + 0.7 + 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.5 = 5.0 min. Dividing by c = 1.50 gives 3.333. Because stations are whole, we round up and the minimum is 4 stations. The fractional part shows that even a perfect balance would leave some idle time, since 4 stations provide 6.0 min of capacity per unit for only 5.0 min of work. That sets an upper bound on efficiency, 83.3 percent, which no allocation can exceed at this cycle time.

Answer: 4

(c)

Start station 1 with the only available task, A (0.8), leaving 0.7 min. Available tasks are B (0.6) and C (0.7); C is the longest that fits, so station 1 holds A and C, total 1.5 min. Station 2 starts with B (0.6); D becomes available (0.5) and is added, then F (0.4), total 1.5 min. Station 3 takes E (0.9), then G (0.6), total 1.5 min. Station 4 takes H (0.5). The rule's allocation is station 1: A+C (1.5 min); station 2: B+D+F (1.5 min); station 3: E+G (1.5 min); station 4: H (0.5 min). This uses 4 stations with total idle time 1.0 min per cycle. The line efficiency is the total task time divided by the stations times the cycle time, 5.0/(4 × 1.50) = 83.33 percent. Station 4 carries the idle time.

Answer: 83.33 percent

(d)

The lower bound on the cycle time with four stations is the total work divided by four, 5.0/4 = 1.25 min, and it is also at least the longest task, 0.9 min. Because precedence restricts which tasks may sit together, the bound may not be reachable. Enumerating every allocation of the eight tasks to four ordered stations in which no task precedes its own predecessor, and keeping the one with the smallest largest-station load, gives a best cycle time of 1.40 min with the layout station 1: A+B (1.4 min); station 2: C+D (1.2 min); station 3: E+F (1.3 min); station 4: G+H (1.1 min). The corresponding output is 60/1.40 = 42.9 units per hour, or 321 units in 450 productive minutes. That is 21 more units per shift than the 300 required, so the line has spare capacity.

Answer: 1.40 min

Problem 4 [A4-049] Static failure theories for ductile materials

A transmission shaft of ductile steel with yield strength S_y = 420 MPa carries a combination of bending and torsion. At the critical surface point the bending stress is σ_x = 180 MPa and the torsional shear stress is τ_xy = 75 MPa, with no other stress components. The design was checked against yielding with a target safety factor of 1.5. During commissioning the driven machine is found to impose a torque 40 percent higher than the design value, while the bending moment is unchanged. The maintenance engineer asks whether the shaft still meets the target, how much more torque the shaft could tolerate before the safety factor under the distortion energy theory drops to 1.2, and why the two common yield theories do not agree on the margin.

  1. (a) Find the safety factor against yielding in the original design using the distortion energy (von Mises) theory. [5]
  2. (b) Find the safety factor against yielding using the maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory. [4]
  3. (c) Find the von Mises safety factor after the torque rises 40 percent, and state whether the target of 1.5 is still met. [4]
  4. (d) Find the factor by which the original torque could be multiplied before the von Mises safety factor falls to 1.2. [4]
  5. (e) Explain why the Tresca and von Mises results differ and which should be used for design. [3]
(a)

For plane stress with σ_y = 0 the von Mises equivalent stress is σ' = √(σ_x² + 3τ_xy²). Substituting, σ_x² = 180² = 32400 and 3τ² = 3 × 75² = 16875, so σ' = √(32400 + 16875) = √49275 = 222.0 MPa. The yield criterion is σ' = S_y, so the safety factor is n = S_y/σ' = 420/222.0 = 1.892. This exceeds the target of 1.5, so the original design is acceptable under this theory. The distortion energy theory is the closest match to experimental yield data for ductile metals, so it is the preferred basis for a safety-factor check, and it is the value used in the what-if analysis that follows.

Answer: 1.892

(b)

First find the principal stresses. With σ_y = 0, σ1,2 = σ_x/2 ± √((σ_x/2)² + τ²) = 90 ± √(90² + 75²) = 90 ± √13725 = 90 ± 117.15 MPa. So σ1 = 207.15 MPa, σ2 = -27.15 MPa and σ3 = 0. Because σ1 is positive and σ2 is negative, the largest shear is half the difference between them, τ_max = (σ1 − σ2)/2 = 117.15 MPa. Yield by Tresca occurs when τ_max equals S_y/2 = 210 MPa. The safety factor is n = 210/117.15 = 1.793. This is lower than the von Mises value, so Tresca is the more conservative of the two for this stress state.

Answer: 1.793

(c)

A 40 percent rise in torque increases the shear stress in proportion, because shear stress in a round shaft is directly proportional to torque: τ = 1.4 × 75 = 105.0 MPa. The bending stress is unchanged at 180 MPa. The equivalent stress is σ' = √(180² + 3 × 105.0²) = √(32400 + 33075) = 255.9 MPa. The safety factor is n = 420/255.9 = 1.641. This is above the target of 1.5, so the shaft still meets the target, although the margin has been reduced by 13.2 percent. Under Tresca the same check gives 1.519, which is slightly above 1.5 as well, so both theories agree on the verdict here.

Answer: 1.641

(d)

For n = 1.2 the permitted equivalent stress is σ'_max = S_y/1.2 = 420/1.2 = 350 MPa. With the bending stress held at 180 MPa, we require 180² + 3τ² = 350². So 3τ² = 122500 − 32400 = 90100, giving τ² = 30033 and τ = 173.3 MPa. The original shear stress was 75 MPa, so the torque multiplier is 173.3/75 = 2.311. The shaft could therefore carry about 2.31 times the design torque before reaching the limit, though in practice fatigue, not static yielding, would almost certainly govern once the load fluctuates in service.

Answer: 2.311

(e)

The two theories disagree because they use different measures of yielding. Tresca takes the largest shear stress, which is the largest difference between principal stresses, and it ignores the intermediate principal stress. Von Mises uses the distortion energy, which depends on all three principal stresses together, and it plots as a circle around the Tresca hexagon in principal stress space. For pure torsion the von Mises theory predicts yield at 0.577 S_y in shear, whereas Tresca predicts 0.5 S_y, so Tresca can be up to 15 percent more conservative. Tresca is simpler and safe, but von Mises is closer to test data. In this case the factors are 1.89 and 1.79, a difference of about 6 percent. For routine design where the cost of conservatism is small, either is acceptable.

Answer: See working

Problem 5 [A4-050] Fatigue: endurance limit and Marin factors

A rotating solid steel shaft of 40 mm diameter, with ultimate tensile strength S_ut = 690 MPa, is machined to final size and carries a fully reversed bending load. The designer estimates the endurance limit using the Marin equation S_e = k_a k_b k_c k_d k_e S_e', with S_e' = 0.5 S_ut for rotating-beam specimens. Surface factor k_a = a S_utb, with a = 4.51 and b = −0.265 for machined and a = 1.58 and b = −0.085 for ground surfaces (S_ut in MPa). Size factor for a rotating round, 2.79 to 51 mm diameter, k_b = 1.24 d−0.107 with d in mm. Loading factor k_c = 1, reliability factor k_e = 0.814 (99 percent reliability), and k_d = 1 at room temperature. The shaft is to run in a hot process area where the shaft temperature is about 250 degrees C, and the assigned value there is k_d = 0.90. The service stress amplitude is 150 MPa.

  1. (a) Find the corrected endurance limit for the machined shaft at room temperature. [6]
  2. (b) Find the endurance limit if the shaft is ground instead of machined. [4]
  3. (c) Find the endurance limit of the machined shaft in the hot service conditions. [3]
  4. (d) Find the fatigue safety factor in hot service at a stress amplitude of 150 MPa, and say whether infinite life is expected. [4]
  5. (e) Recommend how to restore a fatigue safety factor of at least 1.2 in the hot service, and justify the choice with a figure from the calculations. [3]
(a)

Start with the uncorrected limit S_e' = 0.5 × 690 = 345 MPa. The surface factor for a machined finish is k_a = 4.51 × 690−0.265. Since ln 690 = 6.5367, the exponent term is −0.265 × 6.5367 = -1.7322, so 690−0.265 = 0.1769 and k_a = 0.7978. For d = 40 mm, k_b = 1.24 × 40−0.107 = 1.24 × 0.6739 = 0.8356. With k_c = k_d = 1 and k_e = 0.814, S_e = 0.7978 × 0.8356 × 1 × 1 × 0.814 × 345 = 187.2 MPa. The shaft endurance limit is therefore only about 54 percent of the specimen value, showing how much the real conditions reduce the allowable alternating stress.

Answer: 187.2 MPa

(b)

Only the surface factor changes. For a ground surface, k_a = 1.58 × 690−0.085. The exponent term is −0.085 × 6.5367 = -0.5556, so 690−0.085 = 0.5737 and k_a = 1.58 × 0.5737 = 0.9065. All other factors are unchanged: k_b = 0.8356, k_e = 0.814 and the base limit is 345 MPa. Therefore S_e = 0.9065 × 0.8356 × 0.814 × 345 = 212.7 MPa. Grinding raises the endurance limit by 13.6 percent relative to the machined value from part (a), because the finer surface leaves fewer micro-notches to start a crack. The improvement is substantial for a modest finishing cost.

Answer: 212.7 MPa

(c)

The temperature factor now drops from 1.00 to k_d = 0.90, while every other Marin factor stays as in part (a). The endurance limit scales directly with k_d, so S_e,hot = 0.90 × 187.2 = 168.5 MPa. Equivalently, multiplying all factors, 0.7978 × 0.8356 × 0.90 × 0.814 × 345 gives the same 168.5 MPa. The temperature effect removes 10 percent of the fatigue strength, a loss of 18.7 MPa, before any other consequence of heat such as reduced yield strength or oxidation of the surface. Such hot-environment reductions are often found by direct test data, but a simple factor suits the exam.

Answer: 168.5 MPa

(d)

For fully reversed loading, the safety factor against fatigue failure at infinite life is the endurance limit divided by the stress amplitude: n = S_e/σ_a. In the hot service, n = 168.5/150 = 1.123. The value is above 1.0, so infinite life is just predicted, but with a thin margin below 1.2. For comparison, the same stress amplitude gives n = 187.2/150 = 1.248 at room temperature, and 1.418 with the ground finish at room temperature. Hence the hot condition alone cuts the margin from 1.25 to 1.12, and a hot-service design must be checked with the proper temperature factor.

Answer: 1.123

(e)

The required endurance limit is at least 150 MPa, and with a margin of 1.2, the target is 180 MPa. Grinding alone gives 191.4 MPa in hot service (the ground endurance limit 212.7 multiplied by 0.90), which exceeds the 180 MPa target and gives a safety factor of 191.4/150 = 1.28, above 1.2. Grinding alone therefore restores the required margin without changing the shaft diameter, and keeping the shaft cooler, if possible, adds further margin.

Answer: See working

A4 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A4-051] Fatigue design with Goodman or Gerber

A ground steel flat bar of rectangular section, 30 mm wide and 8 mm thick, is used as a cantilever flexure in a test rig. The bending moment at the critical section, about the axis that gives the 8 mm thickness as depth, cycles between 20 N·m and 60 N·m at constant amplitude. The bar has ultimate tensile strength 620 MPa, and the fully corrected endurance limit, including surface, size and load factors, has been found to be 190 MPa. Stress concentration at the section is negligible. Several bars cracked in service after far fewer cycles than the design predicted, and an instrumented test then showed that the moment actually varied between −60 N·m and +60 N·m rather than between 20 N·m and 60 N·m. Use the modified Goodman criterion throughout and treat the stress ratio as fixed in part (c).

  1. (a) Find the fatigue factor of safety for the intended loading of 20 N·m to 60 N·m. [6]
  2. (b) Find the factor of safety for the loading that was actually measured, −60 N·m to +60 N·m, and say what it predicts. [6]
  3. (c) Keeping the intended stress ratio R = σmin/σmax, find the largest peak bending moment that still gives a Goodman factor of safety of 1.5. [8]
(a)

Section modulus Z = b h²/6 = 0.030 × 0.008² / 6 = 320.0 mm³ (3.200 × 10⁻⁷ m³). Peak stress σmax = 60 / Z = 187.5 MPa and minimum stress σmin = 20 / Z = 62.5 MPa. Alternating stress σa = (σmax − σmin)/2 = 62.5 MPa and mean stress σm = (σmax + σmin)/2 = 125.0 MPa. The modified Goodman line gives 1/n = σa/Se + σm/Su = 62.5/190 + 125.0/620 = 0.3289 + 0.2016 = 0.5306. Hence n = 1.885. The bar is safe for infinite life on paper, with a margin of about 89 percent in the load, because the mean stress is moderate compared with the ultimate strength.
