The method rewards stating that the stresses are computed at the outer fibre, that the load is assumed in phase, and that Goodman is conservative for this ductile material.

Answer: 1.885

(b)

For fully reversed bending the mean stress is zero and the alternating stress equals the peak stress. Peak stress is σmax = 60 / Z = 187.5 MPa, so σa = 187.5 MPa and σm = 0. The modified Goodman relation reduces to the endurance limit check, 1/n = σa/Se = 187.5/190. Therefore n = 190 / 187.5 = 1.013. A factor this close to 1 means the bar sits right on the endurance limit, so any scatter in material strength, a scratch, or a small overload gives a finite-life fatigue failure. This explains the early cracks: the design was checked against a much milder cycle. Although the maximum moment is unchanged, the loss of the positive mean shift raises the alternating stress from 62.5 MPa to 187.5 MPa, and alternating stress is the controlling quantity in fatigue.

Answer: 1.013

(c)

The stress ratio is R = σmin/σmax = 20/60 = 0.3333. For any peak stress σmax at this ratio, σa = σmax(1 − R)/2 = 0.3333 σmax and σm = σmax(1 + R)/2 = 0.6667 σmax. Goodman with n = 1.5 gives 1/1.5 = σmax [ 0.3333/190 + 0.6667/620 ] = σmax × 0.002830. Solving, σmax = 235.6 MPa. The moment follows from M = σmax Z = 235.6 × 10⁶ × 3.200 × 10⁻⁷ = 75.4 N·m. This is about 26 percent above the original 60 N·m, showing the original design carried spare capacity. The answer holds only while the load ratio stays at 1/3, as part (b) showed.

Answer: 75.4 N·m

Problem 2 [A4-052] Stress concentration

A 6 mm thick, 80 mm wide steel tie plate carries a tensile load through a drilled circular hole near its centreline, used for a pin connection in a conveyor frame. The first design has a 16 mm hole, and the plate carries 30 kN. For a central hole in a finite-width plate in tension, the theoretical stress concentration factor based on net-section nominal stress is Kt = 3.00 − 3.14(d/w) + 3.667(d/w)² − 1.527(d/w)³, where d is the hole diameter and w the plate width. Maintenance asks whether the hole can be enlarged to 24 mm to take a bigger pin, arguing that a larger hole must be far worse. The material notch sensitivity at the hole radius of the 16 mm hole is q = 0.85, and the corrected endurance limit of the plate is 190 MPa.

  1. (a) Find the peak elastic stress at the edge of the 16 mm hole under the 30 kN static load. [5]
  2. (b) Find the percentage change in peak elastic stress if the hole is enlarged to 24 mm at the same 30 kN load. [7]
  3. (c) For fully reversed axial loading of ±30 kN on the 16 mm hole, find the fatigue factor of safety. [8]
(a)

Net-section area A = (w − d) t = (0.080 − 0.016) × 0.006 = 384 mm². Nominal stress σnom = P/A = 30 000 / 384 = 78.12 MPa. The diameter ratio is d/w = 0.016/0.080 = 0.200, so Kt = 3.00 − 3.14(0.200) + 3.667(0.200)² − 1.527(0.200)³ = 3.00 − 0.628 + 0.1467 − 0.0122 = 2.506. The peak stress is σmax = Kt σnom = 2.506 × 78.12 = 195.8 MPa. Assumptions are linear elastic behaviour, a uniform stress field away from the hole, and a plate thin enough for plane stress. This is the stress a marker expects to see compared with the yield strength when judging a static design, and for ductile steel the local peak is relieved by yielding under static load.

Answer: 195.8 MPa

(b)

For the 24 mm hole, d/w = 0.300, so Kt = 3.00 − 3.14(0.300) + 3.667(0.300)² − 1.527(0.300)³ = 3.00 − 0.942 + 0.3300 − 0.0412 = 2.347. The net area becomes (0.080 − 0.024) × 0.006 = 336 mm², so σnom = 30 000 / 336 = 89.29 MPa. The peak stress is 2.347 × 89.29 = 209.5 MPa. Compared with 195.8 MPa for the 16 mm hole, the change is (209.5/195.8) − 1 = 7.01 percent. The surprise is that Kt falls from 2.506 to 2.347 because the hole is relatively larger compared with the width, but the net-section nominal stress rises by 14 percent, and the product rises only about 7 percent. So maintenance is partly right about direction but wrong about size.

Answer: 7.01 percent

(c)

The fatigue stress concentration factor is Kf = 1 + q(Kt − 1) = 1 + 0.85 × (2.506 − 1) = 2.280. Fatigue stress concentration is applied to the alternating component, and since the loading is fully reversed the mean stress is zero. The nominal alternating stress is σa,nom = 78.12 MPa, so the effective alternating stress is Kf σa,nom = 2.280 × 78.12 = 178.2 MPa. The factor of safety is n = Se / (Kf σa,nom) = 190 / 178.2 = 1.066. This is only slightly above 1, so the connection has almost no fatigue margin even though the static check looks comfortable. Using Kt instead of Kf would have been too conservative, giving 0.97, because the notch is not fully effective in reducing fatigue strength at this hole radius.

Answer: 1.066

Problem 3 [A4-053] Bolted joints preload and joint stiffness

A gearbox end cover is held by M12 coarse-thread bolts with a tensile stress area of 84.3 mm² and a proof strength of 600 MPa. The bolt steel has E = 207 GPa and the effective stretched length of each bolt is 46 mm. The clamped cast members have an effective stiffness of 1.2 GN/m per bolt. The bolts are tightened to 75 percent of proof load, and in service each bolt sees a steady external tensile load of 14 kN from internal pressure. During a rebuild a fitter replaces the metal-to-metal joint with a soft fibre gasket in the stack, which reduces the effective member stiffness to 0.4 GN/m. The preload is re-applied to the same 75 percent of proof value. The designer wants to know what the gasket does to bolt loading and to the risk of the cover lifting off the housing.

  1. (a) With the original joint, find the bolt load in service. [5]
  2. (b) With the original joint, find the load factor against separation of the joint faces. [5]
  3. (c) With the gasket joint, find the bolt load in service. [5]
  4. (d) With the gasket joint, find the load factor against separation, and state whether the gasket has made leakage more or less likely. [5]
(a)

Bolt stiffness kb = At E / l = 84.3×10⁻⁶ × 207×10⁹ / 0.046 = 379.4 MN/m. The joint constant is C = kb/(kb + km) = 379.4/(379.4 + 1200) = 0.2402. Preload Fi = 0.75 × Sp × At = 0.75 × 600×10⁶ × 84.3×10⁻⁶ = 37935 N. The external load P = 14 000 N is shared, with the bolt taking the fraction C and the members relaxing by the fraction (1 − C). The bolt load is Fb = Fi + C P = 37935 + 0.2402 × 14 000 = 41300 N. The bolt therefore sees only 3363 N more than the preload, because the stiff members give up most of their clamp force. This is why a stiff clamped joint is desirable.

Answer: 41300 N

(b)

Separation occurs when the member compression drops to zero, which happens when the external load reaches Fi/(1 − C). The clamp force at working load is Fm = Fi − (1 − C) P = 37935 − 0.7598 × 14 000 = 27298 N, which is still strongly positive. The load factor against separation is n0 = Fi / [(1 − C) P] = 37935 / (0.7598 × 14 000) = 3.57. This means the external load could rise to about 3.6 times the actual 14 kN before the faces open and leak. The result relies on the assumptions of a linear joint, a load applied at the clamped faces, and no thermal change in preload. A marker also expects the comment that the value is well above the usual 2 to 3 design range.

Answer: 3.57

(c)

The same bolt stiffness 379.4 MN/m is used, but the softer members give C = kb/(kb + km) = 379.4/(379.4 + 400) = 0.4868. The preload is unchanged at Fi = 37935 N, as it is 75 percent of proof for the same bolt. The bolt load is Fb = Fi + C P = 37935 + 0.4868 × 14 000 = 44750 N. Compared with part (a), the bolt carries 3452 N more, an increase of 8.4 percent. The softer gasket lets the members spring back faster, so a larger share of the external load goes into stretching the bolt, and a larger alternating bolt stress would follow if the load were cyclic. The bolt stress now is 531 MPa against a proof strength of 600 MPa, still acceptable for static service.

Answer: 44750 N

(d)

The load factor is n0 = Fi / [(1 − C) P] = 37935 / (0.5132 × 14 000) = 5.28. Compared with 3.57 for the original joint, the margin against separation has increased by 48 percent. The soft member takes a smaller share of the external load (1 − C = 0.513 instead of 0.760), so the bolt takes more, and the clamp force falls more slowly as the external load grows, so the faces stay together longer. Leakage by gross separation is therefore less likely with the gasket. The cost is the higher bolt load found in part (c). This trade, a higher bolt load for a larger separation margin, is the reason designers choose soft gaskets for sealing and stiff joints for fatigue.

Answer: 5.28

Problem 4 [A4-054] Bolted joints under fatigue loading

The head of a reciprocating compressor is clamped by M10 bolts with a tensile stress area of 58 mm², proof strength 600 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 830 MPa and a fully corrected endurance limit of 130 MPa for the rolled threads. The gas load on each bolt cycles from zero to 9 kN at every revolution, and the joint constant is C = 0.25. The bolts are tightened to a preload of 30 kN. After repeated bolt fatigue concerns a technician proposes halving the preload to 15 kN, arguing that a lower mean stress must help fatigue life. Use the Goodman line for a bolt with preload, in which the mean stress is the alternating stress plus the preload stress, and the fatigue factor of safety is nf = Se(Sut − σi) / [Sut σa + Se(σm − σi)], where σi is the preload stress.

  1. (a) Find the fatigue factor of safety with the 30 kN preload. [6]
  2. (b) Find the fatigue factor of safety with the 15 kN preload, and judge the technician's argument. [6]
  3. (c) Find the load factor against joint separation with the 15 kN preload, and compare it with the 30 kN preload. [4]
  4. (d) Find the smallest preload that gives a separation load factor of 2.0 at the 9 kN peak load. [4]
(a)

Preload stress σi = Fi/At = 30 000 / 58 = 517.2 MPa, which is 86 percent of proof strength, high (above the usual 75 percent of proof guideline) though below proof. The alternating stress is σa = C P / (2 At) = 0.25 × 9000 / (2 × 58) = 19.40 MPa. The mean stress is σm = σa + σi = 19.40 + 517.2 = 536.6 MPa. Substituting into the given expression, nf = 130 × (830 − 517.2) / [830 × 19.40 + 130 × (536.6 − 517.2)] = 40659 / 18621 = 2.184. The denominator reduces to (Sut + Se)σa because σm − σi = σa. A factor of safety above 2 is adequate for a bolted pressure joint at this strength grade.

Answer: 2.184

(b)

With Fi = 15 000 N, σi = 15 000 / 58 = 258.6 MPa. The alternating stress is unchanged at 19.40 MPa because it depends only on C, P and At. The mean stress is 278.0 MPa. Then nf = 130 × (830 − 258.6) / [830 × 19.40 + 130 × (278.0 − 258.6)] = 74279 / 18621 = 3.989. So the fatigue factor does rise, from 2.18 to 3.99, and the technician is correct on that single measure. The reason is that the lower preload stress leaves a larger Sut − σi in the numerator (74279 against 40659), while the alternating stress and the denominator are unchanged. The argument is incomplete, though, because fatigue is not the only requirement of a pressure joint; separation must also be checked, as the next part shows.

Answer: 3.989

(c)

The load factor against separation is n0 = Fi / [(1 − C) P]. For the 15 kN preload, n0 = 15 000 / (0.75 × 9000) = 2.22. For the original 30 kN preload, n0 = 30 000 / 6750 = 4.44. Halving the preload halves the margin against the faces opening, so although the fatigue factor improved, the joint is closer to leaking. A load factor of 2.2 would usually be considered thin for a gas joint with pulsating pressure, because pressure spikes, thermal relaxation and embedment all reduce the preload in service, and once the faces separate the bolt sees the full external load, which sharply cuts fatigue life.

Answer: 2.22

(d)

Setting the separation load factor to the required value, n0 = Fi / [(1 − C) P] = 2.0, and rearranging gives Fi = 2.0 × (1 − C) × P = 2.0 × 0.75 × 9000 = 13500 N. This is 45 percent of the original 30 kN preload. At this minimum the fatigue factor would be higher than for 30 kN, because the mean stress is lower. In practice a designer would choose a preload somewhat above this minimum, between about 13.5 kN and 30 kN, to cover relaxation and tool scatter, a range in which both the fatigue and the separation requirements are met. The proof limit of 0.75 × 600 × 58 = 26 100 N shows that the original 30 kN was actually above the usual 75 percent proof guideline.

Answer: 13500 N

Problem 5 [A4-055] Welded joints

A steel bracket is attached to a column face by two parallel vertical fillet welds, each 120 mm long, spaced 80 mm apart, with equal legs of 6 mm. A downward load of 20 kN acts in the plane of the welds on a lug whose line of action is 150 mm horizontally from the centroid of the weld group. Treat the welds as lines, with throat thickness 0.707 times the leg, and combine the direct shear with the shear due to the moment about the group centroid. The allowable shear stress for the weld metal is 110 MPa. Examine the end point of a weld where the direct and moment shear components in the load direction add. A designer asks whether spreading the two welds to 120 mm apart would help, and what leg size the original layout needs for a factor of safety of 1.5.

  1. (a) Find the maximum resultant shear stress in the weld for the original layout. [6]
  2. (b) Find the maximum resultant shear stress if the welds are spaced 120 mm apart with the same leg and length. [7]
  3. (c) For the original layout, find the leg size needed for a factor of safety of 1.5 against the 110 MPa allowable stress. [7]
(a)

Throat a = 0.707 × 6 = 4.242 mm. Weld area A = 2 d a = 2 × 120 × 4.242 = 1018 mm². Direct shear τ' = F/A = 20 000 / 1018 = 19.64 MPa. The unit polar moment for two parallel lines is Ju = d(d² + 3b²)/6 = 120(14 400 + 19 200)/6 = 672000 mm³, and J = a Ju = 2850624 mm⁴. The moment is M = F e = 20 000 × 150 = 3.0×10⁶ N·mm. At the critical end point the offsets are x = 40 mm and y = 60 mm. The moment shear components are τx = M y / J = 63.14 MPa and τy = M x / J = 42.10 MPa. Adding the direct shear to τy gives 61.74 MPa. The resultant is √(63.14² + 61.74²) = 88.3 MPa.

Answer: 88.3 MPa

(b)

The area and direct shear are unchanged: A = 1018 mm² and τ' = 19.64 MPa. With b = 120 mm, Ju = 120(14 400 + 3 × 14 400)/6 = 1152000 mm³ and J = 4886784 mm⁴. The critical end point is now at x = 60 mm and y = 60 mm. The moment shear components are τx = M y / J = 3.0×10⁶ × 60 / 4886784 = 36.83 MPa and τy = M x / J = 36.83 MPa. The y component with the direct shear added is 56.48 MPa. The resultant is √(36.83² + 56.48²) = 67.4 MPa. Spreading the welds therefore reduces the peak stress from 88.3 to 67.4 MPa, a reduction of 24 percent, because the larger spacing greatly raises the polar moment, while the farther corner distance raises the lever arm only moderately.

Answer: 67.4 MPa

(c)

Both weld area and polar moment scale directly with throat thickness, so all stress components scale as 1/h for a fixed geometry. The present peak stress is 88.3 MPa at h = 6 mm, a factor of safety of 1.25 against 110 MPa. The required peak stress for n = 1.5 is 110 / 1.5 = 73.3 MPa. The leg size needed is h = 6 × 88.3 / 73.3 = 7.23 mm. A designer would round up to a standard leg of 8 mm. The 6 mm weld gives a factor of safety below 1.5, so it would not satisfy the stated requirement. Increasing the leg size is less efficient than spreading the welds, since the weld volume grows as h² while stress falls only as 1/h.

Answer: 7.23 mm

A4 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A4-056] Helical compression springs

A valve return spring in a pneumatic actuator is a helical compression spring made of 3.0 mm music wire with a mean coil diameter of 24 mm and 8 active coils. The shear modulus of the wire is 79.3 GPa. The spring is loaded to 150 N at full valve opening. The Wahl factor, K = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C with spring index C = D/d, is used to account for curvature and direct shear. A supplier proposes substituting 3.2 mm wire, keeping the mean coil diameter and the number of active coils the same, because 3.0 mm wire is out of stock. The engineer wants the effect on spring rate, stress and deflection quantified before approving, since the actuator stroke is set by the spring deflection under the 150 N load.

  1. (a) Find the spring rate of the original spring. [5]
  2. (b) Find the maximum shear stress in the original spring at 150 N. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum shear stress at 150 N for the 3.2 mm substitute wire. [5]
  4. (d) Find the percentage reduction in deflection under 150 N when the 3.2 mm wire is substituted. [5]
(a)

The spring rate of a helical compression spring is k = G d⁴ / (8 D³ Na). Substituting d = 3.0×10⁻³ m, D = 24×10⁻³ m, Na = 8 and G = 79.3×10⁹ Pa gives the numerator G d⁴ = 79.3×10⁹ × (3.0×10⁻³)⁴ = 6.4233 N·m². The denominator is 8 D³ Na = 8 × (0.024)³ × 8 = 8.8474 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Hence k = 7260 N/m = 7.260 N/mm. The deflection under 150 N is y = F/k = 150 / 7260 = 20.7 mm. The assumptions are small deflections, ends that do not alter the active coil count, and a spring that does not buckle. The stroke is therefore about 21 mm for the original wire.

Answer: 7.260 N/mm

(b)

Spring index C = D/d = 24/3.0 = 8.0. The Wahl factor is K = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C = (4×8 − 1)/(4×8 − 4) + 0.615/8 = 1.1071 + 0.0769 = 1.1840. The corrected shear stress is τ = K × 8 F D / (π d³) = 1.1840 × 8 × 150 × 0.024 / (π × (0.003)³) = 1.1840 × 339.5 MPa = 402 MPa. This is the stress at the inner surface of the coil, where curvature raises the shear. For music wire, whose tensile strength at this size is roughly 2000 MPa, a shear stress near 400 MPa is a low fraction of the static limit, though fatigue duty would need a separate check.

Answer: 402 MPa

(c)

For d = 3.2 mm, the spring index is C = 24/3.2 = 7.50. The Wahl factor is K = (4×7.50 − 1)/(4×7.50 − 4) + 0.615/7.50 = 1.1154 + 0.0820 = 1.1974. The basic stress is 8 F D / (π d³) = 8 × 150 × 0.024 / (π × (0.0032)³) = 279.8 MPa. Multiplying by the Wahl factor gives τ = 1.1974 × 279.8 = 335 MPa. This is 16.7 percent lower than the original wire, because the stress falls with the cube of the wire diameter, with a small offset from the slightly lower Wahl factor at the lower index. The spring is therefore less highly stressed, a benefit for fatigue life.

Answer: 335 MPa

(d)

Spring rate scales with d⁴ when D, Na and G are fixed. The rate of the substitute spring is k₂ = k₁ (3.2/3.0)⁴ = 7.260 × 1.2945 = 9.399 N/mm. The deflection under 150 N is y₂ = 150 / 9399 = 15.96 mm, compared with y₁ = 20.66 mm. The reduction is (1 − k₁/k₂) × 100 = (1 − 1/1.2945) × 100 = 22.8 percent. So the valve would open 4.7 mm less, at the same force. If the actuator stroke is fixed by the spring deflection, the substitution changes the stroke or the force needed, and it should not be approved without checking, because a 6.7 percent change in wire diameter gives a 29 percent change in rate.

Answer: 22.8 percent

Problem 2 [A4-057] Shaft design under combined loading

A solid steel shaft of yield strength 420 MPa carries a helical gear mounted between two bearings. At the critical section the resultant bending moment is 420 N·m, and the shaft transmits 48.7 kW at 1500 rpm. The shaft rotates, but for this first check the stresses are treated as steady, and the distortion energy theory is used for the static factor of safety, with a design factor of 2.0. Stress concentration at the shoulder is ignored for this static check. The plant plans to raise the machine output, and the engineer is asked what happens if the transmitted torque doubles at the same bending moment. The stock size available in the store is a 32 mm diameter bar, and the engineer wants to know whether it remains acceptable before and after the upgrade.

  1. (a) Find the minimum shaft diameter for a factor of safety of 2.0 at the present duty. [7]
  2. (b) Find the factor of safety of a 32 mm diameter shaft at the present duty. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum diameter if the torque doubles with the same bending moment. [4]
  4. (d) Find the factor of safety of the 32 mm diameter shaft after the torque doubles, and state whether it still meets the design factor of 2.0. [4]
(a)

Torque T = P / ω = 48 700 / (2π × 1500 / 60) = 48 700 / 157.08 = 310.0 N·m. For a solid shaft the bending stress is σ = 32M/(πd³) and the torsional shear is τ = 16T/(πd³). The von Mises stress is σ' = √(σ² + 3τ²) = (32/(πd³)) √(M² + 0.75T²). Setting σ' = Sy/n gives d³ = (32 n / (π Sy)) √(M² + 0.75T²). The root is √(420² + 0.75 × 310.0²) = 498.5 N·m. Then d³ = 32 × 2 / (π × 420×10⁶) × 498.5 = 2.4188 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so d = 28.92 mm. A designer would round up to a stock size. This is a conservative static estimate since fatigue from the rotating bending is not included.

Answer: 28.920 mm

(b)

For d = 0.032 m, d³ = 3.2768 × 10⁻⁵ m³. The equivalent moment is √(M² + 0.75T²) = 498.5 N·m. The von Mises stress is σ' = 32 × 498.5 / (π × 3.2768 × 10⁻⁵) = 155.0 MPa. The factor of safety is n = Sy / σ' = 420 / 155.0 = 2.710. Equivalently n = π d³ Sy / (32 √(M² + 0.75T²)). The factor is well above the required 2.0, as expected since 32 mm exceeds the minimum diameter from part (a). The margin is 36 percent over the design target, which is useful because the real shaft will also meet stress concentration and fatigue loading.

Answer: 2.710

(c)

The doubled torque is T = 620.1 N·m. The equivalent moment becomes √(420² + 0.75 × 620.1²) = 681.7 N·m. Using the same relation as before, d³ = 32 × 2 / (π × 420×10⁶) × 681.7 = 3.3076 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so d = 32.10 mm. This is 3.18 mm larger than at the present duty, a 11.0 percent increase, even though torque doubled. The diameter is a cube-root function of the equivalent moment, and the bending moment still contributes, so doubling torque does not double the diameter. The result is very close to the 32 mm stock bar, so the margin is thin.

Answer: 32.100 mm

(d)

The equivalent moment is 681.7 N·m, as in part (c). The factor of safety is n = π d³ Sy / (32 × 681.7) = π × 3.2768 × 10⁻⁵ × 420×10⁶ / (21815.5) = 1.982. This is below the required 2.0 by about 0.9 percent, so the 32 mm bar no longer meets the stated design factor, though it still has no yielding at the working load (n > 1). The engineer should either specify a 34 mm or 35 mm shaft for the upgrade, or accept a lower design factor with a proper fatigue analysis. The small shortfall shows why the stock size should be compared with the calculated diameter, not just rounded.

Answer: 1.982

Problem 3 [A4-058] Rolling bearing selection and life

A deep-groove ball bearing with a basic dynamic load rating of 32.5 kN supports the output shaft of a conveyor gearbox. The load is purely radial, so the equivalent dynamic load equals the radial load. In the original duty the radial load is 4.2 kN and the shaft turns at 1450 rpm. After a production increase the line speed is raised so the shaft turns at 1800 rpm, and the radial load rises to 5.0 kN. Maintenance finds the bearing now fails much earlier than the old service interval and asks for an explanation and a replacement. Use the standard ball bearing life relation, with life in millions of revolutions equal to the cube of the rating-to-load ratio, and calculate life at 90 percent reliability. The replacement must give at least 8000 hours at the new duty.

  1. (a) Find the L10 life in hours under the original duty. [6]
  2. (b) Find the L10 life in hours under the new duty of 5.0 kN at 1800 rpm, and the factor by which the life has fallen. [6]
  3. (c) Find the minimum basic dynamic load rating of a replacement bearing for an L10 life of 8000 hours at the new duty. [8]
(a)

For a ball bearing the basic rating life is L10 = (C/P)³ million revolutions, where C is the dynamic rating and P the equivalent load. With C = 32.5 kN and P = 4.2 kN, C/P = 7.738, so L10 = 7.738³ = 463.3 million revolutions. Converting to hours at 1450 rpm, the revolutions per hour are 60 × 1450 = 87 000, so L10h = 4.633 × 10⁸ / 87 000 = 5326 h. This life is exceeded by 90 percent of a large group of identical bearings, so any one bearing may fail earlier or later. The assumptions are a steady load, normal lubrication, no misalignment, and no life modification factors. The result is about 0.6 years of continuous running.

Answer: 5326 h

(b)

Under the new duty C/P = 32.5 / 5.0 = 6.50, so L10 = 6.50³ = 274.6 million revolutions. At 1800 rpm the revolutions per hour are 60 × 1800 = 108 000, so L10h = 2.746 × 10⁸ / 108 000 = 2543 h. Compared with 5326 h before, life has fallen by a factor of 2.09, or 52 percent. Two effects combine: the load rise of 19 percent cuts revolution life by the cube of the ratio, giving a factor of 1.69, and the speed rise of 24 percent consumes the revolutions faster, a further factor of 1.24. This explains the early failures.

Answer: 2543 h

(c)

The required life in millions of revolutions is L = 60 n Lh / 10⁶ = 60 × 1800 × 8000 / 10⁶ = 864 million revolutions. Rearranging L10 = (C/P)³ gives C = P L1/3. Hence C = 5.0 × 8641/3 = 5.0 × 9.524 = 47.6 kN. The present bearing rating of 32.5 kN is 32 percent too small. A designer would pick the next larger catalogue bearing with a rating above 48 kN, for example a bearing of a larger bore series, and check that it fits the housing and shaft shoulder. Alternatively, a roller bearing, whose life exponent is 10/3 rather than 3, would give a smaller required rating for the same life, but the problem states a ball bearing so the exponent 3 is used.

Answer: 47.6 kN

Problem 4 [A4-059] Journal bearing basics

A lightly loaded oil-lubricated journal bearing supports the rotor of a small centrifugal blower. The journal diameter is 60 mm, the bearing length is 60 mm, the radial clearance is 0.05 mm, the shaft speed is 1800 rpm and the radial load is 3000 N. At the design operating temperature the oil viscosity is 0.025 Pa·s. Treat the journal as concentric and use Petroff's equation for the coefficient of friction, f = 2π² (μN/P)(r/c), where N is the speed in revolutions per second, P the bearing pressure on the projected area and r the journal radius. After a long run the oil overheats and the viscosity falls to 0.012 Pa·s. An alternative remedy proposed by a technician is to remachine the bearing so that the radial clearance doubles to 0.10 mm while the oil stays at the original viscosity.

  1. (a) Find the coefficient of friction at the design condition. [5]
  2. (b) Find the friction power loss at the design condition. [5]
  3. (c) Find the friction power loss after the oil viscosity has fallen to 0.012 Pa·s. [5]
  4. (d) Find the friction power loss if instead the radial clearance is doubled to 0.10 mm with the oil at 0.025 Pa·s. [5]
(a)

The speed is N = 1800 / 60 = 30 rev/s. The projected-area pressure is P = W / (d L) = 3000 / (0.060 × 0.060) = 0.833 MPa. The journal radius is r = 30 mm and the radial clearance is c = 0.05 mm, so r/c = 600. The dimensionless group is μN/P = 0.025 × 30 / 833333 = 9.000 × 10⁻⁷. Petroff's equation gives f = 2π² × 9.000 × 10⁻⁷ × 600 = 19.739 × 5.4000 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.01066. This is a low value, typical of a full-film hydrodynamic bearing. The concentric assumption means that the real eccentric shaft would have somewhat higher friction, but Petroff's value is a standard first estimate.

Answer: 0.01066

(b)

The friction torque is T = f W r = 0.01066 × 3000 × 0.030 = 0.9593 N·m. The angular speed is ω = 2π N = 2π × 30 = 188.50 rad/s. The power lost to viscous shear is H = T ω = 0.9593 × 188.50 = 180.8 W. This heat must be carried away by the oil flow and the housing, otherwise the oil temperature rises and the viscosity falls. The loss is small against a blower drive of several kilowatts, but it is concentrated in a small film volume, so the local temperature rise matters more than the number alone suggests. The calculation assumes a Newtonian oil, laminar flow, and uniform viscosity across the clearance.

Answer: 180.8 W

(c)

In Petroff's equation, the friction coefficient is proportional to viscosity for fixed load, speed and geometry. The new coefficient is f = 0.01066 × (0.012 / 0.025) = 0.00512. The torque becomes T = f W r = 0.00512 × 3000 × 0.030 = 0.4605 N·m, and the power loss is H = T ω = 0.4605 × 188.50 = 86.8 W, which is 52 percent lower than at the design condition. The lower loss looks like good news, but a thinner oil film means a smaller minimum film thickness and lower load capacity, so the risk of metal contact at start-up or shock load rises. Lower friction here signals reduced film strength, not a better bearing.

Answer: 86.8 W

(d)

With the clearance doubled, r/c falls from 600 to 300, so the coefficient of friction halves: f = 2π² × 9.000 × 10⁻⁷ × 300 = 0.00533. The torque is T = 0.00533 × 3000 × 0.030 = 0.4797 N·m, and the power loss is H = T ω = 0.4797 × 188.50 = 90.4 W, exactly half the design value of 180.8 W. The technician's remedy cuts losses by half, a saving of 50 percent, slightly less than the 52 percent from the thinner oil. However, a larger clearance also lowers the bearing's stiffness and damping and lowers the Sommerfeld number, which usually reduces the film thickness ratio and may increase oil flow and vibration. Clearance changes therefore need a full hydrodynamic check, not Petroff's equation alone.

Answer: 90.4 W

Problem 5 [A4-060] Spur and helical gear stress

A 22-tooth cut steel spur pinion of module 4 mm and face width 40 mm transmits 15 kW at 1200 rpm in a packaging machine. Bending stress at the tooth root is estimated from the Lewis equation, σ = Kv Wt / (F m Y), with a Lewis form factor Y = 0.331 for this tooth count, and the velocity factor for cut gears Kv = (6.1 + v)/6.1, with pitch line velocity v in m/s. The allowable bending stress for the gear material is 180 MPa. The machine builder wants to double the pinion speed to 2400 rpm to raise throughput, first at the same power and later at 30 kW once the drive motor is upgraded. The gear geometry is unchanged, and the engineer must check the root bending stress at each stage before approving the upgrade.

  1. (a) Find the root bending stress at the original duty of 15 kW and 1200 rpm. [7]
  2. (b) Find the root bending stress at 2400 rpm with the power unchanged at 15 kW. [6]
  3. (c) Find the factor of safety against the 180 MPa allowable stress at 2400 rpm and 30 kW. [7]
(a)

The pitch diameter is dp = m N = 4 × 22 = 88 mm. The pitch line velocity is v = π dp n / 60 = π × 0.088 × 1200 / 60 = 5.529 m/s. The tangential force is Wt = P / v = 15 000 / 5.529 = 2713 N. The velocity factor is Kv = (6.1 + 5.529) / 6.1 = 1.9064. The Lewis bending stress is σ = Kv Wt / (F m Y) = 1.9064 × 2713 / (0.040 × 0.004 × 0.331) = 5172 / 5.2960 × 10⁻⁵ = 97.7 MPa. The factor of safety against the 180 MPa allowable is 1.84. The Lewis method treats the tooth as a cantilever loaded at the tip, assumes one tooth carries the full load, and uses a factor Kv to cover dynamic effects, so it is a first design estimate.

Answer: 97.7 MPa

(b)

The pitch line velocity doubles to v = π × 0.088 × 2400 / 60 = 11.058 m/s. Because power is fixed, the tangential force halves: Wt = 15 000 / 11.058 = 1356 N. The velocity factor increases to Kv = (6.1 + 11.058) / 6.1 = 2.8129. The root bending stress is σ = 2.8129 × 1356 / (0.040 × 0.004 × 0.331) = 72.0 MPa. This is 26 percent lower than at 1200 rpm, since the halving of the force more than offsets the rise of Kv from 1.906 to 2.813. A higher speed at the same power is therefore easier for bending strength, but the dynamic load and surface durability, which the Lewis method does not cover, become more important.

Answer: 72.0 MPa

(c)

At 2400 rpm the pitch line velocity is 11.058 m/s. With power doubled to 30 kW, the tangential force returns to Wt = 30 000 / 11.058 = 2713 N, the same as the original duty, because force depends on power divided by velocity and both have doubled. The velocity factor is Kv = 2.8129. The root bending stress is σ = 2.8129 × 2713 / (0.040 × 0.004 × 0.331) = 144.1 MPa. The factor of safety is n = 180 / 144.1 = 1.249. This is 32 percent below the original factor of 1.84, entirely from the larger Kv. The margin is thin for a Lewis estimate, so the gear should be rechecked with a fuller method or the face width increased before approving the upgrade.

Answer: 1.25

A4 Practice Paper 13

Problem 1 [A4-061] Clutches

A wet multi-plate clutch in an agricultural tractor power take-off has 6 friction surfaces in contact. Each friction surface is an annulus with inner radius 60 mm and outer radius 100 mm. The lining has a coefficient of friction of 0.08 and the springs apply a total axial force of 2.4 kN. The clutch connects a driver turning at a constant 1500 rev/min to a stationary rotating load of equivalent moment of inertia 1.8 kg·m². During engagement the torque transmitted is constant and equal to the capacity of the clutch. The maintenance crew reports that the clutch grabs harshly, and a colleague suggests that the original design calculation, which assumed a worn-in lining, may be hiding a difference between the two classical pressure assumptions. Treat the friction torque at constant axial force as given by theory only, with no heat flow considered.

  1. (a) Find the torque capacity using the uniform wear assumption. [5]
  2. (b) Find the torque capacity if the clutch is new and uniform pressure applies, and state the percentage by which it exceeds the uniform wear value. [5]
  3. (c) Using the uniform wear torque, find the time for the load to reach the driver speed, and the energy dissipated as heat in the clutch during engagement. [5]
  4. (d) Find the axial spring force that would lengthen the engagement time to 6.0 s, which a technician proposes to remove the harsh grab. State the new torque. [5]
(a)

Under uniform wear the pressure varies inversely with radius, so the mean friction radius is rm = (ro + ri)/2. With ro = 0.100 m and ri = 0.060 m, rm = 0.080 m. The torque capacity is T = N μ F rm, where N is the number of friction surfaces, μ the friction coefficient and F the axial force. Substituting, T = 6 × 0.08 × 2400 × 0.080 = 92.2 N·m. This is the usual design value for a worn-in clutch because wear removes material fastest where pressure and sliding speed are highest, which levels the product of pressure and radius. The assumption gives a conservative torque, since the uniform pressure value is always slightly larger. State the assumption clearly: constant axial force, constant μ, rigid plates.

Answer: 92.2 N·m

(b)

For a new clutch the pressure is taken as uniform over the annulus, so the mean friction radius is rm = (2/3)(ro³ − ri³)/(ro² − ri²). Here ro³ = 0.001000 m³, ri³ = 0.000216 m³, ro² = 0.010 m² and ri² = 0.0036 m². Then rm = (2/3)(0.000784)/(0.0064) = 0.0817 m. The torque is T = N μ F rm = 6 × 0.08 × 2400 × 0.0817 = 94.08 N·m. Compared with the uniform wear torque of 92.2 N·m, the excess is (94.08 − 92.2)/92.2 × 100 = 2.08 %. The small difference shows that the two assumptions do not explain a harsh grab, and the new clutch simply transmits slightly more torque until wear sets in.

Answer: 2.08 %

(c)

The driver speed is ω = 2π × 1500/60 = 157.08 rad/s. With a constant clutch torque T acting on the load alone, the angular acceleration is α = T/I = 92.2/1.8 = 51.2 rad/s², so the engagement time is t = ω/α = 3.068 s. The load kinetic energy gained is ½Iω² = 22207 J. Because the driver keeps its speed, the slip distance exceeds the load rotation: the driver turns through ωt while the load turns through ωt/2. The heat is therefore T × (ωt − ωt/2) = T ω t/2 = 22207 J, which equals the load kinetic energy. The dissipated energy is 22.21 kJ, so half of the energy supplied by the driver is lost as heat.

Answer: 22.21 kJ

(d)

The required engagement time is 6.0 s, so the angular acceleration is α = ω/t = 157.08/6.0 = 26.18 rad/s². The torque needed is T = Iα = 1.8 × 26.18 = 47.1 N·m. Torque is proportional to axial force under the uniform wear assumption, because T = N μ F rm with rm fixed. Therefore F2 = F × T2/T = 2400 × 47.1/92.2 = 1227 N, or 1.227 kN. The torque falls to 47.1 N·m, which is 51 percent of the original, so the grab is softer. The heat generated stays at ½Iω², unchanged, but it is released over a longer time, so the surface temperature rise per second is lower. The clutch must still carry the running torque, so check the load requirement before accepting the lower force.

Answer: 1.227 kN

Problem 2 [A4-062] Brakes

A 1400 kg electric hatchback travels at 100 km/h and brakes to a stop with a constant deceleration of 8.0 m/s² on dry asphalt. The braking system is a four-wheel disc arrangement in which the front axle provides 70 percent of the total braking force, and each front wheel has one ventilated rotor of mass 8.0 kg and specific heat 460 J/(kg·K). Each front caliper holds two pads that clamp the rotor on both faces. The effective friction radius of the pad is 0.120 m and the tyre rolling radius is 0.310 m. The pad friction coefficient is 0.42 when cool. Assume all kinetic energy is converted to heat in the brakes, that the front rotors absorb the energy in proportion to the front braking share, and that no heat leaves the rotor during the stop. After a long mountain descent, the pad coefficient is measured as 0.30 because of fade.

  1. (a) Find the energy absorbed by one front rotor during the stop and the resulting rotor temperature rise. [5]
  2. (b) Find the clamping force required by each caliper (the force on each pad) to give the 8.0 m/s² deceleration when the pads are cool. [6]
  3. (c) With fade (μ = 0.30) and the same clamping force, find the new deceleration of the vehicle assuming the same front and rear braking share. [4]
  4. (d) Find the stopping distance from 100 km/h with fade, and how much longer it is than the cool stopping distance. [5]
(a)

The vehicle speed is v = 100/3.6 = 27.78 m/s. The total kinetic energy is ½mv² = 0.5 × 1400 × 27.78² = 540123 J. The front axle takes 70 percent of the braking, so it absorbs 378086 J, and with two front wheels each rotor takes 189043 J. Assuming no heat is lost during the short stop, the rotor temperature rise is ΔT = E/(m c) = 189043/(8.0 × 460) = 51.4 K. This adiabatic estimate is conservative for a single stop but is the standard first check, because real rotors lose heat by convection only after the stop. A rise of this size is comfortably acceptable for a single hard stop, so thermal limits only matter in repeated braking.

Answer: 51.4 K

(b)

The total braking force needed is m a = 1400 × 8.0 = 11200 N. The front axle supplies 70 percent, giving 7840 N across two wheels, so each front tyre must provide 3920 N at the road. The torque at one front wheel is Fw × rolling radius = 3920 × 0.310 = 1215.2 N·m. A disc with two pads gives torque T = 2 μ F reff, because each pad face contributes μ F at radius reff. Solving for the force, F = T/(2 μ reff) = 1215.2/(2 × 0.42 × 0.120) = 12056 N, or 12.06 kN per pad. This assumes the tyre does not slip, so the deceleration of 8.0 m/s² must lie within the road friction limit, which it does for dry asphalt.

Answer: 12.06 kN

(c)

With the clamping force held at 12056 N, the brake torque is proportional to the pad coefficient. The braking force at every wheel therefore scales by 0.30/0.42 = 0.7143. The same scaling applies to the total retarding force, since the front and rear share does not change. The new deceleration is a2 = 8.0 × 0.7143 = 5.71 m/s². This is a reduction of 28.6 percent from the cool condition. Note that in practice the rear brakes may also fade, but the problem assumes the same proportion, so the whole system degrades equally. The driver would feel a soft pedal and demand more pedal travel or force, which in a hydraulic system means raising the line pressure to recover the lost grip.

Answer: 5.71 m/s²

(d)

The stopping distance for constant deceleration is s = v²/(2a). The cool stopping distance is 48.2 m, using 27.78² divided by 2 × 8.0. With fade, using a = 5.71 m/s², s2 = 27.78²/(2 × 5.71) = 67.5 m. The extra distance is 19.3 m, an increase of 40.0 percent. The distance rises in inverse proportion to μ, so the ratio 0.42/0.30 = 1.40 applies exactly. A driver who allowed for the cool distance would arrive at the end of the cool stopping point still travelling at 14.8 m/s, which is 53 km/h. This illustrates why mountain descents need engine braking and why fade is a safety concern, not just a comfort concern.

Answer: 67.5 m

Problem 3 [A4-063] Belt and chain drives

An open flat-belt drive connects a 7.5 kW induction motor turning at 1440 rev/min to a conveyor head shaft. The motor pulley diameter is 200 mm and the driven pulley diameter is 500 mm, with a centre distance of 900 mm. The belt is reinforced rubber with mass per unit length 0.55 kg/m and a coefficient of friction of 0.30 against the cast-iron pulleys. The belt is allowed a maximum tension of 1800 N in total, including the centrifugal contribution, and is assumed to be on the point of slipping on the smaller pulley. During a wet season the belt surface is contaminated by oil and the friction coefficient falls to 0.18, while the belt tensions are unchanged. Ignore belt thickness, elastic creep and the bending stress in the belt, and use the usual flat-belt friction theory.

  1. (a) Find the belt speed and the angle of wrap on the motor pulley. [4]
  2. (b) Find the centrifugal tension, and the power that the belt can transmit at the maximum tension with μ = 0.30. [6]
  3. (c) Find the maximum power the belt can carry when μ falls to 0.18, and state whether the 7.5 kW load can still be driven without slip. [6]
  4. (d) Find the belt length required for the original drive. [4]
(a)

The belt speed is v = π d N/60 = π × 0.200 × 1440/60 = 15.08 m/s. For an open belt the wrap angle on the small pulley is θ = π − 2 arcsin((D − d)/(2C)), where D and d are the two pulley diameters and C is the centre distance. Substituting D − d = 0.300 m and C = 0.900 m gives sin φ = 0.300/1.800 = 0.1667, so φ = 9.594 degrees. Then θ = 180° − 2 × 9.594° = 160.81 degrees, or 2.8067 rad. The wrap on the larger pulley is greater, so the small pulley governs slipping. The belt speed is well below the 30 m/s typically accepted for rubber flat belts, so a general belt drive is acceptable.

Answer: 160.81 deg

(b)

The centrifugal tension is Tc = m v² = 0.55 × 15.08² = 125.1 N. The maximum tension of 1800 N includes this, so the tight side tension that works against friction is T1 − Tc = 1674.9 N. The belt tension ratio is (T1 − Tc)/(T2 − Tc) = eμθ. With μθ = 0.30 × 2.8067 = 0.8420, the ratio is 2.3210. The effective tension is Te = (T1 − Tc)(1 − e−μθ) = 1674.9 × (1 − 0.4308) = 953.3 N. The power is P = Te v = 953.3 × 15.08 = 14375 W, or 14.38 kW. This exceeds the motor rating of 7.5 kW, so the drive has a margin of 91.7 percent.

Answer: 14.38 kW

(c)

With contamination, μ = 0.18 and the wrap angle is unchanged at 2.8067 rad. The exponent is 0.18 × 2.8067 = 0.5052, giving e−μθ = 0.6034. The tight side tension minus centrifugal tension is still 1674.9 N because the allowable total tension is unchanged. The effective tension is Te = 1674.9 × (1 − 0.6034) = 664.3 N, so P = Te v = 664.3 × 15.08 = 10018 W, or 10.02 kW. This is above the required 7.5 kW, so the belt still carries the load without slipping, but the margin falls from 92 percent to 34 percent. The loss of capacity is 30.3 percent, so cleaning the belt or increasing the wrap with an idler is still advisable.

Answer: 10.02 kW

(d)

For an open belt the length is L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D − d)²/(4C). The terms are as follows. The straight portion is 2 × 0.900 = 1.800 m. The wrap on the pulleys gives π(0.500 + 0.200)/2 = 1.0996 m. The correction for the pulley size difference is (0.300)²/(4 × 0.900) = 0.0250 m. Adding them, L = 1.800 + 1.0996 + 0.0250 = 2.925 m. This formula is the standard approximation for small belt angles and is accurate to a few millimetres here. In practice the manufacturer lists belt lengths in steps, so the nearest standard length is chosen and the centre distance adjusted using the take-up slots to set the tension.

Answer: 2.925 m

Problem 4 [A4-064] Power screws

A square-thread screw jack in a vehicle workshop raises a load of 20 kN. The screw has a mean thread diameter of 36 mm and a single-start lead of 8 mm. The thread coefficient of friction is 0.12. The load rotates relative to a flat thrust collar of mean diameter 55 mm with a collar coefficient of friction of 0.10. The operator turns the handle at the top of the screw and the load is lifted slowly with no inertia effects. The supervisor wants to speed up the jack by replacing the screw with a double-start thread of the same mean diameter and the same thread friction, so that the lead doubles to 16 mm per revolution. The question is whether the faster screw still holds its load without a brake when the handle is released, and what it costs in handle torque.

  1. (a) Find the torque required to raise the 20 kN load with the original screw, including collar friction. [6]
  2. (b) Find the overall efficiency of the jack when raising the load. [3]
  3. (c) Find the torque required to lower the load with the original screw. State whether the screw is self-locking. [5]
  4. (d) For the proposed double-start screw (lead 16 mm), find the thread-only efficiency and state whether it is self-locking. [6]
(a)

The thread torque for a square thread is Tt = (F dm/2)(l + π μ dm)/(π dm − μ l). With dm = 0.036 m, l = 0.008 m and μ = 0.12, π μ dm = 0.01357 m and π dm = 0.11310 m. The numerator is 0.02157 m and the denominator is 0.11214 m, so the ratio is 0.1924. Then Tt = (20000 × 0.036/2) × 0.1924 = 69.3 N·m. The collar torque is Tc = F μc dc/2 = 20000 × 0.10 × 0.055/2 = 55.0 N·m. The total raising torque is 124.3 N·m. Collar friction is a large share here, because a flat thrust collar is a sliding bearing carrying the full load, so its contribution matters when sizing the handle.

Answer: 124.3 N·m

(b)

Efficiency is the useful work per revolution divided by the work input per revolution. The useful work is the load times the lead, F l = 20000 × 0.008 = 160 J. The input work is torque times 2π, so Win = 124.3 × 2π = 781 J. The efficiency is therefore η = 160/781 = 20.5 percent. The thread alone, without the collar, would have an efficiency of 36.8 percent, so collar friction alone cuts about 16.3 percentage points. A low efficiency of this size is the price paid for self-locking, as shown in the next part.

Answer: 20.5 %

(c)

For lowering, the thread torque is Tt,low = (F dm/2)(π μ dm − l)/(π dm + μ l). The numerator is 0.01357 − 0.008 = 0.00557 m and the denominator is 0.11310 + 0.12 × 0.008 = 0.11406 m, so the ratio is 0.0488. Thus Tt,low = 20000 × 0.018 × 0.0488 = 17.6 N·m. Adding the collar torque of 55.0 N·m gives a total lowering torque of 72.6 N·m. Because the thread torque is positive, the thread resists back-driving, so the screw is self-locking. The condition is simply that π μ dm exceeds the lead, which is true here (13.6 mm against 8 mm), and the collar friction increases the margin.

Answer: 72.6 N·m

(d)

With the lead doubled to 16 mm, the raising ratio becomes (l + π μ dm)/(π dm − μ l) = (0.01357 + 0.016)/(0.11310 − 0.12 × 0.016) = 0.2660. The thread torque is Tt2 = 20000 × 0.018 × 0.2660 = 95.8 N·m. The thread efficiency is F l/(2π Tt2) = 20000 × 0.016/(2π × 95.8) = 53.2 percent, up from 36.8 percent. For self-locking the requirement is π μ dm ≥ l. Here 13.6 mm compares with 16 mm, so the condition fails and the thread alone would overhaul, with a back-driving torque of about 7.6 N·m. The collar friction torque of 55 N·m is much larger than that, so the jack as a whole would still hold the load with the handle released, but the thread itself is no longer self-locking and the holding then depends on collar friction alone. A brake or ratchet is therefore still advisable before accepting the speed-up.

Answer: 53.2 %

Problem 5 [A4-065] Material removal: cutting force and power

An orthogonal cutting test is run on a steel tube turned on a lathe. The tool has a rake angle of 10 degrees. The undeformed chip thickness is 0.25 mm and the width of cut is 3.0 mm. The cutting speed is 120 m/min. A dynamometer records a cutting force of 1100 N in the direction of cutting and a thrust force of 420 N normal to it. The measured chip thickness is 0.55 mm. Assume a single shear plane, Merchant's force circle and a constant shear strength on the shear plane. A process engineer wants to know whether a sharper insert with a rake angle of 20 degrees, ground to the same friction angle at the chip-tool interface, would reduce the power drawn by the spindle motor. Ignore the effect of speed on the shear strength and treat the chip as continuous.

  1. (a) Find the chip thickness ratio and the shear plane angle for the test. [4]
  2. (b) Find the average shear stress on the shear plane. [6]
  3. (c) Find the cutting power and the specific cutting energy for the test. [4]
  4. (d) Using Merchant's criterion for the shear angle and the same friction angle, find the cutting force with the 20 degree rake tool at the same feed and width. [6]
(a)

The chip thickness ratio is r = t0/tc = 0.25/0.55 = 0.4545. The shear plane angle follows from tan φ = r cos α/(1 − r sin α) for rake angle α. With α = 10°, cos α = 0.9848 and sin α = 0.1736. The numerator is 0.4545 × 0.9848 = 0.4476. The denominator is 1 − 0.4545 × 0.1736 = 0.9211. Therefore tan φ = 0.4860, so φ = 25.92 degrees. A small ratio r corresponds to a thick chip and a low shear angle, which implies high deformation work. The ratio below 0.5 is common for steel cut at modest speeds, so the measurement looks plausible.

Answer: 25.92 deg

(b)

The shear force along the shear plane is Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ. With Fc = 1100 N, Ft = 420 N, cos φ = 0.8994 and sin φ = 0.4371, Fs = 1100 × 0.8994 − 420 × 0.4371 = 805.8 N. The area of the shear plane is As = t0 w/sin φ = 0.25 × 3.0/0.4371 = 1.716 mm². The shear stress is then τ = Fs/As = 805.8/1.716 = 470 MPa. The units are N per mm², which is MPa directly. This value is typical of a medium carbon steel, which supports the assumption that the shear strength of the work material is constant on the plane and can be carried over to the second tool.

Answer: 470 MPa

(c)

The cutting power is the cutting force times the cutting speed, since the thrust force does no work in orthogonal cutting. The speed is 120 m/min = 2.0 m/s. Therefore P = Fc v = 1100 × 2.0 = 2200 W, or 2.20 kW. The specific cutting energy is the power divided by the volume removal rate. The removal rate is t0 w v = 0.25 × 3.0 × 2000 mm/s = 1500 mm³/s. The specific energy is 1.47 J/mm³, equivalent to 1.47 GJ/m³. This number is useful to size the spindle, and for steel it normally lies between 2 and 4 J/mm³, so 1.47 J/mm³ is somewhat low, which suggests the force reading is on the low side, though it is plausible for a free-machining steel cut with a 10 degree rake.

Answer: 2.20 kW

(d)

First find the friction angle β = arctan(Ft/Fc) + α for the test, since Ft/Fc = tan(β − α). Here β = arctan(420/1100) + 10° = 20.90° + 10° = 30.90°. Merchant's criterion gives φ2 = 45° + α2/2 − β/2 = 45 + 10 − 15.45 = 39.55°. The shear plane area becomes As2 = t0 w/sin φ2 = 1.178 mm². With the same shear stress 470 MPa, the shear force is Fs2 = τ As2 = 553.1 N. The cutting force is Fc2 = Fs2 cos(β − α2)/cos(φ2 + β − α2) = 553.1 × 0.9820/0.6368 = 853 N. The power falls by 22.5 percent, so the sharper tool helps.

Answer: 853 N

A4 Practice Paper 14

Problem 1 [A4-066] Machining: tool life and cost

A job shop turns steel pins, 60 mm in diameter and 200 mm long, on a CNC lathe with a feed of 0.30 mm/rev. The tool life relation is V T0.25 = 300, with cutting speed V in m/min and tool life T in minutes. The machine and operator rate is 60 dollars per hour. Each insert edge costs 4.50 dollars and takes 1.5 minutes to index and reset. Loading and unloading a pin takes 2.0 minutes. The planner currently runs at 150 m/min because that is the figure on the tooling supplier's data sheet. During a rush order the machinist increases the speed by 20 percent without recalculating. The plant accountant asks for a justified speed, and for the effect of the two choices on the cost per pin. Treat the machining as a single pass of the whole length with no approach or rapid-traverse time.

  1. (a) Find the tool life at the current speed of 150 m/min. [4]
  2. (b) Find the tool life when the speed is increased by 20 percent, and the percentage change in life. [4]
  3. (c) Find the economical tool life for minimum cost per piece and the corresponding cutting speed. [6]
  4. (d) Find the cost per pin at the economical speed, and at the increased speed of 180 m/min. State which is cheaper. [6]
(a)

The Taylor relation gives T = (C/V)1/n with C = 300 m/min and n = 0.25. At V = 150 m/min, C/V = 2.000, and 1/n = 4, so T = 2.0004 = 16.0 minutes. The result shows how strongly life depends on speed, since a mere doubling of the ratio produces a sixteen-fold change in life. The tool life of 16.0 min at 150 m/min is reasonable for coated carbide in medium carbon steel. It applies to a defined wear criterion, usually 0.3 mm flank wear, and the constants were derived at the same feed and depth of cut, so the relation is only valid near these conditions.

Answer: 16.0 min

(b)

The new speed is 1.20 × 150 = 180 m/min. Then C/V = 300/180 = 1.6667, and T2 = 1.66674 = 7.72 minutes. The percentage change in life is (T2 − T1)/T1 × 100 = (7.72 − 16.0)/16.0 × 100 = -51.8 percent. A mere 20 percent rise in speed removes more than half of the tool life, because the exponent 1/n = 4 acts on the ratio of speeds, giving (1/1.2)4 = 0.4823. The machining time falls by only 1/1.2, so the net result on cost per piece depends on how tool changes are costed, which is examined below.

Answer: -51.8 %

(c)

For minimum cost the tool life is T = (1/n − 1)(tch + Ct/Co), where tch is the tool change time, Ct the tool edge cost, and Co the machine rate per minute. The rate is 60/60 = 1.0 dollar/min. Then Ct/Co = 4.50/1.0 = 4.50 min, and tch + Ct/Co = 1.5 + 4.5 = 6.0 min. With 1/n − 1 = 3, T = 3 × 6.0 = 18.0 minutes. The speed follows from the Taylor line, V = C/Tn = 300/18.00.25 = 300/2.0598 = 145.6 m/min. This speed is slightly below the current figure of 150 m/min, so the supplier's number is already close to the cost optimum for this edge price and this machine rate.

Answer: 145.6 m/min

(d)

The cost per pin is Co(tload + tm) + Co tm tch/T + Ct tm/T, where tm = π D L/(1000 V f) is the machining time. At the economical speed, tm = π × 60 × 200/(1000 × 145.6 × 0.30) = 0.863 min and T = 18.0 min, so the cost is 1.0 × (2.0 + 0.863) + 0.863 × (1.5 + 4.5)/18.0 = 3.15 dollars. At 180 m/min, tm = 0.698 min and T = 7.72 min, so the cost is 1.0 × (2.0 + 0.698) + 0.698 × 6.0/7.72 = 3.24 dollars. The economical speed is cheaper by 0.09 dollars per pin, so the rush-order speed raises cost by 2.9 percent.

Answer: 3.15 dollars

Problem 2 [A4-067] Casting and solidification time

A foundry pours a rectangular steel plate casting 300 mm long, 200 mm wide and 40 mm thick into a green-sand mould. For this mould and metal the Chvorinov constant is B = 2.8 min/cm², with the usual exponent of 2 and with V and A measured in cm³ and cm². The mould is closed and all six faces of the plate lose heat through the mould. A cylindrical riser with height equal to 1.5 times its diameter is attached to the casting and is cooled on all its surfaces including the top, which is open to the mould. The riser must solidify 25 percent later than the casting so that it can feed molten metal. A customer then asks for a thicker plate of the same length and width, 60 mm thick, with the same riser, and the foundry must decide whether that riser still works.

  1. (a) Find the solidification time of the 40 mm plate casting. [4]
  2. (b) Find the riser diameter needed so that it solidifies in 1.25 times the casting time. [6]
  3. (c) Find the solidification time of the 60 mm thick plate. [5]
  4. (d) Find by how many minutes the riser from part (b) solidifies before the 60 mm plate, and say what that means for the casting. [5]
(a)

Chvorinov's rule gives t = B (V/A)². The plate dimensions are 30 cm by 20 cm by 4 cm, so V = 30 × 20 × 4 = 2400 cm³. The surface area is A = 2(30 × 20 + 30 × 4 + 20 × 4) = 2(800) = 1600 cm². The modulus is V/A = 2400/1600 = 1.500 cm. Then t = 2.8 × 1.500² = 6.30 minutes. This assumes constant mould properties and an even heat flow through every face, which is accurate when the plate is thin relative to its other dimensions. The result gives the baseline against which the riser must be compared.

Answer: 6.30 min

(b)

The riser must satisfy tr = 1.25 t, so its modulus must be sqrt(1.25) times the casting modulus. That gives Mr = sqrt(1.25) × 1.500 = 1.677 cm. For a cylinder with H = 1.5 D, the volume is π D² (1.5 D)/4 = 0.375 π D³. The cooled area is the side π D (1.5 D) plus the top and bottom ends 2 × π D²/4, which together give π D² (1.5 + 0.5) = 2 π D². The riser modulus is therefore V/A = 0.375 π D³/(2 π D²) = 0.1875 D. Setting 0.1875 D = 1.677 gives D = 8.94 cm, and H = 13.42 cm. Because the area includes the neck contact area, an actual design would add a small allowance.

Answer: 8.94 cm

(c)

For the thicker plate the dimensions are 30 cm by 20 cm by 6 cm, so V2 = 30 × 20 × 6 = 3600 cm³. The area is A2 = 2(600 + 30 × 6 + 20 × 6) = 2(900) = 1800 cm². The modulus is 2.000 cm. Then t2 = 2.8 × 2.000² = 11.20 minutes. Comparing with 6.30 minutes for the thin plate, solidification time grows by a factor of 1.78 while the thickness grew only by 1.5, because time scales with the square of the modulus. This is the reason why design changes in section thickness affect feeding far more than the proportional change in dimension suggests.

Answer: 11.20 min

(d)

The riser from part (b) was sized to freeze at tr = 1.25 × 6.30 = 7.88 minutes. The 60 mm plate freezes at 11.20 minutes, so the riser solidifies 3.32 minutes earlier than the casting. A riser that freezes first cannot feed the plate: the last liquid in the casting remains cut off from any supply, and shrinkage porosity forms in the thick centre of the plate. The correct remedy is to enlarge the riser. The required modulus would be sqrt(1.25) × 2.000 = 2.236 cm, giving D = 11.93 cm, noticeably larger than the first riser, with a corresponding loss of yield.

Answer: 3.32 min

Problem 3 [A4-068] Forming: rolling and forging forces

A reversing hot mill reduces a steel slab from 40 mm to 32 mm thick in one pass. The slab is 1.2 m wide and the work rolls have a radius of 450 mm. Over the pass, the average flow stress of the hot steel may be taken as 120 MPa, and width spread is neglected. The rolls turn at 60 rev/min and the rolling force acts at the middle of the contact arc. Roll bite depends on friction, and the limiting draft in the pass is Δh max = μ² R, where μ is the coefficient of friction between rolls and slab. In normal operation μ = 0.25. A roll-cooling problem then causes the surface to become glazed, and friction drops to 0.05 at the next pass. The operator asks whether the same pass can still be taken and what the mill must supply.

  1. (a) Find the draft, the projected contact length, and confirm that the pass is possible with μ = 0.25. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rolling force. [5]
  3. (c) Find the total power required to roll, using the force acting at half the contact length from the roll centreline. [6]
  4. (d) Find the maximum draft available with the glazed rolls at μ = 0.05, and the shortfall against the draft the pass needs. [5]
(a)

The draft is Δh = h0 − hf = 40 − 32 = 8 mm. The projected contact length is L = sqrt(R Δh) = sqrt(450 × 8) = 60.0 mm. The maximum possible draft is Δh max = μ² R = 0.25² × 450 = 28.12 mm. Because 8 mm is less than 28.12 mm, the rolls can grip the slab and draw it into the bite, so the pass is possible. The margin is generous at this friction level, and the answer here is the contact length of 60.0 mm, which is used for both the force and the torque.

Answer: 60.0 mm

(b)

The rolling force is F = Yf w L, where Yf is the average flow stress, w is the slab width and L is the projected contact length. With Yf = 120 MPa, w = 1200 mm and L = 60.0 mm, the contact area is w L = 1200 × 60.0 = 72000 mm². Then F = 120 × 72000 = 8640000 N, or 8.64 MN. This equation neglects friction hill effects, which would raise the force by a few percent, so it is a minimum. The force is carried by the mill housing and bearings, and it sets the stand stiffness requirements. The roll separating force is the same as F for a symmetric pass, so each roll carries it.

Answer: 8.64 MN

(c)

The torque on each roll is the force times the moment arm, which is half the contact length for a force acting at the middle of the arc: T = F L/2 = 8640000 × 0.0600/2 = 259200 N·m, or 259.2 kN·m. The angular speed is ω = 2π × 60/60 = 6.283 rad/s. The power per roll is T ω = 259200 × 6.283 = 1628602 W. The mill has two driven rolls, so the total is P = 2 T ω = 3257203 W, or 3.26 MW. This is the power delivered to the slab as plastic work and friction, excluding the roll bearing and gearing losses. The drive motor must be rated higher still to cover those losses.

Answer: 3.26 MW

(d)

Using the bite condition Δh max = μ² R with μ = 0.05, Δh max = 0.0025 × 450 = 1.125 mm. The pass needs 8 mm, so the rolls cannot draw the slab in; the shortfall is 6.88 mm, and the slab would simply stall or be pushed back at the entry. The machine could not finish this pass until friction is restored. Options include lighter drafts of about 1.1 mm per pass, which is unrealistic, roughening the rolls, or pushing the slab in with an entry pusher. A more practical remedy is to restore the roll surface condition, since friction affects not only bite but the quality of the surface of the product.

Answer: 1.13 mm

Problem 4 [A4-069] Sheet metal forming and bending

A fabrication shop forms a U-channel from stainless steel sheet 3.0 mm thick, with an ultimate tensile strength of 600 MPa. The channel has two outside flanges each 40 mm tall and an outside web width of 60 mm, with both bends at 90 degrees and an inside bend radius of 4.0 mm. The shop uses a bend allowance factor K = 0.40, locating the neutral axis at KT from the inner surface. The bends are made by V-die bending along a 500 mm length of channel, one bend at a time. The bending force is estimated by F = k UTS L T²/W with k = 1.33 for V-die bending, where W is the die opening. The press brake operator initially sets the die opening at eight times the sheet thickness, but a die with an opening of sixteen times the thickness is available, with the same tooling in all other respects.

  1. (a) Find the bend allowance for one 90 degree bend. [4]
  2. (b) Find the flat blank length (the developed length along the channel profile) of the U-channel. [6]
  3. (c) Find the press force needed for one bend with the die opening set at 8T. [5]
  4. (d) Find the force with the die opening increased to 16T, and the effect on the formed bend radius. [5]
(a)

The bend allowance is the length of the neutral axis through the bend, BA = α (R + K T), where α is the bend angle in radians. A 90 degree bend has α = π/2 = 1.5708 rad. The inside radius is R = 4.0 mm and the thickness is T = 3.0 mm, so K T = 0.40 × 3.0 = 1.2 mm. The radius to the neutral axis is 4.0 + 1.2 = 5.2 mm. Then BA = 1.5708 × 5.2 = 8.168 mm. The neutral axis stays at a distance of 40 percent of the thickness from the inner face because the strain on the outside stretches the material more than the inside compresses it. This value is the building block for the flat length.

Answer: 8.168 mm

(b)

The outside setback for a 90 degree bend is R + T = 4.0 + 3.0 = 7.0 mm. Each straight portion is measured from the outside dimensions. A flange has a straight length of 40 − 7.0 = 33.0 mm. The web has a straight length of 60 − 2 × 7.0 = 46.0 mm because it loses a setback at both ends. There are two flanges, one web and two bends. The flat length is L = 2 × 33.0 + 46.0 + 2 × 8.168 = 128.34 mm. Because the problem states outside dimensions, the setback must be removed before adding the bend allowance. The result is the length of blank that must be cut, before accounting for any trimming after forming.

Answer: 128.34 mm

(c)

The die opening is W = 8 T = 24 mm. Converting everything to metres, the strength is 600 × 10⁶ Pa, the bend length is L = 0.500 m, and T = 0.003 m, so T² = 9.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². The force is F = k UTS L T²/W = 1.33 × 600 × 10⁶ × 0.500 × 9.0 × 10⁻⁶/0.024. The numerator is 3591.0 N·m and dividing by W = 0.024 m gives F = 149625 N, or 149.6 kN. This is the force at the bottom of the stroke, and the press brake must have at least this capacity, with a margin of around 20 percent for strain hardening and for variation in sheet thickness, so a rating of about 180 kN is appropriate.

Answer: 149.6 kN

(d)

The force is inversely proportional to the die opening, so with W = 16 T = 48 mm the force is F = 149625 × 24/48 = 74812 N, or 74.8 kN. The force halves. The cost is on the geometry side: in air bending the radius formed is set by the die opening, roughly 0.16 times W, so a wider opening makes a larger radius. The wider die gives about 7.7 mm against 3.8 mm for the narrow die, which exceeds the 4.0 mm design radius. The wider die also lengthens the minimum flange that can be formed. A designer would therefore keep the 8T die for this tight radius and choose a larger press brake instead.

Answer: 74.8 kN

Problem 5 [A4-070] Welding heat input and joining processes

A gas metal arc welding procedure for a thick quenched-and-tempered steel plate uses an arc voltage of 26 V, a welding current of 280 A and a travel speed of 6.0 mm/s. The arc efficiency for this process is taken as 0.80. The plate is thick, so the cooling rate at the weld centreline may be estimated from the thick-plate relation R = 2π k (Tc − T0)²/H, where k = 0.040 W/(mm·K) is the thermal conductivity, Tc = 550 °C is the temperature at which the cooling rate is evaluated, T0 is the initial plate temperature, and H is the net heat input per unit length in J/mm. The procedure qualification was done with the plate at 25 °C. The welding supervisor notices hardness problems in the heat-affected zone on cold mornings, and the metallurgist wants the cooling rate kept at or below 40 K/s.

  1. (a) Find the net heat input per unit length of weld. [4]
  2. (b) Find the cooling rate at 550 °C for a plate initially at 25 °C. [5]
  3. (c) Find the cooling rate if the plate is preheated to 200 °C, and the factor of reduction. [5]
  4. (d) With no preheat, find the maximum travel speed that keeps the cooling rate at or below 40 K/s, keeping the same voltage, current and efficiency. [6]
(a)

The heat input per unit length is H = η V I/v, where η is the arc efficiency, V the arc voltage, I the current and v the travel speed. The arc power is V I = 26 × 280 = 7280 W. The net power delivered to the plate is η V I = 0.80 × 7280 = 5824 W. Dividing by a speed of 6.0 mm/s gives H = 5824/6.0 = 971 J/mm, or 0.97 kJ/mm. This is the figure that appears on a welding procedure sheet, and it is a convenient single indicator of the thermal severity of the pass, although it does not capture how the heat is distributed or the effect of the preheat.

Answer: 971 J/mm

(b)

Using R = 2π k (Tc − T0)²/H with Tc − T0 = 550 − 25 = 525 K, the square is 275625 K². The numerator is 2π × 0.040 × 275625 = 69272, with units of W·K/mm. Dividing by H = 971 J/mm gives R = 71.4 K/s. The units work because W/mm divided by J/mm leaves a per-second quantity, multiplied by K. This is a fairly fast cooling rate for a thick plate, and in a hardenable steel it favours martensite formation in the heat-affected zone. The calculation assumes a semi-infinite plate with a point source, so it is only approximate near the edges or for thin sections.

Answer: 71.4 K/s

(c)

With a preheat of 200 °C, Tc − T0 = 550 − 200 = 350 K, and the square is 122500 K². The cooling rate is R2 = 2π × 0.040 × 122500/971 = 31.7 K/s. The ratio to the unpreheated case is R2/R1 = (122500/275625) = 0.444, so the preheat reduces the cooling rate by 55.6 percent. The squared dependence on temperature difference makes preheat very effective: lowering the difference from 525 to 350 K cuts the rate by more than half. This is the basis on which preheat tables prescribe higher temperatures for thicker sections and higher-carbon-equivalent steels.

Answer: 31.7 K/s

(d)

The cooling rate must not exceed 40 K/s, so the heat input must be at least H min = 2π k (Tc − T0)²/R = 69272/40 = 1732 J/mm. Heat input falls as the travel speed rises, so the limit on speed is v max = η V I/H min = 5824/1732 = 3.36 mm/s. This is well below the qualified 6.0 mm/s, which means the original procedure cools too fast with the plate at 25 °C when judged against the 40 K/s limit. The shop has two practical choices: slow the travel, which lowers productivity and increases distortion, or preheat the plate as in part (c), which allows the original speed.

Answer: 3.36 mm/s

A4 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A4-071] Quality control: process capability and control charts

A honing line finishes the bore of hydraulic pump housings to a drawing dimension of 62.000 mm with a tolerance of plus or minus 0.040 mm. After a tool change the quality technician takes 125 housings and finds the bore diameters are normally distributed with a mean of 62.012 mm and a standard deviation of 0.011 mm. Production is monitored with an X-bar chart using subgroups of 5 consecutive parts and control limits set at three standard errors on each side of the process centre. The supervisor claims that the spread is acceptable and the only problem is that the mean has drifted off nominal. The customer requires fewer than 1000 nonconforming parts per million.

  1. (a) Calculate the process capability index Cpk for the process as it is running, and comment on whether the supervisor's claim about the spread is correct. [5]
  2. (b) Estimate the fraction of housings outside tolerance, in parts per million, and state whether the customer requirement is met. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the technician adjusts the honing stroke so that the mean is brought exactly to 62.000 mm with the standard deviation unchanged. Find the new nonconforming fraction in ppm. [5]
  4. (d) For the re-centred process, calculate the upper control limit of the X-bar chart (subgroup size 5), in millimetres, and explain why the chart limits differ from the tolerance limits. [5]
(a)

Cp = (USL - LSL)/(6σ) = (62.040 - 61.960)/(6 × 0.011) = 0.080/0.066 = 1.212. This only measures the spread against the tolerance and ignores the offset of the mean. Cpk = min[(USL - μ), (μ - LSL)]/(3σ). The upper side is the closer one: USL - μ = 62.040 - 62.012 = 0.028 mm, while μ - LSL = 0.052 mm. So Cpk = 0.028/(3 × 0.011) = 0.028/0.033 = 0.848. A Cpk below 1.0 means the nearer tolerance limit is less than three standard deviations from the mean (here 2.55σ), so the process is not capable as it runs. The supervisor is partly right: Cp = 1.21 shows the spread alone does fit inside the tolerance, since the 6σ band is narrower than the 0.080 mm tolerance band. However, the gap between Cp and Cpk shows that the off-centre mean is costing a large part of that capability. Assumption: normal, stable process with the stated sigma.

Answer: 0.848

(b)

For a normal distribution the nonconforming fraction is the sum of the two tail areas. Upper tail: z = (USL - μ)/σ = (62.040 - 62.012)/0.011 = 2.545, so P(X > USL) = 1 - Φ(2.545) ≈ 0.00547. Lower tail: z = (61.960 - 62.012)/0.011 = -4.727, so P(X < LSL) ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁶, which is negligible by comparison. Total fraction ≈ 0.00547 + 0.0000011, which is 5458 ppm. The customer limit is 1000 ppm, so the requirement is not met by a factor of more than five. Practically, about 1 housing in 183 is a reject. Almost all of the rejects are oversize bores because the mean sits 0.012 mm above nominal; the undersize tail contributes almost nothing. This asymmetry is the signature of an off-centre process, and it shows that centring alone should give a large improvement without any change in spread.

Answer: 5460 ppm

(c)

With the mean centred, both tails sit 0.040 mm from the mean, so the capability is symmetric: Cpk = Cp(centred) = 0.040/(3 × 0.011) = 1.212. The z-value to each limit is 0.040/0.011 = 3.636. Each tail area is 1 - Φ(3.636) ≈ 1.38 × 10⁻⁴. The two tails add: fraction = 2 × 1.38 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.77 × 10⁻⁴, which is 277 ppm. This is well inside the customer's 1000 ppm requirement, a reduction of about twenty to one compared with the drifted process. The improvement came from re-centring alone, with no tightening of the spread, which is the cheapest corrective action available and the first one to try. Note that the usual rule of thumb for a capable process is Cpk of at least 1.33, and 1.21 falls slightly short of this, so the process should still be improved by reducing variation if a stricter customer later demands it.

Answer: 277 ppm

(d)

The distribution of subgroup means has the same centre as the process and a standard deviation equal to the standard error σ/√n = 0.011/√5 = 0.004919 mm. Control limits are placed at three standard errors: UCL = 62.000 + 3 × 0.004919 = 62.000 + 0.014758 = 62.0148 mm, and LCL = 62.000 - 0.014758 = 61.9852 mm. These limits are much tighter than the tolerance limits of 61.960 mm and 62.040 mm for two reasons. First, they describe averages of five parts, which vary less than individual parts by a factor of √5. Second, they express what the process voice says it will do when stable, whereas the tolerances express what the customer will accept. A subgroup mean outside 62.0148 mm signals a shift in the process (for example tool wear or a thermal drift) well before individual parts reach the tolerance limit, which is the purpose of the chart. The chart limits should never be set from the drawing tolerances.

Answer: 62.0148 mm

Problem 2 [A4-072] Process selection and production line balancing

A contract manufacturer is setting up a moving assembly line for a compact gearbox. The plant works one 7.5 hour productive shift per day and the customer's present order is 450 gearboxes per shift. The assembly has ten work elements with times in seconds: A 22, B 34, C 18, D 41, E 27, F 15, G 38, H 24, I 12 and J 29. Precedence is A before B, B before D, C before D, D before E, E before F, F before G and H, G and H before I, and I before J. The first proposed layout uses six stations loaded as: station 1 with A and B, station 2 with C and D, station 3 with E and F, station 4 with G, station 5 with H and I, and station 6 with J. A sales forecast now suggests the order could rise to 540 gearboxes per shift.

  1. (a) Find the cycle time, in seconds, the line must achieve to meet the present order. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the total work content and the theoretical minimum number of stations at the cycle time of part (a). [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the balance efficiency of the proposed six-station layout at the present cycle time, and identify the station loads. [6]
  4. (d) What-if: the order rises to 540 gearboxes per shift. Determine the new cycle time, how many stations of the proposed layout would exceed it, and the best-case balance efficiency once the precedence constraints are respected. [6]
(a)

Cycle time is the maximum time allowed at each station and equals the available production time divided by the required output. Available time = 7.5 h × 3600 s/h = 27 000 s per shift. Required output = 450 gearboxes per shift. Therefore cycle time = 27 000/450 = 60.0 s per unit. Every station must complete its assigned work in 60 s or less, and the longest single element, D at 41 s, is below this, so a feasible balance can exist. The calculation assumes no allowance for breaks, changeovers or downtime beyond the stated productive time, and a production line with a 60 s cycle delivers one gearbox every minute once filled. In practice a planner would normally set the target cycle slightly below this value to allow for stoppages, but the question asks only for the theoretical value needed to meet the order.

Answer: 60 s

(b)

Total work content is the sum of all element times: 22 + 34 + 18 + 41 + 27 + 15 + 38 + 24 + 12 + 29 = 260 s. The theoretical minimum number of stations is the total work content divided by the cycle time, rounded up to the next whole number because a station cannot be fractional: N = 260/60 = 4.33, so N = 5 stations. This is a lower bound that ignores precedence and the discrete sizes of the elements, so a real layout may need more stations. The proposed layout uses six stations, one more than the theoretical minimum, which suggests it is either imperfectly balanced or deliberately loose. The fractional part of 0.33 of a station shows that five stations would be loaded at about 87 percent of the cycle time on average, which leaves very little slack for balancing.

Answer: 5 stations

(c)

Station loads in seconds: station 1 = 22 + 34 = 56, station 2 = 18 + 41 = 59, station 3 = 27 + 15 = 42, station 4 = 38, station 5 = 24 + 12 = 36, and station 6 = 29. These total 260 s, which matches the work content, and all are below the 60 s cycle time, so the layout is feasible. The precedence constraints are also satisfied, since each element is in the same or a later station than its predecessors. Balance efficiency is the work content divided by the number of stations times the cycle time: efficiency = 260/(6 × 60) = 260/360 = 72.2 percent. The balance delay is therefore 72.2 percent subtracted from 100, about 27.8 percent, representing idle time. The loads are very uneven, from 29 s to 59 s, so there is clear scope to rebalance, and the lightly loaded station 6 is a candidate for absorbing elements from neighbouring stations.

Answer: 72.2 %

(d)

New cycle time = 27 000/540 = 50 s. The theoretical minimum number of stations is 260/50 = 5.20, rounded up to 6 stations, which would give an upper-bound efficiency of 260/(6 × 50) = 86.7 percent. Checking the proposed layout against the shorter cycle, the station loads of 56 s and 59 s exceed 50 s, so 2 of the six stations are overloaded and the layout cannot meet the higher demand without rebalancing; the heaviest station would pace the line at 59 s. Six stations at 50 s cannot actually be reached, because of precedence. Element D (41 s) cannot share a station with anything, since the smallest element that could join it is 12 s and 41 + 12 exceeds 50 s, and B (34 s) can only be paired with A (56 s) or C (52 s), both over 50 s, so B stands alone as well. An exhaustive search of every precedence-feasible assignment shows that the fewest stations at a 50 s cycle is 7, for example loads of 40, 34, 41, 42, 38, 36 and 29 s. The best-case efficiency is therefore 260/(7 × 50) = 260/350 = 74.3 percent. This is still higher than the present 72.2 percent, but well below the 86.7 percent bound, because the high volume forces an extra, lightly loaded station.

Answer: 74.3 %

Problem 3 [A4-073] Static failure theories for ductile materials

A solid round transmission shaft of diameter 32 mm carries a gear midway between two bearings. At the critical section the shaft is loaded in steady bending with a moment of 380 N·m and a steady torque of 520 N·m, and no axial load acts. The shaft is made from a ductile steel with a tensile yield strength of 420 MPa.
