The designer wishes to compare two failure criteria, the maximum distortion energy theory and the maximum shear stress theory, and to see how sensitive the safety margin is to a late increase in the transmitted power. Stress concentration at the section is neglected, and the loading is static. A change order proposes to raise the transmitted torque by 30 percent with the bending moment unchanged.

  1. (a) Calculate the bending stress and the torsional shear stress at the outer surface of the critical section. Give the bending stress as the answer. [4]
  2. (b) Find the factor of safety against yielding using the maximum distortion energy (von Mises) theory. [5]
  3. (c) Find the factor of safety using the maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory and state which theory is the more conservative. [5]
  4. (d) What-if: the torque is raised by 30 percent to 676 N·m with the bending moment unchanged. Find the new von Mises factor of safety and comment on the effect. [6]
(a)

For a solid round shaft the surface bending stress is σ = 32M/(πd³) and the surface torsional shear stress is τ = 16T/(πd³). With d = 0.032 m, d³ = 3.277 × 10⁻⁵ m³ and πd³ = 1.0294 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Bending: σ = 32 × 380/1.0294 × 10⁻⁴ = 12 160/1.0294 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.181 × 10⁸ Pa = 118.1 MPa. Torsion: τ = 16 × 520/1.0294 × 10⁻⁴ = 8 320/1.0294 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.08 × 10⁷ Pa = 80.8 MPa. The critical point lies on the surface where the bending stress is largest, and the stress element there has σx = 118.1 MPa and τxy = 80.8 MPa, with the other stress components zero. The point of maximum tension is where the bending and torsion act together on one element. A steady load is assumed, and the analysis does not include the effect of any key seat or shoulder.

Answer: 118.1 MPa

(b)

For plane stress with only σx and τxy, the von Mises equivalent stress is σ' = √(σx² + 3τxy²). Substituting: σ' = √(118.1² + 3 × 80.8²) = 183.2 MPa, because 3 × 80.8² is about 19 580 MPa² and 118.1² is about 13 940 MPa², giving a sum near 33 520 MPa². Yielding is predicted when σ' reaches Sy, so the factor of safety is n = Sy/σ' = 420/183.2 = 2.29. The shaft therefore has about 2.3 times the load needed to start yielding under distortion energy. This theory matches experimental yield data for ductile metals well and is generally preferred for analysis, whereas the shear stress theory is a little more conservative and also easier to apply by hand. The result assumes uniform, isotropic material properties and that the yield strength in tension equals that in compression.

Answer: 2.29

(c)

First find the principal stresses: σ1,2 = σx/2 ± √((σx/2)² + τxy²) = 118.1/2 ± √((118.1/2)² + 80.8²). The radical is √(59.1² + 80.8²) = 200.2/2 = 100.1 MPa, so σ1 = 159.2 MPa and σ2 = -41.0 MPa, with σ3 = 0. Because σ1 is positive and σ2 is negative, the largest principal-stress difference is σ1 - σ2 = 200.2 MPa. The maximum shear stress theory predicts yielding when this difference reaches Sy, so n = Sy/(σ1 - σ2) = 420/200.2 = 2.10. Comparing: Tresca gives 2.10 and von Mises 2.29, so Tresca is the more conservative, by about 0.91 to 1 in this case. The two theories differ most in pure shear, by up to 15 percent, and agree under uniaxial tension. For a safety-critical shaft some designers choose the Tresca value to add a small additional margin.

Answer: 2.1

(d)

The new torque is 1.3 × 520 = 676 N·m. The bending stress is unchanged at 118.1 MPa, but the shear stress scales directly with torque: τ = 1.3 × 80.8 = 105.1 MPa. The equivalent stress becomes σ' = √(118.1² + 3 × 105.1²) = 217.0 MPa, since the shear term rises from about 19 580 to 33 100 MPa² while the bending term stays near 13 940 MPa². The factor of safety is n = 420/217.0 = 1.94. A 30 percent increase in torque therefore reduces the safety factor from 2.29 to 1.94, a drop of about 15 percent, which is smaller than the load increase because bending is unchanged and enters the equivalent stress separately. The shaft still has a margin against first yield, but static yield is rarely the governing mode on a rotating shaft, and the designer must also check fatigue life and deflection before approving the change order.

Answer: 1.94

Problem 4 [A4-074] Fatigue: endurance limit and Marin factors

A rotating countershaft in a conveyor drive is turned from cold-drawn steel with an ultimate tensile strength of 700 MPa. The shaft diameter at the critical section is 45 mm. The designer uses the Marin approach with an ideal rotating-beam endurance limit of 0.5 times the ultimate strength. The surface factor is ka = a·Sutb with Sut in MPa, where a = 4.51 and b = -0.265 for a machined finish, or a = 1.58 and b = -0.085 for a ground finish. The size factor for rotating bending in the range 8 to 51 mm is kb = 1.24·d-0.107 with d in mm. The load factor is 1 for bending, the temperature factor is 1, and the reliability factor for 99 percent is 0.814. Take f = 0.9 for the S-N relation Sf = a·Nb.

  1. (a) Calculate the size factor kb, the surface factor for the machined finish, and the corrected endurance limit Se of the shaft. Give Se as the answer. [5]
  2. (b) The shaft sees a fully reversed bending stress amplitude of 260 MPa at the critical section. Estimate the life in cycles for the machined shaft. [6]
  3. (c) What-if: the supplier proposes grinding the journal instead of machining it. Calculate the new surface factor and the new corrected endurance limit. [4]
  4. (d) Using the ground-finish endurance limit, recalculate the life at the same 260 MPa stress amplitude and state by what factor the life has changed. [5]
(a)

The ideal endurance limit is S'e = 0.5 × 700 = 350 MPa. Surface factor for the machined finish: ka = 4.51 × 700-0.265 = 4.51 × 0.1763 = 0.795. Size factor: kb = 1.24 × 45-0.107 = 1.24 × 0.6653 = 0.825. Load factor kc = 1 and temperature factor kd = 1, and the reliability factor is ke = 0.814 for 99 percent. The corrected endurance limit is Se = ka·kb·kc·kd·ke·S'e = 0.795 × 0.825 × 1 × 1 × 0.814 × 350 = 186.8 MPa. The Marin factors reduce the laboratory endurance limit of 350 MPa to roughly half of that, which shows why a shaft in service cannot be sized on handbook endurance data for a polished specimen. The calculation assumes fully reversed rotating bending, no stress concentration (handled separately), and a normal distribution of endurance data.

Answer: 186.8 MPa

(b)

The stress amplitude of 260 MPa lies between Se = 186.8 MPa and f·Sut = 0.9 × 700 = 630 MPa, so the life is finite. The S-N line is Sf = a·Nb with a = (f·Sut)²/Se = 630²/186.8 = 396 900/186.8 = 2123 MPa, and b = -(1/3)·log10(f·Sut/Se) = -(1/3)·log10(630/186.8) = -0.176. Setting Sf = 260 MPa: N = (σa/a)1/b = (260/2123)1/(-0.176) = (0.1225)-5.68 = e11.93. The result is N = 1.53 × 10⁵ cycles, about 1.5 × 10⁵. At a typical conveyor shaft speed of 600 rev/min this is only 4 hours of running, which is clearly inadequate. The life has been found from the standard high-cycle S-N approximation anchored at 10³ cycles (0.9 Sut) and 10⁶ cycles (Se). Note that scatter in fatigue life is large, so such a prediction should be read as an order of magnitude.

Answer: 153000 cycles

(c)

For a ground finish the surface factor is ka = 1.58 × 700-0.085 = 1.58 × 0.5729 = 0.905. The size factor, load factor, temperature factor and reliability factor are unchanged, so the corrected endurance limit becomes Se = 0.905 × 0.825 × 0.814 × 350 = 212.8 MPa. Compared with the machined value of 186.8 MPa this is an increase of about 14 percent, due solely to the finer surface finish, since grinding leaves smaller stress-raising scratches than turning. The benefit of a good finish increases with the tensile strength of the steel, because high strength steels are more notch sensitive; for a lower strength steel the gain would be smaller. The cost of grinding must be weighed against this fatigue benefit, and a shot-peened or rolled surface could give a larger gain in endurance than grinding.

Answer: 212.8 MPa

(d)

With Se = 212.8 MPa the constants become a = (630)²/212.8 = 396 900/212.8 = 1866 MPa and b = -(1/3)·log10(630/212.8) = -(1/3)·log10(2.962) = -0.157. The life is N = (260/1866)1/(-0.157) = (0.1393)-6.36 = e12.54. This gives N = 2.8 × 10⁵ cycles, about 2.8 × 10⁵. Dividing by the machined life of 1.53 × 10⁵ cycles shows that grinding has raised the life by a factor of 2.8 × 10⁵/1.53 × 10⁵, about 1.8. A 14 percent gain in endurance limit has therefore increased the finite life by about 80 percent, because life is very sensitive to the ratio of the working stress to Se: the S-N line is nearly flat, with a slope exponent near -0.16, so a small change in strength gives a large change in cycles. The life is still short for a continuously running shaft, so grinding alone is not enough, and the diameter would need to increase to reduce the stress.

Answer: 280000 cycles

Problem 5 [A4-075] Fatigue design with Goodman or Gerber

A cast-pulley hub clamps onto a hot-rolled steel axle (ultimate strength 620 MPa, yield strength 450 MPa) in a materials-handling cart. At the critical fillet the nominal stresses, already including the fatigue stress concentration factor, are a bending amplitude of 110 MPa and a steady mean tensile stress of 95 MPa. The completely corrected endurance limit for the fillet has been found to be 190 MPa. The reliability target is the same for all cases. The design engineer must check the axle against fatigue using the modified Goodman line and the Gerber parabola, and against first-cycle yielding, and then examine the effect of a press-fit assembly that adds a steady tensile mean stress. Assume that the mean stress and the amplitude increase in proportion to one another when the load is scaled.

  1. (a) Find the factor of safety against fatigue failure using the modified Goodman criterion. [5]
  2. (b) Find the factor of safety using the Gerber criterion and compare it with the Goodman result. [5]
  3. (c) Check the axle for yielding on the first cycle using the sum of the amplitude and the mean stress, and give the factor of safety. [4]
  4. (d) What-if: a press fit adds a steady tensile mean stress so that the mean stress becomes 200 MPa, with the amplitude unchanged. Determine the new Goodman factor of safety and the new yielding factor, and say which one governs. [6]
(a)

The modified Goodman criterion, written as a factor of safety, is 1/n = σa/Se + σm/Sut. Substituting σa = 110 MPa, Se = 190 MPa, σm = 95 MPa and Sut = 620 MPa: 1/n = 110/190 + 95/620 = 0.5789 + 0.1532 = 0.7321. Hence n = 1/0.7321 = 1.366. The load line from the origin has slope σa/σm = 110/95 = 1.158, so it is a proportional-loading case and this formula applies directly. The result indicates that the stresses could be increased by about 37 percent in proportion before a Goodman failure is predicted. Goodman is the more conservative of the common mean-stress criteria and is widely used for design because it lies below nearly all experimental data for ductile steel, which is why it is chosen when the consequence of failure is serious. The calculation assumes the stresses are uniaxial and that the load is applied in a constant, stable pattern.

Answer: 1.37

(b)

The Gerber parabola for a proportional load line gives n·σa/Se + (n·σm/Sut)² = 1. Writing A = (σm/Sut)² = (95/620)² = 0.02348 and B = σa/Se = 0.5789, the equation is A·n² + B·n - 1 = 0. The positive root is n = [-B + √(B² + 4A)]/(2A) = [-0.5789 + √(0.3351 + 0.0939)]/(0.04696) = [-0.5789 + 0.6550]/0.04696 = 1.621. Compared with the Goodman factor of 1.366, Gerber is about 1.621/1.366 times larger, roughly 18 percent less conservative. Gerber passes through the middle of the experimental data and is the best predictor of average life, while Goodman is a safe lower bound. A designer chooses Gerber when a good estimate of mean performance is wanted, and Goodman when a conservative margin is needed. Because the mean stress is only 95 MPa, the difference is moderate here.

Answer: 1.62

(c)

Yielding is checked on the maximum stress in the cycle, σmax = σa + σm = 110 + 95 = 205 MPa, because the material can yield on the first load application even if the fatigue life would be infinite. The factor of safety against yield is ny = Sy/σmax = 450/205 = 2.195. This is larger than the fatigue factors found in parts (a) and (b), so fatigue controls the design in this case and the section does not yield on the first cycle. If instead the yielding factor had been smaller than the fatigue factor, the yield line (the Langer line) would have been the governing limit, as happens at high mean stress and low amplitude. The check is a necessary supplement to Goodman or Gerber, since both lines extend beyond the yield limit for the larger mean stresses and can give a non-conservative answer on their own.

Answer: 2.2

(d)

With σm = 200 MPa and σa = 110 MPa, the Goodman equation gives 1/n = 110/190 + 200/620 = 0.5789 + 0.3226 = 0.9015, so n = 1.109. The yield check uses σmax = 110 + 200 = 310 MPa, giving ny = 450/310 = 1.452. The Goodman factor of 1.11 is the lower of the two, so fatigue still governs, but now the margin is only about 11 percent, which is too thin for most applications. The press-fit mean stress has cut the Goodman factor from 1.37 to 1.11 even though the alternating stress has not changed, showing that a tensile mean stress is harmful to fatigue strength. Remedies include a larger fillet radius, a shot-peened fillet to introduce compressive residual stress, or a larger shaft diameter. The ratio σa/σm has fallen from 1.16 to 0.55, and the Goodman result assumes the load keeps this new ratio when scaled.

Answer: 1.11

A4 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A4-076] Stress concentration

A flat bar of mild steel in a lifting lug is 60 mm wide and 8 mm thick and carries a central transverse hole of 12 mm diameter. It transmits an axial tensile force of 24 kN. For a finite-width plate with a central circular hole, the theoretical stress concentration factor based on the net section is approximated by Kt = 3.00 - 3.13(d/w) + 3.66(d/w)² - 1.53(d/w)³, where d is the hole diameter and w the plate width. The steel has a yield strength of 350 MPa and the notch sensitivity for the 6 mm hole radius is q = 0.85. A repair proposal would enlarge the hole to 24 mm diameter to accept a larger pin. The load is assumed to be applied through the pin at the hole centre line, and bending of the plate is neglected.

  1. (a) Calculate the nominal tensile stress on the net section at the hole. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the theoretical stress concentration factor Kt for the 12 mm hole. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the peak stress at the hole edge for static loading, and the fatigue stress concentration factor Kf with the corresponding peak stress for a fatigue check. Give the fatigue peak stress Kf·σnom as the answer. [6]
  4. (d) What-if: the hole is enlarged to 24 mm diameter. Calculate the new Kt, the new nominal net-section stress, and the new peak stress Kt·σnom. Give the peak stress as the answer, and comment on the result. [6]
(a)

The net cross-section is the plate width minus the hole diameter, multiplied by the thickness: Anet = (w - d)·t = (60 - 12) × 8 = 48 × 8 = 384 mm². The nominal stress is the force divided by the net area: σnom = F/Anet = 24 000 N/384 mm² = 62.50 N/mm², which is 62.50 MPa. This is the average stress on the weakened section and it is the reference stress to which the theoretical concentration factor is applied. The gross-section stress is only 24 000/(60 × 8) = 50 MPa, so the hole raises the average stress by 25 percent even before the concentration effect is considered. The quantity is defined on the net area, consistent with the given Kt equation, and it assumes the load is uniformly distributed across the net section at a distance from the hole, with no bending.

Answer: 62.5 MPa

(b)

The hole-to-width ratio is d/w = 12/60 = 0.200. Substituting into the given polynomial: Kt = 3.00 - 3.13(0.200) + 3.66(0.200)² - 1.53(0.200)³ = 3.00 - 0.626 + 3.66(0.0400) - 1.53(0.00800) = 3.00 - 0.626 + 0.1464 - 0.01224 = 2.508. This value is close to the classical infinite-plate value of 3.0 and decreases as the hole becomes larger relative to the plate width, because the stress field is less constricted by the finite-width effect. The result applies to a stress on the net section, so the peak stress at the hole edge is Kt·σnom. Kt is a purely geometric property determined by elasticity theory or photoelasticity and is independent of the material, as long as the material remains elastic at the peak stress.

Answer: 2.508

(c)

For static loading in a ductile material the peak stress is σmax = Kt·σnom = 2.508 × 62.50 = 156.8 MPa. Since the steel is ductile, local yielding at the edge of the hole only redistributes the load and the static yield factor is based on nominal stress. For fatigue, the notch is less severe than the theoretical value because of notch sensitivity: Kf = 1 + q(Kt - 1) = 1 + 0.85 × (2.508 - 1) = 2.282. The fatigue peak stress is then Kf·σnom = 2.282 × 62.50 = 142.6 MPa, lower than the 156.8 MPa elastic peak. For information, if the elastic peak were compared with the yield strength of 350 MPa the factor would be 2.23, so the edge reaches local yield only above this load. The fatigue peak stress 142.6 MPa is what a fatigue check would use in a Goodman analysis.

Answer: 142.6 MPa

(d)

The ratio is now d/w = 24/60 = 0.400, and Kt = 3.00 - 3.13(0.400) + 3.66(0.160) - 1.53(0.0640) = 3.00 - 1.252 + 0.5856 - 0.0979 = 2.236. The net area falls to (60 - 24) × 8 = 288 mm², so σnom = 24 000/288 = 83.33 MPa. The peak stress is σmax = 2.236 × 83.33 = 186.3 MPa. Remarkably, Kt has decreased from 2.51 to 2.24, yet the peak stress has risen from 156.8 MPa to 186.3 MPa, an increase of about 19 percent (186.3/156.8 = 1.19), because the loss of net area outweighs the drop in the concentration factor. The factor of safety on yield (350/186.3) is now 1.88, much less safety than before (2.23). The lesson is that a lower Kt does not mean a lower stress: it must always be multiplied by the nominal stress on the section it is based on. The proposal should be rejected unless the lug is widened or thickened.

Answer: 186.3 MPa

Problem 2 [A4-077] Bolted joints preload and joint stiffness

A pressure vessel cover plate is held by M12 × 1.75 class 8.8 bolts, each with a tensile stress area of 84.3 mm², a shank cross-sectional area of 113.1 mm² and a proof strength of 600 MPa. The total grip is 40 mm, of which 26 mm is unthreaded shank and 14 mm is threaded length within the grip. The bolt steel has E = 207 GPa. A frustum analysis of the clamped members (steel plate and a hard gasket) gives a combined member stiffness of 1.40 GN/m. Each bolt is tightened to 75 percent of its proof load. In service each bolt sees an external separating load of 12 kN. A maintenance proposal would replace the hard gasket with a soft elastomeric one that lowers the member stiffness to 0.35 GN/m.

  1. (a) Calculate the bolt stiffness kb, in GN/m, treating the shank and the threaded part in the grip as springs in series. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the required preload Fi, in kN, and the joint constant C. [4]
  3. (c) Find the load factor against joint separation n0 = Fi/[P(1 - C)] for the existing hard-gasket joint. [5]
  4. (d) What-if: the hard gasket is replaced by the soft one (km = 0.35 GN/m) with the same preload. Calculate the new joint constant, the new separation factor, and the peak bolt load Fb. Give the peak bolt load as the answer. [6]
(a)

For two sections in series the stiffness is kb = Ad·At·E/(Ad·lt + At·ld), where ld is the unthreaded length and lt the threaded length within the grip. Substituting Ad = 113.1 mm², At = 84.3 mm², E = 207 000 N/mm², lt = 14 mm and ld = 26 mm: numerator = 113.1 × 84.3 × 207 000 = 1.9735 × 10⁹; denominator = 113.1 × 14 + 84.3 × 26 = 1583 + 2192 = 3775 mm³. Then kb = 1.9735 × 10⁹/3775 = 5.228 × 10⁵ N/mm = 0.523 GN/m. The smaller threaded area controls the flexibility of the bolt since the same force strains it more per unit length. A bolt with more of the grip in unthreaded shank would be stiffer, but in a joint it is normally a softer bolt, relative to the members, that helps by carrying a smaller share of the external load.

Answer: 0.523 GN/m

(b)

The proof load is Fp = Sp·At = 600 × 84.3 = 50 580 N. For a reusable connection the preload is taken as 75 percent of this, so Fi = 0.75 × 50 580 = 37 935 N = 37.94 kN. The joint constant, the fraction of the external load that is carried by the bolt, is C = kb/(kb + km) = 0.523/(0.523 + 1.40) = 0.272. This means 27 percent of the external load goes into the bolt and 73 percent relieves the clamping force on the members. Because the members are much stiffer than the bolt, the bolt sees only a small change in load, which is the reason bolts in a properly designed joint have good fatigue performance. The preload is quite high at 75 percent of proof, so the tightening procedure must be controlled, usually by a torque wrench or a turn-of-nut method.

Answer: 37.94 kN

(c)

Separation of the members occurs when the external load has relieved the entire clamping force, that is when P(1 - C) equals the preload Fi. The load factor against separation is therefore n0 = Fi/[P(1 - C)]. Substituting: n0 = 37 935/[12 000 × (1 - 0.272)] = 37 935/8737 = 4.34. The member force that remains at the working load is Fi - P(1 - C) = 37 935 - 8737 = 29 198 N, so the clamp load is reduced by about 23 percent. A separation factor of 4.3 means the external load could rise to more than four times its present value before the joint opens, which is a generous margin for a pressure-containing joint. The bolt load at the working condition is Fb = Fi + C·P = 41.2 kN, still below the proof load of 50.6 kN.

Answer: 4.34

(d)

With km = 0.35 GN/m the joint constant becomes C = kb/(kb + km) = 0.523/(0.523 + 0.35) = 0.599. Now the bolt carries about 60 percent of the external load instead of 27 percent. The separation factor is n0 = 37 935/[12 000 × (1 - 0.599)] = 7.88, higher than the earlier 4.34, which looks like an improvement. However, the peak bolt load is Fb = Fi + C·P = 37.935 + 0.599 × 12 = 45.12 kN, compared with 41.20 kN before. The bolt is now closer to the proof load of 50.6 kN, and the load swing on the bolt in fatigue, C·P, is more than double. The soft gasket therefore improves the margin against leakage but harms the bolt, and it also relaxes with time and loses preload. For a pressure vessel with cyclic loading the stiff gasket is the better choice.

Answer: 45.12 kN

Problem 3 [A4-078] Bolted joints under fatigue loading

The head of a reciprocating compressor is bolted down with M10 × 1.5 class 8.8 studs, each with a tensile stress area of 58.0 mm², a proof strength of 600 MPa, an ultimate strength of 830 MPa and a fully corrected endurance strength of 129 MPa for the rolled threads. The joint constant is 0.25. Each stud is tightened to 75 percent of its proof load. The gas pressure causes the external load on each stud to cycle from zero to 9.0 kN at every compressor revolution. The fatigue factor of safety for the stud is to be found with the modified Goodman criterion written for a bolt with a known preload, nf = Se(Sut - σi)/[Sut·σa + Se(σm - σi)], where σi is the preload stress. A service technician suggests tightening the studs to only 50 percent of proof load to reduce the stress in them.

  1. (a) Calculate the preload stress and the alternating stress amplitude in the stud at 75 percent preload. Give the alternating stress as the answer. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the fatigue factor of safety nf for the 75 percent preload using the given Goodman expression. [5]
  3. (c) What-if: the technician tightens the studs to only 50 percent of proof load. Calculate the new fatigue factor of safety. [5]
  4. (d) For the 50 percent preload, calculate the load factor against separation n0 = Fi/[P(1 - C)] and compare it with the 75 percent case. Give the 50 percent value as the answer, and say whether the technician's suggestion is acceptable. [6]
(a)

The preload is Fi = 0.75 × Sp × At = 0.75 × 600 × 58.0 = 26 100 N, so the preload stress is σi = Fi/At = 26 100/58.0 = 450.0 MPa. The stud takes a fraction C of the external load, so its load swings from Fi to Fi + C·P, a range of C·P = 0.25 × 9000 = 2250 N. The alternating component is half the range: σa = C·P/(2·At) = 2250/(2 × 58.0) = 19.40 MPa. The mean stress is σm = σa + σi = 19.40 + 450.0 = 469.4 MPa. The alternating stress is small, only about 4 percent of the preload stress, because the bolt is much more flexible than the clamped parts. This is the central fact of bolted joint design: the high preload carries most of the stress and it is steady, so it does not contribute to fatigue damage in the way that an alternating stress does.

Answer: 19.4 MPa

(b)

Substituting into nf = Se(Sut - σi)/[Sut·σa + Se(σm - σi)]: numerator = 129 × (830 - 450.0) = 129 × 380 = 49 020 MPa². Denominator = 830 × 19.40 + 129 × (469.4 - 450.0). Since σm - σi = σa = 19.40 MPa, the denominator is 830 × 19.40 + 129 × 19.40 = 959 × 19.40 = 18 605 MPa². Therefore nf = 49 020/18 605 = 2.635. The studs have a fatigue safety factor of about 2.6, which is adequate for a pulsating load with a good deal of scatter. The expression is the Goodman line passing through the preload point on the mean-stress axis, which accounts for the fact that the mean stress is not zero but starts at σi. This is valid when the preload does not change during service, and it assumes no relaxation of the joint.

Answer: 2.64

(c)

At 50 percent preload, Fi = 0.50 × 600 × 58.0 = 17 400 N and σi = 300.0 MPa. The alternating stress is unchanged at σa = 19.40 MPa because the joint constant and the external load are unchanged, and σm = σa + σi = 319.4 MPa. The numerator is 129 × (830 - 300.0) = 129 × 530 = 68 370 MPa², while the denominator is still 959 × 19.40 = 18 605 MPa². Then nf = 68 370/18 605 = 3.675. The calculated fatigue factor has improved from 2.64 to 3.67, because a lower mean stress moves the working point away from the Goodman line. This result is correct but misleading if taken alone: the lower preload does not make the joint better overall, since the preload is what holds the joint together, and the next part examines what is lost.

Answer: 3.67

(d)

For the 50 percent preload: n0 = Fi/[P(1 - C)] = 17 400/[9000 × (1 - 0.25)] = 17 400/6750 = 2.58. For the 75 percent preload the value is 26 100/6750 = 3.87. The separation margin falls by a third. A factor of 2.6 still keeps the members clamped under the nominal gas load, but in a compressor head the margin has to cover pressure spikes, thermal growth and relaxation of the gasket, and the sealing of the joint depends on the clamp load. The lower preload also makes the stud more likely to loosen under vibration and it reduces the friction available to resist shear. The technician's suggestion trades a small fatigue gain, the factor rising from 2.64 to 3.67, for a significant loss of joint security. It should be rejected: the preload should stay at the high design value, with the torque controlled carefully.

Answer: 2.58

Problem 4 [A4-079] Welded joints

A steel bracket carries a vertical load of 18 kN applied 200 mm to the right of the centroid of a weld group. The bracket is attached to a column flange by two parallel vertical fillet welds, each 150 mm long, with their centre lines 80 mm apart. Both welds have a leg size of 6 mm, so each has an effective throat of 0.707 times the leg. The weld metal has a tensile yield strength of 345 MPa and the distortion-energy shear yield strength is 0.577 times this. The welds are treated as lines, the primary shear is assumed uniform over the throat area, and the torsional secondary shear follows from the polar moment of the weld group about its centroid. A customer asks to move the load outward to an eccentricity of 300 mm to clear a new guard.

  1. (a) Calculate the primary shear stress in the welds, and the total throat area. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the polar moment of area of the weld group about its centroid and the maximum resultant shear stress at the most severely loaded corner. Give the maximum stress as the answer. [6]
  3. (c) Find the factor of safety of the weld against yielding using the distortion-energy shear yield strength. [4]
  4. (d) What-if: the load is moved outward to an eccentricity of 300 mm. Recalculate the maximum shear stress and the factor of safety. Give the factor of safety as the answer. [6]
(a)

The total throat area is the effective throat times the total weld length: A = 0.707 × h × (2 × 150) = 0.707 × 6 × 300 = 1273 mm². The primary shear stress arises from the direct vertical load, assumed to be shared equally over the throat: τ' = F/A = 18 000/1273 = 14.14 MPa. This stress acts vertically downward, in the direction of the load, and is the same at every point of the welds. The primary shear is a small part of the total, since the main effect on this joint is the moment produced by the offset load. The throat is the plane of minimum area of the fillet, at 45 degrees to the legs, which is why the actual leg size is multiplied by 0.707 and not used directly. The calculation assumes the welds have no defects and that the load is shared equally between them.

Answer: 14.14 MPa

(b)

For two parallel line welds of length d separated by b, the unit polar moment about the group centroid is Ju = d(d² + 3b²)/6 = 150(22 500 + 19 200)/6 = 1042500 mm³. The polar moment of the throat area is J = 0.707 × h × Ju = 0.707 × 6 × 1042500 = 4.42 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The moment is M = F·e = 18 000 × 200 = 3.6 × 10⁶ N·mm. The critical point is a corner, at 40 mm horizontally and 75 mm vertically from the centroid. The secondary shear components there are τ'x = M·y/J = 3.6 × 10⁶ × 75/4.42 × 10⁶ = 61.1 MPa (horizontal) and τ'y = M·x/J = 3.6 × 10⁶ × 40/4.42 × 10⁶ = 32.6 MPa (vertical, downward at the right-hand side so it adds to the primary shear). The resultant is τ = √(61.1² + (32.6 + 14.1)²) = 76.9 MPa.

Answer: 76.87 MPa

(c)

The shear yield strength of the weld metal is Ssy = 0.577 × Sy = 0.577 × 345 = 199.1 MPa. The factor of safety is the ratio of this strength to the maximum shear stress in the throat: n = Ssy/τmax = 199.1/76.9 = 2.59. A factor of 2.6 indicates that the load could be raised by about 2.6 times before first yielding of the throat at the worst corner. For a static load on a ductile weld, many design codes call for factors of between 2 and 3, so the design is acceptable but not generous. Note that the throat is assumed to be loaded in pure shear, which is the standard simplification, and that the base metal should be checked separately; the weld is usually the weaker element when the electrode strength matches the plate.

Answer: 2.59

(d)

The weld geometry is unchanged, so A, Ju and J keep their values and the primary shear remains 14.14 MPa. Only the moment increases: M = 18 000 × 300 = 5.4 × 10⁶ N·mm, which is 1.5 times the earlier value. The secondary shear components scale with M: τ'x = 91.6 MPa and τ'y = 48.8 MPa. The resultant is τ = √(91.6² + (48.8 + 14.1)²) = 111.2 MPa. The factor of safety is n = 199.1/111.2 = 1.79. A 50 percent increase in eccentricity has reduced the safety factor from 2.59 to 1.79, a 31 percent reduction, which is less than 33 percent because the primary shear does not grow. Many design offices require at least 2.0 for a static load, and the margin is smaller here than that. The remedy is to increase the leg size (about 8 mm would restore the margin) or to lengthen the welds, and the 300 mm position should not be approved as it stands.

Answer: 1.79

Problem 5 [A4-080] Helical compression springs

A compression spring in a spring-loaded safety relief mechanism is wound from music wire of diameter 3.5 mm with a mean coil diameter of 24 mm. It has 8 active coils, squared and ground ends, and a free length of 65 mm. The shear modulus is 79.3 GPa. The maximum working load is 300 N. For squared and ground ends, the total number of coils is the active number plus 2, and the solid length is the wire diameter times the total number of coils. The Wahl factor for curvature and direct shear is Kw = (4C - 1)/(4C - 4) + 0.615/C, where C is the spring index. A redesign is proposed to increase the number of active coils to 10, keeping the same wire, coil diameter and free length, in order to reduce the rate.

  1. (a) Calculate the spring rate, in N/mm. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the spring index and the Wahl correction factor Kw. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the maximum shear stress in the wire at the working load of 300 N. [6]
  4. (d) What-if: the number of active coils is increased to 10 with the same wire, diameters and free length. Calculate the clearance between the loaded spring and the solid condition at 300 N, in mm, and say whether the redesign is acceptable. Give the clearance as the answer. [6]
(a)

The rate of a helical compression spring is k = G·d⁴/(8·D³·Na). With G = 79 300 N/mm², d = 3.5 mm, D = 24 mm and Na = 8: d⁴ = 3.5⁴ = 150.06 mm⁴ and D³ = 24³ = 13 824 mm³. The numerator is 79 300 × 150.06 = 1.190 × 10⁷ and the denominator is 8 × 13 824 × 8 = 884 736. Therefore k = 1.190 × 10⁷/884 736 = 13.45 N/mm. The rate is the force needed per millimetre of deflection, and the equation follows from the torsion of the wire, with the deflection of each coil proportional to the cube of the coil diameter. It assumes that the ends do not contribute stiffness, that only the active coils deflect and that the wire stays in the elastic range. The rate is a design target and a manufacturer would also hold a tolerance on it, commonly about plus or minus 10 percent.

Answer: 13.45 N/mm

(b)

The spring index is the ratio of the mean coil diameter to the wire diameter: C = D/d = 24/3.5 = 6.857. A moderate index between 4 and 12 is practical for coiling, and this value is well inside that range. The Wahl factor is Kw = (4C - 1)/(4C - 4) + 0.615/C. The first term is (4 × 6.857 - 1)/(4 × 6.857 - 4) = 26.43/23.43 = 1.128 and the second is 0.615/6.857 = 0.0897. Summing, Kw = 1.2177. The factor accounts for two effects at once: the direct shear (which adds to the torsional shear) and the curvature of the coil, which concentrates the stress on the inside of the coil, where the failure starts. The correction is about 22 percent, and it increases as the index falls, so a tightly wound spring has a much higher peak stress than the simple torsion formula would indicate.

Answer: 1.218

(c)

The corrected shear stress at the inside of the coil is τ = Kw·8FD/(πd³). First, 8FD = 8 × 300 × 24 = 57 600 N·mm. The wire section term is πd³ = π × 42.875 = 134.7 mm³, and the uncorrected stress is 57 600/134.7 = 427.6 MPa. Applying the Wahl factor, τ = 1.2177 × 427.6 = 520.7 MPa. For music wire of this size the ultimate tensile strength is roughly 1900 MPa, and a common design guide allows the static shear stress to reach about 45 percent of this ultimate strength, which is about 855 MPa, so the stress here is well within the limit and would leave a factor above 1.6 for a static load. The calculation takes the load as static; a spring that cycles many times needs a fatigue check, because the inside of the coil is where cracks start. At the working load the deflection is 22.3 mm.

Answer: 520.7 MPa

(d)

With Na = 10 the rate becomes k = 79 300 × 150.06/(8 × 13 824 × 10) = 10.76 N/mm, which is 20 percent lower. The deflection at 300 N is y = F/k = 300/10.76 = 27.9 mm. The total number of coils is Nt = 10 + 2 = 12, so the solid length is Ls = 3.5 × 12 = 42 mm. The clearance to the solid condition at the working load is L0 - Ls - y = 65 - 42 - 27.9 = -4.9 mm. The negative clearance means the coils would be fully closed before the load reached 300 N, so the spring would go solid at a load below the working load. For comparison, the original design had a clearance of 7.7 mm, with a solid length of 35 mm and a deflection of 22.3 mm, which is positive but modest. The redesign is not acceptable at this free length: the free length would have to be raised by about 5 mm to reach solid exactly at 300 N (42 + 27.9 = 69.9 mm), and by about 13 mm (to roughly 78 mm) to restore the original clearance of 7.7 mm, or the wire diameter could be changed.

Answer: -4.88 mm

A4 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A4-081] Shaft design under combined loading

A transmission countershaft in a mining conveyor gearbox is a solid steel shaft simply supported on two ball bearings, A and B, 400 mm apart. A spur gear of 90 mm pitch radius sits 150 mm from bearing A and delivers 18 kW at 900 rpm. The gear has a 20° pressure angle, and its tangential and radial tooth forces act in perpendicular planes through the gear centre. Treat the bearings as simple supports and neglect shaft weight, gear weight, axial load and stress concentration. The shaft steel has a yield strength of 420 MPa and is to be sized by the distortion energy theory with a factor of safety of 2.5 applied at the section under the gear, where bending is a maximum and the full torque is carried. Bearing A is a deep-groove ball bearing that must reach a basic rating life of 20 000 hours at 900 rpm, with a load factor of 1.0.

  1. (a) Find the torque transmitted by the shaft. [4]
  2. (b) Find the resultant bending moment at the gear section. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum shaft diameter using the distortion energy theory. [6]
  4. (d) Find the dynamic load rating C required for bearing A. [5]
(a)

Assume steady power transmission with no losses between the gear and the coupling. The angular speed is ω = 2π × 900/60 = 94.25 rad/s. The torque follows from power = torque × angular speed, so T = P/ω = 18 000/94.25 = 191.0 N·m. The tooth forces then follow from the pitch radius: the tangential force is Ft = T/r = 191.0/0.090 = 2122 N, and the radial force is Fr = Ft tan 20° = 772 N. These two forces lie in perpendicular planes, so they are resolved separately into reactions and moments and combined by vector sum in the next part. Keep power in watts and speed in rad/s: using rpm directly in the torque equation is the commonest slip in this type of question, and it changes the answer by a factor of about nine.

Answer: 191.0 N·m

(b)

Treat each plane as a simply supported beam with a point load at a = 0.150 m from A and b = 0.250 m from B, span L = 0.400 m. The reaction at A in the tangential plane is RAx = Ft b/L = 2122 × 0.250/0.400 = 1326 N, and in the radial plane RAy = Fr b/L = 772 × 0.250/0.400 = 483 N. The bending moments under the gear are Mx = RAx a = 1326 × 0.150 = 198.9 N·m and My = RAy a = 483 × 0.150 = 72.4 N·m. Because the planes are perpendicular, the resultant is M = √(Mx² + My²) = √(198.9² + 72.4²) = 211.7 N·m. This is the largest moment on the shaft, since the load is a single point load and the moment diagram peaks beneath it. The reaction RA is carried forward to the bearing selection.

Answer: 211.7 N·m

(c)

At the surface of a solid round shaft the bending stress is σ = 32M/(πd³) and the torsional shear stress is τ = 16T/(πd³). With no axial load, the von Mises stress is σ' = √(σ² + 3τ²) = (32/πd³) √(M² + 0.75T²). The design condition is σ' = Sy/n, with Sy = 420 MPa and n = 2.5, so the allowable von Mises stress is 168 MPa. Evaluating the moment term: √(211.7² + 0.75 × 191.0²) = 268.7 N·m. Solving for the diameter, d³ = 32 n Me/(π Sy) = 32 × 2.5 × 268.7/(π × 420 × 10⁶) = 1.629 × 10⁻⁵ m³, giving d = 25.3 mm. Round up to the next standard size when specifying the shaft. The torque term is weighted by 0.75 because the shear stress enters through the factor 3 inside the root.

Answer: 25.3 mm

(d)

The bearing sees only radial load, with a load factor of 1.0, so the equivalent load equals the radial reaction at A: RA = √(RAx² + RAy²) = √(1326² + 483²) = 1411 N. The life in millions of revolutions is L10 = 60 n Lh/10⁶ = 60 × 900 × 20 000/10⁶ = 1080 million revolutions. For a ball bearing the life exponent is p = 3, so L10 = (C/P)³ and C = P L101/3 = 1411 × 10801/3 = 1411 × 10.260 = 14481 N. The required dynamic rating is therefore 14.48 kN, and a catalogue bearing with a rating above this value at 90 percent reliability should be chosen. Using the larger of the two reactions is correct, as bearing A is the more heavily loaded because the gear sits nearer to it.

Answer: 14.48 kN

Problem 2 [A4-082] Rolling bearing selection and life

A belt-driven pulley shaft on a bulk-material feeder is supported at one end by a deep-groove ball bearing that runs at 600 rpm. When fully loaded the bearing carries a radial force of 4200 N and an axial force of 1300 N, with the inner ring rotating (V = 1). The catalogue gives e = 0.26; when Fa/(V Fr) exceeds e, use X = 0.56 and Y = 1.6. The machine runs fully loaded for 60 percent of the operating time and at half of both the radial and axial loads for the remaining 40 percent, at the same speed. The user wants a basic rating life of 30 000 hours. For a reliability of 98 percent the life adjustment factor is a1 = 0.33, while 90 percent reliability uses a1 = 1. Take the ball bearing life exponent as 3 and assume a load factor of 1.0.

  1. (a) Find the equivalent dynamic load at full load. [4]
  2. (b) Find the cubic-mean equivalent load for the duty cycle. [4]
  3. (c) Find the dynamic load rating C required for 98 percent reliability and 30 000 hours. [6]
  4. (d) A bearing with C = 48 kN is fitted. Find its basic rating life in hours at 90 percent reliability under the duty cycle. [6]
(a)

First test which set of factors applies. The ratio Fa/(V Fr) = 1300/(1 × 4200) = 0.310, which exceeds e = 0.26, so the axial load matters and X = 0.56, Y = 1.6 apply. The equivalent dynamic load is P = X V Fr + Y Fa = 0.56 × 4200 + 1.6 × 1300 = 2352 + 2080 = 4432 N. If the ratio had been below e, the equation would reduce to P = V Fr, and the axial load would be ignored by the catalogue method. The same X and Y also apply at half load, because halving both forces leaves the ratio unchanged, so the half-load equivalent is simply 0.5 P = 2216 N. Marks are given for testing the ratio before choosing the factors, since selecting X and Y without that check is a conceptual error even when the arithmetic is right.

Answer: 4432 N

(b)

With a life exponent p = 3 and constant speed, the damage from each load level adds in proportion to the time at that level and the cube of the load. The equivalent steady load is Pm = (Σ fi Pi³)1/3, where fi is the fraction of time. Here Pm = (0.60 × 4432³ + 0.40 × 2216³)1/3. The cubes are 8.706 × 10¹⁰ N³ and 1.088 × 10¹⁰ N³, so the weighted sum is 5.659 × 10¹⁰ N³ and Pm = 3839 N. Because speed is constant, time fraction equals revolution fraction, so no further weighting is needed. If the speed changed between the two states, each fraction would have to be taken as a share of total revolutions instead. The result is lower than the full-load value because the half-load periods contribute only one eighth as much damage.

Answer: 3839 N

(c)

The adjusted life equation is L = a1 L10, so the catalogue L10 life must be at least L/a1. The required life in millions of revolutions is L = 60 n Lh/10⁶ = 60 × 600 × 30 000/10⁶ = 1080 million revolutions. For 98 percent reliability a1 = 0.33, so the catalogue life needed is L10 = 1080/0.33 = 3273 million revolutions. Then C = Pm L101/3 = 3839 × 14.85 = 57000 N, or 57.0 kN. For comparison, the rating for 90 percent reliability would be 39.4 kN, so asking for 98 percent costs a rating increase of about 45 percent. The candidate should show the reliability factor used as a divisor of the life and not as a multiplier of the load, which is the usual error here.

Answer: 57.0 kN

(d)

At 90 percent reliability a1 = 1, and the life follows from L10 = (C/Pm)³ in millions of revolutions. Substituting, L10 = (48 000/3839)³ = (12.50)³ = 1954 million revolutions. The life in hours is Lh = L10 × 10⁶/(60 n) = 1954 × 10⁶/(60 × 600) = 54289 h, roughly 5.43 × 10⁴ h. This comfortably exceeds the 30 000 h requirement, which is consistent with the 98 percent check in part (c), because C = 48 kN is below the 57.0 kN needed for 98 percent reliability but above the 39.4 kN needed at 90 percent. Hence the bearing meets the life target at 90 percent reliability but would not meet it at 98 percent. Give the life to three significant figures, as catalogue ratings carry that precision only.

Answer: 54300 h

Problem 3 [A4-083] Journal bearing basics

A plain journal bearing supports the impeller shaft of a centrifugal water pump. The journal diameter is 80 mm, the bearing length is 80 mm, and the radial clearance is 0.050 mm. The shaft turns at 1500 rpm under a steady radial load of 6.0 kN. The oil film has a viscosity of 0.025 Pa·s at its operating temperature. Assume the journal runs concentric with the bearing so that Petroff's equation applies, and take the bearing pressure as the load divided by the projected area. All friction work is converted to heat, which is dissipated from the housing surface of area 0.50 m² with a combined convection and radiation coefficient of 18 W/m²K. The designer also asks what happens if the machined radial clearance comes out at twice the specified value, with all other conditions unchanged.

  1. (a) Find the bearing pressure based on the projected area. [3]
  2. (b) Find the coefficient of friction from Petroff's equation, f = 2π² (μN/p)(r/c). [5]
  3. (c) Find the power lost to friction. [4]
  4. (d) Find the steady temperature rise of the housing above the ambient air. [4]
  5. (e) Find the friction power loss if the radial clearance is 0.100 mm instead. [4]
(a)

The projected area of a journal bearing is the diameter times the length, so A = D L = 0.080 × 0.080 = 0.0064 m². The bearing pressure is p = W/A = 6000/0.0064 = 937500 Pa, which is 0.938 MPa. This is a lightly loaded bearing, well below the pressures of several MPa used in the design of heavily loaded engine bearings, so film breakdown by overloading is not a concern at this stage. The pressure is also the quantity needed in Petroff's equation, where it appears as the ratio of viscous term to load per projected area. Care is needed with units: viscosity is in Pa·s, speed must be in revolutions per second in the Petroff equation, and pressure must be in pascals, otherwise the friction coefficient comes out wrong by a factor of 10⁶ or 2π.

Answer: 0.938 MPa

(b)

Petroff's equation assumes a concentric journal, a uniform film thickness c all round, and a Newtonian oil. The speed in revolutions per second is N = 1500/60 = 25.0 rev/s. The journal radius is r = 0.040 m and the radial clearance is c = 0.050 mm = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, so r/c = 800. The viscous group is μN/p = 0.025 × 25.0/937500 = 6.667 × 10⁻⁷. Substituting, f = 2π² × 6.667 × 10⁻⁷ × 800 = 0.01053. This is a typical hydrodynamic value, about one to two orders of magnitude below dry or boundary friction coefficients. The true value for a loaded bearing is higher, since the journal runs eccentric with a thinner film at the loaded side, but Petroff gives the right order and the correct dependence on speed, viscosity and clearance.

Answer: 0.01053

(c)

The friction force at the journal surface is f W, and it acts at the journal radius, so the friction torque is T = f W r = 0.01053 × 6000 × 0.040 = 2.527 N·m. The angular speed is ω = 2π N = 2π × 25.0 = 157.08 rad/s. The power loss is H = T ω = 2.527 × 157.08 = 397 W. This amounts to a small fraction of the pump drive power but all of it appears as heat in the oil film, which is why the thermal check in the next part matters. An equivalent route is H = f W V, with rubbing speed V = ω r = 6.28 m/s, which gives the same answer and serves as a useful check. The sign convention is simple here because the torque always opposes rotation, so the power is a positive loss.

Answer: 397 W

(d)

At steady state the heat generated equals the heat dissipated from the housing: H = h A ΔT, where h is the combined coefficient and A the surface area. Rearranging, ΔT = H/(h A) = 397/(18 × 0.50) = 397/9.0 = 44.1 K. With an ambient temperature of, say, 25 °C, the housing would settle near 69 °C, which is acceptable for a mineral oil. This neglects heat carried away by oil circulation and by conduction into the shaft, so it is conservative. The viscosity quoted is assumed to be valid at that temperature, and if the oil were much hotter the viscosity would fall and the friction would fall with it, so the answer is self-consistent only if the quoted viscosity already reflects the operating temperature.

Answer: 44.1 K

(e)

Petroff's coefficient of friction is proportional to r/c, so doubling the clearance halves it, with pressure, speed and viscosity unchanged. The new coefficient is f2 = f/2 = 0.00526. The friction torque and the power loss are proportional to f, so H2 = H/2 = 198 W, and the housing temperature rise also halves to 22.0 K. This looks like an improvement, but the Petroff model hides the penalty: a larger clearance lowers the film's ability to carry load, because the eccentric operating point moves to a lower Sommerfeld number and the film becomes thinner relative to the surface roughness. In practice the designer would accept the lower friction only after checking the minimum film thickness, which Petroff's concentric assumption cannot give.

Answer: 198 W

Problem 4 [A4-084] Spur and helical gear stress

A 20-tooth spur pinion of module 4 mm and face width 40 mm drives a screw conveyor in a grain handling plant. The pinion transmits 15 kW at 1200 rpm. Use the Lewis equation for bending with a form factor Y = 0.322 (based on the tooth number, stated here), and a velocity factor Kv = (6.1 + V)/6.1 with the pitch-line speed V in metres per second, which suits cut teeth. The pinion material has an allowable bending stress of 220 MPa, taken as the strength to be compared with the calculated stress. Neglect other service and overload factors. The designer wants the torque on the pinion shaft, the tooth load, the stress and the margin of safety, and the highest power the pinion could carry at the same speed before the bending stress reaches the allowable stress.

  1. (a) Find the torque on the pinion shaft. [3]
  2. (b) Find the tangential tooth force at the pitch circle. [3]
  3. (c) Find the bending stress at the tooth root. [5]
  4. (d) Find the factor of safety against the 220 MPa allowable bending stress. [4]
  5. (e) Find the maximum power the pinion can transmit at 1200 rpm when the bending stress equals 220 MPa. [5]
(a)

The pitch diameter of a spur gear is d = m z = 4 × 20 = 80 mm, so the pitch radius is 40 mm. The angular speed is ω = 2π × 1200/60 = 125.66 rad/s. With power transmitted steadily and gear losses neglected, the torque is T = P/ω = 15 000/125.66 = 119.4 N·m. This is the torque the pinion shaft must carry and also the torque that produces the tooth force at the pitch circle. Check the units: with power in watts and angular speed in rad/s the torque is directly in newton-metres. If the speed had been left in rpm, the torque would be wrong by the factor 2π/60, so the conversion is worth showing explicitly for method marks in a closed-book setting where there is no unit-aware calculator to catch the slip.

Answer: 119.4 N·m

(b)

The tangential force acts at the pitch radius, so Wt = T/r = 119.4/0.040 = 2984 N. An equivalent route uses the pitch-line speed: V = π d n/60 = π × 0.080 × 1200/60 = 5.027 m/s, and Wt = P/V = 15 000/5.027 = 2984 N, which agrees and acts as a cross-check. This force is the load carried by one tooth at the pitch point in the Lewis model, which treats the tooth as a cantilever loaded at its tip, and the radial force component, which is not needed for bending in this simple model, would be Wt tan φ for a 20° pressure angle. The pitch-line speed is also needed for the dynamic factor in the next part, so it is worth recording here.

Answer: 2984 N

(c)

The Lewis equation with a velocity factor gives σ = Kv Wt/(F m Y). First the velocity factor: Kv = (6.1 + V)/6.1 = (6.1 + 5.027)/6.1 = 1.824. The denominator uses the face width F = 40 mm, module m = 4 mm and form factor Y = 0.322: F m Y = 40 × 4 × 0.322 = 51.52 mm². Because Wt is in newtons and the dimensions are in millimetres, the stress comes out directly in N/mm², which equals MPa. Substituting, σ = 1.824 × 2984/51.52 = 105.7 MPa. The velocity factor increases the stress to allow for dynamic loading as teeth come into mesh, and a higher speed would raise it. The Lewis model ignores stress concentration at the root fillet, which is why a conservative allowable stress is chosen.

Answer: 105.7 MPa

(d)

The factor of safety in bending is the ratio of the strength to the calculated stress: n = σall/σ = 220/105.7 = 2.08. A value near 2 is reasonable for a conveyor drive with moderate shock, where the service factors have been left out of the calculation. If the designer later introduces an application factor for the screw conveyor starting under load, say 1.5, the effective factor of safety would fall to 1.39, which is thin. Note that surface fatigue (pitting) has not been checked, and it often governs gear life more than root bending, so this factor applies only to the bending mode. Quote the result to three significant figures, but recognise that the Lewis form factor, read from a table, limits the accuracy to roughly five percent.

Answer: 2.08

(e)

At the limit, σ = σall = 220 MPa, and the stress is proportional to the tangential force at constant speed, since Kv depends only on pitch-line speed. Solve the Lewis equation for the force: Wt,max = σall F m Y/Kv = 220 × 51.52/1.824 = 6214 N. The power follows from P = Wt V = 6214 × 5.027 = 31235 W, or 31.2 kW. Because the stress is linear in load, this is simply the present power multiplied by the factor of safety: 15 × 2.08 = 31.2 kW, which confirms the result. The pinion would then have no margin at all, so the usable rating is lower, and the surface durability limit and the shaft bearings would probably restrict the drive to a smaller value than this bending limit.

Answer: 31.2 kW

Problem 5 [A4-085] Clutches

A wet multi-plate clutch couples a diesel engine to a heavy flywheel on a rock-crusher drive. The clutch has six friction surfaces, each an annulus of outer radius 100 mm and inner radius 60 mm, pressed together by a total axial force of 2.4 kN. The coefficient of friction is 0.10 and the lining is assumed to wear uniformly. The engine side turns at a constant 2000 rpm while the clutch engages. The crusher flywheel, with moment of inertia 1.2 kg·m², starts from rest and is accelerated only by the clutch torque, with no load torque during engagement. The steel plates have a combined mass of 3.0 kg and specific heat 480 J/kg·K, and all of the slip energy goes into them with no loss to the oil during the short engagement.

  1. (a) Find the torque capacity of the clutch under the uniform wear assumption. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum contact pressure on the linings. [3]
  3. (c) Find the time taken for the flywheel to reach clutch speed. [4]
  4. (d) Find the energy dissipated in the clutch during one engagement. [4]
  5. (e) Find the average temperature rise of the plates for one engagement. [5]
(a)

For uniform wear the pressure varies inversely with radius, and the frictional torque per surface is T1 = μ F rm, where rm = (Ro + Ri)/2 is the mean radius. Here rm = (100 + 60)/2 = 80 mm = 0.080 m. The axial force F = 2400 N passes through every interface, so the torque capacity of N = 6 surfaces is T = N μ F rm = 6 × 0.10 × 2400 × 0.080 = 115.2 N·m. The uniform wear model gives a lower torque than the uniform pressure model, which would give a larger effective radius, and it is the standard assumption for a worn-in clutch, so the capacity is not overestimated. Hence the clutch can transmit 115.2 N·m before it slips, and while slipping during engagement it supplies exactly this constant torque to the flywheel.

Answer: 115.2 N·m

(b)

With uniform wear, the product p r is constant, so the maximum pressure occurs at the inner radius Ri. The axial force satisfies F = ∫ p 2π r dr = 2π p_max Ri (Ro − Ri), giving p_max = F/(2π Ri (Ro − Ri)). Substituting, p_max = 2400/(2π × 0.060 × 0.040) = 2400/0.01508 = 159155 Pa, or 0.159 MPa. This is the peak at the inside edge; the pressure at the outer radius is lower by the ratio Ri/Ro = 0.6, at 0.095 MPa. The peak is compared with the allowable value for the lining, typically about 1 MPa for wet paper-based material, so this clutch is comfortably lightly loaded. The force F is the total axial load, not a load per surface, since the same load is transmitted through the stack.

Answer: 0.159 MPa

(c)

The flywheel is accelerated only by the clutch torque T = 115.2 N·m, with no load torque, so its angular acceleration is constant: α = T/J = 115.2/1.2 = 96.0 rad/s². The final speed equals the engine speed, ω = 2π × 2000/60 = 209.4 rad/s. Starting from rest, the engagement time is t = ω/α = 209.4/96.0 = 2.18 s. This assumes the engine speed holds constant during slip, which is reasonable for a large diesel but optimistic, as the engine speed would dip under this sudden load. A long engagement time gives a gentle start and a lower heating rate, while a short one increases shock loading on the drive line, so the time is a design choice controlled by the actuation force; the energy dissipated per engagement is fixed at ½Jω² = 26.3 kJ either way (part d).

Answer: 2.18 s

(d)

During slip the relative angular speed starts at ω and falls linearly to zero, and the dissipated power is the clutch torque times the relative speed. Integrating over the engagement time gives E = T ∫ (ω − α t) dt = T ω t/2. Using the numbers, E = 115.2 × 209.4 × 2.18/2 = 26319 J. An energy balance confirms this: the flywheel gains kinetic energy ½ J ω² = ½ × 1.2 × 209.4² = 26319 J, and the clutch dissipates an equal amount. This is a well-known result for a clutch engaging an inertia from rest at constant driver speed: the energy lost equals the energy stored, whatever the clutch torque. The energy is 26.32 kJ per engagement, and a clutch rated for repeated engagements would be assessed on the energy per unit friction area.

Answer: 26.32 kJ

(e)

All the dissipated energy is absorbed by the plates and none is carried off by the oil in this short event, so the sensible heat gives E = m c ΔT. Solving, ΔT = E/(m c) = 26319/(3.0 × 480) = 26319/1440 = 18.3 K. This is a modest rise for a single engagement, but crusher drives engage repeatedly, and it is the accumulated rise between cooling intervals that limits the engagement frequency. If the cycle repeated every 60 seconds with no cooling, the plates would gain 18.3 K every minute, and the lining would be at risk within minutes. The real peak temperature at the rubbing surface is higher than this average because the heat is generated at the interface and conducts inwards, so a designer adds a margin or uses a transient conduction check.

Answer: 18.3 K

A4 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A4-086] Brakes

A simple band brake is fitted to the drum of a rail-yard retarder winch. The drum has a diameter of 0.50 m and is rigidly attached to a flywheel, giving a total moment of inertia of 40 kg·m², spinning at 600 rpm. The brake band wraps 270° around the drum with a coefficient of friction of 0.30. The brake lever is pivoted at a fulcrum, with the tight end of the band attached at the fulcrum itself and the slack end attached 0.10 m from the fulcrum. The operator pushes at a point 0.80 m from the fulcrum. The drum is to be brought to rest in 8.0 s at constant deceleration, and the maximum allowable band pressure on the lining is 0.50 MPa. Neglect the band's own weight and any friction at the fulcrum.

  1. (a) Find the braking torque needed to stop the drum in 8.0 s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the slack-side tension in the band. [4]
  3. (c) Find the force the operator must apply at the lever end. [4]
  4. (d) Find the minimum band width for the 0.50 MPa pressure limit. [4]
  5. (e) Find the kinetic energy absorbed by the brake in one stop. [4]
(a)

The initial angular speed is ω = 2π × 600/60 = 62.83 rad/s. For constant deceleration over 8.0 s, the angular deceleration is α = ω/t = 62.83/8.0 = 7.854 rad/s². The braking torque required to produce this deceleration on the combined inertia is T = J α = 40 × 7.854 = 314.2 N·m. This neglects any friction in the bearings or windage, which would help the brake a little, so the answer is conservative. The same torque must be developed at the drum surface by the difference in band tensions, and it is this value that sets the tight and slack tensions in the next parts. The kinetic energy removed is a separate quantity and is found in the last part, using the same initial speed.

Answer: 314.2 N·m

(b)

For a band brake the tension ratio follows the capstan equation, T1/T2 = eμθ, where θ is the wrap angle in radians. Here θ = 270° = 3π/2 = 4.712 rad, so μθ = 0.30 × 4.712 = 1.4137 and the ratio is e1.4137 = 4.111. The tension difference supplies the braking torque at the drum radius r = 0.25 m: T1 − T2 = T/r = 314.2/0.25 = 1256.6 N. Combining the two relations, T2 (ratio − 1) = 1256.6, so T2 = 1256.6/(4.111 − 1) = 403.9 N. The tight-side tension is T1 = T2 + 1256.6 = 1660.5 N, which is needed for the pressure check. The drum is assumed to turn so that the tight end is the one attached at the fulcrum, which is the layout that minimises the operator effort.

Answer: 404 N

(c)

Take moments about the fulcrum for the lever. The tight end acts through the fulcrum, so its tension has no moment. Only the slack-side tension T2 acts at 0.10 m, and the operator force P acts at 0.80 m. Equilibrium gives P × 0.80 = T2 × 0.10, so P = 403.9 × 0.10/0.80 = 50.5 N. The low value shows why this arrangement is preferred: the operator works against the small slack tension only, with a mechanical advantage of eight. If the drum rotated the other way, the tight end would be attached at 0.10 m and the slack end at the fulcrum, and the operator force would be 208 N, which is 4.1 times larger, so the direction of rotation matters for the choice of layout.

Answer: 50.5 N

(d)

The pressure on the lining is highest at the tight end, where the band tension is largest. At that end p_max = T1/(b r), where b is the band width and r the drum radius, from equilibrium of a short element of band. Rearranging, b = T1/(p_max r) = 1660.5/(0.50 × 10⁶ × 0.25) = 1660.5/125000 = 0.01328 m, which is 13.3 mm. A practical band would be wider than this to allow for uneven wear and for edge effects, so a standard width of, say, 40 to 50 mm might be chosen. The value is small because the loads are modest, and the result also fixes the lining area for the heat check, which has to be done separately for repeated stops. Use the tight-end tension, not the average, because the tight end governs the peak pressure.

Answer: 13.3 mm

(e)

The energy to be dissipated equals the kinetic energy of the rotating inertia, E = ½ J ω² = ½ × 40 × 62.83² = 78957 J, which is 78.96 kJ. All of this appears as heat at the lining and drum, since the load torque is neglected. A cross-check uses the torque and the angle turned: the drum turns through θ = ω t/2 = 62.83 × 8.0/2 = 251.3 rad during the constant deceleration, so the work done is T θ = 314.2 × 251.3 = 78957 J, in agreement. The heat flux on the contact area should be checked if stops are frequent, since the drum temperature rises with each stop and can cause fade. The mean power during the stop is E/t = 9870 W, much larger than the continuous dissipation capacity of a small drum.

Answer: 78.96 kJ

Problem 2 [A4-087] Belt and chain drives

A 15 kW, 1440 rpm electric motor drives a hay-bale conveyor through an open flat belt. The motor pulley has a diameter of 250 mm and the driven pulley 600 mm, with a centre distance of 1.50 m. The coefficient of friction between the belt and the smaller pulley is 0.35, and slip is assumed to occur first on that pulley. The belt has a mass of 0.90 kg per metre of length and the maximum permissible tension in the belt is 1800 N. Account for centrifugal tension in the belt, assume the power is transmitted steadily and neglect pulley bearing friction. The designer wants the belt speed, the arc of contact, the tight and slack tensions at the rated load, the belt length, and the greatest power the belt could carry at this speed.

  1. (a) Find the belt speed. [3]
  2. (b) Find the angle of contact on the smaller pulley. [3]
  3. (c) Find the tight-side tension at the rated load. [5]
  4. (d) Find the length of the open belt. [4]
  5. (e) Find the maximum power the belt could transmit at this speed when T1 reaches 1800 N. [5]
(a)

The belt speed equals the rim speed of the motor pulley, assuming no slip other than the elastic creep that is neglected here. The angular speed is ω = 2π × 1440/60 = 150.80 rad/s, and the pulley radius is 0.125 m, so V = ω r = 150.80 × 0.125 = 18.85 m/s. Equivalently V = π D n/60 = π × 0.250 × 1440/60 = 18.85 m/s. This speed is within the usual range for flat belts, up to about 30 m/s, and it is high enough that the centrifugal tension is significant. The driven pulley turns at 1440 × 250/600 = 600 rpm, which is the output speed of the drive. The belt speed is the quantity that links the power to the effective tension and the centrifugal term in the subsequent parts.

Answer: 18.85 m/s

(b)

For an open belt the angle of contact on the smaller pulley is θ = π − 2 sin⁻¹[(D − d)/(2C)], where D and d are the larger and smaller pulley diameters and C is the centre distance. Substituting, (D − d)/(2C) = (0.600 − 0.250)/(2 × 1.50) = 0.1167, and sin⁻¹ of this is 0.1169 rad. So θ = π − 2 × 0.1169 = 2.9077 rad, which is 166.6°. The contact angle on the larger pulley is the larger value, π + 2 × 0.1169 = 3.375 rad, so the smaller pulley governs slip, as stated. A greater centre distance would increase the wrap and the capacity of the drive, and a smaller ratio of pulley diameters would do the same, which is why belts with large speed ratios use a tensioning idler.

Answer: 166.6 degrees

(c)

The effective (net) tension is the difference between the tight and slack tensions, and equals power over speed: T1 − T2 = P/V = 15 000/18.85 = 795.8 N. The centrifugal tension is Tc = m V² = 0.90 × 18.85² = 319.8 N. With centrifugal effect the friction relation is (T1 − Tc)/(T2 − Tc) = eμθ, where μθ = 0.35 × 2.9077 = 1.0177, so the ratio is 2.767. Subtracting, (T1 − Tc) − (T2 − Tc) = T1 − T2, so T1 − Tc = Fe r/(r − 1) = 795.8 × 2.767/(2.767 − 1) = 1246.2 N. Adding the centrifugal tension gives T1 = 1246.2 + 319.8 = 1566 N, which is below the 1800 N limit, so the belt is safe at rated load. The slack tension is T2 = T1 − Fe = 770 N, and it stays positive, so the belt does not go slack.

Answer: 1566 N

(d)

The standard approximation for the length of an open belt is L = 2C + (π/2)(D + d) + (D − d)²/(4C). The terms are as follows. The straight-run term is 2C = 2 × 1.50 = 3.000 m. The arc term is (π/2)(0.600 + 0.250) = (π/2) × 0.850 = 1.3352 m. The correction for the angle of the straight runs is (0.350)²/(4 × 1.50) = 0.1225/6.0 = 0.02042 m. Adding the three, L = 3.000 + 1.3352 + 0.02042 = 4.356 m. The approximation is accurate when the diameter difference is small compared with the centre distance, which holds here since (D − d)/C is only 0.23. Belt supplier length tolerances and the take-up allowance for initial stretch mean that the belt purchased would be a little shorter than this nominal length, with the tensioning adjustment made at the motor mount.

Answer: 4.356 m

(e)

At the limit, T1 = 1800 N and the belt is on the point of slipping on the small pulley. The centrifugal tension is unchanged since the speed is the same: Tc = 319.8 N. The effective tension is then found from the friction relation: T1 − T2 = (T1 − Tc)(1 − 1/r) = (1800 − 319.8) × (1 − 1/2.767) = 1480.2 × 0.6386 = 945.2 N. The maximum power is P = (T1 − T2) V = 945.2 × 18.85 = 17817 W, or 17.82 kW. This exceeds the 15 kW rating by 19 percent, so the belt has a reserve in strength and friction. The power is not increased indefinitely by speeding the belt up, because the centrifugal tension grows with V² and eventually leaves nothing for transmission; the optimum belt speed for maximum power is V = √(T1/(3m)).

Answer: 17.82 kW

Problem 3 [A4-088] Power screws

A single-start square-thread screw jack lifts a 30 kN load on a bridge bearing replacement job. The screw has a mean diameter of 40 mm and a pitch (equal to the lead) of 8 mm. The coefficient of friction in the threads is 0.12. The load is carried on a thrust collar of mean radius 30 mm with a coefficient of friction of 0.10. The jack is driven by a motor through a gearbox that turns the screw, and the load is to be lifted at a steady 6.0 mm/s. Neglect the weight of the screw and assume the load does not rotate. The engineer wants the torque to raise the load, the overall efficiency, whether the jack would overhaul (run back) when the drive is released, and the drive power required.

  1. (a) Find the total torque needed to raise the load, including collar friction. [6]
  2. (b) Find the overall efficiency of the jack when raising the load. [4]
  3. (c) Find the torque needed to lower the load, and state whether the jack is self-locking. [5]
  4. (d) Find the drive power required to raise the load at 6.0 mm/s. [5]
(a)

The lead angle of the thread is λ = tan⁻¹(l/(π dm)) = tan⁻¹(8/(π × 40)) = 3.643°. The friction angle is φ = tan⁻¹(μ) = tan⁻¹(0.12) = 6.843°. For a square thread, raising the load needs a thread torque T_t = W (dm/2) tan(λ + φ) = 30 000 × 0.020 × tan(10.485°) = 111.0 N·m. The collar adds a friction torque T_c = μc W rc = 0.10 × 30 000 × 0.030 = 90.0 N·m, with the load assumed to act at the mean collar radius. The total torque is T = 111.0 + 90.0 = 201.0 N·m. Notice that the collar friction is nearly as large as the thread friction, so a thrust bearing in place of the plain collar would cut the torque substantially. The collar term is easily forgotten and is worth a clear mark in the scheme.

Answer: 201.0 N·m

(b)

The efficiency is the useful work output divided by the work input over one revolution of the screw. The load rises by one lead l = 8 mm per revolution, so the useful work is W l = 30 000 × 0.008 = 240 J. The input work is the torque times the angle turned, 2π T = 2π × 201.0 = 1263.2 J. Hence η = W l/(2π T) = 240/1263.2 = 0.190, or 19.0 percent. The thread alone, ignoring the collar, would give an efficiency of tan λ/tan(λ + φ) = 0.344, so the collar friction cuts the efficiency from 0.344 to 0.190. A low efficiency is the price of a self-locking jack: an efficiency below 0.5 is a necessary condition for the screw to hold the load unaided, and this one is well under that.

Answer: 0.190

(c)

When lowering, the friction opposes the motion in the same way, but the load now helps the screw to turn, so the thread torque becomes T_t = W (dm/2) tan(φ − λ) when φ > λ. Here φ = 6.843° exceeds λ = 3.643°, so tan(φ − λ) = tan(3.200°) = 0.0559 and T_t = 30 000 × 0.020 × 0.0559 = 33.5 N·m. The collar friction still opposes the turning, so it adds 90.0 N·m. The total lowering torque is 123.5 N·m. The value is positive, meaning a torque must be applied to lower the load, so the load will not run down on its own and the jack is self-locking. Even if the collar were frictionless the thread alone still needs a positive torque, because φ > λ. Self-locking is the condition μ > tan λ.

Answer: 123.5 N·m

(d)

The lead is 8 mm per revolution, so at a lifting speed of 6.0 mm/s the screw turns at n = 6.0/8.0 = 0.75 rev/s, which is 45 rpm. The angular speed of the screw is ω = 2π × 0.75 = 4.712 rad/s. The power at the screw is P = T ω = 201.0 × 4.712 = 947 W. As a cross-check, the useful output power is W v = 30 000 × 0.006 = 180 W, and dividing by the efficiency of 0.190 gives 947 W, which agrees. The motor must supply a little more than this to allow for the gearbox losses, so with a gearbox efficiency of 90 percent the motor would be about 1053 W. The very low screw speed means the gearbox needs a large reduction ratio, about 32:1 from a 1450 rpm motor.

Answer: 947 W

Problem 4 [A4-089] Material removal: cutting force and power

A shop is turning a stainless steel hydraulic cylinder rod and wants to understand the cutting mechanics. In an orthogonal-cutting analysis of a 90° approach turning cut, the uncut chip thickness (the feed) is 0.25 mm, the width of cut is 3.0 mm, and the tool rake angle is 8°. The cutting speed is 150 m/min. A dynamometer records a cutting force of 1250 N in the cutting direction and a thrust force of 520 N perpendicular to it. The chip is measured after the cut and has a thickness of 0.55 mm. Assume a single shear plane (Merchant model), a sharp tool, and that all of the power goes into the cut. The lathe drive has an overall efficiency of 80 percent between the motor and the spindle.

  1. (a) Find the shear plane angle. [4]
  2. (b) Find the shear stress on the shear plane. [6]
  3. (c) Find the cutting power. [3]
  4. (d) Find the specific cutting energy. [3]
  5. (e) Find the motor power needed to sustain the cut. [4]
(a)

The chip thickness ratio is r = t/tc = 0.25/0.55 = 0.4545. In the orthogonal model the shear angle follows from tan φ = r cos α/(1 − r sin α), where α = 8° is the rake angle. Substituting, the numerator is 0.4545 × cos 8° = 0.4501 and the denominator is 1 − 0.4545 × sin 8° = 0.9367. So tan φ = 0.4501/0.9367 = 0.4805, and φ = 25.67°. The shear plane is a fairly shallow one, typical of a ductile stainless steel that produces a thick chip: the ratio r is well below unity. A larger shear angle would mean a thinner chip, a lower cutting force and a lower shear plane area, and these things are all linked through the friction at the tool-chip interface.

Answer: 25.7 degrees

(b)

The shear force on the plane is found by resolving the measured forces along it: Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ = 1250 × cos 25.67° − 520 × sin 25.67° = 1126.7 − 225.2 = 901.5 N. The shear plane area is the width times the uncut thickness divided by sin φ: As = b t/sin φ = 3.0 × 0.25/sin 25.67° = 1.732 mm². The shear stress on the plane is then τ = Fs/As = 901.5/1.732 = 521 N/mm², that is 521 MPa. This is in the expected range for the shear strength of a stainless steel during cutting, where strain hardening and the high strain rate raise the stress above the static value. The result depends strongly on the shear angle, because the area and the force resolution both change with φ, so an error of one degree in φ shifts τ by a few percent.

Answer: 521 MPa

(c)

The cutting power is the product of the cutting force and the cutting speed, since the thrust force does no work as it acts perpendicular to the motion. The speed in SI units is V = 150/60 = 2.50 m/s. The power is Pc = Fc V = 1250 × 2.50 = 3125 W, or 3.125 kW. The feed motion contributes a negligible additional power, as the feed velocity is tiny compared with the cutting speed: with the spindle at about 600 rpm and 0.25 mm per revolution the feed speed is only 2.5 mm/s. For this reason the cutting power is taken as the power at the tool tip, and it is the basis for sizing the motor and for estimating the heat generated in the cut.

Answer: 3.125 kW

(d)

The specific cutting energy is the energy per unit volume of material removed, equal to the cutting force divided by the chip cross-sectional area: u = Fc/(t b) = 1250/(0.25 × 3.0) = 1250/0.75 = 1667 N/mm² = 1.667 J/mm³. The same result comes from power over metal removal rate. The removal rate is MRR = V t b = 150 000 mm/min × 0.25 × 3.0 = 112500 mm³/min, which is 1875 mm³/s, and the cutting power is 3125 W, giving 1.667 J/mm³. Mild steel sits near 2 J/mm³, so this figure is of the same order, and at the low end for stainless steel, which usually needs more energy because it work hardens strongly under the tool.

Answer: 1.667 J/mm³

(e)

The motor must supply the cutting power plus the losses in the lathe drive. With an overall efficiency of 80 percent, Pmotor = Pc/η = 3125/0.80 = 3906 W, which is 3.91 kW. A motor rated at 5 kW or larger would be specified in practice, because a roughing cut at higher depth or feed raises the force proportionally, and a margin must be kept for tool wear, which increases the cutting force by 20 percent or more as the flank wear develops. The thrust force needs no power but loads the tool holder, so the setup must be rigid enough to hold the 520 N without chatter. At the metal removal rate found above, the motor is working at a moderate load for a mid-size lathe.

Answer: 3.91 kW

Problem 5 [A4-090] Machining: tool life and cost

A job shop turns 100 mm diameter, 300 mm long carbon steel shafts with a carbide insert. Two test cuts at a feed of 0.30 mm/rev gave a tool life of 60 min at a cutting speed of 120 m/min and 20 min at 160 m/min. Assume the Taylor tool life equation V Tⁿ = C holds. The machine and operator are charged at $48.00 per hour overhead included. Each cutting edge costs $9.00 and replacing it takes 2.5 min. Loading, unloading and gauging take 4.0 min per part, independent of the cutting speed. The cutting length equals the full 300 mm and the tool approach and overrun can be neglected. The planner wants the minimum cost per part, not the maximum production rate, and will hold the feed fixed.

  1. (a) Find the Taylor exponent n. [3]
  2. (b) Find the constant C in the Taylor equation, in m/min for T in minutes. [3]
  3. (c) Find the tool life that gives the minimum cost per part. [4]
  4. (d) Find the cutting speed for minimum cost. [5]
  5. (e) Find the total cost per part at the optimum speed. [5]
(a)

Two test points on the Taylor equation give V1 T1ⁿ = V2 T2ⁿ, so (V2/V1) = (T1/T2)ⁿ. Taking logarithms, n = ln(V2/V1)/ln(T1/T2). Substituting the data, V2/V1 = 160/120 = 1.3333 and T1/T2 = 60/20 = 3.000, so n = ln(1.3333)/ln(3.000) = 0.2877/1.0986 = 0.262. The value is in the range quoted for carbide tools, between about 0.2 and 0.5, and it is much higher than for high-speed steel, which is typically 0.1 to 0.15. The exponent measures the sensitivity of tool life to speed: a rise in speed of 33 percent here cuts the life by a factor of three, and this is the reason why economic speeds are set well below the maximum the machine can deliver.

Answer: 0.262

(b)

With n known, C follows from either test point, because C = V Tⁿ. Using the first point, C = 120 × 600.262. The power is 600.262 = e0.262 × ln 60 = e0.262 × 4.0943 = 2.9216, so C = 120 × 2.9216 = 350.6 m/min. Checking with the second point as a verification: 160 × 200.262 = 160 × 2.1912 = 350.6 m/min, which agrees with the first result to within rounding. The constant C has the physical meaning of the cutting speed that gives a one-minute tool life, and it is the speed scale of the tool-workpiece pair. The check against the second test point is a worthwhile habit because it catches any slip in the arithmetic of the exponent.

Answer: 350.6 m/min

(c)

The minimum cost per part occurs when the tool life is T_opt = (1/n − 1)(tc + Ct/Co), where tc is the tool change time, Ct the cost per cutting edge and Co the operating rate per minute. The rate is Co = 48.00/60 = $0.80 per minute. The tool cost expressed in machine minutes is Ct/Co = 9.00/0.80 = 11.25 min. Adding the change time, tc + Ct/Co = 2.5 + 11.25 = 13.75 min. The factor (1/n − 1) = (1/0.262 − 1) = 2.819, so T_opt = 2.819 × 13.75 = 38.8 min. This lies between the 20 and 60 minute test lives, so the optimum is within the tested speed range. Note that this is the cost optimum, which gives a longer tool life and a lower speed than the maximum production rate optimum.

Answer: 38.8 min

(d)
