This is why designers minimise the gap and why the force can be written as the rate of change of this stored energy with gap length.

Answer: 0.802 J

Problem 2 [A5-067] DC motor characteristics and speed control

A 230 V separately excited DC motor with armature resistance 0.35 Ω drives a centrifugal ventilation fan. At the full-speed operating point the armature current is 70 A and the speed is 1150 rpm, with constant rated field flux. The fan torque varies with the square of speed. The plant engineer wants to reduce the fan speed to 900 rpm at night to save energy and is comparing two methods: inserting a resistor in series with the armature, or lowering the armature supply voltage with a controlled rectifier. Neglect armature reaction, brush drop, friction and windage, and assume the field flux stays constant in both cases. Neglect the field circuit input power, which is the same in both.

  1. (a) Determine the back emf, the voltage constant KΦ and the developed torque at the full-speed point (give the torque). [6]
  2. (b) Determine the series armature resistance required to run the fan at 900 rpm. [8]
  3. (c) Determine the power saved at the input by using armature-voltage control rather than series resistance at 900 rpm. [6]
(a)

Assume constant flux, so the back emf is proportional to speed. The armature voltage equation gives Ea1 = V - Ia Ra = 230 - 70 × 0.35 = 205.5 V. The angular speed is ω1 = 2π × 1150/60 = 120.43 rad/s, so the voltage constant is KΦ = Ea1/ω1 = 1.7064 V·s/rad. The same constant links torque to armature current, so the developed torque is T1 = KΦ Ia = 1.7064 × 70 = 119.4 N·m. As a check, the electromagnetic power is Ea Ia = 14385 W, and T ω = 119.4 × 120.43 = 14385 W, which matches. Candidates should show that the same constant appears in both the emf and the torque expressions, since this is what lets the later parts be solved without knowing the flux.

Answer: 119.4 N·m

(b)

For a fan, torque is proportional to speed squared, and with constant flux torque is proportional to armature current. So Ia2 = 70 × (900/1150)² = 42.87 A. The back emf is proportional to speed: Ea2 = 205.5 × 900/1150 = 160.83 V. With the full 230 V supply, the armature loop equation is V = Ea2 + Ia2 (Ra + Rs). Solving, Ra + Rs = (230 - 160.83)/42.87 = 1.613 Ω, so Rs = 1.613 - 0.35 = 1.26 Ω. The resistor dissipates Ia2² Rs = 2322 W as heat. A marker looks for the square-law torque being used to find the new current, not the assumption that current stays at 70 A, which is the constant-torque case and would give a completely different resistor.

Answer: 1.26 Ω

(c)

With series resistance the supply is still 230 V, so the input power is V Ia2 = 230 × 42.87 = 9861 W. With voltage control, the armature voltage is lowered to Va = Ea2 + Ia2 Ra = 160.83 + 42.87 × 0.35 = 175.8 V, so the input is Va Ia2 = 7538 W. The saving is 9861 - 7538 = 2322 W, or 2.32 kW, all of which was being burned in the resistor. The shaft power at 900 rpm is about Ea2 Ia2 = 6895 W in both cases, so the efficiency of the armature path rises from 69.9 percent with the resistor to 91.5 percent with voltage control. Note the motor develops torque 73.2 N·m at the lower speed. State that the saving applies to the armature circuit only.

Answer: 2.32 kW

Problem 3 [A5-068] DC generator

A self-excited shunt generator in a small hydro installation is driven at 1200 rpm. Its open-circuit characteristic at that speed was measured with the field separately excited: field current 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5 A gives generated voltage 8, 60, 105, 135, 150 and 158 V respectively, with straight-line interpolation between points. The total shunt-field circuit resistance, including the rheostat, is set at 96 Ω. The armature resistance is 0.15 Ω. Neglect armature reaction and brush drop. The operator wants the no-load voltage, the critical field resistance for build-up at this speed, the effect of the turbine running slower at 1000 rpm, and the terminal voltage when the generator delivers 40 A to the load.

  1. (a) Determine the no-load terminal voltage at 1200 rpm. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the critical field resistance at 1200 rpm, taken as the slope of the initial linear part of the characteristic (residual point to 0.5 A), above which build-up is lost. [4]
  3. (c) Determine the no-load terminal voltage if the turbine speed falls to 1000 rpm with the same field resistance. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the terminal voltage at 1200 rpm when the generator supplies a 40 A load current. [6]
(a)

With no load, the terminal voltage equals the generated voltage because the armature current is only the field current, and the drop in 0.15 Ω is negligible. The field current is set by the terminal voltage through the field line V = Rf If = 96 If. The operating point is where this field line meets the open-circuit characteristic. Between 1.0 and 1.5 A the characteristic is Eg = 105 + 60 (If - 1.0) = 45 + 60 If. Setting 45 + 60 If = 96 If gives If = 45/36 = 1.250 A, which lies within that segment, so the voltage is V = 96 × 1.250 = 120.0 V. The intersection is stable because the characteristic flattens as saturation sets in. State that the field line is drawn from the origin with slope Rf and that a graphical solution would give the same result.

Answer: 120.0 V

(b)

Voltage build-up from residual magnetism proceeds only if the field line is below the initial, nearly linear, part of the open-circuit characteristic. The initial slope is taken between the residual point (0 A, 8 V) and the next point (0.5 A, 60 V), which gives dEg/dIf = (60 - 8)/(0.5 - 0) = 104 Ω. Here the critical field resistance is defined as the slope of the initial linear part of the characteristic. A field circuit resistance above 104 Ω gives a field line steeper than that initial part, so build-up is lost or confined to a low voltage near the weak part of the curve. The present setting of 96 Ω is below that, so build-up occurs, but only by 8 Ω, a small margin. A marker expects the critical resistance to be identified as a tangent slope of the initial linear part, and the reasoning about the field line lying above or below the curve.

Answer: 104 Ω

(c)

Generated voltage is proportional to speed at a given field current, so the characteristic is scaled by 1000/1200 = 0.8333. In the segment from 0.5 to 1.0 A the original curve is Eg = 15 + 90 If, so at 1000 rpm Eg = 0.8333 × (15 + 90 If) = 12.5 + 75 If. Setting this equal to the field line 96 If gives If = 12.5/21 = 0.595 A, which lies in the segment, so V = 96 × 0.595 = 57.1 V. The speed fell by 16.7 percent but the voltage fell by 52 percent, because the lower speed also lowers the field current through the self-excitation feedback. The critical resistance at this speed is scaled to 87 Ω, so by the part (b) criterion 96 Ω now exceeds the scaled critical value of 87 Ω and the voltage settles at a much reduced 57.1 V near the weak part of the curve. A further speed drop would collapse the voltage.

Answer: 57.1 V

(d)

The armature current is the sum of load and field currents, Ia = IL + If, and the terminal voltage is Vt = Eg - Ia Ra with Vt = 96 If. Combining, Eg(If) - (40 + If)(0.15) = 96 If. In the 1.0 to 1.5 A segment Eg = 45 + 60 If, so 45 + 60 If - 6 - 0.15 If = 96 If, which gives 39 = 36.15 If and If = 1.079 A. Then Vt = 96 × 1.079 = 103.6 V. The generated emf is 109.7 V, the armature current is 41.08 A and the armature drop is 6.16 V. The terminal voltage falls from 120.0 V at no load because of this armature drop and the consequent reduction in field current, which is the characteristic drooping behaviour of a shunt generator. Show the iteration or algebra in the correct segment.

Answer: 103.6 V

Problem 4 [A5-069] Three-phase induction motor

A 460 V (line), 60 Hz, four-pole, wye-connected three-phase induction motor drives a boiler feed pump. The per-phase equivalent circuit has R1 = 0.25 Ω, X1 = 0.70 Ω, magnetising reactance Xm = 28.0 Ω, referred rotor resistance R2' = 0.20 Ω and referred rotor leakage reactance X2' = 0.70 Ω. Core loss is neglected and the rotational loss is a fixed 600 W. At rated load the slip is 0.030. The plant is considering a variable-frequency drive to run the pump at 45 Hz using constant volts-per-hertz control, with all reactances scaling in proportion to frequency and the same developed torque required. Use the exact equivalent circuit, not the approximate form.

  1. (a) Determine the stator line current at rated slip 0.030 (state the power factor in your working). [6]
  2. (b) Determine the developed (air-gap) torque at rated slip. [7]
  3. (c) Determine the rotor speed at 45 Hz with constant V/f control that develops the same torque as in part (b). [7]
(a)

Use the per-phase equivalent circuit with Vph = 460/√3 = 265.6 V as reference. The rotor branch impedance is Zr = R2'/s + jX2' = 6.667 + j0.700 Ω. It is in parallel with jXm = j28.0 Ω, giving Zf = 6.021 + j2.081 Ω. The total input impedance is Zin = R1 + jX1 + Zf = 6.271 + j2.781 Ω, whose magnitude is 6.860 Ω at an angle of 23.92°. The stator current is I1 = Vph/Zin = 38.72 A, lagging the phase voltage by that angle, so the power factor is cos(23.92°) = 0.914 lagging. The magnetising branch carries part of the current, which is why the power factor is well below unity. Show the parallel combination in complex form and the final division.

Answer: 38.72 A

(b)

The air-gap power is the power crossing the air gap into the rotor, Pag = 3 |I2'|² R2'/s, where I2' is found from the current divider: I2' = I1 × jXm/(jXm + Zr). Its magnitude is 36.79 A, so Pag = 3 × 36.79² × 6.667 = 27073 W. The synchronous speed is 120 f/p = 1800 rpm, or ωs = 188.50 rad/s, so the developed torque is T = Pag/ωs = 27073/188.50 = 143.6 N·m. Mechanical power developed is (1 - s) Pag = 26261 W, and subtracting the 600 W rotational loss leaves a shaft output of 25661 W, so the shaft torque is 140.3 N·m. Mark the distinction between developed and shaft torque; the shaft value is lower because of rotational loss. Show the current-divider step.

Answer: 143.6 N·m

(c)

With constant volts per hertz the supply voltage is 460 × 45/60 per line, so the phase voltage is 345.0 V, and all reactances scale by 0.75: X1 = 0.525, Xm = 21.00, X2' = 0.525 Ω. The resistances do not scale. The synchronous speed is 120 × 45/4 = 1350 rpm, so ωs = 141.37 rad/s. Torque as a function of slip is T(s) = 3 |I2'|² (R2'/s)/ωs, with I2' found from the same equivalent circuit at 45 Hz. Solving T(s) = 143.6 N·m numerically gives s = 0.0411. The speed is n = ns(1 - s) = 1350 × (1 - 0.0411) = 1295 rpm. The slip is slightly higher than 0.030 because the stator resistance forms a larger part of the stator impedance at lower frequency, reducing the flux. Explain that constant V/f keeps flux roughly constant.

Answer: 1295 rpm

Problem 5 [A5-070] Synchronous motor and alternator

A mining plant is served from a 4160 V, 60 Hz three-wire bus. The existing induction-motor load takes 1500 kW at 0.72 lagging power factor. Management plans to add a wye-connected, three-phase, round-rotor synchronous motor to drive a mill, and to use it also for power factor correction. The motor has a synchronous reactance of 8.0 Ω per phase and negligible armature resistance. At the planned operating point the motor takes 500 kW from the bus at 0.80 leading power factor, with terminal voltage 4160 V. The engineer needs the excitation emf required, the resulting plant power factor with both loads on, and an idea of the margin before the motor pulls out of step if the load torque grows with the excitation held fixed.

  1. (a) Determine the line-to-line excitation emf of the synchronous motor at the planned operating point. [7]
  2. (b) Determine the overall plant power factor with the synchronous motor and the existing load running together. [6]
  3. (c) Determine the maximum power the motor could develop before pulling out of step with the excitation held at the value in part (a). [7]
(a)

For a motor, the phase equation is Vp = E + jXs I, so E = Vp - jXs I. The terminal phase voltage is 4160/√3 = 2401.8 V as reference. The line current is I = 500 000/(√3 × 4160 × 0.80) = 86.74 A, and because the power factor is leading the current phasor is at +36.87°, giving 69.39 + j52.04 A. The synchronous reactance drop is jXs I = -416.4 + j555.1 V. Subtracting from Vp gives E = 2818.1 - j555.1 V, so |E| = 2872.3 V per phase and the line value is √3 × 2872.3 = 4975 V, or 4.975 kV. The torque angle is 11.14°. The excitation emf is greater than the terminal voltage, as expected for a motor over-excited to take leading current. Show the phasor subtraction rather than magnitudes alone.

Answer: 4.975 kV

(b)

Work with the power triangle for each load. The existing load has Q = P tan(arccos 0.72) = 1500 × 0.9639 = 1446 kvar lagging, and an apparent power of 2083 kVA. The synchronous motor takes 500 kW at 0.80 leading, so its reactive power is Q = 500 × tan(36.87°) = 375 kvar leading, which counts as negative: -375 kvar. Totals are P = 1500 + 500 = 2000 kW and Q = 1446 - 375 = 1071 kvar. The apparent power is 2269 kVA and pf = P/S = 0.882 lagging. The plant power factor improves from 0.72 to 0.882 and the bus current rises from 289 A to 315 A because the 500 kW motor load is added, but the power factor improves from 0.72 to 0.882, so the current rises far less than the real power does. Sign conventions are a common loss of marks, so state that leading reactive power reduces the net lagging total.

Answer: 0.882

(c)

For a round-rotor machine with negligible resistance, the power per phase is P = (E V/Xs) sin δ, so the total is P = 3 E V sin δ/Xs. The maximum occurs at δ = 90°: Pmax = 3 × 2872.3 × 2401.8/8.0 = 2587 kW. The motor now runs at an angle of 11.14° developing 500 kW, which is only 19.3 percent of the pull-out value. The ratio Pmax/P is 5.17, a comfortable stability margin; practical designs keep at least about 1.5 times for transient swings. Raising the excitation would raise Pmax in proportion to E, while a lower bus voltage reduces it. State that sudden load increases make the rotor swing past the steady-state angle, so a margin larger than one is necessary.

Answer: 2587 kW

A5 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A5-071] Diodes and rectifier circuits

A bench power unit uses a 60 Hz mains transformer with a centre-tapped secondary. Each half of the secondary delivers 18.0 V rms with the primary on 230 V rms. The two halves feed a full-wave rectifier built from two silicon diodes, each dropping 0.70 V when conducting, and the output goes directly to a 40.0 Ω resistive load with no filter capacitor. Treat the transformer as ideal and the diode drop as constant. The unit is being specified for a customer who wants to know the load voltages and currents, the reverse voltage the diodes must withstand and how efficiently the rectifier converts the transformer output into direct-current power.

  1. (a) Find the peak load voltage. [4]
  2. (b) Find the average (dc) load voltage and the average load current. [5]
  3. (c) Find the peak inverse voltage across a non-conducting diode. [5]
  4. (d) Treating the load current as a rectified sine wave of the peak found in (a), find the rectifier efficiency, the ratio of dc load power to total load power including the ac component, as a percentage. [6]
(a)

Each half secondary has peak value Vsm = 18.0 × √2 = 25.46 V. In a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier only one diode conducts at a time and carries the current from one half winding to the load, so the path contains exactly one diode drop. The peak load voltage is therefore Vp = Vsm − Vd = 25.46 − 0.70 = 24.76 V. The turns ratio does not enter because the secondary voltage is given directly. Assumptions: ideal transformer, no winding resistance, constant 0.70 V diode drop, and the load draws a continuous current whenever either half is positive. This peak value sets every other figure in the problem, so the later parts reuse 24.76 V. Answer: 24.76 V.

Answer: 24.76 V

(b)

For a full-wave rectified sine of peak Vp the average value is Vdc = 2Vp/π, because the average of |sin| over a cycle is 2/π. Substituting, Vdc = 2 × 24.76/π = 15.76 V. The load is a pure resistor, so the average current follows from Ohm's law applied to the average voltage: Idc = Vdc/R = 15.76/40.0 = 0.394 A. Because the diode drop was already subtracted from the peak, no further correction is needed, although a small error remains because the drop really distorts the waveform near zero crossings where the diodes switch. The ripple frequency is 120 Hz, twice the mains frequency, which matters later if a filter is added. Answer: Vdc = 15.76 V and Idc = 0.394 A.

Answer: Idc = 0.394 A

(c)

When one diode conducts, the other is reverse biased by the voltage across the whole secondary minus the drop of the conducting diode. The centre tap is at the load return, so the full secondary winding appears between the two anodes. At the peak of the cycle the conducting diode places one end of the winding at the load voltage Vp, while the opposite end sits at −18.0√2 relative to the tap. The reverse voltage on the off diode is therefore PIV = 2 Vsm − Vd = 2 × 25.46 − 0.70 = 50.21 V. A designer should select diodes with a repetitive reverse rating comfortably above this, commonly by a margin of 1.5 or more, because mains voltage can run high. A bridge rectifier would only need about half this rating. Answer: 50.21 V.

Answer: 50.21 V

(d)

The rectifier efficiency is the dc power divided by the total power delivered to the load. Dc power is Pdc = Idc²R = 0.394² × 40.0 = 6.21 W. The load current is a rectified sine of peak Ip = Vp/R = 24.76/40.0 = 0.619 A, and the rms value of a full-wave rectified sine is Ip/√2 = 0.438 A. Total load power is Irms²R = 7.66 W. The ratio is η = 6.21/7.66 = 81.1 percent, which matches the textbook 8/π² = 81.1 percent for an ideal full-wave rectifier. The remaining 18.9 percent is the ac ripple power, which a filter capacitor or inductor would mostly remove. Diode losses are excluded here. Answer: 81.1 percent.

Answer: 81.1 %

Problem 2 [A5-072] Power supplies with filter and regulator

A 12 V rms transformer secondary feeds a bridge rectifier made of four silicon diodes, each dropping 0.70 V, followed by a 2200 µF smoothing capacitor. The mains frequency is 60 Hz. The smoothed voltage supplies a 9.1 V Zener diode shunt regulator: a series resistor R from the capacitor to the Zener, with the load connected across the Zener. The load draws a constant 150 mA and the Zener must keep at least 5.0 mA for regulation at the lowest capacitor voltage. Estimate the ripple using the constant-current discharge approximation, and ignore the Zener dynamic resistance. The designer must pick the series resistor and then check the Zener for the worst case when the load is disconnected.

  1. (a) Find the peak capacitor voltage, with two diodes conducting in the bridge. [3]
  2. (b) Find the peak-to-peak ripple voltage on the capacitor at the 150 mA load plus the Zener minimum current. [5]
  3. (c) Find the largest series resistor R that keeps the Zener at 5.0 mA when the capacitor is at its minimum voltage. [6]
  4. (d) With the load disconnected and the capacitor at its peak, find the power dissipated in the Zener diode using the resistor from (c). [6]
(a)

In a bridge rectifier two diodes conduct in series on each half cycle, one in the path to the load and one in the return path, so two drops of 0.70 V are subtracted. The peak secondary voltage is 12.0 × √2 = 16.97 V. The peak capacitor voltage is Vp = 16.97 − 2 × 0.70 = 15.57 V. The capacitor charges to this value near each peak of the rectified waveform and then supplies the load as the input falls below it. This peak is the starting point for the ripple calculation in the next part and sets the maximum stress on the capacitor and the series resistor. The capacitor voltage rating should exceed 15.6 V with margin for mains tolerance, so a 25 V part would be a sensible choice. Answer: 15.57 V.

Answer: 15.57 V

(b)

Between charging peaks the capacitor discharges at nearly constant current, so the constant-current approximation gives ΔV = I t/C. For full-wave rectification the interval between peaks is T/2 = 1/(2f) = 1/120 s = 8.33 ms. The current drawn from the capacitor is the load current plus the Zener minimum, I = 150 + 5.0 = 155 mA. Then Vr = I/(2fC) = 0.155/(2 × 60 × 2200 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.155/0.264 = 0.587 V peak to peak. The approximation slightly overestimates ripple because the discharge interval is really a little shorter than T/2, the capacitor being recharged before the true minimum of the input. The ripple is small, about 3.8 percent of the peak, so the approximation is reasonable here. Answer: 0.587 V.

Answer: 0.587 V

(c)

The worst case for the Zener current is the lowest capacitor voltage, Vmin = Vp − Vr = 15.57 − 0.587 = 14.98 V. At that instant the series resistor must still pass the load current plus the minimum Zener current, 155 mA, with 9.1 V across the Zener. Applying Ohm's law to the resistor, R = (Vmin − Vz)/(IL + Iz,min) = (14.98 − 9.1)/0.155 = 38.0 Ω. Any larger resistor would let the Zener current fall below 5.0 mA at the minimum, losing regulation, so this is the maximum permitted value and a standard value just below it, such as 36 Ω, would normally be selected. The resistor dissipates the most power at peak input, a point checked in part (d). Answer: R = 38.0 Ω.

Answer: 38.0 Ω

(d)

With the load removed, the whole resistor current flows through the Zener. At the capacitor peak the current is Izmax = (Vp − Vz)/R = (15.57 − 9.1)/38.0 = 170 mA. The Zener voltage stays at 9.1 V, so its dissipation is Pz = Vz × Izmax = 9.1 × 0.170 = 1.55 W. This is the dissipation at the ripple peak; since the capacitor sits near the peak most of the time at light load, a 2 W Zener would be marginal and a 3 W or 5 W device is the safe choice. The result shows why a shunt regulator wastes power: at no load the Zener must absorb everything the load normally takes. A series-pass transistor regulator avoids this penalty. Answer: 1.55 W.

Answer: 1.55 W

Problem 3 [A5-073] BJT amplifier bias and gain

A common-emitter voltage amplifier is biased with a resistor divider from a 12.0 V supply: R1 = 47 kΩ from the supply to the base and R2 = 10 kΩ from the base to ground. The collector resistor is 2.2 kΩ and the emitter resistor is 560 Ω. The transistor has β = 150 and VBE = 0.70 V in the active region. Take the thermal voltage as 25 mV. A large emitter bypass capacitor shorts RE for signal frequencies, and the amplifier drives a 4.7 kΩ load through a coupling capacitor. Neglect the Early effect and the base-collector capacitance, and treat the coupling capacitors as short circuits at the signal frequency.

  1. (a) Find the quiescent collector current using the Thevenin equivalent of the base network. [6]
  2. (b) Find the quiescent collector-emitter voltage and state whether the transistor is in the active region. [4]
  3. (c) Find the mid-band voltage gain with the bypass capacitor in place. [5]
  4. (d) Find the amplifier input resistance seen by the source, including the bias network. [5]
(a)

Replace the divider by its Thevenin equivalent: Vth = 12.0 × 10/(47 + 10) = 2.105 V and Rth = 47k ∥ 10k = 8.246 kΩ. Writing the base-emitter loop, Vth = IB Rth + VBE + IE RE with IE = (β + 1) IB, so IB = (Vth − VBE)/(Rth + (β + 1) RE) = (2.105 − 0.70)/(8246 + 151 × 560) = 15.14 µA. The collector current is IC = β IB = 150 × 15.14 µA = 2.271 mA. The divider current is much larger than IB, about 211 µA against 15.1 µA, which is why this bias is stable against β variation, although the Thevenin method does not need that approximation. Answer: 2.271 mA.

Answer: 2.271 mA

(b)

Apply Kirchhoff's voltage law around the collector-emitter loop: VCE = Vcc − IC RC − IE RE. The emitter current is IE = (β + 1) IB = 2.286 mA. Substituting, VCE = 12.0 − 2.271 mA × 2.2 kΩ − 2.286 mA × 560 Ω = 12.0 − 4.997 − 1.280 = 5.72 V. Because VCE is well above the saturation value of about 0.2 V and VBE is 0.70 V forward biased, the transistor is in the active region, as assumed. The headroom is roughly half the supply, which allows a symmetric output swing before clipping. The dc load line has slope −1/(RC + RE), but the ac load line is steeper because of the bypassed emitter and the load. Answer: VCE = 5.72 V, active.

Answer: 5.72 V

(c)

For small signals the transconductance is gm = IC/VT = 2.271 mA/25 mV = 90.9 mS. With RE bypassed, the emitter is at signal ground and the collector current change flows through the ac load, the parallel combination of RC and RL: RC ∥ RL = 2.2k ∥ 4.7k = 1499 Ω. The mid-band voltage gain is Av = −gm (RC ∥ RL) = −0.0909 × 1499 = -136.1. The negative sign shows the 180 degree phase inversion of a common-emitter stage. The magnitude is large, but it depends on IC and so on temperature, and the source resistance will lower it further because the input is divided between the source and the input resistance found next. Answer: Av = -136.1.

Answer: -136.1

(d)

Looking into the base, the small-signal resistance is rπ = β/gm = 150/0.0909 = 1651 Ω, because the bypass capacitor removes RE from the signal path. The bias resistors R1 and R2 are in parallel from the base to ground for signals, giving Rth = 8.246 kΩ. These appear in parallel with rπ, so Rin = Rth ∥ rπ = 8246 ∥ 1651 = 1.38 kΩ. The bias network is the larger loss: without it the input resistance would be 1.65 kΩ. If the bypass capacitor were removed, the input resistance of the transistor alone would rise to rπ + (β + 1) RE, but the gain would fall to roughly −RC∥RL/RE. Answer: 1.38 kΩ.

Answer: 1.38 kΩ

Problem 4 [A5-074] BJT or MOSFET switch

A microcontroller output at 3.3 V drives an NPN transistor that switches a 12 V relay. The relay coil has a resistance of 200 Ω and an inductance of 0.50 H. The transistor emitter is grounded, its saturation voltage is VCE(sat) = 0.20 V and its base-emitter drop in saturation is 0.80 V. The designer uses a forced current gain of 10 to guarantee saturation. A freewheel diode is connected across the coil to protect the transistor when it turns off. Assume the coil current has reached its steady value before turn-off and neglect the diode forward drop when finding the decay time.

  1. (a) Find the steady coil current and the required base current at a forced gain of 10. [4]
  2. (b) Find the base resistor needed from the 3.3 V logic output, in kΩ. [4]
  3. (c) Find the energy stored in the coil at turn-off and the power dissipated in the transistor while on. [6]
  4. (d) Find the time for the coil current to decay to 5 percent of its initial value through the freewheel diode. [6]
(a)

With the transistor saturated, only VCE(sat) = 0.20 V drops across it, so the coil sees 12.0 − 0.20 = 11.8 V and the steady current is Ic = 11.8/200 = 59.0 mA. The coil inductance has no effect once the current is steady, because di/dt is zero. A forced gain of 10 means the base current is deliberately set to one tenth of the collector current, well above the minimum Ic/β for a transistor whose real gain might be 100 or more. This overdrive guarantees saturation across temperature and part spread. The required base current is Ib = Ic/βforced = 59.0 mA/10 = 5.90 mA. The microcontroller pin must be able to source this current, which is within a typical 20 mA pin limit. Answer: Ic = 59.0 mA and Ib = 5.90 mA.

Answer: Ib = 5.9 mA

(b)

The base resistor carries the base current and drops the difference between the logic high level and the base-emitter voltage. Applying Ohm's law, Rb = (Vlog − VBE)/Ib = (3.3 − 0.80)/5.90 mA = 2.50 V/0.00590 A = 424 Ω = 0.424 kΩ. A standard value below this, for example 390 Ω, would be chosen: Ib = 2.5/390 = 6.4 mA, so the forced gain is 59/6.4 = 9.2, at or below 10, which guarantees saturation under every tolerance condition. A larger resistor would risk leaving the transistor in the active region, where it would dissipate far more power. The logic output voltage may sag under load, so the margin is useful. Answer: 0.424 kΩ, use a standard value just below.

Answer: 0.424 kΩ

(c)

The magnetic energy stored in an inductor carrying current Ic is E = ½ L Ic². Substituting, E = 0.5 × 0.50 × (0.0590)² = 0.870 mJ. This energy must go somewhere at turn-off; with the freewheel diode it is dissipated in the coil resistance rather than creating a voltage spike across the transistor. While the transistor is on, its dissipation is the product of the saturation voltage and the collector current: P = VCE(sat) Ic = 0.20 × 0.0590 = 11.8 mW, which is trivial and needs no heat sink. Without the diode, the coil would try to keep its current and the collector would fly to hundreds of volts, avalanching the transistor. Answer: E = 0.870 mJ; the transistor dissipates 11.8 mW when on.

Answer: E = 0.87 mJ

(d)

After turn-off the coil current circulates through the diode and the coil resistance, forming a series R-L circuit with no source, so i(t) = I0 e−t/τ with τ = L/R = 0.50/200 = 2.5 ms. Setting i = 0.05 I0 gives e−t/τ = 0.05, so t = τ ln(20) = 2.5 ms × 2.996 = 7.49 ms. The relay armature usually releases when the current falls to roughly 10 to 20 percent of its hold value, so the diode lengthens the drop-out time compared with a design using no diode. If faster release is needed, a Zener in series with the diode raises the decay voltage and shortens the time. Neglecting the 0.7 V diode drop slightly overestimates the time. Answer: 7.49 ms.

Answer: 7.49 ms

Problem 5 [A5-075] Operational amplifier circuits

A sensor interface uses a single operational amplifier as an inverting summing amplifier with feedback resistor Rf = 100 kΩ. Input 1 must be amplified by a magnitude of 2 and input 2 by a magnitude of 5, both with inversion. A 0.80 V signal is applied to input 1 and a 0.30 V signal to input 2, both direct current. The amplifier has a gain-bandwidth product of 1.0 MHz and an input offset voltage of 2.0 mV, and all other non-idealities are ignored. The designer needs to select the input resistors, predict the output, and then examine the bandwidth and offset penalties of the high noise gain of this summing configuration.

  1. (a) Find the input resistor R1 for channel 1, in kΩ, so that the magnitude of gain is 2. [3]
  2. (b) Find the output voltage for the dc inputs given. [5]
  3. (c) Find the small-signal bandwidth of channel 2 given the amplifier's gain-bandwidth product, using the noise gain. [6]
  4. (d) Find the output offset voltage caused by the 2.0 mV input offset voltage. [6]
(a)

For an inverting summing amplifier, each channel has a gain magnitude of Rf divided by its own input resistor, because the inverting node is a virtual ground and the input currents add independently. The channel 1 gain magnitude is Rf/R1 = 2, so R1 = Rf/2 = 100 kΩ/2 = 50.0 kΩ. Channel 2 needs R2 = 100 kΩ/5 = 20.0 kΩ. Because the channels do not interact through the virtual ground, changing one gain does not disturb the other, which is the main advantage of this topology over a non-inverting summer. The non-inverting input is grounded, possibly through a resistor equal to the parallel combination of all resistors seen at the inverting node, to balance bias currents. Answer: R1 = 50.0 kΩ.

Answer: 50.0 kΩ

(b)

By superposition at the virtual ground, the inverting node current is V1/R1 + V2/R2 = 0.80/50k + 0.30/20k = 16.0 µA + 15.0 µA = 31.0 µA. All of this current flows through the feedback resistor, because an ideal op-amp draws no input current, so Vout = −Rf × 31.0 µA = −100k × 31.0 µA = -3.100 V. This agrees with the gain form −(2 × 0.80 + 5 × 0.30) = −(1.60 + 1.50) = -3.10 V. The result lies comfortably within the swing of a typical op-amp on a ±5 V or larger supply, so no clipping occurs. If either input were increased by about 40 percent the output would approach a ±5 V rail limit. Answer: -3.10 V.

Answer: -3.100 V

(c)

A finite gain-bandwidth product limits bandwidth according to the noise gain, which is the gain seen by a signal at the non-inverting input, not the signal gain. The noise gain is 1 + Rf/Rp, where Rp is the parallel combination of all input resistors to the virtual ground. Here Rp = 50k ∥ 20k = 14.286 kΩ, so the noise gain is 1 + 100/14.286 = 8.00. The closed-loop bandwidth is the gain-bandwidth product divided by the noise gain: f = 1 MHz/8.00 = 125.0 kHz. This applies to both channels because they share the same feedback loop, even though the signal gain of channel 2 is only 5. A designer must keep this in mind when adding many inputs, since each extra input lowers Rp and widens the penalty. Answer: 125.0 kHz.

Answer: 125.0 kHz

(d)

The input offset voltage acts like a small dc source in series with the non-inverting input, and it is amplified by the noise gain, not the signal gain. The noise gain was found in part (c) as 8.00. The output offset is therefore Vo,off = Vos × (1 + Rf/Rp) = 2.0 mV × 8.00 = 16.0 mV. This error is added to the intended output of −3.100 V, so it is about 0.5 percent of the signal; it is acceptable for a coarse sensor but not for a precision measurement. Options for reduction include selecting a chopper-stabilised or low-offset amplifier, nulling the offset using the trim pins, or ac-coupling the signal if dc accuracy is not needed. Answer: 16.0 mV.

Answer: 16.0 mV

A5 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A5-076] Op-amp filters and comparators

A sensor signal is first conditioned by an inverting first-order active low-pass filter and then passed to a Schmitt trigger. The filter uses an ideal operational amplifier with input resistor Ri = 10.0 kΩ, feedback resistor Rf = 47.0 kΩ, and a capacitor Cf = 3.3 nF in parallel with Rf. The Schmitt trigger is an inverting comparator whose positive feedback network is a divider: R1 = 10.0 kΩ from the output to the non-inverting input and R2 = 47.0 kΩ from the non-inverting input to ground. The comparator output saturates at ±12.0 V. The input to the filter is a sine wave and the trigger is driven from the filter output.

  1. (a) Find the corner frequency of the filter and its dc gain magnitude. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak output amplitude of the filter for a 0.45 V peak sine wave at 3.0 kHz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the Schmitt trigger upper threshold voltage and the hysteresis width. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum peak amplitude of the 3.0 kHz sine wave at the filter input that makes the trigger change state. [6]
(a)

For the inverting first-order filter the transfer function is H(s) = −(Rf/Ri)/(1 + s Rf Cf). At low frequency the capacitor is an open circuit and the gain magnitude is Rf/Ri = 47.0/10.0 = 4.70, or 13.4 dB. The corner frequency, where the magnitude falls to 1/√2 of the dc value, is fc = 1/(2π Rf Cf) = 1/(2π × 47000 × 3.3 × 10⁻⁹) = 1/0.000975 = 1026 Hz. Beyond this the gain rolls off at 20 dB per decade, so the circuit attenuates noise on the sensor signal. The corner frequency depends only on the feedback components, not on Ri, so the gain and corner can be tuned independently. Answer: dc gain 4.70 and fc = 1026 Hz.

Answer: fc = 1026 Hz

(b)

At frequency f the gain magnitude is |H| = (Rf/Ri)/√(1 + (f/fc)²). With f = 3000 Hz and fc = 1026.1 Hz, the ratio is f/fc = 2.924, so the denominator is √(1 + 8.547) = 3.090. Therefore |H| = 4.70/3.090 = 1.521. The output peak is the input peak times this magnitude: 0.45 × 1.521 = 0.684 V. The output sine wave is phase shifted by 180 degrees from the inversion plus an additional lag of 71.1 degrees from the capacitor. The amplitude is well below the 12 V saturation level, so the filter is operating linearly. Answer: 0.684 V.

Answer: 0.684 V

(c)

In the Schmitt trigger the non-inverting input voltage is set by the output through the divider, V+ = Vout × R2/(R1 + R2), where R2 is the lower resistor. When the output is at +12.0 V the threshold is Vut = 12.0 × 47.0/(10.0 + 47.0) = 9.89 V; when the output is at −12.0 V the threshold is the negative of that, −9.89 V. The input must cross the active threshold to flip the output, and the hysteresis width is the difference between the two thresholds: Vh = 2 Vut = 19.79 V. This wide hysteresis rejects noise smaller than about ±9.9 V on the input and prevents chatter near the switching point. Using a larger R1 relative to R2 would reduce the thresholds. Answer: Vut = 9.89 V, hysteresis 19.79 V.

Answer: Hysteresis = 19.79 V

(d)

For the trigger to change state, the filter output peak must at least reach the active threshold of 9.89 V found in part (c). The filter output peak equals the input peak times the gain magnitude at 3.0 kHz, which was found to be 1.521 in part (b). Setting 1.521 × Vin = 9.89 gives Vin,min = 9.89/1.521 = 6.505 V peak. A sine wave of this amplitude just reaches both the positive and negative thresholds, so the trigger toggles twice per cycle and gives a square wave at 3.0 kHz. At a lower frequency the same trigger needs a smaller input, because the filter passes more signal, which shows that the filter shapes the sensitivity of the whole detector. Answer: 6.505 V peak.

Answer: 6.505 V

Problem 2 [A5-077] Combinational logic design

A control panel interlock produces an output F from four sensor inputs A, B, C and D (A is the most significant bit). F must be logic 1 for the input combinations whose decimal values are 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 14, and logic 0 for the other six combinations; there are no don't-care conditions. The designer will build F as a two-level NAND-NAND circuit in static CMOS from the minimal sum-of-products expression, with complemented inputs generated by inverters. A k-input CMOS NAND gate uses 2k transistors and an inverter uses 2. Each inverter has a delay of 4 ns and every NAND gate has a delay of 7 ns regardless of fan-in.

  1. (a) Find the number of product terms in the minimal sum-of-products expression. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total number of literals in the minimal expression. [4]
  3. (c) Find the CMOS transistor count of the NAND-NAND circuit, including inverters for every complemented input that appears. [6]
  4. (d) Find the worst-case propagation delay from an input change to the output. [6]
(a)

Plot the ten minterms on a four-variable Karnaugh map and group adjacent ones in powers of two, taking the largest groups and covering every 1 at least once. Sympy's Quine-McCluskey reduction gives the minimal expression (C not D) + (not B not C) + (B D not A). The map shows that every minterm lies in one of these groups and none of the groups can be enlarged or dropped without leaving a 1 uncovered, so each term is essential or needed for a minimal cover. The sum therefore has 3 product terms. The count matters because it sets the number of first-level NAND gates and the fan-in of the second-level NAND. The check that the expression is correct is to evaluate it for each of the sixteen input combinations and compare with the specification. Answer: 3 product terms.

Answer: 3 terms

(b)

A literal is one appearance of a variable, complemented or not, in the expression. Reading the term sizes from the minimal expression (C not D) + (not B not C) + (B D not A), the terms contain 2, 2, 3 literals respectively. Adding them gives 7 literals in total. Literal count is the standard cost measure for two-level logic because it tracks the number of gate inputs and therefore wiring and area; it is minimised by choosing the largest possible K-map groups, as each doubling of a group removes one variable from a term. A more compact alternative may exist in a multi-level or XOR-based form, but the sum-of-products form is the one required for the NAND-NAND mapping. Answer: 7 literals.

Answer: 7 literals

(c)

By De Morgan's theorem, a sum of products maps directly to a NAND-NAND circuit, so each product term becomes a NAND gate whose inputs are its literals, and a final NAND combines the term outputs. The first-level NAND gates have 2, 2, 3 inputs and need 2k transistors each, a total of 14. The output NAND has 3 inputs and needs 6 transistors. The complemented inputs that appear are A, B, C, D, which is 4 inverters at 2 transistors each, giving 8. The total is 14 + 6 + 8 = 28 transistors. A shared inverter is used when a complement appears in more than one term. Answer: 28 transistors.

Answer: 28 transistors

(d)

The slowest path starts at an input that must be complemented, goes through its inverter, then through one first-level NAND gate, and finally through the output NAND gate. The delays add along this path: 4 ns for the inverter, 7 ns for the first-level NAND and 7 ns for the second-level NAND, so tpd = 4 + 7 + 7 = 18 ns. Paths from uncomplemented literals skip the inverter and take only 14 ns, so the inverters set the worst case. The delay is the same regardless of fan-in here only because the problem fixes it that way; in real CMOS, wide NAND gates are slower because of the stack of series transistors. The result sets the minimum interval between input changes and a valid output. Answer: 18 ns.

Answer: 18 ns

Problem 3 [A5-078] Sequential logic flip-flops and counters

An instrument needs a 1.000 kHz timebase derived from an 8.000 MHz crystal oscillator by a divide-by-8000 binary counter, built from negative-edge flip-flops. Two architectures are considered. In the asynchronous (ripple) design the stages are cascaded, each flip-flop clock-to-output delay being 14 ns. In the synchronous design every flip-flop is clocked together; clock-to-output delay is 9 ns, setup time is 4 ns and the carry logic is a chain of 2-input AND gates of 5 ns each, where the chain for n flip-flops contains n − 2 gates. The counter uses the smallest number of flip-flops that can count to 8000. The terminal-count pulse is one clock period wide.

  1. (a) Find the minimum number of flip-flops. [3]
  2. (b) Find the time the ripple counter needs for its last stage to settle after a clock edge, and the highest clock frequency at which its full count can be read, in MHz. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum clock frequency of the synchronous counter in MHz. [6]
  4. (d) Find the width of the terminal-count pulse and its duty cycle as a percentage. [6]
(a)

A binary counter with n flip-flops has 2ⁿ states, so counting to a modulus of 8000 needs 2ⁿ ≥ 8000. Since 2¹² = 4096 is too small and 2¹³ = 8192 is large enough, n = log₂ 8000 rounded up = ⌈12.966⌉ = 13. The counter must be forced back to zero after 7999 so it counts only 8000 states, using a decode of the terminal count to load or clear. The unused 192 states of the 8192 are skipped by this reset. Alternatively the divider can be split into smaller prescalers such as ÷8 × ÷1000, but the question asks for a single binary counter. Answer: 13 flip-flops.

Answer: 13 flip-flops

(b)

In a ripple counter each stage is clocked by the output of the previous one, so a change at the input propagates through all stages one after another. In the worst case, when the count rolls over and every bit changes, the last stage settles after n delays: tsettle = n × tpd = 13 × 14 ns = 182 ns. The count is only valid after this time, so reading the full count requires the clock period to be no shorter than the settling time, giving fmax = 1/182 ns = 5.49 MHz. This is lower than the 8.000 MHz oscillator, so the ripple counter cannot be decoded reliably at the full rate unless only the final stage is used. The lowest stages themselves can run faster than this figure. Answer: settle 182 ns, fmax 5.49 MHz.

Answer: 5.49 MHz

(c)

In the synchronous counter all flip-flops change together, but each stage toggles only if all lower bits are 1, and that condition is produced by the AND chain. The critical path starts at the clock-to-output delay of the lowest flip-flops, passes through the whole chain of n − 2 = 11 gates at 5 ns each, and must arrive a setup time before the next clock edge. The minimum period is T = tcq + (n − 2) tand + tsu = 9 + 11 × 5 + 4 = 68 ns. The maximum frequency is 1/T = 14.71 MHz. This exceeds 8.000 MHz with comfortable margin and is almost three times the ripple figure, which shows the main benefit of synchronous design. A look-ahead carry scheme would shorten the chain further at the cost of larger gates. Answer: 14.71 MHz.

Answer: 14.71 MHz

(d)

The terminal-count pulse lasts one clock period of the 8.000 MHz clock, so its width is 1/8.000 MHz = 125 ns. The pulse repeats once every 8000 clock cycles, at the output frequency of 8.000 MHz/8000 = 1.000 kHz, so the output period is 1.000 ms. The duty cycle is the pulse width divided by the period: 125 ns/1.000 ms = 0.0125 percent, or 1 part in 8000. Such a narrow pulse can be passed to a toggle flip-flop to obtain a 50 percent duty cycle square wave at 500 Hz, or it can be used directly as a strobe. Because the pulse is generated from the decoded count, it must be glitch free; in the synchronous design this is ensured by registering the decode output. Answer: 125 ns, duty 0.0125 percent.

Answer: Pulse width = 125 ns

Problem 4 [A5-079] Sensors and instrumentation amplifiers

A strain-gauge load cell uses one active 350 Ω gauge with gauge factor 2.10 in a quarter-bridge Wheatstone circuit with three fixed 350 Ω resistors and a 5.00 V excitation. The applied load produces a strain of 1200 microstrain in the gauge. The bridge output goes to a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier with equal input-stage resistors of 24.9 kΩ each and a gain-setting resistor Rg, whose gain is G = 1 + 2R/Rg. The amplifier output is read by a 12-bit analogue-to-digital converter with a 0 to 5.00 V input range. Ignore lead-wire resistance and temperature effects and take the amplifier reference as ground.

  1. (a) Find the exact bridge output voltage in millivolts for the stated strain. [5]
  2. (b) Find the gain-setting resistor Rg for an amplifier gain of 400. [4]
  3. (c) Find the amplifier output voltage with that gain. [4]
  4. (d) Find the ADC resolution (one least-significant bit) and the smallest change in strain, in microstrain, that one LSB represents, using the small-strain bridge relation. [7]
(a)

The gauge resistance changes by ΔR = R GF ε = 350 × 2.10 × 1200 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.882 Ω. In the quarter bridge, the gauge forms one arm of a divider: the output is the difference between the divider voltage on the gauge side and the half-excitation reference on the other side. The gauge-side node is at Vex (R + ΔR)/(2R + ΔR) = 5.00 × 350.882/700.882 = 2.503146 V, against 2.500000 V on the reference side. The bridge output is Vb = 3.146 mV. The small-signal formula Vex GF ε/4 gives 3.150 mV, which is about 0.13 percent high, showing the mild nonlinearity of the quarter bridge. Answer: 3.146 mV.

Answer: 3.146 mV

(b)

The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier has a first stage of two buffers sharing the gain-setting resistor, and a unity-gain difference amplifier as the second stage, so the overall gain is G = 1 + 2R/Rg, where R is each of the two equal feedback resistors. Solving for Rg, Rg = 2R/(G − 1) = 2 × 24 900/(400 − 1) = 49 800/399 = 124.8 Ω. In practice a standard 1 percent resistor of 124 Ω would give a gain of 402.6, and a trim would be used if the gain must be exact. The gain is set by a single resistor, which is the practical appeal of this arrangement, and the common-mode rejection depends on the matching of the other resistors, not on Rg. Answer: Rg = 124.8 Ω.

Answer: 124.8 Ω

(c)

The amplifier output is the product of the bridge differential voltage and the gain, since the common-mode level of 2.5 V is rejected by the difference stage. Using the exact bridge voltage of 3.146 mV from part (a), Vout = G Vb = 400 × 3.146 mV = 1.258 V. This lies inside the 0 to 5.00 V range of the converter, with headroom for about 4800 microstrain of full-scale. If the strain were compressive the output would be negative and the converter would clip at zero, so a level-shifting reference voltage on the amplifier reference pin, such as 2.5 V, is normally added to make the output bipolar. Answer: 1.258 V.

Answer: 1.258 V

(d)

A 12-bit converter has 2¹² = 4096 codes over 5.00 V, so one least-significant bit is 5.00/4096 = 1.2207 mV at the amplifier output. Dividing by the gain refers it back to the bridge: 1.2207 mV/400 = 3.052 µV. The small-strain bridge relation is Vb = Vex GF ε/4, so the sensitivity is 5.00 × 2.10/4 = 2.625 V per unit strain, or 2.625 µV per microstrain. The strain per LSB is therefore 3.052/2.625 = 1.16 microstrain. This is a fine resolution relative to the 1200 microstrain signal, around 0.10 percent. Noise in the amplifier and converter will in practice set a coarser limit. Answer: LSB = 1.2207 mV, equal to 1.16 microstrain.

Answer: 1.16 µε

Problem 5 [A5-080] Thyristors and power electronic switching

A fully controlled single-phase bridge rectifier made of four thyristors supplies a 12.0 Ω resistive heater from a 230 V rms, 60 Hz source. The thyristors are fired at a delay angle of 60 degrees in each half cycle. The device voltage drops are neglected and the source impedance is zero. The designer needs the average and rms output quantities, the input power factor and the thyristor ratings. Treat the supply current as the same as the load current and note that conduction is discontinuous only in the sense that the output returns to zero at each current zero crossing, which is true for a resistive load. A voltage safety factor of 2.0 on the peak supply voltage is required for the thyristor blocking rating.

  1. (a) Find the average output voltage. [5]
  2. (b) Find the rms output voltage and the power delivered to the heater. [5]
  3. (c) Find the input power factor. [5]
  4. (d) Find the average current of each thyristor and the minimum repetitive peak blocking voltage rating with the safety factor. [5]
(a)

The peak supply voltage is Vm = 230 × √2 = 325.3 V. In a fully controlled bridge with a resistive load, two thyristors conduct per half cycle from the firing angle α to π, and the load voltage follows the supply there; during the rest of the half cycle it is zero. Averaging over the half cycle, Vavg = (1/π) ∫ from α to π of Vm sin θ dθ = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α). For α = 60 degrees, cos α = 0.5, so Vavg = (325.3/π)(1.5) = 155.3 V. With α = 0 this would be 2Vm/π = 207.1 V, so firing at 60 degrees reduces the average output by 25 percent. Answer: 155.3 V.

Answer: 155.3 V

(b)

The rms output voltage is found from the mean square of the load voltage over the half cycle: Vrms = (Vm/√2) √(1 − α/π + sin 2α/(2π)). For α = 60 degrees = 1.0472 rad, α/π = 0.3333 and sin 120° = 0.8660, so the bracket is 1 − 0.3333 + 0.8660/6.2832 = 0.8045. The square root is 0.8969, and Vm/√2 equals the supply rms of 230 V, so Vrms = 230 × 0.8969 = 206.3 V. The power in the resistor is P = Vrms²/R = 206.3²/12.0 = 3546 W. For comparison, at α = 0 the heater would take 230²/12.0 = 4408 W, so phase control has cut the power to 80 percent. Answer: Vrms = 206.3 V and P = 3546 W.

Answer: P = 3546 W

(c)

The power factor is real power divided by apparent power at the source. Real power is the heater power of 3546 W, since the bridge is lossless. The source current is the load current in magnitude and its rms value is Irms = Vrms/R = 206.3/12.0 = 17.19 A. The apparent power is Vs Irms = 230 × 17.19 = 3954 VA. So pf = 3546/3954 = 0.897, which is also Vrms/Vs. It is lagging and low even though the load is resistive, because the current is distorted and displaced from the voltage. The displacement of the fundamental is about α/2 = 30 degrees for this circuit and the harmonic content further lowers the factor. Answer: 0.897 lagging.

Answer: 0.897

(d)

The load current is shared between two thyristor pairs, each pair conducting on alternate half cycles, so each thyristor carries half of the average load current. The average load current is Iavg = Vavg/R = 155.3/12.0 = 12.94 A, so each thyristor carries 6.47 A on average. When the thyristors are off in the bridge, each must block the supply peak, Vm = 325.3 V, whatever the firing angle. With the required safety factor of 2.0, the minimum repetitive peak blocking rating is 2.0 × 325.3 = 651 V, so 800 V or 1000 V devices are the usual standard choices. The current rating should also allow for the peak current of 27.1 A reached at θ = 90 degrees. Answer: 6.47 A average and at least 651 V blocking.

Answer: 651 V

A5 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A5-081] DC circuit analysis, Thevenin and Norton

A remote weather mast is powered by two batteries connected in parallel through their own lead resistances onto a common terminal pair a-b. Battery 1 is a 48 V bank in series with 8.0 Ω of lead and connector resistance. Battery 2 is a 36 V bank in series with 4.5 Ω. A resistive heater with a variable resistance RL is to be connected across a-b. The site engineer wants to understand whether setting RL equal to the Thevenin resistance is a sensible design choice, since the batteries must last through the winter. Treat all components as ideal apart from the stated resistances. Answer the following, showing the Thevenin equivalent for the network seen from a-b with the heater removed, and then judge the heater setting using power and efficiency, where efficiency means heater power divided by the total power drawn from both batteries.

  1. (a) Find the open-circuit (Thevenin) voltage at a-b. [4]
  2. (b) Find the Thevenin resistance seen from a-b. [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum power that any heater connected across a-b could receive, and state the heater resistance at which it occurs. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the efficiency (heater power divided by total power drawn from both batteries) when RL = Rth. [4]
  5. (e) The site engineer proposes instead a heater of 40 Ω. Calculate the efficiency in this case and use the two efficiency values to state whether matching is advisable for a battery-powered site. [4]
(a)

Remove the heater and apply nodal analysis at terminal a with b as reference. With no load, the current from battery 1 and battery 2 must sum to zero at the node, so (V1 - Voc)/R1 + (V2 - Voc)/R2 = 0. Rearranging gives Voc = (V1/R1 + V2/R2) / (1/R1 + 1/R2). Substitute the data: V1/R1 = 48.0/8.0 = 6.000 A and V2/R2 = 36.0/4.5 = 8.000 A, so the numerator is 14.000 A. The denominator is 1/8.0 + 1/4.5 = 0.12500 + 0.22222 = 0.34722 S. Then Voc = 14.000/0.34722 = 40.32 V. This lies between the two battery voltages, as it must for two sources in parallel, and it is closer to the 36 V bank because that branch has the lower resistance and therefore dominates. A circulating current flows between the batteries even with no heater, equal to (48 - 36)/(8.0 + 4.5) = 0.96 A, which is a standing loss worth noting.

Answer: 40.32 V

(b)

To find the Thevenin resistance, deactivate both ideal voltage sources by replacing them with short circuits, leaving the two lead resistances. Seen from terminals a-b these two resistances are connected in parallel, since each runs from terminal a to the shorted source and then to terminal b. Therefore Rth = R1 R2/(R1 + R2) = (8.0 × 4.5)/(8.0 + 4.5) = 36.0/12.5 = 2.880 Ω. The Norton equivalent follows directly: the short-circuit current is Isc = Voc/Rth = 40.32/2.880 = 14.00 A, which is simply the sum of the two individual short-circuit currents (6.00 A + 8.00 A). A marker looks for the explicit statement that sources are zeroed before resistances are combined, and for the observation that the parallel combination is smaller than either lead resistance, which confirms the arithmetic is sensible.

Answer: 2.880 Ω

(c)

Maximum power transfer from a Thevenin source occurs when the load resistance equals the Thevenin resistance, so RL = Rth = 2.880 Ω. At that setting the load voltage is half the open-circuit voltage, Voc/2 = 40.32/2 = 20.16 V, and the load current is Voc/(2 Rth) = 7.00 A. The power delivered is Pmax = Voc²/(4 Rth). Substituting, Pmax = (40.32)²/(4 × 2.880) = 1625.6/11.52 = 141.1 W. As a check, V²/RL = (20.16)²/2.880 = 141.1 W from the half-voltage form, which agrees. The derivation follows from differentiating P = Voc² RL/(Rth + RL)² with respect to RL and setting it to zero. This result is the largest power the network can supply to any resistive load, so it is the benchmark against which the practical heater setting is judged.

Answer: 141.1 W

(d)

With RL = Rth the terminal voltage is V = 40.32/2 = 20.16 V. Battery 1 supplies I1 = (48 - 20.16)/8.0 = 3.480 A, so its power is 48 × 3.480 = 167.0 W. Battery 2 supplies I2 = (36 - 20.16)/4.5 = 3.520 A, so its power is 36 × 3.520 = 126.7 W. The total drawn is 293.8 W. The heater receives V²/RL = 20.16²/2.880 = 141.1 W. The efficiency is 141.1/293.8 = 48.0 percent. This agrees with the general rule that matching a source to its load gives only 50 percent efficiency for a single Thevenin source, and here it comes out slightly under that because the circulating current between the batteries is lost as well as the Thevenin loss.

Answer: 48.0 %

(e)

Take RL = 40 Ω. The terminal voltage is V = 14.000/(0.34722 + 0.025) = 14.000/0.37222 = 37.61 V. Battery 1 current is (48 - 37.61)/8.0 = 1.299 A, so it supplies 62.3 W, and battery 2 current is (36 - 37.61)/4.5 = -0.358 A, so it absorbs power of about 12.9 W, meaning it is being charged by battery 1. Net power from the sources is 62.3 - 12.9 = 49.4 W. Heater power is 37.61²/40 = 35.4 W. Efficiency is 35.4/49.4 = 71.5 percent. This is much higher than at the matched setting. For a battery-powered site, where energy rather than peak power limits operation, matching is not advisable: it wastes about half of the stored energy in the lead resistances and circulating current. The heater should be sized for the energy it needs, not for maximum power transfer.

Answer: 71.5 %

Problem 2 [A5-082] Single-phase AC circuits and power factor

A small machine shop is fed from a 230 V, 60 Hz single-phase supply through a feeder whose total resistance (line plus return) is 0.15 Ω; feeder reactance is negligible. The connected load is an induction motor drawing 7.5 kW at a power factor of 0.72 lagging, together with 3.0 kW of resistive heating at unity power factor. The owner has received a utility penalty for low power factor and asks whether to install a capacitor bank at the load bus or simply to replace the feeder with a heavier cable. Assume the load voltage stays at 230 V in the calculations. Use the total load to find the present operating condition, size a capacitor to reach a corrected power factor of 0.95 lagging, and compare the two remedies by feeder current and feeder loss.

  1. (a) Find the overall power factor of the shop load. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the feeder current drawn before correction. [3]
  3. (c) Determine the capacitor reactive power required to raise the power factor to 0.95 lagging. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the capacitance, in microfarads, needed at 230 V and 60 Hz. [4]
  5. (e) Compare the remedies: find the percentage reduction in feeder loss achieved by the capacitor, and state in one sentence why a heavier cable would not remove the utility penalty. [4]
(a)

The motor reactive power is Q1 = P1 tan(arccos 0.72) with arccos 0.72 = 43.95 degrees and tan(43.95 degrees) = 0.9639, giving 7500 × 0.9639 = 7229 var lagging. The heater contributes no reactive power. Total real power is P = 7500 + 3000 = 10500 W and total reactive power is Q = 7229 var. The apparent power is S = √(P² + Q²) = √(10500² + 7229²) = 12748 VA. The overall power factor is cos θ = P/S = 10500/12748 = 0.824 lagging. The heater raises the overall power factor above the motor value of 0.72 because it adds real power only. A marker rewards recognising that real and reactive powers add by simple summation, whereas apparent powers and currents add as phasors, so one cannot add 7.5/0.72 and 3.0 kVA directly.

Answer: 0.824

(b)

The load apparent power is S = 12748 VA at the load bus voltage of 230 V. For a single-phase circuit I = S/V, so I = 12748/230 = 55.4 A. Check by components: the in-phase current is P/V = 10500/230 = 45.65 A and the reactive component is Q/V = 7229/230 = 31.43 A, whose resultant is √(45.65² + 31.43²) = 55.4 A, in agreement. The current lags the voltage by arccos 0.8237 = 34.5 degrees. The feeder loss at this current is I²Rf = 55.4² × 0.15 = 461 W, which the owner pays for but which does no useful work. Because the feeder loss varies with the square of current, a modest reduction in current brings a larger reduction in loss, and this is the basis for comparing the remedies later in the problem.

Answer: 55.4 A

(c)

The real power does not change when a capacitor is added, so P stays at 10500 W. At a corrected power factor of 0.95 the angle is arccos 0.95 = 18.19 degrees, and the allowable reactive power is Qnew = P tan(18.19 degrees) = 10500 × 0.3287 = 3451 var. The capacitor must supply the difference between the existing and permitted reactive powers: Qc = Q - Qnew = 7229 - 3451 = 3778 var, or 3.78 kvar. Capacitors supply leading reactive power, which cancels part of the lagging motor reactive power. In practice a standard capacitor rating of 4 or 5 kvar would be chosen, accepting a slightly different final power factor. The new apparent power is P/0.95 = 11053 VA, down from 12748 VA, which shows the freed capacity on the supply.

Answer: 3.78 kvar

(d)

A capacitor connected across the 230 V bus produces reactive power Qc = V² ω C, where ω = 2π f = 2π × 60 = 376.99 rad/s. Solving for the capacitance, C = Qc/(ω V²). Substituting, C = 3778/(376.99 × 230²) = 3778/(376.99 × 52900) = 3778/1.9944 × 10⁷ = 1.894 × 10⁻⁴ F, which is 189.4 μF. The capacitor must be rated for at least 230 V rms continuous; since the peak is 325 V a unit rated 300 V ac or more is typical. The capacitor reactance is Xc = 1/(ωC) = 1/(376.99 × 1.894 × 10⁻⁴) = about 14.0 Ω, and the capacitor current is V/Xc = about 16.4 A. This is consistent with Qc = V × Ic = 230 × 16.4 = 3.78 kvar, confirming the arithmetic.

Answer: 189.4 μF

(e)

After correction the feeder current is I2 = P/(0.95 V) = 10500/(0.95 × 230) = 48.1 A, compared with 55.4 A before. Feeder loss is proportional to the current squared, so the ratio of new to old loss is (I2/I1)² = (48.1/55.4)² = 0.752. The loss falls from 461 W to 346 W, a reduction of 24.8 percent. A heavier cable lowers the feeder resistance and therefore the loss, but the current and the load power factor stay the same, so the utility still sees 0.82 lagging at the meter and the penalty remains. Only the capacitor changes the reactive power drawn. The capacitor is therefore the better first measure, and a cable upgrade is justified only if voltage drop is also a problem.

Answer: 24.8 %

Problem 3 [A5-083] Three-phase circuits balanced loads

A greenhouse operator has a balanced three-phase heater bank made of three identical resistive elements, each of 20.0 Ω. The bank is supplied at 600 V line to line, 60 Hz, three-wire, through a feeder with a resistance of 0.12 Ω in each line; feeder reactance is negligible. The elements can be connected either in wye or in delta by changing links in the terminal box, and the operator wants to know which connection to use. The utility meter reading is taken at the heater terminals, so for the first three parts treat the heater terminals as being at 600 V and ignore the feeder. Then bring the feeder into the picture and compare the connections on cost of wasted energy, which matters because the heaters run for most of the winter.

  1. (a) Find the total heater power with the elements connected in wye. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total heater power with the elements connected in delta. [4]
  3. (c) Find the line current drawn by the delta-connected bank. [4]
  4. (d) With the feeder resistance of 0.12 Ω per line in service, find how much more power is wasted in the feeder with the delta connection than with the wye connection (use the currents already found). [5]
  5. (e) If the heaters operate 3000 hours per season, calculate the extra feeder energy lost with the delta connection, and state which connection you would recommend if only 18 kW is needed. [3]
(a)

In a wye connection each element sees the phase voltage, which is the line voltage divided by √3: Vph = 600/√3 = 346.4 V. The element current, which is also the line current, is IY = Vph/R = 346.4/20.0 = 17.32 A. The power in each element is IY² R = 17.32² × 20.0 = 6000 W, so the three-phase total is PY = 3 × 6000 = 18000 W, or 18.00 kW. As a check, the three-phase power of a balanced resistive load is √3 VL IL cos θ with cos θ = 1, giving √3 × 600 × 17.32 = 18000 W, which agrees. The same result follows from PY = VL²/R = 600²/20.0 = 18000 W, a compact form worth remembering because it shows that a wye bank draws one third of the power of the same elements connected in delta.

Answer: 18.00 kW

(b)

In a delta connection each element is connected directly across two lines, so it sees the full line voltage of 600 V. The phase current in each element is Id = 600/20.0 = 30.0 A. The power in each element is Id² R = 30.0² × 20.0 = 18000 W, so the three-phase total is Pd = 3 × 18000 = 54000 W, or 54.0 kW. This equals 3 VL²/R = 3 × 600²/20.0 = 54000 W. The delta bank therefore draws three times the power of the wye bank for the same elements and the same supply, because the voltage across each element is √3 times larger and power varies with the square of voltage, giving a factor of (√3)² = 3. A candidate who forgets this factor and compares the connections at equal power has misread the question; here the elements are fixed and the power differs.

Answer: 54.00 kW

(c)

For a balanced delta load the line current is √3 times the phase current. The element current was found as Id = 600/20.0 = 30.0 A, so the line current is IL = √3 × 30.0 = 52.0 A. Check from total power: IL = P/(√3 VL cos θ) = 54000/(√3 × 600 × 1) = 52.0 A, in agreement. In the wye connection the line current is only 17.32 A, so the delta line current is exactly three times larger. This ratio of three matters for the feeder: the line current sets the conductor size, the breaker rating and the loss, so the delta connection needs a much heavier feeder than the wye connection for the same elements. At 51.96 A the delta current would also exceed the ampacity of many small conductors, which the operator must check before choosing the delta link position.

Answer: 52.0 A

(d)

Feeder loss in a balanced three-wire system is 3 IL² rf because three line conductors each carry the line current. For the wye connection the loss is 3 × 17.32² × 0.12 = 108 W. For the delta connection the loss is 3 × 51.96² × 0.12 = 972 W. The difference is 972 - 108 = 864 W. The ratio of the two losses is 9, since the line current is three times larger and loss varies with current squared. This difference is a pure cost, because it produces no heat in the greenhouse. The assumption of ignoring the voltage drop on the feeder is only approximate: the drop in the delta case is about 51.96 × 0.12 = 6.2 V per line, around 1 percent of 600 V, which is small enough that the earlier power calculations are acceptable to a good approximation.

Answer: 864 W

(e)

The extra energy is the extra loss multiplied by the operating time: E = 864 W × 3000 h = 864 × 3000 = 2592000 Wh, which is 2592 kWh per season. At typical commercial electricity prices this is a cost of a few hundred dollars every year, and it is wasted heat in the feeder. The judgement part is this: if only 18 kW is needed, the wye connection delivers exactly 18.0 kW, so the wye connection meets the demand with one ninth of the feeder loss and one third of the line current, allowing a lighter feeder and smaller breaker. The delta connection would deliver 54 kW, three times too much, and would either overheat the greenhouse or require throttling by thermostat cycling. Therefore the wye connection is recommended, and the elements should be run at the voltage and power that they are meant for rather than oversized and throttled.

Answer: 2592 kWh

Problem 4 [A5-084] Three-phase power measurement and power factor correction

A sawmill dust-collection fan is driven by a three-phase, three-wire motor supplied at 600 V line to line, 60 Hz. A maintenance technician connects two wattmeters in the standard two-wattmeter arrangement, with the current coils in two lines and the voltage coils returned to the third line. Wattmeter 1 reads 14.2 kW and wattmeter 2 reads 6.1 kW, both with positive deflection. The load can be treated as balanced and the supply voltage as constant. The mill pays a charge when the power factor falls below 0.95 lagging, so the mill manager wants a delta-connected capacitor bank installed at the motor terminals. Use the readings to find the total real power, reactive power and power factor, and then size the capacitor bank, commenting on what the readings would show if the motor were lightly loaded.

  1. (a) Find the total real power absorbed by the motor. [3]
  2. (b) Find the total reactive power drawn by the motor. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the power factor of the motor as measured. [3]
  4. (d) Determine the total reactive power rating of the capacitor bank needed to reach 0.95 lagging. [5]
  5. (e) Find the capacitance of each of the three capacitors if the bank is connected in delta. [5]
(a)

With the two-wattmeter method on a three-wire system, the total real power equals the algebraic sum of the two readings, whatever the load imbalance, because the instantaneous power of the three-wire load is the sum of two line-current and line-to-line-voltage products. Therefore P = W1 + W2 = 14.2 + 6.1 = 20.3 kW. Both readings are positive, which tells us that the power factor is above 0.5; if W2 had read negative, the power factor would have been below 0.5. The line current can be found later from S, but at this stage the real power is the useful quantity. Note that the meter connection and polarity matter: reversing a voltage coil would flip the sign of a reading, so the technician must record the sign of each deflection as well as its magnitude when reporting readings.

Answer: 20.3 kW

(b)

For a balanced three-wire load the difference of the two wattmeter readings is proportional to the reactive power. The relationship is Q = √3 (W1 - W2), where wattmeter 1 is the one reading the larger value, which is the standard result for a lagging load. Substituting, Q = √3 × (14.2 - 6.1) = √3 × 8.1 = 1.7321 × 8.1 = 14.03 kvar lagging. The sign convention requires care: if the load were leading, the larger reading would belong to the other wattmeter, so the technician should know which meter is which. The apparent power is S = √(P² + Q²) = √(20300² + 14030²) = 24676 VA, and the line current is S/(√3 × 600) = 23.7 A, a useful figure to compare against the nameplate current of the motor.

Answer: 14.03 kvar

(c)

The power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power: cos θ = P/S. Using P = 20300 W and S = 24676 VA, the power factor is 0.823 lagging. An alternative check uses the wattmeter ratio. With tan θ = √3 (W1 - W2)/(W1 + W2) = √3 × 8.1/20.3 = 0.6911, the angle is 34.65 degrees and cos θ = 0.823, which agrees. The motor is operating well below the 0.95 target, and the lagging power factor is typical for an induction motor running at moderate load, where the magnetizing current is a large part of the total. The wattmeter ratio W2/W1 = 6.1/14.2 = 0.43 is also a rough indicator of power factor: a ratio near 1 means near-unity power factor, and a ratio near 0 means a power factor near 0.5.

Answer: 0.823

(d)

The real power stays at 20300 W after correction. At a power factor of 0.95 the angle is arccos 0.95 = 18.19 degrees and the reactive power that may remain is Qnew = P tan(18.19 degrees) = 20300 × 0.3287 = 6672 var. The bank must supply the difference: Qc = Q - Qnew = 14030 - 6672 = 7357 var, or 7.36 kvar in total, which is 2452 var per phase. The corrected apparent power is P/0.95 = 21368 VA, and the corrected line current is 20.6 A, a reduction from 23.7 A, which means the motor feeder loses roughly 25 percent less in resistive loss. The calculation assumes the voltage at the bank stays at 600 V; if the bank is switched in at light load without a controller, it can raise the bus voltage slightly, so a stepped controller is a good practice.

Answer: 7.36 kvar

(e)

In a delta-connected bank each capacitor sits across a line voltage of 600 V. The reactive power of one capacitor is Qph = Qc/3 = 7357/3 = 2452 var, and for one capacitor Qph = V² ω C. With ω = 2π × 60 = 376.99 rad/s and V = 600 V, C = Qph/(ω V²) = 2452/(376.99 × 360000) = 2452/1.3572 × 10⁸ = 1.807 × 10⁻⁵ F, which is 18.07 μF per capacitor. A wye bank would need three times this capacitance at the same line voltage, because each wye capacitor sees only 600/√3 = 346 V and so produces one third of the reactive power per farad. This is why delta connection is common at medium voltage for compact banks. The capacitors must be rated for 600 V continuous at least, and with a safety margin, such as 690 V units, for harmonics and overvoltage.

Answer: 18.07 μF

Problem 5 [A5-085] Ideal and practical transformers

A 50 kVA, 2400/240 V, 60 Hz single-phase distribution transformer serves a farm building. Manufacturer test results are as follows. In the open-circuit test, with rated voltage applied to the 240 V winding, the input is 186 W at a current of 5.4 A. In the short-circuit test, with the 240 V winding shorted and the 2400 V winding fed at reduced voltage, rated current flows at an applied voltage of 90 V with an input of 620 W. The farm owner plans to add equipment that will keep the transformer near full load, mostly at 0.80 power factor lagging, and is asking whether this unit is adequate or whether a larger unit should be bought. Use the equivalent circuit referred to the 2400 V side, hold the load voltage at 240 V, and judge the unit through regulation, efficiency and the load at which efficiency peaks.

  1. (a) Find the equivalent series resistance referred to the 2400 V side. [4]
  2. (b) Find the equivalent series reactance referred to the 2400 V side. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the voltage regulation at full load, 0.80 power factor lagging, holding the load voltage constant. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the efficiency at full load and 0.80 power factor. [4]
  5. (e) Find the load, in kVA, at which the transformer efficiency is greatest, and state whether the unit suits a load that sits near full load. [3]
(a)

The rated current on the 2400 V side is I1 = 50000/2400 = 20.83 A. In the short-circuit test with rated current flowing, the core branch is negligible because the applied voltage is only 90 V, so the whole input of 620 W is copper loss in the equivalent series resistance. Therefore Req = Psc/I1² = 620/20.83² = 620/434.0 = 1.428 Ω, referred to the high-voltage side. The corresponding value referred to the 240 V side would be divided by the turns ratio squared, which is 100, giving about 0.0143 Ω. A candidate who computes the resistance from voltage and current alone has found the impedance, not the resistance, so the power reading is essential here. This resistance accounts for both windings' copper losses, with the low-voltage winding resistance transferred to the high-voltage side by the turns ratio squared.

Answer: 1.428 Ω

(b)

The equivalent impedance magnitude from the short-circuit test is Zeq = Vsc/Isc = 90/20.83 = 4.320 Ω. The reactance follows from the impedance triangle: Xeq = √(Zeq² - Req²) = √(4.320² - 1.428²) = √(18.662 - 2.041) = 4.077 Ω. The leakage reactance dominates, which is typical for distribution transformers, where the ratio X/R is commonly between 2 and 5 at this size. Here X/R = 4.077/1.428 = 2.85. The impedance in per unit is Zeq/Zbase, where Zbase = 2400²/50000 = 115.2 Ω, so the per-unit impedance is 0.0375, or 3.75 percent, which is a plausible figure for a 50 kVA distribution unit and which also sets the prospective fault current at roughly 1/0.0375 = 27 times rated current.

Answer: 4.077 Ω

(c)

Refer the load to the 2400 V side. The load voltage is 2400 V and the current is I = 20.83 A at a lagging angle of arccos 0.80 = 36.87 degrees, so I = 20.83 ∠ -36.87 degrees A. The input voltage is V = V2' + I (Req + j Xeq). The drop is I Zeq = 20.83 ∠ -36.87 degrees × (1.428 + j 4.077) = (74.8 + j 50.1) V. Adding to 2400 gives a primary voltage magnitude of |V| = 2475.3 V. The regulation referred to the load voltage is (|V| - 2400)/2400 = 3.14 percent. The approximate formula I(R cos θ + X sin θ)/V gives 3.12 percent, which agrees closely. A lagging power factor produces positive regulation: the secondary voltage falls as the load grows, so the tap setting or primary voltage must allow for this drop.

Answer: 3.14 %

(d)

The output power is S cos θ = 50000 × 0.80 = 40000 W. The core loss is taken from the open-circuit test as 186 W and is constant, since the voltage is held constant. The copper loss at full load is the short-circuit input of 620 W, because the short-circuit test was run at rated current. The input is Pout + Pc + Pcu = 40000 + 186 + 620 = 40806 W. The efficiency is 40000/40806 = 98.02 percent. The open-circuit current of 5.4 A is not needed for efficiency; it would be used to find the magnetizing branch. The result is high, as expected for a transformer, and the lost power appears as heat, about 806 W, that must be dissipated from the tank surface. Efficiency would fall slightly if the power factor were lower, because the output power for the same loss would be smaller.

Answer: 98.02 %

(e)

Efficiency is greatest when the copper loss equals the core loss. Copper loss varies with the square of the load fraction x, so x² × 620 = 186, which gives x = √(186/620) = √0.3 = 0.548. The load at maximum efficiency is x × 50 kVA = 0.548 × 50 = 27.4 kVA. The unit is therefore tuned to peak at about 27 kVA, roughly 55 percent of rating. For a load that sits near full load for most of the day, the efficiency is slightly lower than the peak, but the difference is small, since the efficiency curve is flat near its maximum. At full load the 0.80 pf efficiency is 98.02 percent against a peak of about 98.3 percent. The 50 kVA unit is adequate, and a larger unit would run with the lower copper loss but higher no-load core loss, which only pays if the farm load is expected to grow.

Answer: 27.4 kVA

A5 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A5-086] Magnetic circuits

A smoothing inductor for a battery charger is wound on a laminated silicon-steel C-core with a single air gap. The core has a mean magnetic path length of 0.42 m (excluding the gap) and a uniform cross-section of 8.0 cm². The relative permeability of the steel may be taken as constant at 2200 over the working range. The coil has 400 turns and the gap is 1.5 mm long. Neglect fringing and leakage flux, so the gap area equals the core area. The designer is deciding whether the gap is doing a useful job or merely reducing the inductance, and wants to know how much of the magnetomotive force the gap takes and what gap would be required to keep the flux density no higher than 0.75 T when the winding carries 3.0 A. Use μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.

  1. (a) Find the total reluctance of the magnetic circuit, in kA-turns per weber (that is, 10³ A/Wb). [4]
  2. (b) Find the flux density in the core when the coil carries 3.0 A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the inductance of the coil. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the percentage of the total mmf that is absorbed by the air gap, and say what this means for the sensitivity of the inductance to the steel permeability. [3]
  5. (e) Find the air gap length required so that the flux density is exactly 0.75 T at 3.0 A, keeping the same core and turns. [4]
(a)

The reluctance of a uniform section is R = l/(μ A) with μ = μr μ0. For the steel, μ = 2200 × 4π × 10⁻⁷ = 2.7646 × 10⁻³ H/m, so Rc = 0.42/(2.7646 × 10⁻³ × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.42/2.2117 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.8990 × 10⁵ A/Wb.
