The principal stresses are the roots of σ³ − I1σ² + I2σ − I3 = 0. The first invariant is I1 = σx + σy + σz = 120 − 40 + 60 = 140 MPa. The second invariant is I2 = σxσy + σyσz + σzσx − τxy² − τyz² − τzx² = −4800 − 2400 + 7200 − 2500 − 900 − 400 = -3800 MPa². The third invariant is the determinant of the stress matrix, I3 = -590000 MPa³. Solving the cubic numerically (eigenvalues of the symmetric stress matrix) gives σ1 = 136.1 MPa, σ2 = 67.9 MPa and σ3 = -63.9 MPa. As a check, the three roots sum to 140 MPa, the value of I1. The 2D shortcut would have given an in-plane principal stress of only 134.3 MPa, so the full tensor raises the peak tension at the corner by about 1 percent.

Answer: 136.1 MPa

(b)

The smallest root of the same characteristic cubic is σ3 = -63.9 MPa, compressive. A direct check uses the product of roots: σ1σ2σ3 must equal I3 = -590000 MPa³, and 136.1 × 67.9 × (-63.9) = -590000 MPa³, which matches. A second check uses the sum of pairwise products, which must equal I2 = -3800 MPa². Verifying with two invariants guards against a sign slip in one off-diagonal term, which is the usual error when the matrix is entered by hand. Note that the compressive principal stress is far larger in magnitude than the -54.3 MPa smaller in-plane principal stress that the 2D circle gave, because the shear components τyz and τxy couple y with the other axes.

Answer: -63.9 MPa

(c)

The absolute maximum shear stress in three dimensions is half the difference between the largest and smallest principal stresses, τmax = (σ1 − σ3)/2 = (136.1 − (-63.9))/2 = 100.0 MPa. It acts on planes bisecting the σ1 and σ3 directions and is independent of σ2. The in-plane x-y circle used by the original analyst had a radius of √(80² + 50²) = 94.3 MPa, so the in-plane shortcut under-reported the peak shear by 5.6 MPa, about 6 percent. That is non-conservative for a ductile yielding criterion such as Tresca. The reporting error arose because the σz = 60 MPa and the two out-of-plane shears were ignored, and these move both extreme principal values outward.

Answer: 100.0 MPa

(d)

The octahedral shear stress is τoct = (1/3)√[(σ1 − σ2)² + (σ2 − σ3)² + (σ3 − σ1)²]. Substituting: (σ1 − σ2) = 68.2, (σ2 − σ3) = 131.8, (σ3 − σ1) = -200.0 MPa. The sum of squares is 62000, whose square root is 249.0; dividing by 3 gives τoct = 83.0 MPa. This is related to the von Mises equivalent stress by σvm = (3/√2) τoct = 176.1 MPa. Compare σvm, not τmax, with the uniaxial yield strength divided by the factor of safety. Unlike τmax, it uses all three principal differences, so it responds to the intermediate stress σ2. The designer should also not accept the 2D result as a safe lower bound: the von Mises value from the in-plane circle alone would be 168.2 MPa, clearly below the full three-dimensional 176.1 MPa.

Answer: 83.0 MPa

Problem 3 [A7-083] Generalized Hooke's law and thermal strain

A hardened steel insert, 25 mm thick in the z direction, is pressed into a rigid die cavity that prevents any expansion in the x and y directions. The faces perpendicular to z are free. The insert is initially stress free and uniform in temperature, then is heated uniformly by 80 K in service. Take E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.29, thermal expansion coefficient α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per K and yield strength Sy = 250 MPa. Assume the die is rigid, there is no friction on the walls, the stress state is uniform through the insert, and the response is linear elastic until yield. The die designer asks you to judge whether the 80 K service temperature rise is tolerable, and by how much the insert grows in the free direction.

  1. (a) Find the in-plane stress σx = σy in the insert (compression negative). [6]
  2. (b) Find the free-direction strain εz in microstrain. [5]
  3. (c) Find the change in thickness in the z direction. [4]
  4. (d) Find the temperature rise at which the von Mises stress first reaches the yield strength. [5]
(a)

Assume σz = 0 because the z faces are free and, by symmetry of the constraint, σx = σy = σ. Generalized Hooke's law with thermal strain gives εx = (σx − νσy − νσz)/E + αΔT. With both in-plane strains held at zero, 0 = σ(1 − ν)/E + αΔT. Rearranging, σ = −EαΔT/(1 − ν). Substituting: αΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 80 = 9.60 × 10⁻⁴. Then σ = −(200 000 MPa)(9.60 × 10⁻⁴)/(1 − 0.29) = -270.4 MPa. The negative sign shows the walls squeeze the insert in both x and y. Without the Poisson factor in the denominator, a uniaxial constraint would give only −EαΔT = 192.0 MPa, so the biaxial restraint is stiffer by the factor 1/(1 − ν) = 1.408.

Answer: -270.4 MPa

(b)

The z strain follows from the same law with σz = 0: εz = (σz − ν(σx + σy))/E + αΔT = −2νσ/E + αΔT. Substituting σ = -270.4 MPa: the Poisson term is −2 × 0.29 × (-270.4)/200 000 = 7.842 × 10⁻⁴, which is positive because the lateral compression pushes material into the free direction. The thermal term is 9.600 × 10⁻⁴. Adding gives εz = 1.7442 × 10⁻³, that is 1744 microstrain. Judgement: this is larger than the free thermal strain 960 microstrain by 82 percent, so the constraint amplifies the growth in the unconstrained direction. A candidate who forgets the Poisson contribution would report only the free thermal strain and under-predict the swelling.

Answer: 1744 µε

(c)

The strain is uniform, so the thickness change is Δz = εz L, with L = 25 mm. Substituting: Δz = 1.7442 × 10⁻³ × 25 mm = 0.0436 mm. Compare with the free expansion of a part with no walls, αΔT L = 960 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = 0.0240 mm. The walls therefore add about 0.0196 mm of growth in the free direction. Any clearance in z must therefore be at least 0.044 mm, not the smaller free-expansion figure of 0.024 mm, or the faces will jam against the press platens when hot.

Answer: 0.0436 mm

(d)

The stress state is equal biaxial compression with σz = 0, so the three principal stresses are 0, σ and σ, with σ negative. The von Mises stress is σvm = √[½((σ1 − σ2)² + (σ2 − σ3)² + (σ3 − σ1)²)]. With principal stresses σ, σ and 0, the first difference vanishes, and the other two are each σ², so σvm = |σ|. Set |σ| = Sy: EαΔT/(1 − ν) = Sy, so ΔT = Sy(1 − ν)/(Eα) = 250 × 0.71/(200 000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶) = 74.0 K. The service rise of 80 K exceeds this, and the stress of 270.4 MPa exceeds Sy = 250 MPa, so the insert yields. The design is not acceptable; the temperature rise must stay below 74 K, and below about 49 K if a factor of safety of 1.5 on stress is wanted, or else the die must be opened up to relieve the lateral constraint.

Answer: 74.0 K

Problem 4 [A7-084] Plane stress and plane strain

An aluminium alloy (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33) is used in two components that carry the same in-plane stresses σx = 90 MPa and σy = −40 MPa, with no in-plane shear. The first is a thin cover plate, 3 mm thick, free to thicken. The second is a long prismatic retaining wall section cast between two rigid end walls, so its length direction z cannot strain at all, even though the cross-section loading is the same. An analyst proposes using the plane stress formulas for both. Compare the two idealizations, using linear elasticity and small strain, and decide how much the plane stress shortcut mispredicts the strain in the wall section. Report strains in microstrain (µε, 10⁻⁶).

  1. (a) For the thin cover plate (plane stress), find the through-thickness strain εz. [5]
  2. (b) For the wall section (plane strain, εz = 0), find the axial stress σz that the end walls must supply. [5]
  3. (c) For the wall section, find the strain εx. [5]
  4. (d) State the percentage by which the plane stress formula over- or under-predicts εx in the wall section. [5]
(a)

Plane stress means σz = 0 because the faces are free. The thickness strain then follows from Hooke's law: εz = [σz − ν(σx + σy)]/E = −ν(σx + σy)/E. Substituting: σx + σy = 90 + (−40) = 50 MPa, so εz = −0.33 × 50/70 000 = -2.3571 × 10⁻⁴, which is -235.7 microstrain. The sign is negative because the sum of the in-plane stresses is tensile, and Poisson contraction thins the plate. For the same plate the in-plane strains are εx = 1474.3 µε and εy = -995.7 µε. Note that although σz is zero, εz is not: it is a strain and not a stress. A common marking error is to state that a plane stress plate has zero strain through the thickness, which is the plane strain condition.

Answer: -235.7 µε

(b)

Plane strain requires εz = 0. Hooke's law in the z direction gives εz = [σz − ν(σx + σy)]/E = 0. Therefore σz = ν(σx + σy) = 0.33 × (90 − 40) = 16.5 MPa, tensile. The result has a clear physical meaning: the unconstrained section would shorten along z because the net in-plane stress is tensile, and the rigid end walls prevent that shortening by pulling the section in tension. The sign would reverse if σx + σy were negative. This stress is not an applied load. It is a reaction that exists only because z is constrained, and the end-wall connection must be designed to carry it as a real force.

Answer: 16.5 MPa

(c)

For plane strain use the full three-dimensional Hooke's law in x: εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E. The z stress from part (b) is 16.5 MPa, so σy + σz = −40 + 16.5 = -23.5 MPa. Then εx = [90 − 0.33 × (-23.5)]/70 000 = (97.75)/70 000 = 1.3965 × 10⁻³, which is 1396.5 microstrain. It is a common mistake to reuse the plane stress equation εx = (σx − νσy)/E with plane strain data. That gives 1474.3 µε, which ignores the effect of σz and is wrong by the amount computed in part (d). For this problem the correct constrained answer is the smaller value, because the tensile σz acting through the Poisson effect adds a contraction in x.

Answer: 1396.5 µε

(d)

Take the true strain as the plane strain value, 1396.5 µε, and the plane stress prediction as 1474.3 µε. The plane stress formula therefore over-predicts εx by (1474.3 − 1396.5)/1396.5 = +5.6 percent of the true value. Equivalently, the true strain is 5.3 percent below the plane stress value (1396.5/1474.3 = 0.9472), but the error of the shortcut is quoted against the true strain. The effect arises because the end walls introduce σz = 16.5 MPa, and Poisson coupling reduces εx by νσz/E = 77.8 µε. Judgement: for a displacement check, a 5 percent error may be tolerable at concept stage but not for a strain-gauge comparison, so the correct plane strain equations should be used for the wall section, while the thin plate can be treated confidently as plane stress.

Answer: +5.6 percent

Problem 5 [A7-085] Failure theories: von Mises, Tresca, Mohr-Coulomb

A machine designer must choose a failure criterion for a hub at which the in-plane stresses are σx = 150 MPa, σy = −90 MPa and τxy = 60 MPa, with the surface free (σz = 0). Two material options are on the table. Option 1 is a ductile alloy steel with yield strength Sy = 380 MPa. Option 2 is a grey cast iron with ultimate tensile strength Sut = 220 MPa and ultimate compressive strength Suc = 750 MPa, treated as brittle with the Coulomb-Mohr criterion. The same hub geometry and load apply to both. Assume static loading, linear elastic behaviour up to failure and no stress concentration beyond what is already in the quoted stresses. The designer wants the factors of safety so that a choice can be justified.

  1. (a) Find the larger principal stress in the hub. [4]
  2. (b) Find the von Mises factor of safety for the steel. [5]
  3. (c) Find the Tresca factor of safety for the steel and state which of the two criteria is more conservative. [5]
  4. (d) Find the Coulomb-Mohr factor of safety for the cast iron. [6]
(a)

With σz = 0 the Mohr circle centre is σavg = (150 − 90)/2 = 30.0 MPa and the radius is R = √[((150 + 90)/2)² + 60²] = √(120.0² + 60.0²) = 134.16 MPa. The principal stresses are σ1 = 30.0 + 134.16 = 164.2 MPa and σ2 = 30.0 − 134.16 = -104.2 MPa, with the third principal stress equal to zero. Ordered, they are σ1 = 164.2 MPa, σ2 = 0 and σ3 = -104.2 MPa, so the zero is the intermediate value. Every criterion below uses these three. Because the zero lies between the other two, the maximum shear is set by σ1 and σ3, but the zero still has to be carried in the Tresca list and in the von Mises sum to avoid silently dropping a term.

Answer: 164.2 MPa

(b)

For plane stress with principal stresses σ1 and σ2, σvm = √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²). Substituting σ1 = 164.2 and σ2 = -104.2 MPa: σ1² = 26950, −σ1σ2 = 17100, σ2² = 10850, sum 54900, so σvm = 234.3 MPa. The distortion-energy factor of safety is n = Sy/σvm = 380/234.3 = 1.62. This criterion fits ductile metals well because it is based on the shear strain energy in the material, which controls yielding when hydrostatic tension or compression does not matter. A result above 1 means no yielding in static loading; a typical machine-design target of 1.5 would be met.

Answer: 1.62

(c)

Tresca compares the largest principal-stress difference, including the zero principal stress: |σ1 − σ2| = 268.3 MPa, |σ1 − 0| = 164.2 MPa and |σ2 − 0| = 104.2 MPa. The maximum is 268.3 MPa. The factor of safety is n = Sy/(largest difference) = 380/268.3 = 1.42. Since 1.42 is lower than the von Mises value 1.62, Tresca is the more conservative of the two for this stress state: it predicts yielding sooner. The two criteria agree exactly for pure tension and differ most in pure shear, by up to about 15 percent. The designer could adopt Tresca for a simple conservative check, or von Mises for a closer prediction of actual yielding in ductile steel.

Answer: 1.42

(d)

For a brittle material with σ1 > 0 > σ3 the Coulomb-Mohr failure line gives 1/n = σ1/Sut − σ3/Suc, with σ3 the most compressive principal stress. Substitution: σ1/Sut = 164.2/220 = 0.7462 and σ3/Suc = -104.2/750 = -0.1389. Then 1/n = 0.7462 − (-0.1389) = 0.8851, so n = 1.13. The tensile principal stress dominates the result, since it supplies 84 percent of 1/n, and the compressive stress supplies the rest. Judgement: the cast iron has a factor of safety of only 1.13 against fracture, with little warning, while the steel has 1.42 (Tresca) to 1.62 (von Mises) against yielding, followed by ductile deformation. The steel is the better choice for this hub, and the cast iron would need the load cut by about 25 percent to reach n = 1.5.

Answer: 1.13

A7 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A7-086] Strain gauge rosettes

A rectangular (0°, 45°, 90°) strain gauge rosette is bonded to the free surface of a steel pressure-vessel nozzle during a hydrostatic proof test. Gauge a lies along the nozzle axis (taken as x), gauge b is 45° anticlockwise from x and gauge c is along the hoop direction (y). Readings at the proof pressure are εa = 620 µε, εb = −150 µε and εc = −280 µε. The steel has E = 205 GPa, ν = 0.29 and yield strength Sy = 350 MPa. The surface is free of normal and shear traction, so the stress state is plane stress. The engineer on site needs principal strains, their orientation and stresses, and a quick view of the margin to yield by the maximum shear criterion before approving the vessel for service.

  1. (a) Find the larger principal strain, in microstrain. [5]
  2. (b) Find the angle from the x axis to the direction of ε1, positive anticlockwise. [4]
  3. (c) Convert to the larger principal stress using plane-stress Hooke's law. [6]
  4. (d) Find the Tresca factor of safety against yielding at this location. [5]
(a)

For the 0°, 45°, 90° rosette the rectangular strains are εx = εa = 620 µε and εy = εc = -280 µε. The 45° gauge reads εb = (εx + εy + γxy)/2, so the engineering shear strain is γxy = 2εb − εa − εc = 2(-150) − 620 − (-280) = -640 µε. The Mohr circle for strain has centre (εx + εy)/2 = 170 µε and radius R = √[((εx − εy)/2)² + (γxy/2)²] = √(450² + 320²) = 552.2 µε. Therefore ε1 = 170 + 552.2 = 722 µε and ε2 = 170 − 552.2 = -382 µε. A marker watches that γxy is halved when plotted on the circle, a frequent source of lost marks.

Answer: 722 µε

(b)

The principal direction follows from tan 2θp = γxy/(εx − εy) = -640/900 = -0.7111. Using the two-argument arctangent to place the angle in the correct quadrant, 2θp = -35.4°, so θp = -17.7°. The sign is negative, so ε1 lies 17.7° clockwise from the axis gauge. Because γxy is negative, the term (γxy/2) sin 2θ is largest for negative θ, so the major principal strain direction swings clockwise from x. Check by evaluating the strain along that direction using ε(θ) = (εx + εy)/2 + [(εx − εy)/2] cos 2θ + (γxy/2) sin 2θ = 722 µε, which equals ε1, so the orientation is correct.

Answer: -17.7 degrees

(c)

For plane stress the stresses follow from the strains by σ1 = E(ε1 + νε2)/(1 − ν²). The plane-stress modulus factor is E/(1 − ν²) = 205 000/(1 − 0.0841) = 223824 MPa. Substituting ε1 = 722 × 10⁻⁶ and ε2 = -382 × 10⁻⁶: ε1 + νε2 = 611.3 × 10⁻⁶. Then σ1 = 223824 × 611.3 × 10⁻⁶ = 136.8 MPa. Likewise σ2 = k(ε2 + νε1) = -38.7 MPa. Note that the through-thickness strain is not zero here, and we do not use the plane-strain formula, because the surface is free. Quick plausibility check: away from a nozzle the hoop stress in a pressure vessel is tensile and larger than the axial, but here the axial gauge is in tension while the hoop gauge is in compression, which suggests bending at the nozzle junction and not pure membrane loading.

Answer: 136.8 MPa

(d)

Include the zero out-of-plane principal stress in the comparison. The three differences are |σ1 − σ2| = 175.5 MPa, |σ1 − 0| = 136.8 MPa and |σ2 − 0| = 38.7 MPa. Since σ1 and σ2 have opposite signs, the largest is |σ1 − σ2| = 175.5 MPa, equal to twice the maximum shear stress. The factor of safety is n = Sy/(σ1 − σ2) = 350/175.5 = 1.99. Judgement: a value of about 2.0 gives a modest margin at the proof pressure. Because proof pressure is above operating pressure, the margin in service is larger, but the evidence of bending in part (c) means the local stress should be tracked with further gauges before release.

Answer: 1.99

Problem 2 [A7-087] Thick-walled cylinders

A hydraulic press cylinder is a closed-end steel tube with bore radius 40 mm and outside radius 70 mm. The maximum working pressure is 60 MPa internal gauge, with atmospheric pressure outside. The tube material has yield strength Sy = 420 MPa and the tube is initially stress free. Assume linear elastic behaviour, the Lamé solution for a long thick cylinder, and that the ends carry the pressure load through the closure so the axial stress is uniform across the wall. The designer is considering whether the wall could be made thinner to save material, and by how much, if a Tresca factor of safety of 2.0 on yield is required. Remember that the radial stress is not negligible in a thick wall.

  1. (a) Find the hoop stress at the bore. [5]
  2. (b) Find the hoop stress at the outer surface. [3]
  3. (c) Find the Tresca factor of safety against yield at the bore. [6]
  4. (d) Find the smallest outside radius that still gives a Tresca factor of safety of 2.0, keeping the same bore and pressure. [6]
(a)

For a thick cylinder with internal pressure pi and no external pressure the Lamé solution gives the hoop stress σθ = pi ri²(1 + ro²/r²)/(ro² − ri²). At the bore r = ri this becomes σθ = pi(ro² + ri²)/(ro² − ri²). Substituting with ro² = 4900 mm² and ri² = 1600 mm²: σθ = 60 × (6500)/(3300) = 118.2 MPa, tension. This is almost twice the internal pressure, and the value is much higher than the thin-wall estimate p r/t = 60 × 40/30 = 80.0 MPa evaluated at the bore radius, so a thin-wall formula would have under-estimated the true peak hoop stress by about 32 percent (the true value is about 48 percent above the thin-wall figure). The radial stress at the bore is σr = −60 MPa, compressive.

Answer: 118.2 MPa

(b)

At r = ro the Lamé hoop stress is σθ = 2 pi ri²/(ro² − ri²). Substituting: σθ = 2 × 60 × 1600/3300 = 58.2 MPa, tension. The stress falls from 118.2 MPa at the bore to 58.2 MPa at the outside, a drop of 51 percent through the wall, which shows how unevenly a thick wall is stressed. Outer material is therefore much less effectively used than inner material, and this is the reason designers use autofrettage or shrink-fitted compound cylinders for very high pressure. The radial stress is zero at the outer free surface, a useful check that the solution satisfies the boundary conditions at both surfaces.

Answer: 58.2 MPa

(c)

At the bore the principal stresses are σθ = 118.2 MPa, σz = pi ri²/(ro² − ri²) = 29.1 MPa (closed ends) and σr = −60 MPa. The axial stress lies between the other two, so it does not affect the Tresca result. The Tresca stress is the largest difference, σθ − σr = 118.2 + 60 = 178.2 MPa. The factor of safety is n = Sy/(σθ − σr) = 420/178.2 = 2.36. Since the required value is 2.0, the cylinder exceeds the requirement. Judgement: because the factor is above 2.0, material might be removed. It is the radial stress that matters here: a thin-wall calculation that ignored σr would have under-reported the Tresca stress by 60 MPa, which is 51 percent of the hoop stress.

Answer: 2.36

(d)

At the bore, σθ − σr = pi(ro² + ri²)/(ro² − ri²) + pi = 2 pi ro²/(ro² − ri²). Require this to equal Sy/2 = 210 MPa. Then 2 × 60 × ro² = 210(ro² − 1600), which simplifies to ro²(210 − 120) = 210 × 1600. So ro² = 336000/90 = 3733.3 mm², and ro = 61.1 mm. This is 8.9 mm thinner than the 70 mm original wall, so wall thickness falls from 30 mm to 21.1 mm. A real design would add margin for fatigue, since a press cycles the pressure, and for corrosion allowance, so a rounded 65 mm outside radius is a sensible compromise that still gives n above 2.0 while cutting wall thickness.

Answer: 61.1 mm

Problem 3 [A7-088] Rotating disks

A solid steel flywheel disk of uniform thickness, radius 0.25 m, turns at a service speed of 9000 rpm in a test cell. The steel has density 7800 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.30 and yield strength 380 MPa. Treat the disk as thin so that plane stress applies, with no thermal gradient, and no loads other than centrifugal body forces. The rim is free of traction. The test manager wants to know the stresses at the critical points, the highest speed allowed if the peak stress must not exceed half of yield, and what happens if a small central hole is drilled to fit a shaft. Assume the hole is small compared with the disk radius, so the solid-disk results are modified only locally.

  1. (a) Find the stress at the centre of the solid disk. [5]
  2. (b) Find the hoop stress at the rim. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum speed at which the central stress equals half of yield. [5]
  4. (d) If a small central hole is drilled, find the new maximum speed for the same allowable stress. [6]
(a)

For a thin solid disk of radius R the radial and hoop stresses are equal at the centre and reach their maximum there: σr = σθ = (3 + ν)ρω²R²/8. First convert the speed: ω = 9000 × 2π/60 = 942.5 rad/s. The group ρω²R² = 7800 × 942.5² × 0.25² = 4.3303 × 10⁸ Pa = 433.0 MPa. Then σmax = (3 + 0.30)/8 × 433.0 = 0.4125 × 433.0 = 178.6 MPa. This is a biaxial tension, so at the centre the von Mises stress equals the same 178.6 MPa value because both in-plane principals are equal and the third is zero. The factor of safety on yield at the service speed is 2.13, using the peak stress and the 380 MPa yield strength. The centre is the critical point because both stress components peak there, while at the rim the radial component is zero and the hoop component is much smaller.

Answer: 178.6 MPa

(b)

At the free rim the radial stress is zero, so the hoop stress is the only non-zero in-plane stress. For the solid disk, σθ(R) = (1 − ν)ρω²R²/4. Substitution with the group value 433.0 MPa: σθ = (1 − 0.30)/4 × 433.0 = 0.175 × 433.0 = 75.8 MPa. This is 42 percent of the central stress, so the hoop stress falls strongly from the centre to the rim, while the radial stress goes from the same maximum to zero. The disk is therefore most highly loaded at the centre and the rim is lightly loaded. A designer who used the thin-ring formula σθ = ρω²R² would have predicted 433.0 MPa, which is more than twice the true peak and would grossly over-penalize a solid disk.

Answer: 75.8 MPa

(c)

Centrifugal stress scales with the square of speed, σ ∝ ω². The allowable stress is Sy/2 = 190 MPa. Since σc = 178.6 MPa at 9000 rpm, the allowable speed is n = 9000 × √(190/178.6) = 9000 × 1.0314 = 9282 rpm. Because stress depends on the speed squared, a 1 percent speed increase raises stress by about 2 percent, so the margin in speed (3.1 percent above service) is smaller than the margin in stress (6.4 percent). This is why overspeed protection is specified in speed, not stress, and why a trip set point should be placed well below the computed value to allow for tolerance in the speed sensor.

Answer: 9282 rpm

(d)

For a disk with a small central hole the hoop stress at the hole edge is (3 + ν)ρω²R²/4, which is exactly twice the solid-disk centre stress. Substitution: σ = (3.30)/4 × 433.0 = 357.2 MPa at 9000 rpm. The radial stress at the hole edge is zero, so this is a uniaxial hoop stress, and the comparison with 190 MPa is direct. The allowable speed is 9000 × √(190/357.2) = 9000 × 0.7293 = 6563 rpm. Drilling the hole therefore costs 29 percent of the allowable speed. Judgement: if the shaft hole is necessary, the disk must either be run slower, be made from a stronger steel, or be profiled thicker at the hub, since the stress concentration is purely geometric and cannot be removed by a finer finish.

Answer: 6564 rpm

Problem 4 [A7-089] Euler buckling and column design

A bracing strut in a temporary steel scaffold tower is a seamless round tube with outside diameter 60 mm and wall thickness 4 mm, length 2.4 m. The steel has E = 205 GPa and yield strength Sy = 300 MPa. The designer first assumes pinned ends. A detailed review then shows that the strut is welded rigidly at its base and pinned at the top, for which the effective-length factor is K = 0.7. The question is whether the pin-ended Euler formula can still be trusted once the end conditions change, and what load can safely be carried with a factor of safety of 2.5. Use the Johnson parabola for intermediate columns, with the transition between Johnson and Euler where Euler stress equals Sy/2. Assume the load is applied axially and the tube is straight.

  1. (a) Find the slenderness ratio L/r for pinned ends, and the Johnson/Euler transition value. [5]
  2. (b) Find the Euler critical load for pinned ends. [4]
  3. (c) With K = 0.7, find the critical load using the appropriate formula. [6]
  4. (d) Find the allowable axial load using a factor of safety of 2.5, and state whether the end-fixity change helped. [5]
(a)

The inside diameter is 60 − 2 × 4 = 52 mm. The second moment of area is I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64 = π(1.2960 × 10⁷ − 7.3116 × 10⁶)/64 = 277264 mm⁴. The area is A = π(D² − d²)/4 = 703.7 mm². The radius of gyration is r = √(I/A) = 19.85 mm. The slenderness ratio for pinned ends is L/r = 2400/19.85 = 120.9. The transition slenderness is found where the Euler stress equals half the yield strength: Cc = √(2π²E/Sy) = √(2π² × 205 000/300) = 116.1. Because 120.9 is greater than 116.1, the pinned strut sits just beyond the transition and the Euler equation applies in the pinned case. A margin of only 4 percent shows that the strut is close to the transition, so the end-condition change is likely to move it into the Johnson range.

Answer: 120.9

(b)

With pinned ends the effective length equals the actual length, so Pcr = π²EI/L². Substituting E = 205 000 MPa, I = 277264 mm⁴ and L = 2400 mm: Pcr = π² × 205 000 × 277264/2400² = 97.4 kN. As a validity check the average stress at buckling is Pcr/A = 138.4 MPa, which must not exceed Sy/2 = 150 MPa for Euler to be valid. Since 138.4 MPa is below 150 MPa, the pinned Euler load is valid. The result is the benchmark against which the stiffer end condition in the next parts should be compared. A marker also credits noting that the buckling direction is the axis of smallest I, which for a round tube is any axis, so there is no preferred direction.

Answer: 97.4 kN

(c)

The effective length is KL = 0.7 × 2400 = 1680 mm, so the effective slenderness is 84.6. This is less than the transition value Cc = 116.1, so the Euler formula is not valid and the Johnson parabola must be used. The pure Euler load with K = 0.7 would be 198.8 kN, which equals an average stress of 282 MPa. That stress is below the yield strength of 300 MPa, but it is far above the Sy/2 = 150 MPa limit for Euler validity, so the Euler result lies outside its range and overstates the capacity. The Johnson load is Pcr = A[Sy − (Sy²/(4π²E))(KL/r)²] = 703.7 × [300 − (0.01112)(84.6)²] = 703.7 × 220.3 MPa = 155.1 kN. The Johnson result is lower than the Euler value by 22 percent, so using Euler here would be unconservative.

Answer: 155.1 kN

(d)

The allowable load is the critical load divided by the factor of safety: Pall = 155.1/2.5 = 62.0 kN. For comparison, the pinned strut with the same factor would have allowed 97.4/2.5 = 39.0 kN. The base fixity therefore raised the allowable load by 59 percent, a useful gain but much smaller than the factor 1/K² = 2.04 that the Euler formula would suggest. The difference arises because the strut moved out of the Euler regime into the range where yielding limits the capacity. Judgement: the designer should not scale the pinned result by 1/K² and should instead check the slenderness ratio each time the end conditions change, since the governing formula can switch.

Answer: 62.0 kN

Problem 5 [A7-090] Beam on elastic foundation or curved beams

A lifting eye used on a cargo spreader has a curved portion with a solid rectangular cross-section, 30 mm wide and 50 mm deep in the radial direction. The inner radius of the curved section is 60 mm and the outer radius is 110 mm. At the critical section the internal bending moment is 1.5 kN·m, acting so that it tends to straighten the member, which puts the inner fibre in tension. The steel has yield strength 300 MPa. A junior engineer has used the straight-beam flexure formula σ = Mc/I for this section because the member looks only mildly curved. You are asked to apply the Winkler curved-beam theory, find the error in the shortcut, and say what moment the eye may carry with a factor of safety of 1.5 on yield at the inner fibre. Neglect axial force and shear.

  1. (a) Find the distance e between the centroidal axis and the neutral axis. [5]
  2. (b) Find the stress at the inner fibre. [5]
  3. (c) Find the percentage by which the straight-beam formula under-predicts the inner-fibre stress. [5]
  4. (d) Find the largest moment that gives a factor of safety of 1.5 on yield at the inner fibre. [5]
(a)

In curved-beam theory the neutral axis does not pass through the centroid but shifts toward the centre of curvature. The centroidal radius is rc = (ri + ro)/2 = (60 + 110)/2 = 85.0 mm. For a rectangle the neutral-axis radius is rn = h/ln(ro/ri) = 50/ln(110/60) = 50/0.6061 = 82.490 mm. The offset is e = rc − rn = 85.0 − 82.490 = 2.510 mm. The area is A = 30 × 50 = 1500 mm². The offset is small, only 5.0 percent of the depth, but it multiplies the stress sharply because e sits in the denominator of the stress formula, so the result needs several figures of precision. Subtracting two close numbers loses accuracy, so keep four decimals in the logarithm.

Answer: 2.510 mm

(b)

Winkler's formula for bending stress at radius r is σ = M(rn − r)/(A e r), with M positive when it straightens the member. At the inner fibre r = ri = 60 mm: σi = 1.5 × 10⁶ × (82.490 − 60)/(1500 × 2.510 × 60). The numerator is 3.3735 × 10⁷ N·mm² and the denominator is 2.2592 × 10⁵ mm³, giving σi = 149.3 MPa, tension, as the statement says the moment puts the inner fibre in tension. At the outer fibre the same formula gives σo = −M(ro − rn)/(A e ro) = -99.6 MPa, compression. The inner stress is about 1.50 times the outer stress in magnitude, so the stress distribution is strongly asymmetric, with the peak on the concave side of the bend. The factor of safety on yield at the inner fibre is 2.01.

Answer: 149.3 MPa

(c)

The straight-beam flexure formula gives σ = Mc/I with I = bh³/12 = 30 × 50³/12 = 312500 mm⁴ and c = 25 mm: σ = 1.5 × 10⁶ × 25/312500 = 120.0 MPa. This is the same magnitude on both faces. The curved-beam inner-fibre stress is 149.3 MPa, so the shortcut under-predicts it by (149.3 − 120.0)/149.3 × 100 = 19.6 percent. On the outer fibre the shortcut over-predicts the magnitude, since the curved-beam value is only 99.6 MPa against 120.0 MPa. The inner fibre governs the failure, so the error is non-conservative. The ratio of radius to depth here is rc/h = 1.70, below the common rule of thumb of about 5 beyond which the straight formula is acceptable, so the shortcut was not justified.

Answer: 19.6 percent

(d)

Set the inner-fibre stress equal to the allowable stress Sy/1.5 = 200 MPa and solve Winkler's expression for the moment: M = σallow A e ri/(rn − ri). Substitution: M = 200 × 1500 × 2.510 × 60/(82.490 − 60) = 4.5184 × 10⁷/22.490 N·mm = 2.009 × 10⁶ N·mm, that is 2.01 kN·m. The current moment of 1.5 kN·m is 75 percent of this limit, so the member is acceptable with margin 1.34 on moment. If the engineer had used the straight-beam formula the limit would be 2.50 kN·m, which is 24 percent too high, so a design based on the shortcut would have accepted a moment that the real section cannot carry at the required safety factor. Judgement: for a lifting device this error is material and the curved-beam result should govern.

Answer: 2.01 kN·m

A7 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A7-091] Unsymmetric bending and shear centre

A simply supported purlin of span 3.0 m is a cold-formed channel with the web vertical and both flanges pointing to the right. Dimensions are to the wall centrelines: web depth 200 mm, flange width 75 mm, uniform thickness 6 mm. A single vertical load of 4.0 kN acts at mid-span. The site crew has bolted the cladding rail to the web, so the load line lies in the plane of the web centreline. A colleague argues the section would twist less if the rail bore through the centroid of the section instead. Treat the section as thin-walled, neglect the second moment of area of each flange about its own centreline, and assume elastic behaviour. Take the shear centre, not the centroid, as the point about which twist is judged. Assess the two proposals.

  1. (a) Find the distance of the shear centre from the web centreline. [5]
  2. (b) Find the maximum bending stress at mid-span. [5]
  3. (c) Find the torque about the shear centre at mid-span when the load line lies in the web plane. [4]
  4. (d) Find the torque if the load line instead passes through the centroid, and judge the colleague's proposal. [6]
(a)

Treat the channel as thin-walled. Per unit shear V, the shear flow in each flange grows linearly from zero at the free tip to q = V·(h/2)·b·t/I at the web junction, so the resultant force in each flange is F_f = q·b/2. The two flange forces are equal and opposite in direction and form a couple of arm h, while the web carries the whole shear V. The shear centre is the point where the moment of these internal forces about the web centreline equals V·e, so V·e = F_f·h. Substituting I = t·h³/12 + 2·b·t·(h/2)² and simplifying gives the standard thin-walled result e = 3b²/(h + 6b). With b = 75 mm and h = 200 mm, e = 3(75)²/(200 + 450) = 16875/650 = 25.96 mm. The shear centre lies outside the channel, on the side of the web away from the flanges, so a vertical load through the web is not through it.

Answer: 26.0 mm

(b)

The load is vertical and the section is symmetric about the horizontal centroidal axis, so the bending is simple bending about a principal axis and no unsymmetric-bending correction arises. With the flange self-inertia neglected, the second moment of area is I = t·h³/12 + 2·b·t·(h/2)² = 6(200)³/12 + 2(75)(6)(100)² = 4 × 10⁶ + 9 × 10⁶ = 1.3 × 10⁷ mm⁴. The mid-span moment for a central point load on a simple span is M = P·L/4 = 4000(3000)/4 = 3 × 10⁶ N·mm. The outer fibre lies half the web depth plus half the flange thickness from the neutral axis, y = 100 + 3 = 103 mm. Then σ = M·y/I = 3 × 10⁶(103)/1.3 × 10⁷ = 23.8 MPa. This bending stress is the same for either proposed load position, because the position of the load line only adds a torque. The twist stresses are additional and are not included here.

Answer: 23.8 MPa

(c)

A transverse load produces pure bending only if its line passes through the shear centre. Otherwise it is statically equivalent to the same load applied at the shear centre plus a torque equal to the load times the perpendicular distance between the two lines. With the load in the web plane, the load line is the web centreline, a distance e = 25.96 mm from the shear centre found in part (a). The torque at the load point is therefore T = P·e = 4000 N × 25.96 mm = 1.038 × 10⁵ N·mm = 103.8 N·m. The section has very small St Venant torsional stiffness because it is an open thin-walled shape, so this torque is resisted mainly by warping restraint at the supports and by the rail connection. Twisting tends to rotate the flanges toward the side on which the load line lies, which is also the side away from the shear centre.

Answer: 103.8 N·m

(d)

First locate the centroid. Measured from the web centreline, only the two flanges have their centroids off the line, each at b/2 with area b·t. The first moment of area is 2(b·t)(b/2) = b²·t and the total area is t(h + 2b), so the centroid distance is c = b²/(h + 2b) = 5625/350 = 16.07 mm toward the flanges. The shear centre lies on the opposite side of the web, so a load through the centroid is a distance e + c = 25.96 + 16.07 = 42.03 mm from the shear centre. The torque is T = 4000 × 42.03 = 1.681 × 10⁵ N·mm = 168.1 N·m. This is 1.62 times the torque in part (c). The colleague's proposal is therefore worse, not better. Neither position removes the twist. Only a load line through the shear centre, 26.0 mm outside the web, or a stiffening lip or tie that restrains rotation, would.

Answer: 168.1 N·m

Problem 2 [A7-092] Torsion of non-circular and thin-walled sections

An aluminium extrusion for a vehicle frame is a closed rectangular tube. The wall centreline measures 100 mm by 60 mm and the wall thickness is a constant 3.0 mm. The tube carries a pure torque of 1.5 kN·m along its length and the shear modulus is 26 GPa. A fabricator proposes slitting the tube along one side for the full length, to allow a cable run, and argues that since the metal and the thickness are unchanged the member will behave nearly the same. Use the thin-walled closed-section theory for the intact tube and the narrow-rectangle approximation, with the unrolled centreline length as the developed width, for the slit tube. Neglect stress concentration at the corners and the effect of end warping restraint.

  1. (a) Find the shear stress in the intact closed tube. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rate of twist of the intact tube in degrees per metre. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum shear stress in the slit tube. [4]
  4. (d) Find the rate of twist of the slit tube in degrees per metre. [4]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of the twist rate of the slit tube to that of the intact tube, and state the engineering conclusion. [3]
(a)

For a thin-walled closed section, the Bredt-Batho relation gives a constant shear flow around the section, q = T/(2·A_m), where A_m is the area enclosed by the wall centreline. Here A_m = 100 × 60 = 6000 mm², and T = 1.5 kN·m = 1.5 × 10⁶ N·mm. Then q = 1.5 × 10⁶/(2 × 6000) = 125.0 N/mm. Because the thickness is uniform, the shear stress is the same in all four walls and equals τ = q/t = 125.0/3.0 = 41.7 MPa. This is low for an aluminium extrusion, which has a shear yield of the order of 150 MPa, so the intact tube works at a comfortable factor of safety. The calculation neglects stress raising at the inside corners and assumes the cross-section does not distort, which is reasonable if internal stiffeners or end diaphragms are present at the load points.

Answer: 41.7 MPa

(b)

The rate of twist follows from equating the work done by the torque with the strain energy stored in the walls. For a thin-walled closed section the result is dθ/dz = T·∮(ds/t)/(4·A_m²·G). The developed centreline length is s = 2(100 + 60) = 320 mm and the thickness is uniform, so ∮ds/t = 320/3.0 = 106.7. Substituting, dθ/dz = 1.5 × 10⁶ × 106.7/(4 × (6000)² × 26 000) = 1.6 × 10⁸/3.744 × 10¹² = 4.274 × 10⁻⁵ rad/mm. Multiplying by 1000 mm/m gives 0.0427 rad/m, and by 180/π gives 2.449 degrees per metre. A 3 m tube would therefore twist about 7.35 degrees at 1.5 kN·m. This is a modest twist, typical of a frame member that must stay stiff so that suspension mounting points keep their relative alignment under cornering.

Answer: 2.449 degrees/m

(c)

Once slit, the member is an open section and the closed-circuit shear flow can no longer exist. It behaves like a thin strip of width equal to the developed length s = 320 mm and thickness 3.0 mm, which has a torsion constant J = s·t³/3 = 320(3.0)³/3 = 2880 mm⁴. The maximum shear stress occurs at the surface of the thin wall and is τ_max = T·t/J = 1.5 × 10⁶ × 3.0/2880 = 1562 MPa. This is about 38 times the stress in the intact tube and is far above the shear strength of any aluminium alloy. The slit tube would yield and fail at a torque a small fraction of 1.5 kN·m. Safe torque for a shear stress limit of 150 MPa would be 144 N·m, which is about 9.6 percent of the design torque.

Answer: 1562 MPa

(d)

For the open strip, the elastic rate of twist is dθ/dz = T/(G·J). With J = 2880 mm⁴ from part (c) and G = 26 000 MPa, dθ/dz = 1.5 × 10⁶/(26 000 × 2880) = 0.02003 rad/mm = 20.03 rad/m. In degrees per metre this is 1148. That is more than three full turns per metre, so the result is unphysical as an elastic value: the slit member would have long since yielded and the small-angle theory no longer applies. The figure still serves as a stiffness measure, since the elastic torsional stiffness per unit length is G·J = 7.488 × 10⁷ N·mm²/rad, and the same quantity for the intact tube is 3.51 × 10¹⁰ N·mm²/rad. These two numbers allow a direct comparison of the stiffness of the two members, which is the next part.

Answer: 1148 degrees/m

(e)

The ratio of twist rates at the same torque is the inverse ratio of stiffness. From parts (b) and (d), ratio = 0.02003/4.274 × 10⁻⁵ = 469. For the closed tube the torsion constant is J_c = 4·A_m²·t/s = 1.35 × 10⁶ mm⁴, while for the slit tube J = 2880 mm⁴, and the ratio of the two is also 469. The conclusion is that the fabricator's argument fails. The cut destroys the closed circuit, so the torsional stiffness falls by a factor of about 469, and the shear stress at the same torque is about 38 times higher. If a cable run is required, use a hole in the web or a bolted cover plate that restores a closed section, and keep any longitudinal opening out of the load path.

Answer: 469

Problem 3 [A7-093] Castigliano's theorem for deflection

A steel support bracket is an L-shaped member of solid rectangular section, 30 mm wide and 60 mm deep in the plane of the bracket. The vertical column is 400 mm tall and is fixed at its base. The horizontal arm is 600 mm long and joins the top of the column rigidly. A vertical force of 5.0 kN acts downward at the free end of the arm. Use E = 200 GPa and G = 77 GPa, and take the shear shape factor of a rectangle as 1.2. A colleague proposes ignoring axial and shear energy altogether in Castigliano's method. Use the theorem to compute the vertical deflection at the load and judge when the shortcut is acceptable. Treat joint flexibility as negligible.

  1. (a) Find the vertical deflection at the load due to bending of the arm and column. [6]
  2. (b) Find the additional vertical deflection due to axial compression of the column, in micrometres. [4]
  3. (c) Find the additional vertical deflection due to shear in the arm, in micrometres. [4]
  4. (d) Find the arm length at which the shear deflection of the arm equals 1 percent of its own bending deflection, and judge when shear must be included. [6]
(a)

Castigliano's theorem gives the deflection at a load as δ = ∂U/∂P, where U is the total strain energy. Bending energy is U = Σ∫M²dx/(2EI), so δ = Σ∫(M/EI)(∂M/∂P)dx. Section properties: I = 30(60)³/12 = 540000 mm⁴ and A = 1800 mm². In the arm, with x measured from the free end, M = P·x and ∂M/∂P = x, so δ_arm = ∫₀a P·x²dx/(EI) = P·a³/(3EI) = 5000(600)³/(3 × 200 000 × 540000) = 3.333 mm. In the column the moment is constant, M = P·a, with ∂M/∂P = a, so δ_col = P·a²·h/(EI) = 5000(600)²(400)/(200 000 × 540000) = 6.667 mm. The sum is 10.000 mm. The column contributes twice as much as the arm because a constant moment acting over 400 mm bends it much more than the linearly decaying moment in the arm bends the arm.

Answer: 10.00 mm

(b)

The column carries an axial compressive force N = P along its whole height, so the axial strain energy is U_N = ∫N²dz/(2AE), and by Castigliano the contribution to the load-point deflection is δ_N = ∂U_N/∂P = N·(∂N/∂P)·h/(AE) = P·h/(AE). With P = 5000 N, h = 400 mm, A = 1800 mm² and E = 200 000 MPa, δ_N = 5000 × 400/(1800 × 200 000) = 0.00556 mm = 5.56 µm. The arm itself carries no axial force because the load is perpendicular to it. This contribution is a tiny fraction of the bending deflection of 10.00 mm, about 0.056 percent, because a stocky member is far stiffer in compression than in bending over the same length.

Answer: 5.56 µm

(c)

The shear strain energy of a beam with shear force V is U_V = κ∫V²dx/(2GA), where the shape factor κ = 1.2 accounts for the non-uniform shear stress across a rectangle. The arm carries a constant shear force V = P along its length a, with ∂V/∂P = 1, so δ_V = ∂U_V/∂P = κ·P·a/(GA). Substituting, δ_V = 1.2 × 5000 × 600/(77 000 × 1800) = 0.02597 mm = 26.0 µm. The column carries no shear force because the only external load is vertical. Together, axial and shear terms add 0.0315 mm, which is 0.31 percent of the total deflection. The shortcut of ignoring them therefore introduces an error well below the uncertainty in E and in the actual joint stiffness for this geometry.

Answer: 26.0 µm

(d)

Compare the two arm terms directly. The ratio of the shear deflection to the arm bending deflection is (κ·P·a/(GA))/(P·a³/(3EI)) = 3κ·E·I/(G·A·a²). This falls as the square of the arm length, so shear matters only for short, deep arms. Setting the ratio equal to 0.01 gives a² = 3κ·E·I/(0.01·G·A), so a = √(3 × 1.2 × 200 000 × 540000/(0.01 × 77 000 × 1800)) = √(2.8052 × 10⁵) = 530 mm. At the actual arm length of 600 mm the ratio is 0.78 percent, just below the 1 percent threshold. The threshold length corresponds to a span to depth ratio of 8.8, so shear can be neglected when the arm is longer than about nine times its depth. Below that, or for a thin-webbed section with a small shear area, the shear term should be kept.

Answer: 530 mm

Problem 4 [A7-094] Strain energy and virtual work

A wall bracket carries a platform load through two pin-jointed steel bars. Bar AB is horizontal, 2.4 m long, with cross-sectional area 600 mm², pinned to a wall at A. Bar CB runs from a wall pin C, 1.8 m below A, to the loaded joint B, and has area 900 mm². The end B is 2.4 m horizontally from the wall. A vertical downward load of 30 kN acts at B. Use E = 200 GPa. The design requirement is that the vertical deflection at B must not exceed 2.0 mm, and it is currently exceeded. The engineer may thicken either bar but not both, and wishes to use the least extra steel. Use the unit-load virtual work method and ignore self-weight.

  1. (a) Find the force in bar CB. [4]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of joint B. [4]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal deflection of joint B. [3]
  4. (d) Find the area of bar CB needed to meet the 2.0 mm limit if only CB is thickened. [4]
  5. (e) Find the area of bar AB needed if only AB is thickened, and decide which option uses less extra steel. [5]
(a)

Isolate joint B. Bar CB runs from C up and to the right to B, at 1.8 m rise over a 2.4 m run, so its length is √(2.4² + 1.8²) = 3.00 m, with direction cosines 0.8 horizontal and 0.6 vertical. Bar CB pushes on joint B along this direction when it is in compression. Vertical equilibrium of the joint gives F_CB·0.6 = 30 kN, so F_CB = 30/0.6 = 50.0 kN in compression. Horizontal equilibrium then requires bar AB to pull the joint back toward the wall with a force F_AB = F_CB × 0.8 = 40.0 kN in tension. These forces are static results and do not depend on the bar areas, because the structure is statically determinate with two bars and two equilibrium equations at one joint. They are used as the real forces in the virtual work sums below.

Answer: 50.0 kN

(b)

Apply a unit vertical load at B in the direction of the wanted deflection. By the same equilibrium, the unit-load member forces are f_CB = 1/0.6 = 1.667 (compression) and f_AB = 1.333 (tension). Virtual work states 1·δ_v = Σ F·f·L/(A·E). For bar AB, F·f·L/(AE) = 40000 × 1.333 × 2400/(600 × 200 000) = 1.067 mm. For bar CB, 50000 × 1.667 × 3000/(900 × 200 000) = 1.389 mm. Both products are positive because the real and unit forces have the same sign in each bar. Adding them gives δ_v = 2.456 mm downward, which exceeds the 2.0 mm limit by 0.46 mm. The compression bar contributes more than the tension bar despite its larger area, because it carries the larger force over a longer length.

Answer: 2.456 mm

(c)

Apply a unit horizontal load at B pointing away from the wall. Vertical equilibrium of the joint now requires f_CB = 0, because bar CB is the only member with a vertical component and nothing else balances it. Horizontal equilibrium then makes f_AB = 1 in tension. Virtual work gives δ_h = Σ F·f·L/(AE) = 40000 × 1 × 2400/(600 × 200 000) = 0.80 mm, plus a zero contribution from bar CB because its unit force is zero. A positive result means joint B moves away from the wall, as expected when the horizontal bar stretches. As a check, the shortening of bar CB is 0.833 mm, and the joint displacement of 0.80 mm outward and 2.456 mm down projects onto the bar direction as -0.833 mm, which is the same shortening with a negative sign, so the two displacement components are consistent with the bar's own deformation.

Answer: 0.80 mm

(d)

If only CB is changed, bar AB keeps its contribution of 1.067 mm, so bar CB may contribute at most 2.0 − 1.067 = 0.933 mm. The CB term is F·f·L/(A·E), so the required area is A_CB = F·f·L/(E × 0.933) = 50000 × 1.667 × 3000/(200 000 × 0.933) = 1339 mm². This is an increase of 439 mm² over the present 900 mm². The extra steel volume is the extra area times the bar length, 439 × 3000 = 1.32 × 10⁶ mm³. The buckling resistance of this compression bar should be checked separately, since a longer unbraced bar of the new section may still be slender.

Answer: 1339 mm²

(e)

If only AB is changed, bar CB keeps its contribution of 1.389 mm, so AB may contribute at most 2.0 − 1.389 = 0.611 mm. Then A_AB = F·f·L/(E × 0.611) = 40000 × 1.333 × 2400/(200 000 × 0.611) = 1047 mm², an increase of 447 mm². The extra steel volume is 447 × 2400 = 1.07 × 10⁶ mm³, compared with 1.32 × 10⁶ mm³ for thickening CB. Thickening AB therefore uses about 19 percent less extra steel, even though the area increases are almost equal, because AB is the shorter bar. Tension bars have no buckling concern, so AB is also the better choice for design. The decision rests on the volume comparison, not on the area increase alone.

Answer: 1047 mm²

Problem 5 [A7-095] Statically indeterminate by energy methods

A steel cantilever beam of length 4.0 m is fixed at the wall at A and carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its full length. Its flexural rigidity is EI = 16 000 kN·m². To limit the deflection, the free end B is hung from a steel tie rod attached to a rigid roof beam. The rod is 3.0 m long and 20 mm in diameter, with E = 200 GPa, and it carries tension only. Ignore the axial and shear deformation of the beam and the weight of the rod. A designer is considering replacing the 20 mm rod with a lighter 8 mm rod. Use Castigliano's theorem on the whole system, taking the rod force as the redundant, to compare the two cases.

  1. (a) Find the tie rod force with the 20 mm rod. [6]
  2. (b) Find the bending moment at the wall. [4]
  3. (c) Find the tensile stress in the 20 mm rod. [4]
  4. (d) Find the bending moment at the wall if the 8 mm rod is used, and judge the lighter rod. [6]
(a)

The problem has one degree of redundancy, so take the rod tension R as the unknown. With x measured from the free end, the beam moment is M = w·x²/2 − R·x (sagging taken positive), so ∂M/∂R = −x. The total strain energy is U = ∫M²dx/(2EI) + R²·l/(2AE). Castigliano's theorem requires ∂U/∂R = 0, because the roof support does not move. This gives ∫₀L (w·x²/2 − R·x)(−x)dx/EI + R·l/(AE) = 0, which simplifies to −w·L⁴/(8EI) + R·L³/(3EI) + R·l/(AE) = 0. The cantilever flexibility is L³/(3EI) = 64/48 000 = 1.3333 × 10⁻³ m/kN and the free-end deflection with no rod is w·L⁴/(8EI) = 0.0240 m. The rod flexibility is l/(AE) = 3/(314.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 4.7746 × 10⁻⁵ m/kN. Then R = 0.0240/(1.3333 × 10⁻³ + 4.7746 × 10⁻⁵) = 17.38 kN.

Answer: 17.38 kN

(b)

The moment at the fixed end is found by statics once the rod force is known. Taking moments about A for the whole beam, the distributed load gives a hogging moment w·L²/2 = 12(4)²/2 = 96.0 kN·m, and the rod force R acting upward at the free end gives a relieving moment R·L = 17.38 × 4 = 69.51 kN·m. The wall moment is therefore M_A = w·L²/2 − R·L = 96.0 − 69.51 = 26.49 kN·m, hogging. Without the rod the wall would carry 96.0 kN·m, so the rod removes 72 percent of the wall moment. If the rod were rigid, the textbook propped-cantilever result R = 3wL/8 = 18.0 kN would apply. The computed 17.38 kN is slightly lower because the 20 mm rod stretches under load and the beam end can move down.

Answer: 26.49 kN·m

(c)

The rod is a two-force member carrying the tension R found in part (a). Its cross-sectional area is A = π(20)²/4 = 314.2 mm². The tensile stress is σ = R/A = 17378 N/314.2 mm² = 55.3 MPa. This is well below the yield strength of common structural steel at about 250 MPa, so the rod works at a factor of about 4.5 on yield. The stretch of the rod is δ = R·l/(AE) = 0.83 mm, which is also the downward movement of the beam tip. The beam tip would have moved 24.0 mm without the rod, so the rod has cut the tip deflection by a factor of about 29. The rod stress is a modest check, but the connection and any threaded ends should also be checked for the full force.

Answer: 55.3 MPa

(d)

The 8 mm rod has area A = π(8)²/4 = 50.27 mm² and flexibility l/(AE) = 2.9842 × 10⁻⁴ m/kN, about 6.3 times that of the 20 mm rod. The compatibility equation is unchanged, so R = 0.0240/(1.3333 × 10⁻³ + 2.9842 × 10⁻⁴) = 14.71 kN. The wall moment becomes M_A = 96.0 − 14.71 × 4 = 37.17 kN·m, which is 1.40 times the earlier value. The rod stress is 293 MPa, which is 5.3 times the earlier value and exceeds the roughly 250 MPa yield of common structural steel, so the 8 mm rod would yield. The tip deflection is the rod stretch, 4.39 mm, against 0.83 mm before. The lighter rod saves little weight but makes the stress high and shifts load back to the wall. It is not an improvement. The stiffer 20 mm rod gives both lower stress and a lower wall moment.

Answer: 37.17 kN·m

A7 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A7-096] Contact stresses

A bridge crane wheel of radius 200 mm runs on a flat steel rail head. The contact length between wheel and rail is 30 mm and the vertical wheel load is 180 kN. Both parts are steel with E = 205 GPa and ν = 0.30. Treat the contact as two parallel cylinders in line contact, the rail having infinite radius. For this value of Poisson's ratio take the largest shear stress below the surface as 0.300 times the peak contact pressure, occurring at a depth of 0.786 times the contact half-width. The wheel material is surface hardened and the maintenance engineer sets an allowable peak contact pressure of 900 MPa. Check the existing wheel and propose a modification.

  1. (a) Find the contact half-width. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak contact pressure. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum shear stress below the surface. [4]
  4. (d) Find the wheel radius needed to bring the peak pressure down to 900 MPa, keeping the load and the contact length. [5]
  5. (e) Find the contact length that would meet 900 MPa at the original radius of 200 mm. [2]
(a)

For two cylinders with parallel axes, Hertz theory gives a rectangular contact patch of half-width a = √(4·F·R*/(π·L·E*)), where F is the total load, L the contact length, R* the effective radius and E* the effective modulus. The rail is flat, so 1/R* = 1/200 + 1/∞ and R* = 200 mm. For two steel bodies of the same properties, 1/E* = 2(1 − ν²)/E, so E* = 205 000/(2 × 0.91) = 112637 MPa. Substituting, a = √(4 × 180 000 × 200/(π × 30 × 112637)) = √(1.44 × 10⁸/1.062 × 10⁷) = √13.565 = 3.68 mm. The contact patch is therefore 7.37 mm wide and 30 mm long. The load of 180 kN is carried over about 221 mm², which is why the contact pressure is high even though the wheel load looks modest for a crane.

Answer: 3.68 mm

(b)

The pressure in line contact has a semi-elliptical distribution across the patch width, with the peak at the centreline. The resultant force per unit length equals the area under the semi-ellipse, F/L = (π/2)·a·p₀, which gives p₀ = 2F/(π·a·L). With F = 180 000 N, a = 3.68 mm and L = 30 mm, p₀ = 2 × 180 000/(π × 3.68 × 30) = 3.6 × 10⁵/347.12 = 1037 MPa. This exceeds the allowable value of 900 MPa by 15 percent, so the existing wheel is not acceptable by the maintenance criterion. Because the contact pressure varies as the square root of the load, a 15 percent overload would raise the peak pressure by about 7.2 percent. The pressure is also independent of material hardness: it depends only on geometry, modulus and load. Hardness affects whether the material can survive it.

Answer: 1037 MPa

(c)

Beneath the surface of a Hertzian line contact, the principal stresses are all compressive and the largest shear stress, (σ₁ − σ₃)/2, reaches a maximum inside the body, not at the surface. With the given factor for ν = 0.30, τ_max = 0.300 × p₀ = 0.300 × 1037 = 311 MPa. Using the Tresca criterion, yielding would start when this equals half the yield strength, so a material with a yield strength of at least 622 MPa is needed to avoid subsurface yield. The depth is z = 0.786 × a = 0.786 × 3.68 = 2.89 mm. A surface hardening layer must therefore extend deeper than 2.9 mm, ideally with a safety margin, otherwise subsurface cracks begin in the soft core below the hardened skin and spall off flakes later.

Answer: 311 MPa

(d)

From the Hertz equations, p₀ = 2F/(π·a·L) with a ∝ √R, so p₀ ∝ √(F/(L·R)). Keeping F and L fixed, p₀² ∝ 1/R, which gives R_new = R·(p₀/p_allow)² = 200 × (1037/900)² = 200 × 1.328 = 266 mm. The new wheel radius is 1.33 times the old one, and the new contact half-width is 4.24 mm. A larger wheel is heavier and may not fit the end carriage. An alternative with the same effect is a longer contact, since p₀ ∝ 1/√L at fixed radius: a rail head wide enough to give L = 40 mm would also meet the limit. In practice both are limited by edge loading from skew and rail crown, so the designer may choose a modest increase in each, with the product R·L increased by a factor of 1.33.

Answer: 266 mm

(e)

At fixed wheel radius, the Hertz relations give p₀ = √(F·E*/(π·L·R*)), so p₀² ∝ 1/L at constant load. Setting the allowable pressure of 900 MPa gives L_new = L·(p₀/p_allow)² = 30 × (1037/900)² = 30 × 1.328 = 39.8 mm. The half-width depends on the force per unit length, a = √(4·(F/L)·R*/(π·E*)), so a longer contact narrows the patch and its width falls from 3.68 mm to 3.20 mm. A wider rail head or wheel tread therefore reduces the peak pressure. The practical limit is that the load must be shared uniformly along the whole length, so a slight skew or misalignment of the wheel will concentrate the contact at one edge and cancel much of the benefit.

Answer: 40 mm

Problem 2 [A7-097] Stress concentration and fracture mechanics K

A rectangular plate of high-strength aluminium alloy is 200 mm wide and 6 mm thick. It carries a uniform tensile stress of 150 MPa, applied far from the ends. An inspector finds a central through-thickness crack of total length 30 mm, perpendicular to the load. Material data: plane-strain fracture toughness 29 MPa√m, yield strength 480 MPa. For a central crack of half-length a in a plate of width W, take the stress intensity factor as K = σ√(πa)·√(sec(πa/W)), and use net-section stress σ_net = σ·W/(W − 2a). Assess whether the plate can remain in service and whether the linear elastic method is justified for this thickness.

  1. (a) Find the stress intensity factor at the present crack and stress. [4]
  2. (b) Find the applied stress at which the plate would fracture with the 30 mm crack. [4]
  3. (c) Find the critical half-crack length at the 150 MPa working stress. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum thickness for which the plane-strain toughness is valid. [4]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of net-section stress at fracture to the yield strength, and state whether linear elastic fracture mechanics is justified. [3]
(a)

The crack half-length is a = 30/2 = 15 mm. For a central crack in a finite-width plate, K = σ√(πa)·√(sec(πa/W)). The finite-width factor is evaluated first: πa/W = π(15)/200 = 0.2356 rad, sec = 1/cos(0.2356) = 1.0284, and its square root is 1.0141. The infinite-plate value is σ√(πa) = 150 × √(π × 0.015) = 150 × 0.2171 = 32.56 MPa√m. Then K = 32.56 × 1.0141 = 33.0 MPa√m. This is 1.14 times the material toughness of 29 MPa√m. Since K exceeds K_IC, fast fracture is predicted at the present stress, so the plate should be removed from service or the stress cut at once. The width correction raises K by only 1.4 percent.

Answer: 33.0 MPa√m

(b)

Fracture occurs when K reaches K_IC, so the critical stress is σ_f = K_IC/(√(πa)·√(sec(πa/W))). The crack length is fixed at a = 15 mm, so the geometry factor is the same as in part (a), 0.2201 √m. Then σ_f = 29/0.2201 = 131.7 MPa. The operating stress of 150 MPa is 14 percent above this fracture stress, so the plate would already have fractured if it had seen that stress with a 30 mm crack. A load reduction to below roughly 88 MPa, which allows a margin of one third on the stress, would be required to continue operating with the crack in place, but this is not good practice for a crack that is known and growing.

Answer: 132 MPa

(c)

At the working stress of 150 MPa, fracture occurs when σ√(πa)·√(sec(πa/W)) = 29. The sec factor depends on a, so the equation is solved by iteration. First estimate without the width correction: a = (K_IC/σ)²/π = (29/150)²/π = 11.90 mm. Then correct for the width: with a ≈ 12 mm, sec(π × 12/200) = 1.0180, whose square root is 1.0090, which reduces the required a slightly. Iterating converges to a_c = 11.70 mm, which corresponds to a critical total crack length of 23.4 mm. The inspected crack of 30 mm is 1.28 times the critical size. The conclusion is the same as in part (a): the crack is longer than critical at this stress. A tolerable crack at 150 MPa must be shorter than 23.4 mm in total, which is within the resolution of many routine inspection methods.

Answer: 11.7 mm

(d)

A valid plane-strain K_IC test, and hence a valid use of the tabulated toughness, requires the thickness to satisfy t ≥ 2.5(K_IC/σ_y)². With K_IC = 29 MPa√m and σ_y = 480 MPa, (K_IC/σ_y)² = (0.0604)² = 0.00365 m, so t_min = 2.5 × 0.00365 m = 9.1 mm. The plate is only 6 mm thick, below this limit, so the state at the crack tip is partly plane stress. In plane stress the real fracture toughness is higher than the plane-strain value, so using 29 MPa√m is conservative: the true critical stress is probably above the 132 MPa computed in part (b). Even so, the margin cannot be quantified without a test on 6 mm material. Treat the answers in (a) to (c) as a lower bound on safe size.

Answer: 9.1 mm

(e)

LEFM requires the plastic zone at the crack tip to be small compared with the crack and the remaining ligament. A simple screening test is that the net-section stress at fracture must stay well below yield, commonly below about 0.8σ_y. At the computed fracture stress of 131.7 MPa, σ_net = σ·W/(W − 2a) = 131.7 × 200/(200 − 30) = 155.0 MPa. Then σ_net/σ_y = 155.0/480 = 0.32. This is well below 0.8, so the ligament remains elastic and failure is governed by brittle fracture, not by plastic collapse. LEFM is justified for this geometry. If the ratio had been near 1, failure would be by net-section yielding and a plastic collapse check would govern. In the present case the plate fails at about a third of its yield load, which shows how much a crack can reduce usable strength.

Answer: 0.32

Problem 3 [A7-098] Plastic collapse and limit analysis

A floor beam is a solid rectangular steel bar 80 mm wide and 150 mm deep, of yield strength 300 MPa, treated as elastic perfectly plastic. It spans 6.0 m, fixed against rotation at the left support A and simply supported at the right support B, and carries a uniformly distributed load over the full span. The service load is 18 kN/m. A junior engineer states that the beam is safe because the service load is below the load that first causes yield at any point, and that nothing more needs to be checked. Using elastic analysis for first yield and a mechanism analysis for collapse, assess this claim and quantify the reserve of strength beyond first yield. Neglect self-weight and shear.

  1. (a) Find the plastic moment capacity of the section. [3]
  2. (b) Find the uniformly distributed load at which yield first occurs, using elastic analysis. [4]
  3. (c) Find the collapse load by a plastic mechanism analysis. [6]
  4. (d) Find the position of the sagging hinge, measured from the prop B. [3]
  5. (e) Find the load factor against collapse at the service load of 18 kN/m and comment on the engineer's claim. [4]
(a)

For a solid rectangle the elastic section modulus is S = b·d²/6 = 80(150)²/6 = 300000 mm³ and the plastic section modulus is Z = b·d²/4 = 450000 mm³, since the fully plastic section has half the area in tension and half in compression with a lever arm of d/2. The shape factor is Z/S = 1.50. The yield moment is M_y = σ_y·S = 300 × 300000 = 9 × 10⁷ N·mm = 90 kN·m, and the plastic moment is M_p = σ_y·Z = 300 × 450000 = 1.35 × 10⁸ N·mm = 135 kN·m. The ratio M_p/M_y of 1.50 is the extra moment the section can carry after the outer fibres first yield, as the plastic zone spreads inward through the depth. A rectangular bar has a large shape factor compared with a typical rolled I-beam, which is nearer to 1.15.

Answer: 135 kN·m

(b)

For a propped cantilever under uniform load w, the elastic bending moments are a hogging moment w·L²/8 at the fixed end A and a sagging maximum of 9w·L²/128 at 3L/8 from the prop. The ratio of hogging to sagging is 16/9 = 1.78, so the first fibre to yield is at the wall. First yield occurs when w·L²/8 = M_y. Therefore w_y = 8·M_y/L² = 8 × 90/(6.0)² = 720/36 = 20.0 kN/m. The service load of 18 kN/m is below this value by 10 percent, so the junior engineer is right that no fibre yields at service load. The statement only addresses first yield, though. Collapse requires far more load than first yield for a ductile beam with a high shape factor, so the claim leaves out the useful reserve in the section.

Answer: 20.0 kN/m

(c)

Collapse needs two plastic hinges to turn the propped cantilever into a mechanism: one at the fixed end A, and one in the span at distance x from the prop B. Take the reaction at B as R and the hinge moment M_p at both hinges. The sagging hinge forms where shear is zero, at x = R/w, with moment R²/(2w) = M_p. At A, the moment R·L − w·L²/2 = −M_p. Writing w = k·M_p/L², the first condition gives R = √(2k)·M_p/L, and the second becomes √(2k) − k/2 = −1. With u = √k, u²/2 − √2·u − 1 = 0, giving u = 2 + √2 = 3.414 and k = (2 + √2)² = 11.657. Then w_c = 11.657 × M_p/L² = 11.657 × 135/36 = 43.7 kN/m. The collapse load is 2.19 times the first-yield load. This ratio is the product of the shape factor (1.50) and the redistribution factor (1.457) from the indeterminacy.

Answer: 43.7 kN/m

(d)

The sagging hinge forms at the point of zero shear, at x = R/w from the prop. Using the relations from part (c), R = √(2k)·M_p/L and w = k·M_p/L², so x = R/w = √(2k)·L/k = L·√(2/k). With k = 11.657, √(2/k) = √(0.1716) = 0.4142, giving x = 6.0 × 0.4142 = 2.49 m from the prop B, or 3.51 m from the fixed end A. The elastic sagging maximum is at 3L/8 = 2.25 m from the prop, so the plastic hinge forms 0.24 m further from the prop than the elastic peak. The hinge position matters for detailing: web stiffening, lateral bracing and the check for local buckling at each hinge must all be provided at the right places.

Answer: 2.49 m

(e)

The load factor against plastic collapse is λ = w_c/w_service = 43.7/18 = 2.43. The factor against first yield is w_y/w_service = 20.0/18 = 1.11. Typical limit state design requires a factor of the order of 1.5 to 2 on collapse, so the beam has a clear reserve and is safe on this basis. The junior engineer's conclusion is therefore correct, but the reasoning is incomplete. Elastic first-yield analysis gives a lower, conservative bound and ignores the 119 percent of extra capacity that comes from plasticity and redistribution to the sagging region. The proper check is the one made here: compare the factored service load with the collapse load, and also check serviceability, since deflection could govern even though strength does not.

Answer: 2.43

Problem 4 [A7-099] Creep or fatigue crack growth basics

A wide steel web plate in a crane runway girder carries a fluctuating tensile stress with zero minimum, so the stress range equals the maximum stress, 160 MPa. A single edge crack can be treated with geometry factor Y = 1.12, so ΔK = Y·Δσ·√(πa). Crack growth follows the Paris law da/dN = C·ΔKm with C = 2.0 × 10⁻¹² (m per cycle, ΔK in MPa√m) and m = 3.0. The fracture toughness is 60 MPa√m and the girder sees 150 000 stress cycles per year. The inspection method reliably detects cracks of depth 3.0 mm. Determine the safe inspection interval and the benefit of a modification that lowers the stress range by 20 percent.

  1. (a) Find the critical crack depth at the maximum stress. [4]
  2. (b) Find the number of cycles for a crack to grow from the 3.0 mm detection size to the critical size. [5]
  3. (c) Find the inspection interval in months if the interval is set at half the remaining life from the detectable size. [3]
  4. (d) Find the cycles to failure if the inspection method could only detect cracks of 6.0 mm depth. [4]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of the life from 3.0 mm after the stress range is reduced by 20 percent to the life before the modification. [4]
(a)

Fast fracture occurs when the maximum stress intensity reaches the toughness. Since the minimum stress is zero, K_max = ΔK = Y·σ·√(πa). Setting K_max = K_IC gives a_c = (K_IC/(Y·σ_max))²/π. With K_IC = 60 MPa√m, Y = 1.12 and σ_max = 160 MPa, Y·σ_max = 179.2 MPa, and the ratio K_IC/(Y·σ) = 0.3348 √m. Squaring gives 0.11211 m, and dividing by π gives a_c = 0.03568 m = 35.7 mm. Every crack deeper than this fractures on the next load peak, and growth to this size is the endpoint of the life integration in part (b). The result is modest relative to the plate thickness, which is a sign that the design stress is high for a cracked web, and the toughness assumed should be verified for the girder steel at its lowest service temperature.

Answer: 35.7 mm

(b)

Integrate the Paris law between the initial and critical depths: N = ∫da/(C·(Y·Δσ·√(πa))m). For m = 3 the integrand is a−3/2, so N = 2(a₀−1/2 − a_c−1/2)/(C·(Y·Δσ)³·π3/2). The constant part is C(Y·Δσ)³π3/2 = 2.0 × 10⁻¹² × (179.2)³ × 5.568 = 6.409 × 10⁻⁵. The terms in the brackets are a₀−1/2 = (0.003)−1/2 = 18.257 and a_c−1/2 = (0.03568)−1/2 = 5.294, in m−1/2, and their difference is 12.964. Then N = 2 × 12.964/6.409 × 10⁻⁵ = 4.05 × 10⁵ cycles. At 150 000 cycles per year this is 2.7 years of remaining life from first detection at 3.0 mm.

Answer: 4.05 × 10⁵ cycles

(c)

A crack just below the detection limit may be present at one inspection and missed, then grow during the whole interval before the next one. To guarantee at least two chances to find it before it becomes critical, the interval is commonly set at no more than half the life from the smallest reliably detectable crack to failure, so Δt = N₁/2 = 2.02 × 10⁵ cycles. The cycle rate is 150 000/12 = 12500 cycles per month, so Δt = 2.02 × 10⁵/12500 = 16.2 months. In practice the inspection interval would be rounded down to a convenient figure, such as 16 months, or aligned to the regular maintenance shutdown. Where the detectable size is itself uncertain, a larger factor, such as three, could be used. The conclusion is only as good as the assumed Paris constants.

Answer: 16.2 months

(d)

With the larger starting size the same integral applies, but a₀ = 6.0 mm. The bracketed difference becomes a₀−1/2 − a_c−1/2 = (0.006)−1/2 − (0.03568)−1/2 = 12.910 − 5.294 = 7.616. With the same denominator of 6.409 × 10⁻⁵, N = 2 × 7.616/6.409 × 10⁻⁵ = 2.38 × 10⁵ cycles. This is only 59 percent of the life from 3.0 mm, because most of the life in fatigue is spent while the crack is small and the crack grows slowly. Doubling the minimum detectable size costs about 41 percent of the remaining life (2.38 × 10⁵ against 4.05 × 10⁵ cycles), so the interval would have to be cut from 16.2 months to 9.5 months to keep the same margin.

Answer: 2.38 × 10⁵ cycles

(e)

With the stress range reduced to 0.8 × 160 = 128 MPa, two things change. The critical depth becomes larger, a_c = (60/(1.12 × 128))²/π = 55.8 mm instead of 35.7 mm, which lengthens the final growth stage. The Paris constant factor also falls, because it contains (Y·Δσ)³: the new value is 3.281 × 10⁻⁵. The bracket is (0.003)−1/2 − (0.05576)−1/2 = 18.257 − 4.235 = 14.022. The new life is N = 2 × 14.022/3.281 × 10⁻⁵ = 8.55 × 10⁵ cycles. The ratio to the old life is 2.11. The stress cube alone would give 1/0.8³ = 1.95, and the larger critical size adds a further 1.08 times. A 20 percent drop in stress range therefore roughly doubles the life, which is a strong reason to reduce stress by a small amount of added thickness.

Answer: 2.11

Problem 5 [A7-100] Pressure vessel combined loading

A cylindrical hydraulic accumulator shell has an inside radius of 200 mm and a wall thickness of 10 mm, in a steel of yield strength 380 MPa. It operates at an internal gauge pressure of 12 MPa. Pipework connected to the shell end applies an external axial tensile force of 250 kN along the shell axis and a twisting moment of 45 kN·m about the axis. Treat the shell as thin-walled, with the mean radius for all stress formulae, and neglect the radial stress and the local effects at the nozzle. The designer wants an equivalent stress factor of safety of at least 2.0 on the von Mises criterion, and the inside radius is fixed. Check the shell and size the wall.

  1. (a) Find the hoop stress at the existing thickness. [3]
  2. (b) Find the axial stress at the existing thickness, including both the pressure and the external force. [4]
  3. (c) Find the shear stress due to the twisting moment. [3]
  4. (d) Find the von Mises factor of safety at the existing thickness. [5]
  5. (e) Find the wall thickness required for a von Mises factor of safety of 2.0, with the inside radius fixed at 200 mm. [5]
(a)

The mean radius is r = 200 + 10/2 = 205 mm. Check the thin-wall assumption first: r/t = 20.5, which is greater than the usual limit of about 10, so thin-wall formulae are acceptable. The hoop stress comes from equilibrium of a half-cylinder strip, which gives p·(2r) = 2σ_h·t per unit length, so σ_h = p·r/t. Substituting, σ_h = 12 × 205/10 = 246.0 MPa. The torque and axial force do not change the hoop stress in this thin-wall model, because they act in the shell's axial and shear directions. The hoop stress is the larger of the two normal stresses, double the pressure-only axial stress, which is why long pressure vessels split along their length when overloaded. Using the inside radius would give 240.0 MPa, so the mean radius gives a figure about 2 percent higher.

Answer: 246.0 MPa

(b)

Axial stress has two parts. The pressure acts on the closed ends and gives σ_p = p·r/(2t), from equilibrium of the end cap, π·r²·p = 2π·r·t·σ_p. This is 123.0 MPa. The external axial force acts on the wall's cross-sectional area A = 2π·r·t = 2π(205)(10) = 12881 mm², giving σ_F = F/A = 250 000/12881 = 19.4 MPa. Both are tensile, so they add: σ_a = 123.0 + 19.4 = 142.4 MPa. The pipework load adds 16 percent to the pressure-only axial stress. If the piping force were compressive, it would reduce the axial stress and would make the shell safer on the von Mises criterion, but it might introduce a buckling concern.

Answer: 142.4 MPa

(c)

For a thin-walled closed circular tube, the Bredt formula gives a shear flow q = T/(2A_m), where A_m = π·r² is the area enclosed by the mean circumference. Then τ = q/t = T/(2π·r²·t). With T = 45 kN·m = 45 × 10⁶ N·mm, r = 205 mm and t = 10 mm, τ = 4.5 × 10⁷/(2π × 42025 × 10) = 4.5 × 10⁷/2.641 × 10⁶ = 17.0 MPa. This shear stress is small beside the hoop and axial stresses. It matters mainly through the 3τ² term of the von Mises combination. The three stresses are σ_h = 246.0, σ_a = 142.4 and τ = 17.0 MPa. The shear acts on the same wall elements as the two normal stresses, so the stress element rotated through some angle will have different principal values, with σ_h and σ_a no longer principal.

Answer: 17.0 MPa

(d)

With the radial stress neglected, the stress state is plane stress with σ_x = σ_a, σ_y = σ_h and shear τ. The von Mises equivalent stress is σ_e = √(σ_h² + σ_a² − σ_h·σ_a + 3τ²). Substituting, σ_h² = 60516, σ_a² = 20280, σ_h·σ_a = 35033 and 3τ² = 871, so the sum under the root is 46635 and σ_e = 216.0 MPa. The factor of safety is n = σ_y/σ_e = 380/216.0 = 1.76. This is below the required 2.0, so the existing shell is not acceptable. The principal stresses are 248.7 and 139.7 MPa, and the Tresca stress, which is the larger of σ₁ and σ₁ − σ₂ with σ₃ = 0, is 248.7 MPa, giving a Tresca factor of 1.53. The Tresca criterion is more conservative.

Answer: 1.76

(e)

When the wall thickens, the mean radius grows as r = 200 + t/2, and all three stresses change, so the thickness is found by iteration on the whole von Mises expression. Define n(t) = 380/σ_e(t) with σ_h = p·r/t, σ_a = p·r/(2t) + F/(2π·r·t) and τ = T/(2π·r²·t). Trial t = 10 mm gives n = 1.76. Trial t = 12 mm gives r = 206 mm, σ_h = 206.0 MPa, σ_a = 119.1 MPa, τ = 14.1 MPa, σ_e = 180.8 MPa and n = 2.10. Trial t = 13 mm gives n = 2.27. Refining by the secant method converges to t = 11.40 mm, where n = 2.00. A practical choice would be a standard plate thickness of 12 mm or 14 mm, with a corrosion allowance added. The stress falls roughly in inverse proportion to thickness, so a modest increase restores the margin.

Answer: 11.4 mm
